Assassins Creed is one of the most well know Action/Adventure series to date, and rightfully so! I have always been a big fan of Assassin Creed, and owned all the collectors editions on my Xbox, but as I transitions to PC, I really missed Assassins Creed. AC really kickstarted my gaming hobby, and now that it has finally been released to PC, I am more than happy to say it made a smooth transition, with slightly better graphics than on consoles! Director's Cut is not much different than the original game, but is still a respectable port to the PC. I cannot say much about the graphics as they are very outdated by todays standards, but keeping in mind this assassins creed is over 6 years old! Gameplay feels fast paced, challenging, and smooth! Story is pretty basic, and the entire game is basically repeating the same 3 primary missions, over and over again. The whole climb everywhere feature is amazing, and still beats most games to date! I love that we finally got a PC version of Assassins Creed, because it's an outstanding series!
Concept: Honestly very basic, the storyline is very repetitive, following one basic task to the next. 75/100
Graphics: For its time, it's outstanding, everything has a suprising ammount of detail, and is very respectable. 90/100
Sound: Sounds effects are great, but the overall soundtrack is very boring, and feels like it was left to the last second while in development. 75/100
Playability: Using a keyboard and mouse feels great and was very well implimented! Combat is smooth and entertaining, and climbing up buildings feels great! 95/100
Entertainment: Concept is basic, storyline is basic, campaigne is bare-bones, but the amazing gameplay and graphics really boost Assassins Creed: Director's Cut. 75/100
Replay Value: Moderatly low.
Overall Score: 82/100
This game is inferior in every way to Batman: Arkham Asylum

To begin this reviews I have to get the point across, this IS built to be scary; if scary is not what you want go play some Mario! Unless... you are scared of Mario? Nevertheless, this game is my top 10 free-to-play horror experience to date and the reasons are justifiable, I promise! I have spent around 2 hours in-game to understand this is not something horror fans to pass up and you have my word for it.
The Horror gameplay is as you would expect, jumpscare galore, frightening monsters chasing you and the occasional death here and again. The game itself pulls some sneaky tricks which I don't want to spoil for whoever is reading this - use the arcade games they are fun and original, the fighting mechanics are somewhat disappointing but that's not the point of the gameplay! So I won't be deducting any points for that. It was a truly chilling experience waiting for devilish things that seem cute to come at me, literally swearing and laughing due to the silly little things.
I don't know WHY I am in this castle but I don't CARE. It is a challenge I must complete because in order to fulfill my life I must complete all 1000 rooms, sadly, I'm at room 600. There's notes to collect and storie's behind the specimen's which only add to the overall experience, these really add to the immersiveness of the experience, something many horror games seem to miss.
Not much needed here. The level of resilience of the player will vary dramatically but personally I am a horror fan in generally and have a medium-high resilience to this; atleast you would think so. You can complete this game, atleast 95% of you can and you will enjoy every horror gruelling second of it. The ambience really adds to the difficulty, as do the sounds, they fit so well together which is why they need to be accumulated so neither sound sleezy!

The perfect blend of Street Fighter mechanics and a Marvel vs Capcom speed. Definitly worth the buy if you are a fan of fighting games. Although I am still new at the game, there is a lot to learn with combos and moves. Each character is perfectly fleshed out to the core. There is no two characters that are exactly the same. With beautiful sprite work, excellent music and a flawless blend of combat, it is a supurb title for the fighting game enthusiasts.
I highly recommend this to a very specific audience.
People who enjoy indie games, action, fighting, competetive fighting, fast-pased, and budget games.
This game is certainly not for everyone. People who normally play slower-pased games will not get a thrill out of it. However, if you are the gamer who likes to show off your style in a fighting game, this is the one for you.

I am completely infatuated with this game. BEAUTIFUL art style, with main menu attacking with aestethics similar to art deco standards, which instantly bring movies like The Great Gatsby to your head, and the grotesque anatomy of characters with links both to 20s comedy and modern horrors and science-fiction. Awe-inspiring musical blend of jazz and funk (oh God, the main menu theme feels just so good). In-depth tutorial teaching not only Skullgirls-related techniques, but the art of playing fighting games altogether. The "anti-infinite combo system" which really helps fight off abusive tactics. Multiplayer free of major problems (and things like Punkbuster which actually make the multiplayer harder than easier, everything is done through the game without any external apps). Distinctive story mode artworks and the in-game art gallery. Various play styles, ranging from going all-out with one powerful character, or tactical switching between three characters. So similar, yet so different characters. Perfect optimization - plays well even on old PCs and laptops with crappy iGPU.
I swear, never was I so satisfied with money I spent. If you like fighting games - don't even hesitate. If crazy aestethics are your thing - you shouldn't as well. If you don't like fighters in general but seek THAT ONE title that will teach you to fight and love fighters - you just have to try it.

Like many early access games I've jumped in on, Stash has it's share of bugs and various features that need to be optomized, things you should typically expect if you start playing a game in early access during development.  Something you don't expect or see very often is how involved the devs are with their community, playing along side you, finding and going over bugs and discussing with you, in game, how certain mechanics can be changed for the better.  I've been playing a few days now and there have already been several patches to fix issues and make balancing changes, all based on the feedback and bugs found by the community since early release started.
The game itself I find enjoyable and relaxing, my first impression left me thinking about my old days of playing D&D with friends.  There was no form of tutorial or help page when I started playing, but within a day or so a help button was added with a little getting started guide and tips.  There is usually someone around who can help answer specific questions as well.  I now spend most of my time running solo and just chatting with everyone.  Now and then I'll join a party or pair up with someone to clear a dungeon or two.  When my bags are full, I stop by my Base of Operations (BOO) to offload my loot, upgrade my stuff and even do a little cooking when I have the materials.  Then off to town to sell the extra loot to vendors.
I find myself being drawn back into game whenever I have free time, both to keep hunting for loot to upgrade my base and skills, and for the connection to the community.  I see the game become better every day as bugs are squashed and new elements are added and/or rebalanced.  Hopefully I'll see more of you in the game with us soon, helping to make this game everything it has the potential to be.

That being said the Devs are awesome and on the ball with any and all questions or problems you may run into.  There's a good wiki page set up for the game that answers most questions I've come across so far and the in game community is very friendly and helpful.
If you're a fan of Frogdice's other games and like their look and feel then you'll be right at home with Stash.
There's a learning curve, and like I said this isn't finished yet so just think about that before pulling the trigger and purchasing the game.
I'm having fun with it and can't wait to see where this game ends up after they are done with it.

Sure there are harder situations to get around but it just encourages you to try different routes and strategies. Oh and you get to ride a flame throwing robot dog.. Yeah.. fun as hell! As for the negatives and negative reviews. People need to learn patience. I had the same issue with the "error write crash dump" but I gave them my feedback and waited a bit and sure enough it was fixed. As for those saying this is some propoganda game not so quietly backing domestic terrorist groups... No.. learn your history. This game takes place in the 60s. If Nazis invaded the most resistance would be from well armed groups already ready for a fight. The Black Panthers among others were around and might have played a part in that alternate universe.  Also in the game it is far from just the Black panthers resisting. The resistance is a group formed from people all over of many different backgrounds coming together for a common noble goal of freeing the US from the Nazis so they can use the USA to start a worldwide pushback of the Nazis.  If anything this game promotes exactly the message we need right now, to look past our differences and come together around all that we have in common so we can move forward as a society and a species.

Why? Well read on mate...
Personally i think that TNC was heavily leaning on the extreme success of TNO. While TNC is lots more of the fun Rambo styl action of the previous title, It is no where near as good as TNO or even TOB.
Gameplay:
Fun but lacking. The shooting of course was fun, TNC has everything that made the previous game fun and more. However the "more" part is where the game starts to feel unpolished. For example, now that any combinationof weapons can be dualiwielded the devs had to change the weapon wheel, It is now 2 weapons wheels (one for each hand) wish you have to switch back and forth from, However for one the switching speed of the wheels is incredibly slow and selecting a weapon is also feels very clunky and slow therefor both these things (when used) throttle the gameplay speed by a great degree. Luckily however there are hotkeys for dualwield, attachments..etc wich however are also a little slow, However still a better alternative over the weapon wheel.
Aside from that there are new movement abilities to put it short theres is one to reach high places, one to to get into small vents and one to smash through through walls and run over enemies. All of these while seeming very fun and intresting in concept again feel incredibly unpolished and again clunky and dont integrate themselves smoothly into the rest of the movement mechanics and gameplay. There is some very fun energetic level no doubt wisch really show how good of a job Machine Games can do with this franchise, But saddly there was really enough of them especially not when the game is a good chunk shorter than it in my opinion it should be, And what i believe is the worst thing of all about the levels and the gameplay of the game itsself is that there is an insane amount of padding. For example one location of the game was reused MULTIPLE times (yes in different contexts and with different objectives) however is was still the exact same level give or take a few small areas. And what i find especially insulting is that at the end of the (to short) game what you can do is take up missions from the playyer home to go out and kill commanders, But the commanders are mainly in places to already had missions in so basically they are letting you revisit already used locations and getting you to kill a Commander in it and thats pretty much all you do, It feels so much like padding and i expected so much more, And really the commander missions would be fine, infact normally ide say its great that they give you some more stuff to do after the main campaign, a great addtion would it not be for the fact that the main campaign felt a couple hours to short.
Guns:
The guns are fine (even tho personally i think the selection is a bit boring for the regular guns) However the timeline (ill get to that) specific Guns are fantastic and even more fun than the Lasercannon from TNO. However my personally i was extremely dissapointed in the shotgun as it has next to no kick behind it and doesent feel like the powerful shotgun cannons from TNO. But as i said personally i think the selection of weapons is rather bland compared to the previous game (no laser rifles saddly), But on a plus side the Heavy carry only weapons are very fun to use and a great reward for killing mini bosses. And finally the Fire Hatchet wich in this game replaces the traditional knife is also very satisfying to use and i think its a fantastic alternative to the knife, combat and lore wise. Also it creates some fantastic gorey melee kills.
The Story:
By far the biggest dissapointment for me, So first of all the game essentially is split into 2 parts mood wise, The first half being very sad and similar to the general atmosphere of TNO. HOWEVER!! In no way does it do it aswell as TNO. B.J again has inner monologue like in the previous game but unfortunately while being being very reflective of B.Js character and giving us a good insight into his character, it is very poorly written and overall it sounds "whiney" and cheesey, In this first sad half of the game we also get alot of back flashes to B.Js child hood, This i think i actually very good and again provide alot of insight on why B.J is the way he is and they also provide some very intresting gameplay.
Now to the second half of the game wich is alot more upbeat and has alot of humor built into it. While this is refreshing and does create some great moments in the game it can be a little annoying and overwhelming as it does cause a drastic change to the character of B.J, wich not agree with everyone.
However aside from all that the overall Villain of the game is Frau Engel from TNO, Now in the previous game she worked fantastic as a side antagonist as she was a very intresting character, But really she does not work as the main villain, Deathshead was a obsessed evil nazi scientist who performed unspeakable things on innocent people...... and Frau Engel is just kind of a power hungry evil nazi, What im saying is that she is not nearly evil enough to be the main villain of a game wich in previouse iteraions has main villains like DeathsHead or yanno FREAKING HITLER IN A MECHSUIT. Now without including spoilers i have to say that there is so much more they could have done with the character of Frau Engel, They literally just took her out of the TNO and plopped her into TNC without really changing a thing about her, shes not cazier, Shes not more powerful and she in no way is a better or more intresting character than she was in the previous game, Infact ide almost say shes less intresting because we never really get any tense interactive moments with her like the train card game in TNO. ....shes just kinda the ruler of ruler of germany and from time to time she pops up and is a B**ch to you, and then proceeds to further the story a little bit by. But the one saving grace that i have to award her with is that her writing and the voice actors performance are phenomenal. Im a fluent German and English speaker so i could understand every word she said, and it was incredibly well written and sounded very authentic and was alot more natural than in TNO. Aside from that the story is fairly boring, However there is some fantastic characters and other returning characters that are also very well performed. So in conclusion very good characters great voice acting performance but BY FAR  the greatest let down of the game is the ending wich is terrible and completely unsatisfying.
Overall:
Gameplay- 7/10
Story- 5/10
Conclusion:
If you havent played Wolfenstein: The New Order then frankly this game might very well be on your top games of 2017 list, But for people who enjoyed the previouse game and its standalone expansion, Wolfenstein: The New Collossus is an incredibly dissapointment and i personally can not understand how a Dev that created such a fantastic game as TNO would put out a mediocre experience like TNC. I mean seriously normally most of the problems in this game could be looked past but not if the bar was raised to damn high with the previous title. And frankly i would normally definitely recommend this game but seriously the kind of ending they give us in this game is inexcusable for a wolfenstein game.
Seriously if u havent bought this game yet, Save yourself the money and go buy The New Order, its an amazing game you will love it if you into games like DOOM(2016) and mybe even the standalone expansion The Old Blood wich is also pretty good as far as DLC goes. So overall im saying dont buy it now, its not worth your money, but sometime in the future when its cheaper. And also even if your going to buy it atleast wait a while because currently the game is pretty broken and has alot of bugs, But im not going to complain about those to much because they are actively fixing them pretty quickly.

I came late to To the Moon. As a game that’s cheap to begin with and frequently on sale, I bought it early in 2015 and didn’t get around to playing it until December of 2016. After starting it and playing through it all in one night because I couldn’t bear to step away, I can say with absolute conviction that it is not a game to be missed.
To the Moon is a game about love and loss, telling the story of a complex and bittersweet romance from its very end to its very beginning. Without giving too much away (as each moment of it is distinctly touching and impactful in its own way upon in-game discovery), the story’s themes are extremely reminiscent of Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, exploring the true nature and complexity of love as well as the value and effect of memory. You play alternatively as doctors Eva Rosalene and Neil Watts as they use a futuristic machine created by their employer, Sigmund Corp., to fulfill the last wish of the initially mysterious Johnny Wyles, an elderly man on his death bed. Sigmund Corp.’s machine allows Rosalene and Watts to travel backwards through Johnny’s memories – starting with his last – and alter his recollection of his life so that he ends up fulfilling his dying wish.
While To the Moon’s simplistic point-and-click gameplay and some minor mechanical annoyances (such as the pointer still showing options for interaction with people and things during non-interactive cutscenes) might leave some to be desired, the narrative and soundtrack more than make up for it, allowing players a glimpse into the complexity of a lifelong love and all of its warmth, twists, and regrets. Even the art itself, from the character sprites to the lighting effects to the scenery, manages to perfectly encapsulate all of the game’s various themes, feeling creepy, romantic, mysterious, beautiful, and surprisingly realistic all at once. And of course, the game’s writing is fantastic; beyond the narrative itself, the frequent banter between coworkers Dr. Rosalene and Dr. Watts is heartfelt, genuine, and funny, with 99% of the humor feeling natural and well-timed. I was teary, wide-eyed with anticipation, and laughing aloud in equal measure throughout To the Moon and its DLC, but it felt far from an emotional rollercoaster; the jokes and feel-good moments blended seamlessly (and sometimes tragically) with the more serious.
TL;DR: If you’re into narrative-driven games, To the Moon is not to be missed, but be warned – for one reason or another, it WILL make you cry.

Ori and the Blind Forest is by far one of the best games I've purchased on Steam. The story is simple, but heartfelt and beautiful. The world feels fresh and unique, the gameplay is challenging but is completely based on player skill. Whenever I made a mistake within the game I never felt like it was because of poor game design, purely that it was my own skill that was keeping me in the same place. You will die a LOT in this game, I think my overall death count at the end was over one thousand, but it's part of the appeal in a weird sort of way. One top of that the world is stunning, using beautiful colors and each section of the forest is paired with its own incredible music. Movement of your character feels natural, quick, and as you learn new skills it merely adds to the beautiful simplicity of attacks/movement. Buy this game, do it, seriously, you will not regret it. It is beyond fun, beautiful to the point that I can't think of a game that compares to how it looks and feels, and it may just make you cry. BUY IT.

Note: When I bought the game the game was just out, so my review is completely about the main story. Of all the games I have loved and hated, this will be my first review. I feel compelled to write one because the game has impacted me on a deep and personal level. There are very few games that have been able to get inside my mind the way Senua's Sacrifice has. The developers of this game have presented a level of artistry, music and sound in a way that has far exceeded my expectations. Hellblade has conveyed the horror of mental illness in a way that few games, if any, have been able to do and it has used this relatively new media (that we all love) as a tool to paint a picture that has allowed me to take this disturbing journey. And at the end of it all it I am changed me in some small way. Usually we play games to forget our reality. To step into the shoes of some hero or villian and to walk the path of another world that has been born from the minds of the artists and musicians who created it. The path I walked in Senua's Sacrifice was frought with terror and anguish. It is what I wish more games were like. The level of immersion is breathtaking. The sound engineers, voice actors, and the actress who played Senua are on another level. The introduction into the game is one of the best I have ever seen. From the moment Senua paddles to the land of mist and fog and stands on the beach, looking at the bridge to Hellheim is just awesome. Watching the water roll onto the beach and listening to the distant screams of terror is something to behold. I could have stood there for hours watching the fetid waves crash on the sandy beach...
The game follows a strict path but does a masterful job of making you forget that, because it focuses your attention inward toward a darker place of endless torment and boundless suffering. If you are a gamer that needs to explore the cracks and crevasses for nuggets and rewards, or who needs an endless horde of enemies to best, then this game might be a disappointment. There is no leveling up, no rewards, no HUD, no indicators of any kind...and no hope...
Perfect.
Thank you to the Gods who made this game. I will sacrifice someone on your behalf shortly...

I've only played this game for a little over an hour. I was drawn in by the interesting story premise, and the described gameplay. I'm a fan of the arkham series as well as shadow of mordor, so learning the combat structure of this game was disappointing at best. I like the concept of customizing your combos, but as described by other reviews, they are very limiting especially at the start of the game, and the combat mechanics of only dodging attacks vs counter moves leaves you doing hit and run tactics most of the time and not really being able to creatively chain and flow between attack and counter attacks.
The great thing about the freeflow combat type in the arkham and mordor games is it allows for a large margin of players; button mashers will manage to survive and eventually learn the value of timing and combos without making you play a section or battle over and over again. I was initially a button masher when it came to these types of games, having a hard time focusing my concentration in timing and planning. I learned to use proper combos and auxilliary attacks at my own pace while still appreciating the gameplay and storyline. And the replay value of those games are excellent, allowing you to practice and fine tune your technique even more.
With this game, I'm not sure if I would feel the same way if I were still a button masher; probably I would've stopped playing earlier than I did. I tried appreciating the game. But as it progressed, I kept focusing on the negatives as they came about; from repetetive climbing, sometimes annoying camera angles, to lackluster storyline build-up to what could and should be an awesome plot (she's supposed to have been one of, if not the most feared fighter/rebel, and yet why the totally lax supervision and guard on her at the start, particularly she already displayed resistance to the mind wipe?).
Bottomline, after just 1 hour of playing, I'm already regretting purchasing this game. I'll probably find time to try and play this again in the future, but as it stands, I find no motivation, both gameplay wise and story wise, to try and finish the game.

Remember Me takes place in a futuristic Paris and recounts the tale of an amnesic Memory Hunter named Nilin – apparent leader of the terrorist (or in this case, “Errorist”) force opposed to their world's “utopia” where memories can be digitalised and controlled via machines to achieve true happiness – as she gradually rediscovers who she is and how horrible the utopia she lives in actually is.
(TL;DR at the end.)
__
__
TL;DR
Pros:
- Nice story for the length of this game (on average 6~11 hours for the first playthrough depending on how you play and if you accidentally went AFK with the game on).
- Brilliant and gorgeous setting that exploits yet another concept of “utopia/dystopia”.
- Strong female lead without being human; she has her own fears and uncertainties which help to give credibility and depth to the character
- Nice French touches here and there that remind you that this technically takes place in Paris.
Cons:
- Too linear for its own good; the setting feels like it was hard work for naught since you'll never get to explore it.
- Underexploited aspects of the game, as well as predictable outcomes when you reach the final episodes.
- A distinct lack of characters that aren't side-characters besides Nilin.
- Repetitive gameplay that doesn't exactly allow you a whole lot of creativity despite advertising said creativity.
- Absolutely horrible camera that will just screw you over in some places of the game.
Verdict: 7.5/10
I'd recommend this game fully, but only when it's on a big sale as I don't think it's worth a full price of nearly 30 euros; despite its beautiful setting and nicely executed female lead supported by a good voice actress, it's a somewhat short game so you won't get a whole lot of intricacy from the plot. The flaws in the camera also make the simplistic combat unnecessarily difficult from how bad it is at setting itself at a good angle (and it's especially bad once it comes down to fighting in a small arena; the camera just doesn't know what to do anymore).
EDIT: 'Tis once again on sale, go! Go!

Skullgirls advertises itself with "all-new game systems which test the skills of veteran fighting game fans while also making the genre enjoyable and accessible to newcomers."
The former, I don't doubt.
The latter is a blatant lie.
I am about as much a newcomer to fighting games as there can be, having never touched one before this game. In fact, this sparked my curiosity. A fighting game that's easy to learn? Perhaps there
hope for me. Boy, was I wrong.
The first struggle I had to make is button distinguishing in the main menu. What kind of button is "LK"? After finding out that "A" (turning out to be "LP") did the trick and accidentally quitting the game AND skipping the intro cinematic, I found out it's bound to Z. Being a German, I rebound it to Y. Okay.
Then I found the big flashy "TRAINING" option. Well, this looks good. Tutorial? Really! Let's do this!
And with every tutorial step the game really set in. Button prompts in the shapes of arrows were soon replaced with somewhat difficult to understand analog stick icons, having patterns drawn onto them like Zs, or Js, to indicate the order of directions required to input. And this was the tutorial for executing special attacks -- which of course made heavy use of these.
And finally, my breaking point; Chapter 2-1: Defending against Mix-Ups. After a general definition of Mix-Ups being quick attack combos meant to distract and confuse the enemy into a wrong block so any subsequent hits connect and deal damage, I have received the objective of completely blocking three different mix-up patterns of increasing difficulty. And with hit flash after hit flash my patience chipped away even despite the infinite health, and after being met with the fourth repetition of what was supposed to be a blocking tutorial giving me mere FRAMES to input the correct block button, I actually burst into tears, doubting my skill. Think about it this way: The part that was supposed to teach me how to play made me cry and question my ability to push buttons on a keyboard.
So I tried an actual training match against a stationary, non-blocking, non-attacking enemy... and felt though that accomplished just as little, teaching me nothing about how the game worked, or how to enjoy it, or how to play. 5 minutes I just randomly hit the attack buttons, hoping to god something good would come out of it, before calling it a day and writing this review.

Wolfenstein II is a great game. It has fantastic gameplay and production values. But unfortunately, its narrative supports racism even as it claims to fight it.
Normally, I am not bother by game stories or politics, and I'm no SJW or extremist, I just really get bothered by hypocracy, and the narrative was spoiled by the political agenda of the writers.
On on hand, Wolfenstein II continues BJ blazkowicz's fight against tyranny, bigotry, and fascism. We expect the Nazis to be evil, and we have no compunctions fighting the good fight against them.
However, suddenly BJ, our white protagonist (Who is stated early on in game to be a perfect example of the aryan race by the villain), now hates whites. WTH? He was actually decent most of the first part of the game, up until he met our other racist protagonist, Grace Walker.
The instant he runs into Grace Walker, she starts flinging racial slurs about his skin color and strong BJ just let her tirade against his race, taking it like a victim. Oddly enough, in the next scene, BJ himself turns racist suddenly and without any previous tendency, and says about the nazi and kkk alliance that "Those white <expletive> are gonna die".  It's just totally unreal and stupid.
He didn't refer to the enemy as nazis, or fascists, or KKK members, or even white supremacist (none of whom should ever be supported). No, he only referred to them by their skin color. It's flat-out racism right there! Bethesda, I thought you were against this crap? I'm shocked you haven't been called out on this already and crucified by the media.
Now, this has soured my opinion of the game and Bethesda. The politics in the game are very hypocritical. You fight racism as a character that for some nonsensical reason has become the very thing he fights, a racist. If you can get past that, or just want to shoot up a bunch of enemies in a really well made game, by all means buy it and play. It's a great game. I loved the gameplay and the progression system and even some of the characters like Fergus.
In conclusion, unlike it's amazing predecessors, games that don't take things too serious and are just fun FPS games with great characters, Wolfenstein II: The new Colossus's story is marred by hateful political agenda. if that bothers you, stay far away.

Not without its flaws, but a solid sequel to the New Order.
Went back and did another playthrough of the first one for comparison, and came away with this:
Pros:
-No more QTE style boss fights (First one had a few) If you pump enough ammo into it, it'll explode real good.
-Guns! Guns! Guns! (new customization system is nice, and both the LKW and DKW are interesting in thier own ways)
-Improved control setup (throwing kni...er, axes is easier in this one)
Cons:
-All enemies seem to have superhuman senses
-Writing this time around wasn't as good.
-End credits are set to one of the worst covers of an otherwise perfectly chosen song.
Mixed:
-Definitely felt like the middle of the story. Which (hopefully) it is.
Other thoughts:
The gunplay is fun, and the variety of mounted weapons is a plus. Some environments felt bigger, while others felt smaller. Would have been nice to flesh out some of the more interesting non combat sections a bit more, and been given a feeling that the enemy wasn't as omnipotent as they appeared, which was definitely there in the first one (i.e., the sabotaged concrete). Some of the movie segments felt heavy handed and slow, while others fit the story and setting well. More than once I kept trying to hit escape, and get back to shooting Nazis in the face. Having just come from a playthrough of the New Order, some of the more "WTF?" elements are telegraphed in the first one if you look. The twist in the middle is obvious from early on, but I do think how they pulled it off was amusing and well done.
If you enjoyed the first one, you'll most likely enjoy this one as well.
Some people have reported stability issues, but running Win10, i7-6850, GTX970 and had no issues.
Almost forgot:
Emo-Blascowitz is worst Blascowitz. Thankfully, he doesn't stay that way the entire game, or I'd have turned my machine gun on myself.

If this was just more of the same, I would definitely recommend this. There's definitely a lot of improvements, and the narrative is decent with some really awesome twists. However, I'm not sure what made them change the gameplay for this second iteration. It worked well, felt good. But here, it doesn't. Much of it doesn't feel too bad, but then there ecounters where I need to cheese the AI. Just stay in cover and snipe Nazis as they come down a narrow hallway or chase me around a loop. It's not fulfilling gameplay, but it's what needed to be done many times.

The most adorable game to spook you.
You play a history enthusiast whose interests were caught by this rather large creepy house that no one dares to venture in. Upon entering the house, you meet the owner who introduces themselves as 'Spooky', and then sends you forth to explore the 1000 rooms of her mansion.
Looks are deceiving. Not many games can prove that more than this one, because as this begins, you discover that this place is not all it seems to be. Although the enemies you stumble across through the house seem cute and harmless, you'll quickly find yourself running up against more terrifying beings.
Along your journey through the house, you find notes, pieces of journals from those who travelled through before you. You find specimen after specimen that escaped containment. Cracked glass, blood, screeches of unknown things. You run.. Further and further into Spooky's maze of jumpscares.
Oh! I almost forgot.. This glorious little number also includes wonderful little mini-games to keep you further entertained and throws you off even more.
(Tip; put the code -
- in when standing in-front of the blank games machine for Spooky's backstory.)
I won't spoil the ending, but... There is more than one. Try taking a leap of faith. Live or die to see what lies beyond the other side.. The choice is yours.
: Honestly, just as adorable as the rest of the game. The graphics alone set the tone for what the game is trying to bring out in atmosphere and it's just quaint and charming.
For something that has a mostly 'cute cardboard' theme, specimens are also very unique, enjoyably creepy. well put together and thought out.
is just as good when it comes to tying in nicely. I love that it both helps to keep you on your toes, set up the tone even further, bring tension or just make you let your guard down. Each creature has a different soundtrack, chase scenes have specific tracks and it's just perfect spread out to leave nothing feeling blank or empty.
Adorable, entertaining, has depth and clearly shows a lot of work and imagination went into making something truly unique to stand out and give you a game not to be forgotten or passed up. For a free-to-play, I send ample praise to the devs for making a wonderful little thing such as Spooky's house of Jump Scares. It's easily worth the price of some AAA horror games out there on the store.

Refunds should be alotted when development of the product clearly has stopped or the product undergoes such changes as to require new catagorization for the product. This game isn't terrible. It does have some flaws that very noticeable but I think the good out weighs the bad.
The Good
- Controller compatible (D pad didn't work)
- Level designs are small and nice. Smaller levels are for the better considering you spend most of your time running back and forth solving puzzles.
- "Graphics" look nice. Nothing stood out that really amazed me except for the levels where combat was involved.
- Nice art design. Not something I've seen used in many other games.
- Minor platforming/throwback to retro games
- Tutorial was short (Good!)
- Controls smooth
- Inventory Layout and combining of items mechanics simple and worked without any issues.
- Clever puzzle solving and item combining mechanics.
- Description and dialog for most items in the background was a nice detail.
- Interesting "story" and method of telling the story.
- Monster was creepy and unexpected.
- More then just "running away" when confronted with the monster. You can distract the monster by turning on lights to distract him/her.
- Unexpected combat.
- Puzzles not too hard but not too easy.
- Game broken down to different areas to express different challenges for your character.
- Boss fights (kind of).
- Combat system very simple and easy to learn.
- 3 hours of gameplay (Good).
The Bad
- At first it's hard to get the point of the game.
- *Glitch* Doors turned into black squares at one point.
- *Glitch* Couldn't turn lights on at certain points.
- Up and down stairs tedious (Having to hit up and down)(Personal annoyance).
- Changes the story abruptly (A few times) without fully explaining what was previously happening.
- *Glitch* Some long pauses of a black screen and flashes of white or logo.
- After beating the game, screen froze on what I think is the developers logo.
- Puzzles get repeatative.
- No replay value. Except for achievments.
- Price ($16.99 Canadian/$13.00 U.S?). Too much.
- Enemies were easy to avoid/were not very smart.
- Monster would disappear and reappear randomly. Will kill you randomly without warning.
My recommendation for this game IS mixed but not based on whether or not it is a bad game. I would recommend Between Me and The Night simply because it was worth the experience. It's not your typical "jump in for fun" game, so if that's what you're looking for I'd look elsewhere. I'll have a video going up later today explaining my points with examples of the glitches and other topics mentioned.

Remember Me would have made a better movie than a game.
Honestly, it's a well-crafted game. There's really almost no aspect of the game that was done poorly. Except... every aspect of the game is independent of each other. The story, the combat, the art, the level design, the world. It felt like a AAA title, not an immersive experience in Neo-Paris. Rather than thinking about the themes presented by the game, I felt myself thinking about the corporate atmosphere the game was made in. It's a shame, because the story is really good, the combat is interesting(it needs work to become more fluid, but the concept of building your own combos is super cool), the visuals are exactly what they need to be, the level design...is actually pretty mediocre, but there's nothing terrible about it, and the world is, well, it was obviously a passion project, and it shows. But none of it fits together like it should. I got the sense of being handed off from one department of design to the next during gameplay; you navigate the parkour-based level, then suddenly it would stop and you're in a combat sequence, and the combat wouldn't utilize the level design at all, you're just in a mechanically boring arena. Then you finish beating everyone up and you go up a ladder, and the camera angle changes to show off a stunning vista. Then there's a cutscene or bit of dialog and you get some story. Rinse, wash, repeat, and repeat, and repeat.
Also, the controls really need work.

Pros:
-Story is interesting, if a bit cliche in areas
-Level design is inventive
-Music is memorable
-Intro sequence is awesome
Neutral:
-Voice acting isn't terrible or great, just kind of mediocre
Cons:
-The combat system is frustrating, and the game would have been a lot more fun with a more traditional 3rd-person melee combat system.
-Leans on poorly compressed pre-rendered cutscenes a bit much
-The Game can't quite decide what its moral is supposed to be, and the 'Twist' feels a little forced
Final Score: 7/10

Skullgirls advertises itself with "all-new game systems which test the skills of veteran fighting game fans while also making the genre enjoyable and accessible to newcomers."
The former, I don't doubt.
The latter is a blatant lie.
I am about as much a newcomer to fighting games as there can be, having never touched one before this game. In fact, this sparked my curiosity. A fighting game that's easy to learn? Perhaps there
hope for me. Boy, was I wrong.
The first struggle I had to make is button distinguishing in the main menu. What kind of button is "LK"? After finding out that "A" (turning out to be "LP") did the trick and accidentally quitting the game AND skipping the intro cinematic, I found out it's bound to Z. Being a German, I rebound it to Y. Okay.
Then I found the big flashy "TRAINING" option. Well, this looks good. Tutorial? Really! Let's do this!
And with every tutorial step the game really set in. Button prompts in the shapes of arrows were soon replaced with somewhat difficult to understand analog stick icons, having patterns drawn onto them like Zs, or Js, to indicate the order of directions required to input. And this was the tutorial for executing special attacks -- which of course made heavy use of these.
And finally, my breaking point; Chapter 2-1: Defending against Mix-Ups. After a general definition of Mix-Ups being quick attack combos meant to distract and confuse the enemy into a wrong block so any subsequent hits connect and deal damage, I have received the objective of completely blocking three different mix-up patterns of increasing difficulty. And with hit flash after hit flash my patience chipped away even despite the infinite health, and after being met with the fourth repetition of what was supposed to be a blocking tutorial giving me mere FRAMES to input the correct block button, I actually burst into tears, doubting my skill. Think about it this way: The part that was supposed to teach me how to play made me cry and question my ability to push buttons on a keyboard.
So I tried an actual training match against a stationary, non-blocking, non-attacking enemy... and felt though that accomplished just as little, teaching me nothing about how the game worked, or how to enjoy it, or how to play. 5 minutes I just randomly hit the attack buttons, hoping to god something good would come out of it, before calling it a day and writing this review.
This game is about as newcomer-friendly as ARMA 3 is in the genre of first-person shooters.

Not without its flaws, but a solid sequel to the New Order.
Went back and did another playthrough of the first one for comparison, and came away with this:
Pros:
-No more QTE style boss fights (First one had a few) If you pump enough ammo into it, it'll explode real good.
-Guns! Guns! Guns! (new customization system is nice, and both the LKW and DKW are interesting in thier own ways)
-Improved control setup (throwing kni...er, axes is easier in this one)
Cons:
-All enemies seem to have superhuman senses
-Writing this time around wasn't as good.
-End credits are set to one of the worst covers of an otherwise perfectly chosen song.
Mixed:
-Definitely felt like the middle of the story. Which (hopefully) it is.
Other thoughts:
The gunplay is fun, and the variety of mounted weapons is a plus. Some environments felt bigger, while others felt smaller. Would have been nice to flesh out some of the more interesting non combat sections a bit more, and been given a feeling that the enemy wasn't as omnipotent as they appeared, which was definitely there in the first one (i.e., the sabotaged concrete). Some of the movie segments felt heavy handed and slow, while others fit the story and setting well. More than once I kept trying to hit escape, and get back to shooting Nazis in the face. Having just come from a playthrough of the New Order, some of the more "WTF?" elements are telegraphed in the first one if you look. The twist in the middle is obvious from early on, but I do think how they pulled it off was amusing and well done.
If you enjoyed the first one, you'll most likely enjoy this one as well.
Some people have reported stability issues, but running Win10, i7-6850, GTX970 and had no issues.
Almost forgot:
Emo-Blascowitz is worst Blascowitz. Thankfully, he doesn't stay that way the entire game, or I'd have turned my machine gun on myself.

I've been meaning to get this game for a long time. Now I finally had a chance to actually play it, and I must say I regretted not getting it sooner. There was not a single thing I did not like about To The Moon. The story is well-written, the soundtrack is simply amazing, and the art is fitting. The mechanics could have been better but nothing that's stopping me from thoroughly enjoying the game.
John's dying wish is to go to the moon, and the doctors, Eva and Niel, are contracted to fulfill it. To do it, they need to dive into John's memory to find out the cause of that desire. The story uncovers as you gradually dig deeper into John's past one stage at a time. This is a nice reminder that story progression doesn't necessarily means going forward.
The puzzle pieces start to fit together as you go, and you get to know more about the characters, all of which are likeable in their own ways. Although, I find it funny that while the story is supposed to revolve around John, I feel like River is the most developed character throughout the story. I slowly started to understand why she acted the way she did, what she really wanted, how her mind worked, and I felt more sympathetic towards her than any other character. But while it's all dramatic and emotional, it is balanced by the constant comic relief mostly by the dialogue exchanges between Eva and Niel.
The art isn't at all remarkable but it complements the atmosphere of the story very well and I probably won't have it any other way. Despite the rather low quality, they make up for it by using appropriate visual effects and color schemes. Even the subtle sprite movements, such as the eyes and arms, can show you what the characters are thinking or feeling during certain events. The soundtrack is, like I mentioned earlier, simply amazing. Even the simple piano piece that John wrote for River was very soothing and fun to listen to.
Overall, I really enjoyed playing this game and I highly recommend this to anyone looking for a game with good story.

Personally, before playing this game amongst many other things, I felt cloistered and numb to most feelings (primarily due to depression), and coincidentally amongst many other things playing this (or at least listening to the music) helped quite a lot, and felt like breaking this 'shell' of being able to feel less, maybe because of the simplicity of its presentation or the humor [which may be different from person to person, as Dr. Watts can sometimes be a bit too silly], but all these add to the wholeness of detail in the game; lighthearted comic relief, and witty insight in turn. This game would be 'personal' too, on many levels with many people, as far as many reviews can note. Personally, I loved being able to feel--and personally, reflecting on the memory from all exposure within this game brought me to tears.
Happy tears.
Alongside touching experiences that are coming to society's eyes in recent note (Asperger's/Autism, etc), the game is also presents and showing its stuff rather than telling it all (given the dialogue and such) by letting you experience everything through the eyes of characters themselves, or at least those nearest to them to get their story.
The Developers and their team are also very spirited and communicative folks! That's a major plus--including how they treat people, fan and otherwise alike.
Would recommend this game fully--alongside recommending it for generations to come. The DLC (including the comic) are also worth the experience! (Wordless--picture only comic)

Remember Me is a beautiful game with a compelling story. The combat system is sufficiently crunchy while remaining simple enough for button-masher types like me. I did find the game to be somewhat short. I tore through it in about 11 hours compared to 30 in most other RPGs I've played. Nevertheless, all 11 of those hours were spent engaged with the story and wanting to know more.

Despite some imperfections and occasionally frustrating controls, Remember Me is worth buying when it comes on sale if you like a powerful, layered story and complex characters.
Nilin is a memory hunter, an agent who can wipe or alter other people's memories, changing them to suit her purposes. However, as the game begins, she is in the process of being memory-wiped herself, and with only the barest of memories still left, she manages to escape the facility she was being held in, and finds herself fighting for a cause she doubts, against people whose crimes she doesn't understand.
The laser-guided amnesia trope is played straight in this game, but well, since the game is about deleting and altering memories, it is actually justified. Speaking of which, part of the game revolves around altering people's memories to change their allegiances or motivations, with the other part taking place in the real world, focusing on exploration and combat. The memory remixes, as they are called, aren't always intuitive (you don't always know what consequences altering a single memory fragment may bring), but of course, that makes sense, since we don't always know the consequences of small actions in the real world either.
When Nilin isn't rooting around in people's brain boxes, she makes her journey through Neo-Paris, a dystopian future city (aren't they all) with a massive gap between rich and poor, and an underground population of monstrous ghouls, cast-offs whose memories have been so vandalized and corrupted they have become nothing but deformed animals. Most of the time, Nilin makes her way to her objective by platforming, dangling off ledges and leaping from one handhold to the other, and while it can get frustrating to fall to one's death because of a wrong button press, thankfully the game creates lots of checkpoints, making the occasional mis-press not disastrous.
During her journey, Nilin is often attacked by enemies, because of course she is. In combat, everything depends on how well you can string combinations together and which effects you've assigned to which button press. The combat system, despite being combo based, is relatively easy to get a hang of, because no matter which animation or attack Nilin performs, the timing of the button presses is always the same. The only thing that takes more work to master, and which is paramount in the later sections of the game, is to perform mid-combo dodges and continue the combo right after. Once you get this down, though, combat becomes fun and engaging, with only the camera movement eliciting the occasional frustrated grunt.
Combat, however, isn't the main strength of the game, though. In DONTNOD tradition, the main focus is on the story, and Nilin's journey to understanding who she is has a profound effect on players who like to be immersed in a good story. There's the occasional cliché, and yes, also the occasional slightly predictable plot twists, but all this can be easily glossed over because of the fine voice acting (and this time not by the Usual Suspects, but by unknown actors) and the highly credible moral ambiguity the story brings. You'll often find yourself questioning Nilin and the people around her as they achieve their ends by very dubious means.
As mentioned, the story is Remember Me's strong point, as are the scenery and environments, which can be truly gorgeous at some points, and Olivier Derivière's music is memorable without stealing the attention. Combat can be fun, but also frustrating when you're still learning to Miracle Dodge. Once you get it down, though, most of the frustration is left behind, and you can enjoy stringing long, spectacular combos together. But, once again, this game is, in the first place, about story, and again, it's delivered very well. Haters of the Grizzled, Square-Jawed White Male Protagonist will rejoice.
A few of the sequences in the game qualify as DIAS:
. There will be a few sections where the game makes you fail over and over again, with no negative consequence, until you 'get it right', using foreknowledge of where the pitfalls will be. The part where you have to flee from Captain Trace in his gunship in particular is an egregious DIAS offender. A few of the battles, mostly against bosses and mini-bosses, also incorporate quick-time events, and we know how much we all hate those. Botch the QTE, and the boss will resist your 'execution move', forcing you to do the last bit of the boss fight again. Well, at least it doesn't cause a game-over.
Also, 32 seconds of unskippable logos.
Remember Me may have its clunky bits, and I know it got a bad rap by 'professional' reviewers, but the actual user reviews don't lie. Yes, it's a console port, but you hardly ever notice that it is, although playing with a controller is
recommended. It's worth the buy if you like the genre, or if you're a fan of a good story told through a video game. It suffers a bit from the games-as-movies syndrome, but Hell, if it's a good movie, I don't mind.

French studio Dontnod's first game is full of wonderful design, fun combat, strong themes, a decent but spotty plot, and a handful of minor annoyances. Apparently those minor annoyances were enough to drop its Metacritic rating all the way to 65, and unfortunately that fact will keep a lot of people who should be playing this game from giving it a shot.
The game looks beautiful. While it's clearly influenced by other visions of the future, everything from
to
, the futuristic version of Paris has enough touches here and there to make it memorable. The combat also wears its influences, the
games mostly, proudly on its sleeve, but the rhythym of them is a little bit different. It's not a game-changer, certainly, but it's enough to carry a 10-hour action game. At times, you will stumble into some frustrations. For example, the screen gets so busy during most boss battles it becomes difficult to tell what's happening. But I tend to be forgiving of these decisions for a first time developer.
The plot left me with a lot of questions at the end. Mostly not the good kind. There are more than a few character motivations that still don't make much sense to me. But the overarching theme, that making peace with painful memories makes us better people in the end, is a powerful one. It's just a pity that the game never gets the chance to get into the moral problems with your character "remixing" people's memories, but it is an action game and we've got to keep things moving.
Between this and
, Dontnod has quickly moved up high on my list of studios to watch. If nothing else, I have to admire the bravery of developers that genre hop and try to put out clever and original ideas with each new release.

A very fast-paced fighting game, very similar to Marvel Vs. Capcom with a bit of anime style fighting game inspiration. The relatively small roster may be a bit of a turn-off for casual players, but the ability to play as a team exponentially increases variety. With a roster this size, buying the DLC characters goes a long way towards keeping the game fresh. That's not terrible, considering that the game is pretty cheap, and getting all the characters doesn't add much to the price.
Online play is pretty great, but new players will probably get totally dominated without proper preparation. Getting started online requires dedication and willingness to lose a lot and learn from defeat. That's not a massive wall to get over, since the tutorial is really well made and does a good job of helping players move forward, but there's so much information, you might have to go back to it a few times. Training mode is also the best one I've ever seen in a fighting game, and lets you control nearly every possible variable to an insane degree.
Single player is a little lacking in content, with just an arcade mode and a story mode that adds visual novel style cutscenes between fights, but the story mode can actually be very compelling at times. If you get invested in the characters, there are some really powerful scenes in there. The 2nd Encore DLC adds all the DLC characters and several extra single player modes: an endurance mode, combo trials, and a challenge mode. Seriously, the extra content adds a LOT to this game.
The music has a huge emotional range to it, and most of it is really catchy and fits the environments well. Pretty much all of the stages are beautiful, and the visuals and animation are impressive as hell. The character designs are also really, really cool, though the fanservice can be a little distracting at times. Not the worst I've seen in a video game, but it can be kinda weird to see a military commander who wears a really long sweater to hide the fact that she apparently forgot to put on pants this morning. That's more a nitpick than a glaring flaw, though, and some people appreciate that kind of thing anyway.
Overall, I'm hard pressed to find anything bad enough to be a deal breaker with this game. I think it's worth looking at for anybody that doesn't passionately hate the genre. If you don't want to (or for some reason can't) play online, you're really gonna want the 2nd Encore DLC to get the most out of this game, and even with the DLC, it's pretty affordable. Definitely worth a look.

PROS:
+ The game mechanics are simple, yet smart (that is, the use of different kinds of units makes sense…actually more sense than in some overall better games: artillery behaves like artillery (hear that, Order of Battle), the game scale is coherent (that’s for you, my beloved Panzer Corps).

+ The UI is very convenient
CONS

TANK BATTLE: NORTH AFRICA is a fun and very easy to get into wargame. It plays like tabletop wargames of the late 80s and 90s with different ranged fire depending on the unit firing, lethal artillery which can take out a whole unit of infantry with one doom delivering salvo, line of sight and environmental defensive cover. Having the terrain look deceptively peaceful only to move my infantry over a hill and see three or more enemy tanks suddenly appear in the distance is thrilling and fear instilling as my infantry scramble back down the hill into any thick patch of woods for cover.
Music has a 1990s midi feel to it making it relaxing to listen to while motivating me to keep on playing. Sound effects put me into the bomb blasted bullet scarred battlefield with the sound of tank treads and infantry marches going ever forward to victory. At any minute i expect to hear, ' Its A Long Way To Tipperary' by John McCormack playing over the air waves. Oh but wait a minute that was.. another war.
Graphics are well done with a sharp crisp detail and the finest tabletop cardboard piece quality coming to life with fluid animations. I especially like the marching infantry.
TANK BATTLE: NORTH AFRICA for those such as myself who enjoy the likes of Slitherine's epic BATTLE ACADEMY along with many a 1990s classic on pc such as THE PERFECT GENERAL this is a must buy that will bring endless gameplay and tense strategic joy with a sweet release akin to the climax of lover's coupling.

If you enjoyed "Tank Battle 1944", or the "Battle Academy" series for that matter, then you'll have to add this to your library. With "Tank Battle: Pacific" no doubt to come, it's a turn-based strategist's Golden Time.
Incorporating additions made to previous HexWar games, with a zoom feature now added the battles are turn-based and the decisions played out in real time. With HD graphics improving on the looks from the IOS version, the game tackles the rugged and sand covered battlefields of North Africa in 1943. With an 8 part tutorial, the game depsite being a mobile port, which is now a common and sometimes popular choice it, feels more like "Battle Academy" than simpler titles such as "Frontiline: The Longest Day" or"Road To Moscow". The maps are just smaller, and the AI not perhaps as viscious even on Hard. It will give you a challenge, though.
Just don't go expecting "Panzer Corps", "Unity of Command" or a remake of "Steel Panthers".
As with the previous title "TB: 1944", the game focuses on one front, the North African front where the USA and Great Britain fought the German Afrika Korps (as did our boys, the ANZACS who usually always get left out, but proudly adopted the intended insult with the German label "Rats of Tobruk"). While you may at first think you have quite a strong force to take the objectives, you'll be often surprised at having 3 Panzer III's suddenly arriving to block you from three sides. That's Rommel for you, not a cheating AI. Then again, you will often have off-map air and artillery support so it all balances out.
The graphics are seviceable, with my only gripe being the Allies having their units 'painted' in European green (even tan and blue would have been more historically authentic, even if it were only the British who sometimes used that scheme). Might help distinguish Axis from Allies, but if you're a history buff you'd do that by looking at the unit up close. Besides, your units are highlighted with each term. Still, a monor gripe.
The price point is right, and if you are in the mood for a strategy/tactical turn-based game and have any interest in this period, and don't want to spend the extra dollars Slitherine/Matrix demands for it's titles. Then again, if you are totally opposed to mobile ports, which is a bit strange in this day and age (move with the times, or stand still in the past) then it won't be for you, no matter the quality.
If though, like me you enjoy mobile ports like this that fill that important niche where games lasting no longer than 15-20 minutes fit well with real life demands...grab it.

As you cross the swamp in your tiny canoe, you are determined to continue into the heart of darkness, into the heart of hell. There is nothing left behind, nothing to return to, nothing that could make you turn back. The skull of your beloved, cautiously rolled into a linen cloth, is dangling from your belt, while you evenly plunge the paddle into the green water.
The surrounding silence of the swamp remains unnoticed by Senua. She's never alone. From start to end of Hellblade the voices accompany her, accompany you. They won't stop. Constantly gnawing in your head, the voices are the most unique and dominant feature in 'Hellblade - Senua's Sacrifice'. They help you to understand what to do and their comments continuously reveal aspects of Senua's past, which will gradually give you the possibility to understand her history.
There is a reason for the games recommendation to play it with headphones. I did and the experience was extreme. While it's a blast at the beginning, I felt the urge to rip the headphones from my ears towards the end of the game.
As a portrayal of a harrowing live with psychosis the voices undoubtedly succeed. Hellblade uses Senua’s sickness as a route into an excellent story about her inner struggle, love and loss.
The game does not take you by the hand. There's no tutorial, no hud, no objective, no map. Even fighting is not explained but thankfully it's very intuitive. As Senua, it is up to you to reveal your own story, as you wander deeper and deeper into hells circles and if you wish to get the most out of this game, you better don't read too many reviews or view videos of 'Hellblade - Senua's Sacrifice'.
Hellblade unfolds like a beautiful, dark, tense visual novel. The game tells a story of confusion, sadness, fear and loss and it's punctuated by moments of beauty and strength that leaves a lasting impression.
Combat is extremely intense and gripping. To me, the fights are among the highlights of this game, although they are unbalanced in terms of difficulty and only side events on Senua's journey.
This game is something that just doesn't come around every day. And as unique as the story is, are the puzzles. You have to find Norse symbols in your environment and are guided by strange light effects that first made me believe the graphics were bugged. In fact they are not. It's a very smart form of puzzle that's very unique.
Hellblade shows a masterclass of atmosphere, story telling, fighting and puzzles. It all wonderfully comes together to form one extremely unique gaming experience as never seen before.
The true achievement of this game is it creates something exceptional new. Not everybody will like this game, but for sure the developers created a very special game that deserves respect for it's innovations.
Pros:
- incredibly strong atmosphere
- very good, but not outstanding graphics
- extremely intense fights, fighting looks and feels fantastic although the attack and defend options are limited
- very good sound effects, rain, thunder, birds, wind, rustling leaves, burning fire, waves, horns in the distance, waves, all this adds a lot to the atmosphere
- the voices make this game special and they are not only an expression of schizophrenia but also help players understand what to do
- fantastic puzzles with a very unique new idea
- strong, disturbing light and graphic effects that the developers are not afraid to accelerate to an extreme level
- everything feels extremely vibrant
- mainly no music, only sound effects, which strongly adds to the gripping atmosphere
- good music in the few moments it's played
- possibly best ever interpretation of hell in a video game. I'm sure Dante would approve.
- very emotional end (although I didn't fully understand it)
- photo mode lets you stop the game, move the camera and take photos with different filters (I took more than 1000 screenshots)
- very intense aspects of horror
Neutral:
- graphics are softened and grained without the option to disable the graining. I did not mind, but some players might.
- extremely disturbing story, especially towards the end of the game
Cons:
- frame-rate drops at the beginning of the game
- repetitive gameplay
- no map, although it's a linear game I got lost a couple of times walking in the wrong direction
- unbalanced boss fights, some where laughable easy while other seemed almost impossible to beat

Firstly, "what a 'Hell' of a story(pun definitely intended)." I haven't been on a ride like this since Alan Wake and the two are very alike. Alan Wake and Senua's Sacrafice both take you into the deep, dark precipice of the mind and do a great job making sure you're sitting right along with them in the sh**(so to speak) as your character plummets into a downward decent. into madess. However, while Alan Wake's ending completely surprised me and left me baffled, jaw dropped, Senua's Sacrafice consantly had me wondering the nature of Senua's journey; is it literal? Is it metaphorical? Was she cursed and fighting demons? And looking for a way to lift the curse? Or is this 100% in the mind and Senua is really stuck in some nightmare coma? Unfortunately and just as with Alan Wake neither game's ending helps to paint a line of distinction and, therefore, has formulating your own answers to the big ol' "what the flip?" question.
There is also a suggesting of potential DLC and/ or sequel in the game's ending. So I have my fingers crossed for DLC. I doubt there will be a Senua II, it just doesn't seem Ninja Bee's style and, well, sequels historically suck, so, I would not like to see one. I'd much rather DLC continuation and refinement. And since Ninja Bee self-published, like CD Projek, they have the ability to do what the flip they want with enhancements and content.
As it stands the price is well justified. There's simply not enough content call it a $39+ title. There was very little content and very little hours of gameplay and it was not open-world even a little bit...you just follow the rails. It plays more like Dark Souls than anything, but with even less levels, dungeons and labyrinths. I was hoping to be able to explore some nordic ruins on the side etc. perhaps unlock some content and skins for use in other singleplayer game modes, or while repeating chapters. I am definitely disappointed in terms of replayability. NG+ guys! I want to rock through the game with the Hellblade.
As far as gameplay goes, however, I was hoping for a more refined and intricate fighting system like that of Witcher 3, complete with more varied moves, random and spontaneous decapatations of various limbs and head, more than one type of parry(depending on weapon types you parry against), and a much more sophisticated and fluid stepping/ foot pattern system(in combat), dodge rolls, dodge counters...the whole lot. I guess I just expected that games like Witcher 3, or even Tomb Raider would have introduced some nice competition in combat system innovation arena...heck, Heavenly Sword already had a pristine foundation to build off of, in terms of combat mechanics. In many ways I think we assumed Senua's Sacrafice to be a spritual successor to the already perfected Heavenly Sword engine, but, instead, it was completley different and Senua moves sluggishly for her size making it hard to get at the back of your enemy while also lacking in rhythm. It made it hard to believe that this was the same developer. On the contrary, however, having watched the gameplay diaries since 2015 it does at least seem much less rigid and, well, it's technically not broken, but subsequent a two year delay...where is the content?
I really have my fingers crossed for some DLC and would REALLLLY love to see an NG+ or some other sandbox mode complete with skins etc. I would pay!

Overall Rating: 7.5/10
I wouldn't say it's one of my favourite games but it's definitely one of the most memorable and impactful. A poetic and ugly journey of pyschosis and revenge.
Graphics:  9/10
Visually stunning enough to make you want to slow down and enjoy the sights and take in the story within the world. The visual pyschological effects are very interesting and really add to the experience.
Audio: 8.5/10
The voices, sound effects, and music is great (except the ending song). Voices are helpful during combat and also introduces minor story elements. The sound of the storms and waves are incredibly realistic.Headphones are highly recommended for better immersion.
Story: 7
Gets better and better as the story unravels. There are also lorestones scattered throughout the world which also breathes life to the world. I do feel the story could have flowed better. There are brief moments of story, and then long stretches of puzzle solving (with lorestones in between) and combat. However, they do a good job at tying the story together during combat further in the game.
Cinematics: 7
You  really feel for Senua as she struggles with her pyschosis and you can see the toll the darkness has on her as it spreads. I would also like to mention to watch the "Hellblade Feature" in the game after completing your playthrough. You will further appreciate the work put into the game and might even learn something about psychosis.
Gameplay: Puzzles 6 / Combat 8.5
Puzzles are interesting at first but are too simple and way too repetitive. Walk over there, focus on this or activate that, repeat.
Combat is fantastic. The controls seem simple at first (run, dodge, block, light attack, heavy attack, melee attack), but after you realize you can combine actions (ex. run+light/heavy/melee, dodge+light/heavy attack) as variations, charge attacks, and time your blocks to parry attacks, you have a thoroughly enjoyable and satisfying combat experience. "Focus" slows time and boosts the intensity and speed of your attacks which also makes combat super stylish and exciting.
See link for 2m40s video for a taste:

Controls: 8.5
Controls are intuitive and responsive, and the animations are very reflective of how your character interacts with the world.
Challenge: 6.5
This might not bother some people but I did find this game too easy (even on the hardest difficulty). Some would argue it's more about the experience and the journey than it is about feeling like a badass accomplishing difficult feats, but for me, a lot of the satisfaction when playing any game comes from feeling like your life is always at risk and I just didn't feel that way with Hellblade. Perhaps some of the credit is due to the solid combat controls but the "focus" aka "buttonmashermode" mechanic wipes out any chance of failure.

Between Me and The Night is an indie game that focuses around interesting themes and has an beautiful art style. I will add a TL;DR at the end.
The game in itself is fairly simple and ends up dealing with some very heavy themes. In the game you wander across three different parts of the main character's life as you experience his own trip into a sense of madness and paranoia. In your inventory you can hold six items at once while you run around and try to do certain tasks to advance within the game. Sometimes the item could be right in front of you and you could be searching for a long time to find that one item to advance. The story showcases bullying, fear of the dark, and isolation as you explore with the main character. The only thing thing that helps seems to be his videogames, a way to escape his reality. The controls are fairly simple however with controller it would be nice to have the option to switch a button or two.
The artstyle of this game is unique and matches the game really well. Especially how the game is depicted when you are in the Otherworld (the video game). The different monsters and the shadows are interesting to say the least. The music in this game is greatly atmospheric adding to the game’s heavy themes to increase the sense of madness, isolation, and paranoia.
+ Artstyle is beautiful
+ Heavy themes portrayed perfectly to make you see the character’s struggles
+ Good music and sound effects
+ Good story
- Bad save system (saves every chapter, but without looking for help some are long and it is annoying if you have to quit and then restart again from a chapter. Once you figure out the level this is not really an issue. )
- Little replayability unless for achievements
These are my personal suggestions that I feel would improve the game.
- Checkpoint system within chapters
- Ability to change controls
- An option to enable an objective hint giver after being stuck for X amount of time (not to reveal where something is but maybe something like “Am I sure I checked the garage?”)
I was able to enjoy the game very much as I played through it. The art and music are both great and I enjoy games that try to encompass the ideas of madness, fear, isolation, and actually succeed. As much as I enjoy the game however, I don’t like the save system. The save system in my opinion is annoying, especially for someone like me who wants to know when something is saved or likes to always save frantically. The breaks between saves is annoying when I play with no guide, figure every little thing out, then have no option to save as I have to leave the game for the night. Overall I would say Between Me and The Night is a very wellmade and polished game with its story, themes, and visuals making it a good title.
Between Me and The Night has its bumps such as its save system, however the game is a well made title that is able to thoroughly deal with heavy subjects and the thin line of madness people walk. Overall Between Me and The Night has a good story, art, music and is an all around good title to play if you like this type of game or are interested in the themes prevalent within it.

I don't know what to write so I will share a chicken parm recipe with you.
4 boneless skinless chicken breast halves
salt and pepper
1⁄2 cup Italian breadcrumbs
1 egg, beaten
4 teaspoons butter
2 cups spaghetti sauce
4 slices mozzarella cheese
1 teaspoon grated parmesan cheese
Pound chicken to flatten.
Salt and pepper to taste.
Dip chicken in egg; then in bread crumbs.
Fry in butter in hot skillet, turning and browning for 10 minutes or until chicken is done.
Remove from skillet.
To skillet add spaghetti sauce.
Heat thoroughly.
Add chicken.
Place slices of mozzarella on top of chicken.
Sprinkle with parmesan.
Cover and cook until cheese is melted.
Serve with a side of spaghetti.

Pros: Some of the most gorgeous game art I've ever seen, great music, and responsive controls.
Cons: The story completely ruins it for me, I can't tell what point they were going for other than "tear-jerking," which is something that tends to make me blindingly angry rather than sad, particularly when it's done as hamhandedly as Ori was.  Additionally, the multiple "escape" sequences took friggin' long jumps over "difficult" and well into "punishing" territory.  I don't play twitch memorization games because I don't like them, and being forced to play them as a significant part of a supposed puzzle platformer just made me....UGH.  I generally even refuse to play timed chase sequences because they're so aggravating, unnecessary and forced, but I didn't have a choice in this instance.
In short, I really went in wanting to love this game, but I just can't.  90% of it was great, but the Jr High drama class level story and the NEVERENDING ESCAPE SEQUENCES loom so large in my memory that I don't think I'll ever play it again now that I've finished it.
