Hellblade Senua's Sacrifice is great psychological horror that follows Senua's personal journey through Cletic/Norse underworld. Through her manifestations you get a glimpse into the world of psychosis and how it's different effects can be real to many people around the world.
I found this game intense and very enjoyable to play. Although short the overall game play was spot on, I felt the story, cinematics gripping and fights scenes engaging and smooth.
There is no character setup or tutorial so before you start your journey I suggest familiarising yourself with the controls in the menu. I found the a controller to work best, also a good headset is very important.
Over the shoulder you follow Senua on her journey to Helheim , working your way through puzzles and enemies.
The difficulty of the game is, interesting as there is no tutorial so you have to get to grips with the controls relatively quickly.
There are three difficulty  choices in the menu
. I chose hard and found it tasking at times when there wasn't much navigation on what to do. Other than that I held my own in the pretty much in every fight.
A drawback is you can only fight once you are engaged in battle so you are unable to practice swinging your sword, finding out new combinations until you are in combat, easy to learn hard to master.
Although I am sure you will get caught off guard just like me, watch your back.
I found the controller to be the best choice, once I had familiarised myself with them from the menu I picked the rest up on my own.
The controls are not to over complex and can seem a little button bashy when you are fighting if you are unwilling to try new things. Although you can mix up the combo's a bit and get some very nice fight scenes.
If you can time the block nicely the parrying effect is really nice.
This game has steam achievements and all of them but one are story related. The lore stone locations that is a collectibles achievement which can missed if you plan on 100%.
The plot is in-depth and makes the user think relying heavily on inspiration from Norse and Celtic backgrounds. If you have had no experience of mental health issues this game will definitely break the ice.
Highly recommend watching the Hellblade Feature  in the menu after you have completed the game as it shows just how much work went into the making.
The combat system is fluid and smooth and can easily catch you out. Although they could possibly add more styles or combinations but I truly enjoyed the combat in this game.
The sound in the game is brilliant if you are able to use a 7.1 surround sound either on a headset or a TV setup I strongly recommend it to get the most out of the voices.
The graphics are gorgeous in this game and the attention to detail is brilliant.
The cinematic cut scenes, death scenes and endings are great, although sometimes will make you lose focus and causing you to drop your guard at the worst possible time.
Fortunately I didn't find any game breaking bugs, if there were any smaller bugs I did not encounter them so I wish you the same.
Overall I found this game to be a light bearer into the world of psychosis, I hope more games can be created on a similar basis, delving deep into the issues that many can't even comprehend in modern day society.
I personally think this is fantastic and will be looking forward to my second play through soon. I hope other game companies can take inspiration from the detail here and produce similar games like Hellblade.
Hope I helped.

Blink is a smooth, relaxing, and extremely enjoyable experience.
I have been talking, writing, reviewing Indie games for a long time. After a while you begin to see patterns or formulas form when it comes to Indie games. It’s not that they become predictable or boring, on the contrary. So when I say that Blink is a Limbo-like title, I mean that in a good way completely. It doesn’t change the fact though, that this is a Puzzle/Platformer starring a child with a strange power that helps him overcome gaps, and shadowy death monsters with an awesome art style. If Walking Simulator/Roguelike can be a genre, can’t Limbo-like be one?
I am aware that Puzzle/platformers have long existed before Braid and Limbo came to be but they are the bar these days. Games such as BOOR, Inside and Never Alone continue to prove the passion and demand for these types of games. It’s a crowded genre to say the least but one I hold in high esteem and love. One the developers seems to as well. Which is why I’m more than happy then to start by saying I highly recommend Blink.
Blink is about a small child whose father goes missing. No, not at the bar type missing but really missing. Without much explanation you wake up inside a mysterious temple and an invisible voice reaches out to you. It gifts you with a power to slip into, “The Eye.” In the Eye, the laws of physics are different. This begins your quest to find your father and unravel the mystery of the voice and shadow monsters that have begun to plague your village. It’s simple, neat and well told. It’s no Stephen King story mind you, but it gets the major points across without unnecessary complexities.
The story does evolve and even culminates in a pretty awesome boss battle. For most of the game though its a rather monotone mood but in a good way. While the puzzles are challenging and even had me scratching my head at times. I never felt frustrated or angry at my mistakes, certainly not cheated. Blink has fantastic controls and responds remarkably well. The entire experience is very fluid and enjoyable from beginning to end. When I started playing it, I didn’t stop until I had beat the game. It’s that just smooth and enjoyable.
To be fair Blink is a rather short experience, topping out for me at 2 hours of total game time. I am fairly experienced at these titles though and it may take longer for others. This is still a rather short experience but I don’t find the pricing unfair at £4.99/$6.99. Especially when others have charged way more for the same amount of game time. (coughINSIDEcough)
Let’s talk about how puzzles work in this game.
With a press of a button the kid can transport himself into the Eye, a realm where an after image can be used to traverse the terrain. The most basic way to explain it is, you’re using light to create a shadow that acts a platform once you slip into this realm. One important thing to note though is that in the absence of light there is nothing. Which means you will fall into nothing, which happened frequently to me. Also you can’t stay very long in The Eye realm, as it will consume you.
What is very impressive is how well this entire system works. You can use light to trap your enemies inside of barriers, create stairwells for yourself, and use the absence of light to slip through walls. It’s all very strange, but it when you get the hang of it, its awesome. The game does begin throwing in more obstacles as you progress. The Shadow monsters are slow and somewhat stupid but become faster and more feral in the Eye. Some shadow creatures can only see you once you slip into the Eye. This leads to it becoming terrifying as they run you down while you try to move through an area. Later areas throw in lanterns, fog, and platforms that shift into The Eye with you. I cannot stress enough that this is a very smooth and wonderfully done progression. It kept things fun but not stressful. I loved that.
One thing I feel that will perhaps make a person think twice is the art style of this game. Beauty is in the Eye of the beholder in this case. (pun intended.) I will be frank in saying that the sprites for the Humans in this game are weird, and they’re my least favorite part. I felt like I was controlling a hot dog child wrapped in a coat. On the other hand, everything else looks spectacular. The rigid nature of the sprites works well for the shadow monsters and makes them feel alien. The backgrounds and the environments are gorgeous and feel like a painting. I couldn’t stop hitting my screen cap button while playing.
Details are abundant and there was plenty of times I stopped and spoke to some sheep. The final area of the game is, by far, the most memorable and really just tops things off so very well. Of course none of this really works without a good soundtrack. Thankfully, Blink has an orchestral soundtrack and it’s exactly what you would expect for this type of game. It elevates the game and I never got tired of it. Sound effects while minimal, are sufficient but nothing inspiring.
As to the odds and ends, Blink does feature Steam achievements but currently no Steam cards. The game features full controller support. No rebindable keys sadly. Replay value is something that will be lacking for this type of game. You might pick it up again in six months and have fun though. This is standard for most games of this nature. The game runs on flash and has zero options menus, those with higher resolutions will have an experience that may vary. Keep that in mind.
Does Blink bring anything new to the table/innovate? Not necessarily but it does what it set out to do perfectly. If you have played games like Limbo/Braid you know what to expect. If you have never played any of them then this is a great place to start. I never found a bug nor crashed while playing. The nature of the puzzles and mechanics of your powers is executed perfectly. It’s what I took most away from this game. It was just a joy to play. Hopefully more people play Blink and spread the love of Indie Games.

I received this game from one of the developers.  And I have to say its a very solid, fun indie game.
Story: You're a young kid that is looking for his father.  While looking, you run into this being called the Eye where everything it sees is a reality for you but when it closes its eye, the world disappears around you and anything brightly lit up leaves an afterimage burned into the vision of the Eye.  Using the eye's powers, you will explore the world, solve puzzles, find out what happened to the eye's kind and find your father.  The story is nothing to get excited about but it provides a good setting for how the game plays and for the most part provides reasons for everything that is happening.  It would be nice to see more of the world and learn more about the characters, but remember this is an indie game made by a small group of developers.  Frankly its interesting and serves its purpose.  You don't finish the game with questions.
Graphics: The game is colorful and I like the art design.  The shadows and light effects are well done, creating a great puzzle platformer game.  I set the graphics to fancy and I played on a 2K monitor for the entire game and I didn't really see any graphical issues while playing.  But my graphics card has more than enough power to play this game. Kudos to the artists!
Sound: The music in the game is very calming and soothing until you run into the enemies which makes the music tense but not too tense.  The music does not overwhelm the gameplay.  In fact I sometimes didn't even notice there was music playing.  In my opinion the music and sound effects work well with the game.  Its not in your face and its not too soft.  Though I would not get the soundtrack.
Gameplay: I played this game with an Xbox One controller and I recommend playing with a controller.  The controls are simple and its easy to understand how to play the game.  The game does a good job giving you the instructions and what to do in order to solve puzzles. I never felt like the controls made it hard to solve puzzles.  Its a puzzle platformer that has you manipulate light to solve puzzles, avoid enemies and jump on to platforms to move on to the next puzzle.  Its a very ingenious game that will test your brain a little.  There were times for me where I had to think about how to solve the puzzle (different from my usual fare of shooters and strategy games).  There are not hard but sometimes there is no clear answer unless you stop and think.  Puzzles are well done and clever.  There will be some puzzles that frustrate you at first but you will figure it out.  Note: I didn't run into any issues where I messed up the puzzle and I had to restart but there was one puzzle where I messed up and I almost couldn't restart.  If you run into that issue just quit the game and start it again.  Would be nice to have a restart checkpoint option in the menu.
Overall: I like this game.  Its different from my usual fare of shooters and strategy games.  For the price you will get a 2-3 hour game on your first playthrough.  After that you may become a pro and get the other achievements.  I would recommend trying this game out.  Its unique, its fun and its short.  It will definitely test your brain a little bit but in a clever way.  Definitely worth a buy and I would buy this for some of my friends.

You are then granted gameplay at the young age of 3, where you are beckened by your father to come torwards him, after this, you are told about your mother's favourite bible verse. Revelation 21:6\

Assassin's Creed was am amazing game when it was released. The gameplay was novel with fluid movement unlike any video game before, and the plot was intriguing and compelling. The plot is still just as good, but the gameplay has not aged well at all. The game requires a massive amount of grind through the mid-game and most of the end-game, and many games since have surpassed AC1's freerunning and combat (most notably, AC2).
I recommened that players attempt AC1 as the intro point to the series. If the grinding becomes too much to bear, watch the remaining cutscenes and story missions on YouTube and move on to AC2.

I've been meaning to finish this game for a while now. I played Assasin's Creed II first and absolutely loved it. I still haven't completed this one, but I'll get to it some day. From what I can remember, I enjoyed it. Sorry for not being able to give more details.
I will say one thing though: the minimap is rubbish. It doesn't show the outline of any buildings so you can't use it for navigation at all, unlike the second game's minimap. From what I can recall, the minimap is basically a circle with cardinal directions wirrten on it with a opqaue background inside that contains a load of markers for quests and whatnot that the minimap if of no use in getting to.

This game does not require UPlay. That alone will sell it for some people, so I figured I'd start with that.
Still here? Alright.
The controls for freerunning are mostly handled by the game, you simply hold the right buttons down and push the direction you want to go. I'm usually skeptical about letting a game try to decipher what I wanted my character to do based on very little actual control, but in this case, I almost never fell to my death based on a decision the game made for me, which is good. The combat is pretty easy, and the controls are as tight as the sequels. The swordplay is intuitive. Usually, the only time you will get destroyed is if you happen across an elite enemy early on, with many of your advanced skills missing. The combat in this game is very much for fans of the "one-man-army" idea. There is very little actual stealth required. Even if you screw it up and the entire city is out to kill you, you can defend yourself without a problem if you can counter. That said, the stealth is not unfun. The game is very up-front about giving you feedback on everything you need to know about who or what is or isn't your enemy, what you can and can't get away with, and when you are and aren't visible, at all times.
The story is good, but it's better in the sequels. It's also pretty repetitious in this game. After your first or second assassination, you can probably decide for yourself if you will enjoy the rest of the game. The only break from the norm is near the end, where you will be forced to play out the "one-man-army" scenario mentioned above, so again, I emphasize, this is not really a stealth game. It's a hack-and-slash with stealth elements, where both are mostly optional. This means, though, that you are given the choice of how you want to play the game. You can hide in plain sight, mocking your enemies from the crowd, or you can be a total delinquent, make the guards very angry, and kill the beggars that throw rocks at you (the game stops penalizing you for that once the story is completed). The assassination missions also have multiple solutions. You are given a lot of freedom in terms of gameplay, again, except at the end. Stealth is impossible during the final chapter. Overall, I would recommend playing through Ezio's storyline (Assassin's Creed 2, Brotherhood, and Revelations) first, then giving this one a try if you find yourself a fan. The sequels are superior, but this one is also worth looking at.

Gameplay-wise it fits a horror setting (in my view) in that ammo is relatively scarce, though that can fluctuate depending on the seed (more on that below), and the combat itself is clunky but managable. The game punishes you for fleeing but not in a completely unmanagable way and more as an incentive to fight the horror.
Rogue-like elements, including the meta-game progression in the form of birth stars which are allocated before each game and give buffs, are pretty well done though I can see how eventually they may become over-powering. You can delete your history on the game, resetting you, but I guess the life of a rogue-like will inherently depend on how long it takes for you to get bored with it (maybe, I'm not an expert).
Overall, decent enough if you can look past the graphics. Tonally it's consistent, with a focus on prioritisation (personal surivival vs. being a decent person for a bunch of sprites) as well as with an heavy weightiness to it (bad description, think Silent Hill 2?). Um, so yeah, thanks for reading all of this. I'm not an expert but I hope this helps mate (or lady-mate).

In this Dragonball inspired game, you play as a 'rookie caster' who is the only one left to restore the world and defend against the infestation known as the Flanx. This game will have you dashing about at high speeds blasting enemies and altering terrain with several different abilities.

Having bad production value doesn't mean a game isn't fun but unfortunately Caster has very little to offer in terms of gameplay. Caster is a third-person shooter with a camera angle that can very from directly behind the player-character to a top down perspective.  It can be fun to zip around the map and lay waste to enemies but the player won't experience this until at least one hour into the game. Caster requires the player to collect energy in order to upgrade abilities and as a result the first hour or so of gameplay is very slow and tedious. After this first hour there will be a brief moment of mild amusement and then the player is immediately introduced to enemies and situations that require a slower playstyle.
In my opinion the developers would have done well to skip the whole upgrade process that made the first hour or so of gameplay a waste of time and focus on high speed gameplay that this game advertises.

There are many games that attempt to embrace Lovecraftian mythology, but none come nearly as close to it as this one. The gameplay is slow, as it should be, and although it does have the cliché sanity meter, it is a staple for attempting to tackle the world Lovecraft created. You start your journey with next to no information (unless you play as a specific unlockable character) only the knowledge that the world is coming to an end in three days, a car, and some cash in your pocket. Using the runes on the walls of dungeons in addition to notes left behind that give you somewhat detailed information, and the nature of the dungeon and affilation of the monsters you make inference on the god you need to seal. The combat is clunky and your character lumbers about in the dark and dreary environments. This experience, while infuriating to some, people like me find that it brings the game world together. You aren't just managing your resources and sanity in game, the slow gameplay with a time limit grates on your mind in real life as well. All in all if you are looking for a Lovecraftian procedually generated mystery game you won't find anything better than this.

Absolutely love this game. The concept is truly fun, despite being about a dark and terrifying entity and the world's impending doom. Yahtzee is a brilliant writer and it really shows in the descriptions and blurbs of text that bring the world to life.
My only complaint with this game is that the combat can be extremely challenging and somewhat unfair at times. Without powering up your character that you play as, you start with a very modest amount of health and sanity. While health can be restored fairly easily, it is very difficult to keep one's sanity up, especially when an enemy spawns behind you as you're about to leave a room and you end up unintentionally leaving the enemy behind - this causes your sanity to drop a small amount, and after time it adds up fast. Don't get me started on the "you die in one hit" challenges, because so far I can barely even defeat a single enemy without taking damage. Not sure what Yahtzee was thinking when he created those challenges... he probably just wanted to give a big middle finger to everyone who likes collecting achievements.
Although quite short this game is fairly enjoyable, especially with this small price tag.

The premise is clear: the Flanx have invaded Middon, which is short of experienced mages, and you, a noob Caster, gets the job of owning the bad guys.
Right away, you’re put in this action shooter game that has a remind of a 3D Megaman. You’ll be dashing, double jumping and collecting  several diferent weapons that will by fired by your arm and many of which can be charged before firing. Among the arsenal you will find from energy blasts and bombs to seeker missiles and a stunner, including some kind of gravitational gun that will deform the terrain increasing its height. If it was not enough, you can actually deform and destroy all the terrain by all your attacks, which also spices the combat mechanics.
You will face from cockroaches and flying beetles to giant worms. Each enemy is very different in all aspects starting by the models, and including their weapon and combat approach. You should even be prepared for enemies lurking out from the ground and find yourself running while saying ugly words. What is a bit strange is that, having put the time in differentiating the enemies so much, most, if not all, of them just use the same weapons available to you just colored differently.
The game packs 15 short levels and the progress is quite fast. You will start with just an energy gun and the ability to do some small double jumps and dashes and a small health bar. However, in each level you will collect energy by killing Flanx and healing trees, which then you will be able to spend upgrading yourself. There are also some weapons that you will have to find -not that it is hard- to unlock them, and your character will even change color when changing weapon -what does that remind you of, again?-.
Caster can be completed in a couple hours, maybe a little longer, although you won’t be able to upgrade everything -and I mean everything, your jumps height, dash duration, health level, weapons power…-, which may take an extra hour replaying some levels. However, if you really want to play more, you can find mods in the game’s website that will give you some extra content. And you will probably want to play some more, since it’s one of those games where you’re just telling yourself after each level ‘Only one more level and then I walk the dog’ and more soon than later there is no one more level.
About the soundtrack, I should mention it’s not constant. It packs some tracks that you won’t notice to be there and some others that will really pick your attention because they’re actually good.
Overall, Caster is one of these very beautiful indie games that also packs good controls and gameplay and will leave you a taste of wanting more.

This is a game that I found to be very difficult to recommend, or disuade. It sits in the middle ground but ultimately leans towards a thumbs down.
There are a few nagging reasons for this. Like all AAA games, Remember Me is beautiful. The main character is beautiful and looks like she was designed based on actress Hillary Duff (maybe in hopes of a movie tie in or something). The problem with the fact that she is pretty is the character also fist fights giant robots, gets into train wrecks and walks away unscathed. Personally i like the idea of a female protagonist and even more so do i like the idea of an attractive one (as i'll be staring at this character more than any other) but body type is important. Nilin is a runway model. She is anemic, weak and frain by design. If her body was modeled based on a femal olympian or a female boxer it would feel much better to play her.
Athletic women in real life can look both beautiful and gentle as well as tough as nails. Runway models almost always look frain and helpless (regardless of whatever the expression they have in their shots). This breaks immersion for me constantly. Action stars are almost universally in tip top physical condition because what they do is taxing physically. This character looks like a light breeze will break her back, but she still climbs up buildings and flips and flies all over. Its disjarring and the more you play and watch it, the more annoying it becomes.
The second problem that really made me want to put the game down is the blarring one dimensional gameplay and ultra linear pathing. There is only one direction to travel, there is nothing to explore and their are no alternative options. This becomes increasingly annoying over time as the general design becomes very predictable. The problem with this is that in most cases it is an artificial railcar, when the over all design of the levels would allow for a more open world feel with some minor tweaking. This is bothersome.
Lastly combat in this game is pretty boring. Nilin fist fights almost everything and as you fight a group of 5 guys, 4 of them are polite enough to patiently wait until you've killed the one you're focused on. There is no need for crowd control because the crowd never attacks and there is no need for dodging or blocking as the one you're attacking will never attack back as long as you're hitting him. Even when the game does try to break up your combo with a attack from another in the crowd it gives you a giant exclamation point and a way to much time to react. Its too easy. This is just like the pathing system.. ultra linear and insultingly simple. I believe this ended up being fairly lazy design with what could have been really fun otherwise.
Over all I believe there is too much aggrivation in playing Remember Me to recommend it. The positives from the game are strong, but pale in comparison to the negatives. This might have made a great action movie as the story is pretty interesting, the characters are all attractive and having the whole story wrap up in 3 hours feels appropriate. But Here I am 3 hours in and I'm getting bored with playing this game. The sad part is i really want to keep going but it feels un-fun to do so. How should I put this. The game was good! A little short and generic on some bits of mechanics, but good. The generic parts are mostly the linear level design and Tomb Raider style climbing but it doesn't take anything out of the game. The combat was fun due to it being basically a fast hack n slash but with fists. And especially with the combo system. You can create your own combos in the menu, which was just a brilliant idea, too bad most of its potential was left unused. If we get a sequal (which seems unlikely at the point), we should get a better system. There's also small puzzles that you encounter seldom, those that include 'memory remixes' in which you get to literally alter someone's memory with great detail. The music design was very nice because of the way it faded on and off combat, and the music itself was a fitting dramatic orchestra mixed with electronic synthesizers "D blue glitching" the orchestra now and then, making it sound pretty cool.
The story was driving, and the setting was unique. 2080's France (or more specifically, 'Neo-Paris'), where the buying and selling of memories has become the biggest business since anything. But it has gone so big, that it has become a big part of society and culture. It's supposedly a utopia, but we get to see the darkest side of it right at the beginning, the horrifying consequences of having such power, to alter someone's memories. And what becomes of those who get themselves altered too much, or even completely being wiped out of any trace of a healthy human being.
Cons:
Too short.
(I'm not exactly the kind of person that would pay 30€ for a 10 hour game with no replay value)
Pros:
Fun combat and other mechanics.
Decent story and voice acting, interesting setting.

I never write reviews but now I feel like reviewing one of my favourite games.
Ori and the Blind Forest is easily one of the best games I have ever played. Not only it offers a unique environment with so many possibilities and different ways to move and act, it also gives you a gaming experience you will never forget.
I've always been a fan of platformers but I'm also very picky when it comes to them. Some platformers tend to make me feel frustrated but Ori and the Blind Forest, even though it felt difficult to get through some areas, I never got frustrated. Its atmosphere is so relaxing and even breathtaking sometimes that it's hard to just stop playing. Rage quit? Never happened.
I absolutely love the story. It makes me feel happy and yes, I cried a few times. It's simple but beautiful, and the game doesn't have too much boring cutscenes or dialogues, everything actually feels important.
The game isn't hard to learn, vice versa, the learning is easy but not too easy and it's fun as heck! At the very beginning you already feel like a pro and at the end you're a master. You can make a lot of fun tricks with Ori's abilities and that makes the playing even more entertaining.
Some parts of the game are so intense and they come as such a surprise that I have to give props to that. Those parts really have the feel. You know what I mean? They make you feel like you really live in the game, you ARE the game, and you don't have to worry about anything in the "real" world, because the game's world is your world now.
Do I recommend this game? Hell yeah! It's definitely worth its full price and I'm also happy that a definitive edition came out with more stuff to do. If you're looking for an atmospheric, different platformer, this is the game for you!

Lego Harry Potter: Years 5-7 is yet another licensed Lego game and a sequel to Years 1-4. As you can masterfully detuct, it's based on the movies of the last three years of Harry Potter. And yes, the last one is divided into two parts in the game too. Developed by Traveller's Tales and released in 2011. Nope, no talking yet. Nope, still never-ever online multiplayer.
It also was released for Xbox 360, PS3, Wii, NDS, 3DS, PSP, Vita, iOS. From the main consoles you can guess that Wii has the worse graphics. However PC doesn't come as the best, as it's not optimised and they don't sell DLC for it like for consoles: DLC pack of 10 characters and DLC pack of 5 silly magic to shoot at honest people. It doesn't sound important though.
NDS, 3DS, PSP, Vita and iOS are also interesting to mention. As usual, Traveller's Tales can't decide what kind of Lego game to make for portable systems. Years 1-4 had some kind of isometric fetch quest with characters telling you things in dialog box. Years 5-7 seems to be made from scratch and made itself to be like a cutted down version of main game, while occasionally doing unique things. Single-player, yea. It is however nasty that PS Vita was forced to have as much of content as Nintendo DS, despite being much more powerful.
Technically, PC version comes with bunch of problems.
First of all, it's not optimized. Many people reported to have low framerates. Some have it only at start of levels, others have it constantly. Be ready that you may not run it smoothly.
And another one is control mapping. The game doesn't remember them and you will have to rebind buttons on each game's launch. I also had a minor glitch where when I chose USB controller the game would show me square characters instead of words like "button" or "axis".
At least it doesn't freeze or lose save or make progress impossible like Years 1-4 for some people.
Gameplay-wise, yea, it's another Lego game. Casual, can't die, collect-a-thon. That was before characters talked. It still has a hub world of Hogwards and some story missions take place in it instead of separate levels. Mostly for classes. And yes, it's a direct sequel to Years 1-4. It added this fancy magic duel where you just have to attack with same-colored magic as opponent and then button mash to do damage. Though, I must say that magic selection this time around is more fun due to being more varied. They require doing a bit more thing then just moving target over things as game automatically chooses magic for you. Like, there is water-shooting magic.
However, this is the one early Lego game that I beat on a single breath, so to say! I liked Harry Potter books a lot and read them all but I didn't remember books 5-7 much at all. As a result, game acted as refresher. As said, characters don't talk, so new people will not understand much and will not find it fun. But oh boy, I had a lot of it, remembering all the plot twists, reminding myself which one belonged to what year and laughing out at all the Lego jokes. It also wasn't complete comedy as there was a bit of drama, mostly thanks to that awesome soundtrack, so it was quite an experience to me personally.
But then, I am not sure if it's because the game being objectively better than previous Lego ones or my personal bias in this case. Probably the latter.
And hey, it has a level without wand and a 2D-like fancy-pantsy-artsy stage as well.
Also can be noted is that this LEGO game pushed graphics up, using by-modern technical standards. Mostly you will see how shadows look awesome on all those lego details. High-quality and clear and superb lighting. Shame about not-so-awesome optimisation though.
Also, yes, gamepad is recommended.
And yes, I still feel that game mixes battle and puzzles nicely. Most often it's puzzle-only, just very few fights. I approve it in casual Lego games. Ok, not "mixes", more like "pro-puzzle". Still approve.
Anyway, if you are fan of Harry Potter and got a friend, try this one. I liked it a lot. If you are not, then ehhhhhh yet another Lego game.

Then when the game realizes that you probably should have enemies, it spams you with them, so you literally have to stop everything you're doing every few seconds to beat them. It gets repetitive, and shows that the game developers don't realize that there's a big difference between challenging and annoying.
The makers of Candy Crush also have no idea what that line is, but whatever.
Also, all of the best LEGO games have humor, or, at the very least, characterize their characters pretty well. They're fun to watch. That is not the case with this one. I didn't really care about any of them.
Most of the levels feel like busywork instead of actual levels that advance the story. Heck, some of the levels in between the levels that weren't really levels were more interesting than the levels we got.
I'd say that, if the game got one more re-write for the story, it could have been a lot better. As it was, it had a few glaring problems. I'd say no to this one.

As always in LEGO games you destroy the environment, then rebuild, all while the current narrative unfolds. Not everything is LEGO, basically you have 3D models with hand-drawn textures and LEGO parts nicely integrated into them. The music supports the Harry Potter immersion.
I feel like objects have on average more transformations than they had in the first part of LEGO Harry Potter. Some transition to destruction, some recycle. Rooms, i.e. parts of the world with a loading transition separating them, are often larger than in the first part. I don't like that backgrounds tend to blur and I was outright annoyed by the lag in some parts of the game. The first time I played I had to stop after two hours because the lag made me sick to the stomach.
I liked the level where
. Altogether the new skills are nice and work pretty well with the levels. It seems there are more on-screen tips now, like "needs character with key", still there were some situations in which it took me some time to figure out what the game wanted me to do. One related problem is, it's not right away clear what characters can do.
I'd like to see information added to character selections. Make it clear what each character can do. If you don't want to spoil to much only show pictograms as used in levels. Tell me right away whether a character has a key, wrench, is strong, speaks Parsel etc. That way I would have learned sooner about the
.
Another feature I'm missing is a map. The Marauder's map is prominently featured in the stories. Why not provide a variant to the player, preferably with access to known rooms and the Advanced Guide. Also let a level's pause screen show collected character tokens.
Controls are a little less tight than in the first game. Some of the spells feel sluggish and I still don't like the drive mechanism, i.e. vehicles try to go in the direction you indicate in relation to the camera as opposed the car. Possibly part of the missing tightness is that other characters too often get in the way, i.e. they try to keep close and thus move where I want to aim a spell.
There are rarely glitches. Once, I was in a free play level and suddenly left without any character with a wand, some character was stuck in a standing position even while moving while switching to another character showed them constantly even in place. With all the critique above LEGO Harry Potter: Years 5-7 is still a fun game and deserves my recommendation.

Is it an incredible experience? - yes.
Is it a fun game? - well, no.
Ninja theory did everything right when it comes to marketing, making this game and it's unique selling proposition popular. Don't get me wrong, the game
the "mental illness" thing right, at least in the first few hours. Motion capturing and facial animation is good and the acting is something out of this world.
But this game isn't just cut scenes, the developers actually wanted to make it a game. But what do you do if all your budget went into psychology research and motion capturing? - You cut down the game mechanics to the bare minimum.
One of them is, of course, the fighting. What reviewers call "intense" and "intimate" I would describe as repetitive and tiring. There just a handful of enemy types, but the all can be defeated in the same way: dodging and attacking. Dodge - attack - dodge - attack - dodge - attack... The focus mechanic gives you slow-motion for a few seconds, so you can attack some more, before you have to dodge again. Like in Witcher 3, this mechanic makes the fights really simple. Yet, it's not an easy game. That's because the game just swarms you with enemies, especially towards the end of the game. But again, dodging and attack does the trick, just be careful of the enemies that attack you from the back frequently.
The other game mechanic is: wandering around. This makes about 70% of this game. You wander around, looking for things, sometimes runes, sometimes holograms of objects, that you "repair" by aligning your character with the hologram correctly. Other variations are: wandering around in total darkness, wandering around in mazes and wandering around evading enemies. Those activities aren't interesting nor challenging. A few hours in, I just looked up the rune locations online, so I could skip the wandering and go back to the combat, which I actually prefered to those "puzzles".
Hellblade is great game to talk about, but an underwhelming game to play.

I'm playing a fresh Normal run to re-experience the game from the start, and one thing that I'm noticing happening right away is, while I'm still bogged down with resource management and mining, there's more stuff to /do/. And it's easier to to /do/ it. It used to be about finding materials for Warp fuel so you could keep moving to the next system. Now I keep finding new distractions cropping up along the way. Missions, bounties, landmarks, space fights - I have to stop myself and remember that I have the Atlas story path to do still. And then there's the new second story path cropping up that I have to decipher. The game is definately not as bare bones as it once was.
You will still find a lot of deja vu in this procedurally generated universe. There will still be ugly creatures that defy logic. Having been aware of the controversy of this games pre-launch hype and the post launch mess that it was, I decided to still give this game a chance when it went on sale as I have found that some games can provide a good dollar to time ratio. I played this game for a good number of hours before they put out this "Atlas update". The update definitely made the game a little better based on what I saw.
I would describe this game as a Zen game. Theres no immediate goal to obtain, with reaching the galactive core being so far off that it's easy to forget. The majority of the game revolves around exploration, resource gathering, and improving your character.
Exploration is fun, scanning plants and animals and being rewarded for it. You can name your discoveries or leave them randomly generated. However, After about the third planet I got really sick of scanning the stuff I saw. When you look at the prices of good in the game the minute reward you get is not worth it. Aside from scanning you can fly around from point to point to explore abandoned buildings, meet aliens, and sometimes find a trading outpost where you might get an upgrade. This game has a poor tracking system of places you've been. Many time I zoom to a new waypoint only to find I've been there before. In addition, this game respawns resources and boxes. A whole planet to explore and the game seems to want you to only stay in a small area.
Resource gathering quickly becomes tedious, at first it's fun getting what you need to make the first upgrades, but after that it becomes a chore. Your inventory is very limited and there is nothing in the way of storage until you build a base which is a long and complicated process that requires even more resources beyond your ability to get until you finish a covoluted quest line to research those resources.
Improving your character is easier with this patch. Previously you would need to cross your fingers and hope you found a drop pod which contains the Exosuit upgrades for the character. Now you can build a beacon that finds a nearby drop pod for you. Improving your space ship is a needle in a haystack buy. You can sit at trading posts where ships frequent and you can go up to any ship and see if you can purchase it. The ship will either be far too expensive to purchase or equal or lesser value than your own. The prices for these ships are incredibly high and I would spend hours mining rarer resources and still not scratch the price tag. The Multitool mining/weapon gun is also a similar headache. Any outpost with a landing platform will have one for sale on the wall, the quality is the same as a ship only a new one doesn't appear after  Getting blue prints for the Multitool mining/weapon gun or Ship requires a special resource only found by exploring (See exploring for those complaints) or by killing drones that patrol planets. The prices on these blueprints are pretty high so you can only grab a couple at a time if you are searching hardcore. The blue prints are also random so it's rare you will get the blue print you are looking for.
Pros:
I like how this game handles distance. Gives a good sense of scale.
Fun to explore at first.
Cons:
Keeping track of already explored locations is a nightmare.
Game needs an auto pilot because even at max speed it takes some time to get to places.
Upgrades too minimal to feel like they are worth it. +.5s extra sprint time? Oh boy!
Upgrades too rare. In 20+ hours I only found 6 tech upgrades.
Ship purchasing too random. I don't like sitting at  a trade post watching ships coming in praying for the one ship I can buy thats an Upgrade. Most ships are far above what I can afford or are equal or lesser quality of what I have.
Do you get one Hour of gameplay per $6 paid?: Even at sale I say no. It's empty hours. At $60 full price this game is outrageously priced. AVOID.
Ease of 100%: Easy, but very time consuming.
(100% Being all achievements, Unlocks, Upgrades, Ect.)

Got this game over a Steam sale for $1, and am absolutely glad I did so. Caster is a gem in the rough - a rough gem. Quick breakdown below:
Graphics - The graphics might seem a little off-putting at first, but I quickly got over it as soon as I got into the gameplay. The character textures and models could definitely use a lot of work though.
Gameplay - It's got a retro feel to it. That is, a lack of premise, but immersive gameplay. If you're looking for something with a storyline, you'll be disappointed. I've only played through the game on normal difficulty, but even then there were some stages that surprised me (in a good, challenging sort of way). Camera/controls are *occasionally* fidgety, (egs. running on walls in certain maps can be pretty trippy) but it's never enough to really detract from the game. Replay value is so-so. Ending indicates a game that its creators no longer wanted to invest money/time into.
Audio - Hit-and-miss for me. Some tracks are amazing, and really go well with the action, others just sound like cheap techno tracks.
Mods - Rather than mods, I'd call them user-created stages. Downloaded a mod-pack off the game's website, and had a lot of fun with those.
All in all, I got about 3 hours of gameplay from this. Thoroughly enjoyed this, my only major complain being the lack of content (in terms of stages). Maybe there are more mods in forums, but I have not looked at those yet.

After the end of the last game, BJ again narrowly avoids death due to his comrades. However he is not exactly entirely together after his experience, We have a short flashback to make the choice from the first game for a second time, as well as flashbacks to BJ's childhood and his abusive father where you're forced to shoot your dog to "man you up some". To be blunt, BJ's father is an abusive racist piece of trash and the game and acting make you feel what it feels like to be a powerless child in such a household. At least for a moment
and then your submarine gets attacked by a massive floating nazi fortress. BJ demonstrates he is quite handicapable and dispatches nazis from a wheelchair before you're dragged before Frau Engel who proceeds to behead Caroline in a bait to having to make another sadistic choice like The New Order. It actually made me feel tense as I was unsure what was about to happen given they just killed such an important and badass character...
Frau Engel of course ratchets up the crazy sadistic off the charts with what proceeds to happen and it forces her daughter to betray her and join you, you inherit Caroline's armor from the first game..so you must be thinking you're a badass nazi killing Iron Man now right?
Wrong. BJ is still broken, the armor serves as life support, While it allows you to have a bunch of armor, you cant get your health above 50, and its repeatedly made very clear that BJ isnt there. Terror Billy is broken. Years of fighting has taken its toll on him psychologically and physically. He feels the armor is part of Caroline and repeatedly asks her to give him the strength to keep fighting. About halfway through the game, when you finally confront BJ's abusive father years later as an adult things take a turn. First off, gutting him like a fish was quite cathartic... But secondly, he sold your♥♥♥♥♥out to the Nazis and what ensues is you getting captured. Of course our hero will get out of this right?
You watch your first would be savior get mowed down as he tries to sneak in by being your attorney. Frau Engel knew and proceeded to engineer the situation just to give BJ and you some hope, only to have it destroyed right before your eyes so she can further taunt you. Engel doesnt just want to kill you after all, she wants to destroy you more. Humiliate you.
You're dragged into a courtroom, where you get a "fair" trial, you manage to bust free of your restraints and scramble through one of the most tense and difficult firefights in the game... but it was all in your head, a hopeful dream as you're carted out... and then before a live audience and a rediculous spectacle. You are beheaded
Yes. You read that right. You are beheaded. You are dead...
Thank god for Daat Yachud technology. Your friends engineer a plan and save you by nabbing your head and literally giving you a new body. Terror Billy is back. While you cant get the insane level of armor you could get before, you now are back to full health and, as a bonus, you get to choose a fancy toy to play with...
And now its time to make those nazis pay. You and your group spring to action recruiting more allies, this time a moonshine-brewing Marxist from New Orleans who is more than willing to join up with you and fight the good fight..all while chewing the scenery (Christopher Heyerdal did an awesome job here)
Your group concocts a plan to take the nazi flying fortress out, but you need the codes for them from the nazi base on Venus... The plan to get there involves you impersonating an actor to play Terror Billy in a propaganda piece, after all, the Nazis still think you're dead...
And then you get to come face to face with Hitler himself, who in this timeline is still alive... for what thats worth... the actor playing Hitler does a superb job capturing his mood swings and his very rapidly failing health and mental state. As a bonus, yes you do get a chance to kill Hitler, and the sequence alone is one of the most memorable things I've had in a game in a long time.
After getting the codes you travel back and set your plan into motion. Obviously. BJ proceeds to wreck the Nazi flying fortress, and from there they go where Frau Engel is being interviewed on live TV and show her just how very alive, and how very♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ you are. The entire game builds to it and you get the satisfaction of showing the world the inside of her head courtesy of a hatchet, Not to mention embarassing her, as the entire show was about how she was keeping the world safe from you, and gloating about how she killed you before hand.
What followed, at least in my case, was Wyatt reading a moving speech imploring Americans to rise up against the Nazis, to resist, with everything they have, because the nazis can be defeated.
There are side missions where you can help out the resistance, well, resist, and go back to mission areas to retrieve collectables and defeat ubercommanders, Essentially they're commanders dispatched to clean up the mess you made, or to reestablish control, retrieve evidence, that sort of thing. The level replay usually is in a different order and you'll have access to new areas by the time you get to this. I havn't completed all of them yet, but Ive found them very fun.
Like the first game you have all kinds of approaches to the situation, however the game is brutally hard and just running and gunning madly like many may want to do is difficult, if not impossible on higher difficulties. Tactical thinking and good old trial and error are your friends.
The game is brutally serious, but has plenty of humor of varying types, everything from walking in on two of your people having sex in the submarine you need to go out on a mission to a rediculous, over the top, amazing birthday party, Wyatt tripping balls on LSD and the entire Hitler sequence...Much of the humor is dark however, which fits the game.
Additionally the developers did a great job crafting a world that feels so... jarring.. Everything looks like 1960s America on the surface, but everything looks, and feels, off, it does a great job of putting you right there and getting a taste of living under a repressive fascist regime.
I could go on and on, but seriously, the game is fantastic, the story is told amazingly and it was worth every penny of the $60 I paid. Buy it now.

Remember Me is one of those games that had incredible potential but squandered it with weak, nonsensical storytelling and broken game design.
At it's core, Remember Me is a linear, story-driven action-adventure game of a sort we don't commonly see anymore. Think Enslaved: Odyssey to the West and you'll have a pretty good idea what you're getting yourself into. Unlike that game though, Remember Me takes place in a cyberpunk future where the world is dependent on devices called Sensen's that monitor and control memories. This along with several global disasters have created a society where memory is entirely controlled by a corporation called Memorize and while the rich are doing fine, the poor are left broken, living in slums and occasionally losing their minds, becoming what the game calls Leapers because reasons.
You play as Nilin, a former rebel who has had her memories erased and now must listen to a mysterious voice in her head telling her what to do. She has the special power to "remix" people's memories, essentially altering details to change the outcome and thus, alter a person's thinking.
While all of this sounds like a pretty great concept, none of it comes together to make any sense at all. Rebels are fighting against memory control but have these Sensens implanted in them anyway? Why? The limitations of these machines aren't ever adequately explained either. The very first cutscene of the game says that it's basically a  big memory backup machine but it becomes very clear, very quickly that people actually lose the memories they backup. So it's really a mass storage? Later, it's implied that the machine acts as a big hive mind and shares everyone's memories with everyone but people constantly talk about how they've forgotten things. So, which is it?
This wouldn't be such a big deal except altering people's memories is the primary form of combat throughout the game as well as a major plot device used several times. Nilin gets a move called Overload very early on that acts as a finisher but that implies that memories are being shoved into someone's brain and overloading it, right? But other times, she takes people's memories and that doesn't seem to affect her at all. Also, does this mean she's shoving her thoughts and memories into someone else? Wouldn't that tell the enemy what she's doing? Wouldn't that mean she forgets what she's doing? Again, never explained. This is only the start of the inconsistencies as the plot gets more and more absurd, sending Nilin into situations with plot holes large enough to jump through.
Not only do the actions not make sense but the themes don't even tie together well. It's not much of a spoiler to say that the theme of the game revolves around memories and how losing them causes us, as a society and individuals, to lose our identity. Yet throughout the game, Nilin "remixes" people's memories almost without hesitation. The slight hesitation she does feel at times doesn't end up ever having any resolution either so the whole story winds up just feeling hypocritical.
The plot's forgiveable though if the gameplay is alright. The game works as a mix of Uncharted-esque parkour sections and combat sections more than a little reminisce of the Arkham series. It becomes formulaic pretty quickly but it isn't too bad for the first half of the game due to the interesting style of customization. Combat works by executing different combos made up of the X and Y buttons (when using an Xbox gamepad which is HIGHLY recommended). The cool bit is that you can actually customize these combos by giving each button press a different effect. You can't change the pattern of X and Y buttons but you can make certain button presses more powerful, decrease your special attack cooldowns and even recover your health. You unlock these different "pressens" by gaining XP. It's a neat little system with a ton of potential. Throw in five special attacks you get throughout the game and even a gun with different abilities and combat can have a lot of variety.
The problem is in how restrictive the combat becomes. At first, the enemies are basic enough where you can freely experiment with your different moves and it's decently fun, if not a bit repetitive after you find your groove. About halfway through the game though, it seems as though they ran out of enemy ideas so they made new baddies that only respond to one specific way of killing them. The worst are enemies that hurt you every time you hit them so you need to hit them with only regenerating pressens or else you'll lose health quickly. As regenerating pressens make your combos weaker, battles become extremely tedious and these enemies show up in very nearly every encounter. Suddenly, all of your customization plans go out the window as the developers force you down a single path.
The parkour sections range from alright to downright boring and tedious as well. The game is extremely linear with only  minor exploration allowed (think Final Fantasy XIII's endless hallway). The developers tried to break up the monotony by sprinkling collectables throughout every level but since the game is almost entirely linear with narrow corridors, these are pretty easy to find if you give even a minor amount of effort.
If you're still reading at this point, you're probably wondering why I haven't discussed remixing memories yet. It's the major marketing piece for the game and is the gimmick that was supposed to be what the game was known for, right? Well, yes, and to be honest, remixing memories was my favorite part of the game. These sections give you access to the persons memory seen as a recording. You cycle through the recording by rotating the joystick, making it feel like you're editing video frame by frame. You have to find certain memory bugs, displayed as visual glitches, which you can than activate to alter the memory slightly. These sections all have an objective so you need to find the specific glitches that will add up to give you the outcome you require. They clearly put a lot of work into these sections as each bug and combination of bugs activated can give you very different outcomes. One particularly memorable one allows you to alter a medical procedure resulting in the death of a variety of people, depending on what you choose to do.
Some people will find these too base as the puzzles themselves aren't that challenging but I appreciated the variety of outcomes and enjoyed seeing the little nuances of each sequence. The biggest problem is that there are only four of these in the entire game and they are all plot determined. That's right, the gimmick that the game was marketed for barely lets you use it and never freely.
Ultimately, Remember Me is a series of great ideas strung together with terrible implementation. Poorly made enemies, extremely linear gameplay, awful writing and a lack of the game's best feature make this a game to pass on.

No.  Lets make all your swings and combos shift for no reason to a guy standing off to your left.  Want to move the camera to look around?  You can, but the game will feel like it's fighting you.  The amount you have to move the mouse to get the same distance of camera movement in any given direction is CONSTANTLY changing with no indication at any time.  At first I thought it was to try to keep the camera pointed in the way I should be going, but that is not always the case, which just adds to the frustration.  It feels like a console port that didn't take keyboard and mouse controls into account at all.  And for the insanely frustrating user interface I have to vote this game down.  The point of a game is entertainment, not frustration and so at its core, while it may tell a good story, it fails to be what a game should be.

But it does what it needs to do with a somewhat decent variance in landscapes.   The gunplay is fun with the ability to mix and match your guns which is a nice change from the previous games. I will say that Wolfenstein II is perhaps not as revolutionary as New Order but it is still a solid game.  I can accept that people had some issues which may have impacted their reponse to it.  But I do think this is a game worthy of your time.

an easy 8-9/10. fans of old-school fast paced FPS as well as the new-school of slower, cover-based shooters will both find plenty to enjoy here. the arsenal provided is unique and feels fresh (dieselkraftwerk i'm looking at you), and the gunplay is on point. there are special gadgets that you earn throughout the game that also enhance your options of how to fight and press onward. one, for example, lets you compress your body to fit into small tunnels and holes, allowing a more stealthy approach. another sends you up about 15 feet into the air on a pair of robotic stilts, which you can use to climb up to higher locations or to give yourself a brief height advantage in a gunfight.
i also really enjoyed the writing, which i felt was well above par for the genre. each nugget of NPC dialog i overheard in passing made nazi-occupied america feel more alive, and i found myself wanting to know more about my revolutionary comrades. the game also embraces the ridiculousness of it's concept and, without spoiling anything, defintiely doesn't take itself too seriously. i appreciated the not-so-subtle jabs at the alt-right and modern day neo-nazis. plus, you get to fight alongside some bonafide communists, anarchists, and stand-ins for the BPP, with none of them being portrayed in a negative light. cool!
even if you dont care about leftist politics, this game is definitely worth playing for the action alone. i think new order is still slightly better, especially for its level design which is one area in which Wolf2 is lacking. that being said, Wolfenstein 2 has earned its place as one of the better action games of the year.

On PC, this is one of the worst releases I’ve experienced. I stayed up on release day, hitting blue screens and corrupted configurations. At that time, nobody had worked out how to get past these issues. So for the love of god, don’t buy Bethesda games on release. Anyway, this is still a positive review. Once I got the game working, it turned out to be a successful followup to the last game.
Just about everything is better in this than last game. It plays exactly the same, but with sharper execution. Wolfenstein The New Order had decent, but kind of simplistic combat. What elevated it above mediocrity was the story and mood. None of those strengths have been lost in The New Colossus. This still isn't quite perfect, but it's a promising step in the right direction.
In The New Colossus, relations between Blazkowicz and other resistance fighters are presented in an unusually warm, human and sentimental manner. Relationships from the previous game have advanced, so people are having babies. They're fighting for the next generation, not just to avenge their lost friends and families. For the first time in Wolfenstein history, the game explores the backstory of B.J. Blazkowicz. I liked how it was handled, as they had this subplot work double duty. It's not just about B.J., it also explains in more depth how the Americans felt when the nazis took over, and how some collaborated with them for their own benefit. These were people who worked hard, didn't see much for their efforts, and were willing to blame their misfortune on the same people as the nazis. For the price of their souls, they could now get ahead. A lot of people, including Bethesda PR, have tried to tie this story to current events. To me it doesn’t feel like the story was conceived with current events in mind. Instead, this feels like a logical continuation of everything that happened last time. And as such, I'm happy with how it turned out. But if you're expecting this to delve deep into how America would accept a nazi dictatorship, this isn't it. I think it worked, but I can see the missed opportunity here. But the way it ends leaves it wide open to a sequel. So maybe next time?
Combat in the last game could be kind of a mess, as if the result of poor communication in the team. You can tell from how levels are designed how you’re supposed to play a game. In The New Order, combat arenas could either be a series of office corridors where enemies clustered in rows to be mowed down. Or the arenas would be more open like a stealth game, with multiple ways to approach and room to run around and experiment. The problem with the more open arenas was that enemies used hit scan weapons. This was coupled with mediocre sound design, that made all guns sound kind of soft and vague, especially at a distance. This made it easy to lose a lot of health without knowing where the damage was coming from. It encouraged a kind of play where you sat in one spot and waited for enemies to run at you so you could pick them off as they rounded the corner. I’m not sure if I missed something about how you were supposed to play the game. To me, it felt more like I tried to engage with the levels like how they looked like they were supposed to be played, and the game rewarded me with instant death, so I reverted to cheesing the enemy so I could just get on with the story.
Now in the sequel, most of my problems with combat have been fixed. For the majority of the game, I felt like I could play it the way it was “supposed” to be played. Or at least it felt like I was able to understand some kind of designer intent, act on that, and not be smacked across the face. What they’ve done in this game is add more delay between when an enemy sees you, and how quickly they can raise their guns and start shooting. This is especially true for bigger enemies, which were particularly dubious in design last time. The movement in the game emphasizes forward momentum. You move MUCH faster straight ahead than you do side to side or backward. Clear emphasis is put on aggressively moving toward the enemy and blasting them with everything you got. And if things go bad, you can move in the opposite direction at probably 2x the speed enemies run.
I replayed a bit of The New Order a few weeks ago and was reminded of how weak and diffuse the sound design was. None of the weapons packed a proper punch, almost as if it was the explicit intent of the sound designers to make it kind and gentle on the ears. This soft character made it a non-fatiguing game to play for long stretches because nothing grated at your senses. But it felt wrong. It needed more edge and intensity. The soft character is still present in The New Colossus, but they’ve made significant improvements across the board. To hear everything this game has to offer, you’ll need to crank up the volume quite a bit. Then you’ll notice it has a nice multilayered ambient sound design, with tons of attention to detail in each environment. Guns sound more convincing now, and the wide dynamic range allows the game to retain a great sense of clarity and airiness even during the most chaotic mayhem. It isn’t perfect, as guns still drop in volume too fast when they’re a distance away from you. This makes it possible for enemies to be hitting you without you being able to tell where they’re coming from. But overall, this is a big improvement.
The only problem they’ve introduced in this sequel is that it’s often hard to tell where to go once you’ve won a combat encounter. Over and over again I found myself running around empty combat arenas trying to figure out where I was supposed to go. The game has a waypoint marker system, but you need to enable it manually. Ever since waypoint markers were introduced in games it’s been a worry that designers would stop designing levels properly and rely on the UI to direct players in the intended direction. And that’s how it feels here. I’m glad you have to activate the waypoint marker yourself each time. This makes the UI unusually decluttered for a modern game and made my eyes scan environments differently. Waypoint markers cause tunnel vision, and because it’s an overlay, it directly obscures the graphics beneath it. But they somehow managed to make a game here with the worst of both worlds. Level design that requires waypoint markers, and then disabling them by default.
It’s refreshing how old school The New Colossus feels. It's like the developers were allowed to shut the door to the rest of the world and only focus on improving the last game, with no compromises for the sake of modernity. But I wish they had been more ambitious. It's an iterative sequel, with meaningful improvements across the board. But it's not a benchmark title. There are so few good singleplayer FPS made these days. This might be the only one released in all of 2017? That makes Wolfenstein II an easy recommendation, despite my reservations. Do you want to play a new FPS that isn’t multiplayer focused? This is it. It’s good. And it’s all we got.

I was very hyped to play Remember Me. I recall back when I saw release trailers of this game, and wanted to buy it since (sadly I had a very old PC and couldn't run it). When I did buy it, it is sad to say that it did not live up to the hype I heard about it. It has been a while since I have played it, but I thought since I completed it I should write a review. I apologize for any spoilers I may reveal.
Pros:
- As far as graphics go, Remember me is a beautiful game through and through. From simple parts of the game such as running through an area, or in one of the interactive Remix cutscenes, this game left a great impression on me.
- The way you traverse the levels by jumping acrossed obstacles or climbing structures was brilliant.
- The combat system was simple, yet not gamebreaking. While you can buy the combo lab DLC (like I did) and easily cheese most enemies in the game, the vanilla game's combat was just relaxing enough to not overly stress me, but just difficult enough that I couldn't just rely on using the same strategy on every enemy.
- The game mixed up enemy behavior and weaknesses just enough that every combat sequence had to actually be thought out, and new enemies would spawn mid sequence that forced you to switch tactics (for example, the enemies that crawled on walls and shot at you forced you to use ranged attacks to defeat them, while melee enemies still attacked you).
- The story was very gripping for the most part, and even with the limited time there is to play the game (more on that later) the main character's story is still gripping enough to want you to know what happens next in the plot (the ending not so much though).
I do not want to take away from the pros of this game. However, there are, in my opinion, major cons that make me lean towards not recommending this game to others.
Cons:
- First and foremost, this game was really short. The plot left a story that had so much more room for exploration, and the Remix sections of the game were unique in a way that I haven't really seen before or since. However, after 10 hours of gameplay, I just couldn't continue to play. I feel like the ending of the game was rushed, and then left on a cliffhanger (as many plot points seemed forgotten and unfinished after the final boss).
- The Remix system was beautiful, but glitched or bugged out constantly. I was repeatedly looking for an item to interact with, just to find that it wouldn't respond to my tampering, regardless of how many times I rewind to the beginning or restarted the game all together. While the first remix was the one that had the most problems, it was also the most frustrating. Constantly freezing in the middle of a cutscene so important to the main story is a real bummer.
- With the 99 cent DLC package ( I bought on a Christmas sale: price is initially $3.99), combat becomes way too broken. The attacks learned take up the same slots (I.E. X or Y) and can be placed almost anywhere in a combo sequence. However, they do a noticeably higher amount of damage at almost the same speed as a regular jab or kick (even the dragon uppercut somehow was on par with speed, even with the theatrics).
- While it could have been a major joke that went over my head, the Spammer lives up to its name a bit too well. You can literally just run around blasting people in the face until they inevitably die. While it is super weak and takes quite a bit to kill many of the stronger enemies, it is the definition of a cheese weapon. Just run or jump around the arena and shoot the enemy, wait for it to recharge (the recharge time was really fast as well) , and repeat. Along with the built in health recovery system this game has already, it makes you pretty much invincible if you don't feel confident in a hand to hand confrontation (or taking on a large group of enemies).
- I followed the whole story, yet the final boss, in my opinion, makes no sense as to why it is even there. The whole time the story is about the family of the main character, and about those that their influence has effected. Instead of confronting some sort of political figure or person of importance from your past, you fight a giant robot in a virtual reality-like simulation. You defeat the giant robot, and then... game over. It really seems random in a game about political and economic power.
+++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
All in all, I give Remember me a 7/10. I only say "NO" to a recommendation because there is no "MAYBE" option. I wouldn't buy this game unless it goes on sale.

THE GAME
The game is a fighting game with a linear story. Most of the game is basically jumping and moving around to the next destination. -	Graphics /  level Design : The city known as NEO- Paris is stunningly beautiful and well designed
-	Story: The story is somewhat interesting. However, I do feel that it left a lot of plot holes by the end of the game.
-	Gameplay: Different enemy variations and a somewhat good combo mechanic make each fighting section enjoyable.
-	Audio: The best part of the game is the music.
Cons
-	Action / Character development: Most of the characters in the game with the exception of the main character are not well developed.  Also, the voice acting of most of the characters could have been a little better. However, the acting is not too bad.
-	Customization system:  The player can only customize what each hit, button press, of the combo does. Everything else is already determined.
-	No exploration: There is no exploration what so ever. You have one route to follow and that is it.

Drawing inspiration from such blockbusters as Big Rigs: Over the Road Racing and Jurassic Park: Trespasser, elecorn presents to you his magnum opus, Caster. In Caster, you follow the legend of a young boy (or a feminine frame boy), his face tragically crippled at birth by low poly counts, fighting against an unknown alien threat known as FLANX, determined to sit there and do nothing or walk at innocent humans in straight lines as they go about their day. To defeat such a menacing threat our hero is granted the power of super speed and must fly through rin- I mean collect orbs of power, granting him powers such as running up vertical walls, jumping so high he crosses the entire level, and homing missiles that _very_ accurately track their enemies.
The game also features a myriad of references to previous grand slam titles often overlooked by the casual gamer. The ♥♥♥♥♥♥ graphics are a reference to Final Fantasy 7, one of elecom's favorite games when he was 5. The physics reference legendary racer Big Rigs, with the ability to instantly stop while running 172839127 mph. And of course, who could forget the large number of bullets and badly drawn characters, clearly a reference to ZUN and Touhou.
Caster's main strength is in its simplicity and accessibility. With levels lasting between 3 seconds and 2 minutes, you don't have to worry about a commitment when you sit down; you can simply play! The controls are very intuitive; some may critcize the heavy mouse acceleration, but it's by design so that all players, newbies and pros alike, have equal trouble aiming and controlling their character ensuring a balanced experience no matter who's playing.
However, no matter the level of quality of a game there are always a few negative points, and Caster is no exception... one of them being that there are some issues with the PC port of this game. In the optimization process from Linux to Windows and Mac, a large amount of autism was left in. I for one cannot stand for excess autism in my games, and so I cannot ignore this sloppy port job, no matter the quality of the actual game. Further, in his rush to get the game out for the holidays (a goal which he ultimately failed at, thanks to Steam wrongfully delaying his game in their rigorous review process), elecom unfortunately left the game unfinished. Not in the traditional way though, where devs don't have time to add their layer of polish, but actually unfinished. When you attempt to enter the final level you are given a "To Be Continued" screen. What's there is golden, but what COULD have been there could have been so much more...  It's a real shame elecom didn't get to finish his title, as it would have been a good nominee for game of the year.
In the end Caster will be put on the long list of visionary video games tragically cut short by time and budget constraints, dreams brought down by the crushing reality of checkbooks and deadlines. Do yourself a favor and pick up elecom's game. For only 99 cents, you can't really go wrong. You don't need supersize fries anyway. I give this game a 7/10.
