First of all, Remember Me explores an interesting concept of controlling, remixing or deleting
memories that is available for anyone in the society. While at first, the user opens up to a glorious image of individuals being able to share their memories together, or being able to store the memories forever, there is a much darker side to the entire concept that is displayed throughout the events of the game. During the story, the player also explores the concepts of identity that is tied to our memories, as well as the conseqeunces of tampering with memories. The story itself isn't bad, it has its moments, and actually manages to pull off a few nice twists and turns. However, its downside is the horrible pacing of the game. Remember Me feels very slow and at times it can even be called boring. On the flipside, the latter parts of the game lift the story up a notch, but unfortunately the pacing still continues being an issue.
The combat within the game is unfortunately a pretty undeveloped concept. It revolves around mixing and matching different moves to create combos, unfortunately there are only four combos which ultimately makes this system too simple to actually make the combat worth remembering. Furthermore, the enemies are also very predictable and there really aren't any segments of the game that really challenge the player in regards to the combat. The game also features a large portion of climbing sequences which use a simplfied climbing system that  can be seen in almost any adventure game that came out within the last 10 years.
The high point of the gameplay is the amazing design of Neo-Paris and its inhabitants that the user can explore, it is a feast for the eyes and any fan of cyberpunk should enjoy inspecting it.
Overall, I think Remember Me is a good game, but with many ideas that could be further developed and explored. If you manage to persist through the uneven pacing and the somewhat uninspired combat system you may find yourself enjoying Neo-Paris and Nilin's story.

Remember Me is an interesting story based around a classic SF premise; unfortunately, the gameplay is wretched. The demo I'd played led me to believe that I'd be spending most of my time going into people's memories and changing them, but across 8 chapters, you only get to do so 4 times. The bulk of the game is spent running around and fighting.
While navigating the landscape's numerous ledges, ladders and landings is fun, the game constantly stops you for overly-long combat sequences; in a game where your main character is so mobile, it would have been nice to have the option to avoid some of the combats by taking alternate routes. The combat is theoretically made easier by the inclusion of customizable attack combos, but the timing on them is so fiddly that using any but the simplest one is extremely iffy; often you'll get three hits into a combo before the engine decides that you were trying to perform an entirely different combo and starts you over. There are also special abilities that allow you to deal massive damage, stun enemies, perform instant kills, or turn certain types of enemies against the rest, but using them requires you to perform combos to power up your special meter. This gets more aggravating later on when you encounter enemies that damage you when you attack them; you can instant-kill them with the aforementioned special move, but if you encounter multiples of this enemy, you'll have to take a lot of damage while hitting them to build up your meter and reduce your cooldown timers. Boss fights last an unforgivably long time, requiring you to fight off wave after wave of basic enemies so you can use your special move and actually attack the boss. By the time I'd reached the final boss fight, I'd had enough of the combat and decided to watch the ending on Youtube instead, which I'd recommend over playing the game.
I will give Remember Me credit for one thing, though: It's nice to see a game starring a biracial character, though I didn't realize she was one until around 2/3 through the story.

Remember Me is a very cool world, such a cool world that if you are into sci-fi Earth, you should buy it for the story / world-building alone: it's worth it.
Where this game falls short is the outdated controls / mechanics / boss fights. The camera whips around erratically during combat, like it's early Silent Hill or something - or the really early Tekken / MK transitions into 3D survival modes: where someone is doing a flying kick at you, but you have no idea because the camera is very fascinated with a poster on the wall. Quick Time Events were a brilliant idea a decade ago, that were horrible in practice - and this game incorporates them into boss fights: so that's a mess.
With that said, Nihil is an interesting character, Neo-Paris is awesome and gorgeous, and the story is fun. If this had a stealth option like Deus Ex (so that I could avoid all the unenjoyable combat elements) - I'd be in love. Play it for the sci-fi - worth it ;)

So, to start with the most important bit, I have encountered several bugs and technical issues since the launch of the game that patches have yet to fix. First and foremost,
! This has made progressing through the game impossibly frustrating as there's always a large chance that at the end of a level, after defeating whatever final challenge was presented, I have to force-close the game through the task manager and relaunch, resuming from the checkpoint before the fight. This is compounded by the side-missions in which you revisit previous levels of the game to assassinate special commanders. It's almost guaranteed I need to make three or more attempts
. The frustration from this is enough to warrant refunding the game had I not purchased it through Green Man Gaming.
Beyond that, there was an issue with texture streaming where about half the time it would break and stop streaming in high-resolution textures, leaving characters, props, and the world as a low resolution, blurry mess. A far more minor but still valid complaint is that, at some point in the campaign, ammunition broke for one of the weapons and allowed me to infinitely pick up that type of ammunition even though I was already at the cap for it.
As for the game itself, it's a mixed bag. The shooting that
executed so well is back for the most part. It's still tight and weapons feel powerful, but unfortunately, the encounters don't really lend themselves as well to the gunplay this time around. The level design is fairly open, even in the corridor or interior environments. The enemies don't seek cover as much as in the first game and mindlessly charge you. They are also far less resilient, meaning encounters are short and you never feel challenged beyond the occasional times you get caught out and an enemy nukes your health and armor. The level design is just so far below what was offered in the previous title that, aside from seeing new and interesting locations, the game just doesn't play very well. They've also shoehorned in some elements that fail to impress or merit inclusion. You get a few special gadgets that attempt to open up the levels in a manner similar to Arkane (
,
) but the very limited level design and linear encounters aren't enough to make use of them and then end up being an excessive inclusion. Then, there're special missions that you can undertake to revisit past levels to assassinate high ranking commanders of the Nazi regime. These don't offer anything rewarding beyond the ability to revisit places you've already gone to and collect things you've missed, and ultimately they could have gone without, especially since to access them you have to take part in a boring minigame that has no reason to exist.
The story, on the other hand, is mostly of the same quality. It's a pulp comic/dime novel in video game form, and a lot of the game manages to pull off the overly serious and dramatic tone that
did so well. Towards the halfway point of the game, however, it starts feeling shaky and going off the rails. The game has a tone problem, in which is alternates from its serious, bleak themes to almost slapstick comedy that fails to entertain.
Overall,
is a highly disappointing sequel to what was arguably the start of the old school shooter revival. When the first title came out it was a pleasant surprise that left people thinking, "That was
better than anything called Wolfenstein should have been!" But, and this could be attributed to marketing hype and having to live up to inflated expectations, this game just doesn't live up to the first and shows what happens when you change a winning formula.

So, I was more than pleased when I found this little gem. It's amazing how unique and promising this game is opposed to the other.
Plot: A strange and horrific shadow is washing over Great Britain in full force. Cities have been ravished by otherworldly beasts, people have been melded into twisted shells of their previous selves, and in just three days, the country will fall… then the world. All mighty gods known as The Ancients are behind this mayhem, but it’s the player’s job to find out who’s to blame and banish them. You will travel from city to city, all across the UK in search of clues, answers, and knowledge.
As I mentioned before, The Consuming shadow really is its own game, and I doubt you can mistake it for another. Gameplay is rather straight forward, but it works great. You’ve got a plethora of items to find and collect, multiple ammo types, spells to master and more. Dungeons are grid based, and each one has its own objective. This may vary from securing an occult text, finding a missing person, destroying monster nests etc. And let me tell you, this game can be tough, and you will die. Monsters deal vicious damage and conserving ammo is not as easy as you might think. Driving also plays a big role in The Consuming Shadow. Driving from location to location takes time, so it’s important to set a predetermined path as to save every precious hour. But there’s a good chance you’ll bump into random events along the way. You’re usually given two choices to make, and more often than not, my decisions resulted in negative outcomes, like the loss of some health or sanity. There isn’t any pattern behind these events and making the right choice is based purely on luck.
There’s also a sanity meter that must be kept healthy. The madder you become, the more difficult the game is. But, unlike most games in the genera, dying isn’t a total lost. XP is still earned and built up through multiple playthroughs, and each time a player levels up, they’re given an array of buffs before they start their next run.
Now, this is where a complaint of mine comes in. The max level is ten, and if you were to spend all ten of your buffs on health and sanity increases, it makes the game a bit underwhelming. If I’m sporting 456 health, it’s gonna take A LOT to kill me. It also makes your first bunch of playthroughs damn-near impossible, seeing as how you start off with such low stats.
But apart from that… there really isn’t much to complain about, here. The Consuming Shadows accomplishes what it aims to do with flying stars, and apart from a couple gripes, I’d say it’s definitely worth your money.

Here's another one of the ingenious games by Ben 'Yahtzee' Croshaw of "Zero Punctuation" fame. His most notable games are the four games which encompass the so-called "Chzo Mythos Games" quadrilogy of point & click adventure games: "5 Days a Stranger" (2003), "7 Days a Skeptic" (2004), "Trilby's Notes" (2006) and "6 Days a Sacrifice" (2007). While all of these games are really great, I consider "Trilby's Notes" one of the best adventure games of all time. The story alone, interspersed by brilliant flashback sequences, is an amazing experience nobody should pass up. The 2007 puzzle platformer "Trilby: The Art of Theft" featured the protagonist of the Chzo Mythos Games: Trilby, the cat burglar - a character somewhat reminiscent of Garrett from the "Thief" trilogy. The game is a bit like the 2013 game "Gunpoint", however a bit less action-oriented and with a slower pace.
Now, "The Consuming Shadow" is another game which is set in the Chzo Mythos universe, but it's something completely different. This game is a roguelike variant in which an ancient god is about to invade our world. The game mechanics are very exciting and remind a bit of "The Organ Trail" (which was a zombie-themed remake of the classic education game "The Oregon Trail").
You drive around in your car (in "cockpit" perspective), choose your destination on a map and drive from town to town. (Every once in a while, various people also send you text messages on your phone.) Each town is either okay, which means you can stock up on medicine or ammo, or it is threatened by evil forces, so you have to solve the residents' problems. This is done by entering a location in a sidescrolling manner, explore it, finish a certain task and gather supplies, items and information about the ancient gods. These pieces of information can be collected in a notebook, so that you can attribute a specific color, rune, nature and intention to a specific god, figuring out which is the god that's planning to invade our world. This extensive road trip has a final destination, too: Stonehenge, where you can perform a ritual to end the threat once and for all.
Being a roguelike game, The Consuming Shadow doesn't allow saving and loading. However, each time you die, you get a certain amount of points which result in a rating and, better yet, so-called "birth stars" which function like traits or skills you can use when you start a new game. You get, for example, more health points, more sanity points, better lockpicking, a faster car, and some other advantages. This way it doesn't feel like your previous sessions were pointless, but instead serving as a great foundation for your next run. You'll keep coming back for a different approach over and over again (at least that's why I never get bored playing the game).
All in all, I wholeheartedly recommend buying this game. I got the Insanity Edition from the Humble Store, which also includes Yahtzee's novels "Mogworld" and "Jam" as digital downloads. Go get it! It's WELL worth the asking price!

I've already put quite a bit of time into the Humble Store version of this game and I have just recently claimed my Steam Key; so I am checking out all the new features, but I will bring you up to speed on what I already know about this game.
The Consuming Shadow is a roguelike RPG much in the vein of FTL, with the overall goal of the game being stopping a Cthulhu-esque entity (simply called 'the Ancient')  from invading our world. This is done in both of the primary 'game modes' The Consuming Shadow features. The first is the overworld map, where you pick a town on your GPS and drive there via your very slow car to look for clues. Various 'text-only' events can happen both here and in the towns, where you will have to make a choice. These choices like FTL, can give you bonuses to your cash or equipment, or screw you over royally. There are often pieces of equipment you can use to sway these events in your favor, much like FTL.
The meat of your clue-finding will be done in the dungeon crawling sections however, where you enter a 2D side-scrolling section to kill monsters, open locked doors and scavenge chests. It is worth noting that while the keyboard controls function okay here, I found a PS3 or 360 pad is vastly superior. The keyboard controls remind me something of playing Resident Evil on a PS1 emulator, where your hands are spread thin across the keyboard. Speaking of Resident Evil, monsters are plentiful and ammo/health is scarce. You will have to wisely manage your bullets and learn how to melee attack most of the enemies to do well; running from encounters is NOT advisable, as you will take a penalty to your sanity for doing so.
The goal of each dungeon is to find a clue that will help you stop the Ancient, and ultimately you will need two things to win the game: A four-part Banishment Spell and the rune of the invading Ancient. The Banishment Spell is quite easy to attain, but finding the rune of the invading Ancient is tricky. You will need to use logical inferance and vague clues to figure out who is invading, who isn't invading, who is the God of what and so on. This is the funnest part of the game for me, as it balances the action elements with a fair bit of brain-teasing. The Ancient who is invading and what his rune is random on each playthrough too, so don't bother trying to reuse anything for a new run.
There are also a total of four different characters to play as, and unlocking them depends on a good deal of RNG unfortunately, but it's a wonderful way to mix things up. There are also some ties into Yahtzee's other games (Trilby and Chzo) but I haven't touched those yet, so I can't tell you if they are significant.
Overall the Steam version is the same game (duh), it essentially just adds in some extra monsters and challenge modes if you find the main game to be getting stale. None of my complaints about the original game have been addressed; the visuals on some simple things (like your GPS) can be improved, and there should be more backgrounds for the 'text-only' events that happen on the road and in town.
None of this detracts from the gameplay though; if you enjoy Lovecraftian horror, light action and puzzle solving this game will keep you distracted for quite a while.

I'm creating a negative rating to ensure the game stays overall at "very positive," which is how I'd rate this game.  Steam doesn't allow anything other than yes/no, so fault Steam, not me.
The game does so much right that it disappoints me that it couldn't go all the way. Here are the nit-picks:
The game has absolutely beautiful graphics... which make it downright annoying to dodge certain enemy projectiles, and which make it challenging to distinguish foreground from background. Eventually you don't have to be significantly concerned about them, but the emphasis on visual effects does result in gameplay issues.
The soundtrack is brilliant, so much so that I purchased it separately.  The voice acting isn't in English, which may be part of the reason I didn't find the story compelling at all.  I'm a parent, so you'd figure that the story would resonate with me.  But, it didn't.  It seemed a bit artificial, and perhaps alien, somehow.  YMMV, but I'd wager the positive reviews claiming you'd need tissues are all hype.
Combat is... different.  You have a couple abilties which can be used to defeat different enemies.  The enemies are cute and generally enjoyable.  However, the entirety of combat is unsatisfying.  There are no real boss battles.  Combat, and enemies as a whole, are there to either interfere with your platforming needs (e.g., jumping from platform to platform) or to facilitate your platforming needs (e.g., using your skill to use their projectiles to jump to the next platform).  Aside from these two "features," there's no need for enemies to exist in this game.  The real "enemy" is your environment, replete with one-shot-kills.
The gameplay is responsive, interesting, and verstile.  Your character feels nimble, agile, and responsive.  It's completely enjoyable to move around in the world.  But, my *biggest* issue is that this game turns into (devolves into?) a Super Meat Boy clone in many ways.  Heck, there's even a SMB easter egg.  You have a life bar--you can get something like 15 life bars/points, but for much of the game the amount is entirely pointless.  The game is replete--chock-full to bursting--with one-shot-kills.  The first time you face certain obstacles, it's impossible to know if it will damage you or kill you outright.  Some spikes are insta-kill; some are not.  Same for lava.  Same for a thousand other things.  Eventually, you can force-save enough that it becomes merely a tedious process of learning the right patterns and timing for button presses, but that also leads to impatience which leads to more untimely deaths.  That says nothing about the three gauntlets the game has.  Many people complain about the first gauntlet, and I agree, that has to be the absolute worst.  It will crush casual players.  The third gauntlet isn't much better, though.  There is some serious challenge here; this isn't a game for the casual player.
If you're a hardcore, SMB platforming fan, go for it.  If you're looking for a good story and/or a casual game, maybe try for something else.  If you're a fan of the soundtrack, buy it separately.

This is effectively a short story that nevertheless manages to endear itself to the audience in a short span of time.  Clearly a labour of love, Palinurus is both introspective and philosophical.  Treat it as a literary work rather than a technical or flashy display of computer graphics and video gaming, and you would be rewarded with a good read and a special something that strikes an emotional chord deep within.
I would highly recommend interested readers to find the time (1 ~ 2 hrs) to immerse themselves in it from beginning to end.

Palinurus is a kinetic visual novel (that is, there are no choices) about a Passenger on a ship with an AI voyage companion named Budapest.  The story prompt seems simple on paper, but what distinguishes this simple concept from other simple VN concepts is that the quality of writing and storytelling in this VN in particular is exceptional.  Perhaps to make this more impressive is knowing that the main part of the writing was done in a month for NaNoRenO.
As a brief aside to the music and art quality of the game, I would like to say that both are adequate.  I found the music overall to be rather mundane, but there are a few pieces that, in my opinion, fit excellently with the mood of the setting and enhanced the reading experience.  Likewise, the art quality would from time to time switch from mediocre to cute and pretty, but felt somewhat inconsistent, and sometimes unfitting to the mood.  Overall, I would say the music and art were supplements to otherwise exceptional writing.
When I say the writing is exceptional, I don't mean to say "exceptional for a VN writer in particular," but exceptional in the sense that someone (though, there were multiple writers) with a firm control of English rhetoric and emotional storytelling wrote it.  The short story is filled with humor and serious moments that flow naturally and realistically.  At points in their space-travelling, the Passenger and Budapest would frequently tease each other in the same way friends (or perhaps a romantic couple) might, and it feels quite heartwarming and funny to watch the frivolity.  These brief intermissions of happiness, in my opinion, do well in emphasizing the dramatic moments of the game, which feel very heartfelt.  You feel a sense of identity in the deuteragonists of the story and it's easy to form an emotional connection to both of them.  This is the mark of a story largely written by a skilled contemporary writer in the making.
As a brief digression on the emotional impact of the game; even the main develop of Renpy made a comment on his Twitter of the game's sentimentality:
The game is not too long, perhaps an hour's length - shorter if you're a quick reader.  I've refrained from detailing any specific plot points at the risk of making them less dramatic or humorous.  It's a VN that's well worth your time, and I hope will at least make you ruminate about the themes in the game, which are fairly straightforward but otherwise thought-provoking.  It is certainly a beautifully-written game and, I should hope, can become a standard for proficiently written VN's in the future.

Remember those old video arcades? Shops where you had arcade games, pinball machines and so on? And how brutally punishing these games were and how you had to pay for new lifes? Just to try to advance another few seconds into the game before you got wiped out again? That's exactly how Teria plays (except reloading after each death is free).
Monsters spawn behind or inside you and kill you in less than a second. If one enemy spawn-blindsides you, it's survivable, but often enough they double up, basically insta-killing you. So "playing" this game means learning the levels by heart in very small steps, while permanently dying and reloading. Your first weapon seems to have a very short range. So enjoy figuring out how close you have to let those melee dogs come before you can shoot them. Killing monsters triggers new monsters to spawn. Some monsters spawn as just a radar blip and appear only if you step into the correct zone. Wanna pick up that magazine lying on the floor but there is a radar blip right on top of it? Better find a different place to trigger that dog to actually appear, because of course it will appear right inside you if you simply go to the magazine. That's how the whole game plays (not sure if I have seen the whole thing: the dog section, the rifle bots section, the mixed section. The outside section with the dogs, not sure how to survive that).
The game has a few more problems which "add" to the fun: You tend to get stuck while moving close to furniture. You pick up health packs even when you are at full health.
Recommended for people who love brutally difficult egoshooters and learning attack patterns by heart.
Everybody else stay far, far away.

The developers are creating the games engine with a set of easily accessible tools the will enable gamers to easily become modders. They are not just trying to make a game they are trying to build a community of modders that can easily create their own material. I very much respect this view and am excited to see what they come up with. So why should I believe what the developers say?, after all we live in a time EA fever and so many fail to deliver on their grand claims. Well the only reason I have any faith in this company is the willingness of the devs to "throw themselves to the wolfs" so to speak. Any developer that can't or isn't able to deliver usually slowly stops the updating then kind of fades away to rarely be herd from until the game is released with a slimey Plop!. These guys seem to be continuously prodding the community for involvement even when the reactions are hostile!. They have not faded out into the background but seem to be very open about what their goals are as far as development of the game. To me they are holding firm on their vision. Will it work out? IDK! It really depends on how good of a game TUG is when it is released. If it still sucks then no one will want to play it. If no one is playing it then nobody will want to mod for it no matter how good the tools are. If they really put in the effort to create a solid well thought out game then it has a chance. I saw a preview for Remember Me showing off the memory-altering gameplay a few years ago. The game looked fascinating, but I don't think it garnered much attention as I never heard about it actually getting released. I picked it up during the Capcom sale (2015/05) and see it in the summer sale now, so I thought I'd give it some of the love it deserves.
The game has a few similarities to Mirror's Edge, which I loved, but there are also some key differences. Both games have you running/jumping/climbing around a future dystopia, but while ME's setting is pristine and sterile Remember Me takes place in a dirty, gritty, Blade Runnery Neo-Paris. Navigating the levels is fairly linear and you're fairly limited in your capabilities. There's also a lot of emphasis on unarmed combat, which I found very opaque to start with but makes more sense as more combo possibilities are unlocked. The first few fights feel like a chore, and the boss fights have some QTEs I don't really care for, but the combat feels very good once it all comes together.
The main thing I dislike about the game is the camera, which I found generally awkward. When it's in a fixed location you'll wish you could point it elsewhere; when you have control of it you'll wish you didn't. During combat, sometimes it feels like you're fighting the camera more than the mooks.
The highlight of Remember Me is the aforemention "memory remixes." You rewind and fast forward through a scene in your target's mind, altering certain elements one way or another until you achieve the desired result. It's trial and error to find the right combination, but seeing all the different outcomes makes the 'error' part not feel so punishing. I was surprised to find these sequences actually comprise a very small portion of the gameplay -- fortunately the rest of the game holds up.
Remember Me looks great, has some fantastic music, and does some good storytelling with some unique mechanics. If you think it sounds even remotely interesting, it's worth picking up on sale.

This is one of the most thought-provoking games I've ever played, and the experience will be lost on you if you don't go into it reminding yourself that this is a story about psychosis. If you have any experience with psychosis (or even mental health issues in general) the voices are likely to make you uncomfortable at times, but this adds to the experience more than it makes it difficult to play. It is worth stating here though that this is not a game to play if you value mechanics and variety above story telling and atmosphere. The visuals are impressive for a game produced by a non-AAA studio, the sound is effective and I only encountered one bug in the whole game which meant I had to reload the save file. I played the game with and without headphones, and whilst the game can be enjoyed without them, the added directional element adds to the effect of the voices (and also helps in certain battles).
The combat mechanics are somewhat basic and repetitive, especially during the first couple of hours, and whilst this isn't expanded on much more than addding different types of enemies in increasing numbers, the fights are not supposed to be the focal point. I was fine with the 'block/dodge -> counter' formula, although I would have appreciated it if changing target were a little more fluid, especially later in the game. The boss fights do provide reasonable changes from the usual battles though.
The puzzle formats can also feel a little repetitive, and whilst the nature of them never changes, the game does find ways to add variety later on. The runes dotted throughout the game provide interesting tidbits from Norse mythology; it will depend on whether or not you find them interesting as to how much effort you put into seeking them out.
Generally, the game spends the first couple of hours letting you learn the ropes, and then mixes things up a bit. Your enjoyment of it will ultimately depend on how much you manage to connect with it in those first couple of hours, as to whether you have the staying power to get to the end. If you do, you'll experience a game which may be a little paint-by-numbers, but gets you thinking a lot about mental health. I'm still not entirely sure what was real, and what was in her mind, and that keeps me thinking and is one of the reasons I won't forget it in a hurry.

To the Moon costs $9.99 at full price. Some people may say, "Wait for a sale." Well... I have something to say about that...

They could have charged full price ($59.99) for this game and it would still be more than worth it in my opinion.

Invisible Apartment Zero is an interesting peice.  As a prequel to the Invisible Apartment game, once again we are in the shoes of Kasey, a young hacker in a light cyberpunk setting, as her hacking leads leads her to find out things some would rather she didn't uncover.
Before I say anything else, if you haven't played the original Invisible Apartment, it is on steam, and it is -free-.  I would recommend playing that game first, as it establishes the protagonist well and my review is aimed at those who have already played the free chapter.
Mechanically, Zero is identical to its free counterpart. The quicksave button won't give you feedback on whether the quicksave worked or not, so, as with the other installment, clicking MENU in order to manually save is your best bet. I also found that sometimes my clicks wouldn't register in the game, though that also happened with the other chapter and it's possible that it's on my end rather than a game issue.
I was also a bit frustrated with some of the failure states, as some of the choices, from my experience at least, seemed similar enough that discerning the correct option was less about deduction and more about guess and check.  Additionally, your choices might lead you to a few small differences in events, but the major structure of the story won't budge from your input.  To me this isn't much of an issue, but I imagine it could be frustrating to some.
The soundtrack is solid, mostly ambient tones to fit the game, but I thought they worked well.  (As a side note I have no idea where to find the soundtrack on the game's website, and if they have officially posted it somewhere I don't know where that would be.) The artwork is also fitting of the game's tone, and the art style is well represented by the screenshots on the store page. Whether you like the artwork or not is rather subjective so there isn't much to say, other than I appreciated it.
Zero is not a long game, as I beat it in about an hour.  While I like the character of Kasey and enjoyed the game myself, I don't really see myself picking it up for another playthrough anytime soon. Like I said before, the story won't change much from your choices (as far as I can tell,) so i don't see a ton of value in going back and trying to see what few bits I missed.
A six dollar price tag isn't huge by any stretch, but for the length of an hour it might not be what everyone is willing to shell out. I personally thought it was worth the money to see a younger and less confident version of Kasey, but to each their own.
tldr: Hesitant Recommendation.  If you wanted to know more about Kasey's character and appreciated the (FREE) original game then Zero complements the other chapter well. That said, the different story and slightly longer length are the only real changes to the game from the first installment; so if you took some issues with the scope of choice or other aspects of design in the original, then you'll find them here as well.
It was short, but I enjoyed the first game for it's story and protagonist, so it's no real suprise I enjoyed this prequel chapter as well.

This game is not for the faint of heart or easily frustrated. You will die over and over again, It's entirely possible to have 'lost' a playthrough in the first 5 minutes. However, every playthrough grants you a greater understanding of what you need to accomplish and how you are going to do it. The 'Birth Star' or levelling system allows you to customise a characters skills and abillities before a game even starts. Each character is different, with their own playstyles, endings, backstories, pros and cons.
You'll also find yourself in some very uncomfortable situation as you traverse England and Wales in the days leading up to the apocalypse. Do you attempt to save a child from a burning car, injuring yourself? Do you leave your car to join a congregation, only to find that they are minions of the very evil you are trying to banish?
My one nitpick is that the randomness of events,encounters and resource avaliabillity can often lead to certain tasks becoming nigh impossible to complete. It can lead to some frustration but overall it hardly detracts from the overall experience.
If you enjoy rougelikes, Lovecraftian horror and a rich atmosphere and world, you owe it to yourself to pick up this game.

Pros:
1. Great atmosphere, music and sound effects.
2. Using sillouettes rather than actual pictures for sprites makes you imagine what the horrors look like, which makes it much more tense.
3. Driving from town to town builds on feelings of isolation and urgency, adding to the theme of the game.
4. It is incredibly replayable, even with different characters.
Cons:
1. The animation is incredibly stiff. I know I shouldn't dock it points but Yahtzee said two sprites make up the characer; the body and the legs, and it shows.
2. The game is incredibly unforgiving, though this is a small complaint since you are going up against a supernatural force. The odds are indeed stacked against you.
3. Notes and dialog tend to repeat after ten plays or so, even if it is wonderfully written.
In all honesty, buy this game and play it. It's worth the money.

Assassin's Creed is a rather enjoyable game. It has a pretty cool concept, the story is quite alright and free-running from rooftop to rooftop is extremely fun. You really feel like a skilled assassin when you are playing the game, at least for the most part. It gets harder and harder towards the end to dodge enemies and to make sure you're not discovered, but that's to be expected. You need to plan accordingly at times. The story takes place in an interesting era and is quite intriguing but sadly a bit forgettable.
The combat (apart from the assassinations) is somewhat clunky and you can tell that it's a console port. You can play the game with keyboard and mouse but I recommend that you play with a controller if you have one since it's obvious it is meant to be played with one. I had a lot of fun with the game when it wasn't feeling repetitive. Climbing up to the view points was really fun and a few of them was a little bit challenging, too. I found myself enjoying climbing and exploring more than the combat itself.
The visuals are stunning. The game is rather bright and takes place during daytime which is a bit odd for a "stealth" assassin game. The way Altaïr moves is also done extremely well, his movements are very smooth. As a nice treat; Nolan North is the voice of Desmond Miles - and you can't go wrong with that!
A few negative things: Apart from being a console port with somewhat clunky combat, the game can get rather repetitive, especially towards the end. It also lacks subtitles which is crucial for many. Sometimes I had trouble hearing what was said in the game due to the background sounds. This is something to consider if you're like me and prefer to have subtitles. But all in all it's a nice game despite its flaws. It's a good game to start off a franchise with.

I would like to state right off the bat, that I do not hate this game at all. I was actually going to purchase a copy of the game for my wife today to play it together, found out it had been taken off the store, and read the AMA and related info.
This is a complicated game to review, but I felt I would share my thoughts so far. This game has has a lot of heart and love put into it so far, it's very obvious when playing it. It has a very immersive feel as well, via placing objects on the ground, instead of storing hordes of trash in numerous boxes. The feeling of digging out a mine, and having to dump the rock and dirt out the hole, is simple, but adds to that immersion. I also love the sound and effects at night time; That eerie wind and ambience is just mind blowing. Every update to this game, I update and play, as they had been adding tons of unique content.
However, I have to put emphasis on "had." They did work on new biome generation and terrain generation as of last year, which was a big task to do, but there wasn't much else added in. They had a good reputation for releasing small, but potent updates to the game frequently, and highlighting them on their youtube channel, which I would reccomend following if you're at all interested in the game. The youtube channel itself describes what I'm talking about. A lof of the updates come slower than the last, and several of the "in the works" projects being worked on never saw the light of day.  The last major update involved adding a crafting journal, which was great, but those changes were far too small in the scope of what was supposed to be there. It was disappointing to constantly wait to see changes to this game, only to try it out again in a few months, and being disappointed, or bored after a couple hours. It just feels too "barren" for a game that has been in EA this long.
I felt like the game had an amazing direction, of molding your "seed" and it's appearance, which reminded me of Fable in a way. This awesome feeling of exploring a survival world, with less focus  on survival, and more on exploring and progression in a sense and the players making their own "game" in a sense, by offering a diverse solid universe. It seems, and I may be wrong, that they focus more and more on the "pvp" community and pvp in general, rather than coop survival, which seemed like the original spirit of the game. This news comes on the heels of their announcment to make the game F2P, and nothing good rarely comes from a F2P model. While I have no doubt that they will do their best to make it a fair F2P model, if that is the route they choose, it doesn't seem like an idea that makes a whole ton of sense to me.
That being said, the devs are a great team of people, and I have a huge amount of respect for their vision for this game, and have given it nothing but praise up until this point. They are very active in discussions about it, and interacting with the community.I still have the best hopes for this game, and look forward to the final product. I still am in love with that original trailer, and what I imagined it could be. Even in it's current form, it is a good game, to be perfectly fair. In some senses, I don't feel the devs give themselves enough credit, and are too worried about failing. We just need to see content that changes the game, and adds to it drastically. More pets, more mounts, more weapons and armors, more enemies, boss monsters, and places to explore and learn more about the interesting story they've put behind this game. It should also go without mention to how amazing the art is for TUG.
The end note I guess is, that it's great they want to work in a new engine for the game, in a way. But it's a risky move, as we've seen what can happen with games like DayZ, wanting to 'redo' the entire game to make it better. I will still check out the updates from time to time, but it's sad to see that they almost seem to be damaging the game by taking it off the market, instead of trying to promote it more. I know these devs are a small team, and very talented, with a work load far above their numbers, but this just seems like a baffling move. I only wanted to write this because I had a lot of hope for this game. I wasn't a KS backer, but I did buy into EA very shortly after it came out on Steam.
TL;DR Wait until the finished product comes out, and see what they have. (Not that you have a choice now, at least for a year.) If things change for the better, and there's actually content that keeps me invested, my review would change to a positive in a second.

This is one of the most thought-provoking games I've ever played, and the experience will be lost on you if you don't go into it reminding yourself that this is a story about psychosis. If you have any experience with psychosis (or even mental health issues in general) the voices are likely to make you uncomfortable at times, but this adds to the experience more than it makes it difficult to play. It is worth stating here though that this is not a game to play if you value mechanics and variety above story telling and atmosphere. The visuals are impressive for a game produced by a non-AAA studio, the sound is effective and I only encountered one bug in the whole game which meant I had to reload the save file. I played the game with and without headphones, and whilst the game can be enjoyed without them, the added directional element adds to the effect of the voices (and also helps in certain battles).
The combat mechanics are somewhat basic and repetitive, especially during the first couple of hours, and whilst this isn't expanded on much more than addding different types of enemies in increasing numbers, the fights are not supposed to be the focal point. I was fine with the 'block/dodge -> counter' formula, although I would have appreciated it if changing target were a little more fluid, especially later in the game. The boss fights do provide reasonable changes from the usual battles though.
The puzzle formats can also feel a little repetitive, and whilst the nature of them never changes, the game does find ways to add variety later on. The runes dotted throughout the game provide interesting tidbits from Norse mythology; it will depend on whether or not you find them interesting as to how much effort you put into seeking them out.
Generally, the game spends the first couple of hours letting you learn the ropes, and then mixes things up a bit. Your enjoyment of it will ultimately depend on how much you manage to connect with it in those first couple of hours, as to whether you have the staying power to get to the end. If you do, you'll experience a game which may be a little paint-by-numbers, but gets you thinking a lot about mental health. I'm still not entirely sure what was real, and what was in her mind, and that keeps me thinking and is one of the reasons I won't forget it in a hurry.

Hellblade is a phenomenal achievement for what it is: a $30 game that is birthed out of passion and created with a lot of care and devotion. It has the spit and polish of a big title and but the scope is containted so the focus of the game remains clear. It tells a twisted, cruel, gritty, and downright horrifying story that is iterwoven with terrific art and disturbing imagery.
The game also uses audio like no game has before, employing 3D audio to impress the feeling of psychosis where the voices in the lead character's head feels as real as they would in yours. At times, those voices can feel a bit too close, a bit too real, and their constant bikering and negativity can be depressing, so I do implore caution for those that might get affected by it easily.
Both the visuals, audio and some incredible acting executes an "experience" that's worth having. It's dense, dark and full of terrors, which will leave you breathless and horrified. Top props to the level "Sea of Corpses" for being one of the most creepiest levels I have ever played in a video game.
The game isn't without drawbacks, however. The puzzles - where you have to find symbols in environments to open doors - is done with enough repetition that it gets boring real quick. By the end of the game, it was a chore to do, and they aren't as imaginative as the developers would like us to believe. The combat is fine for the most part, albeit aggressively basic that it ends up being a button smash-fest. What peeved me though was that during combat, the game would regularly blind you with either shody camera work or dark visual effects that leaves you more frustrated than filling you with thrills. I hate combat that visually impairs you in any way.
Hellblade is a 10 hour romp and I do recommend it highly. It's not a game you have played before, and it's the perfect showcase of a mid-tier game that I hope is resurrected back again.

Each stage is filled with so many fantastic character designs, that for the most part appear at some point in a campaign and are fleshed out as unique individuals. Overall, Skullgirls is a game I will always remember for reeling me into a genre I would have never looked into before. It's different, unique, bizzare, and full of charm you only get so often with games nowdays. It's a must-by, espically when on sale, and can be loved be anyone, even the most casual players.

I saw a preview for Remember Me showing off the memory-altering gameplay a few years ago. The game looked fascinating, but I don't think it garnered much attention as I never heard about it actually getting released. I picked it up during the Capcom sale (2015/05) and see it in the summer sale now, so I thought I'd give it some of the love it deserves.
The game has a few similarities to Mirror's Edge, which I loved, but there are also some key differences. Both games have you running/jumping/climbing around a future dystopia, but while ME's setting is pristine and sterile Remember Me takes place in a dirty, gritty, Blade Runnery Neo-Paris. Navigating the levels is fairly linear and you're fairly limited in your capabilities. There's also a lot of emphasis on unarmed combat, which I found very opaque to start with but makes more sense as more combo possibilities are unlocked. The first few fights feel like a chore, and the boss fights have some QTEs I don't really care for, but the combat feels very good once it all comes together.
The main thing I dislike about the game is the camera, which I found generally awkward. When it's in a fixed location you'll wish you could point it elsewhere; when you have control of it you'll wish you didn't. During combat, sometimes it feels like you're fighting the camera more than the mooks.
The highlight of Remember Me is the aforemention "memory remixes." You rewind and fast forward through a scene in your target's mind, altering certain elements one way or another until you achieve the desired result. It's trial and error to find the right combination, but seeing all the different outcomes makes the 'error' part not feel so punishing. I was surprised to find these sequences actually comprise a very small portion of the gameplay -- fortunately the rest of the game holds up.
Remember Me looks great, has some fantastic music, and does some good storytelling with some unique mechanics. If you think it sounds even remotely interesting, it's worth picking up on sale.

This game is great! To begin with, it has one of the most beautiful and best realised science fiction worlds ever - we're not talking piles of lore here (although there is a good enough amount of it to fit the game), but the sense of this being a world that's lived in with people actually milling about and in cases where you're crossing destroyed places droids fixing things. The visual design here is some of the best I've seen in any game/movie and it amply deserves the praise it has received. There are many moments where I just found myself stopping to drink in the setting and all the little touches present in the environment, it is better than a moving piece of concept art just about everywhere. The foreshadowing for both characters and places is naturally integrated into the levels for those willing to observe with care.
The port is also well optimised, capable of running smoothly on older hardware as it seems to be using the version of Unreal Engine 3 in Mass Effect 3 producing marvelous visuals with great performance. The audio is fitting and the music is suitably cinematic.
The gameplay is an action-platformer with brawler elements supported by a customisable combo system where the combos are pre-set and unlocked over the course of the game but where the effect of each sequence is defined by which attacks (presens) you equip. This allows you to configure combos for maximum offense, healing or recharging your special powers faster. This somewhat tactical system works well for the most part and has its moments but the cooldown times and limited combos do lead to ocasional irritation. You get to explore many long and interesting levels while largely impacting Neo-Paris and its citizens. There are many collectibles and interesting pieces of lore scattered throughout.
There are a few design issues such as unskippable cutscenes (thankfully most are quite short), the cooldown times getting in the way of unleashing some required special attacks on some bosses and the morality of memory rewriting and the results of Nilin's actions (at least Nilin does feel bad about those). Nilin herself is a well made and strong character whose journey and internal conflicts are well expressed.
For a first game by a new studio this is a stellar achievement and squarely placed Dontnod onto my radar, I definitely want to see what else they cook up!

If you haven't played this game yet, give it a shot. The Consuming Shadow is a very difficult roguelike thats been very well crafted, with a fantastic atmosphere. A chilling rouguelike Survival Horror game, erring more on "survival" rather than "Horror". An ancient god plans to invade the world, so you have to find parts of an ancient banishment ritual to stop them. Delve deep into infested monster dens, take drugs, do whatever you need to in order to save the world.
Or die trying. That will happen a lot.
Pros:
-Many aspects of the game are randomized every time. While you may explore similar locales, there's enough to spice things up every time.
-Real survival horror gameplay. The enemies and atmosphere are oppresive and stressful, but trying to keep your health and supplies up to combat it can be equally stressful. Difficult but rewarding!
-Unlockable characters, challenge modes, beastiary, this game is a Completionist's dream.
-Despite the game's randomization, there aren't any truly "overpowered" item combinations. You'll be clawing your way through this game no matter what!
Cons:
-Like many other rougelike games, you can get some really bad RNG. Be it a map full of monster-infested towns when you desperately need supplies, unfortunate monster spawns, or random events that conspire against your current run. be ready for lots of stress.
-Graphics are simplistic by design. Think of something like Undertale: Not hyper-detailed, but it gets the job done. While I personally don't find this a dealbreaker, I can understand why it might be for others.
-Another "mixed bag" criticism is the game's levelling system. As you complete (or fail) runs, you gain experience, unlocking new perks that can improve future playthroughs. While this is very encouraging, it makes early runs feel like you have an unfair disadvantage.
Conclusion:
A great rougelike game that keeps you on the edge of your seat every time you play it. It's not slow-paced like FTL, but it's not as twitchy and fast as Spelunky; it finds a happy middle-ground of slow, methodical gameplay, along with plenty of monster fighting. This game can be very stressful, but I find it very rewarding.
I love this game and its creator.

I'm a little torn on giving this game a positive review. That said, you'd be hard pressed to find a game more terrifying, and on the first playthrough the game will surprise you more than once, without the use of jump scares. As a horror game, that's probably all we could ask for.
Anyway, on a more objective level, the game isn't particularly good, but on a subjective one, it has a special place in my heart. Maybe it'll carve one in yours with a rusty butcher knife.
(Played the Humble Bundle edition, the differences between that and the Insanity Edition don't change this review.)

The art's not amazing in this game. Right. Now forget that, because it doesn't detract from the game at all.
Basically, it's a Lovecraftian roguelite similar to FTL. You hop from town to town for supplies, quests, and most importantly, "dungeons" to explore. To win, you need to find four parts of a ritual spell, and deduce the identity of the invading god based on various clues offered throughout. The final level can be attempted at any time, allowing you to go in even with just an educated guess. Sometimes, your only choice is to make a guess, because you've got just 60 hours to work out an answer.
Most importantly for this kind of game, there's plenty of replayability. There are multiple endings, characters, and lore to be unlocked, plus the challenge modes new in the Steam version.
Lastly, to address the RNG, the game is a random by nature, but never so much that it can kill you or deny you items unfairly. I have yet to find myself in an unwinnable situation, unless I caused it myself (by not stocking up on health for example).
Oh, and it's not wiki-reliant. Big plus for me personally.
Anyway, it's well worth the $10, but sale or no, definitely consider picking this up.

This game is a love letter for anyone, gamer or non, who loves a good story.

And most importantly, this game dares to deal with mental illness like no other game has before. The developers truly cared and gave the people suffering with psychosis the utmost respect they possibly could. You can tell the developers poured their heart and soul into this game and it shows.
Don't buy this game expecting flawless gameplay, or exhilarating combat. Buy this game for the visuals, the flawless sound design, the lore, and of course, it's story. This game immerses you in ways no other game has or will. It will make you fear and it'll make you feel uneasy, but all in the best way imaginable.
You'll want to find every single bits and pieces of the story, you'll want to explore the entire map, and you'll want to find every single rune containing stories from Norse mythos.
I honestly cannot praise this game enough no matter how hard I try, If it were up to me, I'd buy a copy for every single person in the world because everyone deserves to experience the story and the narrative this game provides. In short, this game is the equivalent of your new favorite book. The one you spend all night reading in one sitting. The one you'd reccomend to all your friends, and the one that you spend your entire life wishing for a sequel.
Please do yourself and the gaming community a favor and purchase this title. I promise you won't regret it.

I would not recommend Painters Guild to others. The other reviews are largely accurate although perhaps a bit forgiving in what they describe as the amount of entertainment you get out of this game. Your gameplay in the first five minutes is your gameplay for the rest of the time you play, only with increasingly menial micromanagement that never gets easier.
The art style, premise, and initial execution of Painters Guild is enticing. This is, unfortunately, where it ends. There is no way to automate behaviours and this inevitably makes progression feel like punishment. Expanding upon your guild and hiring more painters adds more work and doesn't change the game in any significant way. If you have to frantically click and drag your starting painter 5 times a minute, you have clicking and dragging two painters 10 times a minute to look forward to when you expand.
That's not an incentive, and that makes this a management simulation in the sense that you're just adding more responsibilities to your workload. That you can purchase furniture to slightly improve recharge times is nice, I guess, but it'd be better if there were management upgrades you could buy that simply automated these functions.
Progress should feel like progress. Challenge is fine but not if it comes in the form of inundating you with responsibility. Automation and improvement is key for a management simulation and that is something Painters Guild does not offer you.
There's potential for this game if the developer wanted to give it a shot but that does not seem to be the case. Painters Guild is not worth $10 or the discount it currently has at 77% off. The content simply does not justify there being a cost.

I originally bought Trine because it was a platformer that worked on my low spec laptop, and had controller support. I don't regret this decision, and have been "enchanted" by my journey within the Trine world. This is truly one of the great PC puzzle-platformers and deserves its much-loved reputation.
The premise is simple but fun. A wizard, a thief, and a warrior all go searching for an artifact, and find that they are now mystically bound to one another to resolve a problem. Each character has different features and abilities. The thief can shoot arrow, and grab wood platforms with a grapple hood. The wizard can conjure boxes, planks, and platforms. The warrior can shield himself from damage and slice enemies with his sword.
You can't beat the game with one character. You must know which character will solve which problem, and switch accordingly. In this, it has some commonality with an old Blizzard title called The Lost Vikings. Unlike The Lost Vikings, you don't have to guide your characters one at a time towards the exit. You see, all three characters are united in one "presence", and so switching keeps your place -- unless one of your characters dies.
All characters are vastly different from one another. The pensive wizard is vastly different from the sneaky thief who is vastly different from the bold warrior. You really got to be aware of each character's strengths and weaknesses.
When you buy the Enchanted edition, you are essentially buying two different game engines.
There's the "original" game engine which will work on low end machines. It's ambient but simple. I only recomment this engine if you have nostalgia or really just need to use this on potato-level specs.
The "enchanted" game engine is (from what I know) the same engine used in Trine 2. This was has a shock of colour, and really makes use of lighting effects. It's really a testament to the art direction that this holds up after a few years. For anyone who thinks 2D means "retro", take a look at Trine. It's truly beautiful to behold.
The sound has two highlights: the soundtrack, and narration.
First off, I really like the orchestral Medieval music. It's the kind of music I'd like to hear while drinking mead in a cosy pub with a fireplace. It really makes you want to sit down and hear tales from times long, long ago. I loved the soundtrack so much, I had to look up who did it. It was Ari Pulkkinen, apparently the same guy who did the soundtrack to Angry Birds.
And whoever the narrator is, I love that guy. He's got that wistful but world-weary English style about him that makes you realize Trine's universe is both a world of great troubles and great heroes. The moment he talks, I'm hooked on this world.
You can use a keyboard and mouse, and the game is okay that way. However, this game is much better with an x-input controller that features two analog sticks. That means
use the Steam controller, as the trackpad will just annoy you -- especially when you're using the wizard, who uses the right analog for magic.
If you use this with a dual analog stick controller, the game is easy, fluid, and fun.
You'll be happy to know that I've used this game on Windows, Mac, and Ubuntu. It works perfectly on all platforms without a hitch. It also works well on my low end HP laptop, which only has a dual core Celeron processor and 2GB of RAM. I'll also have you know it's got Integrated Intel graphics -- the notion of this having anything by Nvidia is laughable. Yes, Trine works perfectly on that machine without a hitch.
As for relatively beefy hardware featuring an i7 processor and a GTX 1050 Ti? Not only does it work, it looks beautiful owing to the tremendous art style.
A few days ago, I had an argument on Reddit on whether 2D died out with the SNES. Not only is such an idea ludicrous, go look at Trine! Not only are 2D games still being made, they're more beautiful then ever before. If designers in the 80s and 90s could see Trine, they would salivate.
But this isn't just about graphics and sound. This is about entering a vibrant world where you have to interact with unique characters to solve problems. In this, Trine shines. It's a true PC classic.

Tentative Recommendation:
Overall, a decent cyberpunky game with one excellent game mechanic.
First off, most of the gameplay is an incredibly easy version of what you would find in one of the Batman Arkham games. None of the fights are particularly challenging. The one interesting mechanic presented in the game is called "remixing," wherein you watch a memory of a character and then attempt to alter certain aspects of it in order to manipulate their memory. It's a neat idea and pretty fun, but only happens maybe four times total throughout the entire game.
The story itself takes place in a cyber-punky version of Paris wherein memories have become the most valuable form of currency. Again, it's a neat sort of idea but is basically left unexplored and as a result does not make a great deal of sense if you stop to think about the world a bit. The story starts off fairly interesting, but begins to peter out and finishes with a total letdown of an ending.
If you decide to try it, get it on sale for 5-10 dollars or so.

At its core, this game is very simple. A Lovecraftian procedurally generated CYOA with action sequences, simple shadowy graphics and a horrific plot.
But that simplicity in and of itself is what makes it so good. What it does, it does well.
You are the standard Lovecraftian "scholar of the occult turned bastion against the darkness, sacrificing your very self and mind to save the world from the mind tearing evil beyond".
In the main game mode you have 60 "hours" to find the keys to complete the banishment ritual to stop the dark god from entering the world through Stonehenge and warping all creation. To do this, you travel around the UK in your car, stopping at various towns. Some are peaceful and untainted, while others have been infested with the Shadow. In those you may investigate where the infection is and shut it down. Random text messages arrive, both people providing advice and cheering you on, and the Dark Forces taunting you (Cthulu has taught its minions to use SMS, I see...). Theres also random events as you travel around, sometimes leading to more investigation sequences.
All this comes at the cost of your own life and sanity, of course. In the action sequences the game turns into a 2d room by room maze, randomly generated. Search the rooms to find clues to which dark god is trying to get through stonehenge, and items and magic spells to help you in you journeys. Shoot horrid shadow monsters with your trusty gun, or just pistol whip the hell out of them, as you dont have many bullets. After completeting whatever it was that sent you there, sometimes you got to RUN as the dark forces dont like being thwarted. Fortunately theres a handy minimap in the corner that shows where youve been.
Once you have gathered enough clues to piece together which dark god is trying to f'up the earth, get to stonehenge and cast the banishment ritual (magic is used by quickly selecting symbols with RS) to keep it out.
Kind of like a game of Clue, only with much more insanity, Ia Ia Cthulu fhtagn-ing, and terror.
The sanity meter is cool. As you start going insane, weird things start happening on screen. Doors move, things vanish, all hell breaks loose (literally). And in the CYoA text segments, the words in the selection boxes start flicking back and forth between what you are trying to do (ie "Investigate Further", "Return to Car") and "KILL YOURSELF". You can imagine the end result of that one.
The writing in the CYoA segments is *awesome* and totally captures that Lovecraftian feel of flickers at the edge of vision, all consuming darkness, and incredible wrongness, and you are the only one who can stop it, although youd rather just curl up in a corner and die. Graphics are simple, but this game is proof positive you dont need ultra detailed gore to be creepy. In the action sequences you and the monsters are just shadows against a backdrop (rendered appropriately for the area graveyard/park, house, abandoned building etc).
It also has persistant unlocables to aid you in your quests. Extra abilities, items, diary entries, game modes and more unlockable characters provide a feeling of completion, even after watching the last nameless scholar slowly bring his gun to his head to end the madness within for the 10th time.
My only compaint is the XBox controller isnt perfect. Ive had issues getting it to register what I'm doing, randomly shutting off and so forth. Playing keyboard isnt an option for me because of physical issues, so I cant say if the k+M setup has the same control issues. But they are minor issues.
Lovecraft fans will love this one. I'd recommend it to anyone whos far more into psychological horror than gore and jumpscares horror because there isnt any of that (thank f'n god).

Solid game. While some may dislike the art style, I think the silhouette-backlight design actually works in the game's favour, as it leaves more to the imagination and emphasizes the (very effective) sound direction as well. The various challenges and achievements finally add a lot of depth, although the character balance is... debatable. Most bugs have been fixed since the original release. The writing and atmosphere are amazing, especially if you consider it's a procedurally generated roguelike. You do get used to it after a while and you develop a tolerance to the creepiness, but the game can still surprise you occasionally - especially when you're trying for a really hard challenge.
There are some issues. The game could have used more character-dependent flavour texts. The text messages are personalized for each character, but the other situations (mostly) aren't. It can break immersion somewhat at certain points since their personalities are so different. My biggest complaint is that you have to pay birth stars (character levels) to unlock new challenges. This means that a level 10 character can only get 2 (I think) stars at the start with all challenges unlocked, which makes the game even more difficult - as if it weren't difficult enough - and you'd have to play a LOT to make up for those lost stars because the XP requirement for newer levels increases exponentially. I think that area could have used a little more tweaking.
Finally, I'm glad I got this on the day of the summer release for a cheaper price with Yahtzee's two novels thrown in, because the current price is really friggin' high for such a low-production (which is obviously not the same as "bad"), solo developed game in my opinion. Still, there are lots of much worse games to blow your money on with the apparent lack of quality control (Grass Simulator, Accidental Runner and the like, I'm looking at you).

The Consuming Shadow is an excelent mix of horror with retro gameplay. Simple at a glance but surprisingly deep you'll find yourself zipping around a randomly generated British countryside slaying demons and helping wayward souls in your mission to discover the dark god invading the world and the ritual required to banish it.
I could most easily compare the basics of dark-god banishment as a sort of game of Clue, for those who remember the boardgame pasttime, a deductive reasoning experience where you strive to find clues infering what gods are present and what symbols they use with the goal of figuring out which god is invading and what rune holds its affinity. Combing the god's rune with a discovered ritual will allow you to make an attempt at saving the world in Stonehunge, if you can survive long enough to get there.
Combat is hectic and claustrophobic as you battle quick, silhouetted beasties with limited light, pistol-whipping and firing wild shots in oppressively poorly lit dungeons. Choosing the right tactic, ammo and timing are all important.
Magic plays a role as well as you must utilize a collection of runes to both banish dark gods as well as cast spells you may find in your searches, counterspell evil cultists to defeat their magical barriers or to close rifts allowing shadowy creatures into the living world.
Resource management, time management, trigger discipline, reasoning skills and a bit of a gambling nature all play their part in the game. Do you want a few extra hollow point bullets, or the useful piece of gear? Wlil you gamble on your intuition to keep you from wasting ammo on hallucinations as your sanity wanes, or shoot up with illicit narcotics to keep your calm? Should you try and stop the crazed gunman with your words or your hands?
New to the Steam edition are a number of challenge modes including a daily challenge with randomized modifiers, achievements and trading cards. There are several unlockable characters with differeing capabilities and a somewhat gentle progression system that optionally allows you to get a little bit better with each run if you so choose by spending 'birth stars' on a series of randomized stat boosts.
The Consuming Shadows won't be for everyone. Watch some videos and decide for yourself, what you see is what you get. It'll either be amazingly cool or completely out of your range of interests. And don't mind my playtime, I put quite a lot of time into it when it came out in the Humble Store. It will likely grow in time.

Trine is a puzzle platformer with some action thrown in there. You have three characters that you can switch between on the fly, similar to the old Lost Vikings game. You first have the most useful class, the Thief that can use a grappling hook to wooden ledges, a bow, and a flaming bow to light torches. Then you have the wizard that can magically make boxes by clicking or holding the right trigger and draw a box. You can also draw platforms and click and drag specific things to move them or get them out of your way. You can use your boxes and platforms to crush enemies. These first two classes are a lot of fun and have a lot of depth, but then we get to the third class / character, the warrior. He is just your straight up sword swinger, effective melee character.... with a shield that seems pretty useless.
The game is very beautiful, bright and vibrant. It is also very physics based and the physics feel nice. There are nice visuals with diverse settings and instead of cut scenes, the game just uses narrations as you play, which I greatly prefer. Since it is so visually beautiful, it can be a beast on lesser video cards, even at the lowest setting. Your platforms and boxes crush enemies, objects can be thrown into enemies or through destructible walls, the grappling hook lets you swing, and you can wrap hanging spike traps around platforms so they don't fall. I seemed to get the most fun out of unintentional things, such as teeter tauter platforms combine with Ferris wheel like platforms coupled with skeleton warriors jumping and sliding around to fill the room. The platforming dynamic of moving physics based platforming was a lot of fun.
The controls are very simple, and a controller is highly recommended. You have a jump button, a change weapon button, a trigger for drawing boxes or a grappling hook, two shift character buttons, the left stick controls the character, the right stick is like an aim for the bow, to draw platforms and to aim your shield (which is useless when you can easily dodge attacks). You can aim the bow and the longer you aim it, the further the arrow goes. If you don't like switching between characters, you can also play with a friend, but it is sad there is no online co-op.
Each character has their own health and mana bar, but the mana never really seems to run out with enemies constantly dropping potions. If one character dies, they're dead until you reach a checkpoint, even previous checkpoints. If all three characters die, then you simply restart at the last checkpoint. Its a forgiving system, which I'm happy about.
As you progress through the game, you'll level up to get your choice of skill upgrades. You'll also find new tricks and skills.
The enemies seem competent and dangerous enough. The basic enemy is the skeleton that comes in four flavors, standard, shielded, archer and pyro. They will jump over pits, climb, fall and do everything to get to you (except archers that stand and shoot). The enemy AI seems good enough so every situation can be different There are also spiders and bats, but for the most part, that's it.
It is a quick game, about 4 - 6 hours, but still a fun play through (not as addictively fun as Guacamelee). There is some replay value here with collecting stuff from each level and no playthrough feels exactly the same due to the physics and AI. It was a good design choice to have collectables stay collected when you enter each level so you don't waste time getting what you already had.
If you can get it cheaper than $10, go for it. If you're not into puzzles, avoid it, because the combat is pretty shallow.

Pros:
+ Good story with emphasis on the threats of our time.
+ A strong atmosphere is set from the beginning with the intro mission and cut scenes.
+ Great character build. Cpt. Price and the villains are very memorable.
+ Weapons feel superior and powerful. You don't have to empty a whole clip into an enemy's face like in CoD2 to bring him down.
+ The environments where the missions take place help to enhance the feeling of modern day warfare.
+ Lot's of replay value.
+ Tactical approach is supported instead of going in guns blazing.
Cons:
- The game's extremely short, the credits came up when I thought I was a quarter through.
In general:
Video games have it easy depicting modern day asymmetrical conflicts compared to historical battle arrangements. These in-and-out missions with a small number of participants involved go well with the 'one man army' concept that video games are bound to. I hated CoD 2 for that reason. World War 2 was anything but a place for a 'one man army'. It was quite the opposite, there were statistics on how many tens of thousands of men would be needed to advance 3-4 miles in Battle of Normandy and likewise. The gore, the confusion and the feeling of being overwhelmed were just not present in CoD 2. The feeling of having the upper hand on the battlefield feels just right in CoD4: Modern Warfare because the way wars are fought has changed.

I am only going to say two things about this game. First, there is virtue to 'forgive and forget'. Yes, the game was released in a state that would barely be fit to call an alpha at AAA retail price. Yes, it let everybody down after being hyped beyond reason. Yes, the developers promised and talked up what was going to be in the game prior to the actual release. But, its a year on now and, where they could have simply cut and run with our money, those same developers have been working overtime to actually finish the game. Not only finish, but also expand upon their original ideas based on community feedback. So, I say its time to forgive them for their past transgressions. Second, this game really is something special. Even  after the updates, there are still a lot of shortcomings. But, you can tell that an enormous amount of work has been put into it. It goes beyond that though. For example, just recently I found myself standing on the surface of a desolate moon with tendril-like rock formation writhing across.the surface. It was barren, but beautiful, with dramatic splashes of pinks and green soil bursting into full contrast as the sun rose over the horizon. As I looked up at the massive planet looming in the sky against the blackness of space, with the forlorn hollowing of the wind in my ears...well, there's really nothing else like it. Actually, that's the strongest endorsement that I can give No Man's Sky. There's nothing else like it.
