Assassin’s Creed is a game with lots of cool ideas that ultimately fail to come together cohesively. You just get the feeling that the developers were forced to release whatever they had done for the 2007 holiday season, whether it was ready or not. In that way, it reminds me a lot of the first Mass Effect - lots of great ideas, cool story and universe, but ultimately not as good as it should have been (which, like AC, was mostly rectified with the second game in the series).
But first things first... let’s break down what works and what doesn’t. As mentioned above, what works are the ideas the game puts forth, both in terms of story and gameplay. The story centers on a clandestine battle between two orders - the Assassins and the Templars. You play as Desmond Miles, a present-day descendant of Assassins, who has been captured by an organization named Abstergo (the modern day corporate face of the Templars). Using a device called the Animus, Desmond is forced to re-live the memories of his ancestor, an Assassin named Altair, in order to find a mysterious artifact.
The game is played from Altair’s point of view and takes place in the cities of Jerusalem, Damascus and Acre, circa 1200. It is here that you can see where the majority of the work was put into the game. The cities are sprawling, alive, and built with tons of detail. You really do almost feel like you could be in those places at that time. It’s quite impressive, technically. Gameplay centers around two main mechanics - free-running and combat. Free-running allows you to run across streets, rooftops and climb buildings in a fluid manner. When it works, it’s great fun, but oftentimes you’ll accidentally fall off buildings or jump in a completely wrong direction or climb something you didn’t want to, etc. Clearly the developers hadn’t worked out all the kinks yet. The combat is interesting, but nothing special. There are lots of options and it looks great in motion, but it’s not particularly difficult or engaging. Simply mashing buttons usually works in most cases. However, you can clearly see the potential in it. So again... good ideas, but not yet implemented as well as they could be.
Where the game ultimately fails is in the design. Assassin’s Creed 1 can basically be boiled down to the following: go to a city, climb a few towers, beat up a few people (or some other menial task), assassinate a high-priority target, return to home base. Repeat this 9 times and you’re done. It’s all very tedious and gets boring quickly. While there are a few different types of tasks and side missions that you can do in the cities, none of it really rises above being mediocre. The most interesting parts of each chapter are the final assassinations, but even in these cases, the verdict is mixed. Instead of actually being able to sneak around stealthily and assassinate your targets, many of these encounters just end up turning into a big brawl (not exactly what one would expect in a game involving secret assassins).
Ultimately, the game is promising, but flawed. The ideas underlying the story are definitely cool and the environments are really nice (for their time), but as a game, it is simply average in most respects. It also doesn’t help that the Altair character isn’t terribly compelling and nothing really interesting even happens until the very end. That said, this game is worth checking out if the premise intrigues you and you think you might be interested in the series as a whole (which, for the record, DOES get better). If you think that might be the case, my recommendation would be to either skip this game entirely and watch all of the cut-scenes/ending online, or play through it doing only the barest minimum needed in order to continue.
Grade: C
Note: I don’t recommend playing any of the Assassin’s Creed games unless you have an Xbox360 controller (or equivalent-featured gamepad). The AC games have complicated control schemes and were clearly designed with controllers in mind, so proceed with mouse/keyboard at your own risk.

Third person view assassination parkour simulator.
The "simulator" is especially befitting as this is in fact a story of one kidnapped Desmond Miles, set in what appears to be a not so distant future. Machine called Animus s(t)imulates genetic memories of our hero to put him in shoes of his ancestor, assassin Altaïr ibn-La'Ahad, during times of the Third Crusade.
This meta story is definitely one of the highlights of this adventure game. The other being the pretty well executed, smooth freerunning exploration aspect. I also love how the whole Animus business explains lots of acceptable breaks from reality present in video games. But then who will explain the stuff that is going on for Desmond? xD
I would hesitate though to call this much of "action" game or especially "stealth" game. It's rather easy, for one, bar maybe the very end and any area that has water as Altaïr can survive falls from some rather jarring heights but can't swim even in a puddle of liquid. But okay, let it be an action adventure.
For two, however, regarding the stealth aspect. You're not that much interesting to the guards to begin with and then you simply have one button to make you even less interesting, kind of hiding in plain sight (blending). Once you do garner unhealthy interest what you do is run away, break line of sight and hide in some hay or something, often jumping there from some ridiculous heights.
Except you often get this impression it is actually easier and faster to kill dozen of guards rather than to run from them and hide.
In short, the stealth aspect is actually barely present and not that all rewarding, especially compared to something I would call "proper" stealth like in Dishonored or even Deus Ex: HR or Batman. Not mentioning Thief, of course, that's a given. But I imagine I have to set this expectation for the whole series that this is more about the story, freerunning and mass murder rather than stealth. Not saying it's bad, just bit different from what I originally anticipated.
Arguably the most challenging part is gathering literally hundreds of some flags loitered around, yet it gives you pretty much nothing, there aren't even uplay points or steam achievements for that (on consoles you'd get achievos at least). Sufficient to say I gave up on that portion :] Even creator pretty much agreed he was just trolling players with that.
Although I did execute all the "side" missions even if you're required to do only a fraction of them to proceed.
Ah.. the missions.. That's another stab at gameplay. Despite all the open ended nature, it gets pretty repetetive. Maybe that's why they decided not to force all side missions on you.
Overall I'd still say it is a pretty interesting experience, and even if it didn't exactly meet my expectations it did nicely set off the whole franchise and can't wait to play the next installments.

It seems weird to be reccommending a Wolfenstien game for it's story... but just like The New Order, The New Colossus is one of the best stories ever told in a shooter because of just how many big swings Machine Games takes and just how insane the plot is willing to become.
The shooting is pretty good overall, but has one major flaw: The game does not do a good job of letting you know when you are being damaged. This has led to many unexpected deaths. Tough video games are fine, but I feel like the game is sometimes only hard because I don't realize I am being shot/how much I am being shot in the thick of a battle. It's a reletively minor complaint, but in a few giant open shooting sections it became a pretty big deal.
But when the shooting is good, it's reallllll good. Dual Wielding shotgus while running on top of a Nazi airship for example, or shooting fuel tanks to set a group of Nazis on fire. The gameplay side of this game has a lot of good moments as well and while overall the story is the real star here, the FPS portion of this game has its moments as well.
One more element of the game I would like to mention is the soundtrack. With one major exception, every song in this game is increadible and compliments/matches the moment like the PAYDAY 2 Soundtrack or the DOOM 2016 soundtrack. While none of the songs really stuck with me or am I humming throughout the next day, they all work to elivate the game and make you feel like a total sneak-king or complete badass depending on your approach. Of course there is one major exception to this, and you will know it when you hear it...
I think overall this game is a good one. It goes over the top in all the right ways while also managing to have subtly and nuance when it matters (AKA: personal story beats). This game is intense in both gameplay and story, and a perfect pick up if you are looking for a shortish (10-12 hours) single player campaign to enjoy.

BEWARE SPOILERS!!
My take on this game comes from two different places I wanna adress, but before that, keep in mind I -liked- the game, but as much as it pains me, I cannot recommend this title by any means unless it's on a big discount, or the current problems as of the day of this review are fixed.
Having played through the main campaing AND having tried the Freedom Chronicles, I feel confident enough to say that The New Colossus is an unfinished game that needed more time. I will try to keep this simple, might edit stuff later.
As a reference, here's my current rig:
GTX 970, I7 4790k, 16gb RAM, 1920x1080 60Hz, with the last Nvidia driver, the 388.00 version.
Performance:
-On release day, game crashed when alt tabbing, when changing resolutions, got a couple BSODS while playing.
-Game couldn't handle 1920x1080, as there was a configuration error with the DPI scaling
-Game worked pretty stable on Ultra, 60 fps and that, but anything beyond that had mayor FPS drop rates, which might be because my current GPU can't handle Uber (GTX 970). Some levels at the beginning were badly optimized
-Game constantly corrupted my data, was unable to sync with the cloud, for some reason it doesn't detects the console 100% of the times, and because of that, you can't access your game profile, because it needs to be linked with your cloud. This happened a couple of times, and I believe is something that the developers should look at, if they're listening to the feedback at all.
The Game:
Story wise, I got pretty hooked on it from the beggining, it felt fresh and new, and I absolutely loved the character interactions and flavor between the npcs, it felt like a nice touch, with much more richer storytelling than New Order. It's the same ''blazko go blow this♥♥♥♥♥♥up'' kind of momentum that NewOrder has. The game abruptely ends on what seemed to be the middle of the story, the finale lacking an end boss, and Blazko taking revenge on Frau Engel.
The game offers the same beautiful shooting mechanics as NWO, and the game looks beautiful, but it's very, very short. It feels like a story was trying to be told, with cinematics every level, a backstory for Blazko, new characters, a definitive change of pace, but it doesn't feels like Wolfenstein, feels like something ELSE, and I think, had there been more time to add more content to the game, I wouldn't think that. It feels like watching a movie, one I really liked, but it doesn't feels like a complete shooter.
Perks have changed completely, and some of them are almost useless in the game. In new order, it defined your playstyle, and it felt intuitive and natural to understand. Those features feel like achievements in The New Colossus, some of them are useful, some are not. There are weapon upgrades now, for every weapon that you own, except for the heavy weapons. These upgrades are almost MANDATORY to finish the game, especially if you're playing on Uber/Death Incarnate. Takedowns have stayed mostly the same, but the stealth on this game is UNFORGIVING. Some could say this is more realistic and challenging, I honestly don't know what they did to the stealth, but sometimes it doesn't makes sense, as enemies can see you even if you're hidden.
When you finish the game, you can keep playing, and you get to hunt down Uberkommanders, visit locations, and get collectibles. If these were added into the main story, the game would had been very different. They're not a hassle, but story doesn't advances much after that.
Now, on the DLCS.
Freedom chronicles comes with the preorder of the game, and it features mini stories for 3 different characters, each with different abilities and levels made for them. It also comes with combat simulations, something like challenge levels if you wanna play those. By the looks of it, it seems like this is scheduled to be released over time, to add content of the game. I don't mind having more content, (as the game on itself it's lacking some), but it makes you think why wasn't Freedom Chronicles a part of the main game.
Overall, it feels like this game needed more time. Crashes and performance issues on release day, and well after WEEKS these problems keep happening. There is a huge problem with the in-game content, it really feels like Machinegames added features at the end of the game to give it some more lifespan, added with Freedom Chronicles and combat simulations. Is the game worth playing? Yes
Is it worth 10 bucks? Ehhhhhhh... That'll be up to you, of course.
It's a very well written and designed game. Not scary, nor particularly distrubing, but it is very very creepy. The art direction, although very simple, is also perfectly fitting. Even the text assets are acceptable despite being default plaintext, seeing as the character is either typing it out or reading it on typed paper.
The gameplay is uniqe, as far as I know. You simply walk left and right through procedurally generated dungeons and events, shooting, bashing, looting, running, and incanting your way past your foes. You have both health and sanity to monitor, of course. What makes it fun is whodunit take on figuring out which evil entity to banish, piece by piece assembling the know how to save the world. The fittingly abiguious yet descriptive writting also helps. Yes I know that's oxymoronic, but it just works.
The challenge is tight. At first I was sceptical of the difficulty. Then I realized you drain your health kit like a bullet hole riddled tub drains water. Then I couldn't find a way to permenantly restore sanity. Then I had broken legs, a panic attack, an was gushing blood, and proceded to clear three more towns that way before dying.♥♥♥♥♥♥was tense.
Replayability also seems very high, which is good for a session based game like this. If you've played FTL, you'd probably find Consuming Shadow's game sessions similar in length. Besides the main gameplay supported story and unlocks, you also have a daily challenge generator, and an endless dungeon mode. The list of individual challenges you can also unlock is short, but the game makes up for it in other unlockables. It has a diary you can rebuild, page by page. It also has a typical 'bestiary', but one that unlocks word by word, creating a more rewarding 'bestiary' to fill than most every other game has.
In conclusion, sure, the game has problems. The obvious "how did they miss that" graphical bug, the graphics that obviously auto-scale for bigger monitors, and keys can't be rebound in the options. These little problems pale in comparison to everything it does right. Overall, I'd ask you to overlook the rough edges and buy this game if it interested you in any way.

I will start off by saying that I would give 6/10 for the game. But let me explain.
The one thing that I cannot praise high enough for me is the art style of the game. Everything in the game is really well polished and it is a pleasure to look at. It looks really modern and sci-fi without being too far fetched. The art canvas that are unlocked as you play the game are stunning and a good reward for the play through. Congratulations for the artists and designers for these.
With regards to the story, I found the story at times captivating, at others (and most of the time, really) to be a bit obvious. But what I found most interesting was the philosophical discussions and the struggle of the main character when she is still recovering her memory. Having said that, the whole story is very linear.
These two points for me were the highlights. Now, some parts of the game that could improve.
Although I found the mechanic of allowing you to create your own combos, however limited, it was interesting enough to the point that changing it during a battle could prove very helpful. Having said that, I found the battles to be a bit repetitive and fairly easy. Once you get the mechanic of an enemy or a boss, even on the hard difficulty, it was still fairly easy.
With regards to the puzzles like climbing walls, jumping at ledges, climbing pipes, etc, it was a bit simplistic and at times rather frustrating, because as the game is not open world sometimes there were inconsistencies where you can leap up 4 meters from ledge to ledge and sometimes you cannot climb a 2 meters wall where you KNOW there is something behind it. And for me, the most frustrating part was when I was looking for an item (such as health or focus) and because of the linear part, you end up exploring a bit in order to reach the item, which would involve entering rooms to check it out. But if you happen to enter a room that was going to move the story forward, sometimes the door would just close behind you and would not allow you to go back, hence, you will lose the opportunity to get the item. Unless you play the whole game again, because there is only one save slot and the game auto-saves.
The memory remix mini-games were quite interesting, although, it is fairly simple to deduce how to solve, or if you are feeling like exploring the alternatives, just try everything, it won't take long for that and might have some interesting side-effects. These parts are very surreal which, again, congratulations to the art team.
Overall, for me it was an interesting game and experience, but it felt like a one trip pony, i.e. once you play once, it's enough. The replayability of the game is fairly low, because the second time you play, there won't be much novelty, with the exception of getting the missed items because of locked doors behind you.

You'll still have to fight a boss that can only be hurt for a one-second window during which you're still stunned from an unavoidable attack, or you'll be unable to get any health back because time keeps speeding up and slowing down at random, making it impossible to time your attacks for a healing combo. Sometimes tips will pop up and give you really bad advice, too. A lot of the game is kind of fun, but it's gated by really obnoxious parts that aren't "hard" or "challenging", just pointless tricky things you have to do over and over until you succeed and are allowed to continue.

It's not a terrible game, but there are so many more enjoyable games out there that there's no reason to choose this one.

Skullgirls is a love letter to the fighting game genre and also one of the most creative and unique titles on the whole market. It has color palettes, poses, win quotes, and even movesets that are all references to video games and anime. At the same time it has an almost entirely female cast, all of which have drop dead gorgeous character designs, (even the men) and motifs that make them stand out, all of whom are beautifully animated with hand drawn sprites in game.
The gameplay resembles most other 2D fighters. You have six buttons for light, medium, and heavy punches and kicks, and all the characters have special moves that are executed by combining joystick motions with said buttons. Supers are pulled off in the same way as Marvel vs Capcom 1, by inputting a regular special move motion, but pushing more than one punch or kick button. This input in other fighting games would otherwise result in an EX move, which is a mechanic skullgirls doesn't use. And just like every other fighter, grabbing is done by pushing light punch and kick at the same time.
A unique feature of Skullgirls is that you can choose how many fighters you want to use each match. Most fighting games are 1v1; you and your oponent both pick one character. Some games like Marvel vs Capcom 1 & 2, have both players pick 2 characters, where they can then input assist moves from their other fighter, and will play as that fighter when their first one gets K.O'd. Then there's game like Capcom vs SNK 2 or Marvel vs Capcom 3 which have a 3v3 system, that functions the same way as 2v2s, only now  there is obviously one additional character that either player must K.O. in order to win. Skullgirls allows the player to pick any one of these systems, and not only that, but both players are not beholden to whichever mode the other chooses, allowing for 1v3s, 2v3s, 1v2s, and all the other previously established combinations. It's worth mentioning that Skullgirls' 1v1 mode functions in a manner resembling the Darkstalkers series, where the winner of each round does not have their health bar reset to full, and must continue with however much health they had at the end of the previous round, while the loser of the round still gets their health bar reset.
The comabt itself in skullgirls is fast paced because of the fact that the game is permanently in what many fighting games call turbo mode. This speeds up the gameplay, and because of the fact that every light move combos into the medium version of the same move, which THEN combos into the heavy version of the same move, combos are extremely fun to watch and even more fun to pull off. If you watch the top 8 at EVO from any year you'll notice that one combo can last an entire match, and that something like that is not even too uncommon. A unique mechanic in skullgirls is that if you get trapped it in an infinite by your oponent you character will start glowing pink. At this point pressing any button will free your character from the infinite. This forces players to mix up their combos, and deepens the meta game.
The story mode is told through still frame drawings similar to the likes of Street Fighter V, and centers around each girl attempting to find the skullheart, a item in the game's lore which can grant a wish, if the wish is pure. The events involve criss-crossing storylines between multiple factions including mafiosi, scientists, a cult, and the military. The setting could not be more up my alley with the 1920-30s-esque mob film atmosphere. It's even posible that similar to the likes of Super Mario 3, the entire game is a performance put on by the characters. This is supported by evidence like the announcer saying things like "everyone mind you marks" before matches, the film reel motif in the menu, and super combos being referred to as "blockbuster" attacks.
All of this is only helped by the perfect soundtrack. There are multiple jazzy tracks, (once again right up my alley) but also songs from many other genres for the different stages in the game. It is my second favorite video game OST of all time, and I possibly have spent more time listening to it than playing the actual game.
So a hand drawn game about cute girls running around a mob-themed setting, set to a Jazz soundtrack, in a fighting game with inviting but deep combat. For me the stars have alligned perfectly, and it's almost as if the game is directly pandering to me. Even if you're not as enthralled as I am at the very idea of a game with all these components existing, it really is more than the sum of its parts, and everyone should check it out.

What happens when you take the 16bit JRPG pixel style graphics and lay out then use it to convey a visual novel? You get a great game called "To the moon". Ditching the stats and grinding, this one focuses on a solid story with a great sound track.
I'm guessing in the near future we develop the ability to enter peoples memories and change them. Our "heroes" are two scientists who work for a company that does such tasks, to grant wishes to dying patients by changing their memories. Thus making them believe their dreams came true. In this case an old man named Johnny who wants to go to the moon. Along the way of searching his memories to help in this, they uncover some hidden secrets that stand in the way of it's completions...thus creating a moral issue...do you have the right to change a dying person's memory?
It's a great game but short. Lets make no bones about it, the story, pixel graphics, and music are the stars here, not  a new video game play style. This is all old hat, but still done very well.
So spend a day with "To the Moon". You won't regret it....it may even give you the feels!

I like to think of myself as a human being in touch with my emotions. I feel, love to feel and don't stray away from bad or good. I admit, sometimes I tend to overreact, but my opinion is that things like that can't happen if you don't care. However, I am not easily touched by art. The last time I've cried is also the first time, as far as I can remember.
Back in the nineties, when I was five or six, I've watched this movie... I can't remember its title, but I remember the dread and tears rolling down my cheeks during the final movie scene where character visits his buddy's grave. His deceased friend is his circus monkey and instead of flowers, he's bringing him bananas. Something about it disturbed me deeply.
Since then, I had a few emotional rollercoasters where consuming art made it harder to swallow or breathe, but I was never moved completely.
Steam Awards this autumn had To The Moon nominated by a buddy of mine. I was suspicious about it; hey, it's Enterbrain's engine RPG, which means Game Maker, which means, dude, stuff like that can't move you. I didn't really point it out to my friend, but could he feel I was skeptical? Could be, because I've received it as a gift. So, at least I could give it a try, right?
At first sight, To The Moon looks childlishly naive. It's a simple 'walk-in-four-directions' RPG game with limited interactivity and no combat system. It gives an impression it wants you to explore its world, however, soon enough you will discover the game is rather linear.
Dr. Rosaline and Dr. Watts of Sigmund Corp. have a rather peculiar job - they rearrange memories of dying people so they remember their life differently seconds before dying. The new technology allows them to fulfill dying person's wishes. They didn't expect visiting Johnathan Wyles would be anything more than a regular night on the job. However, things turn out to be rather complicated when they find out they need to fulfill Johnathan's dying wish - make him travel to the Moon.
It doesn't take very long to get tangled into a four hour story choke full with symbolism and emotions, aiming and succeeding in shattering you to the core. This is a game that thrives on its lack of stereotypical heroes, big quests and otherworldly ideas. Meeting Johnny (Johnathan's nickname) proves to be a gutwrenching, slowbuilding experience. Nothing in To The Moon happens too fast or too slow; the story is perfectly timed and it's progressing toward the epic finale one step at a time. Both humans and certain objects are pieces of grandiose puzzle. However, motif is not onedimensional - it consists of several layers and, as you piece it together, it takes away your breath, masterfully emphasizing tearjerking moments by utilizing comic relief in form of Dr. Watts dialogue lines which are often used to break the fourth wall and make the world even more beliveable.
And while moving and interacting mechanics are not something that game should be proud of, they're basically non-important. On the other hand, music composed by Kan R. Gao, game's writer and director, proves to be a moving force behind the title and catalyst for game's story. It works wonders in creating atmosphere, be it moments of light comedy or heavyweight anxiety.
As the game progressed, I felt it coming: I knew To The Moon is actually influencing my mental state and changing my perspective with each passing minute. I knew I was getting attached to the characters, their ideas, fears, thoughts, doubts and hopes. By the end of Act 2, it was getting harder to breathe and my emotions evidently grew stronger.
As I was approaching the game's climax, I felt my eyes were burning and body's temperature rising. And then it hit me so hard, the way I wasn't struck by anything in art since that monkey scene from a movie I no longer remember - To The Moon made me cry and it didn't stop there. As I was gasping for air and being thankful I was home alone, I couldn't stop myself. Emotions were too strong, no matter how hard I fought against them. I even tried concentrating, meditating on my breath, thinking crying over game is probably silly because I'm causing pain to myself... But I was wrong. I was so wrong.
To The Moon made me cry during playing, step away from a keyboard and cry for another half an hour after finishing it because it was so liberating. It was an unscrewed valve releasing tons of pent-up emotions from who knows where. A silly little game I knew nothing about proved to be one of my favorite games ever, one I will ALWAYS recommend and the one I will measure interactive art from now on.
Few months ago, I was at home, nervous about some basically unimportant reason (could it be money, or recent  unemployment or what?). My daughter was sitting by the window, her elbows on the window sill. So I was nervously pacing through the room when she turned to me and said: "Dad, come here with me, let's look at the stars."
And I've really turned around, somehow, the fate didn't allow me to miss out on that opportunity. So we sat by the window and we've looked at the starry sky and then she said to me "Look at the stars, Dad. Stay here with me. We'll look at the stars. Aren't they beautiful?"
So I sat there and gazed upon the shiny dots thinking that, as we grow up, society murders something good in all of us and that our kids are the only way we can, at least partially, get it back.
So, just as my daughter on that very night, this game did the same thing for me - with its story of hopes, dreams, fears, love, life and death, it made me feel a little bit more human. And I'm forever thankful for that.

Assassin's Creed is a tale of two games: the one that is an interesting and new intelectual property, and the one that reeks of committee-based game design focus grouped for mass market consumption.  I desperately wanted to play the first, but the second wouldn't leave me be and ultimately became the experience of this game.
Ubisoft's brand of boring and repetitive combat makes its series debut in AC.  Add to that the three virtually identical main set pieces, and you will be left amazed as I was that so bland a game could come from the hundreds of creative people who had a hand in making this title.  Adding more creativity to the production does not necessarily mean more creativity in the final product to be sure.
The tragedy of AC is that underneath all this blandness lies a pretty interesting story of inter-temporal... well... something or other.  The story was obfuscated by the very presentation that was meant to tell it.  I had to youtube the ending and secret story points after beating the game just to see wtf happened.  This obfuscation could have been by design, which is possible as Ubisoft does tend to put the finer points of the game's story into easter eggs to be found by the player.  And maybe that's my fault for not recognizing and engaging that.  But with such a bland gameplay experience, I was left uninterested in anything other than finding something exciting and pulse-pounding about Assassin's Creed, which is ostensibly an action game.  Reading in-game emails and interpreting glyphs on walls would not have qualified as exciting at that point for me.
The final and in my opinion unforgivable F-you from Ubisoft is that this game has in effect no ending.  Clearly Ubisoft had intentions to serialize this franchise, which is fine.  But you have to have an ending in the first release of an IP, even if you have a cliffhanger in it as AC did.  The original Halo did it, Star Wars did it.  It's a rule.  Period.
Assassin's Creed works, and somewhere in there is a compelling story, but you're probably better off with either of Ubisoft's other platforming/action titles Splinter Cell or Prince of Persia.

It seems weird to be reccommending a Wolfenstien game for it's story... but just like The New Order, The New Colossus is one of the best stories ever told in a shooter because of just how many big swings Machine Games takes and just how insane the plot is willing to become.
The shooting is pretty good overall, but has one major flaw: The game does not do a good job of letting you know when you are being damaged. This has led to many unexpected deaths. Tough video games are fine, but I feel like the game is sometimes only hard because I don't realize I am being shot/how much I am being shot in the thick of a battle. It's a reletively minor complaint, but in a few giant open shooting sections it became a pretty big deal.
But when the shooting is good, it's reallllll good. Dual Wielding shotgus while running on top of a Nazi airship for example, or shooting fuel tanks to set a group of Nazis on fire. The gameplay side of this game has a lot of good moments as well and while overall the story is the real star here, the FPS portion of this game has its moments as well.
One more element of the game I would like to mention is the soundtrack. With one major exception, every song in this game is increadible and compliments/matches the moment like the PAYDAY 2 Soundtrack or the DOOM 2016 soundtrack. While none of the songs really stuck with me or am I humming throughout the next day, they all work to elivate the game and make you feel like a total sneak-king or complete badass depending on your approach. Of course there is one major exception to this, and you will know it when you hear it...
I think overall this game is a good one. It goes over the top in all the right ways while also managing to have subtly and nuance when it matters (AKA: personal story beats). This game is intense in both gameplay and story, and a perfect pick up if you are looking for a shortish (10-12 hours) single player campaign to enjoy.

Shoggoth's Scenic Driving Tour of England
Reviewer's Note: Over 50 Hours with Humble Bundle Copy
"It's late. At least, I think it's late. Keeping track of time isn't a priority - wherever I am now... like a purple nimbus cloud crackling with electricity.  What's important is that I've saved the world, and no one will be any the wiser.
…
"Not that I did this for recognition, no! I'm not vainglorious or anything. This was all honestly just a happy byproduct of my pursuit of arcane knowledge, of the Eldritch Truth. I was laughed out of the academy, and the very men and women who found my research so amusing now owe me their insignificant lives. If they had seen what I've seen, fought what I've fought, learned what I've learned, they'd still be laughing -  restrained in padded cells, or worse.
"Now to busy myself for eternity, and let's hope it's a brisk one because I'm quickly running out of reading material."
The Consuming Shadow is great fun. It isn't the deepest or most challenging procedural-type game I've ever played, but it is one of the most unique... like if FTL and Eternal Darkness: Sanity's Requiem finally hooked up and made an unholy union. You play as a nameless, silhouette-y scholar tasked with stopping an ancient alien god's invasion of England (in 60 hours no less) because, let's face it, anything fantastical or magical or evil is innately going to be drawn to England for its rich history, world-renowned cuisine, and year-round pleasant weather.
And it goes without saying you'll have to remain sane, tricky business considering the position you're in.
Sat in your car with a helpful sticky note attached to the rearview mirror (“Don't look back,” Yahtzee's nod to Daenerys Targaryen, one assumes), you must work your way southward towards Stonehenge (the aforementioned ancient god couldn't be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥to research a less obvious pagan site), stopping at  all the quaint villages peppering the English countryside to take on jobs from the Ministry of Occultism, resupply, and generally pop in to make sure all the villagers haven't been replaced with horrible squid monsters and telemarketers.
That's the real pulsating meat of the game – you'll select a destination, drive a ways and encounter a particularly foggy town. Flavor text will inform you that everything isn't as it seems in Lil' Silent Hill, and you'll have to contend with a series of random dungeon scenarios – a hostage situation, sealing a rift, clearing an infestation... run of the mill English stuff, presumably. The dungeons are laid out in a random grid that you traverse like the 2D side-scrollin' badass you are.
Depending on what kind of a dungeon you find yourself in (there's quite a few), you'll get ammo, health, spells, sundry helpful items, and clues to suss out just what kind of an ancient alien god you're dealing with. Of course, you can't enjoy all that ammo, health, spells and so on without killing all the creeping, crawling, and flying horrors occupying the dungeon. The combat is, for me anyway, akin to combat in Silent Hill 2. Your firearm autoaims, and mele is an incredibly viable (read: powerful) option, but you're going to take hits and the combat isn't going to feel amazing... just acceptable. Which is fine! Again, Silent Hill 2-y. I feel like a Joe Shmo fighting unspeakable horror, and I shouldn't feel like his loud cousin Joey Kickass, frequent ruiner of children parties. And if you take too much damage, or dabble too often in the sexy dark arts, you'll encounter some clever little status and sanity effects... nothing quite as memorable as, say Eternal Darkness', but much more impactful on gameplay.
I mentioned that there are clues... see, part of the “stopping an ancient alien god's invasion” is knowing the proper incantation, which you aren't going to just know off the top of your head. Instead, you'll find helpful cultists have left various notes throughout dungeons providing contextual clues like, “the blue god is associated with raucous partying,” “Bytalia hates the ever-loving♥♥♥♥♥♥out of the god associated with the SMH rune,” and so on. Armed with a handy table, you can fill in pertinent information as you find it. This minor aspect of the game is what I found most fun, oddly enough. It felt like I was playing a boardgame. Once you have (or think you have) enough information you can brave Stonehenge itself for either a thrilling conclusion, a hilariously colossal cockup, or something in between.
With each subsequent playthrough you'll unlock new characters (three, each with a slightly different gameplay focus), constellations that let you focus on stats or abilities, and of course flavor text lore in the forms of a diary and bestiary.
The Consuming Shadow is going to have some complaints, and I'm sure a point of contention for some people will be the general aesthetic. While I initially found it less than easy on the eyes, The Consuming Shadow grew on me. There's something absolutely charming about it, I can't quite explain it. I felt immersed, like I was sitting in MY car, checking off a list, sleepily driving towards another cursed township (the otherworldly soundtrack helps a bunch in the ambiance department). My biggest qualm is that I wish there was MORE, which is asking a lot of a sole developer, I know. It's just that after a few playthroughs you'll encounter the same scenarios, same dungeons, same spook text messages, and same sanity effects. I would have loved more flavor text, more horrors, and while I thoroughly enjoyed the English setting I would have really liked some other maps... Australia perhaps, with the ancient god heading towards Uluru, or maybe the ancient god is in the continental United States in search of the first McDonald's.
But I digress. The Consuming Shadow is, as I said, great fun. It's cosmic horror-themed FTL when boiled down to its most basic concept, only instead of being chased by an ironically xenophobic intergalactic rebel fleet you're fleeing from pure, unadulterated EVIL™. The controls are tight and intuitive, the sound design is atmospheric, and... I don't know, it just feels good to play. Yahtzee took a bunch of great retro game mechanics and sensibilities and arranged them in such a way that it doesn't feel like another forced retro indie title.
This is one immersive, engaging, and well-written title. It's fulfilling to flesh out your diary and bestiary, it's thrilling when you finally win (and when you “win”), and it honestly makes for a fun little party game. My friends and I sat around for hours exploring dungeons, filling out the table, and dying.
We died a lot.
And you will too.
I've seen it in the stars.
INSANITY EDIT: the Steam edition includes lots of challenges to keep you coming back for more, PLUS I've noticed a few new denizens occupying the dungeons... definitely a fan of the creepy skitterish guy with more head than can be reasonably explained by natural selection.

It has its moments. The Call of Duty series from 3 and onward had started to become a fairly straight line, with some things to pick up on the way. The series now seems to 'innovate' by the means of inventing a new game mechanic and only using it for a couple levels, never deviating from the Call of Duty formula of straight line run and gun with cinematic moments. This game was the one that did it right before the ones after it screwed it all up. The cinematics don't completely run your game, should you mess up it's your fault, which is a refreshing change if you've played the more recent Call of Duty games before this one like me. Would I say this is a good game? Ehhhhh... would I say it's a good Call of Duty game? Yes, the best after 3; and if the franchise keeps going as it is, that might remain true forever.
In summary, like mentioned above, it has its moments. I didn't feel like my hand was being held during the campaign, and that if I didn't keep close to my squad and work with them that I'd probably get myself or all of us killed. At the same time, the singleplayer doesn't have too much replayability due to its straight line cinematic nature, except to play those key moments in the game again. I'm not going to rate based on the multiplayer, because I haven't played it and I don't really intend to... and multiplayer in Call of Duty games is expected to be good. Given all the information and my own opinion, I recommend this game if you are a fan of Call of Duty and its later games after 3. If you don't really care too much for Call of Duty or never played it, but intend on trying to get in to it, I'd recommend this one for the campaign. It touches on some interesting points, utilizes cool ideas for levels, and despite the occasional hollywood moments, manages to bring a small feeling of actual modern warfare in some of its missions.
Cream of the crop. If you're the type likes  to cream on the crop then it's for you.

An absolute masterpiece. This game is one of the greatest gaming experiences I've ever had; the story is layers-thick and presents new revelations beyond the first playthrough in subtle ways that will grip the player in Senua's world.  This is no game... it's an epic.

I can't even begin to describe the visceral and emotional journey this game took me on...It defies commonly used ways to describe a 'video game'.
This journey, this story, this grab you by the seat of the pants and thrust you into anothers world, perspective, and literally in the case of Senua, her madness...is purely and simply a materpiece in 21st century story telling.
The gameplay is seamlessly woven into the fabric of the setting, the history is amazingly well presented and I felt transported into the horrors of the dark ages, with all its despondancy and terror.  Confronted with Senua's stark future and alienating past I found myself with a deep seated empathy towards her that I have never, EVER, felt whilst maneouvering a protaganist through their story.
And this is so much more than that, the echoes of her mental illness and the way it is dealt with have lead me to take a good hard look at my own perceptions of this subject, how I percieve it and those who are living through it.  I don't mean to generalize in any capacity, quite on the contrary, this game has opened my eyes to how frightening diseases of the mind may be to those who have them.
But this journey also showcases the hope, the joy, the struggle and the love of a young woman stricken by the horrors she is confronted with both within and without her existence...it's like nothing I have ever experienced before in this medium.  This will stand along side some of the most thought provoking movies and novels I have read and reread, watched and rewatched.
I am looking forward to taking this journey with Senua again in the near future, but for now I need to digest, ruminate and  mourn the beautiful and tragic journey...words really can't describe it...
To the developers, artists, actors, performers, programmers and anyone else involved in the creation of this masterpiece, I applaud your effort and can only say I will be recommending this to all those who appreciate such deep and meaningful stories.

Skullgirls is a love letter to the fighting game genre and also one of the most creative and unique titles on the whole market. It has color palettes, poses, win quotes, and even movesets that are all references to video games and anime. At the same time it has an almost entirely female cast, all of which have drop dead gorgeous character designs, (even the men) and motifs that make them stand out, all of whom are beautifully animated with hand drawn sprites in game.
The gameplay resembles most other 2D fighters. You have six buttons for light, medium, and heavy punches and kicks, and all the characters have special moves that are executed by combining joystick motions with said buttons. Supers are pulled off in the same way as Marvel vs Capcom 1, by inputting a regular special move motion, but pushing more than one punch or kick button. This input in other fighting games would otherwise result in an EX move, which is a mechanic skullgirls doesn't use. And just like every other fighter, grabbing is done by pushing light punch and kick at the same time.
A unique feature of Skullgirls is that you can choose how many fighters you want to use each match. Most fighting games are 1v1; you and your oponent both pick one character. Some games like Marvel vs Capcom 1 & 2, have both players pick 2 characters, where they can then input assist moves from their other fighter, and will play as that fighter when their first one gets K.O'd. Then there's game like Capcom vs SNK 2 or Marvel vs Capcom 3 which have a 3v3 system, that functions the same way as 2v2s, only now  there is obviously one additional character that either player must K.O. in order to win. Skullgirls allows the player to pick any one of these systems, and not only that, but both players are not beholden to whichever mode the other chooses, allowing for 1v3s, 2v3s, 1v2s, and all the other previously established combinations. It's worth mentioning that Skullgirls' 1v1 mode functions in a manner resembling the Darkstalkers series, where the winner of each round does not have their health bar reset to full, and must continue with however much health they had at the end of the previous round, while the loser of the round still gets their health bar reset.
The comabt itself in skullgirls is fast paced because of the fact that the game is permanently in what many fighting games call turbo mode. This speeds up the gameplay, and because of the fact that every light move combos into the medium version of the same move, which THEN combos into the heavy version of the same move, combos are extremely fun to watch and even more fun to pull off. If you watch the top 8 at EVO from any year you'll notice that one combo can last an entire match, and that something like that is not even too uncommon. A unique mechanic in skullgirls is that if you get trapped it in an infinite by your oponent you character will start glowing pink. At this point pressing any button will free your character from the infinite. This forces players to mix up their combos, and deepens the meta game.
The story mode is told through still frame drawings similar to the likes of Street Fighter V, and centers around each girl attempting to find the skullheart, a item in the game's lore which can grant a wish, if the wish is pure. The events involve criss-crossing storylines between multiple factions including mafiosi, scientists, a cult, and the military. The setting could not be more up my alley with the 1920-30s-esque mob film atmosphere. It's even posible that similar to the likes of Super Mario 3, the entire game is a performance put on by the characters. This is supported by evidence like the announcer saying things like "everyone mind you marks" before matches, the film reel motif in the menu, and super combos being referred to as "blockbuster" attacks.
All of this is only helped by the perfect soundtrack. There are multiple jazzy tracks, (once again right up my alley) but also songs from many other genres for the different stages in the game. It is my second favorite video game OST of all time, and I possibly have spent more time listening to it than playing the actual game.
So a hand drawn game about cute girls running around a mob-themed setting, set to a Jazz soundtrack, in a fighting game with inviting but deep combat. For me the stars have alligned perfectly, and it's almost as if the game is directly pandering to me. Even if you're not as enthralled as I am at the very idea of a game with all these components existing, it really is more than the sum of its parts, and everyone should check it out.

Gaming has always been a thing my entire life. I grew up with the PlayStation 2 and the few games I had on the many computers I managed to get my hands on in my life before the discovery of got me to where I am today. I manage to play many genres from platforms to shooters, from simple sidescrollers to open world role playing games. With the help of steam, my options have been widened even further to the more meaningful games such as Lisa and Beeswing.

Now how does this relate to skull girls? To be honest I never really got engaged in the idea of fighting games. My first (and only proper) experience was Mortal Kombat for the PlayStation 3 but it was short lived after realizing that having to do tricky manoeuvres with the controller and winning constantly in story mode by button mashing was less engaging then dying over and over again and being determined to play again in Telleglitch: die more edition, ironically. The reason for this review you won’t see many on the steam store page is that it’s coming from an experienced first timer. I will say right now that it’s the best game to start in if you’re interested in the genre because of a proper, in-depth tutorial that you won’t see in many fighting games. But if you’re interested in the other details the game has, I will tell you the lows and highs of this game.

The game itself (if you somehow still haven't noticed) is a fighting game but with a fighting style different from Mortal Kombat and the old street fighter games. The fighting itself is based on the idea of juggling, when you hit someone they are put into a stun lock and the opponent can’t do anything about it, but you can do combos with more finesse and skill put into it then the previouse games i mentioned. But that's easier said than done. You have to put hours into a type of character you want if you get the most out of it because, unlike Mortal Kombat, if you attempt to button mash against an experienced player, you will get knocked out in less than 20 seconds and they would probably mock you, just like what happened to me. But the best thing about it is that you can’t be stun locked forever. If you do manage to do a long combo, the opponent can push you back which makes matches fair. fighters are very well diverse with different fighting styles for any player with a personal preference and all have their strength and weaknesses. You also going to need a controler and amazingly PS4 controlers are combatable with skullgirls and make gameplay smother and let you do faster combos. So it’s best to pick this game if you want to have a balanced fight and, don't worry about the DLC characters because the game gives you open beta which has access to all characters, unless you want story mode and speaking of which-

Like most fighting games, each character has their own story mode with different branches in the universe of skull girls. The story itself is surprisingly dark. The world when you see it for the first time is like what you see in a 1940's cartoon but the events in the game is what you would see in a movie like Goodfellas. It all looks good until the end where you can't trust your friends. If the game secretly slips in the violent imaginations from Neoscavenger (its text based if you didn't figure it out) the atmosphere wouldn't change that much. The stories for the characters always end abruptly so don't play if you want closure in your stories. the art style for the game is gorgeous and its best selling point is the animation. the game holds a Guinness world record for number of frames in each fighter. Each fighter with an average of 1439 frames. you can tell the developers really puts in a lot of heart for its presentation on the world.

To put this into perspective again, if you’re interested in the confusing and scary world of fighting games, get this game. If you bring friends around for some bonding moments the game might make you laugh with some of the characters moves (particularly peacock) if they haven't seen the story mode yet, or go online to get better and make some new friends like me. If you want a deep narrative or some enjoyable brain dead game play, go play Telleglitch, Ubermosh for some simple, yet engaging game play or Lisa or Beeswing for a meaningful and probably life changing experience.

This sad little game that I did not expect to get so emotional with is quite remarkable. The game at its core is generic and dull yet when you go past the introduction the dialogue between the main characters compels and intrigues you.

Taking place some time in the 2500s, you play as a space traveler who boards a single-person space shuttle bound for Alpha Centauri. Along with the traveler is the ship's artificially intelligent navigator known as Budapest who, in order to better interact with passengers, takes the form of a hologram of a young woman. The trip to Alpha Centauri starts off rather routine, but an encounter with meteoroids damages the ship and sends them off course. It is then that the traveler and Budapest must figure out what to do until a possible rescue in deep space.
This game is a kinetic novel, a type of visual novel with no branching story lines, only one ending, and no decisions required by the player. It can be played as quickly as the player can read it.
As it is the main purpose of a kinetic novel, I would say that the story is pretty good. As this is a rather short visual novel, I cannot say too much without going into spoilers, but suffice it to say that I found the story well written with an interesting theme about what it means to be human and to live. Not exactly the most original premise in science fiction works, but the game does a good job of its take on it.
The art itself is passable and pleasing enough to look at, even if it is more standard fare. I thought that the music could have been better as some of the tracks were rather grating to listen to on a loop during certain parts of the game.
Overall, I enjoyed this visual novel. For me, it took a little over an hour and a half to read. If you like visual novels and are looking for an enjoyable story, I would give this a recommend. After all, it is free so it is worth a read.

Palinurus is an agreeable two-hour tour through the cosmos with entertaining dialogue between the protagonist and his vessel's accompanying AI program. During the dialogue something happens. When does a computer program stop being just lines of code, and just what is it that makes a sentient being a sentient being? Reality can blur with cold infinity at your fingertips. In addition to the affable plot I also enjoyed the music selection which varied between classical and what I would describe as 70's-era "Dr. Who"-like synth-pop. All the music selections seemed to fit the moment. The art, while not widely varied, is very well done.
9.5/10. Will likely tour the cosmos again.

The gameplay, while being more limited, is also more focused, as each one of your weapons has their own individual direction on the d-pad instead of a wheel menu which pauses the game and takes you out of the experience. There is only one sword, which means you'll have to get better at the game instead of grinding for upgrades. There are also a lot less canned animations, which while being less pretty, is more satisfying in my eyes. I could go on, but the point is Assassin's Creed is a game that champions gameplay and we need more games like that.

After finishing the story, which was absurd and unbelievable, I decided I would only be playing this game for a review I will be preparing. This means going back and trudging through. Again. Overall, this game does not feel like it adds anything of value that wasn't in Wolfenstein: The New Order. While The New Order surprised me in giving B.J. character, something no other Wolfenstein game has ever done, and had a decent story, The New Colossus ruins everything by trying too hard to continue the series with it's main protagonist, even after the ending of the last game left him dying before rolling credits. The shame of it all is that the DLC clearly shows the devs are capable of producing a worthy new protagonist to fulfill B.J's role, and maybe if the game were built around said protagonist, the DLC characters themselves wouldn't feel so shallow, game play wise. It also felt like the game mocked me for saving Wyatt. My friend tells me he gets a badass gun for saving Fergus, whereas I got a gun I only ever touched when it was necessary to blow open doors that could only be opened by said gun. I attempted to use it in combat situations, but alas, the ridiculously over-powered Sturmgewehrs were the only guns worth using. Wyatt becomes a drug addict and also the most annoying video game character I have ever experienced. Considering I played some of the Gearbox titles, that's saying something. The peek and lean system felt broken for most of the game, as it felt too automated and would not allow me to peek around say, a column because the column stuck out on my side, so B.J. would peek around the little piece that stuck out instead of the whole column. This becomes a non-issue later on in the game where there is practically no cover and the little that is offered does not have weird pieces sticking out, so B.J. doesn't get confused as to what he's supposed to be peeking around. The 3 devices the game offers don't really bring a whole lot to the table. The ramshackles were inconsistent in dealing damage to enemies, as sometimes it would instagib enemies and other times, take 5 rams to kill them. It is also rare, as one can imagine, that running into enemies that have guns would be an effective tactic. The constrictor thing I hardly ever used, as it was a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to line it up properly so B.J. would actually go in the tiny little holes and there were so few of them anyway. The walker I never got. The uber-commanders are annoying, as the levels are just recycled story missions and the bosses have an absurd amount of health, along with being equipped with the Kampfpistole, which is a grenade launcher that deals a ton of damage. Overall, this game left me very disappointed.

Grab the Bottle is one of those games you play to have fun and kill time with only!
If you've ever played the famous mobile game snake, you'll see a lot of similarities between the two games except that the side of view and overal game perception differs!
Another huge plus is that the game follows a story, a story of a curious boy who likes to grab bottles! The soundtrack and the art style of the game give that specific vibe of slacking turning the game into a bottle worth grabbing!

Grab the Bottle is a quirky puzzle game in which the player must stretch their long, Snake-like arm through each level in order to obtain the titular object. A task simple enough in concept, but fiendishly difficult in execution.
The controls couldn’t be simpler, with only four buttons to master: steer left, steer right, grab item, and speed up the rate at which your arm travels (which you won’t be needing much, given that the game is quite fast and finicky enough). From the moment you give each level the thumb-up to begin, your arm continues to stretch out from its starting point until you either fail (by colliding with too many objects) or succeed (by grabbing your bottle after all other collectables are satisfied).
Yes, you heard me right: with the exception of the first level, the game requires you to collect a series of other items BEFORE the holy grail of the bottle itself. Again, this might sound easy enough, until you consider that your own arm is one of the many obstacles you can’t afford to collide with, and the only way to retract (and thereby undo) the twisted convolutions of your loopy appendage is to pick up yet another (non-collectable) type of object, which can be dropped at a strategically-chosen point in order to resume/redirect your arm’s forward motion.
If you think all that sounds kinda confusing, just wait ‘til you attempt to do it in real-time! Make no mistake about it: this is an unapologetic mind-♥♥♥♥ of a game. If you’re in the market for more of a no-brainer, I recommend any number of cheap “indie” horror games recently released to Steam (cheap shot, sorry)! Suffice it to say, this game’s idea of “puzzles” is a little more involved than simply finding a key and opening a door.
Trial-and-error is ultimately the name of the game in Grab the Bottle, unless you're one of those supremely gifted ♥♥♥♥ers who can solve a complex puzzle as soon as glance at it. For the rest of us plebs, this is a game requiring much patience; though once you work out the solution, you'll no doubt appreciate the intricacy and cleverness which went into the level design in front of you.
It's a smartly-made game for smart people. And while I generally fancy myself somewhere in this category, there's unfortunately different KINDS of intelligence, and puzzle-solving isn't one of my stronger suits. I do fair a little better, however, in the persistence stakes, and if you think you sound anything like me, you'll probably enjoy this game in small-ish bursts (longer ones are only liable to lead to keyboard- or controller-smashing antics, and nobody wants that).

Which isn't to say that all the "blame" lies squarely in my court, and that this is a flawlessly-executed product. Ironically, for a game which intends to follow the life of a character from babyhood to senior years, Grab the Bottle does have a somewhat uneven learning curve. To wit: I found levels one to four a relative cinch – once I'd sussed the mechanics out sufficiently – whereas level five was quite the crazy challenge. A chimpanzee of slightly above average intelligence and hand-eye coordination could probably pull off the first four stages, no probs…but good luck, Lancelot Link, with all those steps you have to carefully plot out and smoothly pull off once we hit the fifth level.
I mean, sure, I did get through this level entirely of my own accord, but only after a good fifteen or twenty failed attempts (and a severe temptation to just say “♥♥♥♥ it” and fall back on a walkthrough)! Compare this to my two to four attempts on the prior levels, and you've got a pretty good idea what I mean when I say the learning curve is a tad sudden and steep. Add to this the fact that you only get two "hit points" per level - meaning your arm can bump into a "wrong" on-screen object only twice before you have to restart the level altogether - and even my abovementioned theory of trial-and-error becomes difficult in practice.
Even getting back to the point you were last time to try something different can often be a challenge, and frustration can subsequently ensue. It's definitely a one-or-two-levels-at-a-time proposition for all bar the most skilled and/or disciplined of players.

Aesthetically-speaking, there's certainly nothing to complain about. The visuals have a charming and highly appropriate cartoon-ish feel, and the music and sound effects follow suit. ‘Nuff said.
Grab the Bottle definitely aims first and foremost to be a “fun” game for all ages, and the only trait which threatens to derail this objective is the difficulty level (and complete lack of difficulty settings herein; a mode with more than two “hit points” would be much appreciated). Novel, challenging, and realistically priced for what it offers. A very solid first effort by Kamina Dimension Ltd, and then some.
Verdict: 8/10.

While the game is definitely unique and original, that did not make it fun to play for me.
In this puzzle game, you can infinitely stretch your arm to, surprise, grab the bottle. It reminds of a snake mechanics a bit: your arm extends as far as it can, it cannot bump into obstacles and it cannot crash into itself. After you complete extra level goals (like picking up additional bonuses), you can go and pick the bottle.
•	Style: the game’s style is well defined. Its style reminds of the comic books from 50’s: you know, dotted gradient, combined with colorful, but a bit simplistic images. The way this is done is really commendable, not one element feels off.
•	The Music and Sounds supplement the style, making experience more intense.
•	The humor: the ever-extending arm seems like an absurd thing, but the humor / comic intros before the levels are done well. I found it very refreshing and in that sense, the game really feels “Indie”.
•	The challenge is one and the same on every level. Sure, the elements are differently positioned, but the mechanics are introduced way too slowly. The beginning feels monumentally slow, where you go through easy challenged that try to teach you the game. Maybe the game gets better later, but I’ve played for ~30 minutes and it could not grab my attention during that time.
The game has good attention to detail and overall the style is very well-defined, but ultimately felt slow / not interesting to play for me. You can take a look if you are a puzzle fan, but in that case I’d recommend waiting for 50% discount.
Usually I try to give advice for developers on how to improve the game, but I don’t think I have something to say here: the production quality is good, but the gameplay just does not seem fun and diverse. And this should have probably been understood during prototyping phase. Perhaps it could have been worth trying to speed it up somewhat, both in gameplay (give less space, but make arm slower? The button that speeds up the arm barely helps). As for now, it just looks like a slowed-down snake with some twists.
Just buy it, play it and cry.

grab the Bottle. In short, the name of the game kind of tells you about the gameplay. Sounds easy? It isn’t!
In this game you control a hand with a looooong arm. The controls are easy, moving left and right, grabbing and speed up. But what seems easy on the first look is more than hard on the second.
You have to grab a bottle each level, but there are different obstacles and other items you have to get first before you have access to the bottle. If you hit the wall, solid objects or even your arm while maneuvering around your hand begins to hurt, if you hit something once more you have to start the level from the beginning.
I like the idea of the game. Each level is a photo in a photo album and you begin back when you were a baby, grabbing a milk bottle. As you become older your hand grows (what makes it harder not to hit something) and you prefer other drinks. Currently the game ends when you are still a boy. So we can await much more content and levels. The developer will soon add a multiplayer mode and more single player levels (teen, young adult, middle-aged and senior).
The music is also okey, it doesn’t distract you from concentrating and thinking how to solve that one far too difficult level. Some of them are really difficult and I was sitting there, thinking, getting frustrated because nothing works, tried different ways, over and over again. (at one moment I even tried to find a walkthrough, but aren’t any!) But in the end I managed to solve all of them somehow. Though I think that sometimes I did not do it as it was intended. I even managed to win that crazy level in the end (I began to think, that this was a joke and I’d never win it). This game has no achievements yet (they will add them soon), but the end of each level felt like an achievement already!
There is only one thing in the end. The scene in the last level moves (trees, background) but the “comic-dots” don’t, this could lead to dizziness (I had to rest a bit before making more attempts).
Positive:
+ nice idea with the stretching arms
+ photo album and comic style
+ very challenging
+ controller support
+ soon there will be more levels and multiplayer
+ soon there will be achievements and trading cards
Negative:
- last level caused dizziness
- there could be more level (but they will be added soon)
So all in all this is a really nice and challenging game and if you like to solve puzzles and have some spare time I’d definitely recommend this to you. And as soon as they add multiplayer, more levels and achievements this game will become even better!

Grab the Bottle:
~~~~~~~~~~~~

Wouldn’t it be nice, maybe slightly lazy to a degree, to be born with extendable arms? Well, you could become a superhero, but that’s too cliché in my opinion. No, something far more important! What about the ability to satisfy your thirst at any given time! Need some water, milk or a soda and the fridge is in the other side of the house. No worries mate, there goes my extendable arm to grab the bottle!
Grab the bottle is a casual / puzzle game where you use your stretchable arm throughout levels to reach your main objective, which is to grab a bottle of liquid substance.

As this game is currently on early access, there are about 20 levels to complete at this stage and they gradually increase in difficulty as you progress through them. For the first couple of stages, you will be in your pram, as are all babies born with this type of ability. The liquid you are looking for at that early stage of life is milk. But before you grab the bottle of milk, you must pick up all your dummies within the level.
The trick is to make sure you are not touching items more than twice; tables, chairs, televisions etc - things that can hurt your hand. If that happens you will restart the level. How do you identify which one of the articles to avoid? If an object is part of the background picture, it will have dots over it and your hand will be safe. However, if the entity is prominent and without dots then make sure to avoid it. Another point that’s important to mention is that your arm will also become an obstacle as it elongates. The only way to make it retract is to pick up the objects emanating a blue light, which, by the way, are part of the puzzle. Examples are tomatoes, cheeses and boxes of nails that can be dropped on other object such as plates or small wooden blocks in order to solve the puzzles. Why, you may ask? That, you will have to figure out for yourself.
I like the artwork and the puzzles can be tricky. Control-wise, I use a gamepad and it is pretty responsive. I look forward to seeing further content.
Positives:

-	Good artwork
-	Challenging and well-designed puzzles
-	Responsive controls
-	Multiplayer mode to be added in further updates
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	No Achievements or trading cards
-	Need more content (levels)
This is a solid early access puzzle game. I can’t wait to see more content

Good: Wasteland, Fallout,  Fallout 2,  Fallout New Vegas, Wasteland 2
Bad: Fallout 3, Fallout 4

Don't go into Fallout 3 expecting a deep RPG-experience like FO1 and 2, you'll likely be upset with your purchase.
If you're looking for a vast/interesting open world, filled with secrets and quests, this game may be worth your time and money.
I'll start with the cons:
Fallout 3s perk system is (MOSTLY) filled with what you wouldn't really consider to be perks; a good example being 'Daddy's Boy' which increases your medicine skill by five points. These perks are plentiful and outweigh the more interesting stuff.
It's also possible with the right patience and know-how to reach level 30 (maximum level with Broken Steel DLC) with every Skill and Special stat at maximum...
Critics have complained of the world being Grey/dreary. This is all down to personally preference, of course.
Guns are hit or miss. You'll likely find yourself irritated with the lack of accuracy, early game - feeling the need to rely on VATS. (VATS stops time and allows you to place shots, requiring 'Action Points to use')
The positives:
If you're playing blind, perhaps never played one of the Fallout series, you'll likely fall head over heals for this. The open world is vast and great fun to explore. Many interesting settlements to discover (you won't need to craft the only interesting places in the game.)
Quests are done well, no repetitive nonsense, good and evil choices are plentiful, variety is well done.
There seems to be a never-ending number of Random Encounters - you could play 200 hours and not see them all. These are some of the most bizarre and funny stuff in the game.
Many, many unique items, some very cool (and goofy) stuff to be found!
The five DLC packs are worth it. Each add a considerable amount of time to the game with 'Operation Anchorage' being the weakest link, it's still a good time.
Buying Game of the Year is a huge bargain over the price of just buying vanilla.
With GOTY you get: -The Pitt
-Operation Anchorage
-Broken Steel (overhauls the endgame)
-Point Lookout
-Mothership Zeta
In summary: The game has flaws... Vastly outweighed by positives.

What is it with computer nerds and techno music?
Don't get me wrong: electronic music is a passion of mine, and can be used to considerable atmospheric effect. This effect, unfortunately, goes well out the window the second one puts a jarringly obnoxious thumpy-thump beat to it. Add to this some understandably limited production values and the single LOUDEST music mix I have ever heard in a product released to Steam, and neither my ears nor headphones were off to a good start with this "game".
Fortunately my computer does have a volume switch, and the music tracks after the initial one were actually quite charming and refreshingly beat-free. But they do say that first impressions linger, so it's a good thing I'm such a mutha-♥♥♥♥in' professional and can get past such things, at least enough to be "mostly objective. Mostly" (that's a recent and direct quote from a lecturer/marker of mine in the arts degree I'm currently studying; so if SHE gets to be labelled a "professional", so do I, ♥♥♥♥ you all).
Immersion-breaking beginnings aside, the rest of this product is actually quite aesthetically-pleasing. The artwork is endearing if unexceptional, and the writing is unusually good for a visual novel.
Yes, you did hear me right: unusually good FOR A VISUAL NOVEL. You wouldn't expect it, but honestly, most of these things read like they were written by an especially precocious fourteen year-old (at best), or someone for whom neither English nor written communication skills are a forte (at worst). Unless your visuals are going to switch with every single click of a button, you'd best make sure your VN writer's way with words is at least comparable to that of a lower-level fiction writer. This VN certainly has no problems in that area, and even boasts moments of genuine wit and charm ("it was essentially a primitive form of an escape pod, except roomier and less reliable"). Very nice work, indeed.
So what about the "story" itself? Hmmm. Well, first up, you need to know that this ISN'T an "interactive novel". It's a "kinetic novel", in which you don't make any choices; you just click through a story which unveils in a completely linear and non-negotiable fashion. A slightly spiffier way of presenting a short story or novella, in other words. Obviously this will be fine for some, and a deal-breaker for others.
As long as you're not in the latter category, the story of this VN is, I'm pleased to say...actually pretty darned good (if a tad on the sappy side)! I suspect it's not too much of a spoiler to say it has something to do with the "nature" of Artificial Intelligence, and the curious effects of the cold, vast loneliness of space...so if that sounds like your cup of tea (or, er, tube of space-paste), there really isn't much to hold you back. Especially when the frigger is FREE.
All told, not a bad little effort at all (I even found myself getting the teeniest bit teary by the end)! Just be sure to have the volume turned way DOWN at the start, lest your precious eardrums should be decimated by the initial ill-advised bursts of ruthless techno-thumping.
Verdict: 7.5/10.
