Assassin's Creed is a strange game. The game is built up around assassinations, as you might have guess, but the actual assassination sequences are rather dull, linear and poorly designed and not really worth doing at all. The rest of the gameplay however, the gameplay that's been put in there for no reason other than to claim it's an open world game, is specatular. Running around the cities, jumping from building to building, evading guards is one of the best open world experiences I have had since Prototype.
Your are put into the shoes of Miles Desmond who, through the magical wonder of a machine called "The Animus" get to live the life of his ancestors, or in particular, this one ancestor who happens to be a 12th. century assassin during the crusades. I guess they got lucky when he didn't have to live through the life of that other ancestor that was a 15th. century bar wench.
The story gets quite a bit complicated as the life of Miles and his ancestor gets intertwined in a web of conspiracies and ancient secret societies. You know, the usual stuff. It's not a case of bad writing but it does get a little contrived towards the end and the lack of any strong and memorable characters hurts it a lot.
The fighting is mostly a case of parry and counter facing numerically superior enemies who are, fortunately for you, quite weak. Learning the tempo to this is quite easy however and you'll get bored quickly with the regular combat.
The assassinations, performed mostly with the trademarked "I cut my finger off for laughs" hidden blade, are usually a scripted sequence and often involved a chase scene of some sort. It's not particularly interesting and the amount of fighting and running that needs to be done means you'll never really feel like an assassin.
The open world is where the action is at, the movement is fluid and quick and the scenery is beautiful. Running around the city being chased by a slew of guards is open world at it's best and I'd recommend the game almost purely on that fact alone.
When it all comes down to it, it's a game that fails at what it's trying to do and succeeds at what it's not. It's a strange combination but still a good open world play, even if what was originally intended as the core gameplay is somewhat disappointing.

I don't usually write reviews of games, but as a person who has struggled with mental illness in my own life, I have to say--please buy this game. I followed this project all the way through development via the dev diaries, but I was still a bit leery of the final product really doing justice to the experience of living with a mental illness. But the end product is stunning--and it's not 'just' about mental illness, either. It's something better--a daring, artistic story that happens to be about someone who struggles with mental illness. And it's gorgeous, and well-written, and made by a team who really cares about the industry, their work, and their audience. And one final shoutout--this game can be overwhelming, and I cannot emphasize enough how admirable it is that the developer included a link to mental health resources at hellbladehelp.info.

It's ironic that the title of this game is Remember Me, because the developers and writers seem to forget the theme of the game within an hour of booting it up. Between an unfocused story line, weak dialogue, a hamfisted approach to making the game cinematic, a repetitive combat system, a poorly thought out exploration system (exploration is downplayed because the game is completely linear but there are little pick ups for those willing to take a few steps off the path, some of them flesh out the lore of the game, which could just be available to the player from the start) and a basically non-existent attempt to blend the story and the game aspects, the only real thing going for Remember Me is the distinct visual style. Take a Rube Goldberg device, the game Snake, Mister Fantastic's day off and throw it all in a blender. What do you get? You get Grab the Bottle.

Grab the bottle, aside from being the worst AA catchphrase, is also a puzzle game. The games mechanics are rather simple, use your infinitely stretchy hand to navigate terrain, puzzles, and grab an assortment of bottles. While obviously far easier said then done your hand is also incredibly sensitive. Hitting the wall or objects in the area are a big no-no, do it twice and you have to start from go with all your progress in the level reset.
While the beginnings levels of this twisted puzzler are rather simple, the ante is progressively raised. Side object collectibles will impede your path to a good drink. Want that bottle of milk? Collect various pacifiers while keeping in mind you cannot cross your own path or pull your arm back manually. Where the real daunting challenge of this game lies is in predicting yourself and having a plan from beginning to end. Personally I found this very difficult to wrap my head around in later levels.
One level has you guiding your hand for a tasty bottle of soda through a roller-coaster. Aside from the fact the background is moving, you have to grab items that roll back your hand and then thread the needle again through all the wheels and doors of the coaster. I raged a bit, as tapping anything slightly with your hands sends it flying back and gets you into more trouble rather easily. You are only allowed two mistakes, so expect to repeat levels quite a bit.
Thankfully, the game does feature full controller support and  the controls are simple and intuitive, I didn't feel like I was cheated at any point. The hit box on the hand is a hit and miss sometimes but I will chalk that up to Early Access. The tutorials are rather relaxed in Grab The Bottle as well, which can become frustrating in later levels. Bombs and destructible environments are introduced but it never really tells you how these work but lets you figure it out yourself.
Experimentation is required to figure what you need to do and in what order; which leads to a bit of repetitive death. The game itself is a great mind tickler and I found it quite challenging. What more do you want in a puzzle game?
Well, if you do happen to want more, the developer is planning on more levels beyond the current twenty two. Example of level ideas include: dropping ingredients into a blender in the correct order or actually working a Rube Goldberg device.. The developer has also mentioned a two to four player local multiplayer with various game modes. Steam Cards & Achievements are on their way as well.
The games vintage comic book aesthetic is odd, but Grab the Bottle is odd itself. The level design does take very well to this aesthetic and flows very smoothly. Just expect plenty of dots and scenery that looks like it came from the 1950's. One thing I have to mention is the terrifying faces of these characters. They look like they got hit a shovel, twice.
Weird faces aside, Grab The Bottle is a clever little puzzle game. There is more content coming so a full review will have to wait. Despite that, I feel comfortable with recommending the game if you love puzzle games. It has some really challenging levels to challenge the mind and the game is in a solid state. There is one minor bug I ran into that causes your hand to become invincible, but this only occurred once.  Coming in at $9.99 with more content to come go ahead and see if you can wrap your mind, or more correctly hand, around this one.

Okay, overall, I had fun with this game. I'm certainly not feeling like I was really cheated out of my money, and I can think of several things that make me recommend this game to the community as a whole... That said, this game still lacks a lot of polish and when you carefully look at the game as you play, it's not hard to see that this game wasn't given the full potential that it coulda been.
The story is interesting, and it certainly has me going forward, and there's a lot of material that the game can play with when it comes to the premise that memories can be downloaded and shared just like MP3s today, not to mention be deleted altogether... but it still falls kinda short, like there was supposed to be more that the game could do, but the devs had to cut it short for one reason or another.
The gameplay itself is solid, but lacks some polish. There are moments where you're tasked with 'remixing' memories to change the result, and by extension alter the behavior of that particular character, but they are too few and far between. In addition, the control scheme for these events is somewhat finicky, and it gets frustrating when you have to keep rewinding to change things. Moving about in the game is fairly easy, and anyone familiar with games like Uncharted or Assassins Creed would easily latch onto the standard set of movement mechanics without much trouble. The combat is both interesting and a curse. The combo creation system is a great idea in theory, but the game limits you to changing the effects of the buttons rather than altering the combos themselves. (i.e. you will always have a combo 'X-X-X', and you can alter the last two 'x' presses to any combination of 'heal' 'deal extra damage' or 'reduce cooldowns') It's sometimes difficult to get the right combo going, and it is rather hard to pull off a specific combo when you're in a large crowd (the game claims you can dodge and keep the combo happening, but I haven't had it happen often enough to be reliable.) Finally, there are enemies later game that are really best dealt with by using special attacks, but when you use one, there's a cooldown on that ability that's upwards of 2 minutes.... yes you can use the 'reduce cooldown' effects in combos to lower that, but when you're dealing with enemies you can't attack because it would be either countered, you'd take damage for hitting them, or they're just plain invisible.... yeah, it gets tired quick.
I enjoy this game, I really like the story that's running through it, and I don't feel cheated out of my money. Anyone looking for a brawler-style game won't really be unhappy with it. However, I really feel sad because this game coulda been SOOO much more as a open-world game. I could see a lot of potential in this setting through that. There's a lot of things that you can read about, but would have been so much better if you could GO and SEE these sights.
If it's on sale, go ahead and splurge a little, it'll be fun... But if story-driven games with bugs and less-than-optimal polish bother you, yeah, not really your cup of tea.

Grab the Bottle is a fresh breeze from the field of puzzle games, loaning its main gameplay element from the classic game Snake. You play as a stretching arm trying to reach for that precious bottle of your favourite drink while having to collect, move and break objects that are on your way.
My first concern was if this game would fall in the category of casual puzzle games that are better suited for mobile platforms. With this in mind, I started playing Grab the Bottle and after the introduction levels I was positively surprised. Each level provides you with new challenges, making you progress either with trial and error or carefully planning your way to the finish line. No matter what's your approach, it takes some time to solve each puzzle and it really feels good when you get them done.
The visual style of Grab the Bottle is strongly influenced by the 50s comics and posters and truly, most of the time playing this game I feel like browsing a MAD magazine. The sound design and music go well along with the visuals, although at some point one of the music tracks got a little repetitive.
I found myself a little disappointed because this game doesn't have a grading system to tell you how well you did each level. I would really like a timer or an indicator for how long I had to stretch my arm to get to the bottle. This would give the player more sense of accoplishment and add more replay value for the levels.
When it comes to early access, the game seems to work just fine. I found some bugs when I really, really tried and reported them to the developers. But hey, that's what early access is for!

I've had this game for a very long time. First - when it was still in early early access, it grabbed my attention because, let's face it, OPEN WORLD LEGO BUILDER!!! 'Nuff said. At that time it was very rough, unpolished, unoptimized, but still playable. There was an open world to explore, stuff to collect, blueprints to discover, and limitless area to build upon.

Fast forward exactly 2 years until now - the game gets nicely optimized, works much more smoothly, there's a proper intro, an adventure mode got added; generally it looks and works way better than before and I'm hyped about the adventure mode. But...
Once I entered the game I was greeted by two crashes that made the game return to desktop without any error. The problem is known, from what I've seen, but that does not change the bitter taste that's left in my mouth. On top of that the game seems to be made with controller in mind - keyboard/mouse users beware, you're in for a weird camera behavior (which takes away a lot of fun in my taste). I don't remember if there are key bind options even (if there are - they're well hidden).
Summary: I wish for the game to be enjoyable - the errors and bad design makes it not enjoyable. You can't put LEGO in front of title and hope it does the work. I wish I hadn't bought it in the first place.

This is a puzzle game, where your objective is to... grab the bottle while dodging hazards and environment. The hand behaves very much like the old ''snake'' games, you cant go through your own hand, and you cant back out, unless you pull on an object.
Normal level, consists of collecting a bottle opener (or multiple) and grabbing the bottle in the end. Game is challenging from the start, which is refreshing in the age of handholding games. Theres a good variety in the puzzles and I never felt I was doing the same puzzle again on my playthrough.
Only real gripe I have with the game is the randomness of physics on some levels. You might be doing the puzzle correctly, but something under the hood goes *stranger things* and you fail the puzzle.

Grab the Bottle. In short, the name of the game kind of tells you about the gameplay. Sounds easy? It isn’t!
In this game you control a hand with a looooong arm. The controls are easy, moving left and right, grabbing and speed up. But what seems easy on the first look is more than hard on the second.
You have to grab a bottle each level, but there are different obstacles and other items you have to get first before you have access to the bottle. If you hit the wall, solid objects or even your arm while maneuvering around your hand begins to hurt, if you hit something once more you have to start the level from the beginning.
I like the idea of the game. Each level is a photo in a photo album and you begin back when you were a baby, grabbing a milk bottle. As you become older your hand grows (what makes it harder not to hit something) and you prefer other drinks. Currently the game ends when you are still a boy. So we can await much more content and levels. The developer will soon add a multiplayer mode and more single player levels (teen, young adult, middle-aged and senior).
The music is also okey, it doesn’t distract you from concentrating and thinking how to solve that one far too difficult level. Some of them are really difficult and I was sitting there, thinking, getting frustrated because nothing works, tried different ways, over and over again. (at one moment I even tried to find a walkthrough, but aren’t any!) But in the end I managed to solve all of them somehow. Though I think that sometimes I did not do it as it was intended. I even managed to win that crazy level in the end (I began to think, that this was a joke and I’d never win it). This game has no achievements yet (they will add them soon), but the end of each level felt like an achievement already!
There is only one thing in the end. The scene in the last level moves (trees, background) but the “comic-dots” don’t, this could lead to dizziness (I had to rest a bit before making more attempts).
Positive:
+ nice idea with the stretching arms
+ photo album and comic style
+ very challenging
+ controller support
+ soon there will be more levels and multiplayer
+ soon there will be achievements and trading cards
Negative:
- last level caused dizziness
- there could be more level (but they will be added soon)
So all in all this is a really nice and challenging game and if you like to solve puzzles and have some spare time I’d definitely recommend this to you. And as soon as they add multiplayer, more levels and achievements this game will become even better!

TUG or The Un-named Game is a Survival/Crafting game. You play as a Seed. Seeds have a blue gem embedded in the back of their left hand and are genderless. This later will be an important part of the game. In TUG you can craft an assortment of different items to aid you in everything from farming to combat and even using alchemy and magic.
Currently you have two status bars, Health and Energy. Doing various tasks will use up your energy and require you to eat to refill it. Health is lowered by creatures that attack you or eating poisen mushrooms.
You have the ability to sprint, although not unlimited. Sprinting lasts longer in TUG than most other games and the Sprint Meter refills at a very decent rate.
You can use such items as wood chips, mushrooms and bone meal among others, to brew potions.
The growth potion will allow you to grow crops faster and even turn a baby animal into an adult. (Both of these take time).
You can currently breed goats and cats and even breed them together to get the awesome cogat!
TUG features the unique ability for the character to age, get stronger, faster and even fatter. This is in the very early stages and needs more time before it is finished.
One of the more recent updates has improved biome generation greatly. Biomes feel real and authentic. There is a large assortment of plant life and natural resources.
The game is decently optimized but is lack luster in some areas. You may experience lag spikes or a constant low fps unless you have a decent computer. The devs are working on this and will hopefully have TUG ready for a wider range of computers soon.
Sound effects and graphics are fairly good and offers a unique experience. The higher the settings you can use, the better overall experience you'll have playing.
Currently TUG offers stone age to the bronze age but lacks in content. You'll find it hard to keep going after 15 hours or so, some never make it that far while others make it hundreds of hours.
I recommend purchasing on sale around $10 until more content and optimizations go into the game. Don't get me wrong, I like this game. I would even say I love it but if I'm going to be honest I have to tell both sides.
Watch some videos, check out some reviews and heck, even try purchasing the game and playing for an hour. Steam will refund no questions asked if you've not had the game longer than 14 days or played more than 2 hours.
If you're not comitted to playing an early access game with an prototype level of content and willing to deal with lost saves and bugs, I'd wait. Early Access after all is about helping guide the game to the finish line.
I'd rate the following:
Concept 10/10
Graphics 7/10
SFX 6/10
Content to Price Ratio 4/10

This is a good game.  Not great but good.
You play as 2 protagonists where one tries to escape the confines of Alcatraz while the other finds the location of the loot in San Francisco.  The game is supposedly non-linear where you make some moral decisions during the gameplay; although most of the gameplay will play out one way.  The game is meant for mature audiences only.
A lot of small positives about the game:
-The game has a nice soundtrack.
-Voice acting is good.
-A great setting in the 50's era, post WWII, post prohibition era, where a beatnik generation is making headway into the 60's.  A good cartoony art despite the game's maturity content.
A few major positives to the game:
-I like playing 2 protagonists where the story of each feels different from each other.  Gameplay mechanics are still the same but story, setting, and character feels different.  It reminds me of
where you play two characters but other than character, everything feels the same.
-Although not vast, there is a bit of open exploration in this game.  I think modern point-and-click games follow this format anyway but it still feels refreshing compared to the very old point-and-click games.
-Puzzles aren't too challenging and this may be a good thing.  Compared to Daedalic's other game
, using items to progress the story aren't as frustrating and confusing for most of the gameplay.  I had to use the walkthrough  once for the entire game.
, I had to use the walkthrough many times.
The game is without its own faults.  There are some major bugs to the game.
-A few times, I encountered situations where the game "locks up".  This occurred in a couple of dialogue situations.  The animations on screen are still moving but every function in the game appears disabled.  I can't even exit to the menu.  I would have to go to the task manager to exit the game and start over.  Thankfully, you can save any time and the bug doesn't appear a second time when you start-up the game again.
-Another big bug is that the achievements don't work for some reason; fortunately, I wasn't achievement hunting when playing this game, but it's a shame I couldn't unlock a single one.
-Although not a bug, I didn't feel the moral choices were significant enough to feel like I was in a dilemma.  Sometimes these choices involve trust between the two protagonists.  The problem with this is that I'm playing both characters and the truth behind each protagonists are either revealed or chosen by the player.  By this, hypothetically speaking, if Joe arrives at a situation whether to trust Christine with the money, I would know if she is trustworthy or not since I play her also.
At the end of it all, it is a good game in the point-and-click genre.  I'd recommend it based on the positives.

Another solid adventure game by Daedalic. I wouldn't put it in the same class as the greats, but it is overall a decent adventure game. Its biggest selling points are the setting, the soundtrack, and the backdrops. The game looks great, and I didn't have any technical issues beyond a few nitpicks. Unlike many of their other games, this one opts to use 3D models with 2D backgrounds.
The puzzles are fairly straightforward, and will probably not pose a particular challenge for seasoned adventurers. The characters are suprisingly likeable for the most part. I particularly liked Joe's segments, as they showed off his technical knowledge while fleshing out his backstory. A word of warning, this game deals with a lot of adult subject matter, so it's probably not an appropriate purchase for a younger audience. Sex, drugs, crime, execution-style murder, fellatio, prostitution, etc. Most of it is inexplicit, but it's still worth mentioning.
If I had to nitpick, I have two minor issues with the game. While the 3D models are stylistically fine, though exaggerated, certain scenes were particularly jarring. The protagonists generally looked great in every setting, but certain minor characters looked terrible in their closeup scenes. It gave me Leisure Suit Larry vibes(the 3D ones). I'm not sure if this was due to lighting or low quality modeling, but it was immediately noticeable. The art gallery owner in particular is one that sticks out. I think the game as a whole could have benefitted from a different shading or lighting model, as the 3D models stick out like a sore thumb when placed against the beautiful backgrounds.
My other nitpick has to do with the achievements. They are broken in some way, where the game won't register any achievements without fiddling with the exe's compatability settings, or running as administrator. I finished the entire game and didn't unlock a single achievement. I was forced to fiddle with the game a bit and then rerun the game to unlock everything I should have gotten on the first pass.

About 8 hours of point and click, even if counting the little time spent for rewinds due to buggy user interface (UI). The UI stops reacting to mouse clicks and/or visually breaks otherwise, and this seems to plague mostly the beginning of the game, causing great confusion for some players. But if you can live past the rather rare random UI freakouts, it's all worth the time. At one spot I was able to get the UI fixed by leaving area and returning. One other was that I had to quit the game with Alt+F4 because there simply was no other option, as there was no graphical UI (GUI) elements at all, while nothing reacted to clicks and keypresses had no effect (except the mentioned).
Puzzles are not anything majorly difficult, it was mostly soft flythrough for me with some occasional points where I had to stop for a moment to scratch my head. Even more cool is that you can get past some situations with several ways, greatly reducing the possibility of getting stuck.
One thing I kept constantly forgetting, was that commonly thru the game it's not enough that you have an item in your inventory, you actually have to give it to a person/object to trigger wanted conversation/action. Usually this led into going thru short conversations/monologues yet again. But that was my fault and problem.
One suprising, and in a way somewhat amusing, feature of the game is that it's graphically heavy. I couldn't have full graphics with 1600x900 resolution, because even the menu-view was painful to use - mouse response was heavily lagged and GUI elements moved lagging. So I ended up with 1280x720 with medium-quality graphics, but I must say that I didn't see it ruining anything. On the other hand, I'm currently playing with a cheap-end laptop with external screen.
The most annoying was the constant loading-screen with Christine. Merely opening the town map required it, and if you forgot something, returning to the point where you left required full-time loading. But luckily the loading-times were in seconds mostly, so it wasn't end of the world.
Overall, I'd say that it was worth it.

The game's main selling point - every frame in the spritework oozes with personality and the hand-painted stages set the mood of the fights just as well.
Homages to many other forms of media are frequent in the form of animation and character designs. Prominent are 2D fighters such as Street Fighter: 3rd Strike and Guilty Gear, while the gameplay is heavily based on Marvel Vs. Capcom 2's combo-centricity.
While fighting games generally have inputs made for joysticks in mind, the game is manageable on the keyboard. Most of the special and super moves don't rely on complex execution and negative-edging is optimized just enough for most moves to come out as they're intended.
Systems like the IPS and Dizzy system help make fight less of single-player matches by restricting combo length and repetitiveness. TODs are practically non-existent even in high-level matches, allowing more opportunities for counterplay.
The online playerbase is fairly sparse, so your mileage may be limited if you don't have dedicated sparring partners.
The devs are also awesome as heck. Been following the community since it's release 3 years or so and it has been an interesting ride. The game itself has also gone through tons of balance tweaks since then and the end result's pretty nifty.

It's hard for me to not recommend this game to every single passing human being I encounter. This game has been part of my childhood since it was first released.
If I could give a rough estimate of how many hours I put into just the 360 version alone, I'd have to say about 800 hours. The world is so expansive and enormous. And this isn't even touching the New Vegas world which is even larger and more varied.
Even for its 9 years of age, it still holds up pretty well graphically, especially compared to it's successor Fallout 4. It doesn't run well on newer Windows platforms, so let that be a warning.
The game comes with many bugs that, to this day, have not been fixed. The game world has an ugly green tint on everything. There are many flaws with the combat being solely third person/skewed camera. As par for the course, with any Bethesda-developed game, there are mods that fix mostly all of these issues. Modding this game is the sole reason alone to own it on PC.
Fallout 3 also does another thing well - its DLC. Very few games follow this type of DLC routine anymore, where we would get an entire new section of a map and a story for a relatively cheap price - rather than paying upwards of $20 for map packs, or weapon packs, etc..
Buy this game. Even wait for a sale if you have to. I don't even care if you rarely touch it anytime soon, because keeping it in your library means something. It means that once the gaming industry has come to a figurative crash and every RPG and singleplayer game is tainted with microtransactions and DLC, you can come back and truly enjoy an old classical experience like no other. The same goes double for New Vegas.
Show Bethesda what we want, which is an RPG, not an FPS with paid mods.

Love the game so far. Only played survival mode, which is frustrating and difficult. There are no pop-ups, but there is an infopedia in the options, so unless you like to read, you're kind of on your own as far as learning goes.
Mining and scanning is fun and engaging, simple as it is, seeing as how your survival depends on accruing enough resources to recharge your shields and life support, being on a clock makes the game a bit more thrilling.
Exploration is clearly the main draw of the game. The landscapes are vast and varied, with tons of structures, crates, flora and fauna, and terrain features to keep you interested wherever you go. It's fun to watch little scamps or giant herbivores romp around the planet, and to run from the giant predators.
The intergalactic map is beautiful, but the controls are a bit annoying, as you'd expected to have a free motion mouse, but instead you must use keyboard keys to navigate; you cannot use the map to set a waypoint, only warp drive, nor does it show the names of the planets. Kind of lame.
Trading is interesting. Prices vary by locale, and fluctuate based on your sales and time. Traders frequently come and go from satellite, freighter, and space ports, providing tons of plutonium, zinc, titanium, thanium9, and suspension fluid.
Dog fighting is a serious hassle, as many of the small fugitive vessels move more quickly than even your starter ship.
The narrated dialogue is immersive and descriptive, it very realistically depicts what interactions between various sentient species would be like, kind of like in Mass Effect, shedding light on certain mannerisms and common gestures of each species and sometimes providing unique dialogue responses for each alien.
The only nuissances I've found thus far are one planet where it's colder outside during the day and warmer during the night, can't possibly think of an explanation; and the inventory and options menu. When in the wilderness, it defaults to your ship instead of your exosuit, and each time you change the menu tab, the cursor resets to the middle. Extremely frustrating.
Oh, and don't forget, at the "Initialization" screen, you have to press "E" to continue ;)

As many people know No Mans's Sky did not fully deliver at launch and was missing many promised features, many including myself were dissapointed.
Thing is however, if you wanted the game you saw in the trailers then that is the game your going to get.
With the latest patch 1.3 the game is infinitley better. It now has many features promised at launch and then some.
Here are some of the features in trailers that didnt make it into the base game:
- Ships now have different classes, this system also includes weapons now, which wasnt promised originally
-You can enter and buy giant freighter ships to store cargo or help your travel as a kind of mobile home
- Planet generation was said to be far worse than in the trailers, that isnt the case anymore, planets now have a great deal of variety and are visually interesting
- The graphics and performance have greatly improved, the game is now far more stable
- Factions were "dumbed down" in the base game, this is no longer the case, in some ways they have more depth than was originaly promised
- Crashed freighters now appear and are super cool
- There are many structures seen in the trailer that werent present in the final game. Many of these are back
- Portals appeared but didnt work, now they do and they are great
- Although proper multiplayer is yet to be implemented, you can now "see" other players. Hello Games has also openly admitted that this is the first step towards multiplayer so we are likely going to get proper multiplayers soon
- It was said that the worlds got more alien the closer to the center you were, this is now the case.
Here are some things not promised but none the less present:
- Base building, its easy, useful and super fun to have home amongst the stars
- Vehicles, these are super helpful for travel across planets and gathering resources
- Randomly generated missions to keep you busy
- Farming is now a mechanic and is helful for base builders or people who own freighters
- System economics are now very interesting and trading is no longer gambling
- You can now mince planetary atmospheres
- There are benifits to scanning creatures and learning aobut planets
- Terrain editing is possible
- Space cambat is arguably better than that seen in the trailer.
Now here's the thing, there are a lot of people who give reviews based on things that the game never had, even in the trailer. If you want these things then the game simply isnt for you:
- Realistic simulation of space, the game isnt and was never indended to be remotley realistic. The flora, fauna, ships, space combat, appearence of objects, and the in game periodic table were never meant to be realistic. The game is indented to capture the weirdness of 70s and 80s sci fi, so thats about how realistic the game is.
- Hardcore combat based game. The game can be hard, and space combat can be intense, but if your playing soley for combat then dont be suprised when you get bored fast, combat is fun but its depth never reaches the levels of competitive titles or rpgs. It meant to be a fun exciting thing you do when you are trying to break into a facility or escape a planet with valuable cargo.
- Muliplayer experience. This game was never intended to be "multiplayer" even during pre-realease interviews they were super up front that muliplayer would serve little purpose as the chances of finding other players was so slim in universe-sized digital universe that the game would be impossiible if multiplayer was essential. The increadible difficulty of navigating to a star system where another player resides and getting to exactly where they are is quite large, therefore it would have been a waste of time to make content that was designed for multiple people when players would almost never meet. No Man's Sky is a single player game where you can find others as a personal acomplishment, but thats it.
This game is for you if you are one of these things:
- Someone who likes exploring, there's an entire universe out there waiting for you. And now there are missions, space battles, valuable resouces, and complex trade that will greatly incentivise your exploration. There are also lots of very rare ships, biomes, structures to find.
- Creative people. The game is super open world, its your playground. There's nothing stoping you from becoming a criminal who attacks faction ships for their resources or building an epic base.
- Peopole who want to relax. The game is super chill and there is just a passive coolness to everything you find. You will also find yourself appreciating the finer details of the game as you learn survival tricks to help you along your journey.
- Roleplayers. You dont need to be a neackbeard to be a roleplayer, this simply means thtat you enjoy the feeling of BEING someone. If you decide to play as a trader then you will definitley feel like a cool trader who travels that galaxy in search of wealth. You can be a money obsessed miner if you want, or you can be a pirate and assist them in their raids on star frieghters. You can also be a self sufficient person who lives off the land of their planet, or maybe your a nomad who pilots their freighter into new systems in search of the seecrets of the universe.
- Lore maniacs. 1.3 has brought 30 hours of story gameplay and the lore is quite good. There are monoliths scattered across planets that will each give you a bit of lore and a small reward, if you like reading books in skyrim then you will enjoy monliths in No Man's Sky.
- Screenshot Junkies. If you like taking screenshots then this game has an infinite amount of them. There are literally more majestic scenes of nature and space than you will ever be able to visit and each one will be your own likely no two players will ever photograph the same area. Also with the dedicated photomode it is super easly to get rid of interface, add filters, adjust lighting, time of day, and to get that perfect angle.
Overall this game has grown into a very good title. It truly delivers that feeling of you being in a scifi book cover and as of these last 3 updates there is plenty to do. If you are Starting fresh the game will offer plenty of hours of gameplay for you.

Clockwork Tales: Of Glass and Ink is an extremely well crafted Hidden Object adventure set in a steampunk world, featuring beautiful graphics, a good soundtrack and strong voice acting. It comes with a bonus chapter that serves as a prequel to the main story.
You play an investigator trying to get to the bottom of a mysterious series of earthquakes with a side-plot of rescuing your mentor along the way. Clockwork Tales: Of Glass and Ink is a quite unusal hidden object game set in a steampunk (there are industrial steam-powered machinery literally everywhere) environment and also in what seems to be a fictional version of 19th-century Prussia (which explains why some of the characters use a strange mixture of english-german language). The game is nice to look at and ticks all the right boxes for a HOG, but for me it still seemed somehow half-finished plotwise.
We play as Evangeline Glass, a special agent (who else) who receives a letter from her old mentor requesting assistance: somewhere in fictional Prussia an unnaturally large number of earthquakes shake the ground lately. According to him, these tremors occur near the village of Hochwald, so we travel there right away and quicky discover that a local tyrant/inventor, who seems to be giving orders to the military, is oppressing the locals and is behind the earthquakes. When our scientist friend is kidnapped, we must take matters into our own hands.
The game starts off good with the beautiful snowy highland area and the tense, action filled segments with the soldiers on the zeppelin. The second half though gets uninteresting pretty fast and defeating the villain (whose goals are never revealed) is underwhelming. The game is still fun though since apart from the story (almost) everything seems to be all right.
It is one of those games where we have a helper, a mechanical bird which first we have to repair to make it work again. Besides the usual fetching capability, it also has a camera function, so it can give us information about what we are up against.
In addition to the HO scenes there are fragmented object scenes as well, where we have to reassemble objects (finding missing parts). The puzzles are imaginative and plentiful, ranging from easy to some really hard ones, for example the one with the balls, where we have to roll 5 different coloured balls into their corresponding slots - not only it is hard, but tedious as well (if one of the balls gets into the wrong hole or location, we have to start it all over again).
There are 3 chapters with different looking collectibles (steam insects) for each plus a bonus chapter that precedes the main story in which we have to play as Dr. Ink, the scientist who sends for Evangeline.
The main problem is with the second half of the game in which there's hardly any action and we learn nothing about the madman's further intentions, there's no grand finale, no catharsis, we just solve puzzle after puzzle. The endgame consists of basically a simple wire puzzle. Considering our character is actually a spy, this clueless investigation and lack of resolve is especially annyoying.
I also didn't like the fact that I had to click very precisely on objects so the robot bird would interact with them. It's annoying to realise that you were on the right track, you just didn't click on the right spot and gave up the idea.
As for graphics, the game looks very good, the artwork is unique with all the snowy and steampunk environments. I also liked minor little things such as how the vision changed when I had to put on a gas mask helmet. The music is forgettable and apart from the main characters, the voice-over was terrible. I really mean it, it sounded as if they asked a few people from the studio to provide voices and they were making a feeble attempt to reproduce german accent. I think asking people from the street would have been a better idea. On the other hand the lip syncing looked surprisingly good.
So does this mean I didn't like the game? No. Would I recommend it? I would, since it does almost everything well, all the things people like hidden object games. But if you value a good storyline as much as I do, and expect to play a game that remains exciting all the way, this isn't the best HOG for you.
PROS
+ great steampunk artwork and graphics
+ lots of puzzles and fragmented object scenes
+ mechanical bird helper
+ engaging first half
+ pretty good bonus chapter
CONS
- uninteresting second half, unsatisfying finale
- some puzzles are tedious
- poor voice acting
RATING
6.5/10

I received Clockwork Tales: Of Glass and Ink as a gift from a friend. I had never played a point-and-click before, and wasn't expecting too much as I headed into the game. I figured I'd probably just be bored, with no real story or challenge to the game.
But I was pleasantly surprised!
I'm not going to rid my library of all RPGs and platformers, but I very much enjoyed Clockwork Tales. It's a very different kind of game, a quieter & more thoughtful one. Not something I'll play every night, but when I'm in the mood, it's perfect. As a matter of fact, this is the first game on Steam that I replayed to get 100% achievements, which I'm rather proud of.
The story isn't Pulitzer Prize quality, but it's entertaining and interesting enough to keep you playing. The puzzles aren't difficult, but they do require some thought at times. The graphics aren't overwhelmingly fantastic, but I enjoyed them.
Clockwork Tales was a highly enjoyable play, and I would recommend this to anyone who hasn't tried a point-and-click before, or to anyone who enjoys them.
FINAL RATING: 6/7

This is my first puzzle game from Artifex Mundi, & I really enjoyed it!! Clockwork Tales is a point-and-click puzzle game with a steam punk theme. The art is very beautiful, & there are lots of very fun puzzles. Only 2 of the puzzles were any challenge at all however, so if you are looking for brain-benders then you will be disappointed. The steampunk theme works great for this puzzle game, & because of this most of the puzzles felt very natural in their placement rather than shoe-horned in. There's a good balance of Hidden Object Puzzles along with the other puzzles.
The music is also beautiful, but there are only 3 tracks and it gets VERY repetitive. The game wasn't really long enough for the repetitiveness to get on my nerves however, & the puzzle music track in particular is very pretty! The voice work was also very good.
The only thing that was a disappointment really was the story. It is a fairly simple, linear plot with no character development. There was just enough of a story to connect the puzzles & I just didn't care about Glass or Ink at all really, so it's a good thing that the puzzles were so fun!
Completing the Prologue and the main story took me 6.6 hours, but I wasn't in any rush & took my sweet time so you could probably run through it much faster if you actually focused lol. I bought this on sale at some point but I don't emember what I paid. Definitely was worth the buy for me though.
I recommend this game for someone who likes fun, creative, casual puzzle games, appreciates lovely artwork, & digs the steampunk aesthetic. Since there are no adult themes or language, & the story is simple, with the puzzles being not too challenging, I would also recommend this game for kids. :)

The best sandbox-survival game I've played. I typically don't like sandbox-survival games, but after watching the videos and seeing its potential, I decided to give it a go. I love it!
Like other sandbox games, it focuses on crafting your own materials and hunting wild animals (such as tigers and goats) for resources. The difference, and
with TUG is a higher focus on who you are as a Seedling, that can grow, change, and morph based on what you eat, how much you craft, etc. You can tame cubs, raise them, breed them, and eventually ride them (I hope, given that there's a saddle in game). It's easy to build your own shelter, make farmland and grow your own plants, etc etc.
A lot of negative reviews have low play time and state that it's "hard" to figure out. Well, yes, it's an alpha game. If you're having trouble getting going, check out the TUG Crafting Guide in the Community Hub.
I would recommend it to everyone, really. This game has so much potential, and it's a
of fun!

TUG is a good game with a lot of potential, but there's not quite enough to do yet. The devs are good, transparent and working hard. If you like supporting a worthwhile Early Access game, give this one a buy!
+Graphics: Good mix of cartoonish and realistic.
+Gameplay: Sparse but good, with tons of crafting recipes!
+Audio: Just enough sounds to be effective.
+Workflow: Intuitive crafting/inventory management.
-Gameplay: Only so much to do currently.
-Gameplay: Needs more things to hunt/enemies!
-Audio: Some actions are missing sounds.
+/- Crafting/inventory management can take some adjustment.
+/- It may not exactly be obvious how to do things at first.
TUG is one among many survival sandbox games. It features a fantasy setting and charming, cute, simple-yet-pretty graphics. In TUG, like many sandboxes, you will have to work your way through the tech tree from the ground up. TUG also has an amazingly upfront dev team whose main concern is their game and consumer. So what's it like?
The first time you start TUG you may be alarmed by the long load time, but don't worry, only the first will take that long. When you get into the game, you may find yourself wondering what to do or how to do it. A quick bit of information gathering will fix that.
The first thing you will want to do in TUG is gather objects for tools. To do this you have to tear down a sapling or small tree, leaving you with a wood handle. At this point you will need a properly shaped rock and some vines. Once you find said properly shaped rock laying around (usually near other, larger rocks) and some vines (easy to spot and abundant) you can put them all on the ground together and hit G to craft your first primitive tool!
Hooray! That wasn't so bad, was it? From here on out your imagination is the limit.
TUG, unlike many sandboxes, features a beautiful voxel terrain editor, allowing you to shape the earth pretty much however you see fit. Doing so is a quick and easy process, as you can use virtually any primitive tool. Filling the terrain in with wood or stone, however, is not nearly as quick. So for those of you who hate seeing servers on survival sandbox games where there are tons of halfbuilt or poorly built structures you can rest easy. You can also rest easy in knowing that your buildings will take work and will be an accomplishment.
This leads to a startling revelation: building is fun. building with friends is more fun. Aside from building, crafting, hunting, and farming, there isn't too much to do in the game's current state-but what is there is fun, with more on the way. There is, however, an absolutely EXTENSIVE amount of things to craft, so if you're into making things, you're in the right place.
The graphics in TUG are a treat. Again I will state that they are strangely pretty, considering their simplistic and cute nature. You will find that there are lush biomes filled with dense foliage, as many types of trees as you could ever want, and various bioluminescent plants and resources scattered about.
The colors are at times muted, and almost always earthy, but that won't stop you from finding sand or snowswept locales. As a man that appreciates variety, I was very pleased with both the amount and the look of the biomes available in TUG. Aside from biomes I want to take a moment to talk about the look of buildings. In TUG, when you place a wood block next to a cobblestone block, they will blend together, and this can make for both some pretty--and pretty interesting--ideas and aesthetics.
The presence of fog, various cloud types, sky colors, moon and sun, darkness, etc. make for an overall pleasing and immersive graphical experience that I'm sure you'll enjoy!
The audio in TUG is also a treat, albeit a sparse one, but this is a good thing. In a sandbox you don't want obnoxious music distracting you from you building, fighting, hunting, crafting. You want relaxing music with good atmospheric sounds, and audio cues that would be distinct a mile apart, and in TUG, you have that. The audio stays in the background until it needs to be in the foreground, and I appreciate that so much. While many games try to pull on your heartstrings too much with music and sound, TUG manages to make you feel things by playing the right sound at the right time. The sounds that are there serve their purposes well, although more sounds would be nice, for example, when swinging a weapon.
TUG is a great sandbox with a lot of potential. It already has solid building mechanics and tons of crafting recipes. If you are okay with supporting a vision, give it a buy!

I am a super fan of Lego, not only the video games but also the Lego pieces. Lego means creativity, imagination, unlimited worlds, great possibilities. Highly recommended if you are a fan of Lego.

I've been a fan of Lego and their video games since Creator and Loco days. Back in June 1st, 2015, I heard about Lego Worlds the minute it was released. I'm quite suprised such a high profile company would go the early access but I'm not complaining. Like everyone else, I was hyped and wanted right now. I didn't have the budget at the time to get and remained out of the loop until recently.
Proir to my purchase, Lego Worlds lacked titles in the cutscenes that told which binome you were in and who each Minifig was; map, waypoints, and "quests" per-se. We'll get to the last one in a moment. After my purchase, it had all these features. So while I'm disappointed I wasn't able to get in earlier, I'm NOT disappointed with the game and glad I got in now or wouldn't know what some of the less obvious stuff is.
My only criticism is how you gain new minifigs and pets, the former is to use on your avatar, in the form said "quests". Minifigs and pets are spread out throughout their respective binomes and ask for specific things in a form of a thought bubble. This may not be obvious to you if you watch the day one Let's Plays where you can get on them without having to hunt for objects or just to new to the mechanic in general. Once you have what they needed, they will be available to purchase using the in-game currency. HOWEVER, this is easier said then done.
After you see what it is they need, you etheir check your inventory and hope you're lucky or go and explore, opening thousands of large chests miles/meters away from where you first found them to find said item. Once you got the item you hope to return to the binome you found them or hope to find a new one with same minifigs and their pets.
This method of gaining minifigs and pets is a mixed bag of chips. On one hand, it encourges you explore and gain new items along the way. On other hand, it can get repetitive and or frustrating when you all want is that cute little wolf pup. D:
In a nutshell, ths is basically Lego Creator on an grand and epic scale, encourging you to explore and rewarding you in items, minifigs, and pets to make your world more rich. I'm just kinda suprised a or any "AAA" publisher would go the early access route.
Is it bad or is it good? As of now, they're doing good. So, it's good. Keep it up Lego. I look forward to the future now, 1.0, and beyond. It's simply playable and fun with it's typical rough edges.

I wish Steam had a neutral option. I would recommend this game. However it'll have a big list of ifs and buts, and I can only say get it when it's heavily discounted.
Now to explain my experience:
I was initially intrigued by the game's setting and the concept of stealing memories. It's a fresh concept and started off on a good foot. However, as the game went on, the story started to get less and less interesting, filled with a large number of tropes and cliches, and the worst of all, feeling padded with levels that were way longer than they should've been. The game can be summarized as a collection of cutscenes connected together by tonnes of climbing, combat, and stealth sections, which often repeated in every single stage.
I enjoyed the combat. It was fun stringing together combos and making each hit in a combo do something, like heal self or reduce the cooldown on skills. Getting a chance to dodge whenever I want, and we've got a very dynamic combat, enhanced even further by fun S-Pressen skills, which act like special abilities, such as a short fury burst, or slowing the enemy reactions, or even making machines turn on their allies and self-destruct.
The boss fights were either love or hate experience for me. I enjoyed some of them, like the Zorn robots, but the ones against some important characters were irritating, because most times they were completely invulnerable to everything but one skill, and unfortunately the skill you needed to use would go on a long cooldown after you use it. Even with the help of cooldown reducing skills, this still dragged out the boss fights way longer than they should've been. To make boss fights even worse, you had to finish each boss off with a series of QTE button presses. If you make a mistake, the boss heals some health and you have to keep fighting them.
Another common gameplay mechanic is the climbing. It's very similar to Assassin's Creed style of climbing around buildings and rooftops, except it's pretty much 100% linear. There are no big cities to explore. You pretty much make your way from one ledge to the next the entire time. At times you'd be forced to do stealth sections, where you must avoid getting seen by drones. These drones could insta-kill you if you got in their field of view, so making one tiny mistake meant an instant game over, and not being able to save whenever you want, you'd often be taken back to the last checkpoint.
Lastly, the game also had rather cool memory remix sections, where you had to alter someone's memory and make them think that what really happened was different. It's an awesome idea and I thought it was great, but there were only 4 such sections in the entire game. Moreover, despite how cool they were, I don't see them being fun the second time round, when you already know what to do.
Overall I was a bit disappointed. The game had a nice premise, a cool setting, and both the visuals and music were nice too, but its gameplay suffered for the most part and got very repetitive very fast, and the story got less interesting in the second half. Because of this, I can't recommend it to most players, but I think some players will enjoy it very much.

This game reminds me a lot of the Blacksad comics. Like Blacksad, 1954 Alcatraz is a hardboiled thriller dripping with cynicism, but counterbalances the noir narrative with a cartoonish character design that makes for an unusual gaming experience. Like watching a Looney Tunes episode written by Jim Cain.
You switch between Joe, an inmate at the infamous Alcatraz, and Christine, his wife, as they try to bust him out of prison. The story from there is pretty decent and well-written with some pretty humorous dialogue and a diverse cast of characters. There's also a nice jazzy soundtrack that sets the mood really well.
Here's some hangups, though:
-Twice in the game, the character models would freeze and I couldn't click on anything. I ended up having to restart my computer. Since I save often and with multiple files, this didn't set me back that far, but it was still annoying.
-Occasionally, you reach a couple of points where you can change the narrative. For example: Do you turn the antagonist over to the mafia or keep quiet and save his life? Though you're given a choice, the narrative changes based on it are ultimately cosmetic and don't affect the overarching story that much. There's some changes in the dialogue and that's about it.
-There are two endings, both of which felt rushed and somewhat unsatisfying, IMO. Maybe if they just stuck to one ending and made it a bit longer, I'd enjoy it more.
This is a pretty decent point-and-click, though, and I'd recommend it. If you don't want to spend that much on a game like this, Daedalic occasionally releases this game in a bundle with about ten other titles for an insanely cheap price.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Clockwork Tales: Of Glass and Ink is a point and click adventure game where you play as Evangeline Glass, a women who is sent to the far off village of Hochwald on a mission to rescue your mentor, Dr. Ink, and solve the mystery of what is causing so many earthquakes to rattle the foundation of the mountain village.
For those that have played other Artifex Mundi games, or any hidden object games in general, Clockwork Tales follows the typical game progressions; you’ll have to solve an array of puzzles ranging from painfully easy to somewhat challenging in difficulty. The puzzles probably were the strongest section of the game, combining different elements to create some genuinely interesting puzzles to overcome. However, the story, or lack thereof, and general progression of the game felt hurried and jumbled together like so many disconnected puzzle pieces; it left me wondering when the characters were going to be fleshed out and dissected or when the plot would even be marginally explained. Once the credits rolled, only then did I realize how much this title left out. Let’s review…
As Evangeline Glass, you arrive in Hochwald, a small mountainous village to meet with Dr. Ink. Shortly after your arrival, Dr. Ink is kidnapped by a giant robot  oddly reminiscent of “The Iron Giant”, and whisked away to a fortified castle own by Engineer Barber and his mechanized cronies. Here’s where I had a real issue with the game; the story consists of a thinly veiled plot that tells the reader everything, leaving nothing to be discovered. Let me explain…
The earthquakes are abnormally frequent because they
you so, the guards are corrupt because they
you so, this town isn’t what it used to be because the citizens
you that’s the case. The player doesn’t really figure out any of this for themselves; it’s all stated as fact. The worst trope that the game follows is that the soldiers are the “bad guys” so the game clads them in black, gives them a German accent and slaps on a mustache on them. Combine that all together and you've got the recipe for a generic criminal enterprise to topple.
It might sound a bit harsh, but when you factor in that the paramount points behind these types of games are the puzzles and the story, it makes a bit more sense. One without the other causes the player to lose sight of what they’re doing either due to a lack of interest of a lack of understanding. As mentioned above, the puzzles are the game’s strong suit, while the plot is the weakest portion of the game and ultimately why I cannot recommend it.
For those not interested in plot spoilers or have already played the game, when Dr. Ink is inconspicuously kidnapped by Engineer Barber's 50ft robot in the middle of town and nobody seems to notice but you, you’re tasked with saving him. You dawn a soldier’s Wolfenstein-styled uniform, barter for a helmet, board a zeppelin, repair a mechanical glider out of a box of scrap, infiltrate the castle, defeat a few robots to save Dr. Ink and disable Engineer Barber’s machine with some blueprints, a piece of chalk and a hexagon, thus ending the game.
The only parcel of information that is revealed at the end of the game is that the machine Engineer Barber controls was created by his father, who constructed it to
earthquakes from occurring. However, it has been reverse engineered to produce them instead; the reason for this never being explained. Then again, the backstory in its entirety is never explained. We’re not told who Dr. Ink is, how he discovered this place, why he cares, who Engineer Barber’s father is or why this contraption exists in the first place. At the end of the game, you simply disable, not destroy, the earthquake machine and leave Engineer Barber alone to simply rebuild and continue his work. There’s seemingly nothing stopping him from fixing the damage, firing some security personnel and investing in a gun to put you down the next time you crash land in his courtyard. The plot is just an intangible mess from beginning to end.


Overall, Clockwork Tales: Of Glass and Ink is just one of many hidden object games on Steam. There are better ones out there, several from the same developer and I’d suggest taking the time to look into those instead. With forgettable characters, atrocious voice acting and a subpar plot. If you enjoy hidden object games, I’d suggest looking elsewhere.

It's hard for me to not recommend this game to every single passing human being I encounter. This game has been part of my childhood since it was first released.
If I could give a rough estimate of how many hours I put into just the 360 version alone, I'd have to say about 800 hours. The world is so expansive and enormous. And this isn't even touching the New Vegas world which is even larger and more varied.
Even for its 9 years of age, it still holds up pretty well graphically, especially compared to it's successor Fallout 4. It doesn't run well on newer Windows platforms, so let that be a warning.
The game comes with many bugs that, to this day, have not been fixed. The game world has an ugly green tint on everything. There are many flaws with the combat being solely third person/skewed camera. As par for the course, with any Bethesda-developed game, there are mods that fix mostly all of these issues. Modding this game is the sole reason alone to own it on PC.
Fallout 3 also does another thing well - its DLC. Very few games follow this type of DLC routine anymore, where we would get an entire new section of a map and a story for a relatively cheap price - rather than paying upwards of $20 for map packs, or weapon packs, etc..
Buy this game. Even wait for a sale if you have to. I don't even care if you rarely touch it anytime soon, because keeping it in your library means something. It means that once the gaming industry has come to a figurative crash and every RPG and singleplayer game is tainted with microtransactions and DLC, you can come back and truly enjoy an old classical experience like no other. The same goes double for New Vegas.
Show Bethesda what we want, which is an RPG, not an FPS with paid mods.

Another fine example of what its possible when unleashing the latent potential of videogames.
Hellblade puts you inside Senua's schizophrenic, mind but it's not just another psychological horror. It actually marries the subject of psychosis perfectly with the historical context set on the Viking age, an age of pagan gods, ruthlessness and superstition. This merciless world makes Senua's often doubt her perception, not just because of her condition, but because of the inborn superstition which gripped all of humanity during the dark ages.
But superstition alone doesn't make it any less merciless for Senua, who needs to struggle with her past and the cold, unforgiving present. The game actually makes you feel in your skin the journey she must face. The experience is so real and haunting, it actually makes you physically fatigued - not because of the gameplay, but because of real psychological stress the game constantly puts you through.
Hellblade is definitely the engrossing experience of the year, for me personally, and for many others. It fulfills the basic obligations of any game, with satisfying combat and plenty of exploration, but it goes far beyond. Anyone playing can see right away in the first 5 minutes of play-though that this is no ordinary game, it's an experience. For me, this is where I draw the line when a game stops being just a game, and becomes art.

This is easily, hands down, feet up, one of the best games I've ever played.
It has its flaws, as does every other game out there, sure. However, upon looking at the big picture I can clearly see that Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is a collection of brilliant moments - what I heard, what I saw and what I felt defined this experience as genuinely one of a kind. I have never, ever, played through something like this until now.
Albeit short (we're talking about ~ 10 hours of gameplay, beginning to end) and with a repetitive combat (that is still very awesome, in my opinion), the game really lets you get to know Senua, her fears and her motives. Its strongest points are the narrative, the sounds (soundtrack and sound designs are eargasmic) and the eerie, beautifully crafted scenario. When together, all of these work out for the best; I found myself so immersed in it I couldn't even hear my dog whining for me to throw the ball. And he does that a lot. A. LOT.
It's always been a bit difficult for me to express precisely what I think and feel so, therefore, I believe I'll never be able to properly explain how come this game has just downright entangled me. The best way for you to know is by buying it, supporting the absolutely INCREDIBLE people who envisioned and created it.
If you're the type of gamer who prioritizes gameplay over story content, then try a different approach with Hellblade. You won't regret it if you're prepared for it! :)
P.S. M+KB player here, but this time I tried the game with the Steam Controller and... yeeeeee! Awesomeee!

The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing shows restraint in its obvious inspiration. The ARPG genre is virtually synonymous with "Diablo clone". But it doesn't have to be. So far in my playthrough as Abraham Van Helsing, alongside AI companion Katarina, I have found individuality, charm, and an evolution of genre traditions. But it doesn't fix what isn't broken.
Adjusting Katarina's behavior or sending her off to sell all my loot for gold ("and pick up some health potions while you're out") makes her feel like the best AI companion in in any RPG. Don't neglect to experiment with her behavior settings and skills. A good chunk of the strategy and fun is using her to the fullest.
Switching from ranged to melee with the press of a button, and again toggling between two setups for each, is easy to adapt to and it feels fresh and engaging. Specs unfold at a great pace. Upgrading is rewarding without feeling grueling. The challenge varies as it climbs so you are always on your toes, but never too far from a satisfying rampage.
It's clear a lot of talent and love went into this game. The sound, the visuals, and the balance all feel really clean and tight. I got it on sale for a little under $7, which is Incredible.

Okay... this is gonna be hard one. First, the spirit of the game is awesome. You get a kick♥♥♥♥♥character, very well designed, which blasts through a lot of monsters. You can really feel the way the developpers wanted that game to be: kiss kiss bang bang, with a lot of references and humor.
There's a huge variety of weapons for you to kill your enemies, which are usually quite diversified, and that you can upgrade for even more blasting. The hard mode presents a real challenge, even a bit too hard (but it's hard, what did I expect ?). The scenario, well, it's made not to be too present anyway, so doesn't really matter that it becomes totally faded in the gore after the first chapter.
The art is magnificent, the design also, two thumbs up for it. You really feel in a living world.
Now for the bad parts... the bugs. Oh god... collisions are horrible and you find yourself falling a lot under the ground. The way the levels are made is... good and bad. Usually you'll find yourself at one side of the map, and have to go to the other side of the map to finish the quest, when it's not bugged (happened to me twice during the game, once for the main quest). And then the dash will be your best friend to finally get where you want without it taking you forever. I think the worst part is the monsters not repoping. You travel in an empty map, from side to side.
The UI is okayish, just monitor your life from to time because it didn't strike me much as an element.
The voice acting is... almost not present. For the main characters, no problem, they have their own voices. But for all the other NPCs, you'll get a bad quality recording of the same voice (all of them).
The game offers you to upgrade your weapons, which is good, but for the main weapon (which have self regenerating ammo), you get the choice between a three-shot upgrade or a rail gun. Take the latter, and even bosses won't resist you (final boss took me 15 shots in total). I won't speak about under bosses which are getting one-shot.
Finally, just imagine platform game in isometric view. Sounds good, doesn't work.
In the end, the game doesn't take too long: 10h to finish normal mode, and I had a bunch of bugs forcing me to restart some levels. I would recommend it, for the fun it provides, but definitely not at full price. But just so you know, some parts will get on your nerves.

This game is good enough.
Interesting setting and story
Likable protagonist
Remixing mechanic is novel
The mechanics are solid enough to stay out of the way, but not particularly compelling on their own. This is not Devil May Cry. Play it for the good story, not for the gameplay.
Remixing was underutilized, and would be more interesting if it allowed branching.
Combat mechanics are mediocre. The controls feel crisp, so it passes the first test, but the fights don't feel interesting. The more challenging fights are more tedious than difficult.
Certain enemies require cooldown use to defeat, and you can make those cooldowns available more quickly through the combo system. The problem is that your combos reset every time you defeat an enemy, so if you're fighting a lot of weak enemies, it can be frustrating trying to make your cooldown abilities available again. Aside from cooldowns, it's just unsatisfying in general to be unable to complete combos before enemies die.
None of the enemies ever really felt threatening or difficult to defeat. Instead of those enemies telegraphing their attacks, they show an exclamation over their heads before they strike, the way Arkham Asylum does. The difference is that there's no blocking or countering; only dodging, and you can dodge anything from any enemy. You can pretty much win any fight by hitting dodge every time you see an exclamation.
The result is that the combat feels trivial. Whatever skill you can add to the formula changes how quickly you can end a battle, but your success is never in doubt; I finished the entire game without a single combat death on medium difficulty.
The game holds your hand through all the parkour/jumping puzzles, so that side of the game is trivial as well.

If you're the type of gamer who prioritizes gameplay over story content, then try a different approach with Hellblade. You won't regret it if you're prepared for it! :)

Where to start... I went into this game having only heard about the purging of ones save file if you died to many times and that it was a "walking simulator", but as I dug deeper, I noticed that there was so much more to this game than just that. The heavy psychotic themes and exploration of ones afflictions immediately had me sold. Having always been a fan of games that want to take narration and atmosphere to new levels, this was a game for me.
Right from the start, this game absolutely MUST be played with headphones for the full experience, the distressing feeling of being trapped in your own head but not being alone really makes this game what it is. Just the fact that right from the get go, you have 4 voices talking to you really set the tone for the things to come!
I also really must give credit to Melina Juergens for her outstanding performance as the titular character, just the raw emotion that she manages to convey really struck a chord with me and makes this game one of the best I've played in a while.
Let's break it down shall we?
The pros :
The art style of a dystopic viking universe with really chilling and haunting visuals.
The combat felt heavy and had a satisfying crunch to it.
Again, Melina Juergens performance as Senua really makes the whole psychotic aspect that much more amazing.
Nicholas Boulton as your spiritual sidekick that you encounter on your journey does an outstanding job as Druth, your storytelling companion!
The puzzles felt fun and inventive.
The game really felt polished and ran very well on my computer.
The cons :
The puzzles, while they're fun for the most part, having to look around for symbols in your environments can get a little annoying. Some of the symbols felt wierdly placed, and you had to stand at a very specific angle to get them to be seen.
It can feel a bit walking simulatorish at times, but it doesn't take away from the games other qualities.
In conclusion:
If you are a fan of story driven narrative experiences, this is a game you really must check out! I managed to beat it in around 8 hours. The price tag of 29,99 didn't feel to steep for me. The game runs very well, looks gorgeous and feels very well optimized.
Other than that, I thoroughly enjoyed Senuas journey into the darkest corners of ones self and the exploration of the psychotic and demented themes.
Very well done Ninja Blade, you knocked it out of the park!
9/10 this is a must play if you are even remotely interested!
