Another lovely HOG from the minds of Artifex Mundi! Clockwork Tales is definitely a good game for those who love the steampunk aesthetic, as well as hidden object games! Albeit a bit short, the game has a certain charm to it that I've yet to see in this genre. But, without further adieu, on to the review!
(TL:DR version and Conclusion at the bottom)
The story is a bit interesting. Your old friend, Dr. Ink, has made a discovery correlating to the mysterious earthquakes around the world, and Hochwald, a small mountain town close by to the mysterious castle of the Barber family. You play as Evangeline Glass, and it's up to you to save Ink, and put a stop to the cause of the earthquakes.
While not overly groundbreaking of a story, it's still certainly a little treat. The game is sadly a bit short, in comparison to other games I've played from Artifex Mundi. But, fortunately like other games of theirs, Clockwork Tales provides a prequel story for extra play and to learn more about one of your allies.
There -was- a scene that was a bit... Odd in my opinion, regarding one of the characters having a bit of a unexpected change of heart in it. But, It was just one of those 'come-and-go' moments. Not a reoccuring theme in the game, fortunately.
With the user interface I was a bit disappointed with the lack of a more in-character journal-keeping function, like the ones in the Enigmatis games. However, having the clockwork bird, Matthew, to aid in puzzles and add a extra bit of actual functionality to the game made up for it.
The UI is also well designed, and has it's own artistic flair to it, which I've come to expect from the skilled hands of these developers. So while there isn't an abundance of bells and whistles, there certainly is some eye-catching beauty to the interface itself, down to the pointer.
The gameplay is pretty standard, and as you'd expect from a hidden object game. Artifex Mundi's games are very good about making sure things don't look horribly out of place in scenes, and this is no exception. So while it's not a ground breaker (pun not intended) among their own games, it's still a cut above most the HOGs I've seen and played.
A fair amount of the puzzles in the game I've seen and played before, but that's not necessarily bad. A little lacking in originality, but you know what they say, "Don't fix what isn't broken". And they do have a couple puzzles in here that I've yet to see in the other two games of theirs I've played, which is always a treat.
For those looking for a little more challenge, or to make things easier, there are three different difficulties. Being Casual, for those who are more interested in the story than gameplay. Advanced, for those who want more challenge, but not too much. And Expert, for the people who don't want things to be all that easy on them. The difficulties mainly affect how easily you can see where to go, and how quick your hints recharge. I myself prefer Expert, as I prefer to do no-hint runs.
While the story isn't too impressive, the graphics make up a bit for it. As stated before, Artifex Mundi is good about making both objects and background work together in harmony. So you don't have to worry about seeing horribly stretched images that look like they were swiped off of google. Everything works well in it's environment, and doesn't stick out horribly.
The places you get to explore look lively, and nicely drawn. From the snowy outdoors with storms in the distance, to the vibrant warmth of the inside of the tavern with it's patrons sitting down to warm up.
My only downside, as seems to be common with Artifex' games, would be the talking animations. Which, I'm really hoping they've worked on in their latest games. They did a good job of making sure the person speaking moves their head, as one would do when speaking. But it still looks a little... Odd? Definitely not one of their strong points.
The music is quite charming, and it's enjoyable. Not exactly the kind of thing you'd get addicted to listening to, but it has a elegance to it that is nice on the ears while you concentrate on the game.
The sound effects work nicely, and for the most part, match what is 'triggering' the sfx. So that's always nice. I hope I'm not the only one who finds it so annoying when the sound doesn't match what is supposed to be making the sound. So finding out that this game doesn't have that problem is nice.
The voices were rather well done, and fit the kind of people in the setting pretty well. Some of them weren't exactly.. Well... My cup of tea... But, I won't deny that they at least fit the character speaking. And I'm happy that the game at least has consistant voice acting, rather than some characters being voiced and others not.
I personally love the atmosphere of the game. I'm not one of those kinds of people who are in love with the steampunk aesthetic, but I do have to admit it's a pretty cool style and concept. And the game certainly does keep in touch with the aesthetic, with blimps, and clockwork bugs (which you have to find) as well as steampunk inventions abound!
There aren't really any items that logically would not be in that time period, which I've noticed that this developer is particularly good with. You'd be surprised at how many HOGs can't get that sort of thing down. A cellphone in a middle-aged castle, go figure. Fortunately none of that sort is in this game.
It's definitely a lighter-hearted steampunk game, so it's not all that gritty. The bright artstyle helps to enforce this. It concentrates mainly on the inventions and the victorian stylistic, which is common with Steampunk. So those who are looking for a darker-and-edgier steampunk esque game would not find such in this game.
UI is well crafted, and has a clockwork bird companion (once you fix him).
Lovely Steampunk aesthetic, makes for a nicely styled HOG.
Backgrounds and Hidden Object scenes are nicely executed.
Three different difficulty options to allow players to pick their level of play.
Fully voiced dialogue with characters, which is always a plus.
Achievements! Boy I love me a game with achievements.
Clockwork. Bird. Companion. I think that deserves another mention.
Lighter-toned Steampunk Game, not much nitty-gritty here.
Voice acting! Kinda a "Your mileage may vary" thing.
Story wasn't all that intense.
Game felt way too short, which is the major problem with this game.
Not many puzzles or hidden object scenes. Pretty big downer since that's the point of this genre.
The talk animations... Oooh boy... Do they definitely need some work.

The cyberpunk setting in my opinion is something that is a niche concept, considering that in games it's embraced. With games like Deus Ex and Shadowrun pioneering the Cyberpunk genre/setting Remember Me is a different interpretation of the very Cyberpunk ideal but it does it in such a way that it resonates with the core themes that Cyberpunk present.

I can definitely recommend this game. It has intriguing, well written story, really good graphics (Landscapes are stunning) and enjoyable, dynamic gameplay. The music is also nice. As for the combat system - in my opinion it's simple but enjoyable. Fights are dynamic, some of them are even quite challenging. Looking for hidden objects is a nice addition. The overall concept for game world is interesting and rich in medium and little details creating the full image of the fictional society and its' problems.
The worst part of the game are scripted behaviours of player character. Every few minutes you receive a call, which is of course very important for plot, but during the conversation you suddenly can only walk slowly, it's often impossible to jump through a gap, so you have to wait until the conversation is over. And some other conversations don't have such limits and you can run freely. And of course you can't skip any of the cinematics. Many players won't be annoyed by it on the first playthrough, but on the second it becomes quite irritating.
To sum up: It's a very good game, with great concept, but a few lacks in this concept's realisation. Definitely worth playing.

I have always been fascinated with crime stories. Be it the Goodfellas, Breaking Bad, or a video game like Mafia II. I'm especially drawn to prison stories that are done right so it is no surprise when I tell you that Shawshank Redemption is one of my favorite flicks of all time. So when I sat down to play 1954 Alcatraz for the first time I had high hopes. However do to the history of games that are based on Alcatraz I was very skeptical. So now I will answer the question......."Will I Rage? 1954 Alcatraz"
Gameplay
1954 Alcatraz is an adventure clicker that takes you through the struggle of Joe and his wife Christine. During the game you switch and play between both Joe and Christine as Joe attempts to make his escape from the most notorious prison in America. As you may realize this game relies heavily on the story. Every action will effect how things turn out (kind of). As far as the game play and mechanics of the game they are pretty standard for this type of game. The coolest feature is the seamless transitions from Joe to Cristine. The puzzles seem to lack variety as well as difficulty making it far too easy.
Graphics
I actually really dig the graphics and art in this game. Some people may disagree but I feel it fits the story, game play and time period perfectly. I do understand some people don't like cartoonish or Artsy graphics but for this game it fits amazingly. It could be polished a bit better and made amazing but that's my biggest problem with the game is that the production values seem a bit sketchy.
Storyline
This is the bread and butter of 1954 Alcatraz. The story of Joe and his wife Christine. Joe is in prison for an armored truck heist gone wrong. After an attempted escape he was sent to the rock. Throughout the game you switch between Joe and his wife Christine as both weave their way through the game world to prepare for Joe to make his big escape attempt. The game attempts to give you choices that changes the outcome but isn't very open. In fact, it's more like you take one path or the other really. The story itself is a good one however it never really captivates and feels extremely rushed. Did I enjoy it? Yes. But I wish that they had of taken their time with it more. Instead the entire game feels extremely rushed.
Value
This game has a price tag of $19.99 on steam. It simply isn't worth it. The good news is that this game is on sale for under 5 bucks quite often. If you can get it for under 5 bucks on sale or in a bundle I'd totally suggest the game. It's NOT a bad game. It's just not really a good one either.
Conclusion
I am conflicted when it comes to how I feel about 1954 Alcatraz. I enjoyed my two runs through the game, while at the same time being let down. The colorful cartoon art style was breathtaking at moments. The music and voice acting were also surprisingly good. With the music being exceptionally flawless. Then you get a story that has a ton of potential but in reality is too short and rushed for you to ever develop feelings for the characters one way or another. This becomes a problem when making scandalous decisions doesn't make you feel the least bit bad. All in all if you can get the game on sale for under 5 bucks I'd suggest picking it up. But if you pick it up for the $19.99 price tag..........you'll probably rage.

Just finished it, and it blew me away. The story is great (albeit with an emotional start), the gameplay is amazing (constantly reminding me of one of my favorite games of all time, Super Metroid), the the visual style and quality is wonderful, a perfect mix of simple and fancy.
It's a true platformer, with more emphasis on navigation, exploration, and environmental interaction than on the combat. I'm playing it in Windows with an Xbox 360 controller, and it's free and fluid movement has been fun and natural and really engaging. I find myself thinking back to Oni (another old favorite), where you had such fluidity of movement in a way that few games have had since, though in Oni it was always in a combat context. In some parts of Ori where I have to pass back through an area, I find myself just reveling in the movement and enjoying blasting from a dangling vine to a spider, using the spider's oncoming projectile to blast back off, and then using the spider itself as an anchor point to shoot along on my way. That's compared to, say, Arkham City, which was a great game. In Arkham City it was a ton of fun to fly around the city at first... but then it got old, and traveling around felt tedious rather than free.
Also lots of good puzzles in Ori, and at a difficulty I find satisfying. Hard enough that I had to try several (sometimes many) times to figure them out, yet so far none so hard, or frustrating, or random that I gave up and looked up answers online. Not Mario puzzles, where you want to find that last hidden coin but it's a random hide and seek, but portal-like puzzles where you have to figure out how to interact with the environment to get where you are going. Places where you can't kill the enemy, because you need them as an anchor to let you blast where you need to go, or you need them to bash through a wall for you.
I will say, though, that I doubt it would be nearly as a good on a keyboard. Definitely a game for a controller.

If you would've told me that I would love living the life of a Renaissance painter and running a huge painting business, I would've called you nuts. That is until I started playing Painters Guild, an adorable and addictive Business simulator. You will go from rags to much nicer rags as you begin to expand your colorful empire. Hiring new painters, expanding your shop, and decorating it with all sorts of useful items. The real fun for me in the game is getting the right painters for the right jobs, as taste change and customers demand a style. This is not only tricky but challenging if you only have certain kinds of painters. On top of all that Painters guild is a game that constantly keeps you busy, you won't sit idly by and watch them paint. You must manage your paints, endurance, bills, and most importantly the mastery of your painters skills. Each painter requires training and dedication to see them reach their full potential. While Paints Guild could use more polish in the options/tutorial department, I felt the good far out weighed the inconvenience of such things. So grab your funny hats and paint brushes and start up your very own guild!

This small but enjoyable game may not have all the depth of other management games, but it does have charm that makes it fun to kill time on. Here's a quick rundown of good and bad:
GOOD
- Nice musical score fitting for the backdrop and time period
- The retro graphics are a nice touch
- Easy controls. Just simple clicking and drag-and-drop of objects and characters
- Some character development with with your artists - you make them travel as an Apprentice and then Attempt a Masterpiece to level them up in skills to be better at their work
- Random event generator in game (illness, arrests, sodomy accusations, etc.) keeps things interesting
- The pixelated paintings that your artists create are similar to some historical masterpieces and actually look very nice in-game
- Buy upgrades for your guild building, the furniture, decorations , etc. It's a small amount of items to buy, but it isn't necessary for it to be over the top.
- Some decent business/management gameplay. Have your artists churn out as many paintings as they can to clients or have your artists do business contracts to make great works (painting cathedrals, churchs, etc.) These are the primary ways to keep money rolling in.
- Cheap price $
BAD
- Can become too repetitive for some people. It's constantly having to do similar jobs over and over again.
- The lack of depth in the game and lack of replay value is a concern
- Not a great deal of variety in upgrades and items to buy
Overall, it's a game that you'll play a few times but won't really come back to much. But for what it's worth, it's a good, small game to play for a few hours. Graphics reminded me a bit of Smooth Operators (call center business sim). If you're skeptical about paying $10 on a smaller length game, get it on sale instead.
Grade:   6/10

Remember Me is definitely one of the more unappreciated games on Steam right now. The game's premise is fresh and events take place in a rather stunning dystopian vision of future Paris. The environments are beautifully rendered and greatly contribute to the distressed atmosphere found in most parts of the game. The sound design isn't bad either, although the score may be a hit or miss depending on how open you are in your musical tastes.
The major problems however lie in the extremely linear level design, a terrible camera, as well as some gameplay mechanics that one feels did not go through enough play testing. There's a level for example where you have to fight some invisible enemies using a certain skill, but if you die and reload back into the game, the required skill is on cooldown, making the fight incredibly frustrating. The characters (with the exception of Nilin, who you play as) are fairly uninteresting for the most part and the combat itself isn't particularly fulfilling; it's almost spammy. I hope Capcom/Dontnod do a better job with the sequel. An open world level design would be a nice way to go about it in my view.
Overall, I'd give this a 7/10. The excellent story more than makes up for this game's shortcomings. I am quite looking forward to Remember Me 2! :)

What makes this game great is the mix of beautiful graphics, the interesting female protagonist of color, the combat system, the thrilling story and the adrenalizing soundtrack. It surely isn't the greatest video game ever created but sadly immensely underrated; it offers so much new since you're not in your generic white American town and the plot actually isn't already overused. While the main story only takes about 10 hours to finish and there are no side missions, it has a great replay worth since you can create completely different fighting combinations which, especially on memory hunter mode, give the game a whole new level of difficulty.
Please give this game a try, if you're not willing to spend 30 bucks wait for the steam sales when it drops down to 6, and immerse yourself in the beautiful world of Neo Paris!

Game Menu Option: Two section – Volume and Miscellaneous settings. The volume section has the following: Music and Sound. The miscellaneous section has the following: Custom Cursor, Voice Overs, Difficulty Mode and Full Screen. Wide Screen is automatically supported in the game.
Game Difficulty Modes: Three game difficulty modes – Casual, Advanced and Expert.
Cinematic/Dialogues: All cinematic scenes can be skipped if you do not want to watch them. They can be watch over again under the cutscene section the extras. There is an option for skipping the entire dialogue scene without having sit through it.
Voiceovers: Nothing much can be said about the voice overs asides from that they are well done.
Game Music/Sounds: Nothing much can be said about the music/sounds asides from that they fit well with the game.
Game Graphics: Nothing much can be said about the graphics asides from that they are nicely drawn with a painted feel to them.
Inventory Panel: There is a lock option for the inventory panel. Easy access for the items that are collected in the game.
Notebook: Two sections – Map and Objectives.
Map: The map interactive with useful indicators; map icons/markers. The legend on the map explains the function for each of the map icons. The ability to fast travel to another location and back.
Hidden Object Gameplay: Fragmented items, Traditional word lists, Shadow items with some and/or no interaction required. Most of the hidden object scenes can be replayed in the hidden object section in the extras.
Puzzle Gameplay: Most of the puzzles are fairly easy to solve. Some puzzles has extra puzzles in them to solve. There is a skip button if the puzzle(s) becomes too tasking to solve. Most of the puzzles can be replayed in the puzzle section in the extras.
Game Helper: A steampunk mechanical bird helper called Matthew that can carry out certain tasks that the players can’t complete themselves. Like retrieving items that are out of reach.
Game Ending: There is an ending for the main portion of the game. The bonus chapter is the pre-sequel to the main portion of the game.
Game Achievements: In game and Steam. There are total of 19 different achievements to earn throughout the game. Each of the achievements has certain requirements before they’re obtained.
Game Collectables: Steambug collection – 11 Hochwald & Underground; 8 Castle. 30 steambugs in total.
Game Concept Art/Wallpapers: 6 concept art and 12 wallpapers.
Game Soundtrack: 6 soundtracks from the game.
Game Length: There are eight chapters in the main portion of the game. The bonus chapter portion of the game mostly likely to have at least two chapters the most.
Game Trading Card/Badge: This a special feature only available in the Steam’s version of the game. The game drops three different trading cards only once and the rest of the cards: Community Market, Booster Packs and Trading. The game badge can be crafted after having all the card in the inventory then it can be upgraded four more times.

I was going to leave a negative review but the game eventually changed my mind.
The good:
- More guns than before, and heavy guns are much more viable. They're actually good, but require several upgrades to become powerful.
- Solid level design and variety. Clearly some inspiration was taken from games like Metro, Dishonored, and (obviously) Doom.
- Almost every encounter is play-your-way, either stealth or guns blazing or a bit of both.
- The game is not forgettable like its predecessors - Old Blood etc. I have an easier time remembering obscure shooters from 2000's than what went down in older Wolfenstein remakes.
The bad:
- Steam community makes the game crash. Alt-tabbing makes cutscenes go black, and also makes the game crash. This is like some indie game made by 2 people, is this real life?
- Vaulting.
It's so goddamn awful. Half of the time it doesn't detect the ledge and jumps into it instead, sometimes resulting in a falling death. HOW is it a thing in a 2017 game? Doom vaulting/jumping was excellent, but now this?
- Press ESCAPE to continue.
This is a game about killing. I don't care about pregnancies and random fetch sidequests. Lore is sometimes an actual obstacle to playing the game. Let me kill!
- Excessive nazi bashing/leftist propaganda.
All this focus on interracial relationships and cringe-worthy dialogue by BJ's racist dad. It's blatantly direct and not really necessary, unless you like cashing in on current politics.

- Rambo playstyle is really hard on higher difficulties. What is the point of having dual-wield shotguns if you go down from 100 hp/100 armor to 0 as soon as a single soldier locks in on you?
- The ending/boss fight feels like neither. "Is this it? The entire story?"
If you can overlook these, it's an enjoyable game.

In a nutshell (ha!), Bombshell is a perfectly decent top-down/twin-stick shooter, nothing more, nothing less. It's full of fast-paced action and guns are satisfying. Visuals are decent, gameplay subsystems are fine. That said, I agree, writing is bad, voice acting is pretty mediocre and scenario is next to non-existing. However, here's the thing: Not every games have to be at a Planescape Torment or The Witcher level of writing quality.
There's some games that heavily rely on atmosphere, storytelling and good writing to set up the mood. For some game, the story or characters can actually make or break the game, but here, come on! It's a action-packed, adrenaline driven, silly twin stick shooter? It doesn't pretend to be a cRPG with great narrative or anything, it's just a top down shooter, and at that, it's pretty good.
So, sure, jokes are hit and miss. Sometime it will grab you a smile, sometime it will feel a bit cringy. Sure, the whole scenario could pretty much be written on a post-it note and sure, Shelly sometime feel like a cliché character, a bit like Duke, but without the clever satire. But who care? It let you turn alien to bloody gibs with satisfying weapons in various environment with fast-paced action. It got some rpg gimmick, some extra-story arena challenge, it's chock-full of references, ranging from Duke Nukem to Iron Maiden and the smooth gameplay seal the deal. What's not to like about it?
On the bad side, camera is sometime not really good. On some levels, it feels too close from Shelly and prevent you to see mobs. On these levels, you'll rely more on minimap to shoot at things because they are out of your field of view. All in all, It's solid 7 for general player. If you like the genre, turn that into a 8, because it's a perfectly decent top-down, frantic shooter. It's a bit flawed, nothing exceptional but still good nonetheless.

Playing Bombshell immediately felt like a mix of good and bad. From the get go you are met with a somewhat unique artistic style that comprises of both violence and comic inspired graphics. Getting into the game, you clearly see why someone would immediately think of a Scifi-Diablo from the graphical presentation and the top-down perspective - in combination with the quests and character development parts. However, this comparison only last only you run into combat (which luckily doesn't take long) and you are instantly reminded that this is first and foremost a shooter - with a little RPG sugar added on top.
This game is about the weapons and about blowing stuff up: Enemies, Structures and occasionally Shelly (unfortunately you cannot blow up the GDF forces even though you often feel a burning desire to do so when you hear certain voice-actor's lack of talent throughout the game).
Throwing Bowling Bombs feels awesome and upgraded to Hive Bombs is a serious blast (pun intended).
The Gameplay is somewhat fluent even though it often caters to hit and run tactics rather than strategic skills in attack. Over time it does become both repetitive and shows lack of variety on both gameplay, enemies and their tactics. Furthermore, the top-down and somewhat zoomed-in view comes with a few issues. Downward jumping is really a leap of faith and most of the time you kill enemies before you see them if you watch the radar. For the most part of the game, I played "Kill the Red Dots" and saw few enemies (only when swamped from a spawning lot or a mini-boss). Come to think of it perhaps that was why I never saw much variation of enemies?
The worst part, however, is clearly the one-liners from Shelly. They will drive you mad and constantly makes you want to turn Shelly's weapons against herself and get it over with.
The levels are great from a visual perspective and matches the artistic style of the game, though they often remind you more of a dungeon crawler than that of a galactic interplanetary explorer. Haskell Challenges adds a nice break now and then and is a good addition to linearity of the level designs.
The music is seriously awesome and some of the best and most varied game music I have experienced in a while. Not quite up there with Skyrim, but in my ears a close match with Deus Ex. The guitar play in some of these pieces is crazy good and the main reason for buying the Digital Deluxe-version. This soundtrack is the bomb (no pun intended).
The Quest really lack depths and you feel no engagement or commitment to any of the other characters whatsoever. Admittedly, the Amiga angle had potential with the internal battle between human and machine / Power and Compassion, but it never really reaches that level. Combined with the 90'ies humor spread widely across the game design it is difficult to know whether this game wants to be a serious one with a story to match or just "Duke-The-Fun-Out-Of-It". Still the Gameplay holds up for the most of a couple of hours of gaming before repetitiveness requires a break.
It runs okay - especially compared to when ROTT was initially released, but there is still a lot of bugs in this game and one can only hope that it will get some much-needed attention in this area in the coming days and weeks. There were performance issues when encountering the big boss fights which were quite an issue (Don't get me started on how bad the battle against the Abomination Boss is and ridicously hard compared to the balance of all the levels leading up to it!). At the same time, you didn't really feel that the Boss fights were memorable moments and this is something this game seriously lacks. Those memorable moments where you feel both challenged and skillful enough to just make it (anyone remembers their first encounter with The Butcher in Diablo and this is something each game should have, in my opinion).
One thing really missing from this game is COOP, which would really shine in this weapon- and violence focused trip down interplanetary dungeons with a friend.
Overall the game is quite fun, has solid gameplay even though it becomes repetitive after a while and lacks variety in many aspects. It also had potential for so much more. I mean when you see so many trying to compare it to Diablo (which isn't really fair in any way you choose to compare it) it shows that there is a market for a Deep Character and Story-driven Sci-fi Diablo (perhaps the perfect marriage between StarCraft and Diablo? ... An enticing idea for Blizzard right there!).
Bombshell shows what a small team can do, but also what a small team is limited to. Would I recommend it? The price is a bit high when you compare it to what else you get for the same amount, but it is a small diamond - even though it is rough in many places. Let Interceptor hone it a bit more and I think I'll be a nice addition to most shooter-crazy people with a tendency to classical 3D Realms-based violence and weaponry. Add COOP and a small price discount and you have a must-try recipe for mayhem on a galactic scale!

UPDATE 07/14/16: Just read their last announcement
. I hate F2P games to the bones. Looks like another dev abandoning their game. As many other reviewers have said before me, I need to STOP buying f***ing Early Access BS! This will be my last update. I'm deleting the game from my HDD and placing it in my Trash category.
UPDATE 06/24/15: The game was update again today, so I spend a few hours exploring the new features and stuff they added.
- inventory system: greatly improved to the beginning of the game, still no wearable backpack, but at least the chest and backpack are working inventory wise, which is awesome!
- the tools, armors and weapons that are in game so far are looking great
- building your house is fun, though I wish there were a little more options for decoration and placing the already existing things (like when I have a item in hand that I want to place, a ghost image of said item appears which I can rotate as I want before I place the item)
- combat wise I still can't say much yet, as I have yet to see any hostile mobs, I did some hunting this time, which is ok, but could use some balancing ( a tad to easy i think)
- crafting, the system itself is solid, even though items fly all over the place when you put them down to craft, which is only a minor annoyance though. what I really don't like is the missing help within the game. If you want to know how to craft something, either you just try stuff out until something pops out or you got onto the web to look up the crafting recipes, which is what I did, but why can't there be a small guide (like in The Forest for example) that tells me what I need to craft. doesn't have to autocraft from within the guide, just a simple info book of what I need (just a thought ;) )
- graphics, are awesome, I have the game set to max quality settings and it's running at a steady 60 FPS on my rig (see below), there are a few minor FPS drops now and then, but nothing that ruins the game for me at least, I'm sure future optimization will eliminate most of these as well
Summary: So with the current state of the game and the options available to play, explore, build, etc. I can DEFINITELY recommend this game to anyone. ORIGINAL: First off, the game has definitely potential, BUT at it's current stage I cannot recommend it to anyone, but the most die-hard early access fans, like myself :).

What annoys me personally the most is the lack of a proper inventory management. I like to collect as much **** as possible in these kinda games and TUGs inventory is ludicrously small. You can craft backpacks and chests, but they're only decoration right now. And the stack size of some items is laughable. I assume they are trying to make the game more realistic in that term, but hey ... it's a freaking game ... it DOESN'T have to be realistic. Or they're trying to make the game artificially more difficult by limiting your inventory, which is annoying as hell.

The good parts of the game right now is the crafting system. It take a bit getting used to for Minecrafters, like myself ;), but it is really good. It lacks the variety of recipes that Minecraft has, but I'm sure this will improve with time. I wish there was kinda like a crafting book, that would store recipes that I already discovered, so I don't have to place down all the items each time again and rather just click on the recipe in the book and it would place them for me.

Graphics are pretty good and it fits to the prehistoric (I assume that's what they're going for) very nicely. There are some hick-ups and glitches now and then, but nothing game breaking that I have discovered so far.

Combat system, I can't really tell, since I haven't found myself in combat yet. There are predators in the game and they're supposed to attack the player, but so far I only seen one and I kept far away from it.

Although I had early problems getting the game to work, the devs quickly responded to my issues.  I've now spent several hours in game, and I can't wait for the next few updates.  TUG reminds me of the early Minecraft and Terraria days.  If you want to explore for yourself and figure out the various crafting recipes, you'll have plenty of opportunity to do so.
However, the similarities between TUG and Minecraft/Terraria aren't complete.  It has a unique crafting model, where you place the ingredients together on the ground rather than combining them into a particular shape.
This game is still early beta, but it has a LOT of potential.  I'm looking forward to more.

HOWEVER, this game is still very new and in extreme Alpha, so it does have issues, and not many features yet when it comes to crafting, you can craft everything in a matter of hours and just be doing the same thing after that.  I highly suggest all those interested to research before they buy; by going through the FORUMS and reading up to see if you'd still want to get this game.

While the story and gameplay elements were okay, there were a few more things that I didn't like about this game that makes me want to not recommend it.
I will start with the good.  Remixing memory sequences. You go into the memories of a couple characters and modify (a limited number of) things to change what really happened.
Building your own combo moves.  The buttons are locked to specific sequences, but the "power" of each button is customizable.
That's about all I really liked about it.  So the bad...  Can't skip cutscenes, most of them are quite long, and it doesn't offer any motivation to go back to collect items hidden around the levels if I have to sit through the cutscenes every time.
No counter-move, only dodging, and using it messes with your button combos.  It's really frusterating trying to get a longer combo against an enemy when you're fighting more than 2 or 3 and always having to dodge.
Speaking of combos, while I liked the concept, there weren't enough "pressens" (that's what they are called) to go around to fill out them all, even by the end of the game.  I collected ~90% of the items out there, and still had 2-3 locked button options.
Hidden collectibles, I never get them all in any game and it's a major chore to even think about going back to get anything I missed.  Especially with not being able to skip cutscenes...
Lastly, by the end of the game, I didn't feel all that powerful.  My combos were relegated to healing abilities and/or speeding up the cooldowns on special abilities.  Stealing memories shouldn't have been limited to getting stupid access codes.  All the special abilities and combo moves are unlocked at set points before entering combat with new enemy types.  It would have been way more rewarding to earn new moves through something that tied to the story instead of "oh here's this new move now".

This is, so far, the best HOG I've played on steam or anywhere else.
You control Evangeline, who has been summoned to help her old mentor with his secret project. You arrive just to see him being kidnapped and you have to get him back from the evil robot-controlling villain and save the city. You fix your mentors clockwork bird companion Matthew and he helps you throughout the game.
There is a bonus chapter after you finished the game that is a short prequel to the main story.
The art is beautiful, the voice acting is really good and the music is atmospheric. The one problem I had in this game was the sounds in the engine room, which got irritatingly repetitive, but that might have been partially my fault for being slow.
The steampunk-clockwork world has a really good atmosphere and many neat detail, such as the 'church of science'.
The hidden object and other minigames have a good difficulty, and there's no achievement for not using hints, only for not skipping, which makes life easier.
There is a map and it can be used to teleport. Throughout the game you can collect steambugs, which seem to only be good for the extra challenge and the achievement.
Highly recommended for any gamer, its the kind of game I almost feel bad about buying on sale because it deserves all my moneys.

I find Dungeon Manager ZV: Resurrection to be a very fun and thoughtful little strategy game. In it's simplest form, the goal of the game, is to gradually increase the fame of your dungeon. This will open up new floors, loot and trap upgrades, and entice better equipped
heroes who, in their quest to feed their insatiable lust for shiny tat, are all too happy to risk falling prey to your fiendish traps and ravenous monsters.
However, if your traps are too effective, or your monsters are too good at munching the bones of the hapless, your dungeon will fall into decline. You will need to balance it just enough, that you entice them in, and let
leave, to continue to increase the fame, or infamy of your dungeon.
As your monsters level, you can improve their stats and even merge them to make new monsters... but with bigger teeth! And every real life day, you can take your minions to do battle on the surface.
It's the most fun I've had, from the least amount of money I've spent here on Steam in quite a while. And if you like strategy games at all you owe it to yourself to give this a try. You may like it. There is a basic tutorial at the start and notes in the help section if you need further guidance.

New Review
Pros:
So i have been playing this game quite a bit lately. I will say that this latest update is for sure a step in the right direction. Additional ships, more quests, far more in depth storyline.... Like I actually understand the world as a whole in this game having completed the new missions. I am left feeling more complete.... not totally complete but far more than before. Before the game was either "randomly explore" or go to the center following the Atlas stations for some reason. At least now with the new quest line, there is a real REASON to go there other than simply "thats how you end the game"... The storyline is pretty in depth and full or foreshadowing. It is a proper story. The freighters are great as well. You can sit in the ship bay and watch ships arrive. If you buy one there, there is the option to store it there, giving you another ship. You can have basically a fleet of different types of ships at your disposal. The base building inside it though is basically pointless at this point until they add more base building things.
This game now has an actual LORE! This is something that the game has been missing for such a long time. A lore is a purpose for being in this world. We now have an actual purpose to guide our actions and decisions. We now have more ability to garner actual feelings for other characters and our choices are now influenced by these.
Speaking of base building... as a concept, its good. The building itself allows for simple modular designs, much like how Subnautica does it, or you can build it piece by piece and really design something unique. Unfortunatly, once you build it, there is not much to do with it other than have a few special stations in it.
Cons:
Bugs... Still flying and getting stuck into things like planets, freigters, traders.... like actually flything through the walls and getting stuck in "dead" space.
The base building, though the ability to build complex buildings exists, it is very lacking in customization in pointless design things like terminals and desks and so forth. It leave a player wanting to do more with the bases but there just isnt anything.
Multiplayer.... kinda. Well you can see other players. I have actually and they were a blue glowing ball. Thats about it though really. I have heard you can chat with them but I didnt see a way right off and they made no indication of even noticing me. There really needs to be a better multiplayer. Maybe making it so you can actually play with and see another player and fly in the same ship... something. Instead of making them like another traveler, you could make them one of the races... like a lackey kinda thing.
Overall:
The game is closer to what was promised for sure. It still needs more work though. I would say, the game is justified as is for what it should have been at launch. If future large updates were even put as low priced DLC, I would most likely buy them and not mind. It took a year but it seems like they finally, MOSTLY delivered on what they actually promised. I also have not seen any more of the more absurd animals which is good. Nothing is more unbelievable than something the size of a T-Rex with bat wings and arms longer than its body and legs that are far too short flying after you. So, either I got lucky and didnt see any or they fixed that.
The planets have classes and seem more realistic now. I can look at a scan of a planet and see that it is a hot planet... let me change my gear to fit accordingly.
Either way, I would reccommend this game... but maybe on sale. I would not say its exactly worth the $60 as a game as it is now, but maybe... $40 would be a reasonable price tag in all honesty. I am happy to see though that the devs stuck with the game and kept working on it, even if that one guy went nuts in the beginning and basically tarnished the games reputation from the start.
Finally... I wouldnt say this added 30+ hours of storyline gameplay. They added a good deal but the actual storyline gameplay can be completed in about... what... 10 to 15 hours? This assumes though that you have been playing awhile and already have a rather large collection of materials and can skip much of the farming for materials needed to fly back and forth to everywhere.

For a game about two lovers plotting a prison break while evading the mob,
feels oddly devoid of passion or excitement. Adventure game addicts with money to burn might get an unremarkable fix from it, since it's reasonably polished and provides 6-8 hours' worth of competent point-and-click inventory puzzles. Those looking for anything more -- a spark of life, perhaps -- should give it a pass.
The setup:  Christine and Joe were newlywed lovebirds in beatnik-era San Francisco, until a robbery gone bad landed Joe on The Rock. While Joe hatches a plan to escape the island, Christine tries to find her husband's hidden loot before the local gangsters get their hands on it. The player can switch perspective between Joe and Christine basically at will, though given how the story and puzzles are constructed, it's pretty obvious which one you're supposed to be controlling at a given time. There's also not much you can do as one character until you've completed the immediate tasks confronting the other.
While
supplies the ingredients for a suspenseful lovers-on-the-run caper, the final product lacks much narrative tension or momentum. Most of the game is taken up with Joe and Christine fetching objects across their respective maps, with no sense of time passing or danger building. There are no surprises in the story, and the supposed threat from the mob always feels very distant. The prison break, when it finally comes, is ludicrously simple, lacking in any sense of danger, and over before you know it. The lack of urgency in the story may be partly due to the absence of a fail-state (it's impossible to die in this game), but is mainly due to the slackness of the plot construction.
Another major problem with the narrative is that Joe and Christine's relationship is never adequately developed, despite forming what's supposed to be the emotional core of the story. The game informs us that they're in love, but we're never given much sense as to
they feel so strongly about each other, let alone why they'd risk everything to be together again. I mean, it's not difficult to see why Joe is attracted to Christine: she's cool, literate, a fashionable social butterfly; her sequences have a certain life that the rest of the game lacks. Joe, on the other hand, is wooden, a blank slate, and just kind of... there. It's hard to picture him as either a beatnik or a bank robber, much less holding up his end of a conversation with the vivacious Christine. I realize that opposites sometimes attract, but in the few scenes where we see Joe and Christine together (I counted only two), their dialogue is purely functional and lacks any sort of spark that would have motivated me to see them reunited. The game ends (minor spoiler) with Christine deciding whether to stick with Joe or take off on her own. This should feel like a momentous decision, but given how little time the game spends developing their relationship, her sudden dilemma seems to come out of nowhere, and either decision she might make feels equally arbitrary.
As for the actual gameplay, the puzzles are straightforward and mostly simple, though there are a couple of harder ones along the way. I got stuck a few times, mainly because I wasn't clear on my immediate objective. Pressing the space bar lights up all of the hot spots on-screen, so pixel-hunting isn't a problem. The graphics are reasonably pretty, though some people don't like the 3-D modelling effects. (Personally I didn't mind them, but I wasn't terribly impressed with them either). The voice acting ranges from blandly competent to very good, and the jazz score is terrific. Side characters are amusing but under-utilized, and the '50s-era San Francisco bohemian setting is enjoyable to explore. Though the game's tone is generally light, there are some references to drugs and sex that, while never explicit, might deter parents from letting younger children play the game.
While I'm not recommending
to anyone but die-hard adventure game collectors, I do respect the developer's attempt to make a narrative-driven game with an unconventional story and setting. If the developer can someday marry their appetite for risk-taking and decent grasp of puzzle design with a better focus on narrative buildup and character development, they might produce something really worthwhile.

Ori and The Blind Forest is a
experience. The reasons are:
Favorite platform game of me cause immersive design and powerful gameplay. Looking forward to the Definitive Edition on April 27.

Firstly:
This game looks beautiful and has a fantastic soundtrack.
It also has a fiendish difficulty curve.
Ori and the Blind Forest is easily one of the best platformers I have played so far (and I deeply regret not buying it sooner), it controls well, has creative gameplay mechanics and superb level design with a simple yet powerful plot that really tugs at the heartstrings.
However what really sold it for me was the art and soundtrack. Ori and the Blind Forest has utterly gorgeous hand-painted graphics and a beautiful soundtrack to go with it, throughout the game I was blown away with how damn pretty it was.
My only gripe? When the difficulty curve hits you it hits HARD, this game has a tendancy to go from moderately easy to ridiculously hard at a moments notice with some sections requiring multiple runs and countless deaths before you finally get the hang of it, the upside to this however is that it's immensely satisfying when you finally beat a segment that you've been stuck on for an hour or so.
In conclusion: Buy this game. It's well worth the price and is in my eyes one of the best games to have come out of 2015.

A fun management sim that I did not expect to have as many nuances as it does. I wonder if there's and end-game component, or more historical events/challenges that could be added to the game, but regardless, you really care about your painters, their successes and setbacks throughout their lives as your guild progresses through the ages.
One thing to consider is the portrayal of sexual orientation in the game. There are points for being historically accurate in terms of how society at the time (e.g. church politics) would persecute many brilliant and talented people for how they chose to love others... but one might find the game a bit too dark and perhaps distasteful because of this. There is the ability to ignore or downplay this factor as you play the game, however. In any case, one should bear in mind the ideals of the enlightenment and push on to enjoy a really fun little sim.

This is actually my first review on Steam as I feel quite torn about this game.
On the one hand it's wonderful, the animations and sprite characters are charming, the music is up-beat and cheery (if, at times, a bit 18th Century, as opposed to Renaissance) and the gameplay is both addicting and fun!
On the other hand, all of this is only true for about two hours, because the whole thing lacks depth and content, and this is such a shame. Right now, it feels like a really well polished Beta game, with all the trimings but lacking that last bounty of extra content and final features.
The game tries (and succeeds) to be like the 'Tycoon' games of yore, but whereas those got harder and deeper as the game went on, this just stays the same. There's no extra challenge, all you can do is expand your guild for the sake of expanding, and have more adorable characters just because you can.
The furniture is a nice touch but there's not nearly enough of it, and it'd be nice for the whole 'homosexual' mechanic to have something beyond just the random chance of a death penatly. Maybe other artists could become each others' romantic muses or the like? Leading to increased stats but higher risk of being found out?
Right now, the fundaments of this game are brilliant, but it didn't have nearly enough content to keep me going for more than a few hours. If the developers make more challenge and cosmetic features (as they seem to be doing) then this really will be a first-rate game! As it stands I still recommend it to people, believing that more content is to come! :D

Tomb Raider meets Dark Souls meets What the F***!
This may now be one of the greatest games I have ever played. If you love immersion -I mean amazingly realistic graphics, a deep and rich storyline, and a sense of role play that allows you to become the character- then this game is for you. If you loved the environmental puzzles of tomb raider along with its intense heights and strong female protagonist- this game is for you. If you love the challenging combat of Dark Souls- the unforgiving deaths, the intense boss fights, and the ever-growing fear of failure- then this game is for you. If you wish to walk the dark chasm to hell while accompanied by the insane lunacies and rantings of a psychotic mind in the era of Celtic and Norse mythology- well, then this game might be for you.
It has been said that this game is boring, a point-and-click, too difficult, monotonous, and even pointless. But, No. Allow yourself to be pulled in by the story. This game is about immersion and though I will agree there are times that it can feel slow, the dark and tightly grasping realism of this tale never lost me to boredom. The combat began sparse but grew as the game progressed, in both frequency and difficulty. The small pieces of the story kept me intrigued and forced me to want to learn more. There are element that could be improved upon, such as a more interactive environment, diversity of enemies, and perhaps some flash horror that might make one jump from their seat, though I'm not sure that this game needed any of these elements. It is too short to be monotonous, too intriguing to be boring, too challenging to be simple, and too difficult for sheep.
Wear headphones and do not watch any "making of" videos before first playthrough.
Other thoughts- Hellblade: Rise of Set (Hellblade with Egyptian lore and environment. Prince of Persia meets Hellblade perhaps?)

Even at the earliest playable stages, TUG was something special. The crafting system is wonderfully direct, with the needed materials a logical part of the end product- you know what you need just from looking at it. Materials gathering is also inherently logical, and takes into account both the size & type of whatever you're harvesting from.
With the move away from cubic restrictions on digging and placing of resources, the game's just going to get better- and the modding api they're building into the game means if it doesn't get better in the way you want, you can do something about it.
I'd definitely put TUG on the list of games for people to keep an eye on or give a test run.

Assassin's Creed is a great example of a development studio taking a risk and having it pay off. With it's pioneering of the puppet control system for third person "platformers" and the use of free-running (which later in 2009 spurred Mirror's Edge).
Assassin's Creed has a basic flow. You get a mission in one of five regions, you arrive, you do all the pre-requisite "open world" missions to prepare (such as surveying the area from a perch and stealing valuable information that you can use to better approach the target), then you start the actual assassination.
While others seemed to get annoyed with the preperation phase, I didn't mind it so much as it helped push the sense of how preparation was key for things like this, though some variety wouldn't have hurt.
While Assassin's Creed requires a dual-core procesessor, it does perform quite well on anything that meets the minimum requirements. Unlike most console ports, the frames are smooth and the details are much better.

A story derived from some of the best science fiction of all time. With nods to the Sixth Day, Asimov, and a plethora of other mind-bending steps outside ourself. I highly recommend you play this game with the best video settings on a high-performance pc. It's visual story-telling. It's a cyberpunk novel set in a dystopian future where memories are bought, sold, and traded as a commodity. You play an errorist who has the rare ability to remix memories. In mission one, you parkour you way Tomb Raider-style across neo-Paris in an effort to make it to Headache Tommy's Bar. There, you will begin to unravel your future journey, as well as your own mind.

A game I definitely recommend for any gamers out there.

You gamers out there, you would love the movement of jumping in this magnificent game.

Whats up with ironic names in video games these days? Does developers have a challenge between themselves who can think of most ironic title for a game? Do they then have little award ceremony where the most creative dev gets awarded with a box of Jack Daniels tells acceptance speach and drink himself to the sleep? But I digress, Remember Me is a classic beat 'em up game that is set in not so distant future where everybody is sharing the memories through new technology called SenSen. I can't imagine myself sharing any of my awkward memories with anyone, but in this game it feels like memories are being shared like unflaterring pictres of you on facebook. Game starts with a commercial of different people telling about their experiences with the memory sharing technology and how it has improved their lifes to some extent. After that you see the protagonist somewhere in hospital with her memories being erased. From there you progress regaining her memories and special abilities.
The protagonist is a memory hunter, a person, that steals and sells certain memories of certain individuals. But Nilin is special, she can also remix memories as she pleases. In the very beggining of the game, Nilin's memory is wiped and someone called "Edge" helps her to escape medical facility she's in. As Nilin progress she enters a sever where she encounters her first enemies. Mindless and deformed, these things is an example what happens when you overdose on the memories and overload your SenSen technology. You will meet many variations of so called "leapers" with specific way to dispose of each them. There's plenty of characters you encounter in the journey, but unfortunately, all of them are boring, stale and you can't relate with them on any level. The new task is given to a player: to regain all memories. And so the quest begins.
From the first look the gameplay resembles what would we get if we frankenstein Deus Ex: Human Revolution visuals with Assassin's Creed (1) clunky controlls, but with fists. I wouldn't call it good since it gets boring real fast due to linear corridors and repetitive nature of the game.The only redeaming feature I really liked is assembling your own combination when you want. There's different types of hits you can add to your combination: healing, to slightly reduce cooldown of a special skill, hit that deals more damage and a hit that doubles the effect of previous hit. You then can add them in particular slots which are marked with 'fist' and 'foot'. I found myself using short combos that you get at the very beginning because they are easy to pull off and with good timing you can land them easily, dealing great amount of damage. I expected better scaled difficulty as my first play through I was Memory Hunter difficulty (hardest possible), but all I got was artificial difficulty when enemies deal more damage, you do less damage and it takes a lot more effort to kill bosses. Unfortunately, the unique parts of the game were so short that they were over in a blink of an eye. Thats right, Memory remixing. Another thing I didn't like was quick time events in boss battles. It's especially irritating when you see a strange icon on the screen and you can't tell which button to press and the only way to know is by trial and error. And lastly, the cutscenes are unskippable and it ruins fun for those who already completed the game once. Overall gameplay is pretty poor, but bearable enough to finish it at least once.
The reality is that the game is bad. You can't skip cutscenes, combat quickly becomes a chore, quick time events, lack of customization, poorly written, uninteresting characters and dialogue, boring boss battles. This game won't be temembered, as title suggest.
Awesome game!

Remember Me has been given a raw deal. True the combat gets repetitive at times, the memory remixing is perhaps under utilised and the game is very much "on rails" (to be fair they never said that it was going to be anything but and I'm a strong believer that sometimes it's nice to just be led through a story - Last of Us is pretty much linear for example). However the world the game inhabits is extremely rich, the sounds and graphics add to that. The story is fascinating and gets pretty far out towards the end. It's what I lazily deem "high concept" with some of the ideas - something that rarely goes down well with the mainstream reviewers. It's a real shame though. Unlike some of the other "better" games out there, I sat down and played Remember Me over the course of a week or so and finished it. It drew me in, told a great story and offered some extremely memorable moments....and a fantastic sound track.
Sometimes we really should just celebrate art.

First things first: you, reading this now, the game deserves a chance, buy it! (but not at full price)
I liked Remember Me, actually, i liked it a lot. Primarily because it's a breath of fresh air in this FPS-infested gaming community.
Why? because of its plot (not superb, but really good and interesting for a change), and thus, its setting: having Neo-Paris at your back while you're going around is a blast. Backgrounds and environment all-around are incredible, devs did a great job making you feel like you're in the future, that this could actually happen sometime. Grafics are amazing, quite beautiful.
A very decent combat system (and fun to an extent), New Game+, and some ingenious game mechanics (manipulating memories have never felt so entertaining), adds to the experience and make this game worth playing, with a little bit of replay value.
So, with those strong points, why isn't this game ranked higher? why was it a failure commercially?
Well, as it has very positive things, it also has a lot of problems.
Most notorious issue with the game. Go here, jump here, hit this enemy, activate this button, etcetera, never ending indications. The game makes you follow a predetermined path, without any other possibilites. So, you better follow the non-stop instructions or you'll never go anywhere. Don't try jumping here or there, trying to see if you can go any other path, is pointless.
Is super frustrating: there's the intriguing Neo-Paris on your back and you can't explore it!
I'm not even asking for an open-world game (which would've been epic, none the less), but at least give us some freedom to explore more! I hate when a game has to guide me through it.
Also, please for the love of God, if you despise this too, as I do, never EVER use the "Aug-Eye" feat in the game, as it directly spits on the player's intelligence, telling you how to solve every single situation. Please no.
Only 6 hours, total (could be a lot less), if you don't mind about getting all the optional stuff. Really guys?
It's a breeze, and it's a shame. Because you feel that it ends when you're starting to get into it. Leaves you with a "that's it?" face at the credits.
When this game came out, people said it was "Tomb Raider in the future". No, just... no.
Platforming here, because of point 1, is pointless and so scripted that you'll grow tired of it at some point. Yeah, there are a couple of sections in the game where you've to think a little bit (without Aug-Eye, that is), but doesn't help in this topic.
Combat is decent, batman arkham-like, but fixed combo lenghts and button combinations still restrict you to repeat the same patterns over and over again.
On a side note, how's that this game doesn't have counters??
And the answer is the dodge... because it's an insta-win move. Why? you can dodge EVERYTHING, it's so fast and spammable, that you can keep dodging and never get hurt. You can dodge while doing a combo and if done correctly, the combo won't break and you can finish it. Again, a shame, because it could've been so SO much better. Feels like there's no risk while in combat.
This isn't really a negative point per se, but this game abuses it too much.
There's a great game mechanic called "Memory remix" that its fun, and something new for these kind of games. But, having only 1 valid outcome for them, destroys its potential. Imagine if the devs let us continue the story with other results, setting up your own paths on the story and changing it based on your decisions when remixing. That'd be awesome. But no. At the end, it's just a trial-and-error mechanic.
Finally, after 4 big negative points, why should YOU then give this game a chance? why I still recommend it, when it seems like it wanted to mix so much things that it couldn't reach success in any of them because of that, right??
Well, my friend, because even if the game has important flaws, it's still very enjoyable, and above all, it's a game TRYING TO DO SOMETHING DIFFERENT. This is not you copy-pasta big-budget game, it's a well thought game that couldn't quite get to where it tried to.
There's SO MUCH potential on this, and that's why you should give it a chance.
For me, I'd love to see a Remember Me 2. An almost impossible thing to happen due to its sales, but fingers crossed anyway!

Before I get started I want to make sure everyone knows I recieved a copy of this game from 3d Realms.
First off it was great to see a female protagonist in the game that was strong, independent and fully clothed. Sometimes they pushed the strong/independent part in your face a bit too much but I can live with that. I know what they were trying to achieve. :)
That being said once I got used to the aiming controls I had a lot of fun blowing up aliens and running around getting all the loot! The key to enjoying this game is simple, learn how to aim with both thumbsticks. That particular aiming mechanic could have been made a little clearer in all honesty. Once I got the hang of it, though, I was good to go.
There are some balance issues that need to be addressed. Except for bosses I didn't need to rely on anything other than the base starting weapon you get and bowling bombs. I would switch up to the maxigun if I was getting swarmed but you didn't really need to.
The first boss fight has a decent pattern you can figure out and a little RNG thrown in to make is a bit more challenging... at least for the first 2 stages. The third stage is.... trolly and will have the average player throwing up their hands in frustration.  They know this needs balancing and are dedicated to doing so to make it a far more enjoyable experience. Giving you that challenged yet rewarding experience of beating a tough boss. For that reason I'll recommend this game, for what it is worth, as I believe they intend to improve the things I've mentioned.
Do I recommend the game? As with all things I'll let you decide. Play it for what it is a "B movie plot" game and sheer mindless shooting of aliens. Don't buy into other peoples hype or anti-hype. Use your mind and choose for yourself. Rarely do other peoples tastes match yours exactly.

The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing is a mildly fun medieval style RPG that doesn't take itself too seriously.  Call me a "filthy casual" if you will, but that sort of bugs me because it takes me out of the game a little bit. For example, the town portal system is called a "wishing well" a.l.a. Harry Potter with their magical fireplaces. So they make a joke about it saying that it is a fake & they should just call it a teleporter. I'm trying to get really into my medieval fantasy world here, guys! Why would you crack these little inside jokes like that. I get sort of a campy "Monty Python comedy sketch show" vibe from it. That is not a bad thing but it's just a different mentality I suppose. There is a character who you interact with who has a "never lose" mentality in this game. I get that it's a campy, sort of kooky kind of game that is just having fun with it. I just think of Van Helsing as a title that is for kids or perhaps young teens, as it is not serious enough. Like the Animorphs book series by K.A. Applegate, it is "kid stuff."
A positive aspect of the game is that it is sort of along the lines of Diablo II or Diablo 3 but is set in 1700's Transylvania, instead. That is well & good but for a guy who has a couple hundred hours into D2 & a hundred or two into D3, that doesn't cut anything & doesn't seem impressive or convincing in the least. Basically this game is a disappointment if you are looking for some sort of alternative to the Diablo franchise of RPG games from the company Blizzard, Inc, but better. I suppose it is ok for what it is. Not a popular game. I play a swashbuckling gothic pirate type of person who swoops through the scene every month or so & kills all the rats & evil spiders & such.
Final conclusion can be summed up thusly: "Meh, it's OK." Not really a showstopper or barnburner or "game that changed the WORLD forever" or anything like that. The graphics are a bit old. I haven't played a whole lot of the game. 6/10 would buy but only if it were HEAVILY discounted & there was nothing going on on a Saturday afternoon or Friday evening after working the ol' day job. It does go good with a Starbucks Latte, so that's something I guess. Visiting ASU there in AZ at the moment. On second thought, now that I think about it, save your money. DON'T buy Van Helsing!

First of all this is not only a game, it's an experience and at the same time a love it or hate it experience.
Having said that, for me this was something incredible, and I only got frustrated one time when I was lost in the beginning of the game.
The graphics are amazing and you should play this at high settings to really appreciate it.
You get immersed in this game and my suggestion is that don't use subtitles.
Also if you can, I really recommend playing in the dark because of the dark setting of the game.
I really liked the story, all characters and especially Senua. The voice acting was AAA quality,
the facial animations are probably the best I have seen in a game and the soundtrack is really fitting.
This is a really tense game at times when it needs to be. Finding your way through pitch black darkness
or getting swarmed by many enemies from every direction.
But those are things that I was really enjoying, not knowing what is lurking in the dark gets your heart rate going or parrying enemies hitting you front and back was really satisfying.
The combat is simple but at the same time works flawlessly and reminded me of Bloodborne.
Some people may find the puzzles repetitive or boring, but I enjoyed them as much as the rest of the game.
The thing that I liked the most was the sound design.
All the sounds and voices you hear is just something else and you have to experience it by playing the game.
All in all this is my favorite game of this year and Ninja Theory did an incredible job with it.
Hopefully they will make a sequel or a dlc for this because I was left wanting for more.
Highly recommended.

The game itself is short, about 2 hours of playtime if you're halfway good at solving hidden object puzzles.
The story is mostly there, but has some strange gaping holes in it. There's a lot of stuff that simply isn't explained at all, you're just plopped into the middle of it with no real attempt at backstory or even logical explanations of stuff. The villain is a ridiculously shallow stereotype and there's no real character development.
But, I still recommend it. Mostly because it's beautifully drawn, and while there are holes the atmosphere is immersive and enjoyable. With hidden object games like this, the visuals count for more than anything else in my view, and that's where the game succeeds best.
There's a hard mode for people who are REALLY good at these things (I played through it before trying hard mode and still couldn't get through one of the puzzles) but also a nice and simple casual mode that lets you skip puzzles that just aren't your thing. I'm big into that being important in games like this where I hate being stuck because of one single puzzle.
I liked the voice acting, it's not perfectly timed, but it wasn't awful.
Pros
+ Beautiful art
+ Diverse puzzles
+ Different level settings
+ Atmospheric
Cons
- Shallow story
- Flat characters
- Hard mode is ridiculous

First things first: you, reading this now, the game deserves a chance, buy it! (but not at full price)
I liked Remember Me, actually, i liked it a lot. Primarily because it's a breath of fresh air in this FPS-infested gaming community.
Why? because of its plot (not superb, but really good and interesting for a change), and thus, its setting: having Neo-Paris at your back while you're going around is a blast. Backgrounds and environment all-around are incredible, devs did a great job making you feel like you're in the future, that this could actually happen sometime. Grafics are amazing, quite beautiful.
A very decent combat system (and fun to an extent), New Game+, and some ingenious game mechanics (manipulating memories have never felt so entertaining), adds to the experience and make this game worth playing, with a little bit of replay value.
So, with those strong points, why isn't this game ranked higher? why was it a failure commercially?
Well, as it has very positive things, it also has a lot of problems.
Most notorious issue with the game. Go here, jump here, hit this enemy, activate this button, etcetera, never ending indications. The game makes you follow a predetermined path, without any other possibilites. So, you better follow the non-stop instructions or you'll never go anywhere. Don't try jumping here or there, trying to see if you can go any other path, is pointless.
Is super frustrating: there's the intriguing Neo-Paris on your back and you can't explore it!
I'm not even asking for an open-world game (which would've been epic, none the less), but at least give us some freedom to explore more! I hate when a game has to guide me through it.
Also, please for the love of God, if you despise this too, as I do, never EVER use the "Aug-Eye" feat in the game, as it directly spits on the player's intelligence, telling you how to solve every single situation. Please no.
Only 6 hours, total (could be a lot less), if you don't mind about getting all the optional stuff. Really guys?
It's a breeze, and it's a shame. Because you feel that it ends when you're starting to get into it. Leaves you with a "that's it?" face at the credits.
When this game came out, people said it was "Tomb Raider in the future". No, just... no.
Platforming here, because of point 1, is pointless and so scripted that you'll grow tired of it at some point. Yeah, there are a couple of sections in the game where you've to think a little bit (without Aug-Eye, that is), but doesn't help in this topic.
Combat is decent, batman arkham-like, but fixed combo lenghts and button combinations still restrict you to repeat the same patterns over and over again.
On a side note, how's that this game doesn't have counters??
And the answer is the dodge... because it's an insta-win move. Why? you can dodge EVERYTHING, it's so fast and spammable, that you can keep dodging and never get hurt. You can dodge while doing a combo and if done correctly, the combo won't break and you can finish it. Again, a shame, because it could've been so SO much better. Feels like there's no risk while in combat.
This isn't really a negative point per se, but this game abuses it too much.
There's a great game mechanic called "Memory remix" that its fun, and something new for these kind of games. But, having only 1 valid outcome for them, destroys its potential. Imagine if the devs let us continue the story with other results, setting up your own paths on the story and changing it based on your decisions when remixing. That'd be awesome. But no. At the end, it's just a trial-and-error mechanic.
Finally, after 4 big negative points, why should YOU then give this game a chance? why I still recommend it, when it seems like it wanted to mix so much things that it couldn't reach success in any of them because of that, right??
Well, my friend, because even if the game has important flaws, it's still very enjoyable, and above all, it's a game TRYING TO DO SOMETHING DIFFERENT. This is not you copy-pasta big-budget game, it's a well thought game that couldn't quite get to where it tried to.
There's SO MUCH potential on this, and that's why you should give it a chance.
For me, I'd love to see a Remember Me 2. An almost impossible thing to happen due to its sales, but fingers crossed anyway!

I bought this game because I read somewhere that it had fun parkour like in Mirror's Edge. I doesn't.
I am, however, glad I got this game. It has a great story, great graphics, and I actually like the combat (some seem not to).
The 'parkour' of this game pretty much consists of climbing up walls and jumping from ledge to ledge based upon little orange icons that lead the way. You cannot climb anything that doesn't have the little orange icon. A small disappointment.
The story takes place in Neo-Paris (future France), in a setting that had both utopian and distopian elements (I guess that just makes it distopian, but whatever). The French setting actually works VERY well in this game, and I found myself really getting interested in the lore. The environment is quite immersive.
They also did an excellent job with the graphics. It's not super-realistic, but they really play with the lighting well to make you really get a sense of the area you're in. You might feel claustrophobic in the dark metro tunnels of Old Paris, having your heart suddenly race when you spy the shadow of the dreaded invisible leapers, only to discover the shadow is of an abandoned mannequin. Later, you race through the towering skyscrapers of affluent Neo Paris, where the blaring white purity stands in sharp contrast to the piles of dirty laundry and empty liquor bottles strewn across the apartment interiors.
Finally, combat is actually quite fun. Yes, it can get repetitive, but I've always felt pretty satisfied after defeating a police squad accompanied by flying death robots using nothing but my (character's) fists and feet. The combat just really looks cool, and I felt contantly like a badass playing this game.
I give this game a 9/10 (minus one point for lame parkour). If you like a good story to get into, an fighting like an acrobatic ninja, you'd probably like this game too.

1954 Alcatraz is a Daedalic point-and-click, which is largely the reason I was willing to try it out on a whim due to their games generally being well-made. This one is no exception; you play as a husband/wife pair working together to get the husband out of Alcatraz, and can switch between the two at any time. The things you do as each character can influence the other's path, and their are multiple endings, routes, and puzzles to see depending on how you go about your escape. The only reason I wouldn't recommend the game is the price tag, which is somewhat expensive for a 6-ish hour game, but you can find it for extremely cheap prices on other sites like greenmangaming, where I was able to buy it for $1 on sale.

If you like point & click adventure games then this is a MUST have. It has many elements in a point & click that others seem to forget or lack.  The story is not very deep, but it is rather intriguing. Daedelic nailed it with this one. It also has great replayability value to find the alternate endings.
Final verdict:
9/10
