PLEASE Daedalic make a sequel to Alatraz. There's plenty of scope for these characters, timeframe and setting to develop....
Anyway on to the review a truely beautiful drawn point and click atmopheric cinematic adventure. The music and voice acting is a perfect match for the style of the charming visuals. Christine is a a sassy pouty lead female brilliantly drawn to portray her expressions and attitude. The expressions on the characters faces are particularly good in close ups/cut scenes.
I've seen criticisms of the plot and while it is a little basic and not many twists it keeps you interested and you want to see it progress. I thought the end was maybe a little rushed. There are multiple endings, which adds a little (not much) replay value. I'd like to see extra gameplay and ending for each option. I still only have half of the achievements apparently so maybe there's more replay value.
Some question whether the interracial relationship element of the story could have been explored further but if this was gone into in depth you'd have an awful degree of darkness with the racism of the times. It likely becomes a controversial game and difficult to do justice to the issues at hand.
Gameplay wise it's not the most challenging P&C game, although I did use a walkthrough at times. Puzzles fans maybe disapointing here I suppose. It does give a few hints too making it maybe too obvious for hardcore puzzlers. Personally I don't like spending days on 1 puzzle or needing to constantly break out the walkthrough so I liked the fact it didn't interrupt the story.
It's a solid 8 or 9 out of 10 for me. I was playing this alongside Gabriel Knight and The Secret of Monkey Island. And while I wouldn't say it's better I've played more of it recently and finished it before those too. It's certainly more of a cinematic experience. If you're a hardcore puzzler this maybe not your cup of tea. I'm surprised this has so many negative reviews but maybe that's why. I much prefer this to Deponia although some may prefer the tougher puzzles that game offers. But this is purposely easier, to focus itself as a cinematic atmpospheric story. If you don't buy it now add it to your wishlist as sooner or later it'll be offer and cheap as chips. Not that you'll regret buying it at full price.

I was going to leave a negative review but the game eventually changed my mind.
The good:
- More guns than before, and heavy guns are much more viable. They're actually good, but require several upgrades to become powerful.
- Solid level design and variety. Clearly some inspiration was taken from games like Metro, Dishonored, and (obviously) Doom.
- Almost every encounter is play-your-way, either stealth or guns blazing or a bit of both.
- The game is not forgettable like its predecessors - Old Blood etc. I have an easier time remembering obscure shooters from 2000's than what went down in older Wolfenstein remakes.
The bad:
- Steam community makes the game crash. Alt-tabbing makes cutscenes go black, and also makes the game crash. This is like some indie game made by 2 people, is this real life?
- Vaulting.
It's so goddamn awful. Half of the time it doesn't detect the ledge and jumps into it instead, sometimes resulting in a falling death. HOW is it a thing in a 2017 game? Doom vaulting/jumping was excellent, but now this?
- Press ESCAPE to continue.
This is a game about killing. I don't care about pregnancies and random fetch sidequests. Lore is sometimes an actual obstacle to playing the game. Let me kill!
- Excessive nazi bashing/leftist propaganda.
All this focus on interracial relationships and cringe-worthy dialogue by BJ's racist dad. It's blatantly direct and not really necessary, unless you like cashing in on current politics.

- Rambo playstyle is really hard on higher difficulties. What is the point of having dual-wield shotguns if you go down from 100 hp/100 armor to 0 as soon as a single soldier locks in on you?
- The ending/boss fight feels like neither. "Is this it? The entire story?"
If you can overlook these, it's an enjoyable game.

Written Version:
Before I get into anything, all footage of this review was recorded on the PC and controlled by mouse and keyboard, Computer specs are at the bottom and I was provided review code by the studio to do this review.

Bombshell is an isometric shooter built in the Unreal engine and it looks great.  The texture quality, animations and effects are all excellent and provide that visceral feeling when an alien explodes or when you trigger an execution is very satisfying.  However, as I moved through the levels, I found that I quickly tired of the overly alien terrain that was being reused.  They even start you on the White House lawn, so not getting more earth terrain was disappointing.
Also disappointing from a graphical standpoint is the poor camera and how much it obscures.  You’re stuck much closer to the ground that I would like in a top down game like this, frequently unable to see enemies shooting at you.  Numerous sections of the game also include odd ceiling placements that fade to wireframe for you to see through, which almost make it seem as though the game was intended to be first person initially.  Fading the roof sections and wall sections to a wireframe is a huge mistake.  Fade them out entirely.  Don’t make me look through a mesh to see what I’m doing.

The game has a bit of attitude and if it was 1996, having naught but clever if overused audio clips from the main character to tell your story, that might have been enough, but in the grand scheme of things it falls flat.  Shelly, nicknamed Bombshell, is an attempt at a female duke nukem but the world has moved on from that being enough for a game.  She is certifiably badass to be sure, and while she has a bit of the ole cleavage showing, is not really sexualized which is a nice change of pace.

Bombshell controls best when using a mouse and keyboard.  I tested it with both a Dual Shock 4 as well as the Steam controller and in each case found the move and aim mechanic to be extremely awkward.  This is commonly the case with games of this style, but not addressed or made better by 3DRealms in this case.  Even with the keyboard and mouse move and aim controls is it easy to fall off of a platform or misjudge your aim.  This aspect is made worse with some of the special abilities which include short distance burst movement.

The weapons and abilities in the game are satisfying to use with exceptional sound and visual effects to match.  Each weapon has a different feel to it, whether that be the Ion Maiden or interestingly named MotherFlakker, aptly enough a flak cannon.  It has reasonable variety in other items including medkits, ammo and a few consumable boost items.  Not so few as to be meaningless but not so many as to complicate the game.  You can also upgrade weapons with an alternate firing mode which is pretty awesome.  Though as with my snark earlier about 1996, the menu could well have been designed 2 decades ago as well. And its' not Pipboy retro awesome, it's just old looking.  The game has the usual suspects for Unreal option tweaking, that is to say a lot of them, and as far as performance goes, it runs well.  I maintained 60FPS constantly while playing.  And I didn’t run into much in the way of obvious bugs with the exception of the regular ragdoll physics amusement that can happen.  I’ve heard reports of people having hard crashes and this does not match my experience.

At the end of it all, this is a top down shooter with RPG elements that has very little story, overused dialog and areas that I got tired of very quickly.  Those negatives are mildly offset by exceptional visual effects and some kick♥♥♥♥♥heavy metal music but that’s simply not enough.  Shelly has a similar arrogance and attitude to Duke Nukem but without the funny, and the rest of the title is simply not memorable.  I cannot recommend this game.  You might get a few hours of fun out of it, but I’d wait until its’ in a 3DRealms Humble pay what you want bundle, if at all.  It might be a great game by 1996 standards, but not in 2016.

It took me about 16 hours to play through the entire game, I found it to be a decent ARPG. The story was very blah, simple. It had a ton of action though, and plenty of different ways I could have built my character. I decided to take a brawn approach with my character (side note... I have been doing that a lot recently... my most recent Skyrim character has been brute force kinda guy and my couple newest DnD characters have been Barbarians). This maybe where I struggled a bit, as I tried to max/min the character to a bit but still tried to get as many achievements as I could. This could have definitely tainted my experience with the game.
Overall, I think the game controlled great, never cheated me or anything of that nature, and definitely had a fluid nature. I absolutely adored the fact that I could send my ghost back to town and she would just sell all my crap loot without the need to stop play. I think that is something more ARPGs could handle better, is the amount of loot you attain. But with that being said, I never had that ah ha moment where I just felt like a badass that could slay anything in my path or that I really accomplished anything in general. That with its perceived that it had a shallow system of progression melee or range with a few different types of kickers with the perk system. That's why I would give it a 3/5 stars, but if you are looking for some loot grabbing, enemy smashing, you could go much worse than Van Helsing here.

Clockwork Tales: Of Glass and Ink is a thrilling spy adventure set in a world best described as classic steampunk meets imperial Prussia somewhere around the start of the 20th century. The plot follows a female agent on the trail of her kidnapped mentor, only to find a sinister plot devised by a clichéd spy movie villain, which she naturally promptly foils. It’s cheesy and predictable, but written extremely well and acted out even better… just pure fun!
The video game aspects are done in the usual Artifex Mundi manner. If you know this developer, you will know most of the puzzles and hidden object scene types; although they may provide a few surprises as some of them are devilishly difficult.
But even the difficulty won’t help the short length (3 chapters with only a handful of locations), which makes Clockwork Tales less of a hidden object title and more an interactive adventure movie with puzzles.

You will like this game if you like other HOGs. It is on the shorter side (the main story took me around 2 hrs to complete, which is about half the amount of time I've spent on other Artifex Mundi titles), so keep this in mind, as such a short game may not be worth the $$ to many. This game is different from other similiar games in that it is heavy on the puzzles, light on the hidden object scenes, which could be a good or a bad thing depending on which you prefer. I also found it to be much easier and less complex than other HOGs I have played. If you are familiar with Artifex Mundi, you will also notice that some puzzles were taken directly from other games they've made (or perhaps the other way around...).
Another issue, which I've found to be true with other such games, is that sometimes in the hidden object scenes, you will be directed to find, for example, a "hook," and there will be like 5 hooks in the scene, and you just have to keep guessing until you find the one they are referring to. An annoying oversight on the part of the game makers.
In general the artwork and voice acting are both above average, and the story is super basic but acceptable. But you don't play these games for the story, you play them because you're bored, procrastinating on your work, or you don't feel like playing a "real game." It passes the time... not much else to say.

These are more my impressions so far rather than a review. I picked it up during the summer sale, after the dust had settled from the game's botched launch. It might not have had the best launch ("The canary down the mineshaft serving as a warning of the dangers of hype culture" I think one pundit called it), but it's good to see that Hello Games have been standing by the game and patching in new content to make it align with their promises. I wasn't sure what to expect, or whether or not I'd like it considering all the negativity surrounding it initially; but I have to say I enjoyed it a lot more than I expected. Despite being 'Mostly Negative' it's slowly being turned around and nudged in the right direction.
I can see what Hello Games were aiming at. And in many ways the scope of the game is breathtaking. To be fair, I was already aware that the procedural generation wasn't going to set the world on fire, and it's true that after you've seen a dozen worlds you get a good feel for the range things that are going to be generated. But outside of that, by the time I picked it up in the summer sale there had been enough additional content added on top of that to where the limitations of the procedural engine weren't as big of a deal. That said I do think Hello Games could have done a better job of making worlds, biomes, plants, aliens, spaceships more diverse. The proc gen is so template orientated, that the 'lego parts' analogy some critics used is pretty apt. I can see why people were very negative at launch since at that time Hello Games were leaning very heavily on exploration and '18 quintillion worlds' to discover as being the core gameplay when the proc gen was never anywhere near strong enough to prop that up on its own. The addition of all the new things to do has mitigated that somewhat. The more the procedural generation is pushed into serving as a backdrop by other things to do, the more it becomes an advantage rather than a liability.
Outside of the proc gen there are some aspects of the exploration that work really well. For example the mechanic of learning alien words (that they borrowed from Out There: Omega Edition) and having the words you know be key in determining success or failure at interactions with aliens is a mechanic I absolutely adore. And I enjoy finding derelict spaceships to fix up and claim for my own. As someone who enjoys building things, I like how Hello Games approached bases. They are designed in such a way that bases never tie you down. Building a new one will result in the materials from your previous base becoming available to you to put into your new one. But if you find a spot you like so much that you want to keep your base there, you can continue travelling onwards and still make trips back to it using the portal network. Having a base not only gives you a place to call home, but also encourages you to go out into the universe to find certain materials in order to build the various bits and pieces. And of course the planetary rovers!
It's decidedly not an action game, which might be another reason for it being so horribly missunderstood at launch due to the trailers portraying it very differently from what it is. Instead it's more of a chill exploration experience, on spore style generated worlds, mixed with some survival/crafting, and sprinked with some choose your own adventure style interactions with alien races, and I'm fine with that. It's quickly become the game I play when I want to chillax.
At the time of writing I've managed to while away about 48 hours in NMS without ever getting bored, although to be fair I did get sidetracked building bases for a big part of that so I didn't really make much of an attempt to get to the center of the galaxy. As such I've barely scratched the surface of the story. With the arrival of the Atlas Rises patch, adding many more hours of story, quests, new alien race, new exotic worlds, along with tons of tweaks and improvements I think it would be safe to guess I'll manage another 50 hours.
New favorite feature after Atlas Rises landed is low level flying. It's fun being able to finally weave around the terrain while scoping out places to land. The interface for the Galactic Map got some much needed love too. And, I think they tweaked or improved just about every part of the game in what was a huge 4gb patch (huge for No Man's Sky at least, which is tiny due to the procedural generation). I'm looking forward to discovering the new rare exotic worlds and coming across the new ships.
TL;DR
So the state of the affairs is this: I got my money's worth, that's for sure. I love what they are trying to do with this stupidly big sandbox where you can just jump in your ship and go anywhere, flaws and all. No Man's Sky is now patched to a point where it's a lot closer to what was originally promised. I still have most of the story from the base game still to enjoy, and tons of content from Atlas Rises to check out. I'm excited to see what the future brings for this game because it's clear that Hello Games have a lot of love for No Man's Sky and they aren't going to let it go down without a fight.
This game is now worth every cent I payed back in the day, and what the developers did♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off too trust me, but now they have made it right and given me a game that I look forward to playing.

I've always enjoyed No Man's Sky, even at release, despite being flawed, there aren't many games like it. Yes, it is techically a survival crafting game, it offers a very cool, chill, exploration experience that I really enjoy. I've never really been able to binge on the game for long periods of time, but every time a new big update comes out, I usually play for several more days. Like I said, I enjoyed base No Man's Sky, each of the updates improves on the game significantly. Base building, Land vehicles, and the new one, 1.3, seems to be a major overhaul and rebalance of base game systems and visuals while also adding the groundwork for multiplayer and portals between worlds. I never felt like my $60 was wasted on the game, and each update makes it a better and better deal. I think it is worth full price, but at a discount, it is a steal.

Ori and the Blind Forest (Ori) is a demanding platform game with a brilliant art style and fluid controlls barely found in current games.
The gameplay in Ori is fast and direct and gives a good feeling during the playing process. I didn't played it with my keyboard so I cannot rate this but with a controller it's very precise and intuitive.
In Ori the player unlocks different skills (active and passive) which give him the ability to reach new areas or reduce the damage for example. These skills are often used in more then the straight way.
For example the "Bash" which allows the player to "jump" through enemies, some of their attacks and other specific objects in the environment. But when you use the Bash on an enemy's "shooting" attack the (let's call it "bullet") will be shot into the opposite direction of your jump. Sometimes this is used to open blocked ways.
BUT! For those of you who like chilling gameplay - Ori is fast and merciless - Basically it's pretty hard but not unfair. The most difficult parts in Ori are the escaping scenes which are very fast, very merciless and - which is upsetting most of the people - a non saveable area which means you cannot save in the middle of one of those scenes because the checkpoint you'll be teleported at is the beginning of this challenge.
The story is emotional and good staged. Mostly it's shown with pictures and only some scenes are underlined with text. You shouldn't skip the story!
Gareth Coker is a genius!
The Music in Ori is a master piece of dynamic music in video games. Even if you're not about to play this game you should definitely give the score a try.
The art style of Ori is brilliant. Every little pixel is designed with passion and you can feel it!
I would recomend it as wallpaper ;)
Ori is a masterpiece!
It combines all good which is possible - a brilliant art style, a nice, fast, varied and pleasant gameplay which isn't too easy and even not to hard (in my case), a wonderfull score and story.
You can feel that the development team worked on Ori and the Blind Forest with a lot of passion!

I spent 12 hours and died over 800 times to get to the end. I really hated to put an end to it. Maybe I was just addicted to being tortured by it. In my mind, Ori and the Blind Forest is a really excellent game in story, graphics, soundtrack, and gameplay. It’s flawless, I may say. It creates something new and surprising and remains classic at the same time.

Graphics: Amazing, incredible, fantastic, ridiculously awesome, everything. I was so surprised when I started the game for the first time. The color expression and dynamic effects are perfect, just like a Disney movie! It’s a 2D game but it gave me strong sense of 3D. Shaking branches, leaves in the wind, water waves when raindrops fall in the water...every single detail is so beautiful. Sometimes I felt so delightful just staring at the screen. There are three elements defining three different styles maps: water element, wind element, and warmth element. There are different theme colors for each element. Dark blue for water element, grass green for wind element, red for warmth element. It’s really immersive in different scenes. Especially in the map of warmth element, I just could feel the heat around! There are kinds of monsters in these scenes: monkey, bat, rhinoceros, and some nasty insects and spiders. Every monster was designed delicately especially the monster which could split in many little ones. It’s really disgusting but it’s well done!

Soundtrack: I’ll give it 120 points out of 10. When starting the game, there was a long cutscene. I always skip cutscenes but when I heard the background music of Ori, I stopped myself skipping it. It reminded me of Zootopia, Frozen... It was so Disney anyway! The music changed when I stepped into different maps. When I started with water element, in thorn bush, the music was gloomy and deep, even a little creepy. Was I too sensitive? While after the water was purified and in maps of wind element, the music become relaxing and light which reminded me of those amazing background music in Harry Potter. Then it turned into marches in maps of warmth element which made me really anxious. Besides those different music for different maps, there are exclusive music for three escapes. They almost killed me, literally. They were really stressing and tense but with background music, I was filled with determination and passion. Even if I love these special escapes, they were nightmares with no doubt. Besides background music, the dubbing was amazing as well. I couldn’t actually get what they were talking, but it sounded cute. I liked that!

Story: plot was simple. It was just a story about a little animal influenced enemies with his kindness. It was very simple and enough for a platformer game which lasts about 10 hours in length. Other creatures except Ori didn’t show strong and obvious personalities. But it seemed they were designed to be creatures which didn’t know how to express their feeling so it was fair. I believe most players might be very touched by the big bird’s sacrifice for Ori.
Gameplay: smooth move, excellent combat, fair puzzles, and reasonable ability tree. It was almost perfect... Except the difficulty. When I first saw this game, I thought it was just a little relaxing game for girls which was easy to get finished. But you know what, it turned out to be so unfriendly. Even if I had watched many playthrough, I actually knew what I had to do, when I was literally doing it, it was so different and I really died a lot. You need to be very accurate, and sometimes it was so close, then you would understand why we changed our keyboard over and over again. However, I have to say the skills are very interesting especially “bash”. It was so refreshing when I got that. If you used it correctly, you might probably avoid most damage and attack. It's not often I get choked up by a game, but this one nailed it.  Absolutely beautiful story, beautiful setting and some interesting mechanics.   As the game starts, Nillin is completely amnesiac, so you know just as much of what's going on as she does.  It's hard to write a really positive review about this game when its strongest point is the story, so I'll move on to some of the other aspects of it.
Aside from the story, one of Remember Me's best points is the combat.  It's a free-flow, combo-based system reminiscent of the Arkham series, except that YOU choose the effect that the attacks have.  Extra damage, health regeneration, and a reduction in your special ability's recharge time (more on that in a minute) are the three choices you have, but in addition to that you can use a chain effect which mimics and magnifies the effect of your previous hit in the combo.  These can be changed mid-combat via a menu in the pause screen, to suit your needs in a particular fight.
Nillin gets a TON of character development, but most of the other characters you meet don't really get explored.  Early on you meet someone who is supposedly one of your closest friends, but he never appears again after Episode 3.  This is, understandably, Nillin's story, but the game could have done with a bit more character development.
My only other big complaint is with the climbing.  When you're first introduced to the climbing mechanics, it feels like a tutorial, but the training wheels never really come off.  It has the look of Assassin's Creed-style parkour, but it feels very restrictive and not at all fluid, in several cases almost to the point of immersion-breaking.  I think that if DONTNOD had put some more time into the climbing mechanics, it could have been better than it is.
All in all, weighing the bad with the good, I'd give this an 8.5/10.  The few issues I have with the gameplay aren't enough to really take away from the phenomenal story that this game has to offer, and I can honestly say that I was at the edge of my seat for a fair portion of it.

I only played Wolfenstein: The New Order this year when I got it on sale for super-cheap. I absolutely loved that game, and I was looking forward to The New Colossus.
The New Colossus had a lot of hype behind it, and honestly, I got sucked into the hype. It was the first non-World of Warcraft expansion game I bought at full price since 2013. Did I like it? Well, you can obviously tell I did, since I answered "yes" to "Do you recommend this game?" But it's not without its flaws.
The New Colossus picks up almost immediately after the end of The New Order. BJ Blaskowicz is in a bad way. He and his allies are under attack by a villain from the first game. It's during this introduction that the game gives us a series of Important Story Moments. These moments, and others like it throughout the game, are the best part of Wolfenstein II. The less I say about each one, the better. Some are very sad, some are funny, and some are a combination of hilarious and terrifying.
It's the gameplay where I find the most fault with the game. It's not terrible or bad; in fact, it's very much like The New Order, which was decidedly good! BJ's perks system returns, allowing you to choose how you want Blaskowicz's Nazi-killing skills to evolve. You can still take cover and lean out or above to shoot people. And of course, you can dual wield your guns for that extra punch.
On the other hand, the battles feel a little samey. And a bit more difficult, at least at the beginning. I found myself dying a lot, and I couldn't help but feel like I didn't even know I was barely hurt seconds before collapsing. The damage indicators are perhaps more subtle than they should be; a cursory glance at other players' impressions of the game confirms that I'm not alone in this opinion.
I was a fan of stealthing my way through the areas as much as I could in The New Order. You can do that a lot here too, but stealth feels more challenging than before, and not necessarily in a fair way. I never got a handle on when enemies could see me, although I did get better thanks to some stealth-related perks.
It took me 29 hours to complete the game. I don't play games like a lot of people, apparently. I like to get through a level slowly, exploring every nook and cranny for secrets. I also enjoyed walking around my resistance base and listening to my resistance fighters have conversations. And before I dove into the final level, I did a bunch of side missions, which just use the levels you've visited before (with one exception). Had I not done all of this, I probably could have finished the game in 12 hours or less.
I did have a few technical issues here and there which may have been fixed by a recent patch. None of them were absolutely game-breaking, fortunately.
Overall, it was a good game, but I felt that The New Order was balanced better.

First thing first - it's VERY obvious this game was re-branded after the 2011 court case where they no longer had the duke Nukem license, so Shelly was born and with her BombShell. 3d Realms isn't the one that died back in 2009, this is the new Danish studio.
The main "general", "main villain" and one lines totally are not the duke nukem ones. definitely not. (i beg ye, forgive the sarcasm). The game is a top down Aesthetics much like diablo 3, and tries to emulate the same feel and combat. Sadly for bombshell, it fails.
The Fighting is boring with very limited weapons that range from Bland to Expected (machine gun, mini-gun, shotgun, rocket launcher... you get the idea) and all of this is dukes , er.. shellies special prosthetic arm that is also an AI and turns in to a turret, because the arm is alien tech. the duke nukem cheese story really doesn't hold up in this title, with painfully repetitive one lines and even more painfully bad dialogue & story progression.
The combat is bland, sure shooting and executing enemies is great fun, but sadly the half dozen executions of an equally small number of enemies do bring you to sleep a few hours in.... and the first boss is about 4 hours in. This means digging though "okay-ish" and repetitive mobs to the first actually challenging fight.  While you CAN level your character, the customization is extremity limited boiling down to HP, Shield, Special power as well as a few weapon upgrades (damage + alt fire mode). Also the AI is dummer than a brick and bugs out quite handidly as well. with going non responsive, jumping of ledges and even shooting the wrong direction.
There are no actual drops in the game outside of money (used to upgrade your weapon) and ammo. which drops like candy on Halloween. And there is no physical customization in any way you can control.

Moving on to performance: the game does perform pretty well, with frame-rates in the high 80-90, except when the game decides to magically drop it down to 20 for no apparent reason.
Sound is probably the games best aspect and is pretty well done, but it doesn't make the rest of the game any better. If you're REALLY Desperate for a shooty-runny-action-adventure game... Get diablo or torchlight for better experience.

If your looking for a game that provides fun, excitement and a difference as opposed to some of the most recent games then Bombshell provides that. The game has plenty to offer from such as a wide array of enemies and creative weaponary, which can be used in various ways to counter various enemies and give you the tactical advantage, levelling up and tech trees, dynamic and universal locations and levels. I would recommend Bombshell for those looking for a game with different taste as well as a casual and very fun game.

This review is of the pre-release review copy of the game provided by 3D Realms.
Going into bombshell, you’d be forgiven in thinking, due to its heritage, that you’ll be in for a relentless onslaught of mass destruction and cheesy fun, with characters and tropes ripped straight out of the action hero handbook. Expecting explosions and alien body parts littering the floor as you mercilessly remove every single one of them from the world will sadly leave you feeling disappointed, as it did me.
This isn’t to say that Bombshell doesn’t feature a decent amount of explosive action, featuring a variety of weapons that Shelly’s detachable metal arm turns into. From an average machine gun or minigun to a shotgun, rocket launcher or even to simply detach your arm into controllable vehicle that is otherwise controlled by an AI called Amiga, you’ll have more than a few opportunities to make the aliens go boom.

No matter which way I cut it, Bombshell is a game that for every awesome thing it has going for it, it lets me down with two more. It leaves a good first impression, and man it’s nice to shoot some evil aliens in a 3D Realms game again! But it’s a character-driven action game that seems to have forgotten the character part, and instead just relies on action with no soul. The ten hour campaign was a real slog to get through, with boring levels, standard weapons, weak "role-playing" elements, and an utterly forgettable story. Seeing as there are lots of similar games that do this kind of gameplay better, I cannot recommend picking it up for the asking price of $35. I still look forward to seeing what the team at Interceptor comes up with next, but for me, Bombshell was more bomb than... er... shell.

Having completed a full playthrough (Game Years 1460 - 1620) after the v1.071 patch, I can say definitively that you see the entirety of the game after the first hour or two of play.  By Game Year 1520, I had established a successful guild with 9 solid painters (the maximum allowed). The "hard," flavorful part of the game was over at that point. For the next 100 years, it was autopilot as the game offered no new challenges, no new rewards, and it drastically reduced the number of historical events mentioned.
Unlike other management games (Grand Prix Story, Game Dev Tycoon, etc.), there doesn't seem to be any replay value. The different bonuses for the different cities are not very impactful after about a half hour of play. Nothing unlocks after a playthrough. The game doesn't offer different paths to explore. There really aren't any decisions or choices to make.
The one part of the game I did not explore was hiring the famous artists that we know today such as Botticelli or Rafael. I have no reason to believe, however, that hiring them open new stories. I suspect that they are simply excellent painters – and I had too many of those.

It's an impressive feat that Ninja Theory has pulled off here; with a game that is incredibly harrowing, and utterly engrossing at the same time. While the underlying mechanics at work were generally very simple, I felt like they complimented the narrative well. Actions generally felt good to perform and in many respects, reinforced the oppressive tone the game was driving for.
The only very minor quibble I have with the game was the odd case of a camera getting stuck inconveniently behind a wall during combat; mostly if Senua herself had been driven back into a corner. Thankfully this happened happened rarely and never actually got me killed, so it didn't really spoil my enjoyment.
At the end of the day, Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is an excellent example of a developer tackling incredibly risky subject matter with superb production values that could easily have backfired on them. I couldn't imagine any big publisher greenlighting a project tackling themes of psychosis and mental illness so honestly.
This is a no-brainer purchase if you enjoy horror in any form or if you're looking for an experience unlike any other.

Wow. I just finished the game, and it is certainly one of the most nuanced, thought provoking games I've ever played. If I had to think of another game with a story like this, I would say Spec Ops: The Line, which should tell you a bit about its quality if nothing else.
Like others have said here, I never found the game difficult. I never died in or out of combat, and enemies were generally easy to handle. However, the combat system was surprisingly robust and made encounters feel visceral and impressive, which lead me to not mind the difficulty in the slightest.
This is a game to play for the story, the sometimes suffocating atmosphere, and the incredible depiction of Senua's psychosis. Literally every aspect of the game ties into her mental illness, and once you understand that, the game becomes even more impressive. Even with the combat being easy for me, I still rarely felt safe, and the real(?) and perceived dangers to Senua were unsettling and impactful.
Basically, buy the game, it’s an experience well worth having.

Hellblade has a compelling narrative and is quite beautiful. The combat is repeatative towards the end, but the game mixes it up by giving you different combinations of enemies to fight to compensate for it. The visual puzzles weren't difficult to me but your mileage may vary.
The game's strengths are it's narrative and breathtaking visual / sound direction. The puzzles could be more challenging for me, and the combat was servicable but different types of engagement would make the regular encounters feel more fresh. While I do not consider the combat a detractor from the game, I do not consider it a strength of the game that would bring in players.
Overall I recommend this game. However, I caution that players shouldn't go into this game looking for your next hack and slash action/adventure, as it is not a gameplay driven experience.

I hesitate to call this a "hidden object game" in the traditional sense because the first real HOG screen doesn't appear until over halfway through the game.  They toss in a handful of FROG (fractured object) puzzles, and they give you a "find a bug in each location" challenge, but for the most part this is an extremely casual point and click adventure that happens to have a few hidden object puzzles contained in the mix of mini-games.  (This is not necessarily a bad thing, however I expected something a bit different after playing several of Artifex Mundi's other titles.)
Speaking of the mini-games, I noticed at least three of them were directly copied from "Abyss: The Wraiths of Eden."  I understand that a company needs to meet deadlines, but ripping off your own past work to flesh out your current game is a pretty disappointing tactic.
Due to the sparsity of HOG's, there was no alternate puzzle solution option for this game (such as dominoes or mahjong).  While this is a significantly more simplified level of gameplay than I have come to expect from this studio, it does allow the player to complete all of the achievements in one playthrough.  They also did not include any time challenges for this game.
Aside from the puzzles, the adventure game elements were fairly intuitive, there wasn't too much backtracking, the story was decent enough, the art was good, the character designs and voice acting were well done, and there was even a bit of humour thrown into the dialogue.  I also liked the inclusion of an animal companion who doubles as a special use item (something that seems to be a bit of a trend with this studio's more recent titles).  However, the game is not entirely immersive, and many of the challenges feel like a means to an end, rather than a fun progression of the plot.
Overall I would have to give this game a 6/10.   If you are expecting a HOG, you will be disappointed, but if you are just looking for a casual steampunk adventure game, it fits the bill well enough.

It's hard to fully recommend this game to be honest.  At most times if a game is "eh", I give it a thumbs down only to expression (which I have) that's a thumbs in the middle type of game.  Ori is one of those games.
Pros:
*Beautiful Graphics
*Fantastic Soundtrack
*Tight control (except for jumping - see cons)
*Short but fun 'metroidvania' type of game.
*Crazy chase scenes which are the 'bosses'
Cons:
*Very short for this type of style game (under 10 hours)
*No real boss encounters, however the insane chase scenes make up for it.
*Control is NOT fluid when it comes to jumping:
-- and there are A LOT of those.  You'll encounter crazy complex jumps and you feel you made the jump but you really didn't.  This is where Ori fails to be a fully recommended game in my book.  Nothing is more frustrating than stiff control or bad camera angles!  It's almost not satisfiying in the end when I finished some of the crazy complex jumps.  Folorn Ruins -- I'm speaking to you!
*Not much of a story - there's a story but it's your typical "Metriod" story not much to go with but it somewhat reminded me of Shadow of Collosus which was cool.
For pros and cons me and friend could agree this is similar to Alice 2:  Great graphics and music but the game play not so much.  I recommend this game for $10 or less anything more (especially if you hate stiff controls when in terms of jumping), might not be worthwhile.
Oh and to those who got the no death achievement.  Kudos to you.  You either have A:  NO LIFE or B:  NO LIFE and are just that good.

Received a coupon for 50% OFF this game with some wacky, hilarious-sounding title "Shower with your Dad Sim".  Of course, I had to take a gander.  After I saw that Chris Hardwick had gave it a shout out and also that my 50% off meant that I could obtain this game for 50c, I was enticed to buy it.  I figured that I would most likely be annoyed at spendig fifty cents needlessly... although that's kinda the point (spoilers).
When you first start up the game there does not seem to be much content,  nor will you really necessarily understand what the ♥♥♥♥ is going on at first, but just keep running into some Dad Dongs and you'll figure yourself out.  This game is a vast journey of self-discovery... in game and within your own psyche.  As you progress in the game there are unlocks and mini-games--also an unfolding narrative of the current state of quality control for games on Steam.
The pixel art is trippy and the art/music combo instills a sort of mood reminiscent of Hotline Miami or some other similar ventures.  There is hidden humor in things like trying to change the game Options.  Also, there is abundant humor available for you to Blow of steam with between showers via a bunch of Bad Dad Jokes.
Although this game was presented as satire, it actually transcended itself and became something more.  The games are pretty challenging and fun and will bring you a lot of childish laughs that make it worth your time for a few hours.
My initial review was hyper-focused on the blatant vulgarity of the game and how much  I love it, but the greater message it carries unto the Steam community and the game developer's courage to stick a middle finger up to Valve, I appreciate just as much!

Since some folks may look into puchasing these games individually as opposed to in the "Final Cut" edition which includes all 3 games, I'm going to also post a review of the individual games, taken from my Final Cut review with very slight modifications. I'm going to call this one Van Helsing I (while the sequels will be II and III, of course).
Van Helsing I's content was great. I expected a garbage Diablo clone with a ghost following me around that wouldn't say anything and would be useless in regard to gameplay; just serving as a stand-in for a co-op partner because the game's balancing wasn't made for single player. Boy, was I wrong. That ghost companion is my favorite thing about all three games. Her name is Katarina, she's wonderfully voice-acted, is the best character in all three games, and she is snarky, funny, and great to have around for gameplay purposes, as she has three separate skill trees and levels up on her own. You can boost everything from boosting your hero's critical hit chance, to your Magic Find (item drop quality), to her own damage output, to her own HP, etc. She takes scenes that would be boring in any other game and injects personality and humor into them which make them either enjoyable or less unenjoyable than they would be without her. I cannot properly express how much I like Katarina. If I were given heaps of video game characters to pick from and could choose her, I dare say she would be in my overall top 10 favorite video game characters list.
With Katarina out of the way, the environments in the first segment of Van Helsing I are all outdoors, looking nice with rocks, grass, snow, swampland, trees, etc. It wasn't horribly exciting, but the sheer competence of the combat for a "Diablo clone" took me by surprise. The maps were huge with plenty of monsters to fight, loot to pick up, hidden treasure and a fair number of side quests. By the time I finished the first big leg of Van Helsing I, I was getting a little tired of the outdoor areas. So what does the game do? It goes full-on steampunk. The guns and a few clockwork-soldier-looking-dudes in the wilderness had that vibes, sure, but I never expected a steampunk city with Van Helsing as the hero, but a ghost sidekick, monster allies, and scientist villains. It was cheesy and the vampire ally is practically a cartoon character, but it was all so lovable and fun. There were a significant number of references to movies, film, games, etc., but they never felt like "too much" to me, and added some levity to the game. The third act was more steampunk city, but the classier end of town, so it felt fresh.
The final boss to Van Helsing I was pretty easy, but I'd rather have easy than insufferably hard, because I'm here to have fun, rather than prove something to myself or others. The ending is a to-be-continued sort of thing, but not a cliff-hanger by any means. I thoroughly enjoyed Van Helsing I's original release, and the version you can find in the Final Cut version of the game appealed a bit more to me, thanks to the new skill trees, though that's a matter of taste which could vary from player to player. I cannot speak of the co-op in the original version as I have not tried it, but if it is functional, then I would imagine it's quite fun as it was in the Final Cut version. This is a very good game, though depending on the price, you may wish to grab the Final Cut, even if only to play through the Van Helsing I segment and then quit the game without continuing due to the dip in quality from the sequels.

To the Moon is a different game indeed. First, there's not much "game" to it, besides exploration (and there's not much length to it either, as it's about 4.5 hours of gameplay - though I feel it was just the perfect length for the kind of game it is). There are a few puzzles in the first half of the game, but they add very little (and as such, they're basically absent in the second half of the game). Some other "game" sequences feel so out of place that it almost hurts, and the game could arguably be better without them. Or perhaps not, but as I said, there's not much "gameplay" here, if that's what you're looking for.
Yet, To the Moon wouldn't work as well as anything but a game, because the interactivity and exploration aspects of its gameplay are a very important aspect of its storytelling. As the doctors explore Johnny's memories, you're there too, in a way you wouldn't be if you weren't controlling their actions. The game makes you feel like an invader sometimes, as you uncover intimate feelings and secrets that give amazingly human dimensions to the main characters in the game. It works well with the visual style and the music (FANTASTIC music, I should add) to create a really memorable experience.
And the story is easily one of the best, most humane stories I've ever seen told in any videogames. It is dramatic, but nothing about it seems forced. It is also funny at times (especially where Dr. Watts is concerned). It is also exquisitely well-written, easily topping the likes of Bioware in the quality of its writing. And it's a unique experience, that kind of story that makes you look at your own life and think about what's really important, and what could have happened had things been different. It is effective, it is heart-wrenching, it is brilliant.
In summary, this is not a "game" game. It's all about the story, and how you interact with it. But it's also one of the best stories ever told in videogame form, and the most humane game I've ever played. I highly, highly recommend it. You may not find a "game" here, but you may well find what I've found - a true gem of writing and interactive storytelling, one that is bound to make you relate to the characters like no other game ever had, and possibly make you shed quite a few tears of your own. It is one of my favorite games of all time, and one that I plan to play every year, on my birthday, as a way of revisiting my own life, and remembering what are the really important things after all. And if that's not art, then what is?

Recommended with a caveat: despite an enjoyable story, great art direction and an exciting world, there are serious flaws in the enemy design, puzzles and combat.  These are not wholly visible until suddenly they bring the game to a standstill. You are thrust into fights with enemies and combinations of enemies designed like puzzles but which are ultimately frustrating when presented to you over and over again.
Remember Me suffers from curious game design choices which leave the player confused, when simply working through menus or when he or she should be having fun. The memory remix puzzles are at first exciting, but without any clear goals and precise understanding of cause and effect, you soon realise just how prescriptive the puzzles are and thus dependant on trial and error.
So that's a huge caveat. Why then, do I recommend it? The combat can be worked through with patience. The irritating bosses and memory remixes can be solved with guides. After all that, there is a very interesting world to experience (to a point, as almost nothing is interactive unless its an enemy or game resource) and the story is memorable.
The gameplay, however, can evoke memories you might prefer to erase.

I got this game in a sale and it was worth every penny.  Even at full price this game is worth it compared to many AAA titles that are $60 plus.
It has an engaging story with likeable characters that you grow to care about and the voice acting is spot on.  The atmosphere in the game is really well done.  The game is set in a futuristic Paris where people's memories are a hot commodity and an evil company misuses their power to create a gap between rich and poor.  Overall I liked the story and it last about 7 hours (my gameplay time is higher because I alt+tabbed for a while).
This game would have benefited from being more open as the futuristic paris looked great, I just wish I could have explored it more.
I've seen a lot of people complain about the fighting mechanics, I suspect this is because they couldn't get to grips with them because I really liked them.  You can devise your own combos adding in different elements to change what your attacks do.  You also get a select few "special" attacks which do different kinds of damage.  At the end of the story with them all unlocked you can really pull off some cool combos and techniques.
Unfortunately the game has little replayability value given its very linear story, save for going back to collect things you missed.  Unless you're an achievement hunter though, I doubt you will do this.  There's not much to be gained.
Pros:
- Strong female lead
- Well written and voice acted
- Interesting and at times philosophical story
- Intriguing combat and cool combos
- Great atmosphere and good graphics
Cons:
- Quite short (7hrs, max)
- Not much replayability

I've thought long and hard about this review, so hear me out.
I've been a fan of this series from the beginning, and I mean the very beginning.  I've played all of them, and played many other shooters in my day.  The two most recent Wolfensteins leading up to this one were pretty good.  I had high hopes for this one, and pre-ordered it at full price.  This game just doesn't deliver.  Every other single wolfenstein, including original wolf3D, is better than this one.  So save your money, and go buy one of those.  Or buy this drastically reduced in price on a massive sale.  This game isn't bad, but it isn't as good as it's previous incarnations.
As for the "story"... I can't tell if this is an SJW's wetdream utopian paradise, or how SJWs view the world currently.  You have the "strong" female hero types, a rather saucy black broad with 70's hair and 'personality', a bunch of beta males not worth mentioning, the stereotypical disabled person who takes more screen time in the cut scenes and story than he deserves, oh and of course, the most important thing of all... All white people are evil nazis.  And they actually are!
Political comedy aside, this game is pretty much the only place where this sort of thing is acceptable.  So I swallow the pill hard, and go in to punch nazis... So this brings me to the actual gameplay portion of my review:
-When you take damage, you get no indicators whatsoever.  Like forget about directional... You do NOT get indicators that you are even TAKING damage.  I have read some on the forums state "this is a shout out to the old school style where you had to keep an eye on your health."  That's total BS, like I said, I've been playing DOOM, Wolf3D, and many other shooters since floppy disk DOS days, and you always get an indicator via HUGE RED FLASH and LOUD GRUNT.  This game has nothing.  So you think you're fine, and then you're dead.
-You get to dual wield ANY combination of your guns, this is a FANTASTIC improvement... BUT, you CANNOT control when you reload...  If EITHER gun runs out of ammo, it AUTOMATICALLY reloads that weapon even if you DONT want it to, and still have the other fully loaded to continue SHOOTING at the NAZIS right in front of you... So you die a LOT for this, and find yourself unnecessarily triggering double-reloads on half-full clips in the middle of firefights you otherwise would not want to be doing this in.
-Difficulty is too high not in a fun way.  It's fine if a game is hard, and a challenge.  I am grinding through this on hard afterall, and not backing off.  But it isn't actually a challenge because I need more skill to overcome it... Like the points mentioned above, you feel CHEATED out of every death, not even realizing that you're dying, or what got you.  Forget about one guy behind a random corner and move forward to proceed to the next area?  OOPS, dead GG.  Fired one bullet too many on your dual wielded machine guns and are FORCED to reload against your will when one guy is left in front of you and you have a fully loaded gun in the other hand that could easily blast him... TOO bad DEAD GG. Etc.
Ultimately this game falls short of expectations. Fails to match up to the previous games (which is rare of a sequel in the gaming world).  For the same price point, you can have Destiny 2, or Shadows of Mordor, or TW WH II, or Dishonored 2, etc. all better games.  For less of a price point you can have the previous games, which are better.
Best thing about this game is it's graphics, but that is pretty standard for most next generation games these days.  I'd say hold off for a MASSIVE sale (at least 50%) if you're a fan of the series, really want this game, and have already played the previous 2.  Oh also DOOM is better straight up, get that first too.

It’s kind of sad that future generations are never going to get to experience the simple pleasure of walking around a video store. Aimlessly browsing through aisles of straight to VHS flicks with flashy covers, chuckling to yourself about the ridiculous plot twists described on their back covers, and then finally passing over all of them and picking out a movie you’ve seen before. Bombshell feels like one of those movies you’d pass up on. It has style for days, featuring well designed baddies, unique weaponry, and visceral combat. The game plays great in short bursts, but Bombshell has grander ambitions. It reaches for a rich narrative, platforming puzzles, and expansive levels filled with side missions, but it can’t quite stick the landing, and many players will lose patience with its flights of fancy long before the credits roll.

It's July 4th and aliens have invaded the White House! The President has been captured! A megalomanaical scientist is hell-bent on wiping out humanity! For Shelley "Bombshell" Harrison, it's just another day at the office. The latest shootemup by 3DRealms & Interceptor offers plenty of guns, gore, and gags. However, is that be enough for you to say "Hail to the Queen, baby!" when it's all over?
Bombshell is for all intents and purposes; a shooter molded in the classic style. It's designed to evoke the days of
,
,
,
, and so on. As Shelley, you can hold onto every weapon you acquire, and switching between them is as quick and easy as pressing a numeric key. The campaign is divided into three acts, each with their own set of levels. Aside from inflicting astronomical levels of pain on alien adversity, you'll also do some light puzzle-solving, a little platforming, and uncover a few secrets.
The main difference between Bombshell and the classics of yore is in the overhead perspective. Since you always know what's happening around you, you can expect that enemies will take every chance to surround and overwhelm. While it's fair to say that every strategy devolves into "shoot the bad-guys", your consistently expanding tool-set will give you plenty of evasive and destructive tools. At first you're limited to an ion cannon and a slide. The cannon speaks for itself while the slide offers a quick way to get out of immediate danger.
As the game progresses, your selection of abilities will continue to grow. In true classic-shooter fashion, you will use all of these tools as much as they're available. Everything has risks and limitations though, and you always have to be mindful of the situation. Bowlingbombs are very deadly, because they can home in on nearby enemies and do tons of damage. However, they can just as easily explode in your face if you use them when enemies are close-by. I believe enemy fire can also set them off, so it's not worth throwing them around if you're panicking. A reflector-shield is great for alien weaponry, but it won't protect against melee, acid, explosives, and so on. The energy sword will cut through many enemies, but you're left completely open to attack. Overall, I think this game does a fine job of showcasing how every ability can work, and they're all useful in their own way. I'm especially fond of using the mega-punch to knock enemies off of cliffs.
As far as weapons go, you'll find that they're all unique, especially since each of them have two flavors of sub-weapons. For example, by adding the rail-gun to your ion cannon, you have a solid go-to weapon for doing a ton of damage. However, the other sub-weapon fires shots that bounce off of walls. This might be a better fit for your style of play. Once you decide on a sub-weapon, you're stuck with it, at least until you choose to create a new profile. This level of commitment is balanced out by the sizable arsenal. Over time you'll develop strategies that get the most out of each weapon. This is a great thing, because it's possible that you'll switch between several of them in the middle of a single fight.
Whether it's through story progress, side-quests, or leveling up, you're bound to collect skill-points. These are used to strengthen aformentioned abilities like the reflector-shield and mega-punch. They can also be used to raise health, armor, and energy levels, which aren't quite as necessary or interesting. Weapons can be upgraded through alien currency, of which you'll find tons of scattered around every level. While the upgrades tend to be simple "+x to damage", some add new properties, which help keep the combat dynamic and entertaining.
The encounters themselves are further bolstered by the minor details. As you inflict carnage, you're bound to notice enemies in a near-death state. At this point you can walk up and perform a finishing move. While these finishers don't look nearly as satisfying as a game like
, they achieve about the same effect. During the finisher, you're completely invincible, and your armor replenishes. These opportunities add further dimension to the combat, so you're more inclined to remain in the thick of it.
Like many other games with RPG elements, Bombshell offers a New Game+ mode and two unlockable harder difficulties. The enemies have much more health than before, and they can do more damage. My opinion on the hard setting is mixed. Since enemies are so durable, encounters last longer, and this proves a greater threat to your survival. Taking every advantage and using all of Shelley's tools becomes very important. At the same time, some encounters can drag, and weapons such as the minigun fall behind due to their relative lack of damage. Given the choice, I'd opt for enemies with only slightly more health, but with much more dangerous attacks. Maybe there could be "elite" enemies with weapons & attacks that are unique to harder difficulties.
The process of gaining experience and the subsequent level-ups can also become a grind. Skill-points come at a fairly steady pace, but your level ties into how much you can upgrade your weapons. Even with the increased EXP gains in hard mode, levels can get to be very few and far between, especially after level 15. Weapon-upgrades will also get extremely expensive. Doing all of the side-quests and arena challenges helps, but the difference isn't particularly dramatic. I think the numbers could stand to be changed, just so it doesn't take large chunks of the game in order for players to improve their stats.
Then there's the matter of the long-term. The average play-through should take about ten hours. Naturally this can be followed up by the hard & nightmare modes/new game+ replay. The player can also opt to try a new profile, so they can go through the game with different sub-weapons, and do med-kit-free or even death-free challenge runs. The end result is a fair chunk of time spent, but some players might be left wanting more. The developers have already mentioned that modding tools and Steam workshop support will be available shortly after Bombshell's release, so hopefully this results in plenty of additional content.
So to conclude, Bombshell is a good game. Since the bulk of it consists of shooting aliens, I appreciate that the developers really nailed it. The results of Shelley's high-tech weaponry are suitably gruesome and awesome. Enemies decapitate and explode quite nicely, and the gibs that result from a flak cannon at close-range are always welcome. All of the bits in-between like exploration and exposition are just fine. The soundtrack is also quite excellent, and really helps to elevate the action. If you have the PC for it, this game can also look stunning. The backgrounds are especially well-done. There are some tweaks that could be made, but all in all, this is an enjoyable title.

Alright. Painters Guild. I'm a big fan of management games and simulators. This one looked pretty cool, so I went for it.
After playing for 4½ hours, I've seen everything this game has to offer.
It's not a big game, or a complex game, and there isn't much depth to it..
Honestly, spending 4½ hours with it might be longer than you'd want to. The systems get very repetitive, and I have a hard time putting a finger on what made me keep playing.
I guess it's very soothing. The soundtrack is very nice, the artstyle is cool, and I like the way the paintings look in the 8-bit artstyle.
Spending 8-10€ on it now is probably too much for you. You probably won't get more than 3 hours out of it before you get seriously bored, but it's a cool idea, and it's almost well executed. I just wish there were more things to do in the game.
As it is, you just assign painters to painting that you get hired to do. Then you train them, and make paint for the paintings... You just swap the painters around and you do an ungodly amount of clicking and dragging.
I sound negative, but all in all, i don't really regret buying it. I enjoyed my time, but I'd recommend not buying it at full price. €5 seems about right, and that's when you don't consider that you could get games like Tomb Raider and The Witcher 2 for less on sale...
But like I said, the concept is cool, and the music is actually really really good. It's just a shame that it is as shallow as it is.
So yeah. €5 or less? sure, why not, if you need to burn a few hours (and I really do mean a few..)

Bombshell is an action-RPG developed by Interceptor Entertainment and published by 3D Realms. You play as Shelly “Bombshell” Harrison as you invade an alien world to stop a mad scientist who’s kidnapped the President. While playing I was reminded of cheesy sci-fi action movies from the '80s and '90s. The story is campy and the dialogue even more so. The gameplay is sufficient, but nothing to write home about. In short, Bombshell is much like the sci-fi mvies it takes inspiration from, entertaining while it lasts, but largely forgettable.
To give a little back story, Shelly was once a member of an elite team of soldiers. During an ill-fated mission, she lost her team, and her arm, at the hands of Dr. Jadus Heskel. The game opens with Shelly being called back into service to get revenge on Dr. Haskel who, with an army of aliens called the Kyrr, has attacked the White House in an attempt to kidnap the President, Aurora Skye.
The story seems to be purposefully cheesy and is delivered through mostly competent voice acting. The main characters are voiced well, but the random NPCs that give you side quests deliver their lines poorly and Shelly’s one-liners during combat are woefully overused. For a game that seems to be going for a particular style and attitude, I would have liked to see a little more exposition and character development to sell the world it takes place in. Shelly could have been a great new character had she been more developed, and the futuristic world on display is compelling, but it feels like it only exists to give you enemies to kill.
Speaking of killing enemies, you do that a lot here. In fact, unless you are talking to an NPC or being forced to walk painfully slow during a radio conversation, you are shooting enemies. You fight pretty standard enemies with a variety of different weapons that you collect along the way. None of the enemies I encountered, even the bosses, required much strategy to dispatch; as long as I was shooting them I was doing it right
The weapons you have access to include basic machine guns, shotguns, and even a flamethrower and rocket launcher. You pick up money as you defeat enemies and explore the world, and use it to upgrade your weapons. You can increase the damage they deal and access alternate fire modes, so each weapon is essentially two archetypes. All-in-all the weapons are fairly generic and nothing really stood out to me as being unique. Ammo for everything but your starting weapon is scarce, so I found myself shying away from the other weapons and reserving their ammo for major fights. This meant that I played most of the game with the starting weapon and grew bored dispatching enemies the same way over and over again.
I also felt like game’s controls weren’t as responsive as they should have been. I often resorted to the “spray and pray” approach when enemies were attacking me from off screen or my bullets weren’t going where I wanted them to, which stinks when alternate weapon ammo is limited. I also dreaded anytime I had to jump from one platform to another because the orientation of the camera sometimes made it difficult to judge how far apart ledges were from each other. Most of my deaths were from falling. I tired the game with both a mouse and keyboard and an Xbox One gamepad. Both were adequate ways to play the game, but there were some gamepad quirks like an inability to scroll the fullscreen map which I found odd.*
The RPG elements aren’t limited to your just weapons, you can also upgrade Shelly herself by spending experience points you earn from killing enemies and completing objectives. It’s pretty standard stuff like increasing your maximum health, armor, or energy to perform her special abilities. When you access the menu it has a cool animation that looks like Shelly is glancing down at her wrist which contains a computer. However, I found navigating the upgrade trees and abilities menu to be cumbersome. I think they were trying to mimic an old computer when they designed the menu, but instead just made it difficult for you to be sure you are choosing the right upgrade.
The audio visual presentation is on point. Bombshell isn’t going to win any awards for best looking game, but the action stays fluid even when there are a dozen or more enemies on screen. I wish there was more variety in the levels though. The weapon sounds are also great and change in pitch as you near the bottom of your ammo reserve, giving you an important audio cue that warns you when your magazine is about to run dry. The soundtrack is filled with appropriate rock and metal tunes that I actually didn’t notice as much as I thought I would because the sound effects tend to overpower the music most of the time. Dr. Heskel’s voice acting stands out to me as the best in the game. He is appropriately menacing and taunts you along the way. As I mentioned before, Shelly’s one-liners are overused and by the end I was sick of her quips about her beloved car that we see for a total of three minutes at the beginning of the game. We get it, you liked your car and are upset the aliens blew it up!
In all honesty it’s hard for me to whole-heatedly recommend Bombshell. The $30 price tag may help you overlook some of the game’s flaws, but those flaws are still there. The game suffers from a lack of polish that would have made the game more enjoyable, memorable, and less frustrating. If you’re looking for a somewhat competent action-RPG and can appreciate the campy story, then perhaps Bombshell is worth a look, otherwise you may be better off playing Diablo III and watching a Dolph Lundgren joint.

(Pre-release build / Updated Retail Build provided by 3d Realms)
Duke. Rise of the Triad. Max Payne. These games were not only successful in their era, influencing the popularity of PC gaming in their own right, but also endeared themselves to gamers who still play these games to this day. 3d Realms and Interceptor Entertainment have gotten back to the business of making fun games, and that come with a sigh of relief. Bombshell is their newest IP, an isometric ARPG with noticeable links to the Duke Nukem franchise.
This is a nice looking game, all the graphical flourish you can pack into an Unreal 3 based game is there. Explosions rock the screen, gibs, blood, bulletcasings, enemies, everything melds together rather quickly and suddenly to create some pretty impressive combat sequences. The game's soundtrack is awesome. Easily the best thing about the game, love the power rock mixing into power ballads, and back up again when the action intensifies. Controls well, and for the most part the game is very stable and it's game mechanics are solid.
Where this game falters significantly is in writing, voice acting, and depth. The story is cheesey, although a considerable amount of time is dedicated to explaining races and actions that are rather dull and uncompelling. There is no real depth to this game, it's more A- than -RPG. For example, there are no puzzles to solve, no items to pick up, no skill tree to explore, and no character class customization available. You are able to pick up 9 weapons as the game progresses, each can be leveled up. Their alternate fire modes branch in two directions. You can level up 4 skills or 3 base stats. That's about it. There is plenty to explore but be prepared to a lot of of walking, as quests are simply 'pick up colored crystal and bring back to door' types of tasks.
- Nice visuals, lots of particle effects, nice looking chaotic combat sequences
- The soundtrack is hawt.
- You get to use guns named the Motherflakka and the P.M.S. to tear up 5 story behemoth bosses.
- Not a lot of depth, no items, no detailed upgrading or character customization
- Menial tasks to open doors, and progress to the next level
- Really bad voice acting
- Uneven writing, is it trying to take itself serious? Or not? Is Bombshell irreverant or a heartfelt stab at science fiction? It's never clear.

It's an impressive feat that Ninja Theory has pulled off here; with a game that is incredibly harrowing, and utterly engrossing at the same time. While the underlying mechanics at work were generally very simple, I felt like they complimented the narrative well. Actions generally felt good to perform and in many respects, reinforced the oppressive tone the game was driving for.
The only very minor quibble I have with the game was the odd case of a camera getting stuck inconveniently behind a wall during combat; mostly if Senua herself had been driven back into a corner. Thankfully this happened happened rarely and never actually got me killed, so it didn't really spoil my enjoyment.
At the end of the day, Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is an excellent example of a developer tackling incredibly risky subject matter with superb production values that could easily have backfired on them. I couldn't imagine any big publisher greenlighting a project tackling themes of psychosis and mental illness so honestly.
This is a no-brainer purchase if you enjoy horror in any form or if you're looking for an experience unlike any other.

Wow. I just finished the game, and it is certainly one of the most nuanced, thought provoking games I've ever played. If I had to think of another game with a story like this, I would say Spec Ops: The Line, which should tell you a bit about its quality if nothing else.
Like others have said here, I never found the game difficult. I never died in or out of combat, and enemies were generally easy to handle. However, the combat system was surprisingly robust and made encounters feel visceral and impressive, which lead me to not mind the difficulty in the slightest.
This is a game to play for the story, the sometimes suffocating atmosphere, and the incredible depiction of Senua's psychosis. Literally every aspect of the game ties into her mental illness, and once you understand that, the game becomes even more impressive. Even with the combat being easy for me, I still rarely felt safe, and the real(?) and perceived dangers to Senua were unsettling and impactful.
Basically, buy the game, it’s an experience well worth having.

A finely crafted atmospheric game parts hack'n'slash, part walking simulator, part horror.
It's kind of like Dante's Inferno with vikings. Wait, that doesn't nearly do enough justice... It's an experience into the mind of a woman trying to make sense of a world in which she has lost almost everything. Except her determination and love.
The narrative is quite fascinating. It's a tale of a Pictish warrior who goes on a quest to the Norse underworld of Hel to save the soul of her slain love. While this on the surface seems like a classic Dante's Inferno style story, it soon becomes very clear that Senua, the protaganist, suffers from some form of mental psychosis. She hears voices and sees the world in ways that can turn quite disturbing. Whether she really is going to Hel or whether it's all in her head or even both is up to the interpretation of the player. Many scenes not only draw from Norse mythology but are also heavily implied to be shaped by Senua's own traumatic experiences. It would be easy for this game to fall for classic depction of crazy people, but I felt empathy for Senua. It is clear that she cares deeply for the few people who actually gave a damn about her. A great deal of this game is her fighting her psychosis and coming to terms with it.
Aesthetically, Hellblade is beautiful in both design and graphics. Senua in particular is a wellcrafted virtual character. She can get a little uncanny at times, but considering her state of mind, its hard to judge for it considering that every part of her face was motion captured. Her actress does what I feel is a pretty good job of playing a determined, disturbed woman moving through Viking Hell and confronting both literal and metaphorical demons. The designs of Hel and its denizens are also fascinating, with many foes drawing from Silent Hill in terms of design, as well as Norse Mythology. There's a certain dread towards how most of them walk to the player upright as sentinels rather than simply charging in, especially given their inhuman designs. Some of the environments can get pretty metal as well, but in ways that seem beautiful as opposed to simply crass.
Hellblade is kind of a blur of genres. While on the surface it appears to be a hack and slash game of the Souls flavor, fighting the shadowy Northmen is only a part of the game. A lot of it is actually simply walking around and occasionally doing simple puzzles related to line of sight and focus. And yet strangely I didn't really get bored during these long periods of rest. There are also great moments of tension especially at times when the game enters horror territory.
Combat itself is simple, but effective. When combat is in effect, the camera locks to over the shoulder of Senua, with her foe beyond. Multiple foes can be in the same fight and although switching targets is easy, an important part of it is making sure the enemy does not sneak around you. Thankfully, Senua's own voices warn the player if an offscreen foe is striking, allowing for a nice timed parry. I liked this system because it feels cinematic. The fights feel simple, yet tense. It does feel good to parry or evade a blow that would have floored Senua. Some of the best moments come during the boss fights however, without spoiling them too much I can say that not only is the triumph over them feel great, but the fights themselves feels intense throughout.
Sound design in this game is incredible. I strongly suggest wearing headphones because a big part of the game are the whispers that Senua hears. These furies are both antagonistic and yet also caring. And it can get terrifying when you realize that she has to deal with them for most of her waking life. They also have the advantage of implying what she is thinking at any moment, which delves into her character further. As well as these whispers, an excellent soundtrack plays. Some of the fight music is quite memorable, not going so much into action, but rather determination.
Not that there are not some flaws. The game at the beginning states that there is a permadeath element in which if you die too much your save file is deleted. This is outright false. While I understand the choice, given how it represents Senua's fear of the darkness taken her over, I still feel like it would have been a cool thing to add in for real.
While it is fairly short, going about six to seven hours for a playthrough it's been released to a lower price. Strongly Recommended.
