+ Graphics of Call of Duty 4 was what struck people the most, the previous Call of Duty’s have never achieved its level of realism at the time, so many people were astonished as to what they have accomplished, but its realistic graphics wasn’t the only thing that made COD4 look amazing. The shading and lighting made it atmospheric for night operations in the Campaign, a good example being the prologue mission, it is a stealth mission on a boat in the ocean, and it does an amazing job delivering a stealth operation intense sensation for the player as you try to battle in the darkness and do it quietly without sparking attention. And when it is a warzone, you really do see the worn out battlefield and destroyed environment, giving the player the feeling of what real soldiers see and what they feel when they see it.
+ The sound of COD4 is amazing, from the realistic gun shot sounds, and the collision between bullet and wall, to the reaction of a man being shot. COD4 outdid themselves in 2007 to deliver a very realistic modern war sensation. Then there is the soundtrack, setting the atmosphere for war, when it is a loud war zone, it plays music that would get you hyped and tense for war so you are prepared for the oncoming battle that awaits. And when it is a stealthy quiet mission, the music is very soft and what you mostly hear is the sound of your characters footsteps and the world around you. And the voice actors did an amazing job portraying the characters in COD4, especially Gaz and Captain Price, as Gaz was a very likeable character and Captain Price was that badass boss you would follow around anywhere.
+ Gameplay is astonishing for 2007 games, as COD4 proved to be very smooth and never does it stop or act blocky at any point, you control your character and what stance he/she is in, you control the amount of bullets you want to discharge and you control where you want to go. Everything went according to planned and crashes came almost never, the most frequent crashes came from modders when they tried to mess with the game intentionally.
+ The multiplayer was the most amazing thing at the time and it is easy to know why, it was the first time COD had ever introduced such expansive customization for multiplayer gameplay. So of course people loved that you can decide if you want to take bullets more lightly or deliver bullets harder, or if you want a red dot sight or an acog scope. This paved the way for the amazing multiplayer we see now in Black Ops 2 and Advanced Warfare.
+ The campaign of COD4 is one of the best of all the COD as it delivered a very good story and build up, and introduced a very good way of switching between characters. Switching between the SAS and the USMC. The campaign bears a lot of emotion in the beginning when you finally meet Captain Price to the time you are shot in the face by Al Asad, to the memorable time as Paul Jackson when your bird goes down and you crawl from the debris of the helicopter. COD4 has one of the most memorable campaigns in all of COD.
+ Continuation is what people loved about the Modern Warfare series, as you take from the predecessor and play a same characters to continue the Modern Warfare, and yes I am talking about Soap, that muppet that made it past selection. A lot of people played COD4 because it was the prequel to Modern Warfare 2 which was the prequel to Modern Warfare 3, but there are many people out there that will agree that the only reason they play the other Modern Warfare Campaigns is because they want to pick up where they left off in COD4.
Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare is one of the best Call of Duty’s out there and will be for a long time as it introduced the best features of a game, showing the power and potential they have. The strong story and revolutionary multiplayer, Call of Duty 4 is a must have for shooter and Call of Duty lovers if they want to know one of the shooters that helped build the shooter genre we have today. So yes, I suggest this game to anyone who enjoys shooters or a shooter with a great story.

Clockwork Tales: Of Glass And Ink is a an easy point and click adventure with hidden object and logic puzzles.  I've personally cleared every puzzle without any assistance on the hardest difficulty level.  I'm not trying to brag, but rather I'm the same guy who can hardly solve any puzzles in 7th Guest or 11th Hour.  On the flip side, the puzzles aren't too absurd or abstract, so you're never in a position to randomly guess at a solution.  As for the voice acting and the animated transitions, they are welcoming to break up the monotony of solving puzzle after puzzle.  The overall story though is lacking in material.  The game feels like a chunk of a bigger unwritten story.  The prequel story only creates more questions than it answers.  Overall, I had a great time, even if it was pretty short.  If you like creative puzzles without being overwhelmed, give this a shot.

I received this as part of a sale package containing many games from the developer (Daedalic). I did not realize that all of these games were essentially Point-Click games. And I have come to the conclusion that I do not care for this type of game (P/C). I digress.
This one was actually pretty decent. Dialogue was pretty good. Storyline was intriguing. The fact that you can switch between  two different characters in completely different situations (one incarcerated/one civilian in San Francisco), in hopes to later merge their stories, is a cool concept. I also liked that they covered some mature and progressive social concepts in the game.
All that being said...should you buy this game?
I say maybe. If you enjoy the 1950's Beat era, and you enjoy point/click gaming, then sure go ahead and do it.
If you can find this on sale, even better.
Should you go out of your way to play this? Does this offer a unique "must have" experience? Do I think that this should be in every gamer's collection? Would I play this again?
No.
Personally, I would have rather spent the time and money on something else.
That does not mean it is a bad game, and that you will not enjoy it.
I know there are some of you that will (and likely quite a few of you).
If I could give this a "maybe" recommendation, then I would, but I can't. I think there are enough people out there that could gain enjoyment from this game, and for that reason alone, I will give it a positive recommendation, but just barely.

With the social questions it touches on, the story has a lot of potential that it does not, however, quite live up to. A multi-racial beatnik couple in the 1950s US, wwith gay friends at that, there could be some actual drama. Or social commentary. Or a number of other things. But, for the most part, the game simply falls flat. This extends to certain choices feeling way  too inconsequential (seriously, killing a man who doesn't seem that bad is all just about a Steam achievement?).
Considering this is an adventure that nobody is buying for the graphics (mediocre), animations (bad) or voice-overs (which seem better in German, which of course is par for the course with Daedalic), but for the puzzles (really moronic at times in that you have to do something specific before being allowed to do the blatantly obvious), choices (again, are there, don't feel like they matter), and story (which falls far short of its potential), I can't actually recommend buying this game for itself. It's not that it is that downright bad, mind. It's merely that it isn't actually good, either. Literally every other Daedalic adventure I've played is better - so unless you already own them all, this is not the one you want to get.
For what it's worth, I got this game as part of a bundle deal and basically pennies to the dollar; and I will say it's definitely a much better 'bundle sweetener' than some of the other crap Steam has thrown my way at times.

1954 Alcatraz is a point-and-click adventure with a setting quite well summarised in its title. It features atmospheric music supporting a well voice-acted, believable story. The game has a nice two-protagonist approach but some flaws in its situational progression and is missing some conveniences I expect in adventures.
+ Nice and fitting music
+ Good voice-acting
+ (apart from continuity problems) Believable story
+ Addresses mature themes, sex and violence
+ Good scene art
0 Okay 3D character models
0 point-and-click progression better planned for the first half of the game
- "Cinematic" bars and useless blurring filter in cut-scenes
- Janky animations
- Loading times
- No fast travel
- Waiting for animations
- Janky dialogue skipping
- Some ways to dead-lock the game
- Continuity problems
- Funneling, useless waiting for activation of progression parts
I guess the game wants you to feel like you're watching a movie and an old movie at that. Otherwise the constant "cinematic" bars and a blurry filter don't really make much sense. Anyway, I'd rather have a clear and big picture.
The game addresses a few mature themes generally in connection with moral decisions which I appreciate.
I like the voice acting very much. All of the characters felt right to me that way.
I generally want to be able to fast-forward or skip parts of dialogue. Although available in principle it was a bit off here. At times skipping lines didn't work, sometimes you just skip the subtitles but the audio and video plays out, sometimes skipping resulted in unclickable dialogue choices or vanishing action points outside dialogue, effectively dead-locking the game.
For some reason the intro looks like its graphics were drawn with a sharpie which doesn't really fit the rest of the game and looks almost as if this part was skipped in design in favour of simply showing story board pieces. Well, might be the way the past is portrayed here.
The character models are 3D and look okay but their animations looked odd at times. The background art is hand-drawn and pretty good, liked that.
Loading times, though still measured in seconds, are longer than I'd expect for an adventure game. This was most apparent when navigating Alcatraz which shows an overview of the island as sort of a hub to the sub-locations. The overview is a picture of the island in front of a picture moving up and a picture moving side-ways, plus a few animated birds - no reason for a longer wait. Does the game actually mandate waiting periods in loading times?
Even though rooms are generally close together, I would like to see a fast-travel option on principle, i.e. quickly navigating to accessible rooms and leaving rooms with a double-click - respectively not and not generally possible here.
I think my main problem with the game was its incompletely planned progression, funneling and continuity errors. Besides dialogue going rogue you can also progress in the wrong location (
) and dead-lock the game that way. I didn't like when a game unnecessarily waits for some event before allowing a specific action
. And it feels, like some avenues were just left out of the game.
Additionally the game fails some continuity checks (
).
Despite the few problems I say 1954 Alcatraz is a good game and I recommend it for your adventure cravings.

Received a coupon for 50% OFF this game with some wacky, hilarious-sounding title "Shower with your Dad Sim".  Of course, I had to take a gander.  After I saw that Chris Hardwick had gave it a shout out and also that my 50% off meant that I could obtain this game for 50c, I was enticed to buy it.  I figured that I would most likely be annoyed at spendig fifty cents needlessly... although that's kinda the point (spoilers).
When you first start up the game there does not seem to be much content,  nor will you really necessarily understand what the ♥♥♥♥ is going on at first, but just keep running into some Dad Dongs and you'll figure yourself out.  This game is a vast journey of self-discovery... in game and within your own psyche.  As you progress in the game there are unlocks and mini-games--also an unfolding narrative of the current state of quality control for games on Steam.
The pixel art is trippy and the art/music combo instills a sort of mood reminiscent of Hotline Miami or some other similar ventures.  There is hidden humor in things like trying to change the game Options.  Also, there is abundant humor available for you to Blow of steam with between showers via a bunch of Bad Dad Jokes.
Although this game was presented as satire, it actually transcended itself and became something more.  The games are pretty challenging and fun and will bring you a lot of childish laughs that make it worth your time for a few hours.
My initial review was hyper-focused on the blatant vulgarity of the game and how much  I love it, but the greater message it carries unto the Steam community and the game developer's courage to stick a middle finger up to Valve, I appreciate just as much!

This game is a decent time killer and worth a sale price of about $5, but not really more than that. I'm gonna mark it as "Not Recommended" only because even though it is fun, has some decent comedy, and has very good intentions, there are just too many little issues to recommend someone buy this:
1. The game has a massive bug with newer operating systems that causes it to crash every 15 mins of gameplay. There are workarounds (which I used) to avoid the crashes but it involves editing Windows Services. So if you are not comfortable with that avoid the game entirely.
2. Some bugs remain even nearly 4 years after release date. It's sad because the developers seem active in the community, but are either unwilling or unable to fix glaring issues in the game. Nothing game-breaking, but definitely frustrating.
3. The loot system is not very well balanced. It just tosses GOBS of loot at you constantly and you have to figure out which piece is good for your build. It's not perticularly hard to get anything you need ... in fact you'll probably find 12 copies of what you are looking for in any given outing. The "Go Shopping" option for your companion also doesn't help matters cause it means, unlike other ARPGs, you don't even have to prioritize what you pick up and what you leave behind. Just grab EVERYTHING and send your companion to sell what you don't want for you when you are full.
4. For all the options they give you in character building the actual process of creating a survivable character is pretty linear. You could try and mix up the abilities but in the end you have some key things you will need and not enough points in an average playthrough to get that AND the other stuff that might be fun.
5. Repetitive. Not much more to say here. ARPGs in general are repetitive, but I found this one even more so. Act 3 has some great base defense stuff added in, but it takes too long to get to that point and most people will be bored before that.
Overall it is still a fun game and if you like ARPGs, have played all the better ones already, and are just looking for a new one ... then this is a good game for you. The caveat is, expect minor issues and get it on sale.

This game is a one of mixed perceptions. Just by browsing through the reviews, you can probably guess that your take on this game will depend very much on your luck of the draw in terms of specs, since this game isn't THAT well optimized and certainly not bug-free.
On my first playthrough of the game, I ran into a game-breaking bug where I went into the boss area of the second major area of the game of the first act, but then after the brief dialogue I spawned outside of the lightning barriers that locked in the boss area with no way of opening them.
Loading it up on a new system and making a new profile resolved the issue after many months of taking a break from the game, but by the accounts of everyone else on here, there are plenty of other places for this game to potentially crash, break, or otherwise ♥♥♥♥ with you. So its a bit of a gamble on you actually being able to run this stably.
If you can get around that, its basically a Diablo clone with some nice graphics, a monster-hunter fantasy story, and some solid gameplay that anyone familiar with the genre will probably enjoy.
The story and overall writing is most parody and humorous throughout the whole game. So don't be expecting MUCH seriousness, but I also wouldn't say that its a complete comedy or satire. The banter between Van Helsing Jr. and Katarina is the high point of the game's writing for me. My biggest problem being that the game basically hints at all kinds of other interesting or fun adventures they went on prior to the game's time that I would have liked to have played in this one, but that's a minor greviance.
Gameplay is meh. You're going to be kiting A LOT in this game, especially when dealing with swarms of enemies that love to melee you and do massive damage (which with the expection of certain ranged units is I'd say the majority of the enemies in this game), but the enemies don't respawn and dying doesn't matter THAT much in this game since you can buy immediate respawns with your gold that IMO you're not going to be spending on much else anyway.
I recommend it, with provisions that in buying it you're taking a chance on it working as intended so I wouldn't buy it for that much.

Ori and the Blind Forest is actually the very first platformer that I have played AND completed. I am saying this as someone who up until now has held very little love for these particular kinds of games and their mechanics.
I wil try to be brief and not bore you with too many details:
+ The game was produced by a team that obviously loved its work: from the hand-drawn environment to the excellent music... everything in this game is detailed, harmonious and absolutely gorgeous. A true feast for eyes and ears!
+ The story is not what one would expect it to be. Hold your tissues ready because some of you might need them!
+ The map is large and full of secrets just waiting to be discovered!
+ Battles are not the main focus but can be engaging and demanding at times.
+ Being able to save at your leizure has saved 'me' a lot of fits.
+ Steam achievements give it a great amount of replay value.
~ Concerning the battles: sometimes it is very hard to complete certain stages. Often times, you are surrounded by too many enemies to really move forward or evade properly. Saving at the wrong moment might even get you stuck for a while but you can always pull through.
~ Make sure your system and graphics card conform to the minimal requirements. Mine didn't. The game was still playable but sometimes would stutter at critical moments.
- This game gets very difficult for people who can't use both keyboard and mouse efficiently. It got so bad that I did have to purchase a controller. The gameplay became smoother and easier afterwards.
- I died. A lot. You also should expect to reach a three-digit number by the end of your first playthrough.

If you like the Artifex Mundi style, then you'll probably like Clockwork Tales: Of Glass and Ink. I have to admit, this developer has changed my opinion on hidden object games in general because their titles consistently manage to combine an engaging story with puzzles that are challenging but not taxing or tedious, quality artwork, and music and voice acting that suit the story well. Clockwork Tales delivers, and is probably one of my favorites in this genre.
I really like the Steampunk aesthetic, personally, so I thought it worked nicely into the format of a hidden object game. The bad guys here are militaristic fanatics with suspiciously German-sounding accents, so it's pretty obvious what imagery they were trying to evoke, but (pseudo-)Nazis blend well with the Steampunk style.  I was amused by the effort to include a bit of a science/geology theme in some of the puzzles and in the story, and I also appreciated that (like several of the other AM games I have played) the protagonist of the story was female.
Clockwork Tales is not terribly difficult or long, and the game probably lacks much replay value, It's still pretty entertaining and I enjoyed the few hours I spent playing. The achievements can be won in just a few hours of casual gameplay, so if that's your thing, then this is your game. It's also a family-friendly game as most of the puzzles aren't too difficult and the theme isn't very scary.

Hidden Object games do get a lot of flak, and I must admit to being one of their harshest critics.  This is primarily because some companies who once made standard point and click adventures have instead jumped ship to these games.  Focus Multimedia are an example taking the Art of Murder and Chronicles of Mystery series from point and click to Hidden Object games in their later instalments.
The trouble is that a lot of these games are made on a budget, one that is very tight and they often look it.  The gameplay is often usually a few scenes and some random objects in a list.  There are exceptions however in this genre and I'm please to say Clockwork Tales: Of Glass and Ink is one of these.  DON'T go in expecting a point and click, it is still an HOG but at least it appears to be of decent quality and the game length isn't bad.

I really wanted to like this game, and for the first thirty minutes, I did. The problem is that after about an hour, the game plateaus. You're doing the same things over and over again, and there's no end game or advancement past a certain point.
So why did I log three hours, making it impossible to get a refund for the game?
Because I stupidly kept going for two hours trying to see if eventually anything would change, only to discover after three hours that nothing did. The years progressed, but the tasks (drag canvas here, drag painter there) never varied or progressed in any meaningful way. I maxed out a few painters, then they died and the process started over again maxing out their most skillful apprentices. Repeat ad nauseum. I made it up to the late 1500s before throwing in the towel.
The housing decoration might be something to work towards, but all the housing stuff has stats, so if you want to max your stats you'll just end up with the same room pattern repeated over and over with some different furniture. Similarly, the furniture has stats, so there's little point in buying anything but the nicest stuff, unless you're some kind of gaming masochist.
I guess the main problem is that there is no meaningful progression in this game. It's got one, maybe two hours of decent playtime in it before the repetition becomes too dull and tedious to continue. (Two hours is pretty generous, I think.)
The art style is gorgeous, and it's fun to see the little pixel masterpieces, but they vanish quickly. A gallery of paintings you've unlocked over various playthroughs would be a great way to showcase all the work that went into those little pixel gems and give the overarching gameplay some purpose. Even just making it possible to buy blank canvases to make paintings purely for decoration rather than at a patron's request would be nice. Then you could hang your favorite masterpieces in your guild home. Just *something* to add value to the game's price tag, which is a bit high for the current content.
I hope that the game might be improved upon in future updates. I don't know if it will, but it would certainly be worth revisiting in the future if the dev is active and updates are planned.

However, after you've added your third/forth building and have 100+ prestige the game doesn't offer much else, at 100 prestige it seems you've hit the max level of rich customers and going over that is just to provide a buffer from prestige loss if you have all your artists out on a larger project.

Not an in-depth review, but instead a swift note to concur with many of the players reviewing the day-one experience on this page. It took me nearly eight hours to get the game running in 4K with no crashes, at a decent frame rate, and with no epilepsy-inducing flickering or seasick-inducing frame pacing issues.
Eight. Hours.
Some of that time was spent playing the game of course. Just when you thought you'd fixed it, something else crept in. In fact, only the final couple of levels was everything working acceptably. It took a combination of running windowed mode (4K quadruples the UI and shows you just the top-left of the screen in 1080p otherwise. Turing off some of the graphics features (which are bugged to ♥♥♥♥), and using third-party software like Riva Tuner to ensure 60 frames are evenly distributed across each second.
And yes, of course that destroyed my ability to enjoy the game. I have an absolute monster of a PC and less demanding corridor shooter fare such as this should not require so much tuning/fixing. It was released unfinished. I mean, how can you release a game where switching the resolution up to your monitor's native resolution (in this case 4K) instantly breaks it? How can you not catch that?
And then there are the cutscenes. Yes, they're well-written. Yes they are memorable with great quality animation, but they're also streamed video. Streamed, very compressed video. Meaning there is a chasm of quality between the game and the cutscenes. For decades we've always longed for the graphics during the game to match the cut-scene pre-renders, but with the advent of 4K gaming these low-res, poorly compressed affairs look toxically out of place.
Horizon: Zero Dawn on PS4 Pro has 4K near-lossless cut-scenes to hide loading, and they look seamlessly like the rest of the game. Shadow Of War just released with a 4K cinematic pack that achieves the same thing. These things matter now.
As a shooter, even without the problems, it's average at best. Yes, the characters, writing and cutscenes in general (beyond the poor visual quality) are lightyears ahead of what we're used to seeing in videogames. But this is a shooter. And as a shooter it is NOT a 9/10.

“Shower with your dad simulator 2015” is a indie 2D Scrub-em-up time trial game. You play as 1 of three kids trying to make his way over to his dad, avoiding puddles, wet floor signs, and other, not so friendly dads.
The game is separated into 7 game types, each more ridiculous as the last. Some game modes are locked and unlocked over time, by playing the basic modes. The 2 basic modes, are similar, the first one, you pick your kid and have to race to your dad to add more time, as well as get more points. The second gamemode, you are assigned a random kid, and have to get to that kids, dad, thus adding time, and adding points.
As 2D the game is, it holds its own, graphically speaking. Everything that appears, like obstacles or powerup, are all very clear to the player. The rubber duck looks like a rubber duck, and the wet floor sign looks like a wet floor sign. The music in the game is a mix of fantastic and annoying. The main menu music is clearly stock music from somewhere, but the ingame music is a great loop that oddly doesn't get annoying.
Shower with your dad simulator 2015 does a lot right:
It doesn't take itself serious
It has many game modes so it doesn't get boring
It’s comical, in later game modes
It’s price is extremely low
Its achievements are easy
Shower with your dad simulator 2015 does some things wrong:
Distracting wangs
No real game to be played
Lacks any sort of story
not that much fun after an hour or so
Overall, Shower with your dad simulator 2015 is a good game. Boring at times, but easy to get into, and easy to 100%. well worth the $1.09CAD.

1954 Alcatraz could've been amazing, but Daedelic's adherence to "tried and true" point-and-click mechanics make this game an absolute chore to play.
The story starts off with "Joe", a small-time criminal who ends up at Alcatraz due to a heist gone wrong. With the help of his fellow inmates, Joe must break out of Alcatraz and help his wife avoid the criminal kingpins who suspect foul play from Joe, and demand compensation.
The premise sounds exciting on paper, but the dialogue and voice-acting drag this otherwise intriguing concept through the mud. Each conversation sounds stilted and unconvincing, while the various dialogue options are full of cliches, and downright boring observations from our characters.
1954 Alcatraz doesn't try anything new, and it stays firmly within the boundaries that Daedelic have constructed for their previous point-and-click adventures. Needless to say, what's on display here is far below what we've come to expect from a modern videogame in 2014.
It would be easy to excuse 1954 for it's flaws simply because of it's genre, but recent games like The Walking Dead, The Wolf Among Us, and Until Dawn have proven that these types of dialogue-driven experiences can flourish in new and exciting ways. Daedelic's 1954 lacks ambition, and it does very little to warrant its existence at all. It's depressing to see a developer cling so tightly to old ideas, and archaic design choices.

Should you buy TUG alpha version 0.8.5? It depends:
Do you want to be able to spend a few hours in a row playing a game the way you're used to? If so,
TUG during the Alpha stage of Early Access. You will be disappointed at the lack of content and features. Do you expect a polished and optimized engine? Don't buy TUG yet, it's just not that far along.
On the other hand, do you want to talk with the developers about how things might work
they're added? Do you wonder whether people play games differently when game mechanics change? Do you just like discussing what you love about gaming? Then maybe you'll enjoy owning TUG alpha. (I'm having a blast!)
Don't get me wrong, you will be able to play around in TUG. You can spend a few hours fighting friends, playing around with what harvesting and crafting is there, or building a huge base in creative mode. You can mod many aspects of the game, make fan objects, art. or textures, put up YouTube tutorials, and watch the occasional livestreams. But as of this writing, much of the gameplay just isn't there yet. That is just the way Alphas work.
Early access development is pretty active: updates don't happen frequently, but every new release includes large changes, and several brand new types of gameplay. (Version 0.8.5 added the first version of aging and body morphing, completely revamped how the sky looks and works, and added some new clothing and building material recipes.)
So, before you buy, check out the game forums
, watch TUG's
videos, read through the kickstarter update posts
. Do the features currently in place sound fun? Are you inspired by the vision and possibilities? Are you itching to talk about the ways you love to play?
decide whether it's too early to pay for.

To the Moon is a heart-wrenching story of a dying man's wish and the life he lead. A simple retro RPG visuals combined with a soundtrack that complements the scenes and your progress, there's little to fault this simple yet emotionally powerful game. The story will grab you and will lead you through the history of one man's life, all while discovering the trials and tribulations. The puzzle aspect of the game is straightforward and easy to figure out. But I must admit that some puzzles stumped me at first glance yet fell into place after a couple of guess moves.
The game is very short and is possible to complete in one sitting.  However, it should be noted to take your progress as slow as possible to soak in as much of the content as possible.  Once the story is over, it's difficult to go back in to play it again. Progression is very linear and there's little replay value due to its design (and with only 1 achievement).
The only issues I have are technical ones. First, there is no way to adjust whether or not to play in windowed mode, or to even set a specific resolution to play on. The second is that there's no option to change the audio volume, as my audio setup defaults to full blast and the speakers having volume control.  This makes it unbearable at first but a quick alt-tab out and tuning the software volume is enough to work around this.  Other than these two minor problems, the game runs fine without a hitch.
If the soundtrack is to your liking, it is also available directly. I believe it is worth paying for, as it is one of the rare types where the music complements the game. Plus, a purchase enables you to download it in a variety of formats -- lossless FLAC or lossy MP3.
I recommend picking up this game, regardless of price it is being offered as. Take it slow, soak in the scenery, and have a box of tissues handy.

I would definitely recommend Clockwork Tales: Of Glass and Ink, as it is a beautiful hidden-object adventure game.  The game also has a great little story, with some quirky characters, which makes it highly entertaining and enjoyable.
However, compared to other Artifex Mundi games it falls a little short, and it lacks replay ability.
Other Artifex Mundi games have the ability to skip hidden-object areas for bonus games, such as dominos, or matching memory games.  Clockwork Tales does not have this option, and for people (like me) who enjoy completing the game in every way possible, you lose a reason to replay the game.  It is very easy to play though the game and get all the achievements in one sitting, which while good for some players, isn’t as good for others.
Clockwork Tales is definitely worth playing if you enjoy these types of games, and especially if you enjoy Artifex Mundi games, as they are always very well polished, and highly enjoyable.  Just do not expect the game to last more than a few hours, even if grinding the achievements.  Take Clockwork Tales for what it is, as there is a very enjoyable experience to be had.

As far as Artifex Mundi's Hidden Object Games go, this one is better than Abyss, but still not as good as Alex Hunter. It's almost as though the developer wanted to make their own "Clockwork Man" game, but gave you a robot bird helper instead of a man. At least it utilizes its Steampunk theme way better than that series did. The bird has some useful talents that are actually required to retrieve certain objects, providing a neat twist on the genre. It feels like the actual Hidden Object scenes are getting fewer and farther between in these games, and have an art style not quite up to par with the rest of the game's beautiful scenery, but at least the puzzle-solving aspect is fairly involved, even though many of them are similar to puzzles in other HOGs. Although it's only in the bonus chapter, the sewer cap puzzle in this game is lifted *directly* from Abyss - it's literally the same puzzle and screens. I'm not sure whether to take that as a moment of homage, or as a sign that the developers are starting to rest on their laurels too much.
Oh, and there's a part that involves giving catnip to a cat. I guess that should count for something.
Rating: 3/5

Ori and the Blind Forest has changed my life. I'm not even kidding. This game has swiftly become one of my favorite obsessions. The artwork is simply stunning, the music is captivating, and the story is one for the ages.
Set in the forest of Nibel, the Spirit Tree unwinds a deep plot of destruction and demise as the forest around him begins to die without his essences. Ori, an orphan from the tree, is found and cared for by a loving mother figure called Naru. Slowly, the forest around them begins to wither and die, and only Ori can restore life.
This game is wonderfully designed. Gameplay-wise, it follows the traditional formula of many Metroidvania-style games of platforming, defeating enemies, and unlocking upgrades to your power and health, as well as finding new abilities along your path.
The story does not take very long to complete (It took me roughly 10 hours to finish), but it is one that will leave you wanting more. I heavily anticipate the release of the Definitive Edition, which adds in more areas and more abilities, as well as backstory on Naru.
Ori and the Blind Forest should be at the top of every list of PC games that must be played. Coupled with the visual and audio brilliance, this game does not fail to deliver a memorable experience for the player.

Fallout 3 is truly among the last great Fallouts. It was the first to take the Fallout series from a real-time strategy role-playing game and turn it into a first-person shooter role-playing game, and in doing so essentially resurrected the Fallout series and introduced it to a newer generation.
The gameplay mechanics are fairly solid for a game of it's time, the story; while lackluster sometimes, is interesting, and the lore stays inline with it's predecessors; something unheard of in most modern games. The learning curve also doesn't tend to hold the players' hand throughout the game, which follows the learning curve from the older games. You wander into the wrong end of downtown D.C. at too low a level or if you didn't pay attention to what points you're putting into what when leveling up and you'll come to regret it. There's no warning, no notification saying "hey, you're too weak to be here, turn back".
The only real issues I have with Fallout 3 is that they use the same 5-6 voice actors for nearly all of the NPC's you'll encounter said for a few special NPC's making them feel bland and forgettable, the map feels a little empty given the space it has, and in order to get it to work you'll need to download the .dll files elsewhere as the game doesn't come with them for some reason and edit the configuration files yourself.
Aside from that, there are a lot of amazing free mods on the Fallout Nexus that greatly extend the life and replayability of Fallout 3. At $10.99 Canadian for the Game of the Year edition you really can't go wrong.
Side note: It may say I have only 0.1 hours on this, but on console my main character had well over 4 years on it to the point where I was hemorraging nearly every resource in the game and I use Tale of Two Wastelands quite often, which uses Fallout: New Vegas instead of Fallout 3.
Also Liam Neeson voices one of the supporting characters, what other motivation do you need? XD

If you are looking for a game that is set in a well crafted cyberpunk world, this is the one for you. The game's setting and world are definitely its strong point. From the streets of Neo-Paris to leaper infest tunnels, I'm enjoying it all. Everything is carefully detailed. Vendors have holograms advertisements, news screens highlight story details throughout. Androids can be spotted here and there doing various jobs. The graphics are great and the rendering of lighting effects and textures really compliment everything. Alleys of neon glow over wet concrete, the clash of metals and fabrics on Nilin. The aesthetic reminds me a lot of the style of Half-Life 2 / Dishonoured / Mirror's Edge.
I think where this game didn't meet expectations was the combat mechanic. It seems the devs tried something new this time around instead of sticking to the normal combat in fighting games, and they should be appauded for trying, but it was probably better in theory. My experience with the combo system changed throughout the game. Early on they were intimidating, I thought I wouldn't be able to remember so many buttons. Later on it became tedious and took me out of the fun of combat, and late game I realized that combo building was crutial for some boss fights. Another thing that bothered me was the short delay between attacks or "slow-down". Nilin feels so agile and quick, I would have liked to see what it would play like had her attacks been real time. While the combo system can be annoying, for the most part you could get by just spamming the same attack, it just won't be as effecient.
Platforming is nice and fluid, so is movement in general. I found everything to be responsive, such as opening doors via Nilin's Spammer. As I said Nilin is very agile, she plays like she is very much on her toes. I found the game to be very corridor linear but this didn't bother me too much, except when you move forward past a point and can't backtrack because of a closing door, cutting you off from finding collectable items.
Nilin is a very interesting character. Just looking at her she seems unique and I want to know everything about her. Unfortunately the story doesn't allow for much to be revealed about her til later on. The other characters in the story however weren't very interesting to me.
Story has some plotholes but I feel like it's unique. The idea of a memory hunter is pretty badass. Not sure how she can move objects though in people's memories. Sound assets were neat, lots of glitching going on. Really enjoyed the soundtrack too!

TL;DR, Good game, but as of right now, I'd say pick it up during a sale.
Wolfenstein 2 is, unfortunately, one of my biggest disappointments of 2017. While it starts off strong, the game gets lost in its own narrative, perferring to tell the bulk of the story through cutscenes, rather than gameplay. You'll frequently hit spots where you'll get 10-15 minutes of arena shoot outs, where the AI either flanks and shreds your health in seconds, or lines their heads up to your crosshairs (with no inbetween), followed by 20-25 minutes of expository dialogue, then rinse and repeat. While many of the levels are interesting, New Orleans and Roswell underground especially, they overall fail to live up to the levels presented in New Order both in art and design.
The difficulty also was placed in a weird spot after New Order. While the previous game's difficulties were still brutal on Uber and Death Incarnate, BJ's weapons felt effective against non-armored targets. Meanwhile in New Colossus, weapons feel much weaker (I played up to level 3 on Death Incarnate before lowering it to Terror Billy), compared to your enemies'. Once you unlock the alt-fire modes, the fights feel more even, but that may take awhile.
Lastly, stealth feels broken at best and infeasible at worst. There are several sections where the only way to proceed is through a closed door that you'll just have to hope isn't blocked by an enemy, or long hallways guarded by heavies that like to hide behind objects and can seemingly see through walls. Stealth is never required, so you can just opt to ignore it all together, but as it's presented the game almost implies that it's the better way to approach, making these issues all the more infuriating to me.
The game isn't all bad though, while I felt the game was too dependent on the narrative, it was very well written and acted. It made me hate all the villains, love all the heros and actually cheer out loud once or twice during BJ's successes. There's also some solid level design in the game when you actually get to play, and secrets are well hidden without being obnoxious. They've also amped up the ridiculousness, with overly gorey takedowns and Ramshackle charges, to blood stained weapons whenever you get close range kills, you really get to understand why Nazis freak out when they see you.
Perks are also much better than in the last game,
allowing you to start rushing them from the start, instead of locking them all behind skill trees.
All in all, Wolfenstien 2 works very well as a character driven game, but doesn't live up to the gameplay presented in New Order.

1954 Alcatraz combines simple, straightforward, but not too easy adventure game mechanics with a well-flowing story about love, trust, and a heist that may or may not be the only ticket for a poor couple to a happier life.
1954 Alcatraz is one of the lesser known point ‘n’ click adventure games released by Daedelic Entertainment. As far as their point ‘n’ clicks go, this is probably their most straightforward and featureless one. This doesn’t mean the game is bad, quite the opposite.
The main theme is it is trust. Foremost between the two protagonists, a black man trying to escape prison and his con artist white wife helping him from the outside, while also trying to pay the mob who want to collect the husband’s “debts”. Their stories run in parallel to each other, avoiding the trap of slicing the game into chapters, which helps to keep yourself invested a little bit more.
Almost all relationships in the storyline are put to a test, but none as much as this marriage… to the point where the game even offers multiple endings based on what you uncover about past events and how you choose to handle the trust issues that sprung from them.
It is a mystery why is this set in 1950s San Francisco, as the plot would have worked with any high-security prison. Apart from a few references to the beat movement, the whole era is largely neglected, including the quite important bit that nobody in the whole game is bothered by the fact that you play as an interracial couple in the time when this was outlawed in most parts of the US.
Progression is fluent, thanks to the absence of typical harebrained adventure game logic or tedious, repetitive puzzles. Gameplay is as basic as it can get: you gather items and use them on each other or on certain hot spots. Don’t expect anything fancy, just old-school adventure gaming with an easy-to-use interface.

“Shower with your dad simulator 2015” is a indie 2D Scrub-em-up time trial game. You play as 1 of three kids trying to make his way over to his dad, avoiding puddles, wet floor signs, and other, not so friendly dads.
The game is separated into 7 game types, each more ridiculous as the last. Some game modes are locked and unlocked over time, by playing the basic modes. The 2 basic modes, are similar, the first one, you pick your kid and have to race to your dad to add more time, as well as get more points. The second gamemode, you are assigned a random kid, and have to get to that kids, dad, thus adding time, and adding points.
As 2D the game is, it holds its own, graphically speaking. Everything that appears, like obstacles or powerup, are all very clear to the player. The rubber duck looks like a rubber duck, and the wet floor sign looks like a wet floor sign. The music in the game is a mix of fantastic and annoying. The main menu music is clearly stock music from somewhere, but the ingame music is a great loop that oddly doesn't get annoying.
Shower with your dad simulator 2015 does a lot right:
It doesn't take itself serious
It has many game modes so it doesn't get boring
It’s comical, in later game modes
It’s price is extremely low
Its achievements are easy
Shower with your dad simulator 2015 does some things wrong:
Distracting wangs
No real game to be played
Lacks any sort of story
not that much fun after an hour or so
Overall, Shower with your dad simulator 2015 is a good game. Boring at times, but easy to get into, and easy to 100%. well worth the $1.09CAD.

After hearing about the debale of Yogventures, I was directed to TUG, which seemed to be being touted as the replacement, of sorts, as a game that would allow such a great deal of flexibility and freedom. I thought I'd take a shot at buying it.
The first warning was when my usual PC wouldn't run it, despite it having no problem with things like Skyrim, bioshock infinite and other AAA titles. The game, it turns out, requires DX11, and a 2Gb graphics card, along with a whole host of other outlandish features just to run. That is, if you're missing any of those, it won't run slower, it just won't run at all. The recommended settings are even higher. My higher end PC doen't have the 3Gb graphics card it recommends, but at least it'd run.
After this, I figured this must be a pretty incredible game to have such lofty requirements. I mean, I know it's early access, but they must be doing something with all these requirements, right?
Starting it up, I can't describe how disappointing it is. This looks like a unity game someone game up with in a weekend. The graphics do not look good, for any stage of development. This looks absurdly bad.
The really worrying thing is that this looks like the developers have an engine and are making a game in it, which is fine for an indie game, but it isn't fine when they are devouring resources like this. The state of the game doesn't give a lot of hope they are going to be able to optimise this to run on lower spec machines once there's something worthwhile actually there.
I hope I'm proved wrong, and this becomes the sort of game it looks like it could be, but right now it feels like Yogventures part II. A developer that has lofty goals, a partnership with Yogscast, and an overreaching ambition it can't match.
If you want a game like this to work, maybe take a lesson from minecraft, and focus on getting things to work mechanically before requiring a computer of the gods to run it.

Clockwork Tales: Of Glass and Ink is a point-and-click puzzle game which pays homage to deceased Polish author Jan Brzechwa's series of stories surrounding Pan Kleks/Mr. Inkblot. Developed by Artifex Mundi, it was originally released in August of 2013, and put onto Steam in April of 2014, with achievements and trading cards. The game itself follows Evangeline Glass as she tries to help her mentor and friend, Dr. Ambrose Ink, investigate a series of increasingly violent tremors rocking the planet and seemingly originating in the nestled burg of Hochwald. After his abduction early on, it falls entirely to Evangeline to not only solve the mystery surrounding the quakes and save Hochwald, but rescue Ink from his captors.
The premise is interesting, and to its credit, more involved than a lot of hidden object games, but not quite up to snuff for me. The characters are flat and lacking nuance, the plot as a whole is predictable, and while the environment and all the build up hints at a great backstory and lore that could have been explored and exposited, it all remains veiled in mystery. There's no elaboration about the world the characters live in, how its technology works, or even how our main ensemble got to where they are in their lives; everything is left entirely up to our own interpretation. While that can work well when you're at least given breadcrumbs to go off of, we aren't, and I feel the game suffers as a result. I can't really claim that the game is meant to be played with previous knowledge of the Pan Kleks stories, either, seeing as they aren't mentioned anywhere within the game as a source of inspiration — something that I can't dismiss as being a bit of an odd exclusion.
The goal is outlined fairly early on, and doesn't change at any point thereafter. The ending felt incredibly rushed, and didn't leave me satisfied that things had been finished at all. The dénouement as a whole was fairly lackluster — the final cinematic runs is an expository narrative about how things were all wrapped up off camera after doing the final few clicks, clocking in at less than two minutes long to do so. It came off more as a segue to more story than a resolution, or even a cliffhanger for a sequel.
Gameplay is, of course, looking around and clicking things. While primarily presented as a hidden object game, and indeed offering such as its main minigame challenge, the selection of puzzles is surprisingly diverse. Nonograms, jigsaws, sliding blocks, labyrinths, object interactions, trick locks and associated puzzle boxes… More than a few varieties make an appearance, and can pose a decent challenge depending on your familiarity with each. There are, however, skip options for every puzzle, allowing you to bypass them completely by simply idling for a bit.
Finishing the main story will likely only take you a few hours, with the bonus chapter taking much less. Due to the linear progression and lack of variance in how to move forward, the game has fairly little replayability, but the initial experience can be quite fun. Once you finish a mode, you must play through it again entirely if you want to return to a specific point, as each individual zone of the game is walled of from returning to the previous; the downside to this is that having to go through the game again, as in the event that you miss a Steambug, can be more of a chore than anything else. A post-finish stage selection option would have been quite appreciated for this.
Visually, the game has a virtual painterly aesthetic, with fade-between transitions for a majority of background animations. During cut scenes, speaking characters have their facial expressions smudged about to convey emotion and communication, while the rest of the scene remains static or animated using the fade-between method. Although the smudging effect is one of the more high quality examples I have seen, the lack of use on anything other than the characters' primary features can be a bit jarring, primarily at times when their heads should be moving as well. I would have liked to see the effect used on more areas of the game than it was, as it could have added to give the game a bit of individuality.
Musically, the soundtrack is quite enjoyable; I had no complaints. I particularly liked the track that plays during the nonogram puzzles, although it only makes a single appearance toward the end. Unfortunately, the tracks listed in the Extras menu are not the full selection, and checking the installation directory doesn't offer the raw files, forcing one to pursue other venues to listen to everything on the fly.
The voice work varies between decent and hilariously bad, usually landing somewhere in the middle. A few characters sound absolutely ridiculous, while others are very pleasing to the ears. You can disable voice acting entirely in the options menu, should you so desire.
I encountered no sequence breaking opportunities or unwinnable situations while playing, but I didn't attempt to induce them, either. I did experience a rather annoying issue where the Spy Master achievement didn't go through during my initial Expert run, despite having kept the game set to Expert throughout the entire session.
While the difficulty settings speak of some sort of penalty for misclicks in hidden object puzzles, I was still able to click about at random on both Advanced and Expert and not have it affect anything. I'm not entirely sure if I'm unique in that regard, or if it's simply an aspect that was never implemented. If you're hunting for achievements, and with this in mind, I'd set it to Expert right away so you can get the Spy Master achievement on your first playthrough. The game isn't hard enough nor punishing enough to truly make doing so pose much of an issue, especially if you're accustomed to games of this genre or are willing to utilize the skip function.
The store page is a bit deceptive. You have no control over the glider section, it happens entirely as a cut scene; there's no combat action to the game, as “monster battles” and “defeating mechanical creatures” implies (this action is done entirely via puzzle-solving, and only occurs once); and there are 16 achievements both in-game and on Steam, not 9. The game is very much of the go-at-your-leisure variety, with no timed puzzles or direct fighting involved. These are fairly minor discrepancies, but still a bit misleading as to what one can expect.
As a whole, I would recommend the game to fans of the genre, and those looking for an introduction to point-and-clicks without too extreme a difficulty. The standard asking prices in several currencies are $7.99 USD and AUD, 6.49€, 5.99£, R$ 13,99, and 189 RUB. By comparison as of August 2014, the game is cheapest in RUB. As is par for the course with Steam games, I would recommend getting it while on sale or in a bundle, unless you're a diehard fan of games like it.

I originally had this game from Bigfish, so I knew what I was getting into when I bought it here. The fact that I would purchase a game twice should say something all by itself, but I am biased; I happen to very much enjoy Hidden Object/casual games like this one. What intrigued me the most was the steampunk setting and it does a decent job of making you feel you're in a steampunk world the whole time.
As most HOs, the story is quite short, but what is there is beautiful, fun, and with fun puzzles to solve in your quest to find your mentor and friend, with the help of his mechanical crow, Matthew. First off, Matthew is a sidekick of sorts, chilling out in your inventory and looking awesome, but he's very useful in retrieving items and spying for you where normally you might break your neck if you tried yourself. Matthew is just overall a cool feature, and I wish players got more chances to use him. If you're bored of the crow, there are also hidden robotic bugs in many of the scenes which you can collect for completionist status; a nice little extra challenge, though relatively easy to do. The epilogue chapter helps to add a little more story, gameplay and depth as well. A little more bang for your buck.
Overall, the artwork and scenery in this game is gorgeous, and for once, the voice-acting actually adds to the game rather than takes away from it, even if a few lines are repetitive after asking for Matthews help. The music isn't anything spectacular; it's nothing award-winning but it doesn't make me want to turn it off at any point during the game either. Calm and pretty for the most part - which is exactly what you'll be getting with this purchase. Calm and pretty.

Now, keep in mind I haven't beaten the game yet, so take some of this with a grain of salt.
Remember Me is a game about a society where memories are now a commodity. They are able to be shared, sold, and stolen. The game paints a picture of this bizarre world where (somewhat inexplicably) memories are mostly what run everything. The story follows a memory hunter by the name of Nilin, as she finds herself caught in a maximum security prison with her memories taken from her. She escapes with the assistance of the enigmatic "Errorist" who goes by the name Edge. With Edge's help, Nilin goes forth to take down the corporate overlords who run the show as well as recover Nilin's memory.
Remember Me is a game that has absolutely incredible design. Neo-Paris is a vibrant and strange city, swarming with its own unusual culture and architecture. From what I see, the characters all have some glimmer of interesting traits, but aren't too groundbreaking--their designs, however, are quite interesting if anything. The music is a bizarre mix of electronic and classical instrumentation with a lot chops and cuts in it, I think it might actually be one of the strongest points of the game, as it really has a flavor of its own. Olivier Derivier did a fantastic job on the music for this.
Now for the most weak point of the game, the actual gameplay. It consists of 3rd person action brawling and railroaded parkour. The brawling is vaguely reminiscient of the Batman Arkham series of games, except that instead of mashing punch to win, you alternate mostly between punch and kick buttons to win. There aren't counter moves, but there's some absurdly acrobatic dodge moves you can perform. The decidedly dull combat is only livened up by the Pressen system. With Pressens, you can attach certain properties to each attack in a chain of combos. There's damage, heal, cooldown, and link pressens that all help to try and add some variety to the combat system with varying amounts of success.
Honestly, though, I still think it's worth playing. I approach this game in the same way I approached Alice: Madness Returns, I played that game to experience its art, atmosphere, music, and all-around weirdness and not for the dull gameplay that broke those moments of awe I experienced. That goes the same for Remember Me. I consider it mostly an art experience focused game, and not a gameplay focused sort of thing.
I give it a Gold Star/10

I recently finished this game, and I figured that I should write a very brief review.
Story: The story of this game was really really good. A lot of twists, and events that are a pleasant surprise. It's not perfect, but it's damn good.

Sound: The sound design is really amazing. The guns sound great, and powerful. There is plenty of bass in many of the sounds as well. So if you have a good speaker setup, you will have a bloody good time.
Overall, I highly recommend this game. It surpasses the original (The New Order), and keeps your entertained throughout the whole experience. If you're a numbers person, I would give it a 9/10.

I'm going to leave technical issues aside in this review because you probably know the state of it by now with all the other reviews. This review is just about the gameplay and story.
The gameplay feels like The New Order on steroids. It's incredibly more responsive with a brand new weapon upgrading system. This lets you put stuff likes scopes on guns to make it more accurate, or having armor piecing ammo (which is super important!). I do feel like the difficulty on Death Incarnate is unfair however. It just seems like enemies get a damage multiplier when they shoot at you from long range. I say this because death is fast on this difficulty, but you can recover if you react to the enemy at close range. Now at long range you can go from 100HP to 0HP in less than a second because the enemy can get these combos on you. Not only that, but stealth can really be stupid sometimes. Armored enemies have insane vision, and can spot you from miles away. It gets worse mid game though. Half way through you have the option between three different upgades that you can only choose one of. I chose the worst, and that was the shoulder pads. This allowed me to charge through enemies and go through walls. It sounded like a BJ choice to me so I took that. Unfortunatly, as soon as you get that upgrade, the level design starts to incororate these as requirements to advance through the level. Why's this bad? Because since my shoulder pads can go through walls, I have to go through walls to proceed. The others involve BJ squeezing his body through tight spots and jumping really high, but the shoulder pad charging through the wall while I'm trying to stealth puts everyone on alert! I have no choice, I have to alert everyone, or else I can't proceed. My playthrough on the hardest difficulty would have gone way better if I'd chosen the other two upgrades. I'd say two hours would have been shaven off.
Easily the reason most of us bought the game. So how is it? Well, wanting to stay spoiler free this review, I'll give a brief description of what I thought. The first half of the game is awesome. It feels like a continuation of The New Order as it takes place directly after the ending. A new plot is introduced involving BJ's past as a kid with his mother and abusive father. The opening is shocking, sad, and action packed. BJ already felt like he was battle weary from The New Order, but now he feels like he's just ready to die. There's humor to keep the player from feeling depressed, but I just got this feeling of dread. The game has an absolutely amazing climax, which the game had been building up to. We learn more of BJ's past, and some unexpected things happened that made me go, "What the ♥♥♥♥!?" Easily up to this point the story telling was at its peak. THEN... nothing important happens afterwards.
Honestly, if the game had ended at the half way point, sure it would have been 4-5 hours long, but holy hell that would have been one hell of an ending. Instead, nothing happened, and the game just became... ok. It was no longer amazing, just ok. if you've ever played the 4th episode of a Telltale game you'll know the feeling. Seriously, you could have stopped playing there, watch the ending and have missed pretty much nothing. A lot of really cool plot lines are over after the climax, and not enough interesting ones take their place. Imagine if you killed Deathshead half way through The New Order, but you had to keep doing stuff. There's some side missions to do and the main story having the player gather a group of resistance members. The ending is pretty lame. It's on of those endings where I was like, "That wasn't it, was it?" The best part after the mid game is when BJ becomes an actor... literally. Speaking of BJ, after the climax his inner monolouges occur much less and the game seems to have almost forgotten about him. Other characters take priority. The game focuses way to much on this new chick that joins up with BJ and crew, and not enough with this other chick that joined them. Fergus had some cool moments throughout the game, but feel more like side character, which is a shame because I love Fergus' character to death. I would have liked to have seen more scenes with him like how he was at the intro to The New Order. I don't know about Wyatt as I haven't played that timeline yet, but I'm assuming he has the same amount of screen time with a different story.
Overall, the game is a solid package. It has improved gameplay, an amazing start to mid game story, but just lacks any substance past the half way point. Hopefully the only reason jack all happens at the end of the game is because Wolfenstein 3 has some serious story to tell.

Graphics wise I didn't expect as much as I got. Even with Antialiasing disabled the game looks vibrant and alive (you can force it on through a text file, default with higher resolutions is 0).
As for the controls, I'm guessing it's smoother when played with a pad. Although the pc configuration works, at times it can feel a little sticky.
The game has also some informational value; I for one had no idea how huge the city of Jerusalem really was, before I rode to the walls myself.
I would suggest this game to anyone who likes open world/action/sneaking games or just medieval themes in general.

Ori is a solid metroidvania platformer. It has some of the best visuals I have ever seen for a 2d game and the best narration in a game for a long time (since portal). It has some of the best level design, tricky, yet fair gameplay and amazing character building, exploring each of the characters past and why they are what they are in the present. All of this is done with not a single word spoken. (well unless you count their made up language the narrator uses). In my opinion, no game has come close to perfection. Possibly even hit perfection at some degree. While the story is only about 6 hours long, there's lots of secrets, abilities and upgrades to keep you occupied and some of the hardest achievements in a video game. The game will be best played if you knew none of the story behind it for the emotional response you'll get. I won't be the first to admit this game makes a grown man cry. When you play this game, you'll be immersed in the world, you'll be in awe at the beautiful scenery. This game shows how to make a truly great game. Not some of the garbage that has come out lately. Moon studios show talent and hope to see more great games from them in the future.

To start, I'm a fan of hack 'n slash (devil may cry, dantes inferno) and creepy walking sims (Amnesia, condemned), among many other genres.

Walking simulator 2017 - schizophrenic Celtic edition
Enemy diversity, inventory, power ups, leveling up, NPCs, forget it.   This is not an RPG, it may look like one from the screenshots, but I cannot emphasize it enough, it's not an RPG.  In this game you basically walk through a cinematic story driven experience.
So, is it worth it?  Yes, well, sort of.
To my surprise the game is rather difficult.  I set the game on easy early on because I quickly realized this was a game of story, atmosphere and immersion, and nothing kills those things faster than constantly killing off the player over and over again.  It's essentially an interactive movie, and you want to experience it in such a way.   To my dismay, this is exactly what the game did, it killed me a number of times during a fire escape scene.  You basically just have to run to an exit point in a certain amout of time.  I know exactly where the exit was the first time and bolted for it from the moment go, but alas I didn't get there quite soon enough, I was off by about 1 second and effectively died.  I repeated this process two more times before just barely making it by the skin of my teeth.  This scene is unnecessarily difficult. Replaying a scene over and over again destroys the immersion and the awe of the set piece they're trying to show you, and makes the scene repetitious and frustrating.  This isn't a game of gameplay.  This isn't Dark Souls.  It's a game of story and atmosphere.  Have mercy.  How would you like it if I took a book you were in the middle of reading and throw it across the room every 5 minutes?  Will that kill your immersion in the book?
Graphics and sound?  Good.  I think I read in some review that this was the best looking game they've played to date.  I disagree, I think they're a number of better looking games currently avaible.  The character model looks really good and real.  But the environment does not share that detail.  It's by no means poor, it's very good in fact, it's just not the best thing you will see all year.  And the sound?  It's pretty good, I played the game with headphones, I recommend you do so as well.  What else can I say?  The soundtrack isn't terribly memorable.
Combat.  Yes there's combat in this walking simulator.  Ghosts?  Apparitions? I don't know.   Combat is not one of the things the game does well; there is a hint of variety in the combat structure, and like Ontario, it's yours to discover.  The game doesn't hold your hand and explain the combat keys, so get ready to pull up the key settings during your first combat encounter to figure out your key set.  "You need to focus"  Oh yeah?  What key is that again?  If you want me to press a damn key, then display the key on screen at least once, you know, like every other game. There also little enemy variety.  You have very few enemy models, and you face these type of enemies over and over again during your schizophrenic walk in the park.
In conclusion.  I haven't finished the game yet, and I'm torn actually as to whether or not I should continue on or request a steam refund before I hit the 2 hour mark.  I hear the game is about 6 hours long, and I can tell you now there's little replayablity, if not zero.  So the question then is a one time adventure through a cinematic game worth the $33 CAD for 6 hours of possible enjoyment when it's not frustrating you with unecessary death?  Probably not, wait for a 50% sale and give it a go, and remember, steam offers a refund for games with less than 2 hours of gameplay.

A mature point & click for those who enjoy a good story and some brilliant dialogues. The original setting is deeply interwoven into the narrative and well researched, and it really makes for some fascinating time travelling. The writing is superb all around, with well-developed main characters with shades of grey, and a compelling plot that investigates a few adult themes in a mostly superficial but still enjoyable way. There is also an interesting attempt at non-linearity: you can switch between characters mostly at will, there are a few points that offer different choices and a couple of different endings. All together they provide a sense of freedom in a genre has been mostly stilted and narrow in its storytelling so far. Admittedly that sense of freedom and non-linearity proves to be mostly smoke and mirrors, but I found it an immersion enhancing illusion and it improved my experience rather than letting me down.
The jazz soundtrack is absolutely brilliant and I am genuinely sad not to see it offered with the game or even as dlc. I also thoroughly enjoyed the voice acting, especially when it comes to the two main protagonists. As for the graphics, most of the backdrops are gorgeously detailed and colorful and I seem to disagree with many of the strongly worded criticisms of the 3D animated characters. Yes, better animated games exist, but this one was fine, and it even has some nice moments of attention to detail. Either way, it didn't break the immersion for me.
This isn't a puzzle oriented point & click, but what there was I found relatively simple and logical and not interfering with the flow of the story. There were very few moments when I was actually stuck, but even then there wasn't a great amount of trial and error that was necessary, just a bit of concentration or retracing my steps. However if you're looking for a challenge, you won't find it here.
All things considered, I'm slightly surprised to find this game received such bad reviews from professional critics (mostly due to its graphics and puzzles). So if you have second thoughts, do a bit of reading, see what the world outside of Steam has to say. As far as I'm concerned I enjoyed myself thoroughly. Between the setting, the well written narrative, the fantastic dialogues, the voice acting, the pretty backdrops, and "all that jazz", I personally highly recommend the game.

1954 Alcatraz, Sentenced to Life in Mediocrity

That isn't to say that this is a bad game by any means, but it can leave you stuck between a Rock and a dull place many times.  So, even though the game is relatively short and painless to play, I found myself pushing to finish it since I didn't care about the characters and wasn't really interested by the story arc.  Only really worth a play if you are a die-hard adventure game fan and find it on sale.

: the time is right, the tune is low and guns are smoking. The world is old, yet the life is young. The Beat Generation redefines America with rejection literature, sexual liberation and psychedelic drugs. In this Daedalic adventure game, you take the role of partners in crime, a husband and a wife, to either bring the fugitives to a happy union, or break some more hearts and heads in their run.
The scene opens up to the story of Joe and Christine. Joe participates in a heist and is sent to the Rock, the legendary Alcatraz prison. The money is said to be burned during the car crash, but the mafia have their suspicions. Christine is left with a broken heart and tons of questions in her mind. Joe decides to escape from Alcatraz to meet with his wife, and leave country while Christine tries her best to avoid mafia's advances, discover some truth to events and aid her husband in the coastal districts of San Francisco. They cheat, lie, steal, blackmail and kill to their freedom, with one dream in their visions: a new life in Mexico.
First thing is first: the theme of the game is well thought and interesting. I've never stumbled upon an adventure game that takes place during the Beat Generation. The concept, and the tale of Christine and Joe bears so much potential. The gameplay consists of switches between Joe and Christine. You choose which one's perspective to play at any given time. Whence one of them are stuck due to conditions that they cannot control, you switch to the other to make things progress. Item combinations seem to always make sense according to the narration and the storyline. The backgrounds are nice. The music is catchy and fits the mood at any given time.
The downside is that the game feels rushed. I had some issues about the graphics for example: they are cartoonish and characters do move a bit chalky on the animation department, but that's not the actual bother. The bothersome part is the loading time between scenes. It takes forever to save/load or make a passage to any new area. You kinda lose your interest while constantly waiting for a character to either leave or enter the scene. That needs polishing to say the least. Main Menu and the Save/Load screen glitches terribly and takes time to either save or load. Animations and the voice acting lose their synch quite often - and I'm not even talking about the timing of subtitles. All in all one of the better hidden object games its been my privalige to play and i hope that we get to see MATTEW again as that little crow really has taken a place in my subconscious and he refuses to leave "SHOO crow of with you"...........................see hes not listening".

TL;DR, Good game, but as of right now, I'd say pick it up during a sale.
Wolfenstein 2 is, unfortunately, one of my biggest disappointments of 2017. While it starts off strong, the game gets lost in its own narrative, perferring to tell the bulk of the story through cutscenes, rather than gameplay. You'll frequently hit spots where you'll get 10-15 minutes of arena shoot outs, where the AI either flanks and shreds your health in seconds, or lines their heads up to your crosshairs (with no inbetween), followed by 20-25 minutes of expository dialogue, then rinse and repeat. While many of the levels are interesting, New Orleans and Roswell underground especially, they overall fail to live up to the levels presented in New Order both in art and design.
The difficulty also was placed in a weird spot after New Order. While the previous game's difficulties were still brutal on Uber and Death Incarnate, BJ's weapons felt effective against non-armored targets. Meanwhile in New Colossus, weapons feel much weaker (I played up to level 3 on Death Incarnate before lowering it to Terror Billy), compared to your enemies'. Once you unlock the alt-fire modes, the fights feel more even, but that may take awhile.
Lastly, stealth feels broken at best and infeasible at worst. There are several sections where the only way to proceed is through a closed door that you'll just have to hope isn't blocked by an enemy, or long hallways guarded by heavies that like to hide behind objects and can seemingly see through walls. Stealth is never required, so you can just opt to ignore it all together, but as it's presented the game almost implies that it's the better way to approach, making these issues all the more infuriating to me.
The game isn't all bad though, while I felt the game was too dependent on the narrative, it was very well written and acted. It made me hate all the villains, love all the heros and actually cheer out loud once or twice during BJ's successes. There's also some solid level design in the game when you actually get to play, and secrets are well hidden without being obnoxious. They've also amped up the ridiculousness, with overly gorey takedowns and Ramshackle charges, to blood stained weapons whenever you get close range kills, you really get to understand why Nazis freak out when they see you.
Perks are also much better than in the last game,
allowing you to start rushing them from the start, instead of locking them all behind skill trees.
All in all, Wolfenstien 2 works very well as a character driven game, but doesn't live up to the gameplay presented in New Order.

I recently finished this game, and I figured that I should write a very brief review.
Story: The story of this game was really really good. A lot of twists, and events that are a pleasant surprise. It's not perfect, but it's damn good.
Gameplay: The gameplay is really engaging and exciting. The movement is improved from The New Order, and the mechanics are fun. The guns feel great, and it's a great time killing some Nazis. You will fight many different type of enemies, and they are all fun to fight. There are some puzzle elements, but nothing too complicated to handle.
Graphics: The graphics of this game is superb! Some of the scenes, and locations that you will encounter will leave you watching them for at least five seconds before moving on to the next area. They have done a fantastic job with making the game look amazing in most cases.
Sound: The sound design is really amazing. The guns sound great, and powerful. There is plenty of bass in many of the sounds as well. So if you have a good speaker setup, you will have a bloody good time.
Overall, I highly recommend this game. It surpasses the original (The New Order), and keeps your entertained throughout the whole experience. If you're a numbers person, I would give it a 9/10.
