I'm going to leave technical issues aside in this review because you probably know the state of it by now with all the other reviews. This review is just about the gameplay and story.
The gameplay feels like The New Order on steroids. It's incredibly more responsive with a brand new weapon upgrading system. This lets you put stuff likes scopes on guns to make it more accurate, or having armor piecing ammo (which is super important!). I do feel like the difficulty on Death Incarnate is unfair however. It just seems like enemies get a damage multiplier when they shoot at you from long range. I say this because death is fast on this difficulty, but you can recover if you react to the enemy at close range. Now at long range you can go from 100HP to 0HP in less than a second because the enemy can get these combos on you. Not only that, but stealth can really be stupid sometimes. Armored enemies have insane vision, and can spot you from miles away. It gets worse mid game though. Half way through you have the option between three different upgades that you can only choose one of. I chose the worst, and that was the shoulder pads. This allowed me to charge through enemies and go through walls. It sounded like a BJ choice to me so I took that. Unfortunatly, as soon as you get that upgrade, the level design starts to incororate these as requirements to advance through the level. Why's this bad? Because since my shoulder pads can go through walls, I have to go through walls to proceed. The others involve BJ squeezing his body through tight spots and jumping really high, but the shoulder pad charging through the wall while I'm trying to stealth puts everyone on alert! I have no choice, I have to alert everyone, or else I can't proceed. My playthrough on the hardest difficulty would have gone way better if I'd chosen the other two upgrades. I'd say two hours would have been shaven off.
Easily the reason most of us bought the game. So how is it? Well, wanting to stay spoiler free this review, I'll give a brief description of what I thought. The first half of the game is awesome. It feels like a continuation of The New Order as it takes place directly after the ending. A new plot is introduced involving BJ's past as a kid with his mother and abusive father. The opening is shocking, sad, and action packed. BJ already felt like he was battle weary from The New Order, but now he feels like he's just ready to die. There's humor to keep the player from feeling depressed, but I just got this feeling of dread. The game has an absolutely amazing climax, which the game had been building up to. We learn more of BJ's past, and some unexpected things happened that made me go, "What the ♥♥♥♥!?" Easily up to this point the story telling was at its peak. THEN... nothing important happens afterwards.
Honestly, if the game had ended at the half way point, sure it would have been 4-5 hours long, but holy hell that would have been one hell of an ending. Instead, nothing happened, and the game just became... ok. It was no longer amazing, just ok. if you've ever played the 4th episode of a Telltale game you'll know the feeling. Seriously, you could have stopped playing there, watch the ending and have missed pretty much nothing. A lot of really cool plot lines are over after the climax, and not enough interesting ones take their place. Imagine if you killed Deathshead half way through The New Order, but you had to keep doing stuff. There's some side missions to do and the main story having the player gather a group of resistance members. The ending is pretty lame. It's on of those endings where I was like, "That wasn't it, was it?" The best part after the mid game is when BJ becomes an actor... literally. Speaking of BJ, after the climax his inner monolouges occur much less and the game seems to have almost forgotten about him. Other characters take priority. The game focuses way to much on this new chick that joins up with BJ and crew, and not enough with this other chick that joined them. Fergus had some cool moments throughout the game, but feel more like side character, which is a shame because I love Fergus' character to death. I would have liked to have seen more scenes with him like how he was at the intro to The New Order. I don't know about Wyatt as I haven't played that timeline yet, but I'm assuming he has the same amount of screen time with a different story.
Overall, the game is a solid package. It has improved gameplay, an amazing start to mid game story, but just lacks any substance past the half way point. Hopefully the only reason jack all happens at the end of the game is because Wolfenstein 3 has some serious story to tell.

Remember Me is an odd game.  There are quite a few aspects that are quite enjoyable, such as the visuals and sound.  The voice acting in the game is superb as well. The memory remixes are interesting, but there's not many of them and they make the story ridiculous.  The main character is supposed to be strong and different, but is just another way too thin waif who walks like a runway model and has daddy issues.
The combat is repetitive and boring.  There is an interesting combo system, but usually you'll find youself in large mob fights where you'll never land a combo of more than a few hits because there are just too many enemies coming from all sides for you to land 6 blows in a row.  I found myself going into the combo lab and changing the three punch combo to whatever suited my needs and just landing that.
The game is also WAY too short.  It could easily be finished in a weekend and for the dedicated gamer, a day.  There is simply no replay value.  You'll only unlock art for things you've already seen, character models that simply stand there, or combat moves that you'll never use.

Remember Me is, at it's heart, an action-packed fighting-type game, but don't let that fool you; the interesting take on a 'cyberpunk' future is itself both visually stunning and extremely fresh. In a world where technology has managed to make people's memories more like flash drives, the world is severely corrupted and blinded to what makes them 'human'. As Nillin- a freedom fighter who's had most of her memory removed, you're trying to get your memories back and stop Sensen, the technology that has made these things possible. Nillin also has the ability to change people's memories herself, something that has a variety of consequences and makes for an extremely interesting gameplay mechanic. When you couple the action, unique vision and the emotionally charged story, it becomes a game more than worth checking out.

This one is a hard recommendation. For all the things Remember Me does right, so many others it does wrong. I try to explain following my experience the first time I started the game up to the last second in which I unlocked all achievments for it and deleted it from my harddrive. So here it goes:
==Story==
At first I was confused. I played, things got explained to me, I didn't really care. Something about evil cooperations, and memory hunters of which our lead chracter is part of. We're playing Nilin, who lost her memories and gets guided to her rescue through some dude called Edge before the evil cooperation could delete the rest of her memories. The game is divided into episodes and with each episode we try to help Nilin remember more of her memory and in the end trying to stop the evil cooperation. It's a well written story but it unfolds very slowly and uninteresting. The stories high-point are the interactive memory remixes. As a memory hunter Nilin lets the player break into someone elses memory and alter it to his liking, thus changing persons attitude forwards certain events in the past, affecting the future. Cutscenes in this game can't be skipped.
==Gameplay / Combat==
The gameplay is your typical modern 3rd-person action game. There are linear corridors, climbing sections and arenas in which the Batman-like combat takes places. Combat is fast & fluid. The game allows you to customize from 3 to 8 hit long combo-chains that unlock over time.
The chains can be filled & customized through added presens. There are power presens and even presens that heal Nilin when she strikes. Later special abilities are introduced as well, so called S-presens. S-presens allow to stun enemies, manipulate robot foes, making your invisible for a short time to strike hard etc. Special Abilities have a cooldown. The cooldown can be reduced by adding cooldown reducing presens to your combo chains. There are also multiplier that can be added to the chains. These double the effect of previous presens in the combo chain. In the middle of a combo Nilin can dodge attack enemies and continue her combo. It sounds like a neat idea and it is IF combos wouldn't break each time Nilin strikes a different foe as the one she started the combo at. This can be very frustrating and it is and would explain why people think the combat is bad. But I enjoyed it due the possibility to change my combos accordingly to the enemies I was facing.
==Visuals & Sound==
The game looks gorgeous on highest setting. The only problem I encountered with the game is the constant studder due to Unreal3's texture streaming. There are certain ways to reduce or get rid of the studder on most systems. The soundtrack is a weird mix of electronic noises. The idea behind the music is that during combat a beat is played and each time a combo breaks or Nilin gets hit my an enemy the beat breaks too. But then there are instances in which overly epic music is played too loud that doesnt really fit with the shown scenes.
==Replay Value==
I mentioned that cutscenes can't be skipped. It's tedious to replay certain chapters to collect missing collectibles or to reach a certain point or fight that requires certain actions to unlock missing achievments. Having a collectible / achievment guide by your side comes in very handy. On the plus side: Once you finished the game Nilin will keep all her unlocked abilities and presens (even thouh abilities can only be used from the point onward in which they are unlocked during the story).
==Conclusion==
So why do I recomment the game? It's a short game delivering an well written and interesting story. It takes time to get used to the combat but once combos & presens are fully unlocked someone can have a blast with it. Achievment Hunters can also get their fair share of fun since It's easy to unlock those. But after you have done all that is to do in the game there is no big motivation to return to it. The story and the well done memory remixes are still worth to give the game a go.

The game is a 4/5. It has some weak points, but it is easily worth $10 if it is available on sale. The weak points are mostly minor things.
The game mechanics needed better planning. There are a variety of upgrades for the weapons, but there is no point in getting anything but the base gun upgrade, the ice upgrade, and the explosion upgrade. A person could use the scatter or poison upgrades for enjoyment, but there is no reason to. Same goes for the spell upgrade tree. Ignore them and use the explosion upgrade unless you want variety for your own enjoyment.
The voice acting is kind of silly. I have never understood why games use voice actors who do a poor job attempting a foreign accent, instead of just hiring someone who really has an accent. There are some quality control problems with the dialog not matching the subtitling.
Item pickups are strange. An item might be found at level 10 that is better than items found all the way up to level 20. I think I used a level 20 gun all the way up to level 30 because none of the guns from levels 21 through 30 were any better, even though they were the highest level yellow weapons, and the level 20 gun was just a blue level gun. There is a ring at level 16 or so that boosts mana, hit points and rage to such high levels that it would make no sense to replace it with any other ring no matter how high it's level was. I felt disappointment every time I picked up a yellow ring and had to sell it because there was no place to put it.
There are a few spots where it is impossible to get through without dying, which really irks me. The situations are of the variety "teleport into a setting with 20 guys 4 feet away from you, and if you try running there are 20 more guys 10 feet away in every direction". I want challenges, but impossible situations are cheating.
Other than those minor points, the settings are interesting and well done, the graphics look good, the game engine plays well, the enemy design is varied and challenging, and the music was addicting. I found myself turning the game on just so I could hear the main music play over and over again.

Wow, Skullgirls blew me away. This is by far the best "indie" fighting game I've ever played. It's action-packed, fast-paced, addictive, and incredibly stylish, sort of the lovechild of Darkstalkers and Marvel VS Capcom. It's so easy to pick up and play - its fighting systems are filled with opportunities for advanced techniques and creative play, but it's also extremely beginner friendly for anyone who is new to fighting games. This is the first time I've ever played a fighting game where it just felt so smooth and sweet to chain super moves into my combos. If you come to this game as a fighting newbie, you'll be a combo fiend in no time. The fighting is simply so crisp and satisfying. Every character plays really differently and there are so many chances for exciting match-ups. The netcode is also silky smooth and you'll be able to find a lot of people playing online...just be prepared to get roughed up in your first few matches.
The presentation is also completely fantastic. The animation is *incredible* and filled with so many little jokes and surprises. The amount of detail is crazy...every attack is so weird and funny and full of personality. The character designs are unforgettable and there's a fun amount of anime cheesecake to them. Some of my favorites are Valentine, the sadistic ninja nurse; Filia, who has a powerful parasite living on her head; and Ms. Fortune, the semi-undead cat-girl. The overall setting is really unique - a 1920s-style art deco sci-fi/horror city featuring powerful mafia families, sinister science experiments, and Lovecraftian secrets. The 1920s-esque setting means you'll get some awesome jazzy music. There's a rich story mode and every character gets a moment to shine. I just found it a total pleasure to spend time in this little universe.
My one and only complaint here is that the base game is kind of thin on characters...it only comes with 8 fighters, and one of them, Double, is a shapeshifter who has stolen attack moves from the other 7 core fighters. You can get 5 additional fighters through DLC, including two that I really enjoyed, Squigly and Beowulf, but obviously that requires spending more money. If you get the 2nd Encore upgrade, which includes all the DLC characters and alternate colors, as well as fully voiced story mode and some other modes like survival and challenges, that will bump the total price of the game up to 25 dollars or so. Now, personally, I feel that game is definitely worth that much, at least. However, I can understand if some people feel annoyed that they aren't buying the "full" game when they shell out their initial 10 bucks. Without the DLC characters, the game feels just litle incomplete.
So overall, Skullgirls receives my highest recommendation. This is really a game that should be in everyone's Steam library. If you're interested in fighting games, even a tiny bit, pick it up! In terms of fighting action, music, art design, creativity, and sheer playability, it's absolutely at the top of its class. The DLC issue may be a bit annoying for some people - I think it's important to know that, when you buy this game, you'll really want to get the DLC if you want a meatier, full package. I would encourage you to get both the base game and the DLC upgrade, though, even if you have to wait for a sale: the game is absolutely worth the added cost and the DLC characters are awesome.

Note: If you don't want my long winded review and wish to see the pro's/con's of this game just scroll paste my wall of text. However if you want my personal experience feel free to read.
Now I have little time with this game keep that noted however i've had enough time with it to do a proper review of first impressions. This game starts off as a fun joke with a few cute jump scares, however that mood quickly turns grim. This game does not succeed with it's graphical appearance however the audio and ambience that you overhear quickly makes up for that. This game looks like it's just something some company threw together however if you go into how the monster is announced or how they introduce the new concepts via different room layouts, it quickly makes up for it's lack of looks with well polished audio as well as design.
My first impressions of the game within the first 10 rooms was "This is a joke of a game and dull already." That was until the audio started tugging at the back of my mind and then I paused for the first time with the most creative surprise I had in a while, it was Spooky casually smiling at you through the static of the screen. The reason I mention this is that it was a well done concept that I can honestly say caught me off guard. So all these little things that stick to the back of your mind as you're going room by room pulled by curiosity leaves me to say that this game is definitely a great one. With it's design and use of just a few simple concepts it makes for a good experience. The last thing i'll mention that I liked that made it stand out from other "horror" games is that it right out introduces you the "player" as you dive into this house of horror. This makes for the fact that you directly are introduced, meaning there isn't some dull protagonist that you're hiding behind.
Pros:
1:Audio/SFX is well polished and well used.
2:Design is different than what i've encountered in the past as well as well thought.
3:It slowly takes you deeper into the horror and leads to a climactic build up that was well done from my experience.
4:Gives a nostalgic vibe with the room designs as well as environment.
5:The game is Free to Play and a well done F2P game at that.
Cons:
1:Movement was quite odd and clunky at a few segments.
2:Does not take kindly to players with a lower DPI
3:Textures were bland and reused makes for a dull expirience till the climax. However this minorly impacts the game.
4:Lack of pull factors other than Spooky, and Curiosity and arguably the ambience.
Mixed Factors:
1:Voice acting was a double edged sword, on one hand it was cute and well presented on the other it wasn't executed properly. I personally enjoyed it, but other's could be turned away from the game with such a presentation.
Overall Ratings:
SFX/Audio 9/10
Design 8/10
Voice Acting 7/10
Gameplay 6/10
Character Introduction 8/10
Graphic/Texture Rating 4/10
Overal Rating 7.5/10

Having received Flow Match for free from winning a prize draw, I feel obligated to recommend this game. But having also actually completed the game, I feel obligated NOT to recommend it due to some pretty glaring flaws.
First, though, a gameplay description: Flow Match is a game where you push around crates to form a single unbroken line of crates from one recess in the wall to the other. The first 10 levels are pretty vanilla, the next five involve multiple floors (crates are connected through the floor and ceiling), and the last five involve controlling two characters at once.
The first flaw is obviously that this game is clearly a 2D Sokoban game, but it's rendered in 3D, putting unnecessary strain on my computer's resources. I'd have been happier if this were a Pascal program using only the command prompt, or whatever. (In fact, Unity does have 2D engine capability from what I recall, so I don't see why the developer chose to make it in "glorious 3D" when it's really just a bunch of cubes.)
The second one is its length. As you can see from the statistics on my review, I've only played the game 35 minutes and completed it in that time; as I've stated, the game is only 20 levels long. Even for a cost of 0.63 GBP, the current on-sale price of this game as I write this, that's really not enough, unless the game is made very well (like klocki or Zenge, both short games with higher prices than I think they should normally have). Which, as I shall expound on, it isn't.
Given that this is a Sokoban game, one would expect there to be puzzle-softlock situations, so surely the developer had the foresight to put in an undo hotkey or an undo button, right? Wrong. There is no "undo" function, meaning that a single misstroke of a key requires a level restart... which can only be done by moving the mouse! That's right, there's no level restart hotkey either! It's 2016; this should be a staple in all puzzle games!
The gameplay during the first 10 levels already gets boring by the fifth. None of the levels are particularly interesting, hard, or anything else. By the 8th level, it's just a trudge through the same old, same old. It's clear this game wasn't playtested by anyone who actually plays puzzles regularly.
The next five levels, which involve multiple floors, have a few annoyances. First, you can't see all floors at once (meaning that you sometimes have to push blocks out of the way, perhaps unknowingly softlocking yourself, just to see the whole level). Second, to go from one floor to another, one steps on an arrow and is immediately transported to the next floor; this causes unnecessary switching between floors every time one needs to walk past an arrow to access a different area on the same floor. I would have implemented it so that a keypress (perhaps X, if Z is used for undo) is required to switch floors. Now,
?
At least one level has more cubes than is required. Remember how I said that the crates have to form a single unbroken line? Well, apparently even if all the cubes are joined and there is indeed a single unbroken line from one recess to the other, the game doesn't recognize that as a solution some of the cubes "branch off" said line! That is to say, the game forces the player to use an "suboptimal" solution. But this fact can only be found out on the last level of the multiple-floors set, which is already finicky enough as-is. You can imagine my frustration when I "solved" the level with fewer cubes than necessary. If I were designing this game, I would have put this nuance as one of the first puzzles in the game, where the player is expected to have not yet known all the rules! Then, I would have built a good half of my levels around avoiding multiple paths
Anyway, onto the last five levels; you control both players simultaneously and need to complete two puzzles on two boards. Good twist, but again; none of the puzzles were particularly challenging, illuminating, or
. That's the main gripe I have with the levels in this game.
Now, besides the puzzles and graphics, there is also the story. And the story is not particularly memorable. It's just about some guy whose girlfriend vanishes after he discloses some secret or another, so he makes his way through a desert and a castle, and escapes with his girlfriend. Pretty boring.
Hang on, that seems almost completely irrelevant to the gameplay! Yes, I get that you needed some form of challenge to drive the story, but the story needs to drive the gameplay as well! You don't give us any sort of reason why we should care about pushing boxes around in, what, a desert presumably? The last level, where the two escape from the castle against advancing guards, was by far the most relevant one to the actual story! You could have made a whole game out of that, and expanded the story! Or you could have scrapped the story altogether and just gave us a set of interesting link-Sokoban levels! (under the admittedly weak premise that you're a robot connecting wires in a factory. I'm not too fussy so long as the story's relevant.)
Maybe I'm being overly-critical (the game certainly isn't as bad as some of the games I've played, like Duplexer, May's Mysteries, or Rolling Shapes, and actually is playable), but this whole game seems to have been made very poorly and lazily. Almost zero effort has actually gone into the level design (save maybe two levels in the multiple-floors section), no effort has gone into making the controls aid the gameplay, by the lack of undo button or keyboard shortcuts, and little effort has gone into fusing the story with the gameplay itself.
All in all, a game with mediocre puzzles, subpar controls, and a bland story; and it's too short to bother with. It's not worth your money or the hassle of refunding it.

I thoroughly enjoyed this game!  When I started, I wasn't overly impressed but as the game went on, I got more and more absorbed in the story and by the end I was having a great time.  Or as great a time as you can have as a criminal escaping Alcatraz and his accomplice wife.  There is some freedom of choice that allows you to sort of adjust the likeability-level of your two playable characters (i.e. some choices will make you into a total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥).
+Engaging story
+Excellent voice acting
+Art style is unique (cartoonish but nicely done)
+A variety of endings and variations on endings depending on choices made in the game.
+Solutions aren't nearly as obscure as some point-and-click adventure games.  There is thankfully no "combine a jelly bean and a cat to get a TV antenna" sorts of solutions and I always applaud that (personal opinion that games should challenge without causing unneeded hair-pulling).
-Game length is pretty short - I ran through in about 4.5 hours, getting all three main endings. This makes the full price a little steep but sales and bundles make it reasonably priced.
-There are places you can get "stuck" in progression and have to reload an earlier save (usually when there needs to be an exchange between the switchable characters that is somewhat order-of-events sensitive)
There are a few things to keep in mind about this one:
1.  It is definitely NOT for anyone who is squeamish about violence and sexual acts.  There isn't a lot of it, and what there is isn't graphically explicit, but there are some sound effects that might bother the more prudish consumer.
2.  This takes place in the 1950s and the slang, including racial slang, reflects that.  It is not "politically correct" because there was no such thing back then.  There is also heavy emphasis on the "Beat" culture of that time period, including slang, which might sound very strange if you're not too aquainted with 1950s-era hipsters.
3. $19.99 is a little pricey for the length of the game, so you might want to get it on sale or in a bundle.  Daedelic makes some great games so almost any of their bundles probably includes some games that are even better than this one.

I've played a handful of Artifex Mundi's hidden object games, and I think this may be my favorite one yet.  Based on a popular series of Polish children's books, Clockwork Tales is an imaginative, fun, curious and enjoyable title who's emphasis is more on casual adventure than hidden objects. Set in a steampunk version of the 1700's, you play Evangeline Glass, an intelligent young protégé to the brilliant Dr. Ink.  With the help of Ink's clockwork companion, Matthew the bird, you must save Hochwald and the doctor from the machinations of the evil Grand Engineer Barber.
One of the things I enjoy most about hidden object games is the beautiful and imaginative artwork many have, and this game is no exception.  Everything, including the characters, have a hand-painted look which gives it a storybook-like quality. Even the characters share the art style, which looks so much better than the oddly rendered/animated 3D models in other games.
The game play is your standard IHOG/HOPA, adventure game lite with hidden object scenes mixed in. I always play on Expert to give me a bit of challenge and lengthen my game play, but I found Clockwork Tales to be quite easy, even more so than most games in the genre. This isn't a horrible thing, but considering how much I enjoyed the world that was created, I wanted to spend a lot more time there than a mere 3 hours on the hardest difficulty. Even so, the adventure aspect was very fun with nothing jumping out as being crazy illogical, and the many puzzles were moderately challenging despite most being reused from previous games.  One nice touch was being able to utilize Matthew to collect out of reach items and perform certain tasks.  Most of these aren't too hard to figure out, but it's a nice bit of flavor added to a genre that is very "cut and paste" in most gameplay aspects.
The hidden object scenes are very well done, nicely drawn items without too much clutter, and have a nice range of difficulty, but none of the items were what I would consider unfairly hidden.  Mixed in amongst your standard HOS's are a few FROGs (fragmented object scenes), adding a bit of variety to the gameplay. I noticed, however, that the regular HOS's tend to get more plentiful the further you progress through the game. This wasn't an issue for me as I really like them, but not everyone shares that sentiment.  For those who do not, the number of these scenes are quite low overall compared to other games.
While the setting is one of the best parts of the game, the story in the beginning feels a little rushed and can be a bit confusing.  But once things get going and you move out of the village into the castle, the storytelling smooths out quite a bit.  There are no dark, disturbing themes here (unlike so many others in the genre), and the story isn't deep by any means, but that doesn't detract from it's enjoyability.  This is a game that can be enjoyed by anyone but makes a particularly good family game, especially for parents who are looking for less macabre fair to share with their kids.
One of my biggest issues in previous games from this developer has been the voice acting, but Clockwork Tales is a vast improvement overall, especially with the main characters.  Now I'm not saying these are award winning performances, but they're not jarring nor do they sound out of place given the material, and they don't pull me out of the experience as they would in other games.  Funny enough, the one game in which I find the voice work to be pleasant enough is the one in which we get a toggle for the voiceovers.  The option is still appreciated and I hope we continue seeing it in the future.
This is the Collector's Edition of the game and comes with the bonus chapter (a short prequel to the main story), replayable puzzles and hidden object scenes, wallpapers, soundtrack and collectible "steambugs" that are sprinkled throughout the game.  I'm usually not big on having to find additional hidden items in these types of games, but the steambugs were a treat.  Aside from their imaginative and adorable designs, they're generally not too hard to spot, although it may take you a couple of play throughs to find a few you missed.
All in all, I enjoyed Clockwork Tales immensely and am only disappointed in it's short length.  But the little time that I spent in the game world was time I completely enjoyed.  I will definitely come back to this one again and again.

You defeat an evil German steampunk engineer in this casual hand-drawn hidden-object adventure lasting approximately 4 hours, with the "collector's edition" bonus chapter adding another hour.
The writing and voice-acting is competent if not exciting, the gameplay is linear to the point of having items in the scene disabled whose time has not yet come, there's an extensive help system: on easy, the map is marked where you need to be to progress in the story, and n the scenes there are golden sparkles on the puzzle you need to solve next. There are a few manipulation puzzles and some hidden object puzzles, and they're all fairly small and well integrated into the storyline: for example, with the hidden objects, you are always looking for something (or parts to something) that you'll need to progress in the storyline. I especially liked the dollhouse puzzle: 4 puppets in a dollhouse are looking for pairs of objects, and once you find the objects, you see a small animation where the dolls actually use them - very satisfying.
The storyline has voiceovers, the hints do not: I'd recommend the game for anyone age 6 and up if they can read or have someone who can help them if they get stuck (but with the hint system, that should hardly happen). Also, if you ever wanted your very own steambug collection or find the recipe for the Steam Horse drink ("I'd give up my helmet for a Steam Horse!"), this game might be for you.
The included bonus prequel is about an hour, with the professor in the village using the bits that you could look at, but not use, in the main game.
Some small gripes like light beams colliding instead of passing through each other or minor inaccuracies in the "evil German" grammar (the German subtitles are very well written!) do not detract from an overall experience that is well crafted, even if it doesn't reach the scope or the immersiveness of a "big" adventure like
.

This is my first steam review. I just had to write a review for this game, it deserves all the love!
This game is stunning. From the storyline to in-game artwork to the very captivating sound and music. You are in for a ride!
What makes this game fun to play is the clever level design which incorporates the use of skills / game-mechanics.  Meaning the farther you will get the more skills you will unlock, which you will need to progress in the game (for instance a double jump ability allows you to reach other places on the map).  What is really nicely done is that like this the levels themselves become a puzzle. So in order to reach certain places you will need to use all your skills to get there. I would not say the puzzles are hard, though it does make you think and go 'how am I supposed to do this?'.
And be prepared, there are some levels which will not only surprise you but will have you think on your feet (to the point of severe frustration). These levels are a welcome addition to the standard gameplay of this game and completing them is a reward on its own. Not to mention they are beautifully designed.
I played the game with a controller (PS4 controller and InputMapper), which was working nicely. I would recommend a controller to play the game.
By the way, did I mention this game is beautiful? Well, it is!

tl:dr - Skullgirls is one of the best fighters to buy if you're looking to get into fighting games or enjoy the Marvel Vs Capcom system and/or Anime fighters.
Now for the long-winded version:
Skullgirls is a relatively cheap fighting game which contains some of the best tutorials I have ever played in a fighting game. They seriously wanted you to understand every mechanic and aspect of their engine so that you can use it to your advantage and beat your opponents (whether that's bots or other humans).
With a good story (which is now fully coiced in the 2nd encore upgrade pack!) for every character it offers plenty of .vs bots action if you're simply looking for a fighting game to mash out in your spare time. The online works very smoothly too, running on GGPO which has given me some of the cleanest online matches from many fighting games (I'm looking at you SFV).
The game is also gorgeously animated which Is where I come to the only point which puts most people off. Yes there is fan service (which if this is the reason you're buying the game then there should be nothing stopping you) and it's a shame people instantly turn their heads when they hear it because they're missing out on a ridiculously good fighting game. Try to ignore it if you're put off by it, but it's honestly pretty damn easy to not notice it.
Overall Skullgirls is a crazy good, under-appreciated fighting game which I whole heartedly reccomend to anyone looking to get into fighting games or simply want a new fighting game to play. I mean it's not even that expensive especially compared to other fighting games out there... Why don't more people play this game ;_:
P.S. There's a cyborg made of musical instruments, how can people brush over this so easily!?

January 2012: the month that my gaming perception changed forever.
I bought Fallout 3 GOTY Edition in January 2012, after my parents bought me New Vegas the Christmas before and I loved it. Now, I know you see my profile lists I only have 17.7 hours in the game, but that's simply because I didn't get the Steam version of the game until I bought the Fallout Anthology in 2015. Prior to that, I had to have put nearly 800 hours into the game, easily.
As nerdy and stupid as this may sound, this game changed my life. Much like The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion, I played this game during a unique time in my life. I was getting ready to graduate high school, getting ready to be thrust into the real world, and thus things could get stressful at times. Just as Oblivion offered me respite from my life at that point in time, Fallout 3 gave me an escape from the real world as I adventured in an beautifully bleak world full of destruction, with hopefulness rising from the rubble.
There is no part about this game that I dislike, except for the shooting mechanics which feel a tiny bit clunky. Whether it's the excellent story, the deep gameplay mechanics, the beautiful art direction (RIP Adam Adamowicz), the incredible DLCs, it all just comes together to create a truly unforgettable experience. Despite the fact that New Vegas improved Fallout 3's gameplay and faction play, and despite the fact that Fallout 4 is my favorite in the series (and favorite game as a whole), Fallout 3 will ALWAYS be the one that means the most to me.
The story is a deep story that begins as a child searching for a missing father, and builds into a complex story that addresses morality and its relevance to a world like the one in Fallout, and displays a good portrayal of the franchise's slogan: "War, war never changes." You'll meet good-natured people aiming to truly rebuild humanity. You'll meet seemingly good-natured individuals with their own agenda. You'll meet people whose methods are questionable, but intentions are pure. And then you'll meet individuals whose methods and intentions are just downright nefarious.
Fallout 3's game world feels truly alive and realistic in nearly every way. That is thanks to the art direction and just overall design of the game world. The late Adam Adamowicz captured the classic feel of Fallout in his artwork, and as good as Fallout 4 was, it was sadly missing much of the charm that Fallout 3's art direction had. The ruins of DC, Maryland and Pittsburgh just breathe authenticity, they offer a world that -- despite its bleak and depressing nature -- makes you WANT to explore every place. Well, except for the metro tunnels. Those things are creepy as all get out. Oh, and the Dunwich Building, as well as Vault 87. This game is beautiful, but it also has disturbingly creepy moments as well, which will satisfy many horror fans out there. There are a lot of Lovecraftian elements in the game's various storylines, as Bethesda is notorious for including.
A review of a Fallout game wouldn't be complete without talking about the game's soundtrack. Inon Zur was the perfect choice for this game's ambient pieces, and the radio stations with retro tracks and patriotic marching band music on them are extremely enjoyable and strangely fitting. There's nothing quite like wandering post-apocalyptic DC while listening to Yankee Doodle.
And the DLCs... New Vegas had some great DLC, and Fallout 4 did as well (despite the unjustifiable hate Bethesda got for them), but I think of those three, Fallout 3 had the best DLCs. Being a Pennsylvania native and fan of Pittsburgh (not for its sports teams, mind you), The Pitt was my favorite but all of them were enjoyable in their own way. In The Pitt, you get to explore a section of downtown Pittsburgh in its post-apocalyptic state. Thanks to pollution and the Great War, the city is eternally in a state of brownish, overcast skies which creates an even drearier atmosphere than the Capital Wasteland. It has a morally gray story that truly feels like Fallout. It presents some moral dilemmas, gives great gear and opens up a new area to explore. It's not large by any means, but it's very interesting. Then you have Broken Steel which is a continuation of the game's main quest, boosting the level cap up to 30 and giving players a new plethora of gear to work with. Point Lookout is another great DLC, adding a whole new game world in a swampy wasteland filled with freaky mutant creatures and inbred, irradiated feral humans. It offers an open-ended story filled with lots of dark, demented storytelling. Of all the DLC, that one feels like a true horror movie. It's considered by most to be the best Fallout 3 DLC, but I disagree. It's good, don't get me wrong, but I felt like it just didn't have as many memorable moments as the other DLC. The two controversial DLC are Operation Anchorage and Mothership Zeta, and I can understand the criticism to an extent. Operation Anchorage is a linear story shooter DLC taking place in a simulation of the pre-war Battle of Anchorage, where US forces faced off against Chinese invaders attempting to gain Alaska's oil reserves. It's fun and a nice break from the constant depression of the wasteland, but it isn't a necessity. As for Mothership Zeta, it's a largely humorous DLC that takes place entirely on an alien mothership that has been observing humanity for seemingly thousands of years. It's a Fallout twist on the classic alien abduction stories of the 1950s-1960s. It's certainly the weakest DLC for this game but it's still fun.
Overall, this game is a truly wonderful experience, especially if you're a fan of post-apocalyptic fiction and/or RPGs. I'd consider this my third-favorite game of all time, only outdone by Oblivion and Fallout 4. The GOTY Edition is an amazing value, it comes with the game and all its DLCs, and every single moment you spend in this game is enjoyable in my book. If you've never played a Fallout game before, this is a pretty solid entry point for the franchise. Worth every single penny spent.
NOTE: This game will likely require minor tweaking. It works fine on both my Windows 7 and Windows 8 PCs, but many people experience issues.

I don't normally review games, but I felt obligated to in this rather unusual case.  For those who didn't find Hellblade enjoyable or powerful, it is because you missed the point of what this game was meant to do, and that is to make you think and perhaps understand slightly how someone with a severe mental illness might view their world.
Without giving anything away, I can say, as someone who has suffered greatly, with PTSD, severe anxiety and depression following life trauma, this game truly hit home.  The character, while struggling in ways I don't personally, was very relatable and the writing is truly moving.  This game is emotionally intense and create a vivid and accurate depiction of mental illness without the stigmas surrounding it.  This is one of those games that will stay with you far after you've finished (especially if it hits home for you as it did for me).
While it is a mix of puzzles and sporadic combat (which gets harder later on), this game was far, far more then that and I really hope everyone gains some understanding of what others face through this masterful piece of entertainment.

This game is an interactive art piece. I have never played anything like it. The experience of sublime satisfaction I had after finishing this game is precisely why I play video games at all. I recommend it to everyone who enjoys beautiful, thoughtful stories.
Of note, you must have a pair of headphones to really get the full experience. The sensation of voices talking in either ear, in varying pitches and tones, from the brooding and reverberating voice of Senua's Shadow to the ASMR voice of Senua's narrator, is very unique. A controller is also recommended for the game.
The game is short (about 8 hours) and I feel no need to replay it. I view this as a positive. I have less time to play games now and this game does not waste my time. The game is exceedingly streamlined and filled with memorable messages, themes, and areas. Each encounter presents a new aspect of Senua's character and history. There was never an experience of grind nor was there ever a dip in quality. The combat is also delightful. It plays similar to the Arkham Asylum series or Shadow of Mordor games, but with auditory cues rather than visual. It serves its purpose well, where combat on hard felt desperate and brutal. The entire experience was consistently awe-inspiring. I'm not entirely sure how to describe the game beyond this. Senua's version of paranoid schizophrenia (among other conditions) is tastefully presented and cast over an insightful backdrop of Norse mythology. To detail how masterfully the game intertwines Senua's perspective with mythology would entail spoilers, but it is truly a thing of art.

Spooky's House of Jumpscares doesn't take itself too seriously, but at the same time it takes itself very seriously. This game is kind of wierd like that.
You're greeted by this adorably evil chibi style ghost who tells you to go through her house, and that's the game, you go through her house of a thousand rooms, which is much better than the house of a thousand corpses (that movie was a piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥ this game is fun to play). But going through the house, the first things you'll come across are adorable cardboard cutouts. But the reason these could actually scare you is because of the tension this game throws out at you. The tight corridors create a sense of claustrophobia and later you're worrying about the more dangerous creatures that inhabit this castle.
The next thing I can say is good about this is the amount of parody they give. Whether it's a parody of games like Dreadout, with a creepy school atmosphere lit up by a flashlight that you're holding, or a room that pays homage to the original silent hill games, except in first person, it generally feels like a love letter to horror games that came before it. I think my favorite part about it is the fact that at some points it will change up the gameplay (having to avoid shadow people that can be lit up by your flashlight or even having to be constantly moving and looking at the puppeteer), it gives you more of a reason to come back and play again, just to see what is going to happen next.
The soundtrack is another very well done aspect of the game. At various points I wanted the tension filled music to end so I could know I was safe, this is also the only game that made a very upbeat and happy song drive tension up so high that I was happy when it ended.
Then you have the disturbing mini-games. Which got a chuckle out of me and my sometimes morbid sense of humor. But I won't spoil those for the people who want to give this game a try for themselves.
The best part about it is that it's free, and for a freeware game it's pretty damn good.
My Age Rating: M for blood and gore, and disturbing content
The game may seem all cute at first but then it gets to be very dark and disturbing, not even a quarter through the game.
My overall rating: 8/10
The game is fun and not too punishing for failure. Which is what I look for in a horror game. I like to be scared but I like breaks from the tension, which is something this game gives us and it's all the better fo it. This game definitely wins over my recommendation.

To the Moon is not really the kind of game I would usually play so I went into this with pretty low expectations. I'm very glad I did decide to give the game a try however, because it turned out to be one of the best indie games I've played.
While the gameplay and graphics are simple the game instead focuses on telling a story and what a story it is! There is something heartfelt and honest about this game that you won't find in many other games.
In short, if you can enjoy games where the focus is mainly on telling the story you will probably enjoy To the Moon a lot!

Bravo.
To the Moon is an enchanting and emotional cinematic adventure. The story-driven gameplay couples with world exploration to propel the player through an original and unexpected plot. This is not the game for battles, strategy, tactics, or challenge, so players should be prepared for the interactive mode of storytelling that this game executes with style.
This is without a doubt one of the best applications of music in a game, with the main theme reverberating in a haunting linger well after completing the story. I had plenty to ruminate on by the end, with surprising twists on themes that test the boundaries of contemporary morality. I also found the game to be inspirational as a fresh perspective on thinking about relationship dynamics.
There's not much more that can be said without spoilers. The DLC also provided welcome resolution to the main storyline while still building interest for the sequel. All in all, this has been one of my favorite gaming experiences in years. I eagerly look forward to the next release from this developer.

Reading many reviews of this game, I understand how fortunate I was to have played, or better said, lived through the original Assassin's Creed without reading any reviews beforehand. I enjoyed the game totally oblivious to the "well known facts" that it is redundant, buggy, too easy, and has a confusing ending. I just bought it, started playing and fell out of reality for a week, and loved every minute of it, except the ending - it was really sad to realise that it was finished and I couldn't play any more.
I must admit I'm not a "gamer", I enjoy games since my childhood, but I do not play them professionally, and I'm more on the intellectual side. I get bored with shallow keyboard-smashing action titles, and more appreciate a solid story and an adventure that allows me to use logic to solve the problem. I've never played games like Assassin's Creed before (were there any?), so I was totally blown away. I found it very similar to the original Prince of Persia from 1990, the same cinematic movement animations, same classic approach to a level-based story progression. One fight was a bit too hard for me, but I generally loved the idea of not dying. Since it was a memory, I could not really die - desynchronisation merely meant I was not doing it right. Psychologically it's somehow easier for me than getting actually killed. This game is much more logical than its sequels - here you live through a genetic memory of an ancestor, and you have to follow it very closely. In the sequels you had much more freedom, you could buy property, get various weapons, heal yourself, dress in fancy clothes through uPlay rewards (sometimes losing a finger), visit same place during a day or night - that really broke the concept of a DNA memory and moved the franchise from a science fiction into a non-science... better said: nonsense-fiction genre.
I have found the multi-layer matryoshka-like plot, the graphics and Altair so realistic, I was saying sorry to him each time I was clumsy enough to make him fall off a wall :) I don't understand what "redundancy" people are talking about. I guess I'm not blessed with a consumer's mind, and to me consistency, integrity of a story is more important than the "fun value".
So, if anyone hasn't yet played the original Assassin's Creed and makes up his mind by reading my review, I'd say that if you're jumping through the games while chatting to your friends, and you pay no attention to dialogues and story, this one is not for you, and you will be disappointed with it. However, if you immerse into games and live through them, this is something you'll most likely appreciate.

Assassin's Creed is one of those games that goes out of its way to make you feel badass. For example, when running along rooftops, so long as you're within step or reach of something to jump on, run across, or grab onto (depending on your skills obtained), Altair is going to look badass as hell running around and stabbing people.

Side-scrolling eye candy with mild platforming and forgettable combat/story/upgrades that still remains fun throughout.
Trine shoots pretty much straight down the middle. Nothing blows you away and nothing is completely messed up. The main gameplay idea is that you have three characters who are magically bound together and you can swap between the three. A wizard that can conjure items to drop on enemies or traverse obstacles, a thief with a bow and a grappling hook, and a knight with a shield, sword and brute strength. The idea is that some of the platforming is a puzzle of sorts and you need to use each of the character's strengths at different times. But, in my opinion, the bulk of the obstacles and platforming was mild and easy. I found myself just using one character for most of the game. There were just too many ways to tackle the already easy obstacles. Only towards the end does the platforming really get interesting and option limiting.
The combat is barely toying with average. Bosses don't come often or offer much. And worse, they soon repeat. Overall combat is really just a quick chore that has to be completed so you can get to the interesting stuff. Passive items, leveling, and weapon upgrades try to add some depth but beyond the wizard don't really add much. The story is simple but well narrated. A few lighthearted moments aren't "laugh-out-loud" funny by any stretch but fit the casual, straight down the middle feel of the game.
It was fun for what it was though and save for a jump or two felt right on keyboard and mouse. The visuals are pretty and unique giving the game some atmosphere. It all just kind of works. It was also good enough that I look forward to trying out the sequels to see what, if anything, was polished or improved. Like I said, nothing is going to wow you here. But I can comfortably recommend it at a steep sale or in a bundle to kill an afternoon.

This game wants to be a puzzler, platformer, and 2D side-scrolling hack-and-slasher all at once and fails at all three. The puzzles are never challenging, the platforming is floaty and imprecise, and the combat is just about mashing the attack button and hoping the hits occasionally register. All three mechanics rely heavily on a physics engine that's both jenky and unpredictable.
All in all, it's not a bad game, it's not a good game, it's just a solidly mediocre game. Only get it on sale and if you intend to play with friends, otherwise avoid this.

Remember Me is not perfect. But to be honest, nowadays, what is?
I wholeheartedly recommend this game on a sale, however. Full price, eh. My record of 9.5 hours is pretty much the entire game length on hard difficulty, although I did miss some collectibles. Therefore, 28 EUR is steep. But I got this at -85% off, and I have no right to complain.
The story was VERY interesting, the setting was unique. Neo-Paris, 2084, where SENSEN technology is capable of storing your memory data so that you can erase the memories you don't want, relive memories you hold close, and use your memories as currency... and you're Nilin, an Errorist, who is guided by Edge trying to dismantle this system, which is supposedly "flawed" and should be destroyed.
Soundtrack fits the futuristic theme of the game, it's glitchy orchestral, like a movie soundtrack mixed with electronic and effects. Great support for the events that occur.
Gameplay is primarily three things:
- Combat: (combo-based system, combos can be customized in order to have their elements (pressens) be POWER, REGEN, COOLDOWN REDUCTION and CHAIN; and you also get Sensen Abilities which need a Focus bar which you get from punching your opponents enough. Simple enough.
Some people in the negative reviews might claim "they couldn't get into the game because the combat is too difficult", but you honestly just have to press the right button at the right times, like "right left right left right" with the right delay between them and bam you executed your 5-hit-combo. Not hard, in my opinion.
- Platforming: you need to climb on things, jump on things, move some things around, etc etc. Think of "Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons" and that's pretty much how it goes, except you only move your one character.
- Remix sections: There aren't too many of these in the game, but they hold important plot points, where you alter the memory of others. You'll see if you play. It's interesting. Really.
---- NOW the question is, what did I mean by this game not being perfect?
There were some glaring flaws in some game design elements. Literally a flaw from a game design perspective. In order to learn more of the LORE of this game, you need to find MNESISTS. Now, they wanted to make collectible secret items... and they made those be the MNESISTS. The problem is that without them, you for example won't understand what the hell the Mnemopolis is - but these items are REALLY hidden, and if you don't know where to look, looking for them can be extremely tedious. They aren't indicated well at all, they're just tiny orange boxes, hard to find, and usually you need to go on an alternate path to find them.
So this is like playing in the Mass Effect universe, except you have to look for well-hidden secrets in order to learn the lore of the game, which you're supposedly interested in if you're interested in the plot. I think this was quite silly.
Also, by the end of the game, the enemy versatility kinda falters, they rehash some stuff from previously instead of adding something new.
In the end, it was still a great game.
- PROS:
Interesting story and unique settings
Good soundtrack that supports said setting
Okay combat (others might disagree but they just need to get a sense of timing I guess, it really is not difficult)
- CONS:
Some platforming is a bit tedious
The combat can get repetitive by the end because of rehashed enemies (too much saber force)
THE ITEMS THAT GIVE YOU THE LORE ARE HIDDEN COLLECTIBLES. Terrible decision, even if it kinda makes sense, but not really. Makes looking for them tedious, you might want to use a guide.
The antagonists' motives just aren't very deep by the time you actually get to them. But the plot overall makes up for it.
Recommended. Not at full price, but at a greater discount, definitely.

Remember Me is a game with numerous bugs, an unsatisfying New Game Plus Mode, terrible platforming and a boring, repetitive combat. But you should definitely play this rough gem of a game.
The design and art style is gorgeous, and the landscape of Neo-Paris is one of the most fleshed out and memorable sci-fi vistas I've seen. The game centers around memories and the design actually reflects this. Little things like billboards and graffiti aren't used as purely eye candy but as subtle hints about the story and interesting behind-the-scenes views. Holograms are prevalent throughout the games, and is used in a natural way that doesn't feel like it was just plugged in because it's the future (not to mention how ridiculously well implemented it is). The clash of high neo-Paris society and the desolate slums are shown, These conflicting scenes are used to contrast with each other nicely for story, but also are individually well presented in their aesthetic. The worldbuilding and whole aesthetic feel of Remember Me is definitely it's biggest selling point.
However, this is a game which it's gameplay is sorely lacking. The closest analogy is probably the Batman Arkham style combat with combos instead of constant stringing of individual hits. It sold itself intitially on the Presen combat system, where you can join various moves together to make a combo that can be used to produce various effects (+damage, heal on hit or cooldown reduction). However, while at the start this feels fine, it becomes painfully obvious how limiting this is when you unlock one move one by one, and the combo lengths and button prompts are fixed. This really restricts what the combat could have been like. It could have been where you could string together any combination of punches and kicks, and have near limitless combinations, but it didn't happen. This leads to combat being extremely limited as you merely make each combo specialise in one thing (damage combo, healing combo, cd combo) and use them when appropriate. I would have much rather preferred it if you could have more than 4 combination inputs and much more options to what each move did.
You also have these "super moves" called S-Pressens which have various effects are after being used are set on cooldown. These range from taking control of robotic enemies to doing an AoE stun. In my opinion, these were done nicely and are balanced well. Using the various combinations possible (and the variety of the S-Pressens too) were welcome after having the sour taste of the actual Pressen-combo system.
Platforming is a big part of this game. It has a Assassin's Creed-esque freerunning system, but without the freedom. Instead your forced to only interact with certain, extremely linear paths by the use of an orange UI marker. There's no freedom in the path you can take, because there is literally only one path from point A to B. Jumping is wonky, and Nilin's movements (the protagonist) just doesn't feel nimble or fluid enough for platforming. There are however, some puzzles in the game. There's the more standard puzzles, which are simple but interesting enough to be a nice break from the monotomy of platforming and combat. And there's also remixing, a fun mini game where you interact with people's memories and attempt to alter them. Remixing was definitely a highlight and it's a shame you only get around 4 opportunities. I'd glady pay for a game where half of it was just Remixing, it's actually that fun.
I found the writing to be surprisingly good. A lot of the story is foreshadowed and alluded to, and it's worth it to play it a second time to notice all the cues from the very start. Characters were interesting and the overall story is enjoyable. It's decent enough not to spoil it here in this review at all. I really, really liked the collectables in that they developed the world further and brought character development and behind the scenes information. Voice acting was average. There were some high points such as Edge but some of the characters sounded off and shallow. Nilin in particularly was a mixed bag. At times the VA was fine, but her accent would go all over place from American to British to French and to other less obvious ones. Occassionally she'd also sounds incredibly awkward, especially in emotional scenes.
This game however is terribly unoptimized and bugs are everywhere. I've had regular crashes (I think 1 crash per 1~2 episodes) and frequent audio bugs where the audio tracks would echo on itself.
Overall though, the combat is fine, the designs and story are really well done but there are some very annoying bugs. It's definitely worth a playthrough although it's replayability is soon lost. It's still a fairly unique game combat and story wise and I'd definitely recommend you to play it.

Felt that the plot wasn't too pronounced during the entire gameplay experience, was quite confused at the end. It felt more like no-brainer progression. Adding onto that, the ending was quite abrupt and unexpected as I expected more but it's continued on on part II in which I haven't tried yet (and I don't really plan to due to its negative reviews)
Gameplay was very smooth in general, felt that movement is rather odd if you were to move with a mouse as you can't really move and shoot at the same time, which makes attacking + defending quite choppy.
However, to make up for that, I appreciate the over the top swarms of monsters that can be slain through 1 single AOE attack which makes the experience quite satisfying.
Quite liked the companion option as it allows you to stay behind a tank if you're planning on a ranged character (I played range). Adding onto that, companions allows you to sell items (almost) anywhere in the battlefield with the drawback that you give up her presence for 60 seconds
Felt that the inventory management was pretty dang good considering it automatically optimizes inventory space as you collect more items, it even has a manual sort button there just in case. Your companion also helps in clearing up your inventory space by having a separate inventory space of her own (in which you can send her to sell items too)
Felt that skills were a bit lackluster as compared to games nowadays, felt that they could expand more on the skill tree but I think it is just barely enough for completing the game
Similarly, quite lackluster, the enchantments and upgrades were... not too appealling, it's mostly basic upgrades like HP+, HP Drain, MP Drain, Elemental Damage etc. It doesn't really explore into more experimental elements that a hack & slash game could go with, but as I've said, the basic enchantments/upgrades should suffice for a basic game like this.
The game scales to ridiculous difficulty amounts at further levels (found that after level 20 it becomes annoyingly hard to progress). Though there's a mode for you to farm equipments on with respawning monsters, you can only access it at levels higher than 27 (I believe). Kind of a bit too far away from the point where you'd normally get really frustrated.
One example would be a monster that shoots a bomb, as a ranger, you'd expect yourself to have very little health if you weren't expecting these monsters; it deals immense damage, close to 80% of my health as a ranger and it basically OHKO's you at higher levels if you don't have (very) good armor and health.
No, the problem is that, the area that the game lets you hit the monster is exactly the range of the monster, so you'd have to shoot and run. With the sloppy movement I find it really hard and annoying to kill these monsters, and I don't really even want to go into dealing 2 of these at the same time.
One of my biggest issues would be the camera angle.
First of, the game doesn't allow you to rotate the camera at all, so you're kinda stuck with this 45 degree camera view all the time. The biggest problem is that there will be enemies coming at you from the bottom of the camera (in which is a blind spot), you wouldn't know what's hitting you until you go really close to them or you take a detour. As a ranger, it was a horrific experience most of the time.
Voices were on point, think it is better than that of most games even. The contents of the dialogue were well balanced in comedic value and seriousness, not too much of any in which I feel is a good composition.
Comparing to games nowadays, sound effects here are subpar, if you're very picky in audio, you might find these a bit of a nuisance, but I managed to get over them.
Music was decent, felt that there were some mastering errors here and there (some tracks felt quite muffled for some reason) but it is okay in potraying the mood at their respective positions
Though The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing has its better days in the past, it doesn't have the better perks of other similar games that are out right now.
Think Torchlight II or Path of Exile would be a significantly better choice than this right now, Path of Exile is even free
As of now, wouldn't really recommend it

This is a fun little ARPG. Without DLC there are effectively two options - swordy type or shooty type, and you can switch between them basically at will. Your ghostly companion can be set up as either range or melee as well. The combination is pretty cool.  I've had some success levelling my ghost up as a tank, and sitting back at range and using my guns to finish off opponents which are targeting her. There's also some limited magic which you can use for basic AoE attacks.
Environments are nice. Maps tend to be pretty big, and the sort-of-steampunk atmosphere is a nice change.
The voice acting is a bit hit-and-miss. The main characters are fine, but you'll bump into some real howlers early on who I suspect were voiced by the game's programmers.
The game is a bit more story-driven than, for example, Diablo III seems to be. You get quests popping up all over the place, and finishing them isn't too much of a stretch.
You do have to do a lot of kiting. More than I'm particularly comfortable with. You either get mobbed by a *LOT* of enemies, with no real way to damage more than one at a time... or you'll get one mob which takes a long time to kill, even though it's not particularly challenging.   This is a bit of a flaw, but it's not a major one, all things considered.
I got this on special for $4, and it's well worth that. This holds up nicely, even given the fact that ARPGs aren't really all that hard to come by.
It could do with more character/attack customisation (without DLC) and the loot system is a bit 'meh', but it seems to be a pretty solid, enjoyable game.

This game is stunning. From the storyline to in-game artwork to the very captivating sound and music. You are in for a ride!
What makes this game fun to play is the clever level design which incorporates the use of skills / game-mechanics.  Meaning the farther you will get the more skills you will unlock, which you will need to progress in the game (for instance a double jump ability allows you to reach other places on the map).  What is really nicely done is that like this the levels themselves become a puzzle. So in order to reach certain places you will need to use all your skills to get there. I would not say the puzzles are hard, though it does make you think and go 'how am I supposed to do this?'.
And be prepared, there are some levels which will not only surprise you but will have you think on your feet (to the point of severe frustration). These levels are a welcome addition to the standard gameplay of this game and completing them is a reward on its own. Not to mention they are beautifully designed.
I played the game with a controller (PS4 controller and InputMapper), which was working nicely. I would recommend a controller to play the game.
By the way, did I mention this game is beautiful? Well, it is!

I don't normally review games, but I felt obligated to in this rather unusual case.  For those who didn't find Hellblade enjoyable or powerful, it is because you missed the point of what this game was meant to do, and that is to make you think and perhaps understand slightly how someone with a severe mental illness might view their world.
Without giving anything away, I can say, as someone who has suffered greatly, with PTSD, severe anxiety and depression following life trauma, this game truly hit home.  The character, while struggling in ways I don't personally, was very relatable and the writing is truly moving.  This game is emotionally intense and create a vivid and accurate depiction of mental illness without the stigmas surrounding it.  This is one of those games that will stay with you far after you've finished (especially if it hits home for you as it did for me).
While it is a mix of puzzles and sporadic combat (which gets harder later on), this game was far, far more then that and I really hope everyone gains some understanding of what others face through this masterful piece of entertainment.

This game is an interactive art piece. I have never played anything like it. The experience of sublime satisfaction I had after finishing this game is precisely why I play video games at all. I recommend it to everyone who enjoys beautiful, thoughtful stories.
Of note, you must have a pair of headphones to really get the full experience. The sensation of voices talking in either ear, in varying pitches and tones, from the brooding and reverberating voice of Senua's Shadow to the ASMR voice of Senua's narrator, is very unique. A controller is also recommended for the game.
The game is short (about 8 hours) and I feel no need to replay it. I view this as a positive. I have less time to play games now and this game does not waste my time. The game is exceedingly streamlined and filled with memorable messages, themes, and areas. Each encounter presents a new aspect of Senua's character and history. There was never an experience of grind nor was there ever a dip in quality. The combat is also delightful. It plays similar to the Arkham Asylum series or Shadow of Mordor games, but with auditory cues rather than visual. It serves its purpose well, where combat on hard felt desperate and brutal. The entire experience was consistently awe-inspiring. I'm not entirely sure how to describe the game beyond this. Senua's version of paranoid schizophrenia (among other conditions) is tastefully presented and cast over an insightful backdrop of Norse mythology. To detail how masterfully the game intertwines Senua's perspective with mythology would entail spoilers, but it is truly a thing of art.

January 2012: the month that my gaming perception changed forever.
I bought Fallout 3 GOTY Edition in January 2012, after my parents bought me New Vegas the Christmas before and I loved it. Now, I know you see my profile lists I only have 17.7 hours in the game, but that's simply because I didn't get the Steam version of the game until I bought the Fallout Anthology in 2015. Prior to that, I had to have put nearly 800 hours into the game, easily.
As nerdy and stupid as this may sound, this game changed my life. Much like The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion, I played this game during a unique time in my life. I was getting ready to graduate high school, getting ready to be thrust into the real world, and thus things could get stressful at times. Just as Oblivion offered me respite from my life at that point in time, Fallout 3 gave me an escape from the real world as I adventured in an beautifully bleak world full of destruction, with hopefulness rising from the rubble.
There is no part about this game that I dislike, except for the shooting mechanics which feel a tiny bit clunky. Whether it's the excellent story, the deep gameplay mechanics, the beautiful art direction (RIP Adam Adamowicz), the incredible DLCs, it all just comes together to create a truly unforgettable experience. Despite the fact that New Vegas improved Fallout 3's gameplay and faction play, and despite the fact that Fallout 4 is my favorite in the series (and favorite game as a whole), Fallout 3 will ALWAYS be the one that means the most to me.
The story is a deep story that begins as a child searching for a missing father, and builds into a complex story that addresses morality and its relevance to a world like the one in Fallout, and displays a good portrayal of the franchise's slogan: "War, war never changes." You'll meet good-natured people aiming to truly rebuild humanity. You'll meet seemingly good-natured individuals with their own agenda. You'll meet people whose methods are questionable, but intentions are pure. And then you'll meet individuals whose methods and intentions are just downright nefarious.
Fallout 3's game world feels truly alive and realistic in nearly every way. That is thanks to the art direction and just overall design of the game world. The late Adam Adamowicz captured the classic feel of Fallout in his artwork, and as good as Fallout 4 was, it was sadly missing much of the charm that Fallout 3's art direction had. The ruins of DC, Maryland and Pittsburgh just breathe authenticity, they offer a world that -- despite its bleak and depressing nature -- makes you WANT to explore every place. Well, except for the metro tunnels. Those things are creepy as all get out. Oh, and the Dunwich Building, as well as Vault 87. This game is beautiful, but it also has disturbingly creepy moments as well, which will satisfy many horror fans out there. There are a lot of Lovecraftian elements in the game's various storylines, as Bethesda is notorious for including.
A review of a Fallout game wouldn't be complete without talking about the game's soundtrack. Inon Zur was the perfect choice for this game's ambient pieces, and the radio stations with retro tracks and patriotic marching band music on them are extremely enjoyable and strangely fitting. There's nothing quite like wandering post-apocalyptic DC while listening to Yankee Doodle.
And the DLCs... New Vegas had some great DLC, and Fallout 4 did as well (despite the unjustifiable hate Bethesda got for them), but I think of those three, Fallout 3 had the best DLCs. Being a Pennsylvania native and fan of Pittsburgh (not for its sports teams, mind you), The Pitt was my favorite but all of them were enjoyable in their own way. In The Pitt, you get to explore a section of downtown Pittsburgh in its post-apocalyptic state. Thanks to pollution and the Great War, the city is eternally in a state of brownish, overcast skies which creates an even drearier atmosphere than the Capital Wasteland. It has a morally gray story that truly feels like Fallout. It presents some moral dilemmas, gives great gear and opens up a new area to explore. It's not large by any means, but it's very interesting. Then you have Broken Steel which is a continuation of the game's main quest, boosting the level cap up to 30 and giving players a new plethora of gear to work with. Point Lookout is another great DLC, adding a whole new game world in a swampy wasteland filled with freaky mutant creatures and inbred, irradiated feral humans. It offers an open-ended story filled with lots of dark, demented storytelling. Of all the DLC, that one feels like a true horror movie. It's considered by most to be the best Fallout 3 DLC, but I disagree. It's good, don't get me wrong, but I felt like it just didn't have as many memorable moments as the other DLC. The two controversial DLC are Operation Anchorage and Mothership Zeta, and I can understand the criticism to an extent. Operation Anchorage is a linear story shooter DLC taking place in a simulation of the pre-war Battle of Anchorage, where US forces faced off against Chinese invaders attempting to gain Alaska's oil reserves. It's fun and a nice break from the constant depression of the wasteland, but it isn't a necessity. As for Mothership Zeta, it's a largely humorous DLC that takes place entirely on an alien mothership that has been observing humanity for seemingly thousands of years. It's a Fallout twist on the classic alien abduction stories of the 1950s-1960s. It's certainly the weakest DLC for this game but it's still fun.
Overall, this game is a truly wonderful experience, especially if you're a fan of post-apocalyptic fiction and/or RPGs. I'd consider this my third-favorite game of all time, only outdone by Oblivion and Fallout 4. The GOTY Edition is an amazing value, it comes with the game and all its DLCs, and every single moment you spend in this game is enjoyable in my book. If you've never played a Fallout game before, this is a pretty solid entry point for the franchise. Worth every single penny spent.
NOTE: This game will likely require minor tweaking. It works fine on both my Windows 7 and Windows 8 PCs, but many people experience issues.
