This is a single-player action RPG in a post-apocalyptic sci-fi setting, with first-person and third-person view options. In other words, it's Oblivion with guns. If you've read my review of The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion, also by Bethesda, a lot of it applies here. They seem to have learned from Oblivion, and many improvements have been made to the basic formula. (There will be a lot of comparisons to Oblivion here, as I never played Fallout 1 and 2, which were turn-based RPG titles.)
Fallout 3 takes place in a world much like our own, but where history took a different turn in the fifties, with much more rapid technological progress. It was a futuristic golden age of robots and rayguns for about a century, then America had a nuclear war with China. Oops. Fast forward two more centuries, and that's where our story begins.
During the build-up to the war, many families reserved space in underground cities called Vaults, just in case. You are a resident of Vault 101, beneath the ruins of Washington DC, where the descendants of some of those survivors have lived for generations. But circumstances soon force you into the wasteland above, a lone wanderer fighting to survive.
Character creation uses much the same "make-a-mug" method as Oblivion: Choose a name, race, gender, face, hairstyle, and hair color and you're good to go. The tutorial quests walk you through key moments in your character's young life, from birth to adulthood, and then the main questline kicks off with the mysterious disappearance of your father. The Vault's paranoid Overseer is convinced you have something to do with it, so escape is your only option.
This game also uses much the same control scheme as Oblivion: Mouse to look around, left mouse button to attack, right mouse button to block with a melee weapon or aim with a ranged weapon, middle mouse button toggles first- and third-person views, mousewheel adjusts third-person camera distance, WASD moves you, and most other stuff is nearby. (I bound VATS, use, and grab to mouse buttons.) The keyboard/mouse controls are rebindable and responsive.
Once your eyes adjust to the blinding daylight, you can head to the nearby town of Megaton and pursue leads about your missing father... or not. The main quest can be ignored if you'd rather run around adventuring on your own for a while, and it will still be available to pick up if and when you decide to return to it. There's no shortage of other trouble you can get into in the meantime, from disarming a dud nuke (or not...) to helping a mad scientist write a survival guide. If that doesn't interest you, there are always raiders, radscorpions, and other menaces that have lived long enough...
The combat system is a bit more complex than usual, as hit location can make a big difference to damage and its side effects. Limbs can become crippled, slowing a character or making them drop a weapon, blows to the head can leave you dizzy with a concussion, and many of the meds and chems that are useful in combat are addictive and have crippling withdrawal effects. All of this can be fixed if you survive, but that and weapon and armor degradation are drains on your resources. Repair skill quickly becomes valuable, as you can combine parts from junked weapons and gear to repair your own, or you can pay someone to repair it for you. You can also use Repair to craft your own weapons from various junk items at a workbench, once you acquire the rare schematics that tell you how to assemble them.
The biggest change to combat is VATS, the Vault-tec Assisted Targeting System. The Pip-Boy wrist computer that you use for inventory and such can be used as a targeting system, pausing the action and letting you pick targets and hit locations, then resolving the attacks in bullet-time according to the character's stats rather than the player's reflexes, adding a taste of turn-based combat to the game. Your "action points" for this take time to recharge between uses, however.
In addition to the usual stealth options like sneak attack criticals, you can pickpocket a character and leave them a live grenade or mine as a free gift, with spectacular (and hilarious) results.
Interaction is much more efficient due to various changes, like empty containers being marked as such on screen, and characters with no unique dialogue brushing you off without entering the conversation menu. There's no speech minigame this time around: If a character can be talked into something, there will be a percent chance based on your Speech skill, and you only get one shot. (This can be save scummed, if you insist.) Many also have dialogue options that are only available if you have certain perks or skills, and these always succeed if you meet the requirements. The main difference regarding lockpicking (and hacking) is that locks and computers have a minimum skill requirement, so you can't attempt them with insufficient skill levels. If you want to be a Master of Unlocking, spend those skill points wisely.
There are many bizarre and fascinating locations to be found in the Wasteland, from ancient caves to abandoned shopping malls. A lot of them have a story to tell you as you search through the debris and collect notes and audio logs. If you played Oblivion, do you remember Vilverin, that dungeon you started out facing when you finished the tutorial? Remember how a weird tale unfolded as you went deeper and found more clues? Well, this game has a lot of that in it.
Like in Elder Scrolls, you can play as a good or evil character if you so desire. Instead of the Fame/Infamy system, you have a Karma stat that tracks your reputation. How you choose to finish a quest may have unforseen consequences, and sometimes there are no good options. The "fallout" of your actions can spread far from your original intentions, and in some situations, the only winning move is not to play... or at least, not to play by the rules, if you can change them.
The advancement system is much improved, as you have a more conventional experience point system based on kills and quests completed, and you can improve whatever skills you like when you level up without having to grind them. You also get to pick a new Perk each level: These give you more skill or attribute points, open new dialogue options when talking to some people, give damage bonuses in special situations, and/or grant unique abilties like the Paralyzing Palm.
The game is not without gripes. There are still some random crashes, quest-stopping bugs, and other nuisances that crop up from time to time, and also strange physics glitches, like finding a monster or a junk car floating in midair for no reason, or bodies spontaneously ragdolling again as you return to where you killed them. There doesn't seem to be as much of a "scaling" problem this time around, except for lock difficulties scaling to your level, eventually putting them out of reach of any character without a lot of points invested in Science and Lockpicking. The gunplay could have used an "aim down sights" option, as aiming just zooms your view in, and doesn't help accuracy nearly as much as it should. Completing the main quest (unless you're using the "Broken Steel" DLC) ends the game, making you put it off until you've done everything else you wanted to do.
Overall, despite some annoyances, this game is quite a journey, and still just as compelling now as when I first played it.

A gorgeous world and great story with a suitable score, but let down by painfully bland combat. If you enjoy the exploration elements of Prince of Persia and Tomb Raider, this is definitely worth picking up, but I wouldn't recommend it for those who are after exciting action.

A unique action adventure game in the vein of your traditional hack 'n slash or brawler action adventures. If you're into games like God of War or Devil May Cry, you may take a liking to Remember Me. It combines a fluid brawling mechanic with the Combo Lab, which allows you to construct your own hit combos to your own liking. The combat controls themselves are simplistic, alternating only between punch, kick, dodge, special techniques that trigger unusual conditions in the environment against your enemies, and using a sort of blast gun. On top of this, you get to do some parkour-style navigation and platforming through the environments, which strongly resembles the Prince of Persia games but is fairly simplistic. It even throws in a handful of easy puzzles here and there to mix things up, most notably the ability to "remix" certain people's memories during the storyline to make them change their beliefs.
The setting, story and characters are by far Remember Me's strongest point. It's a very good cyberpunk scenario, revolving around themes of questioning the nature of personal identity and what kind of value you can place on memories. The graphics, sound effects, music, and overall atmosphere are excellent. The story concludes on an interesting ending and the journey there is at times unsettling—in all the right ways, as is appropriate for the scenario's genre.
The game's weakest point is its total length and replayability. I played the game on the highest difficulty from the start, and was finished with the story within 12 hours. Now, this is not to say that it's super-easy or I'm very good, because I felt adequately challenged considering the setting and some fights and bosses gave me quite a bit to chew on till I had figured out how to beat them. The game has an excellently smooth learning curve and maintained an entertaining difficulty throughout. The amount of hand-holding was kept to the minimum of what's expected of modern games and some of the fights and boss scenes surprised me in how the game designers wanted players to think outside of the box and inject some variety outside of the regular brawling with common enemies throughout the game. However, the issue still stands: the length and replayability is extremely limited. Outside of going back to hunt for all achievements and hidden items, because the level designs are very linear and there are no additional challenge modes or anything else to extend the play experience.
Everything gels nicely in this game. Nothing feels contrived or redundant, which is often a problem with games in this genre, where you'll complete the game with abilities you never used or features that you ignored. If anything, I wish it were longer so I could get more use out of its many cool features, and I'm looking forward to any games that DONTNOD produces next. If anything about this game looks or sounds even remotely interesting to you, you should give it a try.

Remember Me is a very cheap game (Can easily find keys for 5 euros), which brings back the old-fashioned wonder of playing an adventure (or i should say "A Story").
In a world filled with first person shooters and sometimes dispersive open world games, "Dontnod" delivered a fine gem.
Not a perfect game, but surely one worth playing.
Remember Me is an action/adventure game.
It somehow reminds me of Uncharted, where you alternate combat phases with some guided platforming.
To be honest it shares the same downsides as the Naughty Dog masterpiece, like a way too guided progression.
The major downside of the game is that there's no room for exploration; you basically navigate a lot of elaborated corridors.
The good thing, though, is that the graphics and setting are so inspired you actually get captivated by the whole atmosphere and you don't think too much about these issues after a couple of hours of gameplay.
The combat mechanics are great.
Ok, you only have 4 combos at your disposal, but you can customise them however you want, by unlocking different "Action Points" (pressens), each one with a specific effect (reduce cooldown/regain health/break guard/double effect ecc...).
The longest combos are hard to deliver (but deadly) and that, mixed with a satisfying variety of enemies and a good selection of special abilities (that are unlocked throughout the story), makes the fights always stimulating.
The developers did a great job balancing the fights, inserting different type of enemies at the same time, so you always need to think and use a new strategy.
The other major feature of the game is it's narrative.
A very simple yet captivating story, that keeps you wanting to know what's going to happen; the plot twists are also great and the game also brings up some existential questions and strong topics.
One last thing i'd like to mention is the "Memory Remixes", a really interesting and fun "Game within the game", although it's featured only for a couple of times.
Remember me is a fine action/adventure game; not perfect but definitely worth the small price you can buy it for.
Strongly recommended to people who can appreciate a good story. Not recommended to people who can't stand "Non-Open-World" games.
Pros:
- Great Story
- Well Orchestrated fights
- Memory Remixes are really cool
- Very inspired level design and atmosphere
- Fairly good graphics.
- Customisable combos
Cons:
- Strictly Guided Exploration
- Sometimes "Claustrophobic"
- More combo slots would have been nice.
- Not That Long (about 7 hours of gameplay)
- It should have "dared" a bit more
To consider:
- Old School Gameplay (You might like it or dislike it)
Recommended

A friend of mine got me to buy the whole trilogy, so I'll review each of the three games on their respective pages.
The game is
pretty, I must say. The environments you travel through are beautiful almost the entire time. There are a few spots that look like generic corridors, but they are not very frequent.
The music is good, but the tracks are very short, meaning the music quickly becomes repetitive to the point of being annoying. You also can't turn it off completely, only lower its volume significantly, so once the music becomes annoying, you can't escape it.
The story is... alright... I guess... Not desperately interesting though. It feels more like an excuse plot than something that was given high priority.
The combat is acceptable, has a nice flow to it, and there are multiple ways to approach it. However, the boss fights aren't particularly interesting. (There are also technically only two bosses. All subsequent ones are copy-pasted versions of them.)
This is what really brings the game down. The most important part of any platformer is to have good... well... platforming. This game does not. You frequently find yourself struggling against inconsistent collision boxes. The grappling hook helps, but it has restrictions on what angles you can shoot it in, and has a tendency to mess up the physics simulation occasionally.
The final level increases the difficulty significantly. It's still manageable, but can easily get frustrating if you haven't yet gotten used to the awkward platforming.
The game is acceptable, I guess... But not something I would recommend. The short music loops and frustrating platforming issues are the main things that bring it down. Most aspects of the game are kinda average, but the visuals are great. I can see how others would like the game, but I personally don't.
(A quick note about the other games in the series: Trine 2 fixes most of the issues that this first game has, and is actually a pretty good game. Trine 3, on the other hand, has a couple of other issues that bring it down again.)
This is without question one of the most beautiful and fun games I have played in a very long time.

PROS
+ Graphics/Visuals
The graphics in Trine are colorful and enveloped in a vibrant bloom, creating a magical and dream-like ambiance. The beauty is even more apparent when playing at 4K resolution or downsampled from such.
+ Music
The music is pleasant and fits nicely with the visual style; also pizzicato strings rule.
CONS
- Faulty Controls
Ironically, controls are wonky considering platforming is a core mechanic of the game. One of my problems was, for example, turning around on a dime and then jumping onto a platform; this often resulted in not grasping onto a ledge and falling, making fast platforming difficult. It was often more practical to give yourself extra space, turn around, wait for a second, and then attempt a jump. If this issue sounds strange, trust me, you would know what I am talking about if you played for yourself. Something else I noticed was that tapping the jump key as oppose to a longer press would cover a shorter distance. As a consequence, if you had to jump multiple platforms in quick succession, you would often fail and have to repeat, making for irksome moments. Finally, the character would at many times fail to grasp onto to a ledge despite clearly being able to do so; once again, leading to frustration.
- Basic Combat
There is nothing special about the combat in Trine; it is quite shallow with no outstanding features. The one character, Amadeus, is next to useless for combat because he has no proper attack. You have to summon a cube, levitate it above an enemy, and let it fall crushing him. Attacking like this is fun at first but gets old, and is far too slow especially when dealing with several foes. With Amadeus being incompetent, only the other two characters are practical for fighting.
- Underwhelming and Skippable Puzzles
Puzzles were not impressive since none really stood out to me. Making matters worse, are the character abilities which make many portions of the game skippable. A prime example would be conjuring Amadeus' triangle block and then using Zoya's grapple to transverse over an area in a way not intended. Even Amadeus alone is a problem since you can summon several blocks and planks to advance effortlessly. You could avoid upgrading Amadeus fully, but self-imposed limitations are never fun.
- Repetitive Gameplay
Trine's gameplay is repetitious due to the reuse of content throughout the game. Not much changes in regards to combat, platforming, and puzzles, thus being a bit of a bore to play.
- Difficulty Curve
Most of the playthrough is far too easy, even on hard; however, once reaching the final level, the difficulty suddenly spikes. In this last level, you have to rush intensifying previously mentioned problems leading one to curse out loud. The difficulty curve which stagnates for the most part and then suddenly shoots up hurts this title big time.
CONCLUSION
The visuals and music of Trine are charming but do little for the overall experience. The combination of core mechanics is admittedly interesting but unfortunately dissonant to the extent of fundamentally breaking gameplay. Then there are other issues adding further insult to injury; I can not recommend this game. Ultimately, I give Trine a PAR of 1.

Immediately change the game to use WASD to move and play the game like that when fighting enemies or it'll be a hassle during tough fights.
The next negative that is important to mention is the bulk of quests have no method to learn what to do, let alone not mess it up since they can't be repeated to get it done correctly. It practically requires using a guide because the game doesn't do anything useful to hint at what to do, or even warn if the quest leads to a boss fight you can't run away from.
I'm still giving it a positive review because those problems can be solved outside of the game, but I will give it a massive deduction in score because of that. The voice acting and dialogue are well done, the atmosphere is something I greatly enjoy and overall, it's worth it if you pay about $5. As of right now, it's not worth $15 because the game has too many issues that should have been solved in development and are obvious how easy they are to fix once the player experiences the bad decisions.

I have to agree with the many other reviewers here, Lego Worlds was much better while it was in early access. (Positive notes in 3rd last paragraph of this review).

From what I remember there used to be a huge procedurally generated world in which you could explore freely and discover new items and props along the way at your own pace and then collect studs to buy them. This was an exciting, fun and relaxing experience which inspired creativity and exploration. Perhaps most importantly, it gave us our own unique, personal adventures.
Now In sandbox mode there is no insentive to exploring the worlds and there is no progression. Everything is just given to you right out the gate. The excitement of discovery has gone which is very sad. Discovering, collecting and purchasing items was my favourite part of the game. I think many others agree with me on this.
There is an adventure mode in which you do quests to progress, and while this is not a bad side of the game by any means, it is much more limiting than what we had in early access and it certainly is NOT why I bought the game! I got bored of adventure mode very quickly (On the day of release) and haven't played this game since.
Lego worlds has an incredible charm to it. It made me laugh many times. The graphics are pretty and the building/terrain editing is impressive. The animations are fantastic and overall this game has wonderful character.
So I won't go as far as saying this is a bad game, but at the moment it sure isn't a great one, like it once was. It has become more boring and limiting.
I will not reccomend this game to anyone untill we get our old features back. Then I will change my review to a more positive one.

JamG is a marble game, which is a real commodity these days. It cites Marble Madness and Ballance as inspirations, and the easiest comparison is to the latest. It has almost the exact same gameplay style, uses very similar graphics and view, and uses a simple yet very dinamic core game mechanic, which is in this case changing the size and mass of the marble on the spot. Based on the trailer, after hours of gameplay I still haven't seen half of the game.
I put together a quick pro/con list, but keep in mind that the game is still in Early Access, so all of the bellow can change in the future.
+ PROS:
Very challenging (might not be a good thing, but works for me)
Easy to pick up and play
Constant updates
Bugs are few and minor, mostly with the UI
Dev seems to actually be paying attention to what people say
Fast paced but gives you time to catch your breath
Hard challenges are always after a checkpoint, so you won't lose much progress
Smooth controls
- CONS:
Very challenging (not everyone likes tougher challanges)
Single player
Early Access
No background, basic textures, simple graphic design
Still has an alpha bug
After a couple levels, challange difficulty becomes hectic
No soundtrack or sound effects yet
No linux compatibility
A word on the puzzles. Sometimes it is hard to find the good solution, which is part of the fun for me, and the game mixes dexterity and wit based challenges in a very good ratio. Thats being said, sometimes the solution seems trivial, other times it feels like my brain is slowly spanked with a sack of lukewarm goat cheese.
I think this review was probably about as much good than bad, but honestly, that's mostly just because I like to complain. The game is engaging, frantic, and frankly hard to put down. For $10 it's not cheap, but if you are a marble game fan you're getting a really good game. I've not even given half the levels a go yet, so I'm sure I will get my money's worth and some. With the promised features and additional levels and content likely to come, i likely to come, it's easy to recommend this game for it's hectic, challenging, and borderline mind-melting fun.

1. Don't believe the people who say this is some politically correct leftist propaganda - no it isn't, so bad reviews saying that it is are trying to misinform you.
2. However, it's simply not a good game. Or a PC game. Or much of an actual game.
TNO had some clear problems and everyone knew it was a port of a console shooter to the PC. However, after tweaking some settings (ffs, the head bob!), it was playable and actually fun. Yes, it was stupidly linear, but you had nazis to shoot most of the time, and even an occasional boss. TOB had a story a bit too stupid for me, but had a cool final boss and had cool low price, so it's all fine.
This thing, though? 90% cutscenes to 10% shooting. ONE good shooting mission which turns out to be a dream sequence (probably was put there post-factum to split how long the cutscene is in actual story line). ZERO bosses. Even the lone shooting mission wasn't as crazy as it could have been (again - console game, no more than 4 enemies on the map at one time, so you kill some and then more of them teleport in), but I died like 10 times and shot thousands of bullets, so that was good fun :) The only fun in this game :(
Perhaps another console artifact was the sound mix and idiotic stereo separation. Unplayable in headphones, a person 15" off the center of your screen can be heard only in one speaker, I was going mad! (Clearly they think the only way to play the game is to have it on TV and listen through the built-in speakers, so this is a work-around for those players?)
And the cutscenes themselves? The story looks like it was written by three 9-year-olds, each one trying to write something else with no actual writing skill. In the end nothing led to anything, or even made sense. There were like 10 new characters on the ship between each mission, but they had nothing to say except call me stupid names. Main characters were a mash-up of cliches, every dialogue was as obvious as it could be with no subtlety or deeper emotion, really like a story I would write in school for homework.
(Actually there was one decent dialogue with well suited music, of course badly mixed but it was cool anyways! Still, you don't buy a €60 game for 1 minute scene, there's Twitch/YouTube for that.)
You start the final mission by talking to a guy about his robotic arm. Really. I didn't want to end the game yet, I had no idea this will be the end. Really caught me by surprise. I was expecting to do this one thing and unlock more of the map.
Oh yes, because even right before starting the final mission, I had no way to actually max out my character. I've decoded 12+ nazi captains and knew where the missing contraption was, but could not enter that mission from the map.
Everything that was left for post-end-game was just going backwards on the same maps you've already seen before, which would have been fine if I could do those side-missions before the end... but I couldn't, except the 3-4 missions I did, everything else actually unlocks after the end.
If you're a completionist and plan to spend more time on replaying the same maps and looking for stuff, then maybe this game will provide you with enough content, especially if you skip all cutscenes, finish the main story in ~4 hours and then play your type of game.
Me, I was in for a single player experience - do everything there is to do until the final credits. but there was nothing to do, no story to tell, no characters to care about, nothing.
Really bad game, esp. in contrast to the awesome Doom of yesteryear. Buy that if you want a good shooter. If you want an interactive movie, still don't buy Wolfenstein II, aim for something with a coherent story instead.

Thanks to various bug fixes, I can now change my solid "no" vote to a very cautious "yes" vote. Tug is an ambitious project that manages to bring enough to the table that's different to not be immediately written off as "just another minecraft style game".
The graphics are smooth and appealing, what little sound there is in the game thus far is very effective, and the crafting system is unique and sufficient once you get the hang of it. Emphasis on "once you get the hang of it", as that's one of the biggest reasons I'm saying this is a good game instead of an outstandingly great one.
The way that TUG is currently set up, when you start out the game they drop you in your world, pants or not, with no instructions what so ever. If you aren't a hardened vet in the genre, you'd better pull up a guide online and make notes, because TUG tells you absolutely nothing in-game. You might figure out how to survive and make some basic tools and so forth on your own with enough trial and error, but some players will give up long before they reach the point where TUG starts to shine because of the complex and unexplained nature of the game's mechanics. That's not the only issue TUG has, but it's still early access so some bugs and issues are bound to happen. It can be difficult to get things like beds to sit flat on your floor instead of lodged halfway through your character, sometimes items will vanish when you leave the room (such as beds) or will cease to be when you merely meant to drop them, for example. If you know what you're doing, these issues are rarely a game breaking experience, but it can detract from your ability to stay immersed and having fun.
The act of mining in TUG is similar in nature to how it is in Minecraft, but like a lot of things, it feels more organic. I never thought I'd be looking back at the tunnel I'd just dug and thinking "Damn that's a pretty tunnel", but digging ends up being one of the most enjoyable parts of the game because of how fluid and unstilted the process becomes. Overall, TUG accomplishes what it sets out to do. It's enjoyable, not too difficult, and pretty to look at. If you've played Minecraft and are looking for something that's a little less precise and a little more organic in both look and feel, watch some videos of TUG and then give it a try. You could do a lot worse with your money on here these days.

I don't get why people are so critical about this. There is not a lot of action games which are not packed full of shooting and guns and/or medieval times. This made me aprieciate Remember me more.
It has an outstanding story, we are guided by a guy who suddenly started talking to us, we have never seen him but everyone seems to know him. Nothing revolutionary, but when we add character development than it gets interesting and of course there are some great story twists. I also loved when Nilin will run through a scary place, she will look behind her back and when it was raining she would get wet. Simple things but made me happy.
Everything is set in the Neo Paris, it's a great place, pretty far in the future but we don't see flying cars and everything, apart from memory hacking, is believable. But, there comes the bigest disappointment for me, level design. I wanted it to be more like Mirror's  Edge, when you still have a little choice of the route and you have markers where to jump, but it doesn't feel so  constricted. Parkour could be a bit more challanging (I died once when climbing and it was because I walked through the wall). I was also not the biggest fan of places where I got attacked. Every time I walked into the arena-type place I knew something will jump on me.
When it comes to battle system - I loved it. Many games introduce everything in the beginning and there is always one powerful attack that is enough to know to kill everyone. In some games I don't even need to know how to dodge  if I press LMB quickly. Remember me  made me learn and appreciate combos, but if you use just the simplest one -3xLMB then I hear you, game could be boring. Part of the fun for me was trying to get the biggest combo and it was harder then in most games when speed is the most important and I used special abilities which I don't usually do. I've seen people comparing this battle system to Batman's but I don't agree. In Batman I didn't have to  use dodge or combinations just hit fast enough and it got boring quickly.
When it comes to boss fights, I like that they were topic-related. I don't think they were boring, but after a while followed a pattern.
I would recommend this game to everyone bored of shooting and sword fighting, but not if you're looking for the next Mirror's Edge.

(Review is completely subjective and based on my own experiences, not others.)
(I may spoil gameplay mechanics, but I won't spoil the story/key facts)
TL:DR
Storyline/Entertainment/Gameplay 9/10
Combat 6.5/10
Environment 10/10
Controls 8/10
Replayability 1.5/10
Overall: 8 - 7.5 /10 - Would recommend to those who are more casual gamers, not intense action shooters.
Details:
I saw this game while browsing the steam store page. Trailers seemed awesome so, *click, buy*. When you enter the game you are immediatly immersed with backstory and introduced to the main character, Nilin. While i won't spoil any of the storyline, I'll overview the general way in which things were layed out. The story is all about discovering Nilin's past while rebelling against the forces controlling Neo-Paris. Where she is, why she is here, what happened to get her in this situation?
Storyline/Entertainment/Gameplay:
This game, to me atleast, is much more a story with interact-able content than a point-and-click adventure. Im not saying that the game was intense on cut-scenes (it wasn't, but ill address this later), but more that each episode of the game is linear (not open world) and would lock doors behind you, preventing exploration backwards in the level. There was never a moment where I was bored during this playthrough, enjoying every little event which happened. Every turn was new and new gameplay mechanics were added continually as you progressed. Although when some mechanics are added, there is no tutorial. So you have to work it out on the fly. The story is spread out along 7 or so episodes, each progressing on the previous to tell the story of the rapidly-evolving state of Neo-Paris and Nilin.
Combat:
To be blunt, I felt the combat was clunky, but innovative. You're rewarded for doing combos by getting a rockin' soundtrack playing in the background. This however is taken away when you take just one hit. Combos are built off of 'nodes' and vary in effect. The first punch/kick is standard and then after that, the combo combinations can either be healing, damage, recharge (of special attacks), or link/extend (boosts effects of previous node). The farther in each combo a node is placed, the stronger effect it is. These nodes can be changed at anytime in or out of combat, allowing for a strong damage combo to instantly be changed out for one that heals if you are low on health, or recharge if you need a special attack and quick! Fighting sequences were well spread and bosses were unique, but each was defeated in similar mannor. Attack when boss is idle, dodge when attacking, and do a quicktime event-like sequence for the final blow. Combat, i feel, could have been removed or re-vamped, but the change in pace from story to combat is pleasant and added to the storyline of the game.
Environment:
All the scenery and graphics were absolutely stunning. I took a few screenshots at key points which really show the beauty of this game. Because of this, it was a bit laggy at times, but i attribute that more to my computer being on the low-end, spec wise, not the game. Each map/area had little areas which could be explored, pick-ups which increase stats, and pacs which give even more backstory to this immersive game.
Controls:
Not much to say for controls. At times, I couldn't hit keys at the right time, but its much more a personal thing then key-mapping. I didn't encounter too many issues otherwise, nothing which was immersion-breaking.
Replayability:
Since this game is linear and follows the same storyline each time (to the best of my knowledge), there is no point to re-play the game unless a period of time has past and you want to re-live the story, or to 100% the game by finding all the little story pacs and power-ups.

This game revolves around its story. It contains a couple "OH♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; moments, and everything you knew about the characters is proven wrong. I literally left the computer in the middle of a level to take a break once, because the plot twist was so unexpected. The characters are believeable, each of them with their secrets.
It's not that complicated unless you play on hard. The enemies are relatively diverse. After a while, it feels lackluster, but it's not the main focus of the game. The customizability of combos tries to make up for that, and it succeds to a degree.
The graphics are good enough, for a 1.5 year old game. Neo-Paris' appearance is appropriate: a city where wealth is highly valued. The way signs and information are displayed via your Sensen is pretty nice too.
This category is represented nicely in Remember Me. Most notably through memory remixes: these allow you to alter other people's memory in order to have them act in specific ways. Unfortunately, there's not that many of them. However, they have a big impact on the story. Then there's remembranes: a nice way to convey information to the player while fitting in the story. The platforming you have to do is similar to combat: not good, not bad, and boring after a while. There are QTEs in this game, but not enough to have much of an impact, be it negative or positive.
I found that a controller is more appropriate for the game. The menus seem to built for controllers as well. They are a bit clumsy at times, but you shouldn't be spending much time in the menu anyway.
You can obtain relatively valueable trading cards. There are many unlockable stories you can read, as well as concept art and 3D models.
Personal Rating: 9.25/10
Objective Rating: 7.75/10

Fighting games are an enigma to review.
Unlike RPGs/Strategy where character/statistical sheets explain how the numbers affects the gameplay, fighting games often are worded for hardcore fans or the information is conveyed through visuals alone. Spectacle fighters are also different because fighting games involve many more characters with contrasting playstyles to emphasize the importance of mastering a character. The result, which is the genre's greatest appeal/detractor, is feeling like when you have spent hours understanding one character you find you barely understand the game when you play someone else.
The TL;DR version is that there are barriers with fighting games from a technical/knowledgeable view as well as the dexterity required to "get gud." Each game has its own quirks, control schemes, tempos for button mashing, etc. that it can be overwhelming to know where to start.

Skullgirls is perhaps the greatest entry for any skill-level as it can accommodate newbs and pros to understand the basics for any other fighting game. If you require in-depth explanations, then you can get the most from the tutorial; if you want to learn as you go, then the gameplay remains accessible to master the game one character at a time.
Skullgirls' training room is often praised by everyone, but it's often not praised enough for how important it is—as well as its many pitfalls. Even as great as the tutorial is for newcomers it falls into the same pitfalls as other games such as forgetting to explain everything.
Many fighting games rely on practice stages with basic AI (or none) to perform button-mashing combos or specific mechanics like blocking. It's acceptable for fans who know what to expect, but it's alienating for those who don't know what to do.
Skullgirls goes many steps beyond the minimum tutorial; it offers a general basics/knowledge chapter noting the differences between high, medium and low attacks, grappling, tag-team attacks, etc. In addition, there is an extensive tutorial for every character to understand their basic combos and special moves, and in the 2nd Encore there are trials that offer high-level challenges for mastering the hardest of combos.
The first category is perhaps the greatest tool for fighting game fans because it can teach you specific skills such as canceling into air-dashes, combining blockbusters with team attacks, mix-ups, etc. The only fault is that sometimes the tutorial UI forgets to explain its abbreviations as you learn the ropes. A simple example is, "hit with c(rouch).LK after a j(ump).HP", which happens right after you learn crouch/jump attacks after being given arrow directions.
The latter categories I often find are more difficult to complete because there is some unknown amount of time between chaining combos to perform it correctly. It would help if the tutorial showed the animation once--to know what you are performing towards--or if the game had a speed setting to work at learning the combinations. The result is some chapters of the tutorial may take an exceedingly long time because you will try something over-and-over with no feedback on your input.
These blemishes, however, do not ruin the enjoyment you may find if you prefer to learn as you play as you can pull up individual character move-sets in-game and use the standard practice mode for training. You might find that mixing in-between them may be the best option, and you can do that from the get-go without any requirements. When it comes to the challenge of the game, it's focused on the refined gameplay rather than a lack of knowledge for difficulty.
As for the game's difficulty, Skullgirls offers a wide range of difficulty options for bots as well as tweaks between the final boss, Marie, for players interested in the Story Mode or Arcade Mode (9 fights and the boss).
There are five difficulty options that affects all the single-player content. When it comes to the final boss the difficulty is lowered by two levels for Story Mode as it was a major complaint about how unfair a fight she is. (Note: Arcade is unaffected by this change.) As a result, if you enjoy to play characters by playing their story-mode the game is now much more feasible even if you are horrid with someone.
Speaking of the Story Mode, the story arcs focus on an artifact that grants one woman's wish every seven years that comes at the price that it may be twisted if it's impure, and thus becoming a Skullgirl. Each character has his/her own reason for seeking the Skull Heart, and as a result some characters may have more story significance than others. Some are outright jokes, and it works because each story offers an opportunity to flesh out a character's personality, which helps if you buy the 2nd Encore DLC to have full voice-acting for every character but it's not required because the writing is effective. The mode serves its purpose of interesting players with its characters more so than immersing the player in its lore.
Other modes are the Arcade Mode, the Versus mode and the Survival & Challenges offered in the 2nd Encore. In these modes, you can choose to fight as a single-character or make a team of two or three. The game is balanced so that you can fight 1 v 3, 2 v 2, etc. without being at a disadvantage by adjusting the health bars. And when it comes to the Challenge mode, it usually revolves around a specific handicap or a unique challenge for a player—or simply catharcism by playing as Marie in two challenges and racking up over a 150+ combo.
When it comes to the roster for the game, I am torn for various reasons. On the one hand, 15 characters (including the DLC) would be a sizable number if two of them weren't clones of the original roster. (Robo-Fortune is a different character in her move-sets, but some of the other possible characters look more interesting.) However, even if you lack the DLC, you can still fight those characters as the DLC only unlocks the ability to play as them. The same goes for the color-palate DLC. It's a unique approach for adding characters to fighting games that I would like to see more often as it keeps the fights being diverse.
It's difficult to judge of how much content vs. hours you'll get out of this game, but if you casually play this game you will find enough bang for your buck—if you are a hardcore fan, you might yearn for more substance as not all the content of the game is meant for those fans.
When it comes to recommending Skullgirls, I find that the most difficult question to answer is, "Can I recommend it for all fighting game players?"
The online network is mostly full of highly skilled players who know each character down to every frame, so it offers little to no entry for casuals; however, there is a local mode option and private lobbies. Some people don't like how there is a system in place that prevents infinite combos. The single-player content, while sparse, is enjoyable if you enjoy the art-styles, characters and other small details of the game as well as being a useful entry point for every other fighting game--but you may want to buy the game with the 2nd Encore upgrade to get all the characters, voice-acting and other modes for the full experience.
Skullgirls is a great game in itself, but I think the only downside is that there is a desire for more content. (More modes, more characters, more of everything.) And aside from the other issues I mentioned beforehand, if the greatest negative quality is that people want more is that not a good enough reason to recommend the game?

Honestly I think this game deserves a better rating, if maybe not a near-perfect one.
I found Alcatraz to be very enjoyable - maybe a little short for a complex, serious adventure game. The game's aesthetic is, let's admit it, pretty damn awesome as long as you use the "50's look filter", I understand all the criticism about the flat character textures, but I can't but wonder if it's done on purpose so that granulated sepia filter looks good on them. It didn't take away much from the game as far as I'm concerned.
I think another "problem" (if we could call it so) is the clash between the cartoonish look of the characters and the pretty much completely serious tone of the rest of the game. I wouldn't be surprised if people expected an adventure game full of gags and dumb stuff, only to hit a huge brick wall of expectations. The game DOES HAVE HUMOR but more in an ironic comment, subtle sarcastic joke way. In the humor spectrum it definitely falls under "serious games", though.
I didn't think the characters seemed two-dimensional - although there are many of them and most don't get that much screen time individually, so there's not a whole lot of room for them to be uber complex and introspective. In fact I didn't feel the game was shallow at all (and I had that expectation after reading the reviews) specially when you consider how they treat various adult themes in the context of the 50s: homosexuality, drugs, interracial relations, racism, sex life and experimenting, adultery, corruption, hipocrisy, social justice in a rather backwards era... All around it's a pretty complex and creative game in terms of characterization and human relations, IMHO.
***SPOILERS AHEAD***
There are a couple different endings and besides the usual "you performed certain actions so you got the good/bad ending" sense, it will affect how the relationship between the main characters develops, which I liked and thought was deep and creative enough to make you feel like you're experiencing a game quite like no other you have ever played. It was refreshing.
TL;DR
This isn't in my top 10 games list and it isn't the most oustanding piece of gaming art ever created, but against all odds (judging by the amount of negative reviews 1954 Alcatraz has) I found this game to be much more enjoyable than I expected, fun and different even if it's true that it fell a little short in some areas and it won't become an all-time classic. I still really recommend you to give it a chance - specially if you catch it on sale - and it might just surprise you.

This game was an unexpected pleasure. The best way I found to enjoy it is to not ask too much of it, and simply let it be the casual gameplay experience it was meant to be. I bought the game because the gameplay videos showed the characters moving slowly and gracefully, and that chill pacing was with me throughout my playthrough. Here's how it breaks down:
The Good - Here is an excellent title if you are looking for some laid-back fun. The game's pacing was just fast enough to keep things interesting, but slow enough to give you the time to take in the visuals and play with the game's 2D physics. The story was present enough to give the game some direction, but was unconcerned with details and complexity just like a picture book (and with the 2D gameplay and rich backgrounds it certainly felt like a picture book sometimes). The character control was pretty tight, not perfect, but close enough that I didn't find myself frustrated trying to jump onto small ledges. All of these elements came together to make for a pleasant few hours.
The Bad - My only real complaint is that I wish there was more content (and I am downloading Trine 2 as I write this review so hopefully that will help). I finished the whole thing in about five hours. I had no technical issues. My controller worked perfectly and the game looked excellent without stutter or other problems.
The Verdict - This is not a flashy game. It is not tense or super-fast-paced. You will not feel the rush of victory or the crush of defeat, because it never feels like much is at stake. But if you play this game with the understanding that it is a casual experience, and you are okay with something a little simpler, then I think you will find this game a comfortable match.

I really loved The New Order, I have played through it twice which for me pretty much never happens(Only other games I have done that with are Spec Ops: The Line and Half-Life 2) so I was pretty hyped for this game.
Without going into spoilers I would recommend The New Colossus. I do think there are some things that might put some people off though, so here are the ones that don't involve spoilers.
- The Tone
The New Order was a pretty grim game. It did have a sense of humour but overall it was a game about a group of people who had lost hope throwing themselves into one suicide missions after the other with the expectation that they had already lost. So it never really got "Silly" at any point and kept a pretty serious tone throughout, which I liked.
The New Colossus is a much more overtly funny game though and the tone is overall a lot lighter. The game has a lot more jokes and a lot more "Silly" moments which I could understand people being down on. However I think the game does manage to find a good balance. One of the things I hate is when a story undercuts a serious moment with a joke, it can work but it is really damn hard to do. Luckily the game never really does that, the silly scenes are silly and the serious scenes are serious for the most part.
The change in tone also makes sense when you consider that we have gone from being a few people literally hiding in the sewers in the first game to being in control of the largest Submarine in the world with a lot more people at our command. I think the change to a more hopeful and somewhat lighter tone is the right move instead of trying to stay dour the whole time.
-The Story
I will say upfront that if you are the kind of special snowflake who is actually angry about the Nazi's being the villains in the game then all I can say is. I'm really sorry you are so sensitive and lacking in a sense of humour, maybe you should go back to your safe space for a breather.
For everyone else, and without spoiling things, I am kinda mixed on the story. There are a lot of great characters in the game with Super Sesh being my favourite of the new additions in this game. However I do go back and forth on if I like Grace and I mostly put that down to uneven writing. When you meet her she is likable and sympathetic but then she turns into an insensitive ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who seems completely self absorbed only to turn back later. Aside from her however most of the game has a for the most part a fun storylines with interesting and satisfying pay offs. Although in some cases it very much feels like they ran out of time and pushed it into the next game.
Which kinda comes to my main problem with the game's story. Whilst I love a lot of the moments and little things that happen the story really does feel like the middle of a larger story. It suffers from the Two Towers problem since it is clear they have plans for a third game to form a trilogy, so you have this game that doesn't have the thrill of everything being fresh but also doesn't have the thrill of being a overall conclusion. It never gets as bad as MGS5 did in that regard but I do feel like I did at the end of Halo 2, blue balled.
It doesn't help that the ending is horribly horribly rushed and unsatisfying. I honestly didn't actually realse that this was the end of the game until the credits started to roll.
On the positive side the game looks great and as I said the story has some great moments. The gun play is as fun as ever and they have also removed the really poorly explained system for upgrading weapons. Now you simply pick up upgrade kits from the worlds and then can use them on your weapons. Meaning you can get the silenced pistol a lot faster and easier.
I did feel like I used stealth a lot less this time round but I think that was just because of the kinda mood I was in. I didn't want to skulk around, I wanted to bust heads. The game also takes a pretty brave move by having your health capped at 50 for a decent chunk of the story. By which I mean you can still overheal to 200 but it will bleed down to 50. Luckily you can also armour as well.
I do think that means I felt more fragile for a lot of the story, which does make sense when you consider you start the game in a wheelchair and unluckily for BJ he used his one time "Murder Nazi Get Legs Back" card in the first game.
I have also been lucky in not getting too much in the way of technicals problems. However I did notice a fair few minor audio glitches like sounds not playing or being far too low. I am aware a lot of people have not been as lucky as me though.
So overall I think it is a pretty great game, it doesn't reach the same heights as the first but it does manage to avoid being a straight retread of the first game and the story takes some turns that I really didn't see coming although I really should have now that I think about it.

A worthy successor to The New Order, narratively complex and equal parts harrowing and absurdly funny. While some parts of the gameplay have been refined upon TNO, some fresh but minor issues have been introduced: items can now be picked up automatically, but the hit detection can be very patchy. Manual saving has been introduced but the automatic saves can be unforgiving. Stealth has been worked upon, but simultaneously seems to be downplayed compared to the previous game (massively if you consider how big a part it played in The Old Blood). The game has some ambitious themes and it's portrayal of BJ in the first half of the game is surprisingly downtrodden, but this allows an emphasis on the themes of catharsis that drive the latter half of the game. Some of the environments can become repetitive particularly when put side by side with TNO, but by no means are boring to explore and are filled with details. Visually the game is a feast with some outstanding mocap performances in the cut scenes, with some very witty dialogue and a surprisingly strong attention to detail. The weapons are satisfying but some greater variety would have been welcome, although the upgrade system allows for some good degrees of personalisation of gameplay styles to suit taste. Likewise enemies are visually well designed and formidable, but can appear to blend in together after a while, but as gibbable cannon fodder they are satisfying to chew up with dual triple barrel shotguns.
Ultimately, not quite the revelation that The New Order was upon its release but the surprises of that game would be impossible to replicate, and so rather Machinegames have instead iterated on the core themes and gameplay to enjoyable effect.
Performance: I have had no issues beyond a mandatory driver update a few days ago, and the game console causing the mouse cursor to overlay on the game when enabled, which happens fairly often due to the proximity to the escape key. The game is fluid on high detail settings on my 1060 card, with a decent i7 processor and 16gb. I see most negative reviews are complaining about performance, but if you have played Doom 2016 or even the previous Wolfenstein releases then you should know what to expect of your hardware.

While I understand that some setups are having issues with this game, I can't really say that I've experienced them, myself.  The issues I have experienced will be in the CON section below.
The game itself, however, is a masterpeice.  This is an incredible sequel to The New Order, and everything about it is amazing.  The mechanics are tight and responsive, the graphics are the toppest of top-notch, the sound and effects are on point and powerful, and the story - the story is what really seals this game as one of the best of all time.  Wolfenstein has always been about killing Nazis, but The New Colossus's focus is more on the people the war affects, how it affects them.  There's a deep human aspect to this game that you wouldn't have expected from this francise, and it makes all the Nazi killing more meaningful and satisfying.

* Fantastic, deeply human story

* Hollywood quality voice acting

Cons:
* Not 100% polished: Game has frozen once, and tabbing out makes it unstable to the point it crashes (but it's stable beyond that).  I've had artifacting in the skybox whenever I'm in an outside area, and I've found graphical glitches in the walls in a few places.  This is with an Nvidia 1080 GTX.
Would definitely, absolutely reccomend this game, especially if you're a fan of Wolfenstein.  4/5, 9/10, 90%, whatever metric you want to use.

There are no words to describe this game; it's just that good.  Beautiful visuals, soundtrack and gameplay.  There are even scenes in this game that give ya the feels.  However, whats a review without giving details on what makes this game so great.
Soundtrack - I'm a huge sucker when it comes to a great soundtrack.  You know it's good when you can't stop listening to the songs.  It's up there at #2 on my list (the others being Kingdom Hearts and Undertale).  The music blends together with the environment and specific events in the game.  Every song has the same melody in it, but feels unique in it's own way.  Although my all time fav song in the sound track is "Restoring the Light, Facing the Dark," very well put together.
Art Style and Environments - The visuals in this game are insane.  Where can I find the artists? I'd like to learn some of their techniques!  The game has beautiful foreground, background, and everything in between.  Colors for the enviornments are well crafted and inserted where they need to be.
Difficulty - I'm not much of a platformer myself, but the difficulty in this game is not too easy, not too hard, but just right.  However, the game is no cake walk, it has it's difficult moments.  Certainly not for casual gamers looking for easy games.  Any gamer that can handle super challenging Mario Maker levels can complete this game with no trouble.
Narration - This game is one of the few that rely heavily on it's visual narration.  It's executed perfectly!  You can tell from the characters actions how they think and what their personalities are like.  During the course of the game, there is text narration told from the spirit tree, who's kind of like the overseer of the world.  Overall, very well executed visual narration.
Immersion - This game will have you immersed in it for quite a while.  I almost completed my first playthrough in one night.  This is also the type of game you wouldn't mind playing over again from time to time.  Even though you've seen the emotional scenes a few times already, they still get to you.  Immersion, 10/10 in this game.
Gameplay - Last but not least, gameplay.  A very crucial thing to get right in every game.  However, this game manages to combine RPG like elements into a platformer seamlessly.  Plus the abilities you unlock as you travel through the game give you access to new areas.  They also give you new ways to kill enemies and use their projectiles to your advantage.  In short, this game knows how to execute gameplay.  Nothing in this game is mundane or a chore of a task.
These six elements of this game blend together perfectly.  It can give you a sense of tranquility, but can suddenly turn into utter panic at times.  The final score of this game is a 10/10, a must have and an eventual classic.  The only thing that I can say about this game is... Ori is just adorable.  I can't wait to see what other games Moon Studios will make.  They have made a great first impression for their companie's name.  You got my support for any future games Moon Studios!

DONTNOD got themselves a new fan after I played Remember Me.
Graphics/Art
I love how much work the designers have put into the environment, characters (fashion for example) and most definitely the lighting and use of contrasts in the game. The game looks visually stunning, running on 1080P on High settings. The Futuristic Neo-Paris setting is absolutely amazing and there have been times where I just had to stop playing and look at the scenery, breathtaking.
Story
The story starts off "fantastic" but slowly degrades to being unfortunately no more than "good", I would've hoped for much more. Nevertheless it is still an enjoyable story that definitely makes you think about what the future could bring to us, and how we as human beings could advance (and maybe how we shouldn't). And I think that is an important part in storytelling as well.
Gameplay
I think the gameplay is one of the mediocre parts of the game that a lot of players seem to have an issue with. The combat feels fresh and new in the beginning by giving you the choice to customise your combos. After a couple of fights it begins to feel quite repetitive and you're more focussing on finishing your combo moves by looking at the buttons at the bottom of the screen, rather than enjoying the fights and looking at the animations.
One of the really new and unique gameplay elements is the possibility to remix someone's memory, and alter how they see their history. This is done by going back to a memory and selecting certain objects which are altered in some ways. For example pushing a table slightly aside so someone might trip over it. The memory starts "remixing" after every altered scene and builds an alternate memory, a memory that becomes the truth to the subject. Too bad that this function is only available 4 times in the entire game, I would have loved to see more of this.
In the end I still think this is a very rememberable (get it?) game, but sadly get an after taste of "what could have been". I would still recommend it if you like 3rd person action/adventure games or Sci-Fi storytelling as I surely enjoyed myself with this one.

First it was Eversion that proved that cute games can be just as disturbing as any others.
Then, Spooky's Jump Scare Mansion comes along and proves that a game can be both humorous AND creepy.
It's a deceptively disturbing game - one could easily think the horror elements can be offset by the cute elements, but in the end, that's far from true. As the player progresses through the game, the cute elements just end up adding to the whole disturbing and creepy feeling the game has.
Being a fan of horror games, I'm usually able to play through games without getting too spooky - most often I just get a few jump scares, but nothing that makes me curse or anything. This game, however, had me cursing out loud during some moments.
The game itself is free, then there's the Karamari Hospital DLC which isn't, but it's cheap - and completely worth the price, actually I'd say it's worth a lot more than its price. It's a small expansion that can be completed in around 30 minutes, but it's definitely worth playing.
If you like horror games, try it out for yourself - play the game and buy the DLC if you like it. The developers deserve it for making such a good game and hopefully we can encourage them to make more in the future.

On top of that the story is pretty weak and the cutscenes are way too long. My screensaver came on during a few because they were more than 5 minutes long. Characters are bland and mostly boring.
Can't replay chapters either... what?
Why do my mouse sensitivity settings (which are WAY high at default) revert every time I launch the game?
I suppose the answer to all of this is "git gud" but I like difficult games if they are rewarding when you figure out how to move forward. This feels like I just figured out the best way to cross a river but the river is full of toxic waste. Difficult games need to COMMUNICATE very strongly with the player as to what is happening and why or else everything feels cheap and you learn nothing.

When I was a kid, I didn't want to play Rollercoaster Tycoon and instead prefered '3D games', but I couldn't afford the newest RC when it came out, so I got this instead. It's fun enough for £1 in the steam sale, surely. I can recommend to begin on a big-ish lot and work your way up. Basically, you begin with however big of a budget you need (starts at 10k, I believe), then you select your advertising preferences, ticket prices, and if you give away free tickets. You don't have to do these things, and can play without. These are limited choices, but it's easy for kids to understand. (And people like me, who just kinda wanna play a bit without actual commitment.)
If you play in sandbox mode, which is what I usually do, the game starts you in your empty lot, if you start with 10k, make it simple at first by choosing a cheap-mid range ride, ticket stand, a generator, a sitting area, bin, two food stalls - either food & drink and a ball game. Theres quite a few to choose from, I usually have one of each, starting with a regular soda stand and a burger one, then advancing onwards towards like Ice cream stand and BBQ chicken etc.
This can be your starting first day to make money. Before you begin your day, go to the menu and click maintence to make sure you have a janitor/repair man. He does everything, I usually get two in my first day. turn your speed to 1/2, close stuff, then repair all the items in your grounds before you start. This is a part of the game that is tedious and annoying, but it's fast enough and takes only a minute. Once you do that, make sure things are open (small stuff like tables and bins open automatically but rides you need to do manually) you can begin your day.
Days end around 10pm and you can start again the next day at 1/2 speed, adding more rides, food stalls, or whatever you need.
I usually start with my basics listed above, and then add onwards. Sometimes if my queue is too long for a ride on the first day, I'll buy another ride to fit in. Just watch your budget.
This is a really simple game and it's enjoyable enough for it's time.
Definately recommended for kids to get them into management games, but theres better ones out there nowadays.
For the price though, it works well on steam and its good enough.

So I bought this game because it was on sale and I'd been wanting it for quite some time. I've unlocked the first two areas and have now hit lv 11 after map completion in both areas. My thoughts so far:
The skill system is neither as balanced nor as customizable as I thought it would be, and the combat is what really put me off.
Monsters don't level with you (which was to be expected), and when entering an area for the first time, monsters are hard to beat. Once you've progressed through the map and levelled up, it gets easier. However, a big issue I have with the game is that it throws monsters at you in abundance. You really can't help but walk into up to three packs that combine into 10-20 (and sometimes even more) monsters, and even when you are overlevelled for that area, they are often deadly. If the area is crammed and you aren't able to use the "run away, attack, run away, attack"-method, you're dead. Which makes the game utterly frustrating and on top of that boring, because you keep doing the same thing over and over.
I had immense trouble completing the second area and went back to the first one just for fun. I one-shot most of the monsters, and the only trouble I was presented with was large packs forming one giant group of monsters. Managable at this point, but still hard.
What really bothers me about this is that it feels like they didn't put any thought into the combat/levelling system and just put a lot of monsters of the same level into an area. There is literally no middle ground between being able to one-shot and running for your life.
In the first area I still thought "this is only hard because I don't have the right set of skills yet", but after several hours of constantly dying despite a proper build for my Hunter, I have to say I don't enjoy the game anymore. I doubt I'll ever finish it.

You hear more of the INCREDIBLE soundtrack, which blends classical and electronic music brilliantly.

Remember Me is a game that was pushed with a large budget and a great concept. While the artists carried through and created a beautiful and immersive setting, the writers and designers failed to distinguish themselves as anything more than "meh".
The combat is boring. Skill really doesn't come into play once you've gotten the hang of the simplistic system. Instead throughout the game you are forced to spam overused combos in fights which are varied in aesthetic only. The "combo lab" which is supposed to provide an individualized feel to the system, fails to do so through lack of any meaningful choice.
The one redeeming piece of design in this game, are the memory sequences in which you rewrite a person's memory. These are entertaining and add a somewhat puzzlish (ish) aspect to the game, however they lack depth and are few and far between.  If the developers had focused more resources on making these sequences long and complex, this game might be something worth remembering.
The game is painfully linear. When I say linear, I don't mean just working your way through a level. I mean there is so little that you can actually do, for most of the game you just do what the game tells you. In the climbing sections the game tells you where to go, which doesn't even matter because unlike a game with a real climbing element, there is only ever one climbing route. Leave your thinking caps at home.
The nail in the coffin is the shameful writing. What could have been the saving grace of the game feels like it was written as a first draft in a highschool creative writing class. The world isn't coherent. The characters lack meaningful motivation. Any backstory is so brief and trivial that a sane person wonders why these characters sound like children who didn't learn to be nice in kindergarten.
The game is beautiful, but thats where it ends. To ask $30 for this game is abhorrent. If you really want it, don't set any expectations, and for the love of steam wait for a significant sale.

After beating the game, I have realized how unexciting it was. While the combat is mildly entertaining, it is fairly repetitive. The introduction of new enemies is not a fresh challenge, but rather an annoying feature, like when enemies are invincible because they are powered by other enemies you must kill first, or turn invible during combat, or hurt you every time you peform damage even when attacking with a range attack. You do climb around like Assassin's Creed, but only through set paths, which again, I found to be more annoying than anything else, mainly due to the fact that you frequently fall and find yourself in trouble. Remixing memories is a puzzle, but once again, because they took awhile to figure out sometimes, I found them more frustrating than anything else.

Sweet graphics, engaging story, what more could you want? How about parkour with great handling. This game has it. The fighting combo system requires gaining proficiency to meet some of the optional achievements, but the story can be completed without mastery.

This is one of the most beautiful games I've ever played. The art direction is fantastic! the music is amazing! And the plot tugs at the heart strings.
The game play is quite great too. It's a platformer in the style of Metroid or Castlevania, where the world map is sprawling and you'll gain new abilities over time that let you explore more of the world.
Controls are responsive and fluid. Each ability you unlock adds fun traversal mechanics, with some that you've most likely not seen in other platformers.
It starts off at a suitable difficulty and ramps up a lot as you progress. By the end, this game has challenging platforming. What keeps it from being frustating is smart check points mixed the manual save point system. You can pick (in most cases) where to save and make checkpoints, so when you are in a challenging spot, you can make a checkpoin right before each new challenge.

This game is art in the classical sense as well as in a gameplay sense. As you can tell from the store page, the graphics are beautiful, and some of the views in-game are breathtaking. The gameplay itself is much like the graphics, fluid and artful when done correctly. Some parts will require simple endurance to get through, but these parts are fairly far between and when completed invoke a true sense of accomplishment. The game itself is a bit short (a few of my hours I spent afk) so pick this masterpiece up on sale. You almost certainly won't regret it.

I shall be one of the lame people who does an actual serious review for this game because.. Why not?
I'll start off by issuing a warning that if you have epilepsy, take all games seriously or you just can't handle pixelated nudity then steer very clear of this, it's not for you.
Developed and published by Marbenx, let's take a look at Shower with your Dad Simulator 2015.
: As difficult as it is to write about; Shower With Your Dad Simulator 2015 is a series of actually challenging mini-games(e.g Endurodad, Dadathon, Dad Divisions, Soapia etc.), topped with pixely nudity, all kinds of dads and a rather addicting streak to it.
: Extremely simplistic, but done in a decent way. The only thing that I dislike is that if you hit escape, the game will close on you.
: Each mini-game has it's own soundtrack that is looped in a pretty non-annoying way even after a decent amount of play time, and it's actually good!
: I found myself getting frustrated time and again over the curve-balls it will sometimes throw you. Something as tiny as a puddle on the floor will have you slide into the wrong dad and make you start over, or lose your streak(depending on which mode you're in). It's a nice challenge that by no means takes itself seriously and I think that's what I enjoy most about it.
It keeps you trying that one more time to beat your previous score, that is the sign of a well put together game for entertainment.
In all, I recommend it if you like simplistic yet fairly difficult games to keep you on your toes. Also if you like Showering with Dad simulators, nudity, showers and pixely goodness.

Fallout 3 is one of my personal favorites. The story is well played and really shows a great example of the Vault-Life. The game was amazing, fun, and emotional at times were the Player-Character bond was just too great. I love this game and would encourage anyone to play this game if they are into RPGs like this one. However, there are some advantages and disadvantages that I would like to mention.
Pros
-Story makes sense, puts you into the shoes of an actual vault resident
-Takes aspects from Fallout 1 & 2 that made them great
-Conversations with NPCs are smooth and have great voice acting
-Real-world situations that could happen in an actual nuclear apocolypse are included
-Many hours of fun and the DLCs just adds to the fun

Cons
-Gunplay is HORRIBLE, might as well resort to just using VATS beacause "aiming down sights" is just putting binoculars on
-If you choose to set off the nuke in Megaton, Moira Brown has no clue that she is a ghoul and probably suffers from amnesia
-It was so easy to get killed just going to the metro to find your dad, a raiders camp of Super Mutants just ambushes you

-Combat is so repeatative, the most interesting battle I was in was with a Super Mutant Behemoth at Galaxy News
-Quests are limited, I couldn't believe it but there are 59 quests without DLCs and 94 with the DLCs included
Overall I think the game is great and would still recommend this to anyone regardless of the cons the game is faced with. I still love the game and bypass any cons that are stated in the list above. Hope you play this game and have FUN.

Let me preface this by saying I know my way around the Metroid games. Metroid is my most favourite series of all time, so I went into this with a very good understanding of what makes a Metroid-styled game fun. For all that is good about this game, and there is a lot of good don't get me wrong, it has three fundamental issues with its overarching design which prevent me from enjoying it. These issues may not be a hindrance for some players, but they were for me, so this review is more a warning as to what to expect from the gameplay if you decide to try this game.
PROS: Very good pixel-art graphics, very atmospheric music, punchy special effects, solid controls. If not for the cons, I would really enjoy this game.
CONS: Player-hostile and strictly linear exploration where you can never go far off the path the game wants you to take, you do a TON of backtracking, find extremely little in the way of bonus items, and any time you find a way to get somewhere tricky the game halts your efforts or simply gives you nothing. Enemies drop nothing and provide zero reason to ever fight them short of when you can't avoid them. Bosses not only range wildly in difficulty, some being really easy others being insanely difficult, but you don't get your energy restored following, meaning you can end up dying after a successful fight just trying to get back to a save point or energy restore point!
