Patch 1.37 review!
This game recieved a lot of criticism for broken promises, lackluster gameplay and 60$ entry fee. Without going into the controversy, a lot has changed since release and I wanted to judge the game on it's own merits as well as comparing it to other similar titles like Elite Dangerous, which I played extensively.
Where Elite Dangerous focuses on tight controls, realism and imerssion, No man's sky feels very arcady (not that this is necessarily a bad thing). In NMS you can't fly into the sun like you can in ED, the planets don't seem to orbit around the sun at different speeds like they do in ED (instead the sun seems to rotate around the planets), the space is not realisticly dark and looks like a rainbow, the ship lacks certain control features from ED (like flying up/down, flying sideways), dogfighting is not as tight as it is in ED, inventory managment is still a problem due to consoly UI, you still are buying ships by running around the space station instead of doing it through a UI like in ED, the game still makes a lot of choices for the player like limiting who you can and cannot attack, and many things storywise still don't make any sense (like why am I gaining reputation for raiding alien outposts, why do some aliens speak my language while others don't, etc.), and lastly there are still quite a few bugs around (nothing gamebreaking, but it needs to be mentioned) - bugs like dialogue sometimes skipping over automatically before you had the chance to read it, graphical seams in the terrain, alien voices sometimes not working during dialogues, shadow glitches from trees and fauna while flying, etc.
Considering all these issues, I can certainly understand people who might still have complaints, HOWEVER to judge a game only on the things it does poorely, while ignoring the good parts is not what makes a good and imformed review imo. I mean, I could just as easily bash ED for not having base building, survival elements, story mode, proper planetary exploration, ability to walk around space stations, proper mod support, it's own share of bugs, or any number of things that NMS does much much better. For example, while in ED you will be doing the same 5-6 things (mining, trading, fetch quests, exploration and combat) over and over again, in NMS there is at least a lot more to do. In ED exploration boils down to traveling far, scanning a system and then selling that information. In NMS this is much more personal since you actually have to land and explore the planet on foot, coming close and personal with planet's flora and fauna as well as overcoming it's geography and hazards. In NMS there are real NPC interactions - sometimes with actual choices, there are puzzles to solve, shrines to visit where you can learn more about alien languages and cultures, there is ground combat, terrain modification tools, multiple storyline paths, freighters, base building both on planets and freighters, farming, and much much more - to the point that now I think ED actually has a real competitor.
Yes, these two games are fundementally different in what they focus on and ED does do a much better job in simulating the basic gameplay loop, but at least to me the number of features in NMS more than make up for arcady quality in it's execution. And with mod support you can fix many of the above mentioned annoyances. It's not perfect and it may not be for everyone, but I can recommend it.
Note: I don't care about multiplayer, so I didn't mention it - but it seems that even that is slowly getting into the game.

That being said its been specified by the developer that this is only the first step towards cooperative gameplay so id say this is a bit like using an alpha/beta feature in a game that will likely get updated in the next. To the games credit they explain the orbs (which I guess are placeholders) as some mysterious glitch which kind of makes sense within the story arc
As far as my review - This game at release was one of the most overhyped games of the last few years and so theres a lot of hate going around for it in the older reviews and a lot of commenters who are still very angry about being lied to in those marketing campains. But in August 2017 If you like Sci-fi and space games with a cool community and loads of content and you see this in a sale its totally a great game now and looks like it will keep improving.

Spoiler-free review.
tl;dr  I recommend this game hands down in its current state (v 1.3), as it stands, it is a fun and unique experience, sure to add ~100+ to my play time.
Originally, this game was a big disappointment, lacking a bunch of features we were expecting. Gradually, with the previous two updates, life was breathed into the game. It was a total breath of fresh air when the Foundation update was released, we knew the game was being worked on, and that the developers were listening.
Now, with the Atlas Rises update, the game has gotten its footing (it no longer feels like early access), and it really shows that this game is a labor of love. I feel like the game is coming in to what we were expecting at launch, and that there will be several more updates to really bring this game up to, and beyond, what we were expecting from the beginning.
I decided to start a new game with the most recent update to get the full experience of the update. I really love the lore of this game; the direction it is going is building up to something great. The initial lack of features is being tied into the lore, and I really appreciate the attention to detail the game now has. Where features once felt lacking, or missing, or clunky, or awkward, they now feel polished, more full, and really help to engage me in the galaxy (it doesn't feel like the grind it previously was, I will note that I have about 10 hours in to the new update). It feels like there is purpose, I want to follow the story and explore. Where I once never felt like getting the center was a priority, I now feel like I need to travel on the Atlas path and get to the center.
If you're on the fence about getting the game, and you like open, resource-gathering, survival (or creative, chill, permadeath) games, pick it up, you won't be disappointed (take it from someone was massivly disappointed at launch) as that is not even a thought that I associate while playing this game any more, tbh, that feeling was dwindling and nearly gone after the Pathfinder update.
8/10 - I feel like this game can easily achieve a 10/10 in the next update or two. This developer truly cares about their game and its community. It shows in how far this game has come with its updates, its community engagement with the ARG, community suggested fixes/improvements being implemented, and a not-so-affordable free giveaway of 10,000 physical Atlas v4 Passes being produced and mailed around the globe. They are doing a great job on marketing their game, a game with substance, a game that has fully captured my attention. I was at a point in my life where video games were starting to feel uninteresting, and I could never find something I wanted to play. NMS has totally brought me back, and I thank them for that.
I won't be saying goodbye to Hello Games any time soon!

Remember Me is an underappreciated story-driven game with stunning visuals but repetitive combat.
In the futuristic setting of Neo-Paris, memories are digitized commodities. You are Nilin, a memory hunter with the rare ability to enter and alter people's memories - a threat. You start the game after having been imprisoned where you've had nearly all your memories wiped, and it's from here you must escape and uncover the full story of who you were.
Visually the game is so covered in detail I found it hard not to take screenshots of every little thing. Environments are meticulously crafted to a point of complexity rarely seen in other titles. You'll find there is a real sense of scale and grandness to the world, and with the nuanced detail given to its citizens and conversations you overhear it begins to feel alive. You can tell a lot of work went into the concept and design of each area.
As you plunge through levels of society including the homes of the rich elite and slums where memory junkies have become mutated forms of themselves, it only gets darker as you uncover the full truth. Each chapter ends with a cutscene where Nilin ruminates on the dystopian society she is newly discovering and tries to see her place in it. While being a bit overly melodramatic in these, Nilin's character is written in such a way as to be insightful and emotive. It was a controversial choice by Dontnod to have a female lead character but they were adamant - and I think her genuine nature is one to be praised.
Unfortunately there are some drawbacks to the gameplay. Where you may wish the game was more open world to explore, it's not. Instead of having any semblance of freedom you're led along a linear path with not-so-dynamic parkour and climbing where your only choice is to jump from convenient ledge to convenient ledge to reach the next objective, usually an uninspired mob fight. Combat also quickly becomes repetitive, relying on pressing a sequence of buttons to do moves and receive chain bonuses. There's not much to it, though special abilities try to keep things interesting.
Alternately, its most creative and compelling implementation is "memory remixing" where you can use your ability to enter people's memories and manipulate events within them. Here you can rewind in a scene to make a subtle change, often only slightly moving a minor object, and watch how new events unfold. Each time is meaningful and fascinating, and in my opinion it wasn't used nearly enough. It emphasizes the idea that altering a single event, or the memory of it, can change a whole life's trajectory.
Altogether, Remember Me is a game to admire for its visuals, storytelling and dystopian setting, and for a small studio it's absolutely impressive. Don't miss checking out the excellent soundtrack too. You'll have to deal with lacklustre combat and linear progression, but ultimately it's the elaborate presentation of the world and its background that make it worthwhile.

Fallout 3, a classic game indeed. This was my first fallout game I ever remember playing in 2008-9. For Bethesda's take on the next Fallout in the franchise, it was very well done. You grow up in a vault, see how cruel Vault-tec truly is, and venture out into the cold, harsh, remains of Capital D.C. in search of your dad. During that time, you chose how you want to develop your lone wanderer. I love the fact that no matter the ending, you have the choice to be a inconsiderate, megalomaniacal, malicious ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. You can be just a regular ole wastelander with no sides at all, or a god-send angel sent from Heaven to save the Capital Wasteland. Fallout 3 made me think a lot about the choices I made, something no other game could do. When I played Skyrim, or Oblivion, I was a mean little elf that ended up leading the Dark Brotherhood and the Thieves Guild. But with Fallout, my perspective changed. I couldn't enslave people, couldn't do evil quests, I even felt bad about robbing someone blind. It gave me something to think about, I actually thought about my choices. V.A.T.S in FAllout 3 was a cool implement, I loved shooting weapons out of raider's hands and watching as they franctically search for a weapon to defend themselves. I loved fighting off behemoths, venturing into the wasteland with Dogmeat, and killing off enclave soldiers with my 10 mm pistol. The DLCS were terrific, I'd love to say as much as I could about them but there's so much to say. Although this game is almost practically ten years old, I wish there was a way to side with the Enclave. In a sense, you can somewhat side with them, but not fully. It would be cool to see how the Enclave would of affected the Capital Wasteland. And lastly, the Good Karma ending is the saddest ending of them all. (spoilers; especially during that 2 second cutscene of Dad and the lone wanderer, i cried so hard) But nonetheless, Fallout 3 was a classic game and I'd love to say much more but there's just so much to say. I love this game with all my heart. 10/10.

Alcatraz is a traditional take on the point & click adventure. It's main mechanic is the acquisition of items and information, found by clicking around on the scenery of each screen, and their combination with either other itens or charcters in order to forward the narrative.
The puzzles to be solved are all presented in a logical light with little incongruity present. At times, the game requires you to fulfill arbitrary, inexplicable requisites before allowing you to take a piece required for the solution of a puzzle, but these are few and far between. For the most part, this is a frustration-free game of logical thought.
The complexity if increased somewhat by the ability to switch between two main characters, who don't meet for most of the game, but nevertheless manage to influence each other's environment trough their actions. Or they should, anyway. This mechanic is seldom used in an interesting manner and for the most part, we are simply playing two parallel, individual puzzle adventures.
We are left with narrative, then: the story of a convict in one of the world's most infamous prisons, and his beat-poet wife, pressed by the mob for cash.
The 1954 setting is by far the most attractive aspect of the game, a cultural and historical period that is all too rare in video games. It is interesting to explore and mostly carries the rest of the game. There are some interesting, well-written characters, - particular highlights are the germ-phobic mob weasel and the loose-canon mad novelist - but the setting is the true star.
In the end, small decisions made throughout the game are revealed to have influence on the ending - or more specifically, on the options available to the characters at the end - but it is hard to care either way.
This game is worth your time if the setting and story setup pike your interest. Otherwise, it is merely a competent point & click adventure.

I'm sorry but this is a rather dull and meatless adventure game.
I'm a seasoned point 'n' click fan and have played a LOT of them ever since I started gaming in the mid 80's. I actually like them so much that even what the general public considers sub par, I seem to enjoy. Also, Daedalic has been in the forefront of the genre for quite a few of the later years and I respect them immensely. It sadly all falls short when it comes to this title.
The premise of the game, it's characters, setting and atmosphere all has potential, but the developer just lets you scratch the surface and never let you get involved and interested. Clearly wanting to provoke some thoughts in us players with including gay marriage, interracial relationships, racism and fatal choices. Even throwing in some adult language and beat slang to top it off. Sadly though, without the ability to get to know the characters and their background better and relatively chopped up writing it never gets interesting and sometimes just feels out of place and added for the wrong reasons. It all feels a bit uninspired and messy. It feels hard to get into the story and even harder to care about the characters. I personally felt so uninspired playing this game I almost didn't want to finish it.
Voice overs are ok I guess, but mostly for the main characters, but here too it seems uninspired. Some other characters are just bad. I usually don't let bad voice acting ruin my experience though, so these are not game breaking.
It's not just the story and characters that seems sloppy. The game mechanics, animations and even some modelling also fails to impress. There's a lot of black-outs through scenes making the whole experience chopped and slow. It also seems you only get to see part of the animations before going black-screen. I just got sick and tired of all those black-screens all the time. There's not a lot going on from scene to scene so I would imagine it didn't need that much loading, but alas. The left-click/right-click mechanics are ok but most of the time it is just totally pointless and I feel in most cases they could have left out the one. Also things can be hidden out of view, even the transition-arrow to go to another screen. Many times because of the pop-out inventory/menu on the left side of the screen. You transfer between the two main characters quite easily using the inventory menu. Shame that the game several times leaves you clueless to when you should change. I've seen this done much better in other games. A simple forced switch would be better in a game like this. The background artists seems to have done a good job at least.
It's not all bad, and for true adventure fans it might be worth a playthrough. I would not recommend buying this game at full price though. Look for a big discount and be prepared for something that feels uninspiring. It should take about 5-7 hours to complete, so it is quite short.

For the seasoned adventure game players, this game is superb - top notch voice acting, challenging puzzles (without being the usual slide puzzle-type puzzles), and involved storytelling. The only issue is that it may have been a tad too short, but maybe that is also just because the characters are enjoyable enough to see what happens next. The mood, the music, the feel of this period was conveyed perfectly and I demand a sequel :) PS Those that complain the game is too hard need to realise that for too many years now these games have been littered with in-game hint systems that ruin the challenge of completing a task on your own. For those people there are 100's of basic hidden object games out there to keep you occupied. Alcatraz is designed for the people who wanna work for their prize :)

The year is 1954, you will be playing the part of two people madly in love with one another. One trapped behind the bars of Alcatraz, the other trapped by the pressure of her lover's corrupt partner, the mob, and even the police. Together you will have to find a way to spring each other from the shackles they hold them down. You will be playing the part of Joe, the convicted bank robber, though no one ever found the money. You will also get to play the part of Christine, a woman who isn't afraid of a little danger, but truly misses Joe.
Graphically this game looks good. Sure there's not a lot to each scene, but what you do have in each scene allows you to take that journey back to 1954. The game is divided into specific areas that you'll have to navigate through and try to find items that could help you down the road. There is quite a bit of loading between the areas and the area map, and there are times were you are going to be doing some serious back and forth action, but the loading isn't too bad where you no longer want to quit. At least if you are able to keep the story going, if you get stuck this because a battle of will.
The music, though simple, is really only one song that is constantly playing in some shape or form. I have to say though that it has this dark and slightly seductive feel to it that just seems to blend into the game. I also like the voice acting in this game, some of them fit a stereotype of people back in the 50s, but at least they are point when they try for that mood.
The controls basically are the mouse that you will use to click on areas, items, people, and more. You will also get to use the Space bar so that you can see all the locations that you can click on (this will save you a couple of times if what you are looking for isn't abundantly obvious
So I have to say that it took a bit of time for me to start really getting the hang of the game. I got to a certain point and then I couldn't find out what to do. At any time you can switch between Joe and Christine, which definitely allows you to see different aspects of the same story, and once things start really rolling in the game you will find that you are going to be jumping back and forth as quickly as possible so that you can solve the next obstacle in the game. For the most part the game helped nudge you along when things got a bit difficult, but apparently I ended up in no man's land, and had a hell of a time crawling out of it. Though once I figured it out, the game took off, and I was completely hooked. There was one small little glitch in the game where Christine magically knew about something that she was supposed to look for before she had the required item to know what she was looking for, but other than that I can't really complain about the game.
The whole cast of characters that you get to interact with are memorable, and have their own life to them. Not one character was a like, they felt alive, and just trying to live their life there way. To me that was quite refreshing that there was definitely some back story and depth to all the characters you were going to have to be dealing with throughout the game.
So if you are looking for a point and click adventure game that will take you to a time from the past, but not too far back, and has a story of lovers scorned, betrayals, and of course cops and robbers, this is the game for you. This isn't a perfect game, but it definitely has enough polish on it that it is not only worth a look, but its worth an entire playthrough. So with that I have to give this game an 8.9 out of 10.

Hoo.
Okay, take a moment to understand that some video games are not something you play because you want to beat them.  Not all video games are products of their mechanics.  Not every video game is something you can master, something you can tweak, something you can optimize.
Some video games are experiences that you can live through.
This is the case with Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice.  This is a game that, while mechanically-competent, beautifully rendered, excellently voiced and magnificently orchestrated, it is not a game ABOUT those things.  It is not a game that is, through its mechanics or its graphics or its acting, impressive.
What is impressive is the opportunity you get to see the world through someone else's eyes.  What is impressive is the experience you get by being put into the shoes of someone who is, above all else, not at home in their own mind.  The game is quick to inform you that this game is a portrayal of psychological complexities and disorders.  Honestly, I felt this "warning" was somewhat frivolous.  Within minutes of starting the game you know that Senua is not well.  You know that she is not safe.  You know that she is going to go through hell.
Beyond this, the game is impossible to speak about without spoilers that ruin the best and most engaging part of it - the experience.  Play this game.  Play it.  Listen, feel, understand.

tl;dr  I recommend this game hands down in its current state (v 1.3), as it stands, it is a fun and unique experience, sure to add ~100+ to my play time.
Originally, this game was a big disappointment, lacking a bunch of features we were expecting. Gradually, with the previous two updates, life was breathed into the game. It was a total breath of fresh air when the Foundation update was released, we knew the game was being worked on, and that the developers were listening.
Now, with the Atlas Rises update, the game has gotten its footing (it no longer feels like early access), and it really shows that this game is a labor of love. I feel like the game is coming in to what we were expecting at launch, and that there will be several more updates to really bring this game up to, and beyond, what we were expecting from the beginning.
I decided to start a new game with the most recent update to get the full experience of the update. I really love the lore of this game; the direction it is going is building up to something great. The initial lack of features is being tied into the lore, and I really appreciate the attention to detail the game now has. Where features once felt lacking, or missing, or clunky, or awkward, they now feel polished, more full, and really help to engage me in the galaxy (it doesn't feel like the grind it previously was, I will note that I have about 10 hours in to the new update). It feels like there is purpose, I want to follow the story and explore. Where I once never felt like getting the center was a priority, I now feel like I need to travel on the Atlas path and get to the center.
If you're on the fence about getting the game, and you like open, resource-gathering, survival (or creative, chill, permadeath) games, pick it up, you won't be disappointed (take it from someone was massivly disappointed at launch) as that is not even a thought that I associate while playing this game any more, tbh, that feeling was dwindling and nearly gone after the Pathfinder update.
8/10 - I feel like this game can easily achieve a 10/10 in the next update or two. This developer truly cares about their game and its community. It shows in how far this game has come with its updates, its community engagement with the ARG, community suggested fixes/improvements being implemented, and a not-so-affordable free giveaway of 10,000 physical Atlas v4 Passes being produced and mailed around the globe. They are doing a great job on marketing their game, a game with substance, a game that has fully captured my attention. I was at a point in my life where video games were starting to feel uninteresting, and I could never find something I wanted to play. NMS has totally brought me back, and I thank them for that.
I won't be saying goodbye to Hello Games any time soon!

This game is a fantastic well-crafted platformer. Full stop. If you like Mega Man, Metroid and the like, you will enjoy this. 8.5/10
PROS:
+Tight platforming
+World changes as you unlock things, making old areas new again
+Plenty of secrets, many are quite challenging to aquire
+Large world, lots to explore -- Despite the world being huge, the design is intuitive and smart. I always had an intuition on which way to go next and I was right 80%+ of the time... Surprislying little confusion on where to go despite the giant map that opens up as you get new tools. Several times I thought "wow, I had an intuition on where to [warp to] [check out] [go], and it turned out I was right". Cant help but feel this is because the designers really thought it out and gave appropriate clues and map indicators to keep you on track. I will contrast this to Axiom Verge, where a large part of the game was spent trying to figure out which of the new paths that opened with [new movement tool] would progress the story.
CONS
-Story is a bit lacking, predictable and simplistic... not much to keep you going there
(MINOR DEBATABLE) CONS
-Basically only 2 weapons... maybe 1. So no variety there... Having just played Axiom Verge, I miss the weapon variety
-Sometimes the secrets are frustrating difficult to *find*, think original NES Metroid at times
-Dont forget to save... sometimes that means backtracking just to save
-Game becomes comically easy when you aquire the final weapon upgrade

First off, don't buy this game if you're looking for some extravagant shooter or action filled ride of destruction or something.  This game tells a story.... what I think is a very good one at that.  Typically gameplay is very linear with no real ability to explore the extremely detailed and awesome looking game world around you.  But, this isn't just a walk in the park.  Actually there's a lot less walking than you think.  Much of it is somewhat similar to parkour with elements of climbing, running, and jumping along the edges and insides of buildings, machinery, and basically anything else that has a handhold.  There are also a number of fights along the way but they almost typically consist of mashing buttons until everyone is lying unconscious... with most of them, little strategy is involved.  It does also have unique gameplay elements involving Nilin's ability to remix memories... those parts are extremely fun and interesting.
I am in love with the futuristic game world that was created for this game.  Truly top notch.  Again, it's a shame the developers don't give you more of a chance to explore it.
The soundtrack is also quite excellent.  This isn't just some synthesized music produced by an audio technician either.  It's performed by a philharmonic orchestra.
The voice acting is also excellent.  I thoroughly enjoyed all the characters and their voice acting really brought them to life.
And then there's Nilin.... Ahhhh Nilin.  Probably one of the sexiest, sultriest, best animated female protagonists in all of gaming.  I really do think the choice of Kezia Burrows was bang on here to voice her.  With her accent she really does portray Nilin as being strong, having an air of sophistication to her as well... almost like a female James Bond.  And sorry to go all pervy here, but you spend the majority of the game following behind her and looking at her backside in all its curvacious glory.  Watching her walk is a real treat.

I really enjoyed this game and totally recommend it. I think the only issue I have with it is that it could have used more of the outstanding elements it already had in place. When a game still feels complete, I feel like that's not the worst problem to have.
My favorite thing about the game was the world it built and the depth of its realization. It feels like the developers left no detail unconcidered when designing Neo-Paris. There's a wealth of information shown about the city's culture and how it was changed with the ability commoditize and rewrite memory. The most impressive thing was that they didn't stop there, the game left details on how outlawing firearms, the prevailence of androids, and how historical strife helped shape the world as well. The drawback to all of this is that most of this is not interactively shown in the game. You walk through the shopping districts and slums and you hear conversations the NPCs have regarding this world but the interaction between Nilin and all of it is relegated to looking. I've heard people had a problem with that and I guess its valid, I was fine with it and loved it anyway.
As for gameplay, it's heavy on the adventure brawler. You make customizable combos with moves that have one of four effects, with supers that can camoflauge you, stun your enemies, make robots fight for you, ect and a long range memory "gun". I had fun with it but it could have used more depth, maybe some integration with the memory remixing would have made it into something totally outstanding.
Now, the memory remixing is probably the most interesting gameplay mechanic of this game. Taking pivotal events in a persons life and rewriting them to suit your needs was interesting, unique, and fun. It was great, I only wish there was more of it in the game (hence the wish of finding a way to integrate it into the combat)
Finally, the visual design was absolutely excellent. It was cohesive, driven, and well delivered in a way that fit the story and world perfectly. I really enjoyed the story with the only issue being that it seemed to waver occasionally to the side of camp when it really didn't need to which led to a few lines that had me roll my eyes when they were delivered.
I played through this on the PS3 and then got it on Steam to play it again and I'm considering a 3rd play through to get all the collectibles. That's really rare for me to do that these days and on that merit alone this game deserves my whole hearted seal of approval. Give it a try if it sounds interesting to you.

One of the best action platformers I've played in years. The controls are smooth as hot butter and the difficulty is the perfect shade of intense. The sound design is fantasic as well as the soundtrack itself. The music really has a character of it's own and sticks with you for hours after you're done playing.
The graphics are a vibrant blend of colors and seemingly hand-drawn artwork. It's breathtaking. I found myself just standing still and enjoying the scenery on multiple occasions during my playthrough.
The play time runs about 5-8 hours depending on how much of the beautiful environment you want to explore. (And you really want to explore as much as possible since there are loads of amusing easter eggs hidden around the secret areas of the game.) But each new area introduces fun new enemy types and variants as well as traps and obstacles to keep the entire experience fresh.
All in all my only complaint is that there isn't more of this gorgeous forest to adventure in.

I really wish there was a maybe option, because if fast paced platforming is your thing, there's some parts in here you're gonna love, If not, you might want to pick another title. Long and short, it loads of fun, but beware the frustration factor.
The Good: This is a beautiful game with a decent story. The controls are great (which is a must for a platformer) and the sound track really helps to set the various moods throughout. Most of the game is a your pace, explore, find the secrets, power ups and kill the bad guys.
The eh: Whether it was to present a challenge or just to add play time I don't know, but the developers took what was like Metroid meets Banjo Kazooie, and added in almost Dragons Lair like action sequences, one wrong move gets you killed and there is no time to think or look around, you just pick a path and hope you're right, if not, start the whole scene all over and try again. While there's a rewarding feeling for having finally accomplished the objective (which is to escape), I don't know that it offsets the frustration of having to rerun the same sequence over and over again trying to get just that last part right.
Honestly, if they'd put an auto save or allowed you to set the pace (there are parts where no matter how fast you go, you're always in peril, there's no buying yourself time to think or look around) this would be a fantastic game, but the repeative nature of key parts, make it, just ok.

Ori is not a long game, it took me 10 hours to beat. Now for me, 10 hours translates to about 5-8 hours for you, not very long at all. However this game is the embodiment of quality over quantity. People use the word aesthetic in totally unrelated contexts, this is one of those applicable contexts, the world sucks you in and doesn't let you go. Everything from the visuals to the soundtrack works together to make you feel totally engrossed.
More about what I like in a moment, here's what I didn't like: I didn't care for the story, mostly because there were so many undefined and unexplained terms thrown at you with no context. I finished it and I still don't know why everything happened. This game also has its own version of Navi which, to be frank, I hated. It really takes the mystery out of the experience when you have somone shouting words at you that won't understand anyway. Lastly, there are optional upgrades that let you see all the secrets in the game which completely spits in the face of every exploration game that came before it.
From time to time I did get the feeling that I wandered in an area that I wasn't supposed to be yet, which is very good to have. Though you could go wherever you wanted the game still felt quite linear. In fact the whole game felt condensed, every room, every crevace you walked into had a purpose, nothing was wasted. This made it fairly easy to predict where the secrets where going to be.
The combat was very enjoyable, sometimes there was no reason to fight an enemy but I did it anyway just for fun. Your primary attack auto targets nearby monsters so you can focus on platforming, and another ability you get later completely blurs the line between the two. Moving around just felt great and satisfying, the movement speed is nice and quick, the animations and little flutters Ori does gives you the feeling that it's enjoying itself. Overall a very positive aspect of the game.
Now for some reason the devs have decided that after you complete a save file, you won't be allowed to go back into it for whatever reason. The game will tell you that you completed it and it will become locked. I'm still baffled at why they would do this, now there's even less incentive to go back and replay it. If there wasn't that damn Navi archetype then maybe I would start a new file but I don't want to deal with tons of unskippable text so one is enough for me.
Is it worth 20 bucks? It wasn't perfect but I can't say I didn't enjoy it so yeah, it is worth it.

Trine is a 2D platformer where you can switch between three different playable characters, each with their own strengths and abilities. The hallmark of the game is its use of physics to manipulate the environment, both to defeat enemies and solve environmental puzzles.
The Enchanted Edition of the game looks really nice, the controls feel smooth and responsive, and there is some really smart level design throughout the game. But for some reason, Trine didn't grab me at first. It seemed like a game I should like, but the early levels failed to capture my imagination. Part of the problem was feeling that I could progress simply by spamming the wizard's abilities. But, I powered through those levels, and I enjoyed the game more as I progressed.
There is an element of "make your own fun" present throughout the game. I recall a few parts of the world that rely on specific character abilities, but most of the game can be solved by any character. This is probably necessary design, in case one or two of your characters are dead when you reach a given part of a level.  But, it also means that if you want to rely on the same techniques with the same character over and over again, you'll probably get by. On the other hand, if you take the time to experiment with the different abilities at your disposal, you'll probably have more fun with the game. At any rate, my enjoyment went way up after I forced myself to switch away from the wizard more often.
In summary, Trine is a fun, beautiful 2D platformer that is definitely worth playing, but to get the most out of it, instead of trying to get through the levels in the most direct, easiest way possible, allow yourself to get creative and experiment with all that it has to offer!

Where to begin with TUG? If your like me and have followed the game for a while you will kind of understand what the game is going to be about. At the moment its a very typical Alpha game and is fairly buggy. All you can do so far is build and explore in creative and play a gamemode called 'survival games'. Survival games is pretty much the hunger games of TUG. You spawn in, you find some materials, craft tools and kill other people. The map is VERY limited compared to how it will be.
At the moment of writing this they are working on new terrain, water etc to make the game awesome!
A lot of the community is focused around the survival server (when it arrives). There will be official servers with lots of people on. A ton of people on the forum have posted concepts for guilds, armies, empires etc? Thats one thing I love.. everyone gets into the spirit of becoming a civilisation and actually being part of the world.
What can you expect?
-Non blocky building
-Indepth survival
-More terrain tools and building tools
-Offical servers
-Proper survival
-TONS more items.
There is so much that is going to be added? So far the lore has been based around the developers (Merylisk in paticular) putting out runes for the community to decode and work out some kind of language for TUG. Eventually the lore will be much more involved in the game, such as finding old ruins etc. The lore isn't handed to you, you can choose to completely ignore it! Or you can go indepth and try to uncover and solve everything you find.
One of the things I love is that the developers seem to understand proper survival! You can't just spawn into the world and create a perfectly made stone tool, you have to scavenge for resources and find materials to add together, it seems fairly reaslistic at the moment and the crafting is very diverse.
If the basic crafting at the moment is the very basics of the game, the advanced crafting such as smelting, molding etc is going to be amazing!
Should you buy this game? I dont know. It depends on what you want. If you want an open world, minecraft-ish (I really shouldn't say that but its the best way to describe it so far) style gameplay with large online trading and fighting, then yeah, buy this game. Buy this game if you like modding, buy this game if you like building. Just buy the game :D
One last thing! The developers are awesome! They always talk to you on twitter or the forums if you message them :D They quite often join in games with us guys aswell.

I wrote a review of 1954 Alcatraz almost one year ago today, ultimately not recommending it.  There were so many things to praise, but a few key shortcomings begrudgingly kept me from recommending it.  After about a year's reflection and a second playthrough, I would like to reverse my opinion and recommend this game to the community.
I still take issue with several things, but they're minor in retrospective.  The biggest issue is that like most point-and-click titles, a guide is almost necessary at a few key points.  Some puzzles are very clear, and the addition of a hint system that pops up when you press spacebar helps a lot of the time, but it becomes a crutch and you're still left trying to figure out a few, key, but nonsensical puzzles.
Still, these issues I consider minor.
This game has a fantastic atmosphere.  The backgrounds are very well-detailed and are just superb.  It has a film noir feel through and through, even if you don’t use the special filter to replicate this effect.  The sound and music, as well as the quality of the voice acting is better than most other titles I’ve played.
There are issues with the writing that I take, in that some of the dialogue seems cut and skipped.  It’s easy to imagine that a character originally had 5 lines but only 1 or 2 made it to a particular section.  The part of the writing that shines through is the world building.  Characters, though extremely stereotypical, aren’t two-dimensional.  They may be static from the onset, showing a hint of growth here and there, but there are many things that make the game work.  It’s a very progressive game that stays true to the era it takes place in.  It doesn’t indulge too much on certain aspects (for instance, there is racism, but it’s written well and not lazily, and only happens with appropriate characters).  Every line of dialogue matters.  I just wish they included more.
All this comes with the expectation that you’ll play through twice.  It is worth it, but it might not seem so before you start your second playthrough.  And give it a month or so.  Maybe longer.  Maybe a year like me.  But either way, this title is a remarkable one and it absolutely should be emulated by other companies.

We were told that there would be multiplayer.
We were told that there would be "a surprise at the middle of the universe," which turned out to be just a way to restart the game.
We were told that there would be an interesting story line, which ended up being just going around talking to aliens and choosing between desicions. Birthing a star sounds cool, right? Well too bad you don't get to know where it is or if you stumbled upon it by accident.
We were told that we could enjoy the game for a long time, but it ended up being so repetitive. Sure, that may have changed with the addition of base-building and specialists, but only to a certain extent. If you want base-building there are many better games which are specifically created for base-building. The specialists simply make you more powerful by giving you upgrades, and don't really add to the story or anyhing.
Seriously regret buying this game.

In many ways wolfenstein is a great game.
The gunplay is solid, with weapons having a great punchiness to them.The story and voice acting are pretty good (I've only played Wyatt's timeline), with some great serious and funny moments.  The music is easily the star of this game, phenomenal stuff, hits all the right notes!
There are however, a few flaws.
The level design can be hit or miss. It feels like the developer wanted the levels to feel a little more open ended than last timel, but wanted to keep the linearity too. However, I don't think was done well. Most areas felt large, but for no reason. All this did was confuse me and gave me a hard time while trying to figure out where to go next. This could've been alleviated with a good map or pathfinding mechanism, but neither is very good. I must also note that in each district, most areas look too samey. There could've been some environmental indication that you are now in a different part of the level.
Stealth is useless. Enemies are placed in such a way that stealth is enormously frustrating. Further, many levels play are created  in such a way that the lighting camouflages enemies. Combining this with enemies that are really alert, with no cooldown makes stealth a tedious way to play the game. I wouldn't mind this if the game didn't actually encourage stealth with the commander system.
The game can feel enormously unfair. Enemies are smart, they will make use of their greater numbers by distracting and flanking you. It makes good use of the combination of light and heavy enemies. My problem actually lies with how squishy BJ is and level design, which makes the smart enemy ai seem over powered.
The latter doesn't allow for fast paced run and dodge gunplay like doom does, nor does it have a reliable way to recover health. Further, though it feels more open ended, the levels are actually still just constricted corridors, with little room to run while keeping tabs on enemy locations. This just leads to a situation where I'm running around, trying to shoot down enemies, but also finding my bearings (running into dead ends is a pain), and losing health really fast with no real way to get some back. I could deal with this during most encounters, but some got really frustrating.
The cover system, which I think was meant to be used often, has not been implemented well. You can go next to a wall or piece  and press the ads button to pop out of cover. However, a large portion of my time trying this system was spent with game not recognising what I wanted to do, or letting me do it, only to randomly pull me out every few seconds. I'd imagine that the game would be a lot easier if it was implemented well. You can also use a key to lean left and right, but similarly, BJ would suddenly be pulled out of the lean, not to mention the large amount of fire fights just mean pinky finger pain.
Finally, while I've already mentioned that the story is pretty good , I thought some of the humour was unnecessary or mistimed.  Further, some scenes seem to have been included, purely for shock value. The ending was also unnecessarily open ended, almost surely setting up a sequel. I preferred the first game, where I could still be pleased with the story as a stand alone thing, while also knowing that a sequel was possible.
All of this considered, I'd have still given the game a solid 8, because most of these issues can be looked past. Combined with solid gunplay and plot, makes for an engaging , fun and hectic shooter.  All they need to do is fix the cover system to alleviate some level design issues that I had (it would reduce the amount of repositioning).

Hellblade is a unique and wonderful game. So far it's the only project I can remember that seriously and meticulously tries to make the player feel what it would be like to have a mental illness. Mind you, it's
I'm talking about; obviously there's been a ton of mad characters in videogames, but so far mental problems (often unexpectedly revealed) were normally used as a plot device. Hellblade is different.
Hellblade was made with the help of people who work with mental illnesses and even those who actually experienced them. In Hellblade realiy shifts and wavers but always makes sense in a twisted way. Senua doesn't know she's sick, and that's why it feels real and scary. Ninja Theory used wonderful methods to represent it, including clever special effects and amazing binaural sound.
It's better not to ignore the game's advice to use headphones: the sound plays a very important role. When I heard the voices for the first time, I got goosebumps. It's not quite like anything else.
On a more technical side, bear in mind that Hellblade is an indie game despite its high quality. It's not very long (although I believe 7–8 hours is the perfect length for this story), it's linear (again, turning it into some sort of open-world crap would never work). There are only a few enemies (but you'll remember them well, especially the bosses). The puzzles aren't too varied (you'll have to solve the same puzzle with seeking shapes that look like runes to open a door many times), but there's plenty of variety in the surroundings, presentations, pace and other gameplay elements. It never feels boring or repetitive. It's a unique, powerful and extremely immersive journey.

Ever since the indie Metroidvania boom I've never found a game that really scratched that Super Metroid itch, until Environmental Station Alpha.
At first glance, the game's graphics will appear simplistic but you will eventually start to appreciate the level of detail that was put in. The animations in the game are well done, and each area seems handcrafted without a single wasted pixel. Some areas even have a dynamic feeling as they undergo change as the game progresses. The soundtrack is also great and fits the ambience of the mysterious station.
Gameplay wise it plays very much like you'd expect where you explore an uncharted area and fight bosses, while also finding tools along the way that allow you to explore more of the world. The grappling hook took you get is particularly fun to use. There are even a few optional upgrades you can get in the game, but they kind of end up making you overpowered.
The game tells it's plot in a wonderful way, where just as you explore the station like it's a puzzle, the story is the same way. It's a puzzle you slowly unravel and even includes a cryptic language for you to decipher to unlock the secret ending.
ESA also manages to mitigate some of the problems other metroidvanias have with backtracking by introducing a fairly substantial teleport system that allows you to easily transport yourself around the map to places you've already been. It introduces this just as the map really starts to open up more.
The only real drawback is the difficulty in the game is a bit uneven. Relatively early on certain boss fights will be on the difficult side, largely because you have limited health. However, during the end of the game most of the bosses end up becoming really easy thanks to having collected HP upgrades and some optional mobility/weapon upgrades.  Plus, as much as I enjoy the different bosses most of them don't involve a whole lot of movement. Instead they tend to be pretty stationary, and you need to dodge their attacks.  Luckily these are both flaws recognized by the developer, Hempuli, and something he is working on for the sequel!.
The game is only $8 and it is a great value, and should take you anywhere from 6 hours if you just power through the mainstory, to over 20 hours if your a completionist and go for the secret ending.
One of my favorite of all time Metroidvanias.

Quite an enjoyable (not to mention content-filled) Metroidvana, with a decent amount of content and secrets. It can be quite challenging for players newer to the genre or less experienced when starting out, but the concept is great, along with the multitude of challenging bosses and endings, along with plenty of secrets (some quite obscure, requiring finding all sorts of secret areas) and powerups. So basically, if you think the premise or trailer is cool (The trailer actually displays rooms from real environments in the game) and you're up for a challenge (certain early bossfights can take 5-10 tries to beat or more) and late-game some areas and bosses can be quite frustrating to navigate if certain completely optional powerups are not unlocked (for example the OP triple-shot module for the gun).
Secondly, before the teleporters are unlocked the fairly frequent backtracking can sometimes get tedious, as earlier in the game the only way to get to key locations is to go through 10+ rooms filled with enemies and obstacles. While it's not extremely heavy on backstory, the general atmosphere and design style of the (absolutely massive) sector-based station is also quite nice
(and, fun fact, the Trailer actually displays rooms from real environments in the game).
So, in conclusion, I would definitely recommend trying this game out, as the price ($8.79 CAD) compared to the hours of content is fair, though as much as I fanboy over this game (being new to the genre) it isn't free of issues to critique, for example the original controls for Keyboard are set to X-jump, and C-shoot, but thankfully in the settings under Keyboard C, they are rebindable, which I recommend taking advantage of, as it's easy to forget the controls after taking a 3-4 day break. (I suggest using the M key for map, as setting it to escape glitches the game out)

I restarted this game three times before I beat it.
ESA is one of those games that's just super hard to come back to after a break. Every time I'd start a new file, I'd have a great time breezing through its opening hours before stopping for the day, and realizing a week later that I hadn't played it since and had no idea what I was supposed to be doing anymore. This wasn't helped by the retro-hard difficulty and some obtuse progression. For a while I was reserved to the idea that I would never complete ESA.
I restarted this game three times, and then it clicked.
I've spent some twenty hours in this game over the past three days. It's consumed my time and my thoughts. I dedicated myself to it, and ESA rewarded my investment.
ESA has a ludicrously dense Metroidvania map.
ESA has an atmospheric world that reacts to your actions.
ESA has enthralling, puzzling endgame content.
ESA has difficult, multi-phase boss fights, and tough platforming challenges.
I can't think of much more that I could want from this game. The only issues I have with it are little polish things that are very understandable coming from a lone developer.
I think this game is very much worth your time.

Finally, after all these years I found IMMERSION again. This game is a work of art.
The visual composition of levels, the quality of the graphic are awesome. The sound work needs it's own level of praise. From the binaural effects to the soundtrack, everything flows so naturally that it feels as part of the world, as opposed to just being pieces of development. Headphones are really, really recommended. The way the sound jumps from left to right to behind is something that must be experienced.
The voices in Senua's head are the second most important and well build character (after Senua herself).
The UI is a minimalist dream come true. There is no UI. It is beautiful, because everything works, and there is no need for anything else to be added. No more "Press "C" to crouch" near every boulder. Simple controls, clear feedback from the environment. All that is needed.
Some criticized the combat because it is too simple and not uniformly distributed throughout the game. Personally i feel that for a game of this length, the complexity of the combat is enough. Simple slash, heavy slash, dodge, block and kick. Some basic combos, that flow naturally. There is no need for more. No unlockable special actions, no super-finishers. Because this game is a tale of a plausible warrior woman. The combat is plausible. It's something a regular fit woman or man could do. And as far as the distribution of the combat, again this feels natural in the context of the story. Some parts are without combat, and that is good.
And a big THANK YOU to Ninja Theory for not making Senua half naked with huge breasts.

Tentative recommendation. I enjoyed the hell out of this... many won't.
First off, this is probably the most simply gorgeous game I've ever played. If you care about graphical quality, definitely check this out. More stylistic than photorealistic, but even still, Senua shows nuanced facial expressions throughout, and manages to avoid the uncanny valley more often than she falls in. The backdrops and animations are simply beautiful as well. Hell has an amazing view at all times.
The story and main character resonated deeply with me for personal reasons, but this game is utterly disturbing and disorienting. It became positively *draining* at times, necessitating a quick break, but I always jumped right back in after a few minutes. It maintains a pervasive sense of dread throughout, far better than most modern horror games.
The gameplay consists primarily of exploration and solving visual puzzles, with combat strewn periodically. The puzzles can get dull after a while, but are mostly simple to solve and easily passed. The combat is tense and rewards patience and proper timing. The camera occasionally gets stuck in an inopportune position during fights, which can lead to some frustration as you try to defensively escape the situation without dying.
Play with headphones or not at all, unless you've got the mother of surround sound systems hooked up.
The game is quite short. I spent roughly ten hours and missed only two of the optional lore glyphs. For the askign price and the quality of the experience, I feel it was well worth it, though others might well disagree. Do not expect to get 70+ hours out of this.
Finally, support it for what the studio's trying to do here. An indie game with this level of production value, still at an indie price point? The quicker we can make this the go-to business model and starve the parasitic AAA publishers out of the industry (or force them to change their ways to accommodate), the better.

I rarely to never comment on a game, be it a good or bad comment. I normally look through the comments to see if others have the same experience and vote those up. I have owned every CoD game except for Ghosts and AW (I have played those, I don't own them). This is one of the games that I had to buy again. Don't let the visuals fool you, this game is hard as balls, and you'll love it for being so.
Need I say more? Everything about this game is beautiful: its graphics, its sound design/soundtrack, its gameplay and its characters.
If you get Ori and the Blind Forest thinking you're in for some relaxing casual fun, you're in for a world of pain. It starts softly, but the difficulty escalates and escalates until you find yourself thinking out loud "holy **** are they ****ing serious?".
I'm not gonna say it's addictive, because it's not. This is the kind of game that you play on the couch for a couple of hours, ragequit and play it again some other day when you're more cool headed. It's not the kind of game that makes you say "this is ridiculously hard, I give up"... you'll get stuck but it will be engaging enough to make you come back and keep trying.
What can I say? The story is worth it. At first it's about finding yourself, and then it becomes a journey to cleanse the forest from all evil.
I have no cons for this game. It's a ride from start to finish, and one of the best platformers I've ever played. One of the most special things about it is the fact that there is no difficulty setting, so it will be hard at first but not-so-hard once you've learned the mechanics of it. Ori and the Blind Forest is a must buy for platformer lovers and those who are looking for a challenge.

What a great game! I'm enjoying it without any crashes! Give me few minutes to explain!
I purchased the Steam edition few years ago (I had Win 7 then 8 then 8.1 then 10). I have installed it two times before the last one (once with Windows 7, and then Windows 8.1). It worked following one guide by installing a mod and modifying the ini file ..etc. But, it never worked well. It also never registered the game spent time within Steam. So, I uninstalled it, and added it to my 'abandoned' category.
Few weeks ago, I thought to try it again as I really want to play it years ago (damn it!). So, I installed it. I did one modification and that is changing the exe file compatibility to Windows Vista! When I run it (no administration rights playing around), it did notify me to install 'Games for Windows - LIVE' s**t, it said, the one I have is not compatible, so I clicked yes and it was installed, but I didn't run it, I just clicked 'OK' and exit.
I run the game and changed the resolution to 1920x1080 and also the details to high. Since then I'm enjoying a great game without any crash for over 20 hours! Now, there are still minor bugs, but those are experienced by all, not only by me (they are very minor, like got stuck between rocks ...etc).
I have checked the installed apps in the settings and found those two:
-  Microsoft Games for Windows - LIVE Redistributable (version 3.5.92.0)
-  Microsoft Games for Windows Marketplace (version 3.5.67.0)
My PC is nothing special at all! i5-4570 with GTX 750 and 8GB RAM. Windows 10 home 64bit with the latest update.
Now, for the game, I think there are really very good reviews about gameplay and everything else. I agree with most that said it is a great game :) I give it 9/10.
Anyway, I might add some notes of my experiences in the game although I'm still level 5 and only 22 hours into the game!
The start was very tough for me (after leaving the Vault), and I found myself to replay the game two times again because my character wasn't what I wanted. I read many advices on how to choose different attributes ..etc, but in the end I found that:
- Whatever you choose, you can't be all-rounder character. You win something but lose something else!
- Physical strength is important especially in the beginning! But it is far from the only thing needed!
- Choose specific weapons and put high points on them. I found Melee weapons come very handy against some mobs and when other ranged weapons useless (almost!).
- Fighting and looting have a major part in the game. Repairing is also useful. so I tend to care more about those aspects. But as I said, you can't have everything, so choose only the ones that suit your style of playing. You might replay the game more than once to understand the mechanics.
- Finding a bed to sleep is not easy in the very start! It is crucial to sleep as it restores health to the max.
- After discovering it, I used fast travel a lot within the world map ;)
- I lowered the difficulty from Normal to Easy (hihihi) What?! It is a damn difficult game! I died a lot! what can I do?!
- Assigning shortcuts for different weapons/armor are very useful in combat. Also for the aid/food.
Now, after knowing where to not go (yet!) and what mobs to avoid, I'm enjoying a great game really. It is a dark story and filled with sadness and a**h***s, but that's life after a nuclear war. I got used to it in the game! After all, it is a very addictive game when you found yourself into it (after few hours from the start though).
I really hope it would work with all, because it is a shame not to play such a great game that suits all players, not only RPG/Action fans.

As a game Remember Me does a number of things right and the rest is either luke warm or a missed opportunity for something greater.
The best thing this game does is easily the visual design. Remember Me pushes the unreal engine to what we all hope to see in games. Everything looks great from models to textures to lighting. If nothing else this game should be played simply on the grounds of how great it looks.
Along this line the sound design is also top tier. It works so well with the world building and visual asthetics that the music blends perfectly into each scene and fight sequence. Voice overs fit perfectly and no voice or person seems out of place.
Character design is also very well flushed out. It's actually refreshing to see a world where the bad guys are not twisting their mustaches and cackling meniacally at the thought of performing evil. Everyone, from the good guys to the bad guys have motives that are understandable and interesting and neither the good guys nor the bad guys end up acting purely towards good and evil.
The story works well too but as with most sci-fi based stories something is lost from the translation of the fantasy world to reality. Sometimes motives, especially of the main character, are lost or not present.
For the most part the game is stable but I did have some crashes and some sound glitches (such as the sound turning off completely.) It's not noticable but hiccups here and there can be a problem. Older machines might have more trouble playing this but I was not able to test that.
As far as gameplay goes there is a lot of promise with the "make your own combo" system but it falls flat when it becomes apparent how to min max. You set up a damage combo and you set up a heal combo. This makes the actual combat more rhytm based system and picking between two or three combos that all do specific jobs.
The exploration sections of the game are as linear as it gets. You go forward, you climb the ledge, it tells you where to go. Basically you hold foward and hit the jump button and you go to the next section. There are small (usually) unobvious branches that lead to collectables but for the most part you are on rails the whole game.
Puzzles are not very complex, once you get a new mechanic you use the mechanic in an obvious way to get to the next section.
Bosses are a bit tedious and sometimes it not apparent what you have to do to beat them. And each boss has only one method to beat them, using a specific mechanic to make them vulnerable then use your combos. Nothing too special.
The most unique mechanic in this game is the memory remixing. It's a fun and interesting puzzle that allows you to change someones memory piece by piece. There isnt much of a fail state for it so worst case scanario you just keep trying things until it clicks. In the end there really is only one way to get the desired result so it is a bit more linear than it could have been. Also these sections appear infrequently, which leaves more to be desired for such a unique mechanic.
The overall story is okay. Motivations are confusing from time to time and the ending is a bit ham fisted. I feel as though a good opportunity for a twist was there but it was neglected. There is nothing to really complain about or praise beyond the core story idea of altering and trading memories. It's unique enough to enjoy but not quite used to its full potential.
The game is short but honestly considering the content it ends up being about the right length. If the gameplay this game length would be considered short.
If you want great gameplay don't bother with this one. It's interesting enough to keep some playing but overall its a move forward and mash out combos game. For those of you who can look past gameplay at the gorgeous visual and music than this game is for you. Still wait for a sale since this game is often at least half off.

This game features some of the most underappreciated graphics I've seen in a while, and that's running the game on medium settings with a low-power graphics card. Altough combat gets less and less exciting the further you progress, the impressive detail gone into the design of Neo-Paris and the storyline accompanying draws your attention away from the more minor flaws.
- Stunning visuals
- Runs well on low spec CPUs
- Interesting storylines
- Memory remixing mechanic is well built
- Customisable combos with different moves
- Voice acting is not too bad
- Fighting is easy and reptitive
- Little variation between enemies
- Camera angles can be ambiguous
- Controls while scaling walls are awkward
- You can backflip away from enemies any time you like?
- Very linear storyline
- Arrows are constantly telling you where to go: all difficulty of finding your way is lost.
My favourite part of the game so far is being able to admire all the scenery and effort that has been put into the level desing - especially while climbing up pipes (you get some of the most amazing views while climbing up pipes on the sides of buildings). The tall, majestic buildings of the city and the deteriorating pits of the slums. I only wish fighting wasn't so easy. You can beat your way through several enemies very quickly by simply spamming the LMB and RMB keys. Even once you have defeated an enemy, if you keep clicking, Nilin will backflip straight to another enemy and continue fighting immediately. There is a very low level of difficulty between most enemies, the hardest being those that can disappear at will.
On the other hand, I do enjoy the fact that you can customise your combos with different moves, or "pressens". However this also can make fighting simple as there are pressens that can regenerate your health. As soon as you equip these very close to the beginning of a combo, any damage you happen to take has virtually no impact as you can just brush it off by beating up more enemies.
TL;DR
If you enjoy games with very appealing graphics and games which aren't CPU intensive, this is the game for you. It has a good storyline, but fighting is too easy and repetitive.

Probably the best "Metroid-like" that wasn't an actual Metroid game that I've ever played. Yes, this includes Axiom Verge. ESA has textboxes to help move the story along as well (something I thought was a huge problem/annoyance in AV,) but I think the fact that the player character was a silent protagonist in ESA, just made the game better. At the very least, there wasn't any balls-dumb writing to the tune of:
"Uhm, HEY? Big scary creature thing that's obviously a hostile boss? I'm like, uhm, LOST? So like uhm, hey do you got a minute? Like, HEY? Whoa, how can my existence real if my hair don't real? Whoa,"
...that you had to slog through, like how Trace was in AV. Still, I think I'd still prefer the silent protagonist, even over a well-written character. That way you can inject your own small motivations into the chracter as you wrestle with the spooky isolation of wandering around a decades-long abandoned research station, which is actually pretty huge, as well as having two old derelict spaceships floating hearby that you can port to and explore, and even spend some small amount of ganeplay down on the planet the startion is orbiting.
Enemy types and their behaviors are pretty standard for this type of game, as well as the types of powerups you find. (Double jump, hori/verti dashing, heat protection, triple shot, charge beam, grapple hook[EVERY game that pays homage to Metroid should have some kind of gapple hook!] sheildy bits that orbit you, life extenders, and a bunch of other things.)
The game is designed so that a good chunk of these things, while extremely helpful, are not necessarily required to reach the FIRST ending. This game has ridiculous amounts of replay value, and last I checked, there are no less than 6 endings you can reach, (I've only found 4 so far,) as well as quite few side quests and a couple secret bosses apart from the "main game."
Bosses in this game (I think there over 19 or 20 of them, secret bosses included,) are pretty challenging, but are actually fun to fight once tyou figure them out, (Again, very unlike AV.) A good chunk of them have two or three phases to boot, so it's not just the same 1 to 3 patterns the whole time. A large part of the challange in ESA stems from how there are no health regenerators dropped by creatures and bosses, at all. The only way you can replenish your health is at a save point or health station, of which there are many located within the game world at fair intervals. This definitely means you can cheese your way through certain situations, but when it comes to bosses, it's kill with what you have going into the fight, or be killed. This might frustrate some people. (This is why it is important to explore and get some powerups that you might not "need," but would certainly improve your survivability. Maybe.)
The music is spooky, grim, desolate, and higly menorable. From an audio standpoint the game is mixed really well.

I joined the hype train in early August last year and preordered No Man's Sky. It was fun to play the game for a good while. But I quickly got bored and moved on. I've never even considered refunding No Man's Sky because it appealed to me. And after the Foundation Update, the game got so much better.
I am currently having a blast with the new Atlas Rises update, and I think it's impressive and awesome that the devs (Hello Games) are still updating and working on No Man's Sky by adding new things and features every update. Sure, they've been quiet for a long time after 1.2, but every time they update the game, I delete my save and start over again to enjoy the new features. It's very admirable to me that with every update, the devs "encourage" people to play again. That is the power of updates.
If you love exploration, space, science fiction, trading and just generally a very chill but sometimes very intense gaming experience, then this game is for you. If not, please don't hate the game because it lacked a lot of features they had promised at release, because it's the updates that matter, not the release. The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing.  Great graphics with dx11 features making the environment pop out right at your eyes. I could barely move without being slaughtered.  After lowering the difficulty down to normal the game was a lot more bareable but I still died several times.  I reset skill and ability points several times trying to find the right build for me and by the end I had something that worked (melee based, i know the most go for range on this game)

You can also dismantle and make essences stronger.  There are a few different ways that can change your character but without paying for the DLC you are damned to only one class, The hunter.  You have a companion, Katarina that will follow you and you can have her help you in different ways.  Also Katarina will level up and has her own ability and skill points.
At the end of the story, it does not have to be the end of the game.  You can keep playing with harder monsters to keep getting better gear.  You can also do all of this with up to three additional friends.  Very fun game, many smooth environments, different skills from melee to range, lots of different ways to build your character.  The game runs great maxed out on an ancient system.  I'm downloading the second one as I type this review!
*also, I played the entire game with a xbox controller, worked flawlessly for melee but aiming could be a little hard when in range.  This game ran smoothly on an old system and I had no bugs.  I did have a couple of crashes when in store or forge, but who knows what that could have been from.

First off, I will say that this game is not for those action junkies that need to be spoon-fed fights non-stop, so if that is the type of player you are, chances are you might not like it.
But, for anyone looking for a very cinematic and rich story, with some interesting twists, then this is definitely a game worth looking into. The devs really put in alot of time and effort dealing with subject matter that tends to be glossed over or ignored as taboo. The facial captures for Senua by Melina Juergens is beautifully done and really brings to life Senua and makes you feel for her and her journey.
The environments are amazing and very detailed. And very much fit the story being told.  The puzzles are quite interesting and some require a little out of the box thinking. True a few can be slightly annoying, but that happens.
Everyone, including the devs recommend the use of headsets when playing, especially with a biaurual setting, I will agree on that, I tried it on the speakers and on the headset, and it is a world of difference.
Overall, this is an amazing game and you can truly tell the devs put alot of work into it to make it something unique and wonderful. I can not recommend this enough.

Here we are again - a retro style 2D topdown shooter that belongs back in the early 1990's.
Again, ripping off Spacewar from the 1960s, but they tried to add a progression system where you upgrade your ship, etc etc.   Star Control 2 did this in the 1990's with far better implementation and quality.
Graphics: Terrible, no 3D, no graphics options, artwork is low effort, even the ship models look awful.  This game tries to look like it's from the 1990's, but if this review was written then, the result would be the same - the game looks bad even when compared to 90's graphics.  Also, it's 2016.
Gameplay: Not as good as Star Control.   Really, quite clunky, physics engine is difficult to control, interface seems half keyboard half gamepad - the developer probably never played any computer games before.
I think it's nice that they tried to add a progression system to the game, but it lacks the depth the developer was hoping for - other games have done this much more richly, and with better graphics and gameplay.  There's no compelling reason to play Space Salvager.  Every game they've tried to copy does what they're doing far, far better, cheaper, and with better visual appeal.
