is an open-world, 2D, story-driven, action-adventure platformer with exploratory gameplay and entertaining combat; the game is visually outstanding as well as sonically masterful with an amazing soundtrack. It was developed by Moon Studios -a group consisting of talented developers spread out over Europe, the Middle East, Oceania, and North America- using the Unity engine. It’s published by Microsoft Studios. The game is currently available for Xbox One and PC.
We’re thrown right into the narrative, as the Spirit Tree begins to tell the tale of how it ‘lost’ newborn spirit Ori to the forest of Nibel due to a storm. Ori, now orphaned, is raised by Naru, a benevolent bear-like creature. Later, a cataclysm leaves the forest in decay, and Naru passes away as a result. Orphaned once more and with his surrounding forest dying, Ori finds Sein, who is ‘the light and the eyes of the Spirit Tree’ and offers to guide Ori in his quest to restore the forest to its previous state: full of life and harmony. In his adventures Ori learns of the events that triggered the cataclysm, and faces several obstacles in his quest. Among them a long-limbed creature named Gumo, who becomes Ori’s ally after making his life a little difficult; a gigantic owl name Kuro, a creature of the darkness who attempts to prevent Ori from restoring light to the forest; and many enemies along the way from whom Ori has to defend himself.
The plot is filled with a wide range of emotions, from carefree bliss to hopeless depression, and includes anything in between: annoyance, humour, curiosity, confusion, kindness, etc... Moon Studios did a marvellous job of tugging at the appropriate heartstrings through various events, resulting in a highly captivating and internalized storytelling experience.
takes influence from animated films like
and
, both of which are coming-of-age stories; in turn,
also feels very much like a coming-of-age story. The narrative has a peculiar tone and style to it, it likes to use vague but guiding vocabulary, allowing the player to infer quite a bit and interpret the themes of the plot (kindness, sacrifice and parenthood). The characters are all wonderfully written; there isn’t any excess, and that (together with its incredible visuals) makes the world surrounding the player feel fluous and whimsical.
I cannot fail to mention the calibre of level design and game mechanics. The gameplay is some of the most fluid and well animated that I’ve had the pleasure to experience. This may be partly because I haven’t played too many games in the past year, or it might be simply because Moon Studios has some immensely skilled devs in their ranks. Ori has abilities and skills that he learns throughout the progression of the game, these skills are learned at the Ancestral Trees. The player can upgrade abilities by gaining experience through finding Ability Cells, or absorbing Spirit Light by defeating different kinds of enemies which have different types of attack mechanisms. There’s so much to do in the game: solve puzzles, defeat enemies, collect Energy Cells and Life Cells (more energy slots and life slots, respectively), use upgraded abilities to explore previously unavailable places, and ultimately restore the forest.
Falling into the genre of ‘metroidvania’, the game definitely takes after classics like
and
, which directly influenced the gameplay of
.
is very much intended as a ‘love letter’ to those games. The map itself is one huge open world; there are no loading screens, just exploration through jumping, climbing, swinging, bashing, etc… It’s no Dark Souls, but if you do not save often this game is very unforgiving.
Writing about the visual aspect of this game is difficult, because I’m at such a loss for words, it is probably the prettiest 2D game I have ever seen. The animations are pure magic and the hand-painted assets and environments are what make the whole game’s atmosphere cohesive. Designers took inspiration from a few well-known works, such as Hayao Miyazaki’s
and Disney’s
. The level “Valley of the Wind” is a straight-up tribute to
. One of the things I think is the coolest about this game is that in the backgrounds there are no recycled assets; one of the two founders, Thomas Mahler, says:
I find this to be amazing because most games today tile their textures or re-use assets already used elsewhere in the game. Unique assets make the game’s environments feel as real, fresh, non-repetitive and original as they possibly can.
Onto the character ‘Ori’, the star of the game. He’s this little creature, a mix between a dog, a cat, a rabbit and a monkey. He’s got a weird little design, but awesome nonetheless; Ori is one of the coolest animalistic characters I’ve had the chance to play as. From his jumping and running animations to the way he interacts with different mechanisms of the game, the character feels as alive as perceptively possible.
Sound is -a lot of the time- as important as the visuals in a video game. The audio of any given game is what gives life to the user experience, a game’s sound is what completes it, what makes you immerse yourself and just forget about whatever’s going through your head.
s soundtrack by itself is serene and beautiful enough to make you disengage yourself from your surroundings. Give it a couple of hours and you’ll completely forget where you are, courtesy of composer Gareth Coker.
The audio design in this game is next to flawless. All the way from footsteps to the environment sounds, to the narration, the audio is simply mesmerizing. The atmosphere, the ambience that the sound manifests, it’s magnificently special.
I dove into this game with minimal knowledge about it, I knew was that it was a very pretty and successful game. But there wasn’t much about it besides the seemingly amazing story and visuals that drew me in - until I read about the developers.
Did you know Moon Studios doesn’t have a location? It’s an independant worldwide collaboration between many talented people all over the world, the two founders (Thomas Mahler & Gennadiy Korol) are veterans in their fields. Mahler previously worked at Blizzard on Starcraft 2 and Korol was Senior Graphics and Tools Engineer at Animation Lab (an Israeli feature-film animation studio). Among their employees Moon Studios has some extremely talented people.
Choosing to play this game was a great call, it provided me with some of the most memorable moments I’ve had in recent gaming and

The fact that it was nominated for so many awards should tell you how well-made it is. And if not, the fact that it WON Best Art Direction among other awards should.

I didn't expect much going in, though I did hear good things about this game. It has an atmosphere and 2D exploratory gameplay most similarly to Metroid, a fact that is pretty much undeniable. Compared to other "metroidvanias," which take on an explicitly different theme or music style, Environmental Station Alpha wears its Metroid inspiration pretty openly on its sleeve. So Metroid fans who are big fans of the series' exploration and atmosphere would do well to check this game out.
Beyond its inspiration, however, it's just a well put-together game in general. Upgrades, bosses, and environments all open up at a very comfortable and easily digestible pace. There's a sense of weight to the robot you control, giving it a different feel from the somersaulting action of Metroid (I'd say the main character feels more like the Cave Story protagonist). Attacking is done with a continuous short-range stream rather than individual shots like in Metroid, giving attacking a more deliberate and precise feel as well.
The map is huge, but not overwhelming, and teleport systems are all in the right places to facilitate fast travel without devaluing the exploration itself. Its biggest accomplishment, however, is the nigh-incredible use of landmarking and identity generously peppered across each and every single room in the game. ESA not only borrows from Metroid's atmosphere and gameplay, but also the distinctiveness of every one of any given entry's rooms. I can still picture the entire station in my head, how it all connects together, without needing to look at the map screen. No area in the game feels dull, and the way upgrades and switches change the landscape just beg further curiosity for the surroundings. In short, it's inspired by Metroid in the biggest way it counts--level design.
I suppose the only negative thing I have to say about the game is that it takes a while before it really gets going, since for a while all you can do is shoot and jump, but it all starts to pick up once you acquire the grappling hook (it's called a hookshot in this game, haha). It immediately makes for a rather fun way to traverse the environment.
It's hard to put into words just how well thought out the game feels, but it's what I'm focusing on because its outward appearance suggests that of a cheap Metroid imitation, so I understand this makes it somewhat of a hard sell. Nonetheless, if you can look past its similarity and try it out for yourself, I think you'll end up being pleasantly surprised with a new Steam favorite.

Atmosphere is very good, the story is compelling and the game in general is very entertaining.
The biggest complaint is that the cut-scenes cannot be skipped. This is a real pain because the game uses a save point system (which is again better than e.g. Batman because it also saves during stages of long boss fights, and in general quite often) and allows you only to replay whole chapters later. Unfortuantely each chapter begins with quite a long cut-scene and this becomes annoying fast when replaying the game for achievement hunts.
Remember Me's atmosphere and storytelling are incredibly compelling. It's a game that is well worth the journey, if you can stomach the rather clunky controls and sometimes frustrating combat design.

Yesterday, I got an early Steam code for a game called Shower With Your Dad Simulator 2015. I instantly took Mad Max and Metal Gear Solid V, threw them out the window and thought no more of them. Showering with my dad was clearly what I needed to spend my day doing as a gamer.
On the surface, Shower With Your Dad Simulator 2015 is a fairly simple video game. You play one of a trio of small children at a set of public showers. These could be at a gym, a swimming pool or somewhere else entierly. You are maybe two or three years old and you have to carefully find and hug your naked dad in the shower.
Hug the wrong naked dad, it's all over.
These game modes increase in difficulty as you progress through the game. Straight razors remove everybody's hair, meaning you have to judge on features like eye colour who is your father. Spots of water on the floor send you sliding across the room without any control, ready to crash into someone else's dad. Wet floor signs slow down your progression across the room.
So, of the game's six modes, the three unlocked from the start are all fairly pedestrian. Where the games gets a little more interesting is when you do well enough to unlock one of the other locked modes.
Without warning I was flying a cyber bathtub through the matrix, collecting holo dads, and filling up a glitching energy bar. Next I was flying a magical bathtub through the clouds, shooting down other fathers to collect 69 of my naked dad. Then dad was the president maybe? I don't entirely know what started to happen.
What's really interesting is that, while these game modes initially feel like they may just exist to be silly jokes, they actually introduce interesting new gameplay mechanics which all function well and feature their own degrees of challenge.
Oh, and there's a bunch of terrible cheesy dad jokes thrown in for good mix.
Shower With Your Dad Simulator 2015 is due out on Steam in "the next few days"

Another isometric hack and slash action with a bit of age, the first instalment of the Van Helsing trilogy plays phenomenally well but isn't without it's share of problems either.
While you may think this is just another tired old diablo clone, Van Helsing's first part delivers some fun that can take you back to the days of Diablo II, and forget that its third sibling came out in the first place. While class selection may be hidden behind a pay wall, the basic hunter class has the potential to answer any and every call you may have when it comes to combat style. Having personally opted for the caster route (just to see if I could), i was pleasantly surprised by the end of the game.
Where Van Helsing suffers the most is in its oddly placed difficulty curve; the game could feel trivial one moment, and then single handedly kill you before you get to quaff a potion in the other. These instances of absolute maddening frustration are an example of the odd power-creep that occurs during the game. Each new chapter feels like you're incredibly behind, but midway through, you'll be breezing through screens covered in enemies without losing more than a few bits of health. Another frustration is that most major bosses have endlessly spawning trash enemies, which add to the nonstop annoyance, and in the case of the final encounter, can be downright infuriating.
Still, despite its flaws, Van Helsing is a solid game, though you may be better off buying the complete edition rather than the episodic content.

I'd like to say in advance, I LOVE Steampunk games, I LOVE Hack 'n Slash, but most of all, I LOVE Van Helsing.
This game is, in many ways, a fantastic one. The behavioral settings on Lady Katarina are interesting and helpful, the loot system is ok, the music and environment are great, and the voice acting is one of the best in Indie gaming history. The Drawback, however, is in the actual "Hack 'n Slash" part. This games Combat is HORRIBLE. and the reasons are that, one, you hold still and sit there everytime you attack which is annoying for ranged players and downright punishing for melee players. The other problem with combat is the fact that the game attacks your targets for you, meaning I, a ranged player, cannot chose which guy I'm gunna shoot at. Instead the game is gunna make me shoot the wolf instead of the wolf handler, or the boss. So I don't get to chose my targets which hurt melee players even more, because, unless they are lucky, can't Dps the highest damage monster and are forced to sit there and take hits from all the guys while they are stuck hit that Fricking wolf that deals no damage whatsoever. So those are the problems with combat. Other problems include the lack of tutorial on how the inventory and level ups and as well as specail attacks work. It wasn't a glaring problem since I am a Dark Souls player and don't need my hand held, but it took me a frustrating 10 Mins to figure out how to equip better gear. My final qualm is this. BlazBlue: Continuum Shift Extend, which I’ll refer to as CSE from now on, is a 2D fighting game by Arc System Works which has been on the consoles for a while, but was recently ported onto Steam for Windows following their success with their port of the first game in the series, BlazBlue: Calamity Trigger.
Gameplay
A lot of people find it rather difficult to play fighting games using the Mouse and Keyboard setup, so the game does support controllers, along with local versus mode so you can play against your friends. When compared to other fighters such as Street Fighter, Blazblue’s mechanics are more complex and deeper so its not as great of a pick-up for players looking to learn how to play fighting games but like all things, if you’re dedicated enough to practice, you’ll be able to play the game no problem, though it may take some time compared to people with experience in other fighters. However, if you’re just looking for casual play with friends,  the game comes with a beginner mode, called Stylish, which gives the user one-button combos, similar to Persona 4 Arena’s combat system. ss+(2014-12-12+at+07.48.55)Whether you’re new to the BlazBlue series or fighting games in general, CSE offers a fairly in-depth tutorial on the game’s mechanics and general advice for each character in the game so players wanting to learn the franchise can do so without pressure in the tutorial and training modes.
Other gameplay modes included in the game are:
Versus – A standard 1v1 match against a friend or a computer.
Score Attack – 1 player fights various computer controlled characters to get a high-score.
Unlimited Mars – Score Attack with smarter bots and enemies have stronger and alternate abilities.
Challenge – 1 player attempts to perform combinations of moves (combos) fluidly on a passive bot.
Abyss – A pseudo-dungeon where players can buy upgrades to their characters to fight against regular and Unlimited Mars
For collectors, you earn currency to buy items with in the gallery, such as the boss characters from Unlimited Mars and the Story, artwork, and additional voice-packs. In addition to all these extra modes that provide plenty to do, especially if you’re still a beginner and have a hard time completing certain modes, the game also comes with a story mode, which I thought was rather long and text-heavy for a fighting game. Some people may like it, others probably won’t since fighting games aren’t usually known for their story. The story is fully voiced in English, also Japanese as DLC which is currently being included for free, presented in a similar style to visual novels, with the character model appearing on screen standstill, and occasional artwork.
2014-12-12_00004
The game’s main story is coherent enough and even gives you a playthrough of the previous games’ main plotline, but the writing itself made various out of place references to internet culture and was, in general, so bad that you hope they were trying to be ironic. They have to be right? No one could possibly think naming your main character The Bloodedge was a good idea. Right?
2014-12-12_00005
Apart from the main storyline, is a series of lore, entitled, Teach Me Miss Litchi!, which doesn’t offer anything in terms of gameplay, but creates some humorous skits and touch upon the world’s lore, which I admittedly do not follow very well since anything that has to do with multiple universes and time travel just flies right over my head.
The game’s online is rather barebones, but functions without any major hiccups. The standard amount of settings for 1v1 versus like, the number of rounds, duration of each round, how many players can be in the lobby, who gets to participate in the next round, usage of special characters, and whether to make a private/public/ranked (to play for Player Skill Rating and earn a spot on the leaderboards) lobby are all included, but not much more.
Graphics
Being a 2D fighter, the game’s graphics were never that demanding to begin with so being on the PC doesn’t offer as much in terms of graphical improvements as it would with other genres. While it does output in “native” 1080p compared to the consoles’ 720p output, it doesn’t seem to do anything as the graphics both in-game and in the menus look identical to their console counterparts, even with Anti-Aliasing set to 4x (the maximum the game allows).
Click on the image for a full-size view.
Click on the image for a full-size view.
The artwork and in-game backgrounds are very visually appealing, but doesn’t really mean much when the in-game character models and even the menus are so jagged.
Audio
The game’s voice acting was done fairly well in both the English and Japanese dubs of the game. I thought the game’s soundtrack was really solid, but lacked variety as  pretty much every track in the game was a variation of fast-paced, anime theme song, so people who don’t enjoy that style of music probably won’t enjoy this game’s soundtrack either. The game’s sound effects were varied enough too so you have a good idea of what’s happening and won’t get confused by the verbal diarrhea that tends to occur when people start executing faster combos since all the game’s characters seem to love shouting out what move they’re using.
Verdict
One of the issues of the game I didn’t talk about previous was that this was a port of a game originally released 4 years ago on consoles, with the DLC included in the Extend edition only being a year younger. In that time, consoles have already received the series’ next installment, Chronophantasma, which is likely to be ported onto Steam eventually as well. The game also carries a $30 price point on Steam while you could it for $20 on consoles rather easily.

The game is also a hard sell since the game’s price point is extremely high for a port of a 4 year old game, especially when you know the sequel is already out on consoles and probably will be ported to the PC as well. Amazing metroidvania game.
Simply put: This is exactly what a metroidvania game should be.
The exploration is great, and doesn't feel tedious, even when backtracking through areas you've already been through.
The platforming is emphasized perfectly. Lots of very fun platforming puzzles that are very rewarding, and fun to find.
The battles are well designed, focusing on learning patterns to defeat an enemy, rather than fussing aroud with which weapon would or wouldn't be optimal (since there is only 1 weapon)
Amazing secrets, from simple secret entrances for a basic powerup like a health container, all the way to the suprisingly massive (and well hidden) post-game content.
Great difficulty curve. I feel this game sets the standard for difficutly curves in metroidvania games. You'll be trying to beat each boss multiple times (for me, it was around 3-5 tries per boss), as you learn their patterns, and the exploration is just dangerous enough to keep you on edge, but not too difficult to be constantly dying while exploring.
Going off of difficulty curve, there's no ammo or health, or any pickups besides powerups/collectibles. This means you don't worry about ammo for a weapon, and you heal at save points (and some other designated spots). This is great because it means you are never farming enemies for health/ammo/etc.
Amazing post-game. You defeat the final boss, and have most (if not all) of the map unlocked, but as you continue to play, you don't even realize that there is a very large, challenging, and well planned post game which is very satisfying for those completionists out there.
Really this is everything I could've asked for in a metroidvania.
If you're a fan of the metroidvania genre, you will NOT be dissapointed here!

Fallout 3 is a great game, and I recommend it. However, if this is your first time playing it, you should know what you're in for.
STORY:
The main quest line in FO3 is...good, but not great. The prologue is pretty much universally hated -- don't judge the game until you exit the vault. Really, the prologue is bad, but just push through it. Beyond that, the first half of the main quest line is basically running around from place to place following the path your father took. It's a little bit "your princess is another castle"-ish. However, it does get better closer to the end.
If you're used to the detail-rich factions of Fallout 1 and 2, you should be prepared: Fallout 3 has no nuance in that regard. One faction is good, others are bad, and there's pretty much no explanation for it other than that's the way it is. FO3 is set up very well in that there are always multiple ways to resolve quests, but the choices are fairly black and white -- good karma or bad karma. In short, there's little of the nuance regarding, for example, the philosophy of the super mutants in Fallout 1. Super mutants are just bad in this game -- they are giant ogres who kill people. They cannot be reasoned with, they cannot be aligned with.
GAMEPLAY:
All in all, there is a lot of freedom and flexibility in this game. There are great melee weapons, small guns, big guns, and energy weapons, and you're free to choose a character that suits your style. Energy weapons are a bit weak, even with maxed out energy weapons skills, but closer to the end there are some good energy weapons available as well. The world is absolutely littered with items. Lots of junk, but lots of useful stuff as well, with guns, ammo, books to upgrade skills, etc. FO3 was also the first game to introduce crafting mechanics into the Fallout universe. It's not as extensive as in the later games, but repairing your weapons and armor is a critical part of the game, and you can find instructions for crafting unique homemade weapons at various points in the game as well. All these add up to a lot of freedom to create the character you want.
On a practical note, I played this game on Windows 10 and had no real issues; however, on very few occasions the game did crash. I would recommend looking into the Unofficial Fallout 3 Patch mod and the CASM mod that periodically autosaves the game. That can prevent a lot of frustration if you do run into problems, and the patch mod especially fixes a lot of issues with the buggy DLC areas. But with regard to Windows 8/10, I had few problems, but your mileage may vary.
EXPLORATION AND SIDE QUESTS:
Fallout 3 has a huge open world, and that's great! But at times it can feel extremely sparse. There are a total of 18 side quests in the entire game. The DLC adds another 26 main and side quests, but I found the DLC in general very lacklustre. More on that later. But sure, you're running around a wasteland, of course it's going to be sparse! However, most of the locations you will find out there are mostly just there to fight enemies and collect loot. There's little backstory, even in places where I expected I might find a little backstory. The locations just...exist. And you can scavenge stuff from them. This was the aspect of FO3 that I found most disappointing. I spent a long time exploring new areas, but in the end I didn't feel very rewarded at all for it. Moreover, the buildings start looking extremely similar after a while. Apparently every company in existence uses the same filing cabinets, the same computers, the same desks, the same wallpaper, etc. At times it just got really, really repetitive. Find another generic building with the same generic office supplies, and loot the area for the same weapons and ammo. In general, my recommendation would be to read up on the wiki a little bit and be intentional about the places you go to explore. Go to the places with side quests or collectible items, and skip the rest.
DIALOGUE:
This was the first Fallout game to have voice acting for all characters. And that's nice, but it seems as though their budget might not have been high enough to make it work well. Perhaps part of the reason for the lack of nuance in the different factions might have been because that would drive up the cost of voice actors. Most characters have little back story, other than a basic "this is my current motivation right now". You might also find that you can recognize voice actors who voiced multiple characters, but I actually found this a little endearing. I think there were a total of two child actors -- one for male, one for female, but I could be wrong.
One of the major issues with the dialogue system, however, are the speech checks. These are essentially a dice roll, so the higher your speech skill the more chance you have of succeeding. I don't have a problem with that, but when you succeed it felt so unnatural that I largely stopped using the speech checks. Here's a random example:
NPC: "No way, you can't come in unless you do X, Y, and Z."
You: "[Speech: 80%] I think you should let me in."
[SUCCESS]
NPC: "You know what, come right in!"
Each time I succeeded at a speech check, the NPC had such an immediate 180 change of heart, that it felt like I had hypnotized the person and made them bend to my will. It felt completely bizarre. Speech skills weren't a way to reason with the person and make them come to see your point of view. It was an immediate "No, you should do what I want." "Oh okay, you're completely right!" It was downright creepy at times. And in most cases, the speech checks are there to either (a) skip past entire quests, or (b) convince them to give you more money for doing something. Honestly, I think you'll have more fun if you bypass the speech check options. I did, anyway.
DLC:
In my opinion, the DLC is a little hit and miss, but ultimately worth playing. I really enjoyed The Pitt, and Point Lookout was pretty good as well. I wasn't a fan of Operation: Anchorage, and I absolutely hated Mothership Zeta. But that's entirely subjective, and you might feel differently. Broken Steel is worth getting simply for the fact that it raises the level cap and lets you play the game indefinitely. However, I think it does so at the cost of completely ruining the original ending of the game. But I'd recommend leaving all the DLC until you are at least level 20. They're quite challenging. They are also apparently quite buggy, though I didn't experience any problems. It may be because of the Unofficial Patch mod I mentioned earlier.
To summarize, there is a lot to like about Fallout 3, and translating the isometric world of Fallout 1 and 2 into the sprawling 3D open world of Fallout 3 opens up a whole new way of enjoying the Fallout universe. I put 135 hours into the game, and overall I enjoyed myself. But the game has its flaws, and I think knowing them up front will help you look past them to enjoy the good aspects of the game.

It's a fairly standard sprawling yet linear adventure: think Half-Life 2 and The Last of Us.  Though it is completely on rails, it feels vast, like you're carving a natural path through a huge mega city.  It is also GORGEOUS.  Constantly.  I mean, it may not be the most technically advanced game out there, but it has world design on par with HL2's City 17.  Combat is button-mashing combo junk like Assassin's Creed or Shadows of Murder with annoying QTEs capping off boss fights, which is really the only disappointment the game presents (aside from very restrictive "platforming" segments filling out most of the game).  More pleasantly, maybe it's the agile woman protagonist in a French sci-fi setting, or maybe it's thematic parallels between memory access technology and photography, but I feel the spirit of Beyond Good & Evil in abundance here.  As a fairly enjoyable hop and skip through a fantastic dystopian future landscape, I would recommend it for the visuals alone.

The story is so remarkably well-crafted that the linearity isn't any sort of issue (to be honest, anything else might just detract from it).
The characters are believable and interesting.
The aesthetic, while simple, is beautiful.
The music is phenominal.

Does it have its flaws? Of course. Do I care? Not a lick.

(Disclaimer: I have played about 3,5 hours of a non-steam version of this game, this copy comes from Humble Bundle.)
As a person who has played a lot of good Hack 'n' Slash games in their life, and really enjoys the genre, I am sorry to say that Van Helsing does not hold up to the competition.
There are a couple of VERY important elements that every game in this genre has to absolutely nail to make the the gameplay loop, that is inherently repetetive, fun and enjoyable to the point of of not minding the repetition. I'm going to quickly explain how VH fails at each one of them:
1. Animations and effects: Fighting must look flashy and dynamic, that goes for both the player and monsters. There lies the first fault of this game, both player and monster animations are lethargic, nobody looks like they actually want to fight each other. Weapon swings are slow and unnatural, and some of the animations look downright silly (dual blade swinging looks like some kind of oriental dance, not fencing!). Spells and other effects don't look too good either, some of them actually made me laugh at how bad they are.
2. Feedback: Maybe the most important of all is the feedback player gets when smashing through hordes of enemies. How much fun we have with the combat depends on how well everything sounds, how awesome do spells and abilities feel, how much impact there is behind every blow we make, etc. Why would I play the game that is all about killing things, when I feel like I'm swinging blindly in the air, instead of smashing the opponent's face? Why would I cast the spells that look and feel like throwing glowsticks or lighting up deodorant? Yeah... Van Helsing is exactly that, plus it sounds painfuly mediocore at all times.
3. Loot: That's the drive that keeps us all going. The more interesting you make your loot, the more interested we are at playing your game. Now, I have only played for about 3,5 hours, but I have not seen a SINGLE cool piece of equipment at all. All passive stats and basic effects not worth mentioning. Just take one look at Diablo III items, and you'll see what I mean. Maybe it gets better later, but I should have to get the good stuff only in the end of the game, I want to have fun on the way as well!
Summary: In my opinion, VH fails as a H'n'S in every way. The main things that make a game in this genre fun are not present. There is absolutely no reason to buy it, especially because it exists on the market where we have things like Path of Exile: free game that's a better Hack 'n' Slash in every aspect, or Torchlight 2: a game that costs about the same and is infinitely better. Unless you are a lotal addict, avoid at all cost.

Going to warn you right off the bat - I'm going to rant. I'm frustrated about the current condition of a game that I used to love, and even more frustrated that nothing will ever be done about it. TL;DR if you wish, I know this is a bit long, but I could have written more.
The thing about games like these, more often that not, is that it's the people playing that make the game great, not the game itself. I could say the same about Halo 2 or 3, or Garry's Mod, or Battlefield, or any decent MMO, or what have you. Seeing as I recently built a gaming PC, and in observation of the console hackfest, I bought the PC version of this once-great shooter to try and rekindle the feeling of brotherhood and teamwork I got playing with friends years ago.
Unfortunately, due to its age and some other factors, CoD4 has lost this glimmer.
As far as the game itself, it's the last good Call of Duty, honestly. I faithfully played the Xbox 360 version until around the time MW3 came out, by then it became so infested with hackers that it became difficult to play a legitimate game. The PC version's dedicated servers have, for the most part, kept hackers at bay, but since Punkbuster is a pain to deal with, I don't feel like installing it, and thus have to play on unprotected servers. (I have Windows 8.1, and I'm honestly surprised CoD4 runs as well as it does on my system. The last time I tried installing Punkbuster for CoD4, it gave me a whole bunch of random errors that I didn't feel like dealing with.)
One thing I liked about Call of Duty in the past is that it was relatively simple, CoD4 being no exception. WaW and even leading up to Black Ops things were still pretty simple. In MW2 I used to be able to tell, just by its firing sound, what weapon was used to kill someone, and relatively how far away. Now, in Ghosts, there's a whole bunch of stuff that I'm not willing to put in the effort to comprehend. I can't even imagine what Advanced Warfare is going to be like.
Call of Duty as a whole has become a pit of despair. ...There seems to be a thing about golden guns that really seems to get at people, and the effect it's had on the industry is not good. A lot of free FPSs that I play to kill time feature golden guns, but can only be bought with its respective premium currency - I can only deduce that this is due to the popularity of golden guns in the Call of Duty series, and they have been implemented as an attempt to make more profit. But, sorry, I'm going off on a tangent. I should be writing about CoD4.
Back in the day, you used to be able to grab a few friends, party up on Xbox Live, and play a good game of Search with good people. It was great. The feeling of brotherhood I got during those days was only matched by Halo 3. Now, I can't find a legitimate game. I was playing TDM today, with 40 players on Killhouse.
40 PLAYERS ON KILLHOUSE!!
That's TOO MANY PEOPLE. Now, maybe this is because I can't use Punkbuster, but I can't find a server with a good population that has less than a 30-player cap. 30 is too many! The maps are too small and the game is too fast-paced for that kind of a cap. 30 players is more of a low-population Battlefield server, which has the size of maps needed to support that.
And another thing - the darned auto-balance is horrible. Way to separate me from my friends while we're playing, server...I think that feature is stock, but it's still bad. This never happened on console, and we never had any issues with balance.
Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare has a very special place in my heart. It's painful to see it in this state - not just the PC version, but across all platforms.
I *want* to recommend it. But I can't. It's not worth $20 for a completely ruined game. I'm sorry.

Putting such a simple story into the game can makes hundreds of player cry. The music is a master level piece and touches your heart all the time. The art is amazing and different all the time. Review:
This game is amazing, after beating the whole games, I cried at least 5 times. Put you in game, the first 5 minute already threw the tear gas at you. The game is a decent puzzle game with a really smooth animations. Arts in the games is amazing, the music is top class.
The story is about Ori, the little light cutie who got adopted by Naru, which is the purple creature. One day the forest orb got stolen by the huge bird, everything in the forest starting to be destroyed and infected. Invade by all the evil creatures. The whole forest became a mess and you Ori need to save the forest. I am not going to tell you what's happened before that or after that. The characters in the game all have their own story that makes you cry and reflect about.
The game is definitely challenging , I died countless of time and perhaps a bit angry sometimes. However, the story after is worth it. Your skills will level up through time and you can unlock news skills from exploring places. There's secondary level up but it is not a "Must" to have them, but they sure will make the game easier for you. After spending 7 hours in game, with a play style like speed running just for the story, there's a tons of areas that I haven't explore yet, the game can last longer than 8 hours in my opinion.
The games does have some cons, because there's no teleport or fast travel, once you arrive the location, it would tell you to go somewhere else further. From your starting locations on the left side through the right side, then at last it will tell you to go back near the beginning. Therefore, it will get kinda boring. Personally think that the game's simple story line and music overpowered and left the game behind. Sometimes, I just dont really care about the gameplay and just want to know what's going to happen. Therefore, you will miss alot of things when you trying to avoid enemies and get to the location as soon as possible. It is a place to place pattern, no side quest and only got one straight storyline, so sometimes you might just ignore the locked areas and just wanted to proceed your journey.
I will suggest this game to people who likes to play puzzle games or platformers, the gameplay is challenging and smooth, if you like the feeling of being chased or escaping, this is probably the platformer you are looking for. But you will still need to die a few times to understand the map and how it works, later on the skills will increase, you will forgot about the bottons and things just get a bit complicated, but you will work it out anyway since the game will always give you some puzzles for you to refresh your memory. I would'nt suggest this game to people who don't like stories telling, "People who never cried because a movie" or "I am a smart person, intellgent over feelings" because this game's stories is what makes you motivative, it is like a rollercoaster and playing around with your feelings. If you don't like the touching theme, you won't like to proceed the game since we play the game to feel.

I've also spent a lot of time collecting the golden bricks and these quests often didn't make any sense to me and I failed a few because I just didn't figure out how to complete them. A good example is one quest in the beginning, where I had to bring chickens and pigs into a stable. Each time I managed that, another pig or chicken escaped the stable. So I was basically expected to have a speedrun to complete this quest.
In the end, I just gave up as I decided the game wasn't fun for me anymore. Maybe at some point I'll have a look at it again.

A lot of fun, an incredible game that doesn't seem to end (until, well, you kind of finish the main "Golden bricks" collecting which is a little sad).
The UI might not be the best thing ever, as well as the overall controlling, as it can feel clunky at times but this game is full of content and stuff to do; I remember spending countless hours making my own racetracks by terraforming, and playing on them with the different vehicles I collected was just so natural, finding new biomes and structures for the first time is always the best part, knowing there is so much left to do, the curiosity fuels the entire purpose of LEGO Worlds.
The only major downsides are how finding chests, which contain new, sometimes essential items and stuff is more of a grind instead of an actual adventure, the other problem is the rather complicated building, it's just not easy, at least not the brick by brick way, so whenever I got asked to build a house for an NPC I just spammed the "place brick" button until the objective was met. Don't get me wrong though, when it comes to exploring and finding creatures it really gives some sense of accomplishment, when you get to a place you have never been, or when you see a character you want to be, you actually feel good about it.
There are countless good things about this game, and I surely don't want to spoil anything but the game is awesome, and maybe not perfect, but it surely occupies a place in my LEGO heart as all the animals and characters are just so unique and charming in their own ways (Don't ask me why but the pigs in particular are somehow very cute).

At the time of this review, I have only finished about half of the game. I will likely come back to it some day, but I have too many good games in my inventory to bother with this right now.
I had high hopes for this game, and really wanted to like it.  It has a lot of the stylistic appeal of
, with some added super-cool
-style interfaces.  Unfortunately, it seems to have taken all their effort to get this far, and the combat and environment suffer for it.
One of the biggest complaints I have might be poo-poohed by folks, so I'll get it out of the way.  After 5
games, 3
games and
, gamers have been trained to respond to an attacking enemy in this style of game by pressing "Y".  To have this game copy everything else control-wise in the other games
that is a bit of a hurdle.
Ok, now to the main points:
: this is the worst part to me.  There was so much promise in this city--slums and ledges and boxes and rooftops. To find yourself unable to even climb on a box in the street is insulting. To then have these hidden items in places that are not easy to locate is just trolling.  Such a rich world, but it quickly becomes apparent that it's just a hallway with fancy wallpaper.  On the few occasions when a puzzle needs you to interact with the environment, it is often so poorly indicated that I couldn't even tell there was a puzzle there.
: So, first there's the whole "can't block" issue that killed me plenty of times.  I'm willing to write that off to poor playing on my part.  Unfortunately, that's not all that's bad about the combat. The next thing is the "combos".  you get a series of combos, but they are all variations of X and Y, so there can only be a few.  On top of that, the shortest combo is 3 strikes.  The next one is 4, and then 5.  This sounds fine, but since dodging breaks the combo and getting hit breaks the combo, I was rarely able to string more than 3 attacks together when fighting more than 2-3 enemies. So, effectively, I had one combo.  The last issue leads into the next one...
: You learn to remix memories pretty early, and then....don't use it for a long time.  As a central core of the entire world they have built, you'd think they would do more with it.  Really, it is used for the very rare remix, and for exchanging information via high-tech implanted electronics that in centuries past would have been passed via a map scribbled on a napkin.
So the point of all this is that really, they had a great idea for this game but didn't have the money, time or talent to pull it off.  Which is really a shame.  You can see true greatness peeking out from behind the bars of
, but sadly it will never see the light of day.  I will instead believe that the game was so great that it threatened to destroy the world, and so the government and dontnod conspired to create this game and erased the original from everyone's memory.
EDIT: Oh!  I can't believe I forgot this.  The developers speak French, and I don't.  And even
was offended by the pronounciation of the French words in the game (Saint Michel, La Bastille, etc).
:
I finished the game the other day, and have a few things to add. You do a lot more remixing later in the game, so that is something. In fact, it gets a little tedious, which is kind of funny considering the huuuuuuge gap at the beginning.  The combat is still highly repetitive and still sucks, though I was able to pull off longer combos. It was still difficult to know when an area was open and when it wasn't, although later in the game you spend more time inside, so it's more clear.
The story is amazing. The world they made is amazing. But the gameplay is just not up to it. If you can get it for <$10, do it. Beyond that...go play
again.

F3 is open world roleplaying, FPS and survival game. The Fallout universe paints a picture of a dystopian future. It exists in what people on the cusp of the atomic revolution in the 1950s saw as the sci-fi world of tomorrow. if several thousand nuclear bombs were dropped on it. It's a quaint sci-fi view of a future filled with atomic cars, robot servants, and incredibly basic computer terminals. A nuclear war has taken away most of these technological comforts, providing the backdrop for a game with a dreary, desperate atmosphere filled with glib and dark humor. It's a world that is both fantastic and somehow believable. And it is one that's exciting to explore.
You play as the Vault Dweller, a blank slate for you to write your story on. The game begins with your birth and then quickly moves through childhood with snapshots of pivotal events, such as the day you get your Pip-Boy 3000. You live in Vault 101, a bunker designed to keep its occupants alive through the nuclear war that ravaged the surface. At the end of your childhood, you awake to alarms and confusion. Your father has opened the vault entrance and taken flight. The fragile existence of the other vault inhabitants has been shattered. Nothing will ever be the same, especially for you since it is your charge to leave the relative comfort of Vault 101 and search for your father out in the wastes.

Another of the little known projects that Grasshopper picked up and published. A stylized and exceedingly lush visual presentation is the highlight of the game, and every fan of the schmup genre should at least try it out. You won't be going for high scores as much as other games but the veteran mode is decent enough for me and gives me a good challenge. Arcade has an Insane mode for those looking to go higher.
The games stages are varied and beautiful, featuring some really cool bosses that fight you through multiple tiers and angles. Design wise in the art department this game is tops. Nothing else like it really. It is probably the pinnacle of visuals in a shmup so far to be honest. Soldner-x 2 on PS3 is about the only one to give it some heat. Not many new ones are made and this one clearly had some work put into it. That alone does give it worth.
The gameplay is pretty solid too. Various pilots and weapons are available. It doesn't quite have all the options and varied modes of Raiden IV but not many games do. For 10 bucks and much less on sale you really cannot go wrong here. Story mode is a great little jaunt and Arcade is fun for picking your own custom way through the game. Fast Forward button is working for me and makes playthroughs a lot smoother in the cutscenes. The mechanics are varied enough for at least a good ten hours, though, the story is somewhat interesting if a little weird and disjointed.
I see no reason to hate on this game at all. Buncha whining babies if you ask me. We barely get these games. To trash the ones we do have, especially when they are this high quality, is perverse and ridiculous to the extreme.
At any rate it's one of the best looking shmups ever made. Look in the FAQ and max it in the command line Steam options. Prepare for some decent bullet hell.

What can I say about Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice that hasn't been said already?
Well, a lot actually.
The game starts off by warning you that the game deals with psychosis, and my first thing to tell you is that you should probably look it up because it most likely means something different than what you think it means. But before I can tell you about the game, I have to tell you a little about myself.
I suffer from mental illness and deal with psychosis. I had a period in my life a few years ago where I really went off the deep end but somehow managed to find my way back to reality on my own... or at least I think I did. Playing this game was something that was extremely difficult to start doing, and once I started, it felt somewhat disturbing in that I was experiencing symptoms again. However, I found this game more cathartic than anything. Playing this game made me feel like someone understands what I deal with, and not just someone who's lived through it themselves. It made me feel not so alone in the world while I was playing it.
There's a popular YouTuber named Rags who said in his review video that a drawback of this game was that it didn't have replayability. I must say that I have to sternly disagree with him. If you haven't lived through this experience in your own life, then you didn't pick up on everything that the game offers. This game is absolutely flawless in it's portrayal, from the helplessness you feel with the controller at the beginning of the game to all the little details, including how Senua moves her eyes. These aspects you will most likely take for granted your first time playing the game. Sure, you'll acknowledge it, you'll understand why things are the way they are in the game, but you won't feel it. That's why any good movie needs to be watched at least twice: the first time so you can figure out what's going on, the second so you can better put yourself in the characters shoes.
There's a video that comes included with the game that talks about what the developers did in order to make the experience the way they did. If you want the full experience of the game and to better understand what people with this condition deal with, then I suggest that you play through the game, watch the video, and then play through the game again.
But for me, Senua is so relatable, I have to question whether or not this game is real.

The good and the bad!
Graphics: The graphics in Lego Worlds are not amazing but they are Lego, they fit the game perfectly and the 3D effects of the Lego itself are really good! The explosions, digging, clouds, vehicles etc are all super fitting for this game, seriously they stand out and make it feel like apart of the Lego Universe!
Audio: The audio is simple, seriously! Nothing massive or heavy needed, no voices needed for character, only the narrator at times who talks over the top of you, with a slightly Little Big Planet feel (PS Game) Clicking, Clacking, Boping, Digging are all sounds that are basic but at the same time, it is Lego and what audio effects would you like?
Controls: The controls.. This is where the game falls! I cannot stand the controls in this game and for some unknown reason you cannot remap the keys and MUST be played with an Xbox Controller! The keyboard controls are all over the place and not helpful or fitting in anyway, but then using an Xbox controller did make it easier but was not better completely and I often found myself forgetting the keys and pressing the wrong one!
Gameplay and everything else: I suspect that a lot of people are going to jump into this expecting Minecraft, but I highly suggest you do not! - There is no eating or survival system in this game, but there is a survival DLC!
The game has all sorts of Lego comedy going for it which would bring children into the game to play, too which you can play with two people on one PC, which is awesome for parents or kids alike to play together at a cheaper cost!
One annoying issue, when playing Adventure mode with a friend online, the stuff created, explored and progressed ONLY effect the host and not the other player! This I found was a huge let down for the other friends in the game!
You can use Sandbox if you just want to create anything and everything, with all items open which is seriously enjoyable!
Adventure mode is basically like a campaign too which you can do this with a friend, but if you are doing Adventure mode and want more, then make sure you complete the first 3 worlds right up until you get your 10th golden brick and then quit to main screen, once there a code section is unlocked and there, you can enter these codes:
LY9C8M – Lock & Roller – NEXO KNIGHTS.
XP3BN2 – Lance's Driller – NEXO KNIGHTS.
P42FJ6 – Police Car – LEGO City.
BG7DWK – Getaway Car – LEGO City.
U98BR2 – Pizza Van – LEGO City.
BR1CK5 – Unlocks All Bricks.
F1XTRS – Unlocks All Windows And Doors.
The world sizes start off small in Adventure mode, lots of people get this confused thinking world size is tiny but just wait! When you upgrade your ship more and more, you are able to increase the world size as you progress through and they are very large!
Caves, dungeons, treasure, chests, zombies, skelentons, pirates, monsters, exploring and soooo much more.  There is a fair share of content in this game to keep you going if you love the Lego world!
Creating things is confusing I found! I do not like the way you create a building from scratch in this game, that being the controls and the way you move around in one, which makes it confusing and very slow to create anything and everything! - Good easy way is, once you get the scan and copy tool... If you find an item, building, statue, volcano, etc etc ingame that you really like the look off, then you are able to scan the entire size, save and then import it into any world you like WITHOUT having to recreate it block for block yourself!
Riding animals is weird but deeply fun for kids.. Yes, you heard that correct! I could of singled out a horse or pony but no, you can ride pigs, octopuses, giraffes etc and it makes for some seriously weird stuff but deeply amusing!
Children will love this game and they can go off and explore with a few friends if they all own the game or one other on the same PC, but adults too can also enjoy the universe too which create!
You can discover items but having enough ingame money, getting your discover tool out and pressing X on the controller so discover, this then unlocks the item for ever, so it is highly suggest to go around every single world with this tool out if you want them all unlocked to use at a later date (No need to do this if you only want to play Sandbox, this is for adventure mode only) Also, using the tool, you can fire out animals (HIGHLY AMUSING) and other items instantly dropping them into a world of your choosing.
Would I recommend this game? Yes, why not! I love Lego and this is as close as I can get to playing in an open world Lego universe with doing anything from building to exploring!

Somewhere far into space there is a biome conservation station. On it, many scientific experiments happen. Conundrums that are going test your might, agility, space orientation, intuition and patience. Especially patience. You land your craft in its bay. You're neither a tourist, nor a scientist. You are about to get tested.
This is the essence of Metroidvania genre. Ironically, it's also one of the cheapest price-wise from the bunch. The exploration aspect of this game has people talking. ESA features so many secret rooms, reading story bits, boosts and easter eggs, both included in story mode and optional, that it takes a precise map and sincere effort to find them all.
To master this game means to master mechanics such as jump, dash, hook, charge & spam shot. The controls are what you expect them to be, no awkward combinations or button layouts. Alternatively, I've never got comfortable with dash mechanic in Hyper Light Drifter, a similar in a sense game, where you have to direct gamepad's trigger with inhumane speed. Thus I couldn't have found a number of unlocks and secrets, hidden behind trials which required continious dashing through spikes or disappearing tiles. In ESA there's an instadeath spike maze and dash sections, but oppositely I was in control of them.
While this game is undoubtedly hard, you can count ridicilous rooms on one hand. ESA'a gritty flavor is where you fall in love with it. It tries hard to seem harder than it actually is. It loves showing you the pick ups through the walls in a yet unaccessible room. Then It taunts you with empty rewards room while you are at 1 HP, saying, "The upgrade - it's missing, move along". But the upgrade is there close by, hidden. There are bosses that turn the screen into a bullet hell, however there are openings where you can reduce them to half of their health in a matter of seconds. If you are looking for an idealistic Metroidvania experience, you've come to the right address.

This is a surprisingly atmospheric, pixel-graphic metroid-style game.  It's tough, clever, and intriguing.  If you look at this and think, "I bet I'd like that, but I've been burned before", don't hesitate.  I think you'll seriously enjoy it.

Long story short, this is a simple-looking but surprisingly complex and satisfying Metroid clone.  If you like Metroid clones, you should give this a try, period, though there are flaws.
Essentially it's what you'd expect from this sub-genre of game; a 2d platforming interface with a large map to explore and upgradesd throughout.  I use Metroid clone rather than Metroidvania to describe it since it lacks any of the RPG elements usually associated with the -vania affix; this is pure, oldschool Metroid style, not unlike Axiom Verge or AM2R.  Of course, it's a bit less 'pretty' than those games, opting for an ultra-simplistic 8bit style with 8x8 tiles (rather than the 16x16 you'd usually see in this style of game), yet it still manages to get the job done with surprising flair and quality in this approach.  As well, the soundtrack's quite nice and aesthetically the game pulls off a great eerie, lonely atmosphere.  It basically pulls off something similar to Super Metroid's tone using only tools a bit closer to Metroid 1's, which is impressive in and of itself.
As far as gameplay goes, it's for the most part about as simple as this kind of game gets; you run, jump, and shoot, with upgrades that increase your ability to do most these things in various, simple ways.  Once or twice you'll encounter a somewhat unique upgrade such as the grappling hook which comes with a surprisingly deep physics system that allows skilled and clever players to sequence break with it alone, but most everything else is almost disappointingly bland given how crazy powerups in this genre have gotten (again Axiom Verge is a good example).  What's more, and this is the game's deepest fault IMHO, the feeling of increasing in power as you traverse the game -- perhaps the single most addicting element of this genre -- is stifled in myriad ways.  Not only are the powerups themselves generally small and rarely make you feel a full order of magnitude more powerful in and of themselves, but the game does all kinds of things to keep you feeling modest.  Most notably, as you go through the game and power yourself up, the station "comes alive" more and more and traversing the gameworld actually becomes
difficult, even if you can techinically reach new places... though occasionally you'll even be locked completely out of previous zones until later still!  And even at the very end, when you're fully geared and the whole map should be your oyster, it's kind of a nightmare to get from place to place, even with the teleport system you unlock.  And on top of all that, the endgame is absolutely full of challenges that limit your powerups or force you to turn them off or punish you for using certain ones... it truly makes you feel almost bad for powering up at several points, and that's not a great thing.
And speaking of endgame... yeah... well.  It's hard enough as it is, definitely a challenging game to begin with and most the bosses will give you a run for your money until you've memorized them quite well, ESPECIALLY toward the end... but oh, no no no, even beating the difficult final boss isn't really the end, of course.  At this point you're meant to solve some intensely crazy, ARG-level puzzles throughuot the game, complete all kinds of wild challenges (several of which force you to turn off your meager powerups or punish you for using them, as stated) and complete "hell areas" to get the "real" ending, and... honestly?  This is where I gave up.  I love to do everything in these types of games, and surpass all the challenges, but ESA... between the difficulty of traversing the map, the mostly-weak powerups and the meek feeling brought about by their limitations, the fact I even got lost as to what to do next with use of guides at this point, and the brutal difficulty and myriad things to do... this endgame was just too much.  Of course, some of you may be salivating at the sound of that challenge, so it's not necessarily a bad thing, but just beware.
Even with all those criticisms, I'd still recommend this game if you're a fan of the genre.  It was truly an out-of-nowhere surprise and if you're very patient and curious you may get a hugely rewarding experience -- and even if you're like me and quit after the 'bad' ending, it'll still be worth the time and money.

Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus is by far one of the best shooters I’ve played this year, rivaling last year’s Doom 2016 by id Tech, Wolfenstein II is the definitive example of what it means to be a modern first-person shooter. Wolfenstein II is yet another nod to the classic Wolfenstein 3D originally released back in May of 1992. Deemed the father of all first-person shooters the Wolfenstein series still has plenty of life left and I can’t where to see where the series goes next.
At it’s core, Wolfenstein II is a massive upgrade over the previous game in the series. Both the visuals and the gameplay have greatly improved offering players new ways to play and create encounters with enemies varying level to level. Players can chose to approach any combat situation in a stealth-base manor, all guns blazing or a combination of the two. Be weary, the enemies in Wolfenstein II are also a lot smarter than they were in the last game, flanking the player and predicting your next movements. Best of luck to players wanting a real challenge with the plethora of difficulty modes found in the main menu.
Wolfenstein II sets the bar extremely high and is most definitely the best in the series. Unlike its predecessor, Wolfenstein II greatly balances the mindless shooting aspect and the narrative driven gameplay found in most shooters. You’ll always want to be shooting something, but you’re constantly reminded why you’re shooting throughout the story and the cause that you are fighting for. The characters in the game are extremely memorable and you’ll soon learn to care for them more than you ever have in any other first person shooter game.
As for performance, Wolfenstein II sees a different level of optimization and scalability across different hardware configurations. Unlike Wolfenstein: The New Order, Wolfenstein II is a bit more demanding cranked all the way up, as it was designed for more current hardware, but in turn it offers many more settings than its predecessor such as resolution scaling and additional anti-aliasing methods for those less fortunate. There are also specific rendering modes for both AMD and NVIDIA graphics cards. Its up to you to find the best balance of settings based on your current hardware configuration if you don’t quite meet the system requirements.

Simple game: 4 slow moving divers with limited vision, must team together against 2 fast moving sharks. The divers get an array of weapons and tools. The sharks choose from different breeds (Great white can block damage, Thresher can deal damage with its tail, etc).
This is a very fun game, but has a high skill curve. You can often predict match outcomes by looking at the number of games played previously by the sharks vs. divers. And expert players on either team are a menace to new players, especially when the teams are overall uneven.
I like this game because it is very simple basic mechanics, but lots to learn. Learn the advantages of the different shark breeds on each map. Learn to use the array of diver weapons and tools. The game evolves very differently based on the choices and ability of the two teams.
If you are new, invest a little time, playing as both shark and divers, accept that you will lose to expert players. But it's a fun learning curve! Learn the maps. Eventually you too will be a terror in the deep!

I played this game in two sittings over two days. I've never finished a game (besides portal) that quickly. I loved Nilin, she was a very diverse character. I could connect with her throughout many points in the story. The small clues that eventually led up to the, well, two big reveals, I definitely didn't pick up on until I really thought back on it. The fighting was a tad bit difficult to learn and VERY repetitive, but the story made up for that. All in all, I REALLY liked it.
Note that most thumbs down reviews don't have many hours logged. Trust me, there's a reason: at first, the game is a bit uninteresting and slightly boring, but as you play, it becomes a LOT better. If you don't look at the game critically, it's fun and easy to play once you get the hang of it.
My only real complaint is the repetitiveness of the boss fights and not being able to explore much. Neo-Paris is so gorgeous that I would have loved to just get lost in the city. I also would have liked more to do with the memory remixing.
It's a hugely story driven game, so if you like that kind of thing, this is definitely the game for you! (as long as you're cool with some combat too).
Ease of play: 8/10
The concept of fighting is easy to grasp, but can be repetitive and annoying that it just frustrates the crap out of you. It's a relatively easy game; your paths are clearly pointed out for you and the game gives lots of helpful tips. It's easy, yes, but is it a bit... too easy? Maybe.
Graphics: 7/10
I ran this game on Windows XP with the minimum graphics card. With all settings on medium, honestly, the game looked fantastic. I'm sure it would look even better on a computer with higher specs. I rated this aspect from my personal experience with the game. YMMV.
Story: 7/10
I loved the concept, and the story is a HUGE part of Remember Me. I loved learning about Nilin and Edge, and the two major plot twists at the midpoint and end of the game honestly shocked me. It was a bit boring at some times, but overall, it was fun to learn about the world of Neo-Paris and uncover the secrets behind Memorize and the Sensen technology.
Overall: 7/10
I liked Remember Me a LOT, and I think it's an underrated game. If you're not sure, wait until the price drops (I personally got it for $8 and it was VERY MUCH worth it. The Incredible Lag of Van Helsing
Generally I don't write bad reviews about games, but this time I have to.
The main reason why I give this game negative score is because the technical aspect of this game is on the same level as that garbage of this game's steampunk scenery:
1. It is badly optimized
2. Quests get bugged all the time
3. Ability sets don't get saved
4. The game tends to crash after minimizing it
To eleborate:
1. You will need
hardware you think for this game to be playable, the recommended settings I can consider to be lies. Even if you tinker the settings to get FPS up, the game still suffers from annoying stuttering and screen-tearing. V-sync will dump your performance even more.
2. Scripts, gate openings, cutscene launches after booses - such quest related things routinely fail to execute, but hey - the devs got a "solution", open chat and type "/FixQuest" then space and a number, which quest needs fixing... it is better than nothing but such cheap solution is an insult to paying users - why the hell wasn't the game released in a proper condition in the first place?
3. Similar to other hack and slash games, you can switch between saved skill combinations, the thing is, they are resetting to basic attacks after each loading screen. I have asked about this, the support quickly replied and said they will look into this, kudos to them, but that problem actually happening was just another drop to my already aggravated patience.
4. Oh, another quest bugged? Just Google, which quest number should be entered now for the command, you minimize the game and it crashes...
Even apart from technical problems, there are other things:
1. The fights in this game get extremely overwhelming, you are attacked by a lot of enemies at once who charge at you from large distances, in some areas the enemies simply keep respawning indefinitely after you've killed a wave...
2. Abilities feel they have low impact. Nothing you throw makes a lot of difference, in most of the game you'll be orb-dancing and spamming ranged attacks, constantly drinking potions and waiting for Katarina to respawn.
3. Katarina doesn't understand the concept of tactical retreat. You can adjust her combat behaviour but it doesn't make any noticable difference.
Now positive qualities:
1. Humour.
There are funny situations and interesting dialogues between the main character and Katarina - the ghost companion.
2. Visuals.
The game does look good, despite unreasonably high
system requirements.
Note that if the technical part of this game would be fine, I would give this game positive rating, there certainly are some interesting ideas and nice sceneries, however - in the condition how it is now I just cannot recommend anyone to pay for this.
I am glad I bought this on sale, not for full price! And speaking of money - you can play only ONE class in this game, you are asked to buy DLC if you want other classes...
It is NOT worth the money!

The last good Call of Duty game.
Campaign is short, entertaining with great setpieces and a decent story that gets to the point without dragging on unnecessarily; the engine felt functional and the gameplay wasn't awkward; and most importantly, the game was properly built around a server browser rather than peer to peer matchmaking.
CoD 4 was the omega of the franchise. On one hand, the game was good fun and not simply an annual source of income on Activisions ledger. On the other hand, it is also where you can start to see how the franchise went completely down hill in terms of quality. CoD4 introduced kill streaks and perks, with ridiculous mechanics like AI helicopters in multiplayer, dogs, martyrdom, and a host of other "rewards" which replaced skill in the game with unbalanced characters.
People do still play online, so if you don't own this game and you must own a Call of Duty that has assault rifles, you're better off buying it than CoD 12 this November.

I have mixed feelings about this game.  On one hand, it's an extraordinarily well crafted Metroidvania style game.
The controls are smooth and responsive.  The music is minimalistic, yet evocative.  The graphics are simple, yet beautiful.  There are a plethora of secrets to discover.  It's a satisfying and immersive exploration-based experience.  I really love this game!  Highly recommended!
On the other hand, it can be incredibly frustrating.
Some of the bosses, even after I figured out their patterns, were butt-kickingly tough.  I had to restart the game in easy mode, just to have a chance.  Only gamers with elite platforming skills should try the normal difficulty.
Precision platforming using the swinging "hookshot" mechanic is required to progress.  The hookshot is lots of fun, but it's difficult to master, so there were many repeated attempts before I got lucky and landed where I needed to land.  It was especially frustrating when I had to link several precise swings while being shot at by turrets, as any damage will disrupt your arc.
Backtracking: Most power-ups allow you to access new areas all over the map.  So, when you get the ability to destroy the red blocks, you have to try to remember all the places you encountered red blocks, and seek them out.  I don't mind backtracking; it's part of the fun of exploration games.  But this game is on the verge of getting carried away...
I completed this game with the "bad ending" on easy mode, achieving a 94% completion.  That's good enough for me!  I'm really glad I played through this game, and I definitely got my money's worth.  But I have neither the patience nor the skills to unlock any of the other multiple endings.

Skullgirls is a game about girls fighting over the Skull Heart, an entity(?) (it seems sentient) which will grant you a wish in exchange for possessing you. It seems that the purity of the wisher plays a fact into how long it takes for the Skull Heart to fully possess you.
The game reminds me of Darkstalker in art and character design. Every (main) character is female, every character is sexualized out the wazoo, and it's a 2D fighting game. It doesn't feel particularly inventive, although there's only so much you can do with fighting games. Maybe this isn't a good genre for me to review. The character stories are rather lame. Divekick had better character story than this and it was literally a two button game. You dive, and you kick. (It's quite brilliant, I highly recommend Divekick) The campaign for each character is fairly short (thank goodness). I had to watch a YouTube video to deal with one boss (on Normal mode no less, Christ) but other than that button mashing will get you through the game. And that's the problem, isn't it. Sure, learning the combos will make you competitive against real players but against the AI you can using a rolling pin and win. Of course... this was on Normal mode...
You start the game with six characters, you can unlock three more by completing the campaigns (which is a point against the game if you ask me). The forgivable thing about the unlocking process is that you have more fighters to choose from. If you could only use one fighter at the start or one fighter for some duration of the game, then I'd be a little more sore about it. Of course the campaigns are so short it doesn't really matter. I had every character unlocked within an hour. That excludes the DLC characters, to which I say SHAME ON YOU. I already bought the game and now you want more of my money? No way Jose.
There's really not much to review here. So the question is, do you miss 2D fighters with needlessly complicated command chains to execute special moves? Do you miss cutesy chicks? Do you like watching beach balls bounce about? If you answered yes to all of these questions, Skullgirls is for you.

Skullgirls is a labor of love, through and through.
Ignore the DLC for now. The base Skullgirls: Encore package has some of the most incredible polish you'll see in a fighting game, with 9 criminally well-balanced characters. Each character plays completely differently, allowing you to best find your niche.
Don't know anything about fighting games? No problem--Skullgirls' tutorial mode might not be the best under the sun, but it *will* make you find your way around fighting game mechanics. Whether you've been plopping quarters since Street Fighter 2 classic or only popped in because you dig the character design, you can rest assure that this game will make sure you feel at home with the many commands.

Cons:

I picked up the game about a year ago and finally got around to playing it... And oh my god, I wished that I had played it as soon as I got it. The non-fighting scenes such as the parkour scenes were a good brake from an all out adrenilin pumping precision button smasher scene, the small cinematics and quick comm scenes also gave life to the vibrant game.
The atmosphere of the game was spared no shortcuts either, being one of the most active environments ever with cool and interesting quercks such as the holgraphic prompts everywhere and the interactable scenes were very fresh and gave a new look on what are normally very inactive and dead environments. To sum this game into a finishing paragraph will be hard becuase the game really does break all the boundries of genres in gaming and forces them into one seemless act of incredible storytelling, enthralling gameplay and outstanding plot line.
