Lemme start this off with the positive aspects of the game.
I love the setting, which might be due to my having a soft spot for cyberpunk.

The aesthethic is beautiful, the orange/white color contrast works well and is integrated into the architecture, posters, graffitti, Sensens, and just about everywhere while not being overbearing. There is also nice contrast between the higher class and lower class parts of Neo-Paris. Luxurious shops, finished roads, well-furnished homes, and even a ritzy android brothel can be found in the Saint-Michel district. Slum 404, however, right next to the district, has no roads. The buildings are dilapidated, Leapers run abound with their home, the sewers, being just next to the slum, and there are no stores - merely stalls, stands, and bar put together by scrap metal. The world was well fleshed out and I wanted to explore more of it.
Sadly, you don't really get to explore it since the level design is very linear. If you liked the world of Mirror's Edge but hated that you didn't get to explore it much, Remember Me has the same issue.
The premise of the game is interesting too, with memories becoming a commodity. I love the opening of the game, showing the moving, heart-felt, well-intentioned marketing for commoditizing memories - then the stark reality of how prisoners in La Bastille are abused by having memories taken away, and how the wardens and doctors are basically thought police.
Also, I think Nilin is cool and a badass. I like her character design. I did roll my eyes a few times during the game towards the end when she said things that just made you go "Wait, what?" because they felt uncharacteristic and shoveled/ham-fisted in for the sake of "drama". Female representation in video games has been a hot topic lately, so I figured that was worth mentioning.
Ok, now for the bad stuff and why I can't recommend the game for $30 in good conscience.
The gameplay is lackluster and easily the weakest part of the game. Mostly just memorize 1 or 2 combos, swap out the Pressens you need for the situation, and press the spacebar + a/w/s/d whenever you see a big red "!" on some part of the screen - often the direction you dodge in doesn't even matter and can be cast during any attack. The platforming/parkour is very fragmented, lacking the flow of Mirror's Edge or Assassin's Creed while having less depth. It being slow and easy makes it incredibly boring and tedious .
Being boring and tedious seems to be a common theme, even in the memory remix portions of the game. Memory remixing is just a matter of moving through the scene and trying all the possibilities until you get the outcome the game wanted. There isn't any challenge, risk, or open-endedness to how you reach the outcome. Memory remixing is basically a point and click adventure game that lasts 5 minutes at most.
Also, UNSKIPPABLE CUTSCENES. If you're a completionist like me, this will make 100%'ing the game a royal pain. Rewatch every monologue by Nilin, watch Nilin put her hand to ear and walk at a snail's pace until Edge is done talking to her, watch a Leaper attack an enforcer to the ground, watch a conversation go on and on, watch the memory for its full duration at normal speed before you remix it, etc.
Verdict:
If you do not already own this you're probably better off just watching a let's play or waiting for it to go on sale for about $10.
If you do own this, it is worth a playthrough at least.
Hopefully if DONTNOD Entertainment get a sequel going they can polish the gameplay to make it more engaging, allow you to explore Neo-Paris or another city in this dystopian setting, and allow you to skip cutscenes.

The first game in what would become a series a three, was released by Neocore Games in May 2013. At first sight,
doesn't seem to offer much new or original to a well-established gaming genre: the fast-paced action rpg, played from an isometric point of view. After all, we had the
and
series, which did a pretty good job at delivering extremely enjoyable games.
From my first impressions with this game, it was clear that Neocore Games knows its classics: they stayed true to the core of this particular genre, which is the combination of the fast-paced hack 'n slash (or shoot 'n bewitch) gameplay with the development of your character and the endless craving for loot. After all, what's more rewarding than mowing down horde after horde of enemies, in order to find dozens of lootable items, among which there might be just that one special items? Or breaking hundreds of barrels, hoping to stumble upon a golden ring belonging to a named set?
Actually,
goes several steps further than most other action rpg when it comes to loot, objects and what you can accomplish with them. I've played through the entire game twice (first as a gun-oriented hunter, than as a melee character), and both times I found myself busy with objects for a fair amount of time. There's not only an incredible number of weapons, armour, rings, boots, gloves, hats, capes and trophees, there's also the possibility to enchant and even enhance them with small magical pieces, "essences". The best items come with a slot for one or more essences, and it's great fun to upgrade one's armour or items in this way. The game gives you a huge amount of customization options over your character (although you can only play as Van Helsing himself, obviously) too: upon levelling up, you can spend 5 ability points (to build your character's strenghts) and 3 skill points (spent in a very extensive skill & spell tree). Part of the immense fun this game provides, lies in building a well-balanced, skilled character that's up to the task and to the items he can wield. There are "perks" too, which offer a general or more specific buff and which unlock after meeting certain requirements.
But Neocore Games went even one step further by introducing a companion to Van Helsing: a female ghost, who can help you defeating the enemies in several ways (melee, range or simply by enhancing your capabilities). Even better: Katharina also gains experience and can be upgraded, can learn skill and can be equipped with weapons, rings and armour. All of which can be upgraded and enchanted, of course. So if you like that sort of finetuning a character,
offers a fantastic experience. And Katharina even helps to solve to everlasting problem of having too much loot but too little inventory space: you can send her off to town to sell some items for cash, or for potions.
Compared to such an extensive character building & enhancing system, the actual gameplay is a little more bland, although it's still pretty solid and enjoyable. With the aid of good weaponry, skills, spells and aura's it is great fun to mow down entire legions of enemies, which the game keeps throwing at you. But towards the latter part of the game it becomes clear which skills are best suited to your style of playing, and the gameplay starts to show some repetition. The story itself is decent enough - nothing special, but it does the job of keeping the game going, and Katherina is a humorous sidekick in many situations. The user interfaces (and the extremely important inventory screens) are a marvel of lay-out and offer whatever you want at a mouse-click. This game offers the perfect example of how developers can make life easy and enjoyable, even in the most complex of situations.
And if all of this were not enough,
offers perfect integration with Steam through leaderboards, co-op multiplayer, and nearly one hundred achievements which offer an extra challenge and a great fun to hunt after. The three main dlc's are pretty useful too: they offer two new sets of skills & spells so that you can play either as a magic character or as an "arcane mechanic" (have to try that one out sometime). The third dlc offers a new set of skills for your female companion.

After reading through some of the reviews, I wanted to share my views on Depth. First tried it on a free weekend, then decided to buy it on sale.
Matchmaking is unbalanced, you could have 4 level 100 divers vs 2 level 1 sharks. But levels are just for show, they don't affect gameplay. No P2W, items are cosmetic. So no worries about smurfs, you can die to anyone at any level. Your own performance is determined with a personal "score" regardless of winning or losing the match, I find it better to look at it instead of the match outcome. With my wooden PC and terrible FPS skills, I usually end up doing worse than lower-leveled players...
No ranked games, just lots of quick play. Speaking for myself, I prefer casual games anyway, so this doesn't affect me. Any disconnects or RQs replace the player with a bot. Most of the time these bots do better than the original player anyway, AI is pretty good.
Game does get repetitive after repeated plays, but there are daily quests/missions which encourage you to change up your tactics (e.g. use a net gun instead of your usual harpoon). I play some games, take a break when I'm bored, then come back again later. It's not an adventure/RPG type of game where you rush to finish the game and never go back.
Overall: recommended, to play as a shark swimming faster than a plane, or to shoot said shark with a poisoned speargun

With the 192+ hours and my $20 that I've spent on this game. I think I've finally gathered enough mental energy to write the best review I could possibly do for this game.
--So What Is This Game About?--
I think by just looking at the image and trailer for this game, you can already tell that it's obviously a diver vs shark game and it is, but there is a lot more to it than just that. The diver's have 2 objectives to complete each match and that is to either escort and defend a really sluggish robot called S.T.E.V.E through checkpoints, until it has reached the final one or kill the sharks that try to kill them or destroy S.T.E.V.E. The game is almost like a "Last-Team Standing" game and the "Escort the Payload" mode in Overwatch, thrown into a blender and made into a fine paste with each team having 30 lives that goes down each time a diver or a shark dies. Gold is a "thing" that divers can collect to upgrade or buy weapons and equipment, although you can only do this when you die which I find really annoying sometimes (also S.T.E.V.E collects 1000 gold each time he finishes a checkpoint). The sharks have something similar to gold except they don't find it lying on the ground or have a machine collect it for them, instead they get it by killing diver's and they could use it for buying certain perks that make finishing the match slightly easier.
--Gameplay--
When using terms like "defend" and "escort", you could definitely tell that this game is heavily orientated around teamwork, communication, and sometimes strategizing. Don't play as shark thinking that camping is still a cancerous strat, because it's quite literally one of the best ways a diver can survive and defend S.T.E.V.E throughout the entire match, which may make the game sound boring but think about it, in a real-life scenario do you really think a human can survive a Great White Shark attack? But if camping in a small confinement waiting for a robot to collect your salary isn't your cup of tea, then you could always feel free to leave and stay in the open abyss shooting down any enemy sharks.
--Gameplay Mechanics--
Well, if the trailer wasn't enough to soil the under garments of any galeophobe who might be reading this, then you're first match most likely will. The devs are really ♥♥♥♥ing cheeky for adding the sounds of your diver's heart thumping everytime a shark is nearby, it's a really good way for the player to be more on edge and focused for the next attack, it's also a brilliant way to tell the player when they're out of the checkpoint looking for a medkit or an ammo box to get the ♥♥♥♥ back inside before a shark tears their♥♥♥♥♥apart.
--Controls--
The overall control scheme is great and doesn't really require any sort of adjusting, but the movement of the diver feels rather stiff when it comes to "sprint-swimming" when your diver does this, he/she only does it in these short bursts which makes it really annoying when you're trying to escape the jaws of death and you're stuck furiously tapping the Shift button. Aiming down sights might also be nauseating to certain newcomers, because gravity practically doesn't exist underwater  and you're free to aim in almost any direction and if you really tried then you could possibly get a kill upside down, although you might do like 5 flips during the process. Shark controls aren't too bad, but the act of having to thrash your mouse left to right, to kill a diver will most likely bother some newcomer's.
--Is It Worth It?--
For a $20 price tag? I don't think so. I feel like this game misses the potential (in-terms of content) to give it an extra "umph". Sure there may be a good handful of sharks and guns, but some more maps and gamemodes would definitely be nice. I'd like to give credit where credit is do though, the devs are genuinely nice people and are always listening and reading to what people have to say about the game and  have actually changed and added a couple of things, because of the communities feedback. In conclusion, I think it is an amazing game and a $10-$15 price range might be a reasonable price for the game, if you're interested in this game you should wait until a sale when the game drops down to around $5.

Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus is by far one of the best shooters I’ve played this year, rivaling last year’s Doom 2016 by id Tech, Wolfenstein II is the definitive example of what it means to be a modern first-person shooter. Wolfenstein II is yet another nod to the classic Wolfenstein 3D originally released back in May of 1992. Deemed the father of all first-person shooters the Wolfenstein series still has plenty of life left and I can’t where to see where the series goes next.
At it’s core, Wolfenstein II is a massive upgrade over the previous game in the series. Both the visuals and the gameplay have greatly improved offering players new ways to play and create encounters with enemies varying level to level. Players can chose to approach any combat situation in a stealth-base manor, all guns blazing or a combination of the two. Be weary, the enemies in Wolfenstein II are also a lot smarter than they were in the last game, flanking the player and predicting your next movements. Best of luck to players wanting a real challenge with the plethora of difficulty modes found in the main menu.
Wolfenstein II sets the bar extremely high and is most definitely the best in the series. Unlike its predecessor, Wolfenstein II greatly balances the mindless shooting aspect and the narrative driven gameplay found in most shooters. You’ll always want to be shooting something, but you’re constantly reminded why you’re shooting throughout the story and the cause that you are fighting for. The characters in the game are extremely memorable and you’ll soon learn to care for them more than you ever have in any other first person shooter game.
As for performance, Wolfenstein II sees a different level of optimization and scalability across different hardware configurations. Unlike Wolfenstein: The New Order, Wolfenstein II is a bit more demanding cranked all the way up, as it was designed for more current hardware, but in turn it offers many more settings than its predecessor such as resolution scaling and additional anti-aliasing methods for those less fortunate. There are also specific rendering modes for both AMD and NVIDIA graphics cards. Its up to you to find the best balance of settings based on your current hardware configuration if you don’t quite meet the system requirements.

An interesting and quirky experience for me. Almost the entire game involves going through one room to the next, of which there are 1000, some short and straighforward, some longer and more complex, but all being a few seconds long at most. Occasionally, you'll be chased by monsters which, despite coming in many variations, almost universally require you to simply go through rooms as fast as possible until they cease their pursuit. Very few moments require solving puzzles or obtaining keys to proceed, giving the player little reason to explore unless forced to. Because of these characteristics, the game feels like a very long chase sequence and, with 1000 rooms to be overcome before the game is over, it can get very repetitive despite being a very short game, clocking at around 3 hours for completion. Fortunately, there are save spots every 50 (later 100) rooms, which allows the player to take a break if necessary.
Difficulty-wise, it's not hard; almost all the monsters can be avoided with little hassle, and it's entirely possible you'll miss several of them depending on how efficient you are at going through the rooms. However, the game leaves little room for error, as the enemies tend to deal high damage and some can even one-hit kill you if they manage to get in close enough. It all depends on how well you can manage to keep to your goal of sprinting and reaching the next door.
In regards to atmosphere, it's a blend of humor/cuteness with horror, which can be verified by looking at a few screenshots. The humor consists mainly of cutesy characters and dialogue, which are peppered throughout the gameplay (but become increasingly rarer). The horror portion involves surprisingly disturbing imagery and sounds, most of them from the monsters that chase you, and I didn't find myself detracted from it by the occasional humor, so I believe the game was successful in its atmosphere. In my opinion, that is the highest point of this game - seeing what monsters, environments and dialogue will come next.
All in all, if you're a fan of horror games, I'd say give this at least a try. It's different and has a charm to it that I believe adds to the overall experience and makes it quite unique.

If video games can be art, then Hellblade: Senua’s Sacrifice is a stunning example of that potential, and if video games can’t be art, then Hellblade is an exception. A terrifying but beautiful exploration of loss, grief, fear, and hope, Ninja Theory’s creation shows that great games can aspire to more than mindless fun.
I should point out that not everyone will enjoy Hellblade, but that is to be expected. Good art turns many people off, and this particular game contains quite a bit that might hamper some people’s fun. The total length of the game, for one, is very short, and there is supposedly a “perma-death” feature if you die too often (there is some speculation that this last point is a hoax, but that goes beyond the scope of this review). Each of these elements, however, serves an important purpose.
Yes, the game is particularly short, but I honestly wouldn’t have it any other way. A game as dedicated to narrative as Hellblade is should be short. There is little to no bloat in this story, and it goes on for exactly as long as it needs to in order develop and come to a conclusion. Other reviewers have alluded to the expectation for games to offer many hours of enjoyment, so we can see the risk that Ninja Theory took here. That risk, however, was entirely necessary. At the end of the day, a nice tight narrative is sometimes better than a sprawling and seemingly endless series of side plots and fluff.
As for the “perma-death” thing, what better way to give the player a sense of anxiety in regards to death. Just the threat of a premature end (and, as I have alluded to, it may be just an empty threat) can lend the game-play an appropriate sense of gravitas. The game-play becomes tonally tied to the narrative, creating a cohesion that many games do not have.
Having defended some of the seemingly questionable choices that the developers made, I think it is time I address the artistic merit of Hellblade. In the video game industry, generally speaking, the bar for what constitutes a good story is pretty low. I am aware that this is a controversial opinion, but I would argue that most of the best video game narratives are kind of trashy, at least if we compare them to film or literature.
Having established that position, I am glad to say that Hellblade raises that unfortunately low bar. This is a tale where every element works perfectly, whether tonally, thematically, or aesthetically. Tackling the difficult issue of mental illness, namely psychosis, the game paints for the player an enlightening picture in the heroine. Senua is not a stock character, and by the end of the game we see that the last thing that we should do for the mentally ill is to invalidate their unique experiences. Mental illness is a struggle and potentially a disability, but it is not a fault or weakness.
Hellblade: Senua’s Sacrifice is perhaps the most perfectly balanced game, in terms of narrative versus game-play, that I have ever played. It is certainly the most beautiful, a term I use in a broad and somewhat nebulous sense. It has proven to me that games really can have artistic value, and I hope to see more games like it in the future.

The good, the bad, and the ugly. Let's start at the bottom!
The ugly - Strange optimization issues for PC. Some strong setups seem to struggle, whilst some medium setups do well. Personally, the game stutters for me every 10 or so seconds, so it's liveable, but decided to buy it on PS4 anyways (only $20, why not)
[Edit] This seems to have been cleaned up A LOT since 1.3, I now have stable 60 FPS with no stuttering.
The bad - Space pirates can be an annoyance. With the lack of hotkeys, it's annoying trying to recharge your shields whilst getting♥♥♥♥♥♥pounded by bandits. This is mostly alleviated once you have a decent ship, though.
The weather mechanics can be a bit boring, at the moment all they do is indicate whether you're on a toxic, hot, cold, or radioactive planet, and they deteriorate your suit. I feel HG could have taken these mechanics further (like radioactive planets interfering with your scanners, cold planets slowing down your movement speed, etc etc) which would give the planet types a bit more depth.
The good - Free updates, and continual support. After the crap that these devs went through, for them to still be on this game and supporting it for free just goes to show how much they care about their game. Every update brings more content and depth, it's becoming more and more like the game they originally advertised. If they had spent an extra year in development, I believe they'd have hit their mark. Unfortunately, it seems like perhaps Sony forced an earlier release.

At its surface the game is a high-quality retro adventure platformer one green visor away from a Metroid fangame; but Environmental Station Alpha sadly suffers from Too Much♥♥♥♥♥♥Going On Syndrome, indistinct foreground vs. background tiles, and the delusion that extravagant difficulty is the sole criterion of a good game, which was getting old back when Newgrounds was still relevant.
- Bosses routinely boast two or even three phases, each more impossible and bullet hell-y than the last
- Numerous & agile enemies in unavoidable places
- Lots of ordinary-looking blocks that are actually disappearing blocks
- Standard gameplay themed on ability physics exploits not expressly explained to the player (the hookshot corner-jumps stopped being fun after the 20th time)
- Generally unfair & unintuitive expectations
The game gives the strong implication it was designed by a Super Metroid speedrunner, and even includes an early-game portion expecting the player to run through the volcano biome without any heat-resistant gear (a strategy of EVERY Super Metroid speedrun.)
Casual players heed this warning: You'll lose interest in this game by the third or fourth boss (Serpent 5), if you manage to get that far.
But coolkids & masochists? This asinine game beats out Dark Souls any day.

What starts as a simple plot to fulfill a dying patient's dream of reaching the moon quickly evolves into a complex foray into the depths of the patient's past. This game, along with the Batman: Arkham series has re-invigorated my interest in action games.
Firstly, let's talk about the game quality of Remember Me. Aside from Nilin when she's talking (lips don't always match her speech), and another when one of the enemy bosses temporarily left the area I could fight in, I noticed no errors. There wasn't any empty map areas, there wasn't any low quality texturing anywhere, and everything I interacted in worked flawlessly.
However, there are a few problems. First is the fighting 'combo' system. While it's good and innovative, the lack of time between enemies (especially when they're rather aggressive and you're trying to fight back 5 of them) means anything other than the first combo of 3 punches is likely to get unused, especially late game. The powers available are a mix of good and meh. Sensen Fury is a good power but unfortunately useless for the majority of late-game due, normally due to the ammount of enemies you're facing meaning one is always ready to strike you and break the combo, and the fact there's more useful powers available.
Some of the enemies are hard to defeat too. The large robot, for example, unleashes a shockwave power you have trouble escaping from, and then has a vulnerability which, if you get caught in the shockwave, cannot get to in-time to attack the robot. Some boss battles are hard to do due to lack of guidance (e.g. you need to do power X and then Y).
The upgrading system is good - it's not as you level up, it's as you find parts of the upgrades... which is a good ploy for you to search the maps for upgrades. However, you occasionally have a hard time finding said upgrades. While I'm talking about collecting, might I add how hard it is to find all the Scarabmechs.
The story, however, is the crown jewel of Remember Me. Thoughtful, logical, and if you have a good mind, you can link up so much of the story elements as you play you can link things together, often before the story reveals them to you.
Lastly, the soundtrack. From stirring pieces to real gritty, electronically re-cut "you're about to poop yourself" moments, I have never heard such a good soundtrack. There's parts where it sounds normal, and others where it's been remixed in such a way it blends in with the whole experience.
Remember Me is - without a doubt - one of the best games I've ever played. It joins my pedestals of other excellent games, like No One Lives Forever 2, Railroad Tycoon 2 and Sid Meier's Civ series from 4 onwards.

Wolfenstein II: The New Colussus has managed to beat the first one by a mile, and that's quite an achievement!
Let's talk about performance first, a lot of the complaints are about that specifically about that.
(My specs) GTX-1070 8GB, i5-6400, 16GB DDR4  and the game is not installed on a SSD.
The load times are very fast! It feels like it's on a SSD, but it's not. And I've yet to experience any performance issues like lag or stutter. (Frames are not going below 60, hasn't happened yet, and this is being played on the "High" setting) Though the game does crash now and then.. Mostly when minimizing the game and only once I've experienced a crash from picking up a collectible.
Optimization: Perfect (For me - Average-High Spec PC)
And now bugs!
I've only experienced a very minor amount of bugs so far.. Visual glitch in the outside Manhattan area when looking into the sky. And a glitch with Maria when she's washing one of the Heli-jets where her head would go inside her body (She's attempting to look at the player)
Bugs: Only the common ones you find in just about any other game.
On to the story! (No spoilers)
The story here picks up right after the first one, so you will miss absolutely nothing!
I very much appreciate the large hub that is added between missions (The U-Boat from the first game which is inspired by a real never built U-Boat that was supposed to the be the largest ever made. This one is called Eva's Hammer which is most likely a reference to Eva Braun, the wife of Adolf Hitler) This allows you to do small side missions and some much bigger stuff away from the main campaign that you should experience yourself! I feel BJ and the rest of the group has been vastly improved since the last game.. And this one really makes you feel for William Blazkowicz.. Emotionally and... well... Have you seen how many times he has been blown up and tortured by just about everything you can imagine? He just walks on like a god damn machine! I love it!
Story: Fan-freaking-tastic!
Some gameplay praise now.
The player shadow is a direct shadow from the player. (Legs, arms, head and weapon) the body doesn't move with the mouse precisely, it has a slow delay like in a 3rd person shooter.
Weapons can be dual wielded separately.. Pistol/Rifle, SMG/Laserkraftwerk or whatever you want!
Stealth and combat executions has been improved by a mile! Dynamic and glorious!
10 out of gosh dang 10!

BB Vet here, It's a bit pricey but at the end of the day you get what you put in.
PROS:
-Beautifully stunning spritework, backgrounds and HUD, especially for a 2D fighting game.
-Each character is unique in their own way, even with an in depth backstory.
-Hours of fully english dubbed(or japanese if you want) story modes.
-4 button layout is easier for new players being introduced to fighters than your average 6.
-Full Fightstick/Controller support.
-Comes with a special artbook and the soundtrack with some of the battle themes in it.
-Tutorial mode can teach you everything from the bread and butter of a fighter to special character exclusive combos.
-If your a fan of rock/metal THIS SH!T WILL GET STUCK IN YOUR HEAD.
-Specials and astrals, though sometimes difficult to pull off, look stunning.
CONS:
-Lots of characters are NOT noob friendly (I'm looking at the Clovers and Arakune).
-Barely anyone plays online anymore.
-Ragna and Jin are easy for new players, therefore we have an online scene with nothing but them.
-IMPOSSIBLE to play on keyboard
-A bit outdated (Chronophantasma coming january 2k16)
-A tad awkward to configure controls.
It's a solid fighter, but at the same time though miniscule, it has its fair share of problems. I can reccomend this to anyone that's a fan of flashy overthetop (Shonen basically) anime fighters. If you or a friend wants to get into Blazblue, then I highly reccomend this over Calamity Trigger, though I will reccomend playing with someone your skill level or some of the easier CPU's before stepping online. In Short: It's just a plain ol innocent collectathon that encourages creative thinking. Not for those seeking a EPIC story or action.
In Full: Your objective is to travel to different worlds and unlock tools to help you collect Gold Bricks, which allow you to unlock more tools and more varied worlds to explore. Rinse and repeat, seems like it would get boring right? Especially when some missions can be as simple as painting a house, which can be achieved by spraying random colors in no order or style. But heres the thing, this is a game about building block toys, so the FUN comes from using these opportunities to make something really special.
DO NOT go into this game expecting a epic story like in previous lego titles. The adventure mode is simply ment to be a source of inspiration for the player. This is evident in the way it allows players to put as little or as much effort into completing tasks, as mentioned with the painting missions. For example: I played a mission where the objective was to help finish building a house. Now you could just make a box, slap a door on it and call it a day. But I spent time with it, made a nice roof, and decorated a bit. Why?
The Building in this game is fantastic. It is in my opinion more comfortable to build with a controller than with a mouse. The simple controls and large variety of brick shapes allow for very detailed designs to be made rather quickly. Speaking of overall controls, they are decent for controller, but not so intuitive for keyboard and mouse. To move the camera you have to hold the right mouse button... so when you arent holding it all you see is a cursor. This is not very useful while exploring, as even while trying to interact with the world with the cursor it would sometimes select something in the foreground, rather than what I was pointing at. I honestly didn't spend much time at all with K/M so maybe one could get use to them.
ONE HUGE PROBLEM WITH THIS GAME is the User Interface. When building, objects are not organized, so if you dont already know where a item is it might take you a while looking through foilage bricks and furniture before finding the window you want. It desparately needs either a folder system to organize everything or a search bar that can check both item name or some associated tag. I was trying to find medival looking items to make a world themed around it but it took a lot longer than I would have liked. Would be nice to search "Medieval" and have all associated items appear. But this is only really an issue in sandbox mode or end game of adventure mode when you have all or most items unlocked.
Also not a fan of the First Person mode, as you still have to attack with the default attack button  (X button on xbox controllers) so unless you can play claw, don't expect to trick shot a skeleton. Vehicles have trouble traversing the lego terrain and I have gotten bigger vehicles like trucks stuck on terrain many times. I Mean STUCK, I had to delete the car and spawn another. Combat seems slightly worse than main series lego games. Hand to hand combat is a coin flip, and some weapons and enemies can spam rediculously overpowered attacks that stun and kill you in a few seconds (example, dragon mage dude that rapid fires flame balls). Combat boils down to simply outclassing your foe with a better weapon.
There also needs to be more intelligent AI for the lego people, and more customization options. I placed alot of knights for my kingdom but they had no weapons and were getting shredded by enemies, or they would walk right past an enemy, stand next to them and do nothing for a minute or two before fighting. Id like to spawn them with weapon or other held items to make them more useful. Also, auto spawners would be nice... but im getting off track.
POINT IS I love this game, but I see potential for it to be something truely never seen before. crappy combat and UI just doesnt ruin the pure joy of building a secret base in a large cave, or a futuristic palace high above the world. If you want a building game (and think Blockland was very dissapointing...) This is the game for you.

Depth Hunter 2: Deep Dive is a very calm and ambient spearfishing game. Its very straighforward, you get 5 areas to hunt (without dlc) with objectives (find and spear this species, find these treasures in this area, take a photograph of this species or location) and you scuba into the depths of the ocean that your in to complete the objectives. A very enjoyable game if your looking for a serene experience with small challenge. The controls are very tight, where you aim is where the spear goes and the swimming is surprisingly easy to control.
The visuals in the game are very pretty with the changing landscape, the different species of fish and the occasional wreckage here and there which adds greatly to the feeling that your actually in the ocean.
The soundtrack and the ambient noise in the game is incorporated very nicely that they complement each other, but if your in the mood to only hear the ocean you can change the preset. The sounds do immerse you into the atmosphere of the ocean, which is a good bonus for me.
Pros: Beautiful game, great atmosphere, different locations and challenges.
Cons: A little on the short side, but you can replay the levels and complete the achievements which adds to the total time played. DLC add more locations and species. If price is a turn off, you can complete the base game with 100% achievements and buy when its on sale.
9/10 If you've been scuba diving this will bring back memories of that experience. Great atmospheric game.

If video games can be art, then Hellblade: Senua’s Sacrifice is a stunning example of that potential, and if video games can’t be art, then Hellblade is an exception. A terrifying but beautiful exploration of loss, grief, fear, and hope, Ninja Theory’s creation shows that great games can aspire to more than mindless fun.
I should point out that not everyone will enjoy Hellblade, but that is to be expected. Good art turns many people off, and this particular game contains quite a bit that might hamper some people’s fun. The total length of the game, for one, is very short, and there is supposedly a “perma-death” feature if you die too often (there is some speculation that this last point is a hoax, but that goes beyond the scope of this review). Each of these elements, however, serves an important purpose.
Yes, the game is particularly short, but I honestly wouldn’t have it any other way. A game as dedicated to narrative as Hellblade is should be short. There is little to no bloat in this story, and it goes on for exactly as long as it needs to in order develop and come to a conclusion. Other reviewers have alluded to the expectation for games to offer many hours of enjoyment, so we can see the risk that Ninja Theory took here. That risk, however, was entirely necessary. At the end of the day, a nice tight narrative is sometimes better than a sprawling and seemingly endless series of side plots and fluff.
As for the “perma-death” thing, what better way to give the player a sense of anxiety in regards to death. Just the threat of a premature end (and, as I have alluded to, it may be just an empty threat) can lend the game-play an appropriate sense of gravitas. The game-play becomes tonally tied to the narrative, creating a cohesion that many games do not have.
Having defended some of the seemingly questionable choices that the developers made, I think it is time I address the artistic merit of Hellblade. In the video game industry, generally speaking, the bar for what constitutes a good story is pretty low. I am aware that this is a controversial opinion, but I would argue that most of the best video game narratives are kind of trashy, at least if we compare them to film or literature.
Having established that position, I am glad to say that Hellblade raises that unfortunately low bar. This is a tale where every element works perfectly, whether tonally, thematically, or aesthetically. Tackling the difficult issue of mental illness, namely psychosis, the game paints for the player an enlightening picture in the heroine. Senua is not a stock character, and by the end of the game we see that the last thing that we should do for the mentally ill is to invalidate their unique experiences. Mental illness is a struggle and potentially a disability, but it is not a fault or weakness.
Hellblade: Senua’s Sacrifice is perhaps the most perfectly balanced game, in terms of narrative versus game-play, that I have ever played. It is certainly the most beautiful, a term I use in a broad and somewhat nebulous sense. It has proven to me that games really can have artistic value, and I hope to see more games like it in the future.

Favorite game on Steam thus far - possibly favorite game ever! I can't understand why this little gem with a huge Metroid-like world is such a sleeper? Why hasn't this indie title spread to consoles and gained more notoriety? The game has it all. It has the retro feel with uncomfortably pixelated graphics (at first; then, somehow, your mind gets accustomed to it - and actually likes it!), tight as hell controls (rivaling Super Meat Boy), exploration, exploration, exploration, tons of tough as nails bosses (I do have complaints about a couple, but, overall, well done) and just grade A platforming.
Here are my pros and cons:
Pros:
- Tons of bosses
- Tons of hard bosses (this also has a con)
- Profound feeling of satisfaction once a difficult part is completed
- Cool upgrades that, like Metroid-style games do, allow you to explore more areas and get more cool upgrades
- Wicked story with an other-worldly feel, a la Super Metroid
- I haven't played any portions post-campaign, but I hear there's a ton of extra content and an additional difficulty setting that promotes replayability
Cons:
- Boss fights can be a bit unfair by design. The controls are tight, yes, but the perspective can blind you from attack. One boss, in particular, took more than a few of my tries. The room was enormous, and the boss itself had 3 iterations that forced you to use almost the entire room. If the dev blew up the perspective so that almost the whole screen could be seen, it would be more strategically effective as well as more visually imposing. Don't get me wrong, I loved it!
- That's it.
To sum it up, this game is a classic Metroid-style game with a twist - you'll see it. It's much tougher than Metroid ever could be, so it's not for the faint of heart. But, when you beat that grueling boss or get that seemingly impossible upgrade (you know which one it is if you've played the game and reached the end), it's so unbelievably satisfying. For $10, you really can't beat it. From what I've seen in some YouTube post-game walkthroughs, there's a ton of additional content with some cool unlockables and puzzles. There's also a secret that you can find in the game that shows you how to unlock a super hard mode - that is, if you're a masochist! Anyway, much respect to the dev - so much content and so well-integrated. Please make another game like this! And, for those of you still reading this, what are you waiting for? Buy this game!

I was very surprised and delighted by how much I loved this game. 5/5, fantastic job Arvi "Hempuli" Teikari, you earned yourself a fan.
The biggest criticism I see here is that the game is hard. Yes, it's a challenge, and though I haven't tried it myself there is an easy mode. It hardly needs it though, because though it is difficult it is never unfair. Every obstacle is learnable, every boss can be beaten without taking a hit, and each time you try again you make progress. This contrasts metroid, where you can power-through bosses if you've found enough health upgrades, that option doesn't exist here, you have to adapt. I love this in a game, and I'm sure I'm not the only one.
Level design is fantastic, I was never lost but always felt like I was exploring on my own. Powerups are all novel and feel great, always changing up the gameplay subtly to keep it interesting. Gameplay is sharp and accurate, perfectly designed for the platforming and enemies.
With all love I give the game, I do offer some criticism though. At the beginning of the game, the aethetics sometimes interfere with the mechanics, I didn't know what I had to kill, or what to stand on at times, by the end of the game this is a non-issue though. The post-game content is... confused. The post-game feels vastly different from the main game, not an extension of it as it should be, and it isn't nearly as polished, though it IS deep (post-game took up 16 hours of my 24 hour play time, for the lazy that means it took me 8 hours to get to the end). I'd only reccomend flying blind to the dedicated players, but don't feel ashamed of following a guide, the extra bosses are absolutely worth it. It's also a bit weird that there are a ton of secrets in this game, but very few are truly discoverable until the post game. I was begining to think there were no secrets at all, and then I found a bunch all at once. Shoutouts to the bike.
TL;DR: If you like pattern-based or precision side-scrollers, this game is a diamond in the rough. I went in with zero expectations, and now it's one of my favorites, and it could be yours too.

I've yet to beat this game, however I feel like it's important to note some things about the game so far so new players will be aware going in.
First of all, ESA is a good platformer with some interesting mechanics and backtracking for upgrades and secrets. It is not, however, much of a metroidvania so far. Shortly within my first play session I had noticed a rather strong linearity to the game, and further in I'd found that it seems to actively prevent and discourage exploration by denying any sequence breaks. Often times I'd reach an area (whether through intended means or not) only to immediately find that just past the obstacle was some new one that I yet lacked the upgrade to bypass, rendering most of my backtracking worthless.
Secondly, enemies do not drop anything. While this does have benefits, it also takes away any incentive for combat in the game. Oftentimes you'll be able to encounter rather strong regular enemies in somewhat out of the way locations, but these almost miniboss like encounters provide no benefit. It is a simple and easy matter to completely bypass them.
Third, at a certain point in the game I was tasked with flipping a switch in one part of a level to reach a boss. Upon flipping the switch, the layout of the entire region was changed with new platforms that often blocked off your old paths. However, the relationship between that button and the new platforms appearing doesn't make any sense from a logical perspective, and they block off areas I could access before, but have yet to find a different route too.
In closing, ESA will be plenty of fun if you want a good platformer and don't mind exploring a bit. Don't go into it expecting a metroidvania though. The game's constant barricading, infrequent optional upgrades, and outright denial of sequence breaking prevent that.

I can say after giving this game and it's sequel the old college try that I cannot recommend this game. At first, the game was light and funny, but the big aspect of this game (what with being a diablo clone) is combat, and if you are lacking in that aspect, then the rest of your game is going to suffer; and that is almost exactly what happened to this game. The game is quite laggy almost all the time, and the game swarms you with so many enemies with so much health that fighting them feels like trying to knock out a mountain with nothing but a toothpick. I'm not saying that fights should be easy, but even on normal mode, trash mobs take way too much damage before they go down, and more attacks should have more effective AOE.
I chose to play as a ranged character after giving the game a few early tries, and found I was nothing but frustrated. Enemies which were basically living artillery were able to instakill me as soon as they saw me, and I found myself running around like a madman taking 5-8 shots to take out a single enemy which had 20 others just like it right behind. In brief, combat was long, tedious and I would see future mobs coming at me not with the glee of popping their heads off, but with resignation as they were just another obstacle between me and my final goal. An obstacle which, I had wiped out at least 12 of in the past play session.
In short: Even after putting all my skillpoints into body and dex, I still didn't have enough health to survive encounters, or enough damage to make fighting monsters not feel like a chore. In Diablo, I can wipe out a dungeon in 15 minutes on high torment levels. In this game, I'd be lucky to wipe out a map section in what feels like three times that.
And as a final tip to the developer: writing achievements is fine, but DO NOT make an achievement that says "Don't kill a monster type" in a game where you have been patting my back for killing everything that moves, then putting that monster type all over the map, then having them attack me with flamethrowers doing an insubstantial amount of damage, and when I do kill it not allow me to go back and un-kill that monster. Same goes for that "Fight the final boss without destroying any spawn towers", because I sustain Fulmugati will be almost indestructible if you don't.

I agree that this game had and has its problems. I too was disappointed by the game upon release. Atlas Rises / 1.3 is NOT just another update, even though more is coming after it. I am currently starting new saves for almost every gamemode after quitting for several months, and I have already found much has changed even since 1.2 "Pathfinder." Even though I was not one of those who refunded the game, I'm still returning to it almost as if I had just bought it.
If you are on the fence about this game again or for the first time, keep in mind that it is a niche game, and is not for everyone. The quirks of procedural generation still do exist even though they have been smoothed out for the most part, and probably always will to some degree.
Overall though, I would recommend NMS in its current state for sure.

This game used to be pretty good, in my opinion. Not the best game ever, but certainly enjoyable. However, that seems to have changed.
When I installed the newest updates, I hadn't played in quite a while. When I last played, the game was still in early access. I expected everything to be somewhat similar to what I had left behind, probably because I didn't read the update announcements very carefully. Naturally, I came to wish I had.
There were a few things I noticed right off the bat:
1. By all the moons, what happened to the menu? It became a cluttered mess, or rather more of one. Before, the menu wasn't the best, but I could still figure out where everything was. It took me a few minutes just to figure out how to make a new world.
2. World generation. To be fair, I never messed around with it too much before, but as with the menu situation, the new update didn't do anything to help. After some trial and error, I got it working. This one isn't really that bad, so whatever.
3. The in-game tools became a cluttered mess. I didn't struggle TOO much with finding everything, but the selection screens also seemed buggier than before. There were times I would mean to press one button, only to accidentally press another. This happened both with kb/m and a controller.
Now then, on to a quick pros/cons list:
Pros:
+ Lego-esque graphics. I've always been a fan of Lego games, and their characteristic art style.
+ Building options.
+ Pre-built structures, because I'm too lazy to make everything on my own.
+ World variety.
Cons:
- All the problems listed above.
- Unlocking stuff is now more tedious/difficult/whatever term you want.
- (Sometimes) buggy controls and movement.
- Buggy camera.
- Lots of areas feel very empty.
- Even with friends, not that enjoyable.
- (Occasionally) odd/poor/unpolished animation. This isn't all the time though.
Final verdict- If you must get this game, get it when it's on sale. Otherwise, don't get it at all.

Spooky's House of Jump Scares is worth your time. Being free (as of this review), this is the only benchmark the game has to pass. If it's worth your money, and worth your time, you should play it. While I have very little experience in the horror genre, Spooky's House of Jump Scares is pretty transparent with its premise. There's plenty of cute and lighthearted moments, some jump scares, and a thin thread of plot which goes deeper than the surface level. There are 1000 rooms, so you'll spend most of your time wandering from room to room, taking less than a second to move through one of the many repeated corridors. And, while the enemies are spaced out well enough to keep you interested, they can sometimes be a bit underwhelming. However, there are a couple of genuinely scary moments, and the game has enough charm that you may want to stick around to see it all.
If you're looking for simple jump scares this game has you covered, and if you're interested in some horror game mechanics in a boiled-down scenario, check it out.

I would have given a positive review but there are a few elements of the game that really bother me. I would however like to see a sequel made where they improve the flaws in this game's design.
Don't get me wrong, there are many good things about the game: such as the setting, the graphics, the story and the main character (it is nice to have a brown coloured main character for once and the main character's design is really well done).
But the good things aside, it is the flaws of the game that really hold it back for me and ruined the overall experience, for me.
The first issue is the combat; it uses preset combos that you can customise, from the moment the game introduced the combat in this way I knew immediately - oh boy this game's combat is going to get very repetitive very fast! The issue when you have combos that are completely fixed with the same identical animation and same identical button combo each time is that it means you just have to keep pressing the same button combinations over, and over, and over the entire game long. Yes, you can change the combos but all it changes is the effects and the animations of the combo; the button presses remain the same. E.g. left click, right click, left click, right click. Sorry but I can only stand repeating this so often.
There is a power for Batman style freeflow combat, but it is only temporary and feels a lot less satisfying than doing a combo which actually seems to do more damage than the freeflow power. It would have been cool if the freeflow power allowed unlimited combo as long as you could keep the combo going without a break in the combo (yes, I know, like Batman). This would have helped quite a bit. There are other powers you can use and if you damage some opponents enough you can use finishers, which are cool. But these only go a short way in helping the overall issue that is the combat in this game. It may have been interesting if you simply could customise the combo effects at different stages of the combo and the animations simply cycle through the ones they have made for that effect - this way at least you have more animation variety and this would allow them to give greater customisation to the combos. E.g. you could pick speed over damage and such too, which currently is not the case. Picking the same type of combo attack with a different animation does only that - same damage, same speed, just different animation.
In addition, they could have allowed constant freeflow attacks but that do not give you a bonus effect and also reduced damage. These are just a few ideas and I'm not even a game developer.
Then there is the platforming, in general it works but it has many issues with the controls and doesn't always work or do what you want. There are times I've made the same identical jump two times, one time she just randomly decides to fall right through the ledge she was supposed to grab, the other time she grabs it no problem. Then often while going around corners or trying to jump across a gap she just refuses to go the direction you want no matter what key press you push. I don't know if this is due to the port or if this was also an issue on the console versions but definitely is something they should have fixed. If not at launch, at least with an update!

There is not that much to tell about this game: it's a very casual fishing/diving simulator, in which you spend all of your time underwater, swimming gently along some nice (sub-)tropical settings, mostly reefs. The gameplay consists of either catching the required fish, or of exploring the surroundings - either by taking "perfect" photographs of several fish, or by searching for lost treasures. There is a small element of advancing through the game, since you gather experience and money with every catch or find with which you can buy better equipment.
The main game consists of three diving locations, to which several can be added by buying the different dlc's. Every location can either be completed by fulfilling the different "mission goals" (which are mostly very basic), or can be just enjoyed swimming along in a free mode. This swimming, looking around and catching fish definitely has something very relaxing about it - this is the perfect game to play after a stressful day at work.
But the game does lack some features which would make it more attractive - I'd love to get some more information on the different fish swimming around me, and the diving-simulator part really is extremely basic. Everything is being handled automatically, which in a real-world dive surely would not be the case. Some element of action or even tension would have been incorporated here.
All in all, this is a game which offers just what it aims to do: a relaxing, nice experiencing, without any difficulty whatsoever. The Steam achievements are mostly easy to get, except for some overtly grinding ones (I don't expect too many people to spend 24 real-time hours underwater in this game).
Simple diving and exploration game, relaxing music with nice graphics.

How to even start with this game, on one hand its probably the best game of this year narrative wise, on the other it has glaring issues that really should stop me from recommending it. So I'm just going to structure this into sections because I think it will let me back up my points coherently.
The Good:
The narrative and character presented in Senua offer a very unique story and one I don't want to go too much into detail about as I think knowing too much could ruin the experience but I will say this, the mental condition is something not many games or films have ever gotten spot on and the condition in this game (psychosis) is one of the driving forces of the plot and adds a lot of tension to not only Senua, but you as well. The voices that the character experiences not only get to her, but can even put doubt and distraction in the players mind as they constantly ramble and talk during puzzles, fights and just trying to figure out what to do next.
The cut-scenes are also beautifully shot, every angle and adjustment feels like it is showing emotion. The wide angle shots making you feel distant and disconnected from reality and the close-ups feeling like you are in-closed in Senua mind just like the voices; which I feel was almost definitely intentional as the camera is almost representative of a character, Senua constantly turns and talks right to it which may seem weird to some but I think it really helps convey her emotions.
A consistently creepy and engrossing atmosphere also really helps you get immersed into this world that NinjaTheory have created. It also doesn't overstay its welcome, constantly keeping things fresh and pulling you in more and more after every level.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I feel I should dedicate a paragraph to the PC settings "and all that jazz". The game doesn't run poorly but nor does it run incredibly well either, I had around 50-60 fps with either +10 or -10 on that in some sections, It really wasn't an issue however and it never crashed nor seriously dropped into the 20s or 30s.
The settings are decent, not amazing but decent, It is a shame however that to turn off motion blur (without going into files maybe, idk I didn't try) is to lower all post processing but It once more really wasn't an issue so no need to deduct points for me, its only in here in this separated tap as It may be very important for some.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I Could go on and on about tone and how detailed and nuanced the story really but if you like what you've read so far then I implore you to buy this game if this is what you want, as the flaws really come no where near to outweighing the positives; supporting indie (yes this game is independent) games like this is very important to restoring the glory days back where almost every AAA game isn't an exclusive. Anyway if you want more on this point, watch this video by Raycevick, he explains it way better than I ever could
The Bad:
While the combat isn't terrible and it shows glimmers of greatness, it is below par overall and It maybe should have been given more time, especially from the creators of DMC. It also gets a bit repetitive, the puzzles especially, once again, not amazing but passable and they certainly get better.
Let me prefix this one, I think that Melina Juergens did a great performance and she is very talented but something about her delivery on some lines seemed off, maybe it was bad direction but It did throw me out a few times and that isn't something I can ignore in a game that is as immersive as this one. It really felt out of place and you may notice it as well.
Overall:
This is an outstanding game but not one without flaws, it is also an important game and I wish it the most success possible but it is a shame a lot of people will never get to experience this game one way or the other. But it really is so close to that masterpiece mark and I'm guessing Hellblade will have a cult following within the next few years.

Hellblade centers around a Celtic warrior named Senua, who travels to the north in order to revive her lover with the help of Norse gods. It's a classic hero's journey, but not quite what you'd expect based on this description alone. In several ways.
A game with a title such as "Hellblade" can only be a hack & slash game. There's simply no other way. But here's where Hellblade already defies expectations: While the game does feature combat, it takes a backseat in favor of some good old puzzle solving. The puzzles consist of finding runes and scanning your environment for matching patterns. Basically, the player progresses by looking at things. When you do get to slice up foes, the dance of blades is meaty and graceful, but overall rather simplistic. Light attacks and parries for regular enemies, heavy attacks for larger enemies, guard breaks for foes bearing a shield - you've probably seen it all. Plus, there's walking. Lots and lots of walking. Genre-wise, Hellblade can be best described as a mix of third person action, puzzle game and one of those infamous walking simulators.
Mechanically speaking, Hellblade would never set the world on fire. And yet, it's weirdly captivating. The reason for that is the game's gripping atmosphere. Everything about the game is dripping with gloom and the visuals only emphasize that. Of course, there's also the character of Senua. Promotion material already makes a big fuss about her mental illness. The twist is that Senua's journey to hell in order to overcome grief is symptomatic of her psychosis, from her obsession with patterns in mundane objects (see: puzzles) down to her delusion that a Norse god might bring her lover back from the dead. It's nothing American McGee hasn't done already, except Hellblade goes one step further to put the player in the shoes of such a troubled individual. The player will frequently encounter visual glitches or whispers mocking, confusing, sometimes encouraging him. Said whispers also serve as audio cues for when the player is stuck, or during combat when an enemy is about to strike from off-camera, which is pretty much the only trouble you will have in this game.
For the most part, developer Ninja Theory treats the topic of mental illness with respect. There is no easy solution, no tear-jerking and no pretense - like Senua, the player has to accept it for what it is. You won't gain any new insights on the topic of mental health either. It would be the wrong medium, anyway. And apart from a few hammy moments, Hellblade also works well as a psychological drama, although cutscenes tend to occur more often and run longer than they should. Plus, though Hellblade is lovely animated, in those cutscenes Senua has a weird habit of exposing her front teeth for no reason, which looks off.
If you can enjoy a video game for something other than how they play, Hellblade might be worth a spin. It offers an atmosphere that is as depressing as it is absorbing, conveyed primarily by the game's visual and audio design as well as by dealing with rather dark topics like mental illness. On top of all, it's a journey that feels personal. Hellblade's themes would be easy to dismiss as a mere gimmick if they didn't tie in beautifully with the game. It's just sad there's not more of a game in here.
On a different note: VNV Nation during the credits? Oh Tameem, will you ever grow out of your goth phase?

After much work to get this application to work on 64-bit Ubuntu, 16.04 and forks:
Open Source Drivers on Ubuntu 16.04
1. Installing DRICONF.
2. Installing the ST3C support.
3. In the .drirc file of your /home directory should have the following under the application name of default:
<option name="force_s3tc_enable" value="true" />
<option name="allow_glsl_extension_directive_midshader" value="true" />
Both are necessary for the game to get to the main menu and be usable.
However, following the directions from FrozenByte, the sound is still really bad and buggy. It jitters, stutters and overall just horrible. It doesn't matter what version of libvorbis you use, the floating point or integer based variant. I can't recommend this game for any Linux player because there is no guarantee it will work on your system and it doesn't automatically install the dependencies needed for this game to work when you click the play button in Steam.

Environmental Station Alpha is a brilliant little gem of a game, and as far as I am concerned - the best metroidvania on Steam by a wide margin. A Metroidvania wrapped around an insane hours-long trail of riddles, optional bosses and crazy challenges leading to alternate endings. Two things to keep in mind, though - firstly, Normal is actually really hard, so don't be afraid to play it on Easy if you're not looking for a serious challenge. Secondly, the game's map will outright lie to you about how many exits there are out of a given room. There's a bit of rubbing up against walls to figure out which one's fake and there isn't always an exit shown on the map, or enough of a hint that there is one at all.

The boss battles are cheap, unfair, painstakingly repetitive and slow. A series of long lasting easy to dodge moves followed by the boss sporadically flailing around or shooting sprays of bullets in an impossible to avoid manner during the only time you can actually damage them.
I regret buying this game. beating this game means you're lucky, not skilled. I would not recommend this game even if it were on sale. If the bosses weren't complete BS I would gladly pay more than the current price. Even then it has many other flaws.

Thoroughly enjoyable game. Make sure to read the negative reviews before deciding whether the "Mixed" rating is sufficient to discourage you from buying it. Most of the reasonable ones were technical issues (which I definitely sympathize with and which I would have been equally♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥about had I experienced any game-breaking bugs), and then there are the ones from Nazi sympathizers complaining that this 36-year-old series about killing Nazis still involves killing Nazis. (In some quite satisfying ways, incidentally. Whether you like chopping Nazis apart with an axe, or burning Nazis alive with diesel bombs, or vaporizing Nazis with lasers, or good old-fashioned killing the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of Nazis with fast-moving bits of lead, this game can fit your playstyle.)
A lot of the mechanics are basically the same as in New Order, which some people have complained about, but for me there was enough novelty with the power armor in the first half of the game and the contraptions in the second to keep it interesting.
Another complaint I've seen is that the Übercommander side missions are all in places you've already visited, so they don't really expand the game as much as one might like, but I treated them like a way to revisit levels and gather collectibles and readables I missed the first time through, which was a lot better than just replaying the same missions to acheive the same goal.
One criticism I found more understandable (if minor) was the lack of a final boss fight the way there was in New Order. There is what amounts to a fairly difficult boss fight near the end, but the enemies are just the same nameless, faceless Nazis you've been killing all along, only more powerful.
If it runs on your machine (which, being Bethesda, is always a significant "if") and if you don't need a safe space for your fragile pro-Nazi sentiments, it's absolutely worth playing.

Blazkowicz barely survives a present from general Deathshead. After some time in recovery, the story continues. Not much of a spoiler, really. Immediately, things start to go crazy, and will get crazier still. It's different from previous two games, cause it's less personal. The whole focus is not just Blasko, it's about the whole crew and organizing a revolution. And that's fine, cause we get to know better many other characters, which are very different from what we're used to and from each other. They all have great voice acting and keep the atmosphere in the base lively, which is a rung above the previous games. Main characters models are somewhat changed, especially in cutscenes. I liked them better before, they shouldn't have changed that.
Graphics and details are improved aswell, but you do need a serious rig for High or above. Even on Medium setting it looks amazing, but on High i got some fps drops with my GTX 970.
Gameplay is easily the best thing about this game, and if for nothing else, you gotta play it for this. Perks are still here, weapon upgrades too. But there's something new too - contraptions. I love ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t like this :)  It's a really interesting mechanic that makes it very fun to play. It spices up stealth, combat and exploration. Doesn't matter how realistic it is, after all it's a game, it should be unrealistic.
Plenty of collectables, and they're cumulative for a savegame slot as before. They do add value to the story, as you find out more about your enemies and the people involved, if you don't mind reading them, but you should.
Stealth is also more rewarding, cause you get to eavesdrop on enemies and listen to their conversations, which is always fun. And you don't have to defeat armies of enemies, which would be challenging on higher difficulties.
This is the first game i payed full price for, and i have absolutely no regrets. I really wanted to play it right away and find out what happens next. It's not boring, even when you're just hunting collectables, cause it looks so good, just running around is satisfying. And it has more content, took me about 40 hours in previous games for a single pass 100%, i'm at 60 hours in this one, and that's gonna go much higher while pursuing the rest of the achievements, and that's all before the DLCs. In a market filled with many games focused in loot and quests it may be hard for some games to get the recognition they deserve and with The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing I can honestly say that it was such a pleasant surprise that I hope it’s not something to go under your radar. As you can expect, you plan as Van Helsing while also having with your ghost friend and companion Lady Katarina. The world from the game is a mix of wilderness in forests, swamps and secret lairs with a combination of cities inspired by the gothic architecture that blends perfectly with the theme of Van Helsing.

The Story is easy to follow and it is told in a very casual manner without taking itself too seriously by adding one little joke here and there. As you advance in your main story you will be asked to do another tasks, which, while entirely optional they are highly recommended to do since it will show you different enemies and different worlds. The best part of doing these side quests was that, not once I felt overwhelmed with a ridiculous amount of tasks to do, it’s just about the right amount of content if you just want to play a 20 hour long game without the need to grind by keep killing the same old monsters or soldiers over and over again.
With the option to choose between a more ranged or melee approach to kill your enemies, the variety in the customization is also a pleasant surprise. Depending on the style you choose how you want to engage your enemies you can engage them from far or close and personal so it’s really up to you how to tackle them. There’s also a decent selection of Auras, Skills and other powers and abilities for you to explore and learn as you level up. Lady Katarina, your companion, is also customizable and you can even order her on how to approach your enemies as well what to you want her to do. She can attack from close or long range, focus on the weakest enemies or on those harming you not to mention you can ask her to go sell your unwanted loot or even to buy some health and mana potions, saving plenty of time to explore a bit while she’s shopping for you.
It’s a very easy-to-follow game and fairly enjoyable. I never felt frustrated or bored and the game did not felt repetitive, something that may be common in these types of games. I had an enjoyable experience from start to finish while listening the pleasant soundtrack and the funny sayings from lady Katarina from time to time.

This game used to be pretty good, in my opinion. Not the best game ever, but certainly enjoyable. However, that seems to have changed.
When I installed the newest updates, I hadn't played in quite a while. When I last played, the game was still in early access. I expected everything to be somewhat similar to what I had left behind, probably because I didn't read the update announcements very carefully. Naturally, I came to wish I had.
There were a few things I noticed right off the bat:
1. By all the moons, what happened to the menu? It became a cluttered mess, or rather more of one. Before, the menu wasn't the best, but I could still figure out where everything was. It took me a few minutes just to figure out how to make a new world.
2. World generation. To be fair, I never messed around with it too much before, but as with the menu situation, the new update didn't do anything to help. After some trial and error, I got it working. This one isn't really that bad, so whatever.
3. The in-game tools became a cluttered mess. I didn't struggle TOO much with finding everything, but the selection screens also seemed buggier than before. There were times I would mean to press one button, only to accidentally press another. This happened both with kb/m and a controller.
Now then, on to a quick pros/cons list:
Pros:
+ Lego-esque graphics. I've always been a fan of Lego games, and their characteristic art style.
+ Building options.
+ Pre-built structures, because I'm too lazy to make everything on my own.
+ World variety.
Cons:
- All the problems listed above.
- Unlocking stuff is now more tedious/difficult/whatever term you want.
- (Sometimes) buggy controls and movement.
- Buggy camera.
- Lots of areas feel very empty.
- Even with friends, not that enjoyable.
- (Occasionally) odd/poor/unpolished animation. This isn't all the time though.
Final verdict- If you must get this game, get it when it's on sale. Otherwise, don't get it at all.

Preface: I mostly play Normal mode on PS4. I only got the PC version on sale to play at work after the 1.3 update and have never touched Survival, Hardcore, or Casual game modes.
I've enjoyed this game since release, but it definitely won't be for everyone.
Good:
- Basic exploration of an infinite number of proceduraly generated worlds.
- The best option I'm aware of for a sci-fi game that allows you to transition seemlessly between planets in a solar system. You're not limited to a single solar system, but the transition between stars breaks the illusion of being a real place for me.
- Mindless resource collection with decent crafting options.
- Very low stress.
- Continuing to receive free updates.
Bad:
- A lot of grinding.
- Game doesn't have a lot of variety, at least before 1.3. Yes, the worlds and animals are technically all different, but they also tend to feel very similar.
- Not exciting or demanding in any way. Surface combat is never challenging, and space combat is usually the same. If you do happen do die, it's more of an inconvenience than anything else.  NOTE: This may be different in the Survival and Hardcore game modes. I wouldn't know.
- Not much multiplayer interaction before 1.3. I understand you can now see and hear other players in-game. I'm not very familiar with how well this is working, but you still have to go out of your way to encounter other players anwyay.
- Slightly bug-ridden. No surprise, really, given the size of the studio, but it's frustrating to lose progress when the game crashes. Thankfully, there are frequent auto-save points. I recommend triggering these (by leaving your ship) before ever attempting to warp between systems by any means.
- Filled with questionable User Interface decisions. This is a game that requires a lot of inventory management, especially in the early game. However, even after dozens of hours, I sometimes find myself having to reorganize materials between four different inventories in order to build a necessary upgrade.

All this comes with a caveat:  I am not a min/max hardcore achievement hunter.  Those guys are a different breed and you should read their 1.3 reviews, not mine.
That said, NMS has evolved from a hard-to-recommend tech demo into a full fledged game.  The 1.3 patch, which is essentially the game they should have released last year, makes for a fantastic voyage into the unknown.  I can't vouch for survival mode or permadeath (not my style), but the standard and creative modes now rival many crafting survival games that excel at the genre.
Simply put, it may not be worth 60 dollars yet, but a thirty dollar sale, absolutely.
Instead of recounting my hours with NMS (only half of them were on PC), I'm going to list those who should buy and those who shouldn't:
You should buy NMS if:
You like scifi tropes and fictional space as a backdrop.  Read: familiar SciFi fantasy.
You like to work from the lowest of the low into an interstellar combat/trading/exploration tycoon.
You just wanna build a base.
You like steady and constant upgrades culminating in a sandbox type game.
You like wandering aimlessly.
You like following a defined path (you can be aimless or directed in this game).
You like feeling small in the face of an uncaring and mysterious universe.
You should not buy NMS if:
You need top notch twitch FPS responsiveness with no input lag and headshots.
You think space flight is going to be like Elite:Dangerous.
You think you'll never see the same animal (or 1% offshoot) twice.
You want to be a god among men. (Cheats/Mods notwithstanding)
You can't stand minor imperfections.
Temper your expectations.  This is not the end all be all game.  I obssessed about NMS with all the initial release hype and I was let down hard.  But I still put many hours into the game and I will put in many more.  This is not a blockbuster sandbox like Minecraft.  It is quirky and beautiful and frustrating and overwhelming all at once.  It challenges you to find your own path while giving you a goal to work with.  1.3 only enhances all of this and I can't yet tell how the story they put into place will play out.  But it's the basis of a game (now with rudimentary MP) that lets the inner explorer and completionist share the same room together without tearing each other to pieces.
TL:DR - It's a good game now.  Buy it on sale and sink 40 hours into it.  Totally worth it.
