{TL;DR:
Pros- Excellent female protagonist, good story, and beautiful environments
Cons- Game wants to be a movie, my knowledge of physics keeping the combat from being more than a bad joke}
Set in a perfectly realized cyberpunk future, Remember Me is deeply satisfying. The environments are beautifly detailed and complement the free running elements of this title, even if it can turn into a "look at the pretty skybox" stlye staright path a times. On the subject of free running, you might expect a free running brawler to include some moves that include jumping on your enemies from a higher point, but this is sadly not the case, despite some of your early enemies utilizing this exact tactic. Instead you, playing as asmall, skinny woman, must stand on the same level as larger, sometimes hulking, enemies. Of course the protagonist does this with great ease, you don't want to design a game to be too frustrating, after all. I'm not saying Nilin should be weak and helpless like so many other female characters in games, in fact, I think she maybe the best example of a female protagonist in a video game yet. That said, while I can imagine that anyone of her size who can run and jump all around the obstacles Nilin encounters just on her way to the local bar to have the endurance and speed to hold up in a fight, the boss fight against X-Mass Kid is a mahor breaking point of this logic.
Regardless, the combat is simple, yet fun. Besides, the size difference isn't the biggest problem with the game, the problem is that Remember Me desperately wants to be a movie. I may have only just started episode 3 (something Valve can no longer use as an excuse), but a good chunk of the game, about 1/3 of my playtime, has been spent in cutseens, scripted sequences and "pretty skybox" segments. I know this might be the "no" moment for those considering playing this, but hold on just a second. It turns out that the story is really good, so the "want to be a movie" problem is very neglegable. Also, in my opinion, the exploration and combat parts (you know, the game part) of the game show up enough to keep the movie bits from overstaying their welcome.
All in all, this is a nice story with some fun, anarchist-cyberpunk brawler action. There are some flaws, as there are with any game, but nothing that can't be ignored when put next to the better elements.

There's a lot to like to this one, but although I would recommend it, it still leaves much to be desired.
The concept is interesting and pretty unique. It is very linear and story-driven, but it doesn't utilise the core mechanic of memory remixing much at all. At it's core it's a third-person fighting game with some shooting tacked on. The combat mechanics were average at best despite the pressens adding an interesting touch. Shooting is sloppy thanks to a sluggish and unresponsive camera and some mechanics were badly interpreted for a mouse/keyboard player.
This is a console port though, so that's why it has these problems with controls. Despite this though, I got used to it and didn't end up grumbling too much in-game from control-related failures.
The story is very good though, but I won't spoil. The dystopian future is pulled off very well with some amazing level design with very few complaints. They even tried a bit of a puzzle element, which was completely out of place but a cute effort.
I do recommend this game. It's not a 'must play', but it certaintly is a'should play'.

First impressions:
I went into this game expecting something like Skyrim meets Dark Souls…I was wrong, very wrong.  Hellblade stands alone in terms of game play, at least from my experience.  The very first thing I noticed were the multitude of voice’s inside of the protagonist’s head.  At first I thought this was a bit distracting, but after a while it became a very unique way of expositing the story.  No reading, no narration, just the protagonist’s thoughts…and it’s awesome!
Game Play:
Third person, over the shoulder; about what you would expect from the Unreal engine.  Movement is simple and fairly standard, making it easy to pick up and go.  One of the most interesting things I noticed was how the environment changes as the protagonist’s mind set changes.  The combat was interesting, seeming like a simplified Dark Souls style, but it is also very intense.
And that is a great way to describe this game as a whole: Intense.  The game play is incredible and engaging and the psychosis effects are awesome and together create one of the most interesting games I have ever played.

How to even start with this game, on one hand its probably the best game of this year narrative wise, on the other it has glaring issues that really should stop me from recommending it. So I'm just going to structure this into sections because I think it will let me back up my points coherently.
The Good:
The narrative and character presented in Senua offer a very unique story and one I don't want to go too much into detail about as I think knowing too much could ruin the experience but I will say this, the mental condition is something not many games or films have ever gotten spot on and the condition in this game (psychosis) is one of the driving forces of the plot and adds a lot of tension to not only Senua, but you as well. The voices that the character experiences not only get to her, but can even put doubt and distraction in the players mind as they constantly ramble and talk during puzzles, fights and just trying to figure out what to do next.
The cut-scenes are also beautifully shot, every angle and adjustment feels like it is showing emotion. The wide angle shots making you feel distant and disconnected from reality and the close-ups feeling like you are in-closed in Senua mind just like the voices; which I feel was almost definitely intentional as the camera is almost representative of a character, Senua constantly turns and talks right to it which may seem weird to some but I think it really helps convey her emotions.
A consistently creepy and engrossing atmosphere also really helps you get immersed into this world that NinjaTheory have created. It also doesn't overstay its welcome, constantly keeping things fresh and pulling you in more and more after every level.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I feel I should dedicate a paragraph to the PC settings "and all that jazz". The game doesn't run poorly but nor does it run incredibly well either, I had around 50-60 fps with either +10 or -10 on that in some sections, It really wasn't an issue however and it never crashed nor seriously dropped into the 20s or 30s.
The settings are decent, not amazing but decent, It is a shame however that to turn off motion blur (without going into files maybe, idk I didn't try) is to lower all post processing but It once more really wasn't an issue so no need to deduct points for me, its only in here in this separated tap as It may be very important for some.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I Could go on and on about tone and how detailed and nuanced the story really but if you like what you've read so far then I implore you to buy this game if this is what you want, as the flaws really come no where near to outweighing the positives; supporting indie (yes this game is independent) games like this is very important to restoring the glory days back where almost every AAA game isn't an exclusive. Anyway if you want more on this point, watch this video by Raycevick, he explains it way better than I ever could
The Bad:
While the combat isn't terrible and it shows glimmers of greatness, it is below par overall and It maybe should have been given more time, especially from the creators of DMC. It also gets a bit repetitive, the puzzles especially, once again, not amazing but passable and they certainly get better.
Let me prefix this one, I think that Melina Juergens did a great performance and she is very talented but something about her delivery on some lines seemed off, maybe it was bad direction but It did throw me out a few times and that isn't something I can ignore in a game that is as immersive as this one. It really felt out of place and you may notice it as well.
Overall:
This is an outstanding game but not one without flaws, it is also an important game and I wish it the most success possible but it is a shame a lot of people will never get to experience this game one way or the other. But it really is so close to that masterpiece mark and I'm guessing Hellblade will have a cult following within the next few years.

Sine Mora is a bad SHMUP. Let's get that out of the way before anything else. Random scoring, a poorly defined central mechanic (which you cannot even use if you want to score well) and boss/enemy designs that just feel cheap plague this game. The enemies don't stand out from the background well enough, and projectiles are a variety of colors that can sometimes blend in (one boss even has orange/red projectiles which are flanked by a SUNSET, and the screen gets 'brighter' as if blinding you during the fight). Skip this and go get Jamestown. Sine Mora is a terrible excuse for a SHMUP, and a poorly designed, yet beautiful game.

This turned out to be a really visually interesting arcadey shmup, and I had a blast just looking at and discovering things for the first time. It's incredibly well designed and tight with a great depth of options for replay value, it's just such a damn shame that it's so short on levels and content.
The focus and budget on Sine Mora clearly went into the set designs, which are a really compelling mix of 3D environments played from a 2D point of view. The world is varied and interesting, and the art style is sharp but still arcadey enough to be mostly upbeat and fun. The enemies are all different and while they mostly play the same (take out section X -> move forward or flip angles and take on section Y -> survive through bullet-hell section Z to defeat the enemy) there are a few unique sections where the screen will rotate and it's about accomplishing various objectives, or you'll be dodging more than shooting, or vice versa. These all help to mix the gameplay up and make the enemies interesting.
The other thing that makes this title shine is the story elements and good writing everywhere. Every character has a well introduced backstory, and not just to give them depth, it also fits them into the story. There's a fantastic encyclopaedia available in the menu screens that helps you understand each aspect of the world and history of the characters more, and the introduction to enemies is very interesting in game. It feels more mature than you'd expect from a typical shmup, especially one with an arcade style gameplay like this.
By far the biggest problem with Sine Mora is the lack of content. Clearly it was never intended to be longer than a few hours, and the focus went into the beauty and design of those levels, which shows. But despite the replay value offered by multiple characters, aircraft, unlockables and different gaming modes like score attack and arcade, it's just boring and repetitive after more than a few hours. If you're not a completionist, a die-hard shmup fan, or both then you're unlikely to have reason to play the story more than once or twice.
The other failure or complaint is that shmup fans typically want to strive for high scores and competitive speedruns, etc. They're the type of gamers who expect more than just a score attack, and get annoyed at things like random score multipliers, random powerups and things that take away from the real competitive aspect of the game. Sine Mora seems to have tried to appease new players and die-hard shmup fans and has failed on the latter as a result.
Available for £7.99/9.99€/$9.99 on Steam and while it's pretty short, it's still fair value when compared to competitors like Jamestown and Raiden III Digital Edition at the same price. When it's on sale, in my opinion it's probably the best option on Steam for a modern entry level shmup for someone like me who isn't heavily into the genre but wants to give something more casual like this a try.

All of the Jackbox games are excellent party games, and this one is no exception. Some of the games have a single-player mode (e.g. You Don't Know Jack) but for the most fun, try and get a group of people together. Great party game, plenty of fun and some decent options to keep things varied.

For streaming it would more sense to buy Fibbage XL and Drawful 2 separate, as You Don't Know Jack 2015 doesn't stream well. Lie Swatter + Word Spud are sort of play-once throwaway titles, you'll forget you even have them. I've also experienced a glitch multiple times in the first Drawful in which the game softlocks.

The Original Jackbox Party Pack still holds up fairly well since it's release. It includes 5 great party games that anyone can easily learn to play and join in on.
YOU DON'T KNOW JACK 2015: A hilarious trivia game with a charismatic host, Cookie Masterson.
FIBBAGE XL: Write lies to fool other players thinking its the truth.
WORD SPUD: Like hot potato, pass around a word and add to it before the timer runs out.
DRAWFUL: The drawing game where you dry a strange thing and others try to guess what it is.
LIE SWATTER: Hosting up to 100 players, determine if the info on the screen is a fact or a lie.
SOME NEGATIVES: You cannot pause the game, unlike other packs where you can pause by hitting ESC, you cannot pause the games, which is kinda annoying at times. (This may not be a negative to some) There is no family-friendly mode, which when playing with younger ones can't be all that fun, but this may not apply to some.
To conclude, TJPP is an overall great pack of games bound to bring hours of fun and laughs. Aside from it's few quirks, the pack is well worth the price considering that it is very replayable and it is so handy that anyone can play via their device (phone, tablet, PC, etc.)

Hey everyone and this is my review about the game!
This is a Action Co-op PVP game.
There are many resolution sizes available.
There is fullscreen, windowed mode and borderless window.
There is a brightness volume slidebar available. 80% - 120%
There is a master volume slidebar available. 0% - 100%
There is a music volume slidebar available. 0% - 100%
There is an interface volume slidebar available. 0% - 100%
There is a gameplay volume slidebar available. 0% - 100%
There is a tutorial available.
You are able to play with a controller.
There is microphone, chat and quick-chat wheel.
You are able to change the controls.
You are able to change the look of your crosshair.
You can choose between a Shark player or a Diver player. Each of them plays differently.  Each team (2 sharks and 4 divers) has around 30 life tickets. The game could be dark at times, so boosting up your brightness or darkening your own room will make the game a bit more brighter.
Yes there are consumables to make some area's a bit more lit up or certain maps are brighter than others, but trust me. IF you are making your own room darker, the game gets brighter.
You can choose between a couple of sharks such as "Tiger, Great White, Thresher, Hammerhead, Bull, Mako and the Goblin shark". Each shark has different abilities, stats and a may have a different gameplay. Tiger sharks are fast, squishy and has the ability to go invisible while the Hammerhead shark is doing tons of damage with the environment.
Shark has a third player camera (Camera is behind the character) and they have 2 ways of winning. They will have to destroy The gold robot "S.T.E.V.E" or killing the divers until they ran out of tickets. Each kill will grant the shark at least 10 evolution points which they could spent to make their shark stronger. Giving them Bleed effect, Faster movement, lifesteal, upgrading their ability and many more. Skills building depends on which shark you are using. There are also seals swimming around and they are waiting to be eaten by a shark which will heal the shark.
You are able to buy certain weapons or tools in the beginning and perhaps consumables. Divers will need to collect gold that are scattered around the map in order to buy new consumables, modifiers or even stronger weapons. Consumables are really important and could change the outcome of a game.
Divers have the first person shooter perspective and they also have 2 ways of winning. They will have to survive and make sure that the gold robot "S.T.E.V.E" will make it back to the boat after opening 4 loot cases or by killing sharks until their ran out of tickets. Gold could be difficult to find at times but by buying the "Sonar" or "DPV" it will save you alot of time. The Gold could be spend for modifiers such as "Bleed, Toxic, Tag shots, scopes and many more" but they can also be spend on consumables to buy medkits, mines, Flares, Supply kits and many more.
Good Graphics.
Good Music/soundtrack.
The game keeps track of your stats and how many shark/diver matches you have played.
There are 12 maps.
There are events ingame which are totally for free and you are able to get some skins for in return.
You are able to buy skins, skins are pure cosmetic and has no game impact. So NO pay to win.
Matches are really short (5-20 Minutes a match).
Game could be repetitive at times.
There is no matchmaking which will mean that a level 1 can fight against a level 58. But that is normal in these pvp games as there are smurfs on other pvp games as well. So if anyone says, there is no matchmaking, There never was a matchmaking in any game due smurfs.
There is a leaderboards available with each of a different tracking. (Shark kills, Diver kills, gold collected and many more).
There is a level system and once you have reached the max level which is 100 you will get a crown. (Level system doesn't have an impact on the game)
The game is often for sale for $5 instead of $20. You may want to wait if you are unsure about the game but in the end it will pay off if you do like the game.
It has a small community, but an active community and so are the developers.

This game isn't as bad as people say but in it's current state its hard to recommend.
First and formost this game should NOT have been released off of early access yet for a number of reasons. Firstly, most the quests are broken and the ones that aren't are laughably boring. If you like painting (literally just changing the colour of bricks) or finding items that are nowhere to be found, then this game is for you. Secondly, the game holds most of itself away from you until you find "gold bricks". How do you find them? Well since most of the 'quests' (if you can really call them that) are broken you'll spend most of your time searching for them in chests that are ALWAYS buried underground and you have to dig them up (once you've unlocked the landscape tool). I could go on, don't get me started on any of the vehicle controls. This game had a LOT of promise in early access, a chance to build and explore your very own lego world? Take my money! Discovering items and characters was exciting (and didn't require giving items you never have only to find ONE and they take it out of your inventory!) and the biomes were unique. But all we got was a cheap, rushed game that forces you to do things the hard way to lengthen what little content and experiences it offered. Don't get me wrong, walking around for the first time is amazing, and finding your first town is the coolest! But the gimmicks wear off fast and after grinding your first 50 bricks for a world size that isn't tiny you'll start to loathe this game.  There are only a limited amount of bricks to build with and you have to unlock them all too! One by ONE. There's no difference between adventure mode and sandbox except sandbox has unlocked everything and has no quests. Which is what most people will probably play. And don't expect to see giant lego cities like Lego City undercover either, towns are tiny to say the least. As it is right now, there are way too many bugs, glitches and broken mechanics to enjoy Lego Worlds. I'd hope for future updates but seeing the trailer for the 'classic space pack' DLC we'll probably have to shell out more $$$ to play a decent game. Why make DLC for an unfinished game?
Sorry for the rant, I don't hate this game. I just REALLY dislike it.

Remember Me never quite meets it's full potential but it's still a robust experience overall.
For starters, it's one of the most visually striking games I've ever played. The graphics and art direction are absolutely phenomenal. I'd almost solely recommend this game on the strength of it's visuals, it's that good.
The game has a very uneven story though it's bursting with originality. The writing is smart enough to ask to right kind of questions and there are some truly memorable moments in the 9 chapters that comprise the story.
Nilin, who already stands out from most video game protagonists by being a woman of colour, is written with the right balance of emotion and toughness. She feels vulnerable but is always capable of getting the job done. In between each chapter Nilin monologues about what's she done and how she feels; there are some genuinely interesting moments of pathos for her that flesh out her personality. She's much more interesting that other characters in these types of games such as Kratos or Dante.
Remember Me's biggest fault is the gameplay. This is a character action game with a total of 5 combos. Changing what your combos do is a good idea in theory and having multiple enemy types helps but it doesn't change that you essentially are pushing the same combination of buttons for the entire game. This is going to be a problem for many people, especially if you're looking for a challenging experience. The combat doesn't nearly have as much depth as competing games in the same genre.
If you're new to the action genre, or you want an adequate action game with a good story, then I recommend Remember Me. If you want a highly polished action game, look elsewhere.

This is atrocious.
I tried to stick it out in the end to see how the story played out but I couldn't stomach another bugged boss fight where I spend 15minutes with failed dodged mechanics and inexplicable QTE. Then to only to be rewarded with the game not proceeding and having to repeat the entire experience.
The premise of this game is interesting enough, you have a memory hunter, an "errorist" of the most extreme sense a political terrorist to take down the big bad corporation. Yadda yadda ya. First big problem: game crashes on Ch 0. Worrisome. Game cache to fix, downloads 1.1gb of missing data.... okay? How on Earth was that not installed?
The story gives an illusion of choice. There were huge forks in the story where a good/bad moral choice system good have been implemented but Capcom decided to go on an rails route- which really makes for a wholey underwhelming story. The character debates through internal dialogue scenes about how her floating head compatriot Edge might be "good or bad" and he's "super militant"- that's great- but we literally have no say, and we're shoved around in the story to do his bidding. If we just had our memory wiped (this is no spoiler, you're literally exposed to that in the first second of game play) wouldn't we approach things with a different perspective?
The game mechanisms are boring, the combo system is boring and has no rewards. I just set up the 5 and 6 combo to basically be healing and maximum PMP/recharge gain. Never died unless I wanted to.
Summary of this stupidity:
Gameplay: 4/10- at least you could combo somewhat seamlessly, the finishers had no variability and no bonuses for using them

It's a good game for three bucks.   Very relaxing.  Basically you swim around and either A) go harpoon fishing, where you single-handedly reduce the Pacific ocean's fish stocks by 50% with a speargun, B) Look for treasure, which is floating around the reef floor and pick up ancient plates and statues and such, or C) take photographs of various underwater attractions, like sunken planes and ships, coral reefs and other fauna, and underwater ruins.
All three are fairly relaxing, though fishing becomes tedious quickly because of the relatively small number of fish you're allowed to spear (no dolphins or sharks or sea turtles, I'm afraid).   Trying to find every piece of treasure in a given area can get a bit tedious as well, so I would say photography mode is my favorite.  Exploring the wrecks is especially interesting.  I wish it were possible to turn off the navigation points within them though (maybe it is but I didn't see the option).
Along the way you'll gain experience and money that can be used to unlock levels and purchase new gear, like flippers that let you swim faster and a camera with better zoom or more storage, or let you go longer between surfacing for air (because apparently you aren't SCUBA diving, but are in fact a snorkler with the world's greatest lung capacity).  It's all pretty easy to do and there isn't much in the way of grinding involved.
So, yeah for three bucks it's a fun little diving game.  It's a genre that's been underserved for a long time but now there are a few games for it, the other main one being Subnautica.  That's much more of a tense survival game, but there's much more to it than Deep Hunter 2.  Then again, that one takes place on a fictional planet so you won't see real-world animals in it, and it isn't three dollars either.

So, 7 years after release, i decided to buy the game again. This time on Steam...obviously.
And guess what ? It still stands its ground. People saying that it's the best CoD game in the franchise are not full of shait or blinded by nostalgia.
I first started up the singleplayer campaign. Finished the boat mission and when the text, "Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare", appeared after the end of the first mission, i got chills. Really. It felt just like the first time i ever played the game.
And it isn't the nostalgia talking. It was like a new experience...only re-lived.
The music, the atmosphere...everything in here is so well done.
Atmosphere...a little sense of realism and characteristics...these are something that are missing in the latest CoD games.
Since Black Ops 1 it has been just about explosions and over-the-top action.
I love explosions...and i love the silly, uber-soldier action...but CoD went too far with it. You don't feel close to the characters anymore. You don't get sucked into the stories or into the world...no. It's just nonesense action. The characters in Blops games or Ghosts, they don't feel like soldiers anymore. Hell, they are not soldiers. They are superheroes.
When i play a CoD game i want a game with soldiers, not a Marvel movie directed by Michael Bay...it's like Marvel Transformers...ugghhh...
The campaigns in CoD4 and MW2 are the only good campaigns in the new era of CoD. Old era (CoD 1-3) is ofc good aswell, but the gameplay in the latest CoDs is just way better.
EDIT: OK, WaW campaign is quite decent aswell and i did enjoy Blops2 campaign 'cus it tried to be fresh and innovative but the story and characters were still just "MEH!".
Now the multiplayer. This is where CoD4 shines. This is where the roosters at! It still holds up.
I expected a dated character movement and gunplay but i was dead wrong. The gunplay is amazing! The gunplay is, in fact, better than in Blops or MW3.
Sure, the character movement is a bit smoother in, say...Blops2. But everything else is better in here.
Yes, the multiplayer is still alive! Hundreds, if not thousands, of servers full of people! There are 8vs8 servers, 12vs12, 16vs16, 20vs20 even!
Latest CoDs only have 8vs8 and that's about it...maybe 12vs12 max but not more.
CoD4 is the only CoD where you see 40 people in one server.
It also has one of the best multiplayer maps. MW2 had some really cool maps too and Blops2 had couple of decent maps (Nuketown and Hijacked) but CoD4 takes the cake! Pretty much every map is a masterpiece in here!
CoD4: Modern Warfare is a must have for every FPS fan!

*As its been announced that Chrono Phantasm Extend is coming to PC, I thought I'd make this review*
This review is lengthy and If you don't have time to just sit and look through it, read a shorter condensed review.
Rare, very rare is it for me to find a game that actually will allow you the chance at a tremendous gameplay and story. Myself, I've never liked the 2d fighting games, but Blazblue really helped change that if only because of its incredible story.
One thing to note though: My original intention for me buying the game was for the story, but the fun gameplay and character variety changed that.
Story wise you won't find much that can compare to some of the complexity that Blazblue is. If you played the original Blazblue and didn't look up anything to understand what was happening and trial-and-error it yourself, you are a trooper. The story is so complicated at times that its hard to distinguish the "right" path from the "wrong" path. Some people take this either good or bad.
For this installment however, they changed the story portion around a bit as its not as complicated to figure out. They also added a bonus for people who did (or didn't) play the original Calamity Trigger. However, that story was reduced in depth and for those who played it, will notice a lot of dialouge change. That however wasn't a bad thing since it gave us a better grounded way to understand this game.
One of the major perks I found with this game's story: It's entirely voice-acted. EVERY single character has a unique voice that's different, they all have a personality, and MY WORD does Hazama sound bloody awesome. Sometimes I wish that Ufotable would just take the dialouge, then animate it into glory. For most of the between people dialouge, I just sat back, closed my eyes, and after the end of their talking, casually hit the A button to proceed to the next. It's so much fun to understand this story.
A flaw to this game however (and to MANY people) is that the story is quite frankly, complicated as stated before. Each characters story takes place at different set, key points, and if you don't have a guide on you, your gonna have a hard time pieceing the story together. To newcomers however I say --- DON"T GIVE UP!!! There is a magnificent story behind this game and you'll miss out if you don't work to understand!
Gameplay is the typical 2d fighting with various moves that are unique to each character. However, they all have a unique way of playing style, feel, reach, and all add some sort of variety to prevent that "stale" air of copy and paste fighting characters. That itself helped me like it more.
For those who know it, theres nothing like pulling off a Astral Heat against an opponent. Oh, the satisfaction.
A great game that shouldn't be missed, wonderful story, characters, completely voiced, hilarity, fun gameplay, and more.

Hellblade centers around a Celtic warrior named Senua, who travels to the north in order to revive her lover with the help of Norse gods. It's a classic hero's journey, but not quite what you'd expect based on this description alone. In several ways.
A game with a title such as "Hellblade" can only be a hack & slash game. There's simply no other way. But here's where Hellblade already defies expectations: While the game does feature combat, it takes a backseat in favor of some good old puzzle solving. The puzzles consist of finding runes and scanning your environment for matching patterns. Basically, the player progresses by looking at things. When you do get to slice up foes, the dance of blades is meaty and graceful, but overall rather simplistic. Light attacks and parries for regular enemies, heavy attacks for larger enemies, guard breaks for foes bearing a shield - you've probably seen it all. Plus, there's walking. Lots and lots of walking. Genre-wise, Hellblade can be best described as a mix of third person action, puzzle game and one of those infamous walking simulators.
Mechanically speaking, Hellblade would never set the world on fire. And yet, it's weirdly captivating. The reason for that is the game's gripping atmosphere. Everything about the game is dripping with gloom and the visuals only emphasize that. Of course, there's also the character of Senua. Promotion material already makes a big fuss about her mental illness. The twist is that Senua's journey to hell in order to overcome grief is symptomatic of her psychosis, from her obsession with patterns in mundane objects (see: puzzles) down to her delusion that a Norse god might bring her lover back from the dead. It's nothing American McGee hasn't done already, except Hellblade goes one step further to put the player in the shoes of such a troubled individual. The player will frequently encounter visual glitches or whispers mocking, confusing, sometimes encouraging him. Said whispers also serve as audio cues for when the player is stuck, or during combat when an enemy is about to strike from off-camera, which is pretty much the only trouble you will have in this game.
For the most part, developer Ninja Theory treats the topic of mental illness with respect. There is no easy solution, no tear-jerking and no pretense - like Senua, the player has to accept it for what it is. You won't gain any new insights on the topic of mental health either. It would be the wrong medium, anyway. And apart from a few hammy moments, Hellblade also works well as a psychological drama, although cutscenes tend to occur more often and run longer than they should. Plus, though Hellblade is lovely animated, in those cutscenes Senua has a weird habit of exposing her front teeth for no reason, which looks off.
If you can enjoy a video game for something other than how they play, Hellblade might be worth a spin. It offers an atmosphere that is as depressing as it is absorbing, conveyed primarily by the game's visual and audio design as well as by dealing with rather dark topics like mental illness. On top of all, it's a journey that feels personal. Hellblade's themes would be easy to dismiss as a mere gimmick if they didn't tie in beautifully with the game. It's just sad there's not more of a game in here.
On a different note: VNV Nation during the credits? Oh Tameem, will you ever grow out of your goth phase?

This game is a throwback to the days of old (like half of everything on Steam is, these days) but it fails to recapture the excitement of those bullet-hells-gone-past by changing the formula in ways that it didnt need to be changed, and passing up on the opportunity to change it in ways that it did.
For starters, the game is too damned easy. I see all of these reviews talking about how challenging Sine Mora was... and all I can think is, "Maybe I didnt play long enough to see the later levels?" I got about four and a half levels in, before I got bored, and I never died during that time. The problem with the games difficulty is that, compared to older bullet hells  which typically only allowed you to get struck once or a very few times before dying, Sine Mora allows you to get hit as often as you like, replacing the classic "lives" system with a timer that gets decreased every time you are struck, and which can be replenished by killing enemies. Doing poorly really only lowers your score, because you can survive many strikes as long as you always kill all of the enemies on the screen in the process. Couple this with a bullet-time esque super power and the game seems devoid of tense situations, despite the abundance of enemies and bullets on the screen at any given time.
This is a very strange departure from the classic formula, and one which I think was as much for the worse, as it was unnecessary. And, meanwhile, the game fails to address the most important mechanic of bullet hell games: the weapon upgrade system. Or, more specifically, how you balance weapon loss with weapon advancement, so that the player neither has too strong, nor too weak, of a primary weapon.
Classic bullet hells simply emptied your guns when you died, and forced you to start from scratch when you respawned. This meant you were quite likely to get little farther than however far you made it on your first life, because you needed maxed out guns to handle leter stage enemy waves. It's a great tactic for soaking up quarters in the arcade, but it was largely abandoned when the genre came home to private consoles. Super Nintendo and Genesis bullet hells typically employed some kind of self-balancing mechanic which would give you weapon upgrades more frequently after respawning, and slower once your weapons were more advanced, so that you always had firepower appropriate to the stage of the game you were at.
Sine Mora however, doubles down on irritation of the former, poorer, mechanic by using a system that ostensibly allows you to recover lost weapons immediately, but actually serves to be even more frustrating. When you are struck, one or more of your weapon upgrades will fall off of your ship and you have to race forward, often into harms way, to catch them. You will very likely be struck again trying, and thus loose more upgrades. The more advanced your weapons are, the more parts you will lose with each hit. While playing, I found that because the game created no real fear of failure for me, the only reason I was worried about being hit, was because I got incredibly frustrated chasing down my upgrades... even though I really didnt need them, because the game gave me enough bumbs/special attacks to eliminate most boses without a problem.
On top of the general gameplay problems, I found the constant cinimatic interuptions to be EXTREMELY irritating. They seemed to occur every fifteen seconds or so, with no purpose other than to show off the games pretty scenery. The enemies often enter the plane of action from behind it, and I frequently found myself firing at enemies I wouldnt be able to hit for another few seconds, while I waited for them to "enter" my field of fire. The story is delivered in pages of text two or three times each level, the characters are all bland and unlikeable, and the story is so dark next to the bright, colorful levels, that it was almost mood killing.
This game was just... not fun. It got my interest the second I saw it in the store, and it lost my interest in just under an hour. The game mechanics are bad, the controls are equally as bad on mouse, keyboard, and gamepad, and I could not wrap my head around the design decisions these developers made. Many of the levels take place UNDER WATER, even though you are very clearly flying a WW2-era inspired fighter plane.
I didnt enjoy this at all, and I dont recommend it, especially not to fans of bullet hell games.

I'm a big fan of unconventional FPS games and Shark Week, and Depth blends the two wonderfully.  With Depth you can choose to be the hunter or the hunted in the form of divers or the predatory sharks.  Each round begins with the Diver team having a lead start to strategize and maneuver into defensive positions.  About 30 seconds later the Shark team is released into the waters.  This amounts to pitting 4 divers versus 2 sharks, and from my experience, the team Shark is the most fun and unsurpisingly the most popular.  This is to say if you're in the lobby and having a hard time finding a game, switch to a diver and your wait depletes.
But underneath these straightforward mechanics is a deep ability system that keeps the game competitive and gives you the sense that this game certainly isn't just a glistening novelty.  Each shark brings it's own set of advantages and disadvantages.  Large, brutish sharks do more damage but swim much more slowly.  Likewise, the more difficult to master weapons employed by divers are the more leathal.  This gives players a great sense of mastery and reward.
And what's more?  All of this takes place in a very well thought out and, at times, scary atmosphere beneath the waves.  If you're looking for a change of pace from the usual FPS, or even the novelty games here and there, this is a competitive contender and a solid buy.

This is a great Humans vs Sharks video game with many different elements from games like Dead By Daylights heartbeat indicating the enemy sharks for human players and the ability for sharks to see enemy divers from a short distance (can be extended with ability upgrades for longer ranges).
A large selection of weapons for Divers to use although the available range of weapons that you may buy depends on the money you currently hold in-match (e.g $400 for the cheapest basic pistol, $4500 for a basic harpoon which is the most powerful weapon in the game and can be upgraded with purchasable weapon mods). You can earn this currency during your matches, which you start with $700 to begin with, kind of like with CS:GO.
The reason for this large arsenal is to give you options to fight particular sharks. Net Guns = used to trap enemy sharks for a few seconds, which can be increased, although sharks have an ability that helps them break out quicker, more effective on bigger sharks as they have a bigger hitbox. Harpoon = The most powerful weapon in the game and is preferably used to take out the tankier sharks such as Great White, Hammerhead and Bull Sharks.
For sharks it is very different as they get stronger by spending evolution points earned by killing Divers on increasing their main abilities (Tiger = Cloaking, Great White = 50% reduced damage, Goblin = Hallucinations of goblin shark clones, Hammerhead = regain stamina when hitting environment when ability is active etc.) as well as abilities that reduce effectiveness of modded ammo from Divers (such as bleed, toxic and tagging ammo mods).
In terms of gameplay the 2 teams are made up of 4 Divers vs 2 Sharks, so it tends to take more skill to play Sharks compared to Divers although to make it more balanced the Sharks are deadly in their own right. The probability of victory is dependant on the performance of each team and requires strategy so teamwork is highly important in order to win.
All in all this game is pretty fun and has a decent gaming community compared to communities in other games, hacking is very rare in this type of game so you won't need to worry about it when thinking whether its worth buying this game.
The game itself doesn't require top of the line hardware in order to run it but I imagine it would be hard to run on a potato computer even on lowest settings, any gaming computer rigs from a few years ago should be able to run this game fine at least maybe on medium-high settings at solid 60fps just fine.
I'd recommend the game as it is fun to play, especially with friends if they have this game. I personally have found this to be quite fun although the only thing that annoys me is how it takes 2-7 minutes to find a game when matchmaking.

I picked this game up in a sale a while ago, because what I had previously seen and read of it sounded interesting, but initial reviews weren't really encouraging. It took me a long time to actually play this game - and boy, am I glad I finally did!
On many accounts the reviews were probably correct, especially in regards to the combat system. The fighting is ARPG style, similar to other brawlers like Batman or the recent Shadow of Mordor, and mainly takes place in smallish arenas along the path. Fights can be quite challenging, because of the many emenies attacking from all sides, requiring you to dodge and evade, and stringing together an 8-hit combo can be rather tricky. The bit that falls flat is the "combat lab", which allows you to create your own combos out of different moves. All moves have the exact same timing, albeit different animations. The only difference is in their effect. Some moves heal, others reduce cooldown on your super moves or give you bonuses for your next combo. Overall this seems more like a gimmick than a fully fledged system. Because as mentioned above, stringing together longer combos is already quite tricky.
However, it is not so much the combat that kept me playing, but the intricately realized, dystopian world in which Nilin, the main protagonist, tries to make sense of her purpose and fights to regain her memory and identity. The game is beautiful to look at. Vibrantly coloured, high fidelity environments give Neo-Paris a believable not-so-distant-future vibe. Between fights, Nilin will have to frequently traverse rooftops, building facades and other obstacle courses, Tomb Raider style. This breaks up the pace really nicely, and makes room to get the story moving while exploring.
The story is another strong point of this game. The tale as such is nothing groundbreaking, but it explores some interesting themes through unconventional means, like the memory manipulation scenes. These sequences let you re-arrange an NPCs memory of past events, to effect a different outcome in Nilin's timeline. All of these are tied neatly into the overall narrative, and provide some very welcome depth to Nilins character development, which overall is very strong - for a game...
I am very happy that I didn't just let this one pass me by! If you like Tomb Raider mixed with a bit of Deus Ex, you should have a look at this title.

This is a great game, one of my favourites. From slums to the heights of society, every level is exquisite and well designed. In the nicer parts of Neo-Paris the enviroment has this polished clean look that adds to juxtaposition of the ramshackled slums and sewers. Overall graphically it is a very stunning game.
Now gameplay. There are few things to talk about here. One is combat mechanics. This game takes an interesting approach to melee Arkham like combat. It has customizable combos, which can be accessed and altered at any time through the Combos Lab. This is a really cool idea and I love the game even more for it. The second thing to talk about is the memory remix sections. This is where you remix a person's memory so that their perception of reality is shifted in one case turning enemy into ally. This is a part of the story and part of the more morally questionable aspect of the protagonist Nilin.
Lastly the story. I have to say I loved it. But then again I'm a huge fan of the Cyberpunk genre. If you don't like cyberpunk stories than you probably wont like this one. I thought is was a brilliant depication of a dystopian society masquerading as a utopia.
Last advise: If you plan to get this game use a gamepad. With these melee combo centred games I prefer to use a gamepad. It just feels better.

Usually, the word "interesting" doesn't bode well when discussing art, but Remember Me is interesting in the best possible way. Derivative combat mechanics and uninspired platforming are a small price to pay for the marvelous, high sci-fi world building and characters that are drawn with tenderness and depth. There are sparks of brilliance everywhere, and they burn just about long enough to leave you intrigued rather than frustrated. Being able to customise attack combos is a stimulating diversion, even though there are extremely few options to choose from. The handful of "memory remix" sequences are narratively arresting, but ultimately amount to an exercise in trial and error, albeit beautifully realised. Remember Me is a game that lacks conceptual focus and falls back on a lot of tried and tested gameplay conventions to make up for it. However, the gorgeously realised world, compelling plot and fantastic presentation mean that you should definitely give it a chance. I for one will come back for a second playthrough.

This is an incredible bit of artistic game design; a glimpse into a world most people cannot imagine, told with such style and nuance as to stagger the mind.  Because it's primarily art, however, the mechanical gameplay can sometimes be frustrating, unclear or repetitive - I wouldn't have wanted more combat (sometimes the combat they do have is horribly paced, dropping you into a well of hacking and slashing for your life between long stretches of nothing) as that would have undermined the intensity of the storytelling but maybe less fetchy puzzles.
Aside from those issues, however, this has been an amazing experience and while the run time may be short (8-10 hours) it doesn't feel overpriced for what it delivered.

Hellblade is, by far, one of the most emotionally-driven games I've ever played. The protagonist (Senua) travels through a Viking hellscape constructed by the devices of her own psychotic mind. And let me tell you, experiencing the perspective - regardless of being simulated - of a person ailed by schizophrenia/psychosis in a manner this direct and in-your-face was nothing less than mind-blowing and powerful. The level of detail and the research that was done by Ninja Theory to accurately depict the phenomena experienced by Senua is astouding, and leading her through her journey was one of the most painful, but satifying endevours of my gaming career. The things that poor Senua sees are horrific to say the least, and the experience can easily leave the player perturbed and shaken.
In terms of gameplay, the combat was one of the most buttery-smooth systems I've ever played with. The mechanics are simple, but just diverse enough to let you find your own methods for taking down an opponent (or twenty). And let me tell you; killing brutish monsters and dancing around your enemies like a Pict ninja is oh-so satisfying. There is no leveling system for your character; the arsenal you have at your disposal never changes. It's completely up to the player to adapt to enemies in order to survive.
My one complaint about the combat is that it was a little too easy. I played my first playthrough on Hard (hardest difficulty) and managed not to die a single time from combat. My only deaths came from puzzle areas. But I still cannot emphasize just how satifying the combat is.
Which leads me to one of the most important aspects of the game; the puzzle and challenge areas. The developers approached these sections of the game to shed light on some aspect of Senua's psychosis. For example, there is an area where the world goes dark because of a mental phenomena known as neural blindness, and the player navigates Senua "blindly" through a pitch-black world. But most prominently, the player is going to find a load of puzzles that revolve around finding patterns amongst the mundane world (buildings, trees, shadows, ect.) - patterns that most people would never find. While some of the puzzles were challenging and enjoyable, most of them were far too tedious to make the experience enjoyable. Finding the solutions was often time-consuming and slightly aggravating. But I must say, there was a healthy combination of puzzle areas and combat sections organized throughout the game. Simply said, the game is designed and organized well.
Overall, Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is one hell of a game, and at an amazing price! The story is extremely rich and it does an excellent job of immersing the player into Senua's world. This game sheds light on a very contraversial topic, and it did so in a beautiful, artistic, and most importantly - fun perspective. If all of this information hasn't swayed you to buy this game, then at least do it to support Ninja Theory's revolutionary economical development system they used specifically for Hellblade. They created a triple-A title with a fraction of the budget, which allows us gamers to buy our favorite games for half of the normal price!
This is not just a game. It's an experience.

Top notch audio and absolutely gorgeous! Add incredible voice/face/motion performance and this is the best looking and sounding game I’ve played in, well, maybe ever. The dark fantasy environments span from beautiful glades to the depths of hell, and goes to the surreal extremes of something like Demon’s Souls. Senua is rendered with frightening detail, becoming increasingly torn up throughout the game with only 2 flaws that I noticed: no pupil dilation and she’s still ripped in flashback before she became a fighter. The monsters are all pretty faceless, but have nice random variations.
I’ve heard complaints about the combat, but I found it to be a smooth combination of timed blocks, dodges, guard breaks, and attacks. It’s basically what you would expect from a post-Arkham Asylum beat-em-up, but a little more ground level and frenetic. Depending on the mood of the scene it can be brutal thrashing or the spectacle fighter ballet seen in their previous game Heavenly Sword (there’s probably an implied antithesis given the name ‘Hellblade’). The boss fights do a good job of building on the skills you’ve learned. There’s no on screen prompts, so I had to check the options screen to learn how to play on occasion.
The puzzles are the weakest element being at best BORING because they’re easy clichés or at worst BORING because you’re circling the same area for the 5th time wishing there wasn’t a puzzle. They all make use of some nice visual tricks, but I never feel clever for stumbling through the solution.
The story is completely bizarre in the best ways possible, seamlessly jumping between hallucinations, flashbacks, monologues, intrusive thoughts, remembered conversations, and often several of those at once. It can get intense to the point of discomfort, especially with Senua having horrific meltdowns including violent self-mutilation. It can feel like slogging through a montage Tomb Raider Reboot failure sequences and her suffering is a bit much to take in while trying to unwind after work, but it’s also motivating to see what Senua overcomes compared to my minor neuroses. And despite being so intense from the start, it manages to repeatedly outdo itself by turning up the crescendos all the way to the end. The narrative treats the player like an adult and trusts them to piece together the shattered symbolic moments and characters.
I found the quick dives into Norse mythology particularly interesting, it’s not setting that I'm usually attracted to, but this version is portrayed with such relatable clarity. Which makes it such a shame that some of the stories fade out if you continue progressing through the level, forcing you to stay still or miss out. That’s my last nitpick. The storytelling and technical craft are an absolute masterpiece. The gameplay itself is a little rough, but doesn’t outweigh the interesting aspects of the game. If you’re looking for something a little darker give this game a shot.

I have to start this review with a confession: I didn't love Cave Story. I thought it was an alright game and very impressive for a one man job, but it didn't hit me in the same spot as everybody else. I always felt it couldn't really decide if it wanted to be gameplay or story driven and in the end neither portion of the game felt like the "complete" experience. I guess, it just wasn't my cup of tea but if you love it, I'm happy for you.
With that in mind, I was absolutely blown away by the beauty of Environmental Station Alpha. I'll go as far as to say, I felt like this is the best Metroidvania that isn't a Metroid I've ever played yet. (And yes, I've played Axiom Verge.) Simple in design, strong in execution. Little to no unnecessary dialoge or other gameplay interrupting cutscenes. The focus stays on exploration and progress and that's what I enjoyed oh so very much about ESA.
The game is not perfect (nothing is) of course. The difficulty is always somewhere between challenging and too damn hard; I had to repeat a few boss fights quite often and the only thing that kept me from rage quitting was the very awesome boss music. Unfortunately, I felt that the very last boss of the game was just artificially unnecessary hard and the ending I got after that fight was everything else but satisfying. It hurt me a little that a game that started so amazing ended so disappointing, BUT I haven't yet found all the extras, so there might be a special ending somewhere.
While sound design is not outstanding and the music does nothing interesting, I fell in love with the soundtrack immediately. The feel of uneasy calmness is perfectly captured in the lo fi psychedelic tracks and accompanies your travels through the deserted space station. If you want to play a simple Metroidvania that doesn't give you too much handholding and keeps the atmosphere mostly in the level design instead of the story, you will like Environmental Station Alpha!
Highly recommended.

How does an indie Metroidvania stand out from its peers? The way Environmental Station Alpha does it isn't through a notable gimmick but rather through craft. It is a quality and cohesive title that, barring difficulty issues, could be a real treat for you.
It's the classic story of an abandoned research facility and an agent sent in to investigate where it all went wrong. The player takes control of a robot that will explore ES Alpha and discover the truth behind its downfall. Along the way the player will explore, fight, and powerup in traditional Metroidvania fashion.
The powerups are cool and have that great mix of unlocking new areas in Alpha while assisting in moment-to-moment combat/traversal. You will explore many diverse regions of the Station that are memorable as they are fun to traverse. The game provides many interesting scenarios including the player speeding through a region while their health is slowly drained by the intense heat. These are interesting biomes that are fun to traverse the first couple times. That brings me to one of the game's few flaws.
To get around, even with teleportation, you'll have to go over lots of ground that you likely have already trekked through because even with all the powers you obtain, the paths through ES Alpha are labyrinthian and don't open up as “wide” as they should. One must take the long way around to get anywhere, even late in the game. It can be grueling or tedious and it's only exacerbated by the game's difficulty.
Now I won't tell you if the game's difficulty is bad or not, but it's a hard game that can be unforgiving at times. For example, not only are a couple bosses very difficult and long, the game utilizes a very draconian save system. There is no autosaving, there are no checkpoints. The player must go to save rooms to record their game. If the player beats a boss and then dies without saving, the player will have to load in to their last save and do the boss over again and if there's a long gauntlet on the way to the boss, the player will have to do that too.
Bringing it back to the positive, ESA employs a pixel art graphic style that is one of the most considered pixel artstyles in modern indie games. The music is similarly great with lots of memorable ambient sounds that have real emotion and story behind them. The game's simplistic presentation goes very far.
ESA also has a very involved post-game (or extended ending, if you will). It highlights what's already interesting about the plot and expands on it. Warning though, conquering the post-game involves a cipher puzzle so if that bugs you, you might want to employ a help guide. The secrets of ES Alpha truly feel forbidden enhancing the otherworldly, alien tone of the game.
If you want a Metroidvania that relishes in its quiet, lonely tone and can tolerate some occasionally vicious difficulty, you'd be doing yourself a favour by checking out Environmental Station Alpha. It's engaging, it's interesting, and it's a real gem in the genre.

Thirty-one minutes in and I HAVE to write a review and share my thoughts!
Most of that time was spent figuring out how to save and repeating the first 50 floors a few times, and there was one time where the game almost crashed on me while I tried to stream it to a friend, but still, the time I actually DID play was agonizing. And only the first 50 floors, too.
Games like these are ALWAYS waaaay scarier when you actually play them for yourself. I could barely ever bring myself to play the original Five Nights at Freddy's (I have it here but not through Steam itself) for two reasons: I'm horrible at conserving power and it's actually legitimately terrifying. But anyway-
The gameplay is so dreadfully simple, but also so dreadfully dreadful. You just make your way through simplistic rooms (again, I'm not past 50 [EDIT: 100] yet, so that could very well change) just waiting for something to come out at you. And these aren't regular jumpscares either. They actually make sense. Most of the negative reviews here already say what needs to be said about this game, so I'll make this one kinda short and express what I disliked about the game.
Sine Mora is very pretty and flashy, but is completely lacking in the depth of mechanics and overall design that make a good shmup. The time system is usually too forgiving, making long boring sections of stages with a few meagre enemies where there's no threat of death whatsoever, and is completely useless when most of the deaths you'll have is due to false difficulty when you hit what you thought was a piece of the background and explode instantly. So everything in the game takes away time when you get hit... except tiny bits of tile that blend in with the background? I don't know how the game manages to be easy to get through, yet so frustrating and unfulfilling at the same time. It just doesn't feel as though it tests your skills as a player.
The worst part of this game's design, though, is the scoring. Enemies will drop power-ups and points at random, and the point items themselves are randomized as well, to go from somewhere around 1000 points to 100000, I think. Even as more of a casual shmup player I can see how terrible this idea was: point systems should NEVER have this kind of rng involved. With no reliable scoring, half the brilliance of enjoying shmups is gone down the drain.
One last thing to mention: the story is also a mess. It's not one of those "you just don't get it" stories: there's barely anything to get. I do like the designs of the pilots as anthro animals (hi StarFox) but these characters have nothing to them as well.
While far from unplayable, Sine Mora isn't going to get much more time from me at all. Even on Steam I think there are much better shmups, such as Ikaruga, Kamui, Mushihimesama, Eschatos, and Crimson Clover, and outside of steam there are of course hundreds of other great titles available. Can't recommend it less.

So I just played this for not even an hour and I'm already sick of it.
There's story mode, and there's arcade mode.
In story mode, nothing makes any sense. Just a lot of fictional facts and talk about revenge, no context and no character background was given. Which would be ok... If it weren't for the fact that all the cutscenes, dialogues, infodumps and such kill an already slow pacing. In an arcade shmup? That's unacceptable. This isn't Metal Gear Solid. There's even moments where the dialogue in-game literally obscures a good part of the screen while enemies are still coming at you.
In arcade mode, you only get play on hard or insane difficulties. If you want to focus on getting to know the mechanics well before going into hard mode (which is imperative when you don't have lives but time), you have to hear that damn story.
The gameplay has its pros and cons.
Some boss attack patterns and stage moments were pretty nice. But you often find yourself against walls of bullets without the possibility to slow the ship (or "focus") because this doesn't exist in Sine Mora. There's somethink like it, called time capsule, which slows time (but not your ship), and it's finite. Once you've run out of it, the only way to replenish is through randomized drops from enemies.
Some attacks, specially during boss fights, are clearly unavoidable without fast reflexes and time capsule, and that would be actually cool if it was possible to refill it systematically, but you can't so you are screwed if you have finished it.
You sometimes find yourself (specially in caves) wondering where you can move because you'll sometimes run against rocks or stuff that you thought was just in the background.
Once you take a hit, you lose some shot power upgrades that go flying around and that you won't be usually able to recover unless you want to risk jumping in the middle of a group of enemies, which might mean losing even more shot power.
Graphics and artstyle are very nice, but music? It was so forgettable that I don't even remember if there was some background music to begin with, and I'm not even joking. Bossfights are also nothing special to be honest, and they are much more nice to look for their design that fun to beat for the challenge they pose.
Oh, and you don't get to choose your ship. The game does it for you in story mode. Level after level I found myself with different ships that had different sub-weapons every time.
I gave up after using all my continues in a part where you had to do something otherwise everything around you would just explode. It was most definitely explained in one of the dialogues before, which I clearly fast-forwared because of how annoying they were, and guess what? The dialogue didn't come back up after you died. I was just repeating the same part and exploding again trying to figure out in the few seconds you had what you were supposed to do. Nice.
Overall, this game not only lacks impact, but it's a big mess and fails at being both arcade and story-driven. What's nice in Sine Mora is the bling, the graphics, the designs and all these things.... Stuff which I don't really care about in a shmup when it doesn't even have it's basics covered.
The game can get very cheap during big discounts so if you don't trust me you can give it a shot. It's more bad than good but not so bad that you would regret spending a dollar or two to see how it really is with your own eyes.

I bought this game on a Steam Sale, but, trust me on this, the Jackbox Party Packs are worth the full $25. If I had a nickel for every time I've packed my laptop to a house party JUST FOR THIS GAME, I'd have enough money to buy the trilogy. You just need your laptop and an internet connection to start it up. Listen, the game uses your phone as the controller, which means literally every single person you ask to play with you immediately have a frame of reference for how it works. That's priceless. No teaching controls, no explaining mechanics, just "look at the TV, go to that site, enter the code." I don't care if you have an Android, iPhone, or cheap knockoff iPad; if you have an internet browser, you can play this game. The games offer the prompt, then your phone's browser lets you submit your response. Super easy. I've seen socially reserved people suddenly become the funniest f***er at the party, not because they're social butterflies, but because they were witty with their lies on Fibbage.
PLUS, the games are presented in such a way that it can behave like either Apples to Apples or Cards Against Humanity. It's good to play with kids, college students, or adults and still have a good time. The prompts are never inappropriate, but you're responses can definitely be. Players can adapt the game to suit your own friend bubble's sense of humor and it's brilliantly handled. There's also a secondary prize in most games (the best ones at least) based on who had the most liked responses, which people can pick after the answer has been revealed.
This one comes with 5 games and all of the best ones have an 8 player cap. Each game takes about 10-15 minutes to play, but they have TONS of questions and prompts, so you'll almost never hit one you've seen before and it's pretty easy to corral people to try it out because of the play time. Each game has an announcer that briefly explains the game and the rules, while also presenting the prompts. They're sorta funny; they get some laughs for being super cheesy. You won't want to turn it off for being annoying, at least. They're a little self aware, honestly. Fibbage XL and Drawful are THE games you need, though.
YOU DON'T KNOW JACK 2015 is basically a trivia game with some quirks. Not much to say about it, but I'm not crazy into trivia games. The series has been around since (at least) the original Xbox, so they know what they're doing with the whole "digital trivia" thing. If you like trivia, you'll probably like this.
Fibbage XL is one of the games you're buying this for. It's a trivia game at it's heart, but the questions are less "fact heavy" and much more obscure/funny. Sometimes someone will know the answer, but most of the time you're guessing. After everyone has sent in a guess (or the time limit goes off), the game presents a list of options to pick from, which are composed of everyone's responses mixed in with the answer. If someone pick your guess, you get points. If you pick the right answer, you get a lot of points. That means you can win for being convincing with your answer, rather than actually knowing it. Really, really fun game.
Drawful is the second game you're buying this for. It's Pictionary, except everyone draws at the same time and you're drawing on a phone so it's really not going to be a masterpiece anyway. Basically, the Drawful announcer tells everyone to start drawing, then everyone gets a unique prompt on their phone to make a little sketch for. Then, the drawings come up one after another on the TV. Like Fibbage, everyone says what they THINK the answer is and everyone picks from a combined list. If it's you're prompt, you get points for every person who picks the correct answer. If not, you get points for picking the correct answer and some points if someone picks your guess. Very fun, probably the best game here, IMO. They even made a standalone sequel and it's also great.
Word Spud is essentially a fill-in-the-blank game. Much more abstract and toned down than the other games. This one is about just hanging around and chilling. Not a huge fan.
Lie Swatter is better than Word Spud, but is really just a spin on how trivia games work. Up to 100 players can play this game, which is really it's main draw. You're basically given a succession of prompts and have to tell whether it's a lie or not. You get points for picking out the lies and more points for being the first to respond.
Seriously, though. Get this. It's a great game to break out at a party or just with a small group of friends. I wish I had this when I was studying abroad and staying in hostels.

16 people made this.

This game was made by a little studio in the UK consisting of less than 20 people.

A decent game with an interesting story that has 2 neat twists towards the end (that you may or may not see coming) but it's held back by the repetitive and lackluster combat. Indeed, the game was touted as having a ground-breaking combat system where you can design your own combos but that isn't the case at all: the combos are pre-set and the only changes that you can make to them is to modify what effect each of your attacks within the combo have (health regen, added damage and shorter cooldowns). You'll end up using the same handful of combos over and over again with a few initially cool finishers but that quickly get old as you end up having to use them regularly without the respite of fun & varied combat to even things out. The boss battles on the other hand were rather enjoyable as they each had their own disctinct mechanics and were therefore more challenging.
Also, the other pioneering aspect of the game was its supposed memory-rewinding which is indeed really cool when you get to use it but it is only accessible at 4 specific plot points which is a damn shame.
It's also unfortunate that the amazing futuristic environments of neo-Paris aren't fully explorable and that the player is always constrained in their movements. The game would have been so much better if there was an element of free-roaming where you could go around weakening the despotic government by targeting a series of key political & military figures and altering their memories. You could either take them completely out of the fight by breaking them mentally, causing them to commit suicide or joining them to your cause. The game had so much wasted potential :(.
TL;DR: Basically get it for the neat story if you don't mind so-so combat.

So this game caught my attention since I last saw the trailer from Gamescom 2016; you can see that the atmosphere of the game was decided since early stages of development. Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice isn't a game for the easy going, light-hearted and shallow players. The game has more heart and soul than most of the story driven games I've played (Quantum Break, Alan Wake, any AC, Batman... you name it). Within the first minutes of the game it is percieved that it has a psychological edge to it, making it to stand out from the bunch because of it's masterful sound and use of binaural sound. Yes, it is sometimes a slow paced game. There are areas filled with nordic lore and stories that fit perfect to what the protagonist is feeling and experiencing. Combat wise is masterful (it is not a hack and slash). Every hit that you land on enemies feels real and impactful. There are no set combos and the more you progress through the story the more harder the fights become. Gritty, nerve-wrecking and real would describe my feelings for the combat without mentioning the permadeath system that only adds stress to the player in every battle (specially on harder difficulties).
The purpose of the game is to be immersive, there are no tutorials, no hud and the only help you get is from sound cues delivered in a unique way. Let the game flow naturally, don't expect anything similar and stay vigilant on every detail that sets this game apart from the others. It is almost impossible to concieve that a team of only twenty people made this game (so I pay them proper respect), including the actress for Senua, who also worked in the game.
Been gaming for more than twenty years, and I havent had this lasting impression from any other game. Bravo Ninja Theory!

How to optimize fallout 3 for windows 7, 8, 8.1, and 10
Step 1: Run as Administartor
Go to your Fallout 3 install folder within Steam.
Default location: C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\Fallout 3 goty.
Right click the Fallout 3 application file and select Properties.
Select the Compatibility tab and tick the Run this program as an administrator box.
Step 2: Run fallout 3 in compatibility mode
Go to your Fallout 3 install folder within Steam.
Default location: C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\Fallout 3 goty.
Right click the Fallout 3 application file and select Properties.
Select the Compatibility Tab and check the box that says Run this program in compatibility mode for:.
Check the drop down box and troubleshoot with different Windows versions.
Optionally, you can try compatibility with Windows XP SP3 .
Click Apply and OK
Step 3: Edit your Fallout.ini file
Open your My Documents folder.
Under My Games, open the Fallout 3 folder and select the fallout.ini file.
In the fallout.ini file, find the following line: bUseThreadedAI=0.
Change this line to read: bUseThreadedAI=1.
Add another line after it that reads: iNumHWThreads=2.
Run the game.

Where does an older gamer begin with Hellblade. It's worth the price, well made, well told, and well acted. The use of 3D audio to place you into her head fits very well. Its haunting, its rewarding, and it tells a story that leaves you shattered mentally, and wondering just what is real, and what is self-induced psychological nightmare. This is a game based on story, combat is mild, yet rewarding. The puzzles make you think, yet can slow the story down slightly but I found this to be cleverly used to push the narrative of the main character in a mental state of chaos. For $30 you will get a high production value for your dollar with a game focused on telling you a story. This is not a typical game, combat is very basic, yet requires patience, awareness, but once mastered becomes a part of the story but never the main part of the story. The game is shorter at around 5-8 hour depending on your speed or play style. Best utilized with slower, controlled, observence of the beauty of the world created for you to explore. This game is a welcome change of pace in what I have seen as AAA mess of gmaes half finished, and over priced garbage. This is fresh, amazing, and worth each dollar of their $30 price tag. It is wonderful to see game developers try something different, twist an old walking sim/story to a new branching path, and bring the player along to experience a mental breakdown of the main character driven by a full mental disorder that is relatable and at the same time so very foriegn.

Trine is a delightfully charming platformer that is fun to play both by yourself and with others. Both playthroughs I enjoyed.
Pros:
- Absolutely gorgeous world! The colors are amazing, everything looks crisp, and the whole game looked mystical.
- I like the switching through characters. Every character has his or her own abilities, and they are all distinct. Playing as each character is a different experience and way of getting from A to B.
- Solid character controlling for the most part. I appreciate any side scrolling game with a good idea on how jumping and moving around should feel. No awkwardness here.
- Playing this game made me happy. I don't know how else to explain it.
Cons:
- Sometimes the game would freeze. That's never fun.
- The drawing button for the wizard and the move objects button should be different! Ahh! The only button mapping that bugged me.
- The segments at the beginning of the levels are dumb. You stare at a map while you wait for the narrator to finish speaking. Very rarely do narrators in a video game work.
- Come to think of it, the voice acting in general was meh.
- Was that even a story?
- What is the point of mana? The meter would decrease but never enough to make me think "man I wish I had more mana" because there are checkpoints frequently.
