The game is very much focused around exploring a huge map with varied environments to find new power-ups that help you explore further. This is coupled with finding random HP upgrades that are often hiding behind breakable walls and discovering the lore of the area you are exploring.
Overall the game plays well. The controls are far more responsive than the game it pays homage too, which assists greatly in the epic boss fights and some incredibly difficult platforming segments. ESa makes very good use of allowing the player to traverse the environment using it's various power-ups even before the correct power-up for a certain segment is found. There were numerous times where determination and precision got me to an area I would have normally required a power-up I didn't have to get to.
Speaking of bosses, they are balls hard. You can't take very many hits, so most boss fights require the player to know all of the boss' attack patterns and how to deal with them. This is both a strength and weakness of the game. On one hand the bosses being so difficult made defeating them feel really satisfying. On the other, losing repeatedly to the same boss in it's last phase is frustrating as hell. This frustration also partly comes from having to reload from the last save point, which is only near a boss about half the time. The other half of the time you have some walking to do.
The only other gripe I had with the game was a brief segment in the middle where the game gave me no direction on where to go next. I still hadn't discovered enough power-ups to really explore the station fully on my own and I spent about 5 hours trying to figure out where the way forward was. This really messed with the pacing of the game.
Overall I quite liked the game. I'd recommend it if you are looking for a Metroid-like experience, or you like games that are old-school hard.

Environmental Station Alpha is the Metroid game I\'ve been waiting 12 years for. It\'s got tight controls, an environment rich with life and detail, and it brings an eerie ambiance and mystery. This game is definitely worth the $8 - I highly recommend it!

One of the coolest items you earn in the game is the hookshot. An entire platforming game could be built around this mechanic alone, and it\'s very well done.
In terms of playtime, I\'m already nearly 10 hours in.
Multiple endings, aliens, blowing stuff up, this game is A++ and one of my favorite games of all time. Beat the game? Keep exploring. You may find more.
Don't get trickied by the oversimplistic pixelized graphic style, this game is polished to the moon. Well thought out, precise and fun.

I'm no veteran shoot 'em up player, but I'm not a complete beginner either. I've spent a great deal of time playing Xenon, Tyrian, Raptor or recently Jets'n'Guns. That being said, even the normal difficulty setting of this game is brutal for me. You are under constant pressure of a strict time limit which you need to replenish by killing enemies, so avoiding them too often is not an option. Enemy hitboxes are small, number of bullets to dodge is often insane, usage of special powers is limited and you lose weapon upgrades after being hit. Also after 10 deaths you have to restart the whole chapter. I gave up at the beginning of Chapter II after 20 minutes of trying to beat the short turrets+lasers stage. Either the enemies or the time limit itself always got me.
The graphics are fantastic, can't argue with that. Level design and bosses are pretty impressive too. On the other hand the storytelling is unnecessarily complicated and confusing, it lost me shortly after the prologue. Hungarian voiceovers didn't help either.
TL;DR - If you're a hardcore shoot 'em up player this might be your thing. Casuals stay away.

I have mixed feelings about Sine Mora: its fabulous art direction and fun-but-challenging gameplay are good even for the shmup genre, but it presents major flaws that I cannot ignore.
-The storyline is convoluted, and conveyed almost exclusively in walls of text.  Most people will just skip these parts, but folks who take the time (like me) to read through will be left disappointed.  It isn't even that the story is particularly bad, it just isn't given the attention it deserves.
-There is a very challenging portion of the game, and if you manage to beat it your character is instantly and unavoidably killed.  It's enough to make you throw your controller.
-It is sometimes unclear what hit your ship or how you died... not a problem for completing the game on easy mode (you have lots of health) but really terrible if you want to spend the time to truly master the game.
-I experienced some graphicals glitches putting black boxes across parts of the backround.  The game is otherwise so beautifully made, it was dissapointing.
-3d is not used very well.  Without true depth perception, it is very difficult to see what is in your pane of existence.
-Random powerups and score system?  Really?  This fact alone completely changes every level every time you play it, and most of the time for the worse.

This is a spoilerfree review of the game played on the easyest difficulty.
This was easyly the best shmup I have ever played.
The story contains time manipulation so it is rather hard to follow, after you beat the game you get an encyclopedia though that gives informations about the game world. that kind of makes it easyer, the wikipedia article on the game erases any questions that should have remained.
Anyway, aside from time being part of the story it is also a game mechanic, as you can slow down time when the hell the bullets put you in is to big. it has a meter though so you cant just slowmo yourself through the game. There is also a limited amount of time you have before dying that gets a few extra seconds every time you kill an enemy and that gets reduced when you are hit, so its also kind of your health.
aside from that you really just shoot the stoff coming at you and dodge what you cant shoot, with different subweapons depeding on the  pilot and you pick up powerups on the way. after death you have a limited amount of continues that let you start again from the last checkpoint (though I often had moments of "WHAT? Way back there was the last checkpoint? god damnit") if you get a total gameover you only have to restart a story chapter not the entire thing.
That description doesnt do the game justice though. What amazed me is the variety the game offers.
You will never really encounter the same enemy for to long, the areas all feel unique and all of it looks gorgeous. the bossfights are numerous and epic, like seriously you get thrown against one epic machine of doom after another.
I cant say anything about the difficult difficulties, I do know however, that even the easyest difficulty will sometimes require restarting a chapter because it still is bullethellish after all.
The downsides:
First and foremost the length. If you dont play this to get all the achievements, if you dont play this failing every 20 seconds because you chose a difficulty that is way to high for you, then you should, like me, get two hours out of this. those may be the best two hours you have ever had with a shmup but it is still questionable if that is worth 10 euros/dollars/billion simbabwe dollars/whatever. so I would reccomend waiting for a sale.
btw I checked on the achievement guide, and if you want to get all of those you can count on 50 hours or more worth of gametime. I think id quickly lose the fun in that though.

I was hesitant to give this game a thumbs up. The actual gameplay/combat is exceptional, and since its a fighting game that (of course) matters the most. But I really wanted to give it a thumbs down because of how absolutely terrible the story mode is. It's like watching a particularly terrible anime, and you have to deal with shuffling through hundreds of dialouge boxes just to get through it. The voice acting is irritating, and I know that they over-act on purpose, but that doesn't make it any better. Just like a lot of anime there are a bunch of made up words thrown in your facee to make it seem like the plot is well thought out and or complex (but its not). All of the characters are rehashes of over-used cliches. The dialogue is awful, but it's not even bad in a comedic way, it's just painful to listen to. I found myself skipping past entire conversations between characters without any consequences because again, a lot of the dialouge is pointless. Was the story worth my time? No. Is the actual fighting fun? Yes. And it's a fighting game after all, so I gues a lackluster story is nothing to be ashamed of anyway.

Read this if you have a Qanba or PS3/PC only fightstick! Otherwise, uh, have fun with your game that luckily works for you?
The game is rad, but this port is terribly sloppy.  There are like, six companies that make decent arcade sticks for the PC, and unless you happened to buy a stick that is XINPUT friendly (which, if you have a PS3/PC compatible joystick it won't be!), good luck mapping your buttons to anything that makes any sense whatsoever.  I literally couldn't get this game to recognize the start button on my Qanba Q1 (a fine joystick that works great with Skullgirls or USF4), and had to use some sort of DLL wrapper workaround to get it to recognize any inputs at all.  After much fussing around, I was able to get something acceptable, except for the fact that one of the attack keys was irrevocably bound to the "record dummy action" key in training mode, and another was bound to "play recorded action".  So you can just imagine for yourself how that went.  This is not a difficult problem for Arc System Works to fix, and yet here we are, several months after release, with nothing. I hope that they will be more considerate in the creation of future PC ports of their fighting games, because their games are actually quite good (as I'm sure this one could be!).

Ah, BlazBlue Continuum Shift II, the first game of the series I played. I've seen videos on it, I've heard people talking about it. So when I got a system that could play it, I bought it. Sadly it was for the Nintendo 3DS meaning I could not play with others online, just local. Not to say BlazBlue was bad on 3DS, just it could of been better, though too be fair it at least had an animated background unlike a certain Street Fighter port. . . For 3DS. Well my 3DS broke a couple months ago so no more BlazBlue for me, as well as other games I loved playing on that system. But then I saw that BlazBlue Continuum Shift Extend was released for PC and so I used the money I made from selling my most prized possession in all of Gaming to get BlazBlue. . . and other games. Well how is it? Basically the same really, there's probably some technical changes but overall everything seen in Continuum Shift II is all here, the only true noticable differences will be the intro cinematic and the addition of a new character, Relius Clover, or Carl's messed up Father who thought it be cool to turn his Mom and Sister into puppets. BlazBlue can have a heavy story line, or be not-serious-at-all comedic. But who plays games these days for Story? Well you'll probably get curious on it eventually because why not? But out of seriousness the Story will be long, doesn't matter which character you choose so may want to have some snacks around. Although there will be Gag stories which sometimes they're funny and other times they're just, eh. And then there's the arcade mode, you played Street Fighter? Same thing. Only different here is you can do Fatalities. Okay so they call it an Astral Finish but still it's the one move that can instantly finish off a character in an epic display. . . except Arakune who turns into a giant floating ball. Speaking, the characters, you'll either love them or hate them. Each character is different than the other, and each character has a very different personality. From Ragna's troubled ego, Jin's super obsession, Taokaka's hyperactivity, and of coarse Hazama's trollish attitude. And then there's the character who you can't tell the gender because BACKSTORY. . . also has a clear Male and Female voice which reason for being is (again) Backstory. Then there's the special content where you can see concept and fan art as well as seeing some shorts about the series. BlazBlue is clearly not going to be for everyone out there, but it's still a fun game none-the-less. You'll get a sense for other large name games while playing a different game. I say at least try it if you ever get that chance.

When I initially bought the game and posted this review, I thought it was one of the best fighting games I've touched in a long while. While I wouldn't say that was wrong at the time, with more experience under my belt I would say it's not that worth touching.
To put things into perspective, back then my experience with fighting games was Ultra Street Fighter 4, Skullgirls, Guilty Gear X2 #Reload, Street Fighter 3rd Strike, and a few games from my early childhood that are too fuzzy in my mind to recall. Out of those, the only ones I still like are X2 and 3rd Strike.
After playing this game, I see it has room for better combos while the pacing of the game is really bad compared to other airdasher/anime fighting games. I'd still recommend it as an introduction to the series if you care for story at all, but otherwise just play the sequels or check out the Guilty Gear series. Still a fine game and can recommend, but it doesn't hold up nearly as well as I thought.

A decent game with an interesting story that has 2 neat twists towards the end (that you may or may not see coming) but it's held back by the repetitive and lackluster combat. Indeed, the game was touted as having a ground-breaking combat system where you can design your own combos but that isn't the case at all: the combos are pre-set and the only changes that you can make to them is to modify what effect each of your attacks within the combo have (health regen, added damage and shorter cooldowns). You'll end up using the same handful of combos over and over again with a few initially cool finishers but that quickly get old as you end up having to use them regularly without the respite of fun & varied combat to even things out. The boss battles on the other hand were rather enjoyable as they each had their own disctinct mechanics and were therefore more challenging.
Also, the other pioneering aspect of the game was its supposed memory-rewinding which is indeed really cool when you get to use it but it is only accessible at 4 specific plot points which is a damn shame.
It's also unfortunate that the amazing futuristic environments of neo-Paris aren't fully explorable and that the player is always constrained in their movements. The game would have been so much better if there was an element of free-roaming where you could go around weakening the despotic government by targeting a series of key political & military figures and altering their memories. You could either take them completely out of the fight by breaking them mentally, causing them to commit suicide or joining them to your cause. The game had so much wasted potential :(.
TL;DR: Basically get it for the neat story if you don't mind so-so combat.

Mind games done right
"Remember me" is a well crafted game in a beautiful setting. Neo Paris is simply stunning. The presentation and artwork "Remember me" offers isn't seen very often and I can't praise the level of detail enough.
When you start the game your character Nillin had forgotten nearly everything. She has to escape from a dystopian prison in which the prisoners are robbed of their memory. In the grand scheme the story is nothing really new, but I really liked the character development Nillin undergoes and the the fact that all the characters in the game have a real motivation for their actions which you can understand. The twists in the story aren't as obvious as in other ganes but at some point you'll know in which direction the writing will go. And while the story may be not original, it is told really well while it doesn't start to get boring. Overall I needed about 10 hours to beat the game and I enjoyed every second of it.
You acquire a variety of skills and abilities which you can use while fighting or while solving little puzzles. All of the abilities are enjoyable and useful. You will need every combat skill from time to time which is assured through the variety of enemies you face. While the combo system could have been a little bit more thought out, it still was fun to switch around the different kicks and punches.
The boss fights were memorable, at least three of them were really great. The amount of enemy waves you have to face sometimes can get a bit tedious but most of the time I didn't thought that I was just fighting for the sake of it. I'm not really a big fan of platforming so Remember me did it exactly right for my taste which means, it is easy as hell. It's really hard to miss jumps and even in situations where you're under pressure you can always count on the auto save system of the game which is never far behind in case you die.
The most fun I had in the game was when I mixed my first memory. With the help of a mind controlling glove you can go into the mind of certain NPC where you're able to play with the memory of a certain event. I really felt like I was playing "Final Destination - The Game". You try out different scenarios in which you try to kill certain characters. While all only happens in the memory of the person you're mixing at the moment it still has big consequences in the end. Mixing plays a huge part in the story and is really well implemented.
Overall I had a great experience, the game may not be perfect in every aspect but it did a lot of things really well. I was satisfied with the ending and the experience I had. In the second half of the game I became emotionally invest in the characters and how their story might turn out which doesn't happen very often in those type of games. If you're remotely into brawler games with a good portion of platforming and a great story, you should try it out.

Where does an older gamer begin with Hellblade. It's worth the price, well made, well told, and well acted. The use of 3D audio to place you into her head fits very well. Its haunting, its rewarding, and it tells a story that leaves you shattered mentally, and wondering just what is real, and what is self-induced psychological nightmare. This is a game based on story, combat is mild, yet rewarding. The puzzles make you think, yet can slow the story down slightly but I found this to be cleverly used to push the narrative of the main character in a mental state of chaos. For $30 you will get a high production value for your dollar with a game focused on telling you a story. This is not a typical game, combat is very basic, yet requires patience, awareness, but once mastered becomes a part of the story but never the main part of the story. The game is shorter at around 5-8 hour depending on your speed or play style. Best utilized with slower, controlled, observence of the beauty of the world created for you to explore. This game is a welcome change of pace in what I have seen as AAA mess of gmaes half finished, and over priced garbage. This is fresh, amazing, and worth each dollar of their $30 price tag. It is wonderful to see game developers try something different, twist an old walking sim/story to a new branching path, and bring the player along to experience a mental breakdown of the main character driven by a full mental disorder that is relatable and at the same time so very foriegn.

Now a lot of the reviews of this game are just people saying which character they like or is "their waifu" without giving any info of the actual GAME. When I was looking for an actual review of the game to see what I would need to know, I was left completely in the dark. As a noobie to this game, I think I can offer some advice to other fellow noobies just picking up the game or even people thinking about buying it (which you TOTALLY should buy this game).
Now starting off I would reccomend that you play this game with an arcade stick/pad, as it, along with most fighting games of this nature, are practically near IMPOSSIBLE to adjust to without one. Playing with a controller may be appealing to some but DONT use a keyboard. So, in short, Arcade Stick > Controller > Keyboard.
Next, I would suggest going to the training center to learn everything that there is to know, the devs really put some time and effort into making a new player feel welcome and it shows. It may feel discouraging to keep messing up on a single action at first (especially the super moves), but you will get the hang of it.
Finally, I'd reccomend that you play with every single character to start off and see who you like and fits your playstyle. Just choosing the character with the biggest tiddys or the most revealing clothes won't do you any favors except to your willy.
Now I know this isn't much of a review of the game as it is just advice of how to start but I truly think that noobies and people willing to buy this are alone in the dark when it comes to advice, sorry for sounding like an episode of Neds Declassified School Survival Guide guys.
But, if you're still on the fence about this game, I'd just like to list off a few other great traits that this game has to offer:
-Amazing and Fluid Animation
-Art that will blow your MIND
-CRAZY COMBOS
-Unique cast of characters
-INSANELY GOOD Soundtrack
-Intriguing Presentation

Metroidvania with tight controls.  Fun, hard, fair (at least for the first couple of hours.  Cool upgrades.

Environmental Station Alpha is capable and well-crafted metroidvania, notable for an extra-low-fidelity aesthetic (and plot) and its high demands on player reflexes and muscle memory.  That degree (or two... or three) of increased difficulty over its most obvious inspiration -- Super Metroid, perhaps my favorite console game of all time -- causes the fun to devolve into frustration more often than I would have wished... primarily during several of the many boss fights.
In all likelihood, I would have enjoyed ESA more if I had played on Easy Mode; but by the time I reached this conclusion I was already too far along to want to start over again.  Even so, I can easily recommend it to those players who don't mind a bit of frustration with their entertainment, particularly if they harbor any nostalgia for Metroid/Super Metroid.
Nota bene:  I completed the game at 100%, but cheated (increased my HP) to get the Dash Booster X and didn't really pursue any of the (seemingly) substantial post-game content.  I also played using a keyboard, though I suspect a controller might have worked slightly better.

This is everything I wanted out of La-Mulana but without the absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t factor tacked on.  Gobs of areas to find your way through that are packed with small details, secrets upon secrets around every corner that will have you using a notebook to keep track, multiple endings, and so much more all on top of crisp controls and a fantastic set of tools to work with.

"This space station has gone quiet. Go find out why."
That's about all you need, and all you get, to start exploring Environmental Station Alpha. Despite its simplistic appearance, there is a lot of atmosphere and mystery surrounding the space station. As you explore, you find upgrades that let you explore more, and you eventually discover what went wrong. So now you know what you need to do to save the day.
But ESA doesn't just ask you to find out "what" went wrong. It also poses the questions "Why?" and "How?", and therein lies the trap.
My first run through the game clocked in at 5 hours. Literally, exactly 5 hours. 5:00:00, on the dot. Navigating certain areas, and figuring out where to go, is generally obvious enough thanks to mission objectives being marked on the map but there are moments in the game where you're just left wondering where you're supposed to apply the new upgrade you just got. There could be 20 unexplored rooms, but only 1 of them is where you need to go next. Repeat this for each upgrade and it quickly becomes tiresome. Bring a notepad; ESA doesn't have any sort of "Map markup" feature that lets you leave notes on your map, but it does explicitly state which tile on the map grid you're on at any given time, and maybe just writing down "red blocks at 18-12" would be enough.
That isn't my biggest gripe with the game, though. As I said, I got through the main story in 5 hours, which I'm assuming isn't too bad for a first-time without the use of any guides. However, the ending leaves you feeling unsatisfied, as if there was another approach you could have taken for a more satisfying resolution.
Well, there is. This game is absolutely loaded with secrets. I don't mean cute hidden upgrades (though there's a couple of those), I mean new areas, new bosses, new endings, the whole shebang. And it is absolutely esoteric. Is it worth it? Honestly, I want to say no. The post-game content is great (exploring the new areas, fighting the new bosses) but it's so bogged down with pointlessly esoteric nonsense and repetitive filler tasks that the effort involved to get there is far greater than the payoff. The two fights with You-Know-Who were a blast, but it took me close to 8 hours of faffing about in order to unlock what I understand is the True Actual Final Boss.
I like that the game offers a rather deep rabbit hole to go down if you're willing, but because of all the dead-ends, invisible walls, and one-way doors, it's too much of a chore to fully complete. As much fun as I had fighting the post-game bosses, I can't say that all of the filler content in between them was worth the time and effort. The base game, however, remains a solid experience, and I can recommend the game on that point alone.

Environmental Station Alpha (ESA) is a challenging Metroid-like that focuses on exploration and interesting platforming mechanics. You play as a robot who has just discovered an abandoned station somewhere in outer space. You'll explore to unravel the mystery of the dissapearance of the station's crew, and the strange things going on in the local computer system.
Pros:
- excellent movement & controls
- unique upgrades add to interesting platforming
- great soundtrack; atmospheric and fits the retro theme
- optional upgrades & rewards for further exploration
- Checkpoints/warps/shortcuts to areas keep the game interesting up until the final stages of the game so things don't get too repetitive.
- The most hardcore challenges of the game are often optional, however, a completionist is going to have intense difficulties to overcome in the end-game.
Cons:
- Some bosses are annoying if they're too challenging. The jog back to the bossroom is often short, but any time I have to face a boss more than 10 times just to get lucky can get old (I know, I know, git gud... ;)
- No Steam achievements
- *edit: i had a complaint about the ending, but continued playing and realized I hadn't actually finished the game :P
Similar to other classic action/puzzle games, in ESA the player finds upgrades and power-ups throughout the world (Charge Shot, Dash, Energy Upgrade, etc.) and uses these new tools to gain access to new areas. Don't think this is just a clone, however, because ESA adds a number of unique upgrades that become integral to your movement and survival throughout the game.
Developments in the storyline will tell the player their next objective on the map, but ambitious players will be rewarded (sometimes with with killer, optional upgrades) for further exploration into the many different routes and rooms hidden throughout the world. The developer also did a great job with keeping things interesting while backtracking through previously explored areas - new enemies and traps emerge to prevent you from taking the easy path back to an objective.
I don't want to spoil too much in this review, but suffice to say that when I beat the game I did not get the best ending possible. It looks like there is still A LOT for me to explore in this very involved and complicated map. It's clear to me now that the developer just might be a sadist and has likely lured many a gamer into obsession with this completionist nightmare. And yet we must be stalwart and overcome the challenges presented us.
For a game that borrows so heavily from one of the greatest and most influential series in gaming history, ESA is a shining example of a great idea made better with creative innovation.

Sine Mora is exactly what you'd expect from a bullet hell game made in the 10s. Wonderful graphics, a terrific storyline laden with sorrow and grief (I MEAN it) and a polished, well-made feel to it. As a graphic designer, I can say that the whole game exhales good taste, from the menus and interfaces to the choice of using the voice acting in the original language of the developers (hungarian), which just adds to the whole experience. Expect huge bosses, hundreds of power-ups (but no leveling system) and lots of noise from all the explosions and destruction. Pay close attention to insta-kill gimmicks, for they might catch you offguard.
Only negative aspect in the game, in my opinion, is the soundtrack. I know the name behind it is a great one (Akira Yamaoka, known for the Silent Hill series), but the songs are not remarkable and don't have much presence in-game. Also, make sure to use a gamepad for maximum enjoyment (though a regular keyboard setup will still do the trick nicely!).
All in all, if you have at least a little bit of interest in the genre I'd highly recommend giving it a try. As I said, it's a game made with good taste and attention to detail, truly a piece of good craftsmanship if that makes any sense. Oh, and pay close attention to the story, it's worth it!

Fun game, but it is first and foremost a brawler. If you don't like mashing left and right click several hundred times every few minutes, it will be very unpleasant.
You can customize your combos in limited ways. Performing the 2nd-8th maneuver in a combo can give you either bonus damage, health, or reduce the cooldown on your S-Pressins (special attacks).
The combos are as follows:
Punch-Punch-Punch
Kick-Punch-Kick-Punch-Kick
Punch-Kick-Kick-Punch-Kick-Kick
Kick-Kick-Kick-Punch-Punch-Punch-Punch-Kick
You will unlock a number of the Pressins (slotted combo pieces) as you progress through the game, and each one is restricted to kick or punch. So if you only have free 2 health punch Pressins, you cannot make anything more complex than the simple 3-punch combo.
Each stage of the combo does progressively more of the perk (i.e. a step 5 health Pressin will give more HP than a step 3 one), but don't expect to regularly reach anything beyond the 5-combo, because you will get interrupted all the time. You have to hit a stun S-Pressin or have 1 enemy remaining to get a long combo to completion.
Some of the combos can just be easy cheesy, like Punch-Health Punch-Chain Punch. Such a combo will give you significant more HP than you lose by attacking an enemy that damages you when you hit them.
Using a  6 combo of Punch-Cooldown Kick-Cooldown Kick-Cooldown Punch-Cooldown Kick-Chain Kick will allow you to completely remove the cooldown on the stun S-Pressin before it even wears off (you do have to perform it twice during the stun).
There is some serious platforming, but the camera will change to fixed locations when you do certain areas. This can make it hard to see the indicator that you can make a jump or whatnot because you're looking at a 2D indicator from the side. When in these fixed camera locations, when you turn a corner, the camera jumps to a new fixed location and it can be disorienting, as well as your character will keep going on inverted controls for a second (pressing A to go left, then the camera changes, you character will go right while holding A until you let up for a second).
The bosses LOVE to turtle. They will be unattackable unless you hit them with the stun S-Pressin, and will otherwise hurl explosives and minions at you endlessly until the stun S-Pressin comes off cooldown. Once you have managed to injure the boss to a critical state, the finishing move will be a Quick-Time Event. Failing the QTE will return them to non-critical health and you will be on cooldown for the stun again. A cooldown-heavy combo is highly suggested if you don't want to hear the boss repeat their lines for half an hour.
Remixing memories is what we're all here for, and they're amazing how you can change little details to change a person's memory to a more favorable outcome for you. Unfortunately there are only 4 of these events, and pausing the memory on the glitches that you can interact with can be frustrating, as sometimes you have to hit the pause button before the "glitch here" icon appears onscreen.
All-in-all, a fun game to get on sale. Replayability would be pretty subjective to the player, but I would think it to be low unless you just want to get all the collectables, as the cutscenes are unskippable and the fights tedious.

Could have been great, exploring the possibilities of memory alteration and its ramifications, but ended up as one long massively glorified quicktime event.
I kept wanting to like this game. I kept going back to it in the hopes it would get better or grow on me.  I really did want to like it.  The graphics, music, story and characters truly are all great and I loved the artistic world that has been created.  The game truly does *look* great.  What lets it down is everything else.
The trailer gives you the impression that the game centers around being able to modify peoples memories.  From that I had gotten the feeling that you could "stealth around" enemies or convert them rather than rely on direct confrontation every time. Sadly though the memory remix moments are few and far between and they are (like the game in general) far too linear, there being only one "right" way to remix the memory.  This seems like a bit of a missed opportunuty in my opinion, there could have been so much more focus on the memory scrambling and altering abilities in the game.
What little story there is between chases, telegraphed bosses and too-long quicktime chain cutscenes made me want to carry on to see how it went. The story is actually compelling and interesting and I wanted to see if/how the character could grow.  But time and again the QTE based fighting and QTE based running away along with the stiffling train-track limited "open" world the game was just ruined.
I liked the main character, her self questioning, her reassessment of what she had become forcing us to question our own motives and morals.
But with a combat system that is more an exercise in futile button mashing and enemy avoidance than actual combat I really cant recommend this to any but the most die-hard of QTE fans.

Remember Me is a game with obvious strengths and weaknesses, but overall it is very much worth the price of admission, if you can catch it on sale. The atmosphere is fantastic, with top notch graphics and music immersing the player in the story set in a futuristic dystopian world. Combined with an intriguing storyline, Remember Me is a work of art for the senses. Several times I found myself halting the game just to admire the sheer beauty of the world it is set in. That alone is a compelling enough reason to give this game a try.
Speaking of the "game" part, how does it perform? It's a mixed bag, with many positives, but a few shortcomings and annoyances. The first is that for a 3rd person view platformer, it is extremely linear, to the point that paths rarely allow any deviation, giving the feeling that the game is a platformer on rails. This is a real shame, as I would have loved to be able to wander around and explore the world a bit just because of how impressive it is audiovisually. Combat can be both fun and frustrating, with the (lack of) targeting becoming a huge annoyance when fighting large groups. If you miss a secret, you will need to replay the level most of the time, as pretty much every checkpoint is a point of no return.
Replay value depends on how much you want to go back and find all the missed collectibles and achievements. Other than that, despite the game being quite short, there is not much reason to go back to it, other than to re-experience the story and beautiful world. Still, even just one playthrough is definitely worth the experience.

I've played this game on PS3 and now I'm doing another playthrough on PC and I thought my opinion would change, but it hasn't. Remember Me is (unfortunately) one of those games that should've been great but instead it was... average.
I'll start what I personally disliked the most: the combat. There's a great idea in there somewhere, putting together your own combos like that and in the first 2 chapters I enjoyed it. But it stays the same pretty much throughout the whole game and it soon becomes tedious. It becomes a chore, something you have to get through in order to move the story forward. The fact that I dislike the combat so much is really overshadowing the game's great protagonist and story, because combat comes back so often. Unlike memory remixes, which really only happen a few times (which is odd).
As for the rest, I'll sum them up in pros and cons. Starting with the pros:
+ Great protagonist. Nilin is a well-written character. She's not forced to be sexy or witty. She's just a strong, smart character. I really enjoyed her monologues after each chapter. (Why isn't she a poet?)
+ Edge is another good character (who should just become a poet). At first, I did not understand his purpose in the game but it all becomes clear in the end.
+ Beautiful environment.
+ Memory mixes.
Cons:
- Unenjoyable combat. I wouldn't necessarily call it 'bad', but it's just... not satisfying at all. And the fact that there's a fight pretty much every few minutes does not help the matter.
- Pretty much zero interaction with environment. Neo-Paris is (probably) a wonderful place to be. It's beautiful, it's alive. Also, all the stores are closed. Those who are open do not allow you to get in. You will not be able to wander off to that crowd of protestors, or talk to the woman who mutters something about you as you walk by. This game is basically forcing you to take a linear approach (aside from the few collectibles there are to gather).
- Not enough memory mixes!
That's about all I can say about this game. It was such a promising idea and I still consider Nilin and her story to be great, it's just unfortunate that she's in a game that's unenjoyable to play.

I started playing this game because I didn't really feel like playing Diablo 3, and all in all I'm pretty happy with my choice.
Story:
I was expecting the game to be a Diablo-clone in most ways, so having the big bad be a  instead of a  was a pretty nice surprise. Fighting robots(?) in a steampunk-ish world also felt a bit fresh compared to fighting the same old demons and mythological creatures (some of which do appear in this game as well). The basic story is of course the good old "hack your way through a bunch of enemies to defeat the big bad trying to take over the world (or country?)", but there's nothing wrong with that.
Gameplay:
If you have played Diablo or any other ARPG you will probably recognize the play style right away. You use your mouse and a couple of buttons to dash out various spells while keeping an eye on your health and mana. The addition of rage, which refills when you kill a creature and can be used to power up your spells, was a nice touch. It gives you an extra thing to do during fights, as well as more ways to personalize your skill tree, so an extra plus there.
Graphics:
The graphics were fine. Not great, not bad. Some creatures looked pretty good, some looked pretty bland. The same can be said for the environment. Personally I enjoyed the city zones more than the nature zones. The (few and short) cut scenes were pretty meh, especially compared to the Diablo cut scenes, but that's acceptable.
Music:
While playing the game I thought that the music fit the mood pretty well, but as soon as I stopped playing I forgot the soundtrack right away.
The voice acting in this game... At first I thought that the voice acting was just really, really bad, and almost lol'ed a couple of times during the first few hours of the game. But then I realized that that was what they were going for (probably?). Sort of cheesy, over-the-top voice acting, that when you get used to it fit the game really well, and was sometimes just really funny (in a good way!). Some of the comments from both Van Helsing and Lady Katarina were just hilarious, although by the end of the game Katarina was becoming quite annoying.
Overall:
Overall I enjoyed this game, even my second playthrough, which was a little unexpected. I don't really want to call Van Helsing a Diablo-clone, since there were a couple of things that set it apart from Diablo, so let's just call it a decent option if you like ARPGs. I recommend this game, even at full price if you don't want to wait for a sale, however I do have a couple of warnings:
1. There are some bugs in the game, the most common being corpses stuck in walls or terrain that can't be looted. I also found a couple of chests that I couldn't open for whatever reason. The biggest bug I faced was a door leading to the next zone being closed, forcing me to start over with a new character. (Luckily this didn't happen with my hardcore heroic character.) There was a fix posted on the developer's forum to fix this, but that fix didn't work for me. On July 2nd 2015 they added the "Mantis Bug Tracker" to the game, which should help fix more bugs, but I wasn't able to test this out myself.
2. If you care about achievements you can get most of the achievements by playing through the game twice. None of them are really that hard to get, as my first playthrough was on hardcore heroic difficulty (=perma-death), and I only died four times, so the game is fairly easy. However, there is one achievement that is just plain stupid. It requires you to get 500,000 kills, which is a lot, seeing as you only get about 10,000-15,000 kills per playthrough. Luckily there is a way to make Lady Katarina afk farm kills for you, which she is doing for me as I am typing this, but just be aware that there is this one really annoying achievement if you (like me) want to clear the game 100%.
But all in all, a really good game.

Don’t be intimidated by the terrifying atmosphere, because underneath the initial impression of underwater horror lies a very solid and enjoyable game. In asymmetrical teams, sharks and divers use any means necessary to secure what is rightfully theirs; the sharks their aquatic sanctuary and the divers their treasures of gold. Depth is fast, fierce and rarely forgiving. Your view on the ocean’s top predators is likely to change, for better, or for worse.
Variety in gameplay is offered through different species of sharks, maps, weapons and upgrades, which allows players room to strategize, combine tactics and think on their feet (or fins). The community may be small, but it consists of a highly dedicated player base and developers that put a lot of care and effort into the new content that is released for the game. Frequent updates and active curation keeps Depth alive and well, which will hopefully still be the case in the years to come.

I pre-ordered the game, Collector's Edition, and I was very excited. Upon release I was looking at nearly all reviews and was quite worried at how many negative reviews there were, specifically in terms of optimization and the game being too short. I  was relieved, however, when I found that I could run the game properly without any gameplay issues on my custom-built pc which is decent but now older, and I found the game to be enjoyable, and taking about as much time as I thought it might to complete. I do have a few issues which I will address.
The only technical issue I had was when the game would crash if I tabbed out, but it stopped after a few days.
The combat felt different from the New Order in a negative way; I found stealth to be difficult at times without later upgrades connected with story advancement. Certain situations almost force you to engage in loud explosive combat, which would likely be frustrating in higher difficulties. The first 50% or so of the game leaves your health at 50 instead of 100 and you can only regenerate from under 10 health to 10 health instead of 20. This may seem like a minor issue, but the enemies take more hits to kill, especially from the starting weapon, which made the enemies feel like bullet-sponges. I felt like I was playing on the hardest difficulty in The New Order but I was in fact playing on the average difficuly.
The story was decent, although there's a laughably convenient situation in the game (which leads to your health being doubled and causing the combat to be more fun), and one character is quite mean to my boy Fergus, but the very end, when you see credits, was really really dumb and I felt like there was much more to be done, despite the length of the game.
I would say I enjoyed this game greatly, and will continue to enjoy this game on harder difficulties. I would recommend this game to anyone who owns the New Order and wants more. I think the New Order is superior gameplay-wise and has more content and is often reduced to the low price of $8.99 during a number of sales. Any one in the review section who says it was as short, or was shorter than The Old Blood probably sped through it or has a misconception of just how short the Old Blood is.

There are some thematic spoilers in this review, but I try to avoid specific details.
This game has been a mega disappointment for me and I don't get where the critical praise is coming from.  You go down corridor after corridor, and just when you get a taste of an open area, boom, a new corridor.  Time to go to Roswell, that'll be cool, won't it?  Nope, you're in a tunnel that looks like every other ♥♥♥♥ing tunnel in the game.  The characters that were added to this game are just bad.  Grace is bordering on stereotypical and includes dialogue that just sounds forced, like criticizing the use of the phrase "you've got balls" to mean you are brave.  *LIGHT SPOILER*Then she's put in charge of the group because....reasons I guess?  Why not...anybody that was already a part of the group?  Doesn't make sense to me, but maybe I missed a critical explanation in the story, but I don't think I did.*END SPOILER*  Then there's the caricature of a southern racist for BJ's dad that somehow comes off as worse than the damn Nazis in the same game...It's just strange.  He shows one genuinely human moment with BJ, but it's encapsulated within the caricature they have already protrayed him to be so it doesn't do much to develop his character.  BJ's mom doesn't show a lot of depth either, which is a shame, because they made it very clear she was a major source of inspiration for BJ and I would have loved to see more interactions between them.
I really don't have much good to say about this game.  It has some genuinely great story moments that I won't spoil, as well as some neat interactions between Nazi's and citizens in Nazi America.  The game somewhat subtly handles the descrepancy between morality and legality in a neat way that may make you think for a bit.  It's prettier than The New Order.  Gun play feels okay enough, maybe a little better than The New Order.  However, now take this with a grain of salt, I've never played a game that felt worse with a controller.  I had to turn off aim assist for it to be playable with my xbox controller, and ultimately opted to play with mouse and keyboard.  In single player shooters, I prefer to kick back with a controller, so that was a bummer.  Level design is bad.  The first level of The New Order blows away everything in The New Colossus.  You never feel like you are really going anywhere in this one.  This is probably due to never getting much perspective on where you are within the world...and most of the levels look similar.
This game also contains some severe difficulty spikes.  I completed The New Order on Hardened without too much issue, and this game threw a couple engagements at me that had me lowering the difficulty to the lowest because I'd get instantly melted.  A couple friends didn't seem to have this issue though, so maybe I just suck.
As for technical issues, this game isn't home free.  I've had a few crashes as well as some graphical glitches that require a full restart to fix.  Performance is decent, running at mostly 60 fps at 1440p on a GTX 1070 maxed out.  Dropping to 1080p keeps me in the 100s most of the time, but I opted to stick with 1440p.  I tried playing on my TV, and the game does not work properly on 4k screens.  It has scaling issues if you use the Windows DPI scaling above 100% and has artifacting issues, at least on my rig.  The dynamic resolution setting does a very poor job of targetting 60 fps as well, making it useless if that is a feature you are interested in.
♥♥♥♥ it, I'm gonna go down this road.  I don't care what the devs say, this game most certainly contains commentary on contemporary extremist politics.  It will date the game very badly.  It just makes you eye roll.  Nazi's have a conversation about pacifism (feel free to look up the quote), which is supposed to be satirical of the far right in the modern day in a very obvious way.  It just rubs you the wrong way, it brings you back into reality, and kills the experience.  The game also manages to squeeze in a "fat shaming is bad" message...it's just a weird thing to choose to showcase when portraying the atrocities of Nazi Germany.  BJ also has a scene where he uses "white" in a derogatory manner, which is also a strange choice.  Doesn't really bother me, but I find it odd considering the type of person he's been this whole time.  There's a few moments that make you feel like you are playing a power fantasy for the far left more than a game about fighting the Nazis.  Those sound similar, but there's a difference.  The New Order didn't have that problem.
I was so excited for this game and it really let me down.  I loved The New Order, but the issues I listed have really kept me from enjoying this game much.﻿  If you play games as an escape to any degree, stay away, it's just an upsetting experience in that regard, and the rest of the game isn't necessarily worth your time.

Sine Mora is eyecandy, writ large. It proves that Shoot 'Em Ups don't need to be against a flat-panning or blank backgrounds, but can instead tell a story within lush landscapes. This is an older game that sees a 75-85% price drop around 5 or so times a year. However, I've noticed it has wider availability alongside its steep discounts on deal sites like Humble Bundle, Indie Gala, Bundle Stars and so on. If you're looking to pick it up sooner than later, a steam key from a service like that might be your best bet.
This game gets a lot of flack for being difficult, as well as many other negative comments I downright balk at-- I simply don't see where they're coming from. If you come in expecting a Shoot 'Em Up, you're going to be put off by the amount of projectiles on the screen. If you come in expecting a bullet hell, you'll hate the slower pace and Galaga-esque waves. Approach Sine Mora witih an open mind and try to appreciate it for what it is, and remember that User-generated tags are sometimes inaccurate. I don't know about you though, but Sine Mora is nirvana for me. It is absolutely tragic that it has to be a casualty to my "No thumbs up for broken achievements" rule, because it's simultaneously in my top 10 favorite games of all time.

As far as Metroid clones go, Environmental Station Alpha is very faithful to the original and Super Metroid in terms of design, for better or worse, though it feels more like a mixture of Super Metroid and Fusion in terms of atmosphere. In many ways, the game does retain a distinct Metroid feel throughout, but unfortunately it falls off where those didn't with a very limited arsenal, infrequent pickups, and combat that starts to feel like a chore after a while. Traversing the station was a lot of fun, and I liked the segments where I had to explore far more than any time the game tested my combat ability, which, because of a lack of any long beam, felt like a repetitive slog through boss mechanics.
The graphics leave something wanting as well, as the environments feel sparse and retro, which works very well, but anything which animates is far too simplistic, and I found it straining to look at after a while, especially the player sprite.
A worthy sendoff to Samus this is not, but there is some fun to be had as it isn't a shallow parody of a Metroid game, merely an underdeveloped love-letter to one. I recommend only for those truly hungry for an isolating exploration platformer.

It's everything I hoped it would be. Requires more thought than the average game, reminds me very much of Super Metroid - the way the game works as well as its ambience -, and there is plenty of content.

Enviromental Station Alpha (ESA) is a masterpiece. At first ESA is a well built metroidvania game where there are surprisingly few powerups however, ESA choses quality over quantity in that every single powerup is very useful. There's no running around trying to find everything little, mostly useless, something-container.
As you're playing, if you are really trying to explore everything, at some point before the end you'll realize you've actually been playing a puzzle game the whole time and you've completely ignored countless clues along the way. The developer himself said "There are no empty rooms in Enviromental Station Alpha."
With that in mind, there is a thread in the community forum with most, if not all, the answers if you get stuck on something, but for nearly every puzzle you come across you'll have seen a hint for it somewhere and just not remembered to write it down.
Overall, most of the thrill of ESA comes from solving a puzzle yourself by vaguely remembering seeing something and going back through all the rooms to find it.
A testament to the human imagination.

To start off, like many others have said, this game is gorgeous. The visuals are stunning, the effects, the lighting, it all adds to the atmosphere of the game. The music is beautiful as well, I really want the soundtrack. The gameplay is excellent; the controls are top notch. I played strictly on an Xbox 360 Controller and had no problems with gameplay at all. While the story isn’t heavy, and a little on a “we’ve seen this before” level, it is still solid, and you WILL get put on a few feels trips.  The character design is super cute, I just adore Ori, even if I thought he looked like “Ghost Stitch” the first time I saw him haha.
The overall game was quite good, with a few small exceptions. One, the “escape” sequences are BRUTAL. The difficulty spike on each of these is just insane, and you WILL go through a few dozen lives on each one. I didn’t really care for the sudden difficulty spikes, but at least it wasn’t too often. Two, the fact that you can’t go back into your save file once completed is a HUGE disappointment. (yes, I know there is a “fix/hack” you can download to get back into previous areas, but that’s not the point). I like being able to 100% my game AFTER I finish the storyline if I need to, and not being able to is a huge issue for me. I shouldn’t be punished and forced to replay an entire game for a single object.  I hope this is something that gets patched.
In the end, the game is excellent and for anyone who likes a good platformer, give it a go.

The game is a metroidmania type of game; a 2d view side-scroller where you can movie both ways and access hidden and locked areas later once you've aquired certain abilities. There is backtracking but it felt more like exploration.
Supberb music and artwork, it was a joy to play through and sometimes found myself waiting for a while, just to look at everything and take everything in.
It makes you feel like a good player; the way the gameplay it set up for chaining abilities and how easily they are accessed makes the flow of the game very apparent; big windows of opportunity makes combat fun. Instead of dreading enemies you look forward to them so you get to try out new combos or use the enemies themselves to access new areas. The platforming itself is more difficult than the combat -  some quite difficult sections, but the on-demand save system handles it quite well.
Some rpg elements are present like the rudimentary ability tree; you'll eventually get all of them and some are more important to get first than others, but luckily there is little focus on this so that you can focus on the gameplay itself. The choices does not make or break the game.

From beginning to end, Remember Me stays true to its name in a variety of ways that I leave to you to discover through its satisfying gameplay and story. That said, some commentary:
As is with many games, the avenue that the character must follow through each map has but one successful approach, so there is some suspension of disbelief that a character who can leap as Nillin does is yet at other times unable to jump over the smallest of obsticles in her way at other times, unless the game needs you to in order to move forward. That will hurt replayability, but some will enjoy going back to old chapters to find the collectables that were missed the first time through.
I appreciated that the game provides tips during gameplay if you seem to be stuck with how to defeat an enemy or proceed forward - the game typically waits a healthy amount of time to give you a chance to find a solution, then sharing a hint before frustration truly kicks in.
The environment and effects are fantastic. Combat is a bit of a puzzle at first, but once you figure out it revolves around structuring good combos, it works well. Between puzzles, memory games, remixes, combat and jumping around, gameplay remains interesting throughout - as does the story and its characters, good and bad, as they evolve.
Highly -
- recommend the use of a game controller for this game. Keyboard/mouse controls are unreliable, misleading, and will cause you no end of frustration during more complicated combats.

I found Remember Me to be a pretty epic game, although I thought it a bit flawed.
The world the game takes place is amazing, graphics are great (apart from some plastic lookig skin textures on the main character) and the developers seem to have spent much care in making a detailed world. The lore and backstory to the world is a different take on usual dystopian scenarios. On the downstide for the most part the game couldnt' get much more linear if it was a simple straight line. And I'm sure "invisible walls" went out many years ago. Or are at least better disguised. But those are minor points.
Soundtrack is also awesome and fits in well with the game.
Story was great. (I'm sensing a theme here :) )
The combo system was an interesting mechanic I haven't really come across in other games. It worked well, albeit somewhat frustrating. In fact, my main peeve with this game was the damn combat as it's mostly nothing but mashing the left or right mouse button (with a few special actions thown in as you progress). Another letdown was the combat scenarious as time and time again they would trigger some foes to fight, then as soon as you dusted them off, they doubled the number of foes and had you go at it again. I didn't enjoy that, although the difficulty wasn't that hard really.
Gameplay wise was nothing special - lots of platforming and with some akward camera angles at times. It worked though.
As I said, the story was interesting, thought provoking, and easily capabably of producing a range of emotions. Without going into specifics for spoilers, I found one aspect of the remix sequences to be somewhat disurbing, doubly so when it was revisted towards the end of the game. However, as with so many things, it's down to personal experiances - and if you've never experianced this thing in RL, then you probably won't be fazed by this sequence in game either.
So I found the combat flawed and the story disturbing at times but everything else top notch and well worth the play time.
Hopefully some other games in this world will be released in the future.

Game #7 - Sine Mora (PC)
November 8, 2014
My love for Side-Scrolling Shooters dates back to my earliest gaming years. I think I was about 6 when I played Defender on my 2600 and even though it was a mess of huge pixels on a Black and White 11" Tube TV, it was the challenge that I truly enjoyed. Since then, I have played almost every shooter that I could play. Some have been outstanding and others have been downright horrible. Sine Mora is more of the former than the latter.
The striking thing about this game is the story. It's almost so heavily weighted on dialog that it's 50% of the entire game, which in story mode is only about 3 hours on the normal difficulty setting. It was pointed out on my Cast that the game seems to be similar to Star Fox in many ways, almost an 2D homage to the series. I'd like to think that the developers brought that into the game as a tribute, but regardless the story and characters are solid. Additionally, the graphics of Sine Mora are great, hands down they are gorgeous. The enemy types are in abundance and the Boss Battles are challenging without being insurmountable. Overall, the game is as solid in the Shooter category as any contender out there.
Although the game Story Mode is shorter, there are multiple game options from Arcade to Challenge Modes. Each of these game types offer multiple difficulty settings to extend the game experience. I would suggest that you could get 10+ hours out of this game if you played each option through to completion. As for the price, Steam sells Sine Mora for $9.99, but I know that different Holiday sales have brought the title down to below $3. I would suggest waiting till one of the sales just to feel better about the e extremely short Story Mode.
The average Metacritic score is 77 based on review sites across the Internet. I feel that a solid 8 would do this game justice, and especially if you find it for sub $5. Even if you have to pay full price for this title, you should enjoy the overall experience and have a lot of fun on your hands.

Wonderful follow up to one of the best franchise reboots of all time.  I thoroughly enjoyed this game from start to finish. This game achieved something truly amazing. Between it's absolutely solid gameplay, well crafted, intentionally flawed characters, and intriguing storyline that appropriately bonunces back and forth between comical and serious.
Performance: First off, in my 14 hours of playing this game I had no crashes, frame drops, or system restarts. I was able to play the game completely uninterruppted by any bugs (besides the disagreement the game seemed to have with Nvidia Overlay). The game delivered a beautiful and well-optimized experience without sacraficing quality.
Gameplay: Absolutely fantastic. Some of the best gunplay out there. It's responsive, beautiful, and the bullet impact truly feels like it packs a punch. Stealthing your way to two commanders plaguing an area feels just as good as improvising a full force, guns blazing, attack with reinforcements being thrown at you. While most of the game is the usual Wolfenstein bullet fest that felt fantastic in the New Order, there are some parts of this game where the developers effectively manage to characterize the protagnoist, situation, and further develop the plot through gameplay segments rather than cutscenes, which is something absolutely spectacular that I feel too few games achieve.
Cutscenes: The cutscenes in this game were beyond impressive. Not once did I ever feel annoyed by the short breaks in gameplay taken to watch these amazingly well directed cutscenes that were both bold in composition and mesmerizing at the same time.
Characters: This is something I really hope more people pickup on and come to appreciate about this game. The NC does something that is without a doubt lacking in storytelling, specifically in video games, and that is it deploys a set of intentionally flawed characters, BUT does not directly address the fact that they are flawed, rather it leaves it to the players notice. It's something that I cannot simply explain here without spoiling, so do yourself a favour and see for yourself.
Frau Engel was absolutely brilliant in this sequel and will leave you feeling downright uncomfartable at times.
Additionally : Finishing the game around 14 hours the game in no way overstayed its welcome and the story at no point lingered or felt like it was simply trying to increase playtime by adding unncessary garbage.
The mapping and directions for quests are useless.  I really had high hopes for the game, but it has no in-game direction.  What a waste of $60.

Even after the update (and updates to drivers) the game will crash for no reason. I'll have long sessions with no crashes, then suddenly crashes for days. At times, sound effects won't play (dog barks, doors getting kicked open), damage indications don't show up on the screen (red splotch in the direction of the damage), sometimes blood won't show up during an assassination/execution (other times it does every time), sound effects from executions sound deafened for no reason, death animations not playing in full (lasting a couple of seconds and sometimes lasting what feels like the proper length), collectible reticles popping into existence in locations inaccurate to where they are (or for collectibles already collected) and many other instances that I can't figure out of it's an intentional design, unintentional design or broken due to a bug.
While I personally have found the story and gameplay sacrifice consistency for one another and often to the detriment of the player, made worse due to the inconsistent issues and bugs are making it significantly less enjoyable than what it's trying to offer, and I've found it to be lacking regardless.

It is rare when I am stunned by a game.  Often games can be entertaining, visually stunning or encompase complex story arcs, but rarely do they acheive all three.
Remember Me is a beautiful game.  I lost count how many times I just sat back and looked at the environment, often getting attacked in the process.  The combat is not complex (once you get used to it) and by the end you flow around your enermy, dancing between blows like a ballet of violance.
The story is imaginative, thoughtful and well written, with strong voice acting and presence.  In the end you drift past the combat, knowing that your enermy will meet their poetic demise, because all you desire is to understand the next glimpse of your fractured memory.
This game is a cross between Deus Ex, Mirrors Edge and a film I used to love called Renaissance (2006 staring Daniel Craig).
If I were to critic this game, and I am loathed to do so, it is a little short and I completed it in about 10 hours.

So I just be the game today and here's my take on it. Hope it helps for those considering to purchase this game!
Story, Art, and Characters - Simply amazing. Everything in the game has great textures and you can see the developers really focused on making sure the graphics in every scene were done carefully to ensure a complete masterpiece. The story is very interesting, as you watch the main character struggle to find her identity, struggle with morality, and the broken society. If you like philosophy, you may enjoy this game as it quotes some historic guruus.  The cutscenes are unskippable which makes replaying some levels a pain. Also this is a straightforward, single-result (meaning no different endings) type of game with no side-missions or quests.
Gameplay - Standard fights are repetitive, relying on the same button combos and limited variety of enemies. Often, I had to put the game down because the gameplay was too repetitive and not fun. However, the "remixing of memories" a feature used 4-5 times in the entire game was a blast and I wish the developers made that more prominent in this game. In addition, it took me about 8 hours of gameplay to beat it once through without searching for hidden items or achievement hunt.
If you like a game that has beautiful art that takes "Inception" to a completely different level and that you don't mind putting down due to repetitive fighting and moving around the areas, then this should definately be a consideration to add to your library:

Remember Me is actually quite a good game and a prime example of why you shouldn't listen to critics or pretty much other people - including me. The graphics are quite impressive, on PC, even though if you examine each thing in the game individually the textures don't appear to detailed or high resolution, and there are plenty of beautiful scenes and vistas in the game. Combat is accomplished with a "customizable" combo system in which you can replace certain pre-determined buttons with various different types of attacks which increase your power, restore  your health, decrease your "Special" cooldown time, and others. Ultimately the combat is not too complex and usually consists of very simplistic patterns like X Y Y X Y Y, or X X X, but it proves fun regardless when combined with later abilities gained and new enemy types to which you must adapt.
The story isn't exactly "new", as it builds upon concepts floating around the science fiction world and even Hollywood for decades. You are tasked with correcting the "wrongs" of a Paris, neo-Paris, in which Dumbledores pensieve has become commercial technology for every citizen to use - leading to memory junkies, and all sorts of weird "digital" modifications as well as multiple oddly labelled "memoriel" concepts which Capcom seems to have made up.
Remember Me's platforming isn't remotely as challengng as some harder platformers, but really it's a lie to say that any 3D platforming game is difficult. That's one of the only things I remember people complaining about, that the platforming was pretty much on rails and the camera always told you where to go (during platforming) with it's focus. Regardless, the game is some good fun without putting forth much effort. On top of that, the graphics in many parts of the game are surprisingly brilliant for a low-key console game - and, it gives me hope that if Capcom actually got their act together, they could use many of the lighting effects and creepy environments in Remember Me as a good example of how to fix some of the atmospheric problems of Resident Evil.
Really the only thing I do not like in this game is the memory remix system. The controls are just unintuitive for PC because they were meant for a controller. Even playing with a controller, they are still bad. If not for that, the memory remix sections would be quite cool and they actually give some depth to Nilin and the Errorists overall, making you see that even though they are the protagonists, they are kind of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥- getting people killed indirectly or bending people to their will.
The themes in this game are very old school scifi and oddly enough, they have not been explored much at all by modern media. It's all very Phillip K.♥♥♥♥♥♥"Do Androids Dream of Electric Sleep?"-esque and the only things I can think of that have given this any exposure have been Inception and Total Recall, and a fantastic Stargate SG-1 episode titled "Collateral Damage."
Overall, Remember Me is a pretty decent game, though it is often held back by infuriatingly inept movement controls and hand-held platforming, and quite possibly one of the worst combat cameras in the history of video games.

While the mechanics contain nothing new, perhaps apart from the create-your-own-combos system, this game has perhaps the most compelling story I have played in a long time. The combat gets slightly repetitive, the quicktime event-ridden (mini)boss fights are bland, and the puzzles are easy.
With that said, however, I absolutely adored the setting in all its grim, dark glory. The visuals are astonishing, the score is brilliant, and the story appealed to me in every way.
TL;DR: if all you care about is innovative gameplay, skip this one. But if you enjoy a good story and some beautiful design, do give this a spin.

A perfect example that tells you why content is not king. This could have been a really memorable game: dreamy music, fantastic artwork, a good balance of detail and flow in storytelling etc... But it is one of only a hand full of games I have rage quitted in like 25 years of gaming. It is not impossible but seriously... spending several hours on an escape sequence just kills the joy. What is the point they are trying to make? If it is that you need to gain the skill to pass it, here is my answer: half way through the sequence there is completely random chance of certain projectiles being at a certain place which you need for escaping. you go through the brutally difficult process of getting there and without a chance to save, you have to start over. I died hundreds of times in a few hours of playing the game. I am not a professional gamer, but hey, I am not really THAT bad. And my experience with platformers goes back to the 8 bit era so yes, I can handle difficulty. This is not difficult. It is broken. Here is why: When you are making a game you should not think your audience are going to play it on your machine with your skills with your joypad/keyboard/mouse. People have different skills and different hardware. When something gets to this level of difficulty, miliseconds of reaction time from your hardware start to become a thing. And that is what makes the whole experience change. That, plus: When I have to repeat a task times and times for a chance of something happening, it very much resembles the repeated killing of the same monster for a chance to get a rare loot. We all openly criticize MMORPG games for forcing us to grind. They just do it to add to hours of our gameplay. Why is Ori and the Blind Forest doing it? I couldn't find any answer.
I believe this and I stand by my statement: It could have been a great game. But it is broken because the difficulty is 1. not justified. 2. not adjustable. Add the fact that controls are not customizable and you have a game which could have been great but fails just because its gameplay fails.

I'm six hours into the game, so I think I have a fair grasp on the game to write a review. First thing's first, if you're a fan of unfair games, this is the sort of game you might want to pick up. That's not to say it's unbeatable, just have fun re-loading because you took one hit in the gauntlet before the boss chamber.
Pros: Graphics, sound, and gameplay are all good. The graphics are low-bit, but done in a style that works. Music is just phenomenal. The gameplay is pretty fluid and easy to get the hang of. The atmosphere is done absolutely wonderfully.
Cons: There really aren't any outside of my personal gripes, to follow. It runs smoothly and if the extreme unfairness is your cup of tea, then all the power to you.
Gripes: The game is unfair and difficult. The hard spots are hard enough, but you find yourself taking a lot of cheap shots in a lot of places. Unfortunately, taking a hit or two on the way to a boss means you either have to have the boss down pat and not be off by a microsecond with any of your moves, or just re-load. Health is far too scarce for it's own good, and when you do happen across an upgrade, it's usually completely inacessable until much later in the game. There are exceptions of course, though the game pretty much just taunts you with health that you desperately need, especially on later bosses. There are no health pickups whatsoever, and what little they did to assuage that quickly becomes inadequate. You need to just get used to the controls and avoid taking hits rather than actually staying and fighting. Especially when everything you encounter starts to hit you for more than one point of damage, because even at max, normal mode's HP cap is 30. You wind up being incredibly flimsy. Oddly, I found the difficulty varies rather harshly from one boss to the next, one boss will beat you over and over and the next one you'll beat on your first or second try.
At the end of the day, I have to say that these games are the most fun when your effort is actually rewarded, and your efforts are usually rewarded with obstacles you can't pass.... yet. Kinda takes the wind out of exploration. I found myself tentative about even exploring, since if it wasn't the right way to go, there would be no payoff. And that's just no fun. And now to actually beat this game...

I'm conflicted on this because it's basically two games, where the first one is good, but the second one is, well, not.
The first game is basically to Metroid what Castle in the Darkness is to Castlevania: Heavily inspired by the older game's ideas, but with 8-bit-esque graphics and some degree of unnecessary cheapness, but never so much that it becomes unbearable. It's fun to play from start to finish, satisfying to find things, and mostly just the right level of difficulty. Only at one point (a boss with WAY too many "gotcha" extra forms) did I seriously consider a ragequit. My main complaints here are that several hidden things (including some exceedingly useful upgrades) are hidden in a completely unclued manner, or put in places that communicate to the player "come back later" rather than "keep trying", and that the ending you get for finding what the game considers 100% is thoroughly unsatisfying and predictable.
The second game is for people who thought Fez wasn't cryptic enough, and also needed some combat and cheap insta-death precision platforming. It basically just feels like a long drag of purposeless padding, along with a section that asks the player to go through a ridiculously, unnecessarily cheap section two or three different times. Basically you have to do a bunch of random-seeming running around through sections of the game you've been to already, followed by going to a cryptic secret section, followed by a dumb maze, followed by more running around including said cheap section again and the maze again and possibly twice, and when you're all done running around you have to start mostly over again in a new game+ and beat the whole thing all over again, and just...ugh.
Worse still, most of the instructions on what the game wants you to do in this part are locked behind a weird alien language that I honestly have no idea how anyone ever translated, as the only way I was able to know what any of it was saying was by reading a walkthrough. I mean, even Fez had a "Quick brown fox" room. And no, I don't think that discovering any of this latter part of the game myself would have been any more fun, because it probably never would have happened. There's a decent boss fight or two buried in this section, but it's mostly just not worth it. As of this writing I've basically lost my enthusiasm for playing the game thanks to this part, especially since the only endings that aren't the two that suck from the aforementioned first game require completing pretty much the entirety of this part.
So..I have to recommend this game entirely on the gameplay of the first part. And the fact that I'm willing to do so should tell you just how solid that gameplay is.
