Although I had never heard of Environmental Station Alpha prior to it showing up on a friend's activity feed, I went ahead and bought it on a whim, only to enjoy it more than any other game I played in 2015.
The game is inspired by Super Metroid to the point of saturation, but still manages to stand as a brilliant game in its own right, with tight controls, outstanding boss battles and an excellent soundtrack. Many reviews both positive and negative will touch on the difficulty of the bosses, but each of them behave consistently enough that victory is not a matter of luck, but figuring out the correct counter-strategy and perfecting its execution. Enduring defeat long enough to establish this muscle memory admittedly requires equal parts humility and stubbornness. However, the sense of accomplishment that follows defeating each boss easily justifies each failed attempt.
Beyond the excellent boss fights, the game's greatest achievement is the fact that exploring the station is not only fun from the very beginning, but becomes even more enjoyable as the game continues. The various power-ups obtained over the course of the game -- and I strongly recommend tracking down the optional ones -- allow for smoother, quicker movement as long as the player has the necessary platforming skills, and the computer terminals scattered throughout the station build enough backstory that the game never feels quite as lonely as its spiritual predecessor did.
For those that remain hungry after completing the game, there is an overwhelming amount of post-game content to challenge the player. Post-game content aside, completing the game through the first ending provides the player enough challenge, wonder and thrill that there is no reason for fans of the genre not to pick Environmental Station Alpha up at its single-digit price point, even if only on a whim.

Senua's Sacrifice is a short, uniquely brilliant gem. Step into Hel and piece together Senua's story as she tries to rescue her beloved. The game is an audiovisual masterpiece.

It's very different from anything on the market. I've been playing video-games my entire life. Now, I'm what people would describe as a "young professional." Work keeps me busy and I find it very difficult for games to keep my attention, particularly story-driven games or RPGs. They're difficult to get into after being away due to life suddenly getting busy.
A lot of games that come out nowadays offer nothing new. I've experienced it, or at least some form of it, before. All has happened  before and will happen again. The games fall into the same tropes using the same designs. It feels like a repetitive slog and the experience ends up feeling like a chore. Or, worse yet, comletely and utterly forgettable.
Without spoiling anything, Senua's Sacrifice does things very differently. You can tell by the level of care and attention to detail Ninja Theory put in the game. Every minute is rich with things to experience. Each minute is a step closer to piecing together what happened to our tragic heroine. Words have meanings and double meanings. Best of all, the game can be completed from start to finish within seven or so hours -- short enough to keep me invested in the story.
:
This is, by far the best part of the game. There's a reason why the game recommends you to use headphones. The audio is scripted in a way that builds suspense and helps add to the atmosphere of the game greatly.  Melina Juergens does a fantastic job with her debut as Senua. Without spoiling anything, the rest of the cast includes the renowned Steven Hartley (Eredin in Witcher), Chipo Chung, Oliver Walker and Nicholas Boulton (my personal favorite VA). They all perform flawlessly. It was an absolute joy to hear the narration or about Norse mythology whenever a runestone was interacted with.
:
I'm running it on 1920x1080, 60FPS with highest settings. It is a visually magnificent game, with starkly contrasting settings. One minute, you'll be running around a hell-ish swamp while the next you'll be in a lush-green garden. The juxtaposition is done really well. Each of the areas feels very memorable and purposeful. They all tie into the story, slowly unraveling what you've got yourself into. Graphical bugs were minor and a non-issue. You should definitely check out their Dev Diaries to see how it's made.
- A great mix of exploration, puzzles, survival, world-building and combat.
- If you die, you accumulate rot. If the rot reaches your head, Senua's journey starts a new.
- The voices are quite unnerving.

This game achieved something truly amazing. Between it's absolutely solid gameplay, well crafted, intentionally flawed characters, and intriguing storyline that appropriately bonunces back and forth between comical and serious.
Performance: First off, in my 14 hours of playing this game I had no crashes, frame drops, or system restarts. I was able to play the game completely uninterruppted by any bugs (besides the disagreement the game seemed to have with Nvidia Overlay). The game delivered a beautiful and well-optimized experience without sacraficing quality.
Gameplay: Absolutely fantastic. Some of the best gunplay out there. It's responsive, beautiful, and the bullet impact truly feels like it packs a punch. Stealthing your way to two commanders plaguing an area feels just as good as improvising a full force, guns blazing, attack with reinforcements being thrown at you. While most of the game is the usual Wolfenstein bullet fest that felt fantastic in the New Order, there are some parts of this game where the developers effectively manage to characterize the protagnoist, situation, and further develop the plot through gameplay segments rather than cutscenes, which is something absolutely spectacular that I feel too few games achieve.
Cutscenes: The cutscenes in this game were beyond impressive. Not once did I ever feel annoyed by the short breaks in gameplay taken to watch these amazingly well directed cutscenes that were both bold in composition and mesmerizing at the same time.
Characters: This is something I really hope more people pickup on and come to appreciate about this game. The NC does something that is without a doubt lacking in storytelling, specifically in video games, and that is it deploys a set of intentionally flawed characters, BUT does not directly address the fact that they are flawed, rather it leaves it to the players notice. It's something that I cannot simply explain here without spoiling, so do yourself a favour and see for yourself.
Frau Engel was absolutely brilliant in this sequel and will leave you feeling downright uncomfartable at times.
Additionally : Finishing the game around 14 hours the game in no way overstayed its welcome and the story at no point lingered or felt like it was simply trying to increase playtime by adding unncessary garbage.
The mapping and directions for quests are useless.  I really had high hopes for the game, but it has no in-game direction.  What a waste of $60.

This, in it's current state, regardless of my feelings towards the story or the gameplay is irrelevant considering the amount of issues plaguing the title. Even after the update (and updates to drivers) the game will crash for no reason. I'll have long sessions with no crashes, then suddenly crashes for days. Alt+Tabbing, opening steam overlay, picking up a collectible and any random action will cause an issue for reasons only the game can tell, but refuses to divulge. Not only that, but the gameplay is afflicted with inconsistencies as well.
At times, sound effects won't play (dog barks, doors getting kicked open), damage indications don't show up on the screen (red splotch in the direction of the damage), sometimes blood won't show up during an assassination/execution (other times it does every time), sound effects from executions sound deafened for no reason, death animations not playing in full (lasting a couple of seconds and sometimes lasting what feels like the proper length), collectible reticles popping into existence in locations inaccurate to where they are (or for collectibles already collected) and many other instances that I can't figure out of it's an intentional design, unintentional design or broken due to a bug.
While I personally have found the story and gameplay sacrifice consistency for one another and often to the detriment of the player, made worse due to the inconsistent issues and bugs are making it significantly less enjoyable than what it's trying to offer, and I've found it to be lacking regardless.
Good game, poor optimisation. When I buy a product I expect it to be well tested and polished. Not seeing it here. Refunded.

Man, I wish this game didn't have the bugs it has so I could give it a perfect review. The gameplay is thrilling, as is the plot, and it feels a lot more open-ended than the previous game. In that respect, I'd give it a perfect score.
In terms of bugs, I had frequent issues with explosions rendering, but I was playing on lowest settings, so that may be the cause. There were also a few parts of the map you could get caught on or even stuck in, and a bit of terrain that was unnecessarily difficult to traverse, but besides breaking immersion a bit, there was nothing that really ruined the gameplay.
Mechanically speaking, this game is just as intuitive as the previous one; get a gun, follow the objectives, kill any nazi you meet from here to there. As with New Order, there were a few times I found myself confused, so don't expect to do a no-deaths run your first time playing, but it all sorts itself out with a bit of environment exploring, and once you get the hang of the game mechanics (which you should be able to do very quickly), the gameplay makes a lot of sense without being easy. There were a few times I had to turn down the difficulty a bit, and I'd say this one's noticeably harder than New Order, but in the end that just adds to the fun, in my opinion.
Oh, and it's no more political than the previous games, you still just kill nazis and save the world. I'd even go as far as to say it's a solidly patriotic game, it holds very true to the idea of America as the land of the free and the home of the brave. Inclusion of the KKK is new, but then again, if you're one to rush to defend the klan, this game probably isn't for you.

Depth Hunter 2: Deep Dive is a rather interesting game. It is meant to be a diving simulator, but is more of an underwater fishing, treasure-hunting, and exploration game. The landscapes are absolutely beautiful, there are Three major locations around the world for you to explore and each has various missions you can complete. I spent the majority of my time playing, scouting for gold coins on the ocean floor and looking for relics. The music is relaxing, the scenery is calming and peaceful, this was a very enjoyable game to play.
The underwater hunting aspect of the game, or spearfishing, is overly simplified I think. I would like for this to have been more difficult. Killing so many fish in one area should attract predators, but in this game there are none, taking away a lot of the challenge. The closest thing to predators the game offers are crabs. Still, it has it's positive qualities, the underwater scenery being the biggest one. You can take pictures underwater and just explore if you are so inclined. Depth Hunter 2: Deep Dive was worth picking up.

Well , what we got there ? Continum Shift Extend ? Wow , everybody believed it would never be released ,  and i have currently it in my library . As a great fan of the first game , BB Calamity Trigger , i will be quick on the pros of one of the greatest fighting game ever made :
Pros:
-a technical , and yet easy-to-learn gameplay . Lots of combos and strategies , but beginners won't be lost.
-BBCT lacked of characters  , but with this game you get the double of playable characters ! ( and each of them are unique and full of charisma : contrary to other mainstream fighting like Street Fighter , the fighters have personnalities and you can see it simply through their sprites and animation ! ( i particularly appreciate Hazama , the great evil of this sequel ^^ )

Cons:
-The story is  complex and hard to understand , even though you played the first game ( but the story remains great ,and worth it )
-You must appreciate mangas / anime design ( i know not everybody appreciate it ... )
-Some bugs from times to times
- That's all !
Conclusion : CCCSE is an upgraded version of the first BB game : more characters , more features , online mode , solid gameplay...

Sine Mora is a shoot 'em up from Digital Reality, the company that gave us games such as Imperium Galactica, Haegemonia and Platoon. I guess Sine Mora is one of the first indie games they have developed so far - an attempt at something different with lower production costs and a now not very common genre.
Do note that this game is very difficult! Even on normal difficulty setting it is easy to perish and boss battles do not make it easier. There is a constant swarm of enemies and as typical of the genre the longer you survive without being hit the stronger you can become by picking up all the various power-ups lying about.
Graphics are decent and there are cutscenes incorporated in the narrative that make the game look even more fantastic. I liked how the camera focused on the plane as we were transitioning from one place to another. The story takes place in a fictitious world and it is a tale of, mainly, revenge. Its steampunk approach renders it a unique atmosphere - even more interesting is the Hungarian audio that - per default - you will hear.
Greater difficulty levels and various story modes available make Sine Mora a long-lasting experience. If you like the genre and you are in for some challenge pick this one up

I don't think the story is completely the "regular cliche story" - there are archetypes for "journey" models that are pretty much the staple of computer games through time immemorial, hero, discovery, realisation, gaining power etc.  But I think this had a little more to offer.  When I was thinking through the story in retrospect it did haunt me a little.
I would love to see a sequel, as all the faults that people mention (ie boring combat, sub par exploration etc) are all pretty valid, however it's just one of those games where if you go into it with no expectations, will take you on a great ride.
As an aside I would love to have Richard Morgan tunring this into a novel, that would kill. :)

As far as shootem' ups go, I think mechanically Sine Mora is competent if not pretty standard. The weapon upgrades are sufficiently meaty, there's a good variety of secondary weapons useful in their own specific contexts, and the controls are responsive and accurate. Where I feel it shines is in the boss battles; each world boss is very unique and many are grand in scale. All of them are really fun to play.
Ironically, for me the strongest part of this game has been the narrative. While I'm 99% sure the language is a fictional one, it seems to be inspired by eastern European/Slavic languages. The voice acting and story are surprisingly good considering this genre typically just focuses on mechanics, but for those not willing to invest the time, following the plot and reading the huge walls of text will be just another thing to mash the "skip" button through.
On the technical side, there seems to be some goofy issues with controller support. Half the time I try to play my 360 pad works beautifully, the other 50% of the time it refuses to recognize it at all. This would be more of an issue if the controller never worked because the game is unplayable with the keyboard in my opinion, but as it stands it's more of an annoyance/inconvenience.
Overall, a great "shmup" title :)

The memory remix scenes are conceptually some of the coolest stuff to come out of games in a long time -- you can dive into peoples' memories and change little details to radically alter how those memories play out and affect them -- but in execution, it's pretty much just trial and error.
Pick it up on sale and for the price of a movie ticket you'll get a story and effects worthy of a fun summer sci-fi flick. Just don't expect much of the mechanics.

I've been playing this game since release.
At launch i simply hated it......tried to get refund many times but wasn't able to......and i'm glad i didn't.
Graphics were bad, there was nothing to do other than farming elements to craft some items that would allow you to further explore the big empty space of NMS. The story was boring and the finale was a lackluster disappointment.
Then, they release 2 updates, Foundation and Path Finder.
Pathfinder added ground vehicle, organized ships into classes and other improvement for the planet generation of biomes and objects...improve relationship with aliens and the ability to contruct bases.
Then, they released the Atlas Rises update......A huge update that overhauled the game.
Improved graphics; improved planet generation. Improved main story. Procedural quest that acts like those guild quests from Skyrim or missions from Elite: Dangerous.
Better ship handling. The combat was improved with more weapons, different ship handling and better enemy AI. And the infamous addition of multiplayer co-op.....while its very basic with only a VOIP system, not even player avatars, its a small step into something that was supposed to be single player only.
Better galactic economics, trading, deeper crafting and base buildings, this Atlas Rises update gave a new beginning for the game.
But all this aside, the simple fact that Hello Games is still trying to improve the game and gives support for the game with huge updates that further changes it speaks volumes. A really small company that really tries to make something different and gives way more support than other big AAA veteran companies who tries to milk their famous franchise to pander to a part of the community that doesn't even play their games (You what game).
Still, the game isn't for everyone, but if you like old-school sci-fi books like "Foundation" or "Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy" and always wondered how would be to explore a enourmous universe on your own, i recommend this game. It's not a masterpiece or some thought-provoking, mind bending experience, but its decent enough to get you immersed in its universe.

For those that are familiar with Metroid Fusion, Environmental Station Alpha is similar in construction. A robot is sent to a multi-sector research station to discover why contact was lost. There are biomes to explore, logs to read, bosses to defeat, upgrades to acquire, and secrets to discover. Just remember: while it is similar, this is no Metroid adventure.
The few pixels that make up the cute little robot controlled by the player should be an overall indication to how threatening it can be. Movement options are fairly limited most of the time, so the environment, enemies, and bosses can seem unforgiving at times. Some powerful upgrades exist, but get used to short-ranged weaponry, four directions of fire, and no health drops. Since save and restore points are the only sources of health in the game, ESA gameplay rewards a conscious and patient player.
Exploring the station is fun. Each environment feels unique with its own aesthetic, music, pace, and enemies. Even though backtracking is a major part of the game, know that the areas in Environmental Station Alpha aren't always as they were, be it new enemies in old places, closed off routes from overgrowth, and activated security systems adding challenges to original paths. Teleporters can used to get around the station quickly.
Even though exploring is fun, be prepared to get lost. A lot. Areas that seemingly lead elsewhere are often out of reach with the player's current upgrades, or, there are hidden rooms behind walls that have little or no visual indication, contrary to other areas that may have cracks or color variation where blocks can be broken or passed through. Players may find that shooting and dashing at every wall conceivable seems like the only way not to miss something. There are times when the next destination is obvious, as certain events update the map with markers, but other times when players might feel at a complete loss as they try to decipher riddles.
Environmental Station Alpha executes the retro feel excellently. The game features a darker, more neutral palette with pops of bright color that references the original Metroid and Super Metroid. The sound design appears to draw inspiration from those games as well. The soundtrack has Brinstar-like catchy tunes, but also has many atmospheric songs and sounds that enhance the feeling of isolation as the player delves deeper into the station's secrets. Some of the music gets quite eerie.
The story is driven primarily by logs, so be prepared to read. I'm typically not a fan of story progression through text logs, but I don't mind it in ESA because the text logs are fairly short and sprinkled throughout. The subjects of these logs can seem confusing at first, but as players progress, more pieces of the puzzle are assembled regarding the events that transpired across the station before the robot's arrival. Some of these logs are filled with riddles, which may become clearer as they're revisited after exploring new areas.
Each boss is a unique experience of varying difficulty and technique. There are a number of optional and secret bosses that test players' understanding of the game's physics. I find that the bosses of Environmental Station Alpha are a major highlight.
The game goes surprisingly deep with optional power ups, secret areas, an alien language, hidden rooms, easter eggs, and inside jokes, all of which the game doesn't spoil for the curious explorer. Close to--if not half of the game--includes the postgame secrets. Good luck to those that set out avoiding a guide for the postgame content. "Involved" is an understatement, but another area where Environmental Station Alpha shines.
Gamers that enjoy the Metroid franchise will likely enjoy Environmental Station Alpha. It's undeniably influenced by that series, but most certainly no imitator. This isn't a cheap and short indie game. In fact, it's a big game for the low price. It is similar in length to Metroid, and even deeper with its secrets. For those that think they'll have Samus Aran's familiar arm cannon and powerups, they're in for a pleasant surprise.
Mechanics are fun and very challenging and the bosses are unforgiving. Excellent game that reminded me of Metroid Fusion.

It's good.  It's real good.  I am still enjoying the game thoroughly, even though I beat it hours ago.  It's one of those games that sucks you in while you're playing it, and stays on your mind when you're not.  The controls, graphics, atmosphere, and music all come together into a nice polished enjoyable experience.
I'll get the flaws out of the way first.  I really only see two, and they are quite minor:
- If it's your second or third time through, the game probably plays fairly smoothly start to finish.  However, on the first try you will likely spend a fair bit of time searching for the next powerup, switch, or boss that advances the game.  I ended up revisiting the same dead ends a couple times, and this was occasionally frustrating.
- The map is a necessity to the game.  However, often times when looking at the map it appears there may be two similar paths from your current location to the place you want to go, but only one of them is passable in the direction you are traveling.  It's sometimes very frustrating to almost get to your destination only to find out that “you can't get there from here”.  More than once the only way there is not the obvious way.
These are very minor gripes.  Minor, because of the nature of the game's strong points, like:
- The game is large, and so much more full of variety than you could have possibly expected out of an 8x8 tile set and an “imaginary sound chip”.  There's so much to see and discover, and it all looks fantastic in its low-fi splendor.  Every portion of the station has its own look and atmosphere, its own enemies, and its own set of unique and interesting challenges.  So when you're not sure where to go next, just go somewhere.  It's nice there.
- The controls are tight.  They have enough predictability so that getting through a difficult area is much more a matter of practice than it is luck.  More than once I encountered a room or a boss where my first reaction was, “You've got to be kidding me, this looks impossible.”  However, after a few attempts (yes, you'll be retrying things regularly), the precision and repeatability of the controls becomes evident, and the completion of said room or boss is a very rewarding payoff.  Several times I found myself saying, “Wow!  I really pulled that off!  I'm amazing!”  Which brings me to:
- Accomplishing a difficult series of jumps, finding that one secret spot that looks a little different than the others, and beating that punishing boss are usually good enough rewards in and of themselves.  However, occasionally you'll find an optional powerup that is just a joy to use.  You know what I'm talking about, because you've played other Metroidvania-type games.  It's that powerup that lets you go back through other areas that were difficult the first time, and completely tear them up.  Blasting through them so much faster than before while wearing a big stupid grin and giggling a little.  Yes, this game rewards its players for a job done well.
- Not really the obvious hints that tell you where to go next, but rather subtle hints like difficulty that say, “Maybe you should turn back.  This will be easier later.”  Usually if you encounter an area or enemy that seems unfair, it probably means you're headed in the wrong direction.  HOWEVER.  Several times throughout the game I stuck with it and muscled through an area ahead of schedule.  Not necessarily breaking the order of the game, but possibly to get a health or weapon upgrade a little early, so that I could have a little breathing room in the challenges ahead.  Very rarely was there ever an “all that work for nothing” situation.
- The graphics, animation, and music put you there in the game.  Occasionally you'll spot inspiration from other beloved games in the genre, but it all really stands on its own, even if you're not bringing all that rosy nostalgia with you.  The water area is calming yet dangerous.  The lava area is close and oppressive.  The jungle area is verdant and lush.  At every point along the journey, the game draws you in to its amazing atmosphere.
- Yep.  The game received an update recently which included an optional new (seemingly large) area with new music, enemies, and graphics.  It's clear this developer enjoys their work.
Like I said, I beat it, but I'm definitely not done with it.  I'm not a completionist by any means, but the game still has so many interesting things to do that it will be keeping me entertained for a good number of gaming sessions yet.  If you've ever enjoyed a Metroidvania game, this is definitely one to add to your library, and it seems almost criminal to be buying it for under ten bucks.
P.S. My biggest request is for a Linux port.  Streaming it to a Linux machine has a number of issues that other games do not, and it has some deal-breaking control issues when played under Wine.  So if you want to play it on your Linux machine, you're fairly well out of luck unless you're better at troubleshooting strange issues than I am.  Since the game is built on MMF2, a Linux port (while not directly supported by MMF2) should be possible and mostly hassle free through a 3rd party library.  I think this developer has a bright future, and hopefully a Linux port can put a few extra dollars in their pockets, and help speed them along through their next project.

Like many other games in the genre the hints to Metroid are plenty and often apparent. ESA, like Axiom Verge, sometimes gets a bit too close when it comes to lifting graphical assets and enemy movement patterns from Metroid to not annoy me (if I wanted to play Metroid or Super Metroid I will play the originals).
ESA does, however, offer a good experience at a good price. Although not graphically intricate or inspired, the game does look nice from a pixel art perspective. Like mentioned, I do feel the hints to Metroid when it comes to some of the tiles and enemies are a bit too much.
The game has quite a bit of backtracking and a surprisingly large map. Music is a delight. Sounds are nothing spectacular, but don't detract from the overall experience.
Boss battles are my primary gripe with this game. Although not very inspired, they do offer more than decent challenge, which I enjoy. It does annoy me to no end, though, when the HP bar is almost empty only to suddenly refill and the boss enters another state. I can live with this as a chocking WTF-kind-of-thing once, but it happens often and occasionally even twice with the same boss.
The backtracking also becomes quite tedious towards the later part of the game when suddenly the station is powered up and you get shot at from all kinds of thingymajigs.
Pros:
Music
Art style
The challenge

Sounds
Cons:

Wouldn't mind if the developers had ventured further from the Metroid graphical concept

Ori and the Blind forest... I'm not sure where to begin.
I'm not someone who is easily impressed. I tend to be fairly critical. I can enjoy a game if it is well made enough to look past the flaws it has.
Ori and the Blind Forest has absolutly blown me away, surpassing any and all expectations I might of had for the game. This easily is one of the best games I have ever played.
The gameplay is extremely smooth and fluid. The controls are simple, but the ways you can use them lend themselves to complex use.
The game is both easy to pick up, yet challenging. It has some spikes in the challenge but nothing that can't be overcome with a good application of skill.
If I had to give any complaint about the gameplay it would be sometimes it puts too high of a mark on intuitivness. You have to figure out how to apply an old skill to a new situation with objects you never, or rarely, used the skill with before.
Downright amazing. Its an appealing middle between pure fantasy and reality. Its bright and colorful, and gloomy and atmosphric when it needs to be. Even on the very low reslution i had to use the graphics still look far better then many HD games these days.
Perfect marks. The sound effects are fitting, and none of them annoying or grating. And the music is extremly pleasant to listen to.
The only thing I can critize is that the official soundtrack doesn't have the title them on it.
This proves very well that less is more. The story isn't over the top complicated... or even really complicated at all. It is told through sparse dialoge and a few cutscenes. It pulls on you before the prologe is over, and leaves you a little fuzzy after its over.
The game will take you a while to beat on your first run, there is a lot to figure out. It certainly harkens a replay too, or several.
As great as the game was there were a number of technical issues that I have to address.
The game is very demanding graphically, I had to keep its resolution settings on 640x480 to play smoothly. There is no options to otherwise lower its visual demands on the machine, limiting the amount of computers that can play it.
The text seems to be prerendered images. When the resolution is set low instead of the font point size lowering it instead becomes pixalated and hard to read, if not impossible.
Occasionally the screen would stop scrolling so i had to move back and forth to get it to lock onto Ori again.
And the last techincal issue would be, for me at least, the cutscenes kept self pausing while I was watching them.
This is by far one of the best games I have played, period. Satisfying gameplay, smooth graphics, great audio, and a story that has you from begining to end. I would recommend picking this game up.
9/10

If you like either or both, the Diablo series and the Titan Quest series of games, you will love The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing. All of the familiar action is here, along with the addition of an interesting story, great character, original world, and monster design; nicely designed quests, good loot, deep and satisfying gear/weapon customization, challenging boss monsters, very good soundtrack, and wonderful voice acting.

One of those rare instances where the zerg rush has been perfected outside of an RTS. The first in a trilogy of games, Van Helsing's Hack and Slash adventure offers some surprisingly diverse game play, witty banter, teeth grinding moments, and an overall good experience in one package.
The game allows for easy switching between ranged and melee attacks. You're ghostly companion is also useful, as well as buffs you. The game itself is well done, with a pletora of items, stats, askills, and abilities to tweak to your hearts content. It also gives you the ability to adjust your stats and skills (for a price) so you don't have to worry about making a mistake in your build. The story is also interesting, with some good humour written into it.
The game itself is a little buggy. Music tends to dissapear at times, and the melee skill habitually dissapeared, very annoying during a fight. Even on normal, enemy density is quite large in some areas, resulting in the veritable zerg rush that can quickly get you killed if your not ready for it. While it does force you to put some thoughts into tactics, it can also be quite annoying at times (waaaaaay too much zerg on the last boss).
The other potential issue, is that the other two classes, and the ability to manually level your companion, have to be acquired via dlc.
Overall however, this was an excellent and enjoyable game that is worth trying if you are into diablo-esque games (though you may want to try and pick it up on sale so you can get the all the dlc at a good price). Let me preface this by saying that I'm personally really enjoying the game, shooting nazis has never felt this fun to me. With that being said, I feel that the game has too many flaws at the moment for me to give it a recommendation.
First of all, it seems that Machine games decided to put its focus on the story, and unfortunately, I'm not really enjoying that much of it. Most of the side characters are one dimensional and boring, the dialogue isn't that well written and the villain is a female bootleg joker wannabe. Furthemore, the game has some scenes that just don't fit the tone of the game. You're introduced to Blazkowicz' father in the game and his character was just badly written. He's written for the sole purpose of being hated. He's racist, sympathetic to the nazis, homophobic, a wife and child beater, and the only reason for him to show up after his brief introduction at the beginning of the game is to serve as a plot device to set up a series of events later on. I don't mind having sensitive topics in a game but this is clearly written to be emotionally manipulative, as opposed to actually serving a point. Not to mention the myriad of "activist" scenes literred in the game with obvious political leanings that you can't help but roll your eyes everytime they're played. The only saving grace in the story is the character of Blazkowicz, it's very rare to see a protaganist with nuance and vulnerability in these sorts of games and it's a nice touch to add to the game.  I honestly still wouldn't care about the story not living up to expectations if they didn't sacrifice gameplay length to focus on the story, as this game is quite a bit shorter than its predecssor.
I still would've seen myself recommending this game, if not for the large amount of issues that plague it, from texture flickering to memory leaks to crashes. The game would've definitely benefitted from a couple of months for polish.
Overall I'd say that the game is well worth buying on sale (and possibly full price had the bugs been fixed).

Here are the cons though:
- Gameplay wise is very linear, with the places you can explore limited, and the things you can interact with pre-determined for you (i.e. you can't walk back to places that you've explored before).
- Combat is interesting, in that you can chain combos, but that's where the lackluster bits come in. The type of combos you have is pre-determined for you (i.e. you can't create your own, but have to live with the ones built into the game), and you have to "unlock" them based on how many enemies you kill so far
- Most of the game has you climbing and jumping all over the place, with a few nice interesting puzzles to add to the mix
Summary:
This game is definitely worth getting when it's on offer. Replay value is limited. I'm not likely to play this again unless its to see how the various memory mixes play out, or to get the rest of the achievements/extras. Let me get this straight, you want me to tell you a review about this game? Whoever you are, you might as well go to the curators, because if you've come for a review on this game, you've come to the wrong place. However, if you have come for an outstanding chocolate chip cookie recipe, you've come to the right place.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Ingredients
1/2 cup (1 stick) unsalted butter
3/4 cup packed dark brown sugar
3/4 cup sugar
2 large eggs
1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
1 (12-ounce) bag semisweet chocolate chips, or chunks
2 1/4 cups all-purpose flour
3/4 teaspoon baking soda
1 teaspoon fine salt
Directions
1. Evenly position 2 racks in the middle of the oven and preheat to 375 degrees F. (on convection setting if you have it.) Line 2 baking sheets with parchment paper or silicone sheets. (If you only have 1 baking sheet, let it cool completely between batches.)
2. Put the butter in a microwave safe bowl, cover and microwave on medium power until melted. (Alternatively melt in a small saucepan.) Cool slightly. Whisk the sugars, eggs, butter and vanilla in a large bowl until smooth.
3. Whisk the flour, baking soda and salt in another bowl. Stir the dry ingredients into the wet ingredients with a wooden spoon; take care not to over mix. Stir in the chocolate chips or chunks.
4. Scoop heaping tablespoons of the dough onto the prepared pans. Wet hands slightly and roll the dough into balls. Space the cookies about 2-inches apart on the pans. Bake, until golden, but still soft in the center, 12 to 16 minutes, depending on how chewy or crunchy you like your cookies. Transfer hot cookies with a spatula to a rack to cool. Serve.
5. Store cookies in a tightly sealed container for up to 5 days.
For a Rocky Road Bar:
1. Lightly butter a 9 by 13-inch baking pan. Make the batter as per cookie recipe and fold in 1 cup chopped walnuts along with the chocolate chips. Spread batter in prepared pan. Bake until the edges are light brown and the batter sets, about 45 minutes. Cool slightly and cover surface with 4 cups marshmallows and 1 cup chocolate chips. Broil at least 8 inches from the heat until marshmallows turn golden brown, about 2 minutes. (Keep an eye on the marshmallows, and turn the pan frequently--they go from golden to char in a wink.) Cool, cut and serve.

This game was an unfortunate casualty of an over populated genre and ended up getting overlooked by most people last year, myself included. This is a shame because Environmental Station Alpha actually brings a lot to the table:
• Atmospheric sound design with rich sound effects and good music.
• A rather high difficulty level that will challenge veterans of the genre.
• A lot of boss fights, most of them well designed.
• Manuevering mechanics that are fun to master.
At the time of this review, my first playthrough took 7 hours with 84% item completion, and I can tell that squeezing out those final collectibles is going to be even more challenging than what I've already braved.

What is this game? It's a 8 bit styled metroidvania in the style of the very first metroid game. It's no ripoff however, it features a well fleshed out story, gameplay, upgrades, reward for effort, secrets, and more. It comes with a good price at the cost og graphics, performance, and level design, but despite these issues this is definetely a game recommended for all fans of metroidvanias.
pros:
- original upgrades and weapons
- true metroid feel
- good story
- amazing music and ambient sounds
- great gameplay and feel
- supercharger upgrade is amazing
cons:
- really bad level design at a few (three) areas (the "room" at the very bottom of the map right after the boss there is the worst designed level I have ever seen in my life).
- bad performance (2D unity issues)

- supercharger, once located, can take hours of attempts to actually get (but its well worth the effort)

Not really a in depth review but I just wanted to give this game a thumbs up because it is by far the best "Metroidvania" game I have played since Super Metroid. The music is amazing, the boss fights are fun and rewarding and its got to be the best $10 I've spent in a long long time.

Amazing game. The areas are well designed and connected together. You also have a good selection of bosses to fight, and many of them are nicely thought out. The soundtrack, while nothing extraordinary that you will listen to beside the game, is decent enough and serves its purpose. But the strongest point of the game is exploration. There are ton of secrets to find, and it feels damn good to find them. I see many people compare this game to La-Mulana. This game is nothing like La-Mulana. La-Mulana is garbage that throws insane and cryptic stuff at the player from the beginning. This game I beat with 92% completion rate without using a guide and knowing nothing about it. This game respects the average-hardcore player, and offers a fairly challenging main game that is beatable, while also providing insane postgame riddles and puzzles for the masochist people to figure out. That is why this game is brilliant.
If there is one thing I would complain about it is the research outpost area. I thought it was badly designed compared to the rest of the game. I feel that there are many parts of it that you can't pass without taking tons of damage. Also I found the enemies that counter charge and dash rather tedious and frustrating.
All in all, a brilliant game that is a must for metroidvania fans.

I don't generally recommend things in a public place, because it seems a little pointless, but I hope this helps someone make a decision.
I've played every 2D Metroid, I've dabbled in more recent Castlevanias, I've done a lot of platformers. ESA managed to hold my attention for over 75 hours of exploration, trying somewhat challenging things, and more exploration. This is Hempuli's first commercial release to my knowledge, but he spent about 3 years tinkering with this game and trying to make it better. This is a better-designed metroidvania than Super Metroid was. There's no arbitrarily huge amount of health that you need to recover by grinding off of little enemies spawning out of pipes. You find a save, you get your health back, you fan out in multiple directions and see if you can find anything. The only real negative I can think of when it comes to ESA's exploration is that you don't find some little missile pack buried in each room, stuffed in a wall. You don't get that momentary gratification and pointless increase to the capacity of a weapon you'll never use. Instead, when you find some health or a bonus item, you feel massively more rewarded. That's not for everyone, but it's certainly for me.
I see a lot of complaints about ESA stemming from its difficulty. "This boss has too many phases", "I don't have enough health", "I don't know where to go", all that kind of deal. The boss pacing definitely feels off in a couple of places. Some of the earlier bosses are decidedly more challenging than later ones feel at the time. The reason this doesn't bother me is because each boss actually feels very unique. Each boss has its own mechanics and feels complex in its own way, aside from a couple which are designed to teach you basic mechanics and one that acts as an item progression gate. Health, and dying a lot, are also not issues. There's an easy mode available directly from the start if you can't progress on normal, and it increases your maximum health, lowers enemy damage, and starts you with more maximum health. ESA also does a great job of directing you to where you need to be if you interact with terminals you find. Similar to Zero Mission, ESA will explain where you need to go through highlighting the target square on your map for you, which continues for quite a long time to allow you to continue progressing and exploring on the way to your destinations. You can also get around the game much faster than it initially seems due to the eventual introduction of a quick travel mechanic, eliminating a lot of pointless backtracking. Save points are generally positioned well and are used to prepare you for a boss so that you have a minimal run to get back to a boss. There are very few exceptions to this.
The amount of optional content in ESA is also very impressive. There are secrets hidden everywhere, optional upgrades you can find, and with the introduction of a recent patch an entirely new area to explore. On top of this, once you've beaten the main game and reached an ending, you may have some questions about things you have found in the past that seem to have had no effect. This is where your postgame starts, and there are plenty of clues about how to progress postgame that can be found simply by continuing to investigate each unfilled square on your map. The secrets of ESA are not like a missile expansion hunt you would experience in a Metroid game. They are targeted and explained if you look carefully. There are only a scarce few entirely self-contained bonus rooms having little to no indication of their existence; almost all the things you want to find have a directing point somewhere. The postgame secrets are handled in an entirely different way than the traditional metroidvania style and require a different mindset to continue delving into each step in the chain of hidden information, which is a wonderful changeup so late into the game.
The soundtrack was also handled very well. Every track fits into the area it belongs in and helps set the mood particularly well. The instrumentation used in ESA's soundtrack really goes well with the style of game and manages to call up memories of old SNES titles while not being some shameless ripoff. There wasn't a single instance where I felt "Oh, this track is obviously inspired by another game". My single complaint with ESA's soundtrack is the lack of variance in boss music. There's one track used for almost every boss in the game, and it became noticeable after a while. I definitely would have appreciated a bit of variance in the boss music, even if it was just one extra track on some bosses. Luckily, this isn't a huge issue, because most bosses are intense enough or go down quick enough once you know their patterns that the music doesn't feel repetitive.
The graphics are the only point where it starts to break down for me a little. For the most part, ESA functions visually, but there were definitely times where I felt that the player character was blending into the background a bit too much. The low-pixel style also impacted how enemies and environments appeared, and more than once I was a bit confused as to what I was looking at until I took a second to inspect it. This isn't a major issue, but I would personally have appreciated more pixel density for ESA so that I could better interpret what was going on in each area. It's easy enough to tell what you're looking at in 95% of the game, but that other 5% is what I wish had more to it. That said, each area in ESA is quite visually distinct and the environments never felt samey or repetitive. Each room, even, is visually memorable, which is pretty impressive.
Hempuli's put a lot of time into making ESA great. Any time a bug has come up, it's been fixed as soon as possible. There's still a persistent issue with some people running the Mac version where the game runs at decreased speed or lags, but from what I understand this might be fixed soon with a change in the Wine/Wineskin wrapper and is a result of a recent Mac OS update. Linux, unfortunately, does not jive with Multimedia Fusion. At the time of this review, your best bet is going to be playing this on Windows or using a dual-boot (which I guess people might have anyway because of Linux?), and the Mac version may be improved pretty soon to have few or no issues. There's one issue in particular where the Mac version will not support a controller natively, but using Joy2Key or any other program you like is a very quick workaround for this, and the keyboard controls function totally fine on their own. As far as the content of the game itself goes, bugs that have been reported to be negative for people have been ironed out pretty quickly, and nothing currently stands out as being broken. This is a game which has been examined and improved upon consistently since its release, and I really can't recommend it enough. Hempuli knocked it out of the park and has done all that was required of him as a dev, plus a free update with an entirely new area and its own secrets. Some people seem put off by ESA because of how it looks and from the apparently intimidating difficulty, but I promise that even a little patience goes a long way. I hope those who pick this up decide to keep at it even if a boss initially feels impossible or exploration feels initially unrewarding, because it is ultimately worth it.

I never write reviews for anything cus it's lame, but felt like i should for this as it's really really good and whoever made it should get credit. I've played almost all notable 'metroidvanias' that have come out over the past few years (and believe me, my parents are proud) and it's by far and away my favourite genre. This is a perfect example of it doing almost everything right.
The controls are straightforward, the artstyle is crisp and the exploration is very fun. There's still a bunch of secrets I still haven't figured out - while others may find this offputting ('cryptic' puzzles as another review mentions) it's personally what i enjoy and not intergal to the main 'stpry'. I also enjoy the "difficulty" that others have brought up, i didn't think it was too hard and unforgiving and requires good timing and patience, and mostly just being careful of your surroundings. The boss levels are pretty challenging and I died quite alot but it felt pretty good beating them eventually.
It doesn't break the mould too much in terms of upgrades, but the physics-based grappling hook is really fun and and allows for some small sequence breaking if you're precise and patient. Also, plenty of little secrets and stuff to find by the same means.
Overall, it took me roughly 20 hours to complete the game with 90% of the map (but im really slow), and from the top of my head there's at least three puzzles I haven't solved - maybe i'll look up how to solve them. Surely there's a couple more hours behind these.
I sort of bought this because I needed something to tide me over so i didn't burn through Axiom Verge too quickly, but i found myself pacing this game because i was enjoying it too much. And it's also really cheap ( i think when i bought it was like three quid on sale). Can't really fault it if you're a weird obsessive of the genre (or not), unless you find it too difficult. Great stuff, well done to the people who made it. Admittedly, i dont actual play many games anymore but this is definitely one of the most enjoyable ive played in years.
EDIT: After posting this, i went back into the game to explore the map fully and get the post endgame content♥♥♥♥♥♥and i'm glad i did. All the little cryptic puzzles and stuff dont need to be solved to finish the game, they're just bonus game. I assume when i do what needs to be done i'll get to the research station update thing. Fun.
Edit 2: after playing the post-game stuff, it's really surprised me how the game is different to the main game (so far). It's like La Mulana a bit, but nowhere near as obtuse and difficult.

Played on an Inteli i7 2600K with a 970GTX graphics card and 8MB RAM at 1080p with high graphical settings and ran lovely without any issues.
Summary: Finished after 13.5 hours of play (in-game time). Was a fun game, but would have benefitted from a bit more vaiety towards the end.
Pros:
+ Engaging story. Outstanding cut-scenes.
+ Well fleshed-out NPC's that you spend time with between missions and start to really care for by the end of the game.
+ Fun gunplay. Enemy soliders seem to posess sqaud AI and will regularly flank you and try to flush you out. I played on "Do or Die" difficulty and this posed just the right level of challenge for me.
+ Some great locations.
+ One of the most well realized and perfectly chilling villains I've ever seen in a computer game.
+ Multiple ways of approaching battles, and weapon customizations add a tactical element to the gamplay.
Cons:
- Stealth AI can be .. questionable. Luckily the game doesn't focus too much on stealth, so this is not a big issue.
- Some long cut-scenes. We're talking 10 or 15 minutes. They're good, but after a few of them, occasionally feel like they get in the way of the shooting.
- No pause button in said cut-scenes.
- I felt it peaked at about 3/4 of the way through and then didn't offer much new material while getting to the end.
All in all, one of the best single-player linear FPS games I played in a long time. Would recommend.

An excellent port of my favourite fighter! Mad props to the devs and publishers for finally releasing this gem on Steam. ♥
Each fighter utilizes distinct mechanics and play very differently from each other, which makes for an extremely complex yet very comprehenshible combat experience. For example, Iron Tager can
his opponents to draw them in close. Rachel Alucard deploys traps around the stage and brews up
to manipulate position and momentum. Platinum the Trinity cycles between a range of different weapons and Arakune aims to
his opponents in order to deal extra damage with a swarm of insects.
also features a couple of game modes designed to teach players some proper mechanics, such as an extensive hands-on Tutorial and a demanding
where you can train combos and learn all about each fighter's unique quirk and play style. Even though BlazBlue can be very demanding when it needs to, it is still fair toward new players, both to the game itself and to fighters in general.
Personally, the most pleasing aspects of the game lies in its gorgeous visuals and charming narrative. Though the story is your typical run-of-the-mill anime (science vs. religion, WW2-alluded cataclysms, obnoxious lolis, catgirls, scruffy men, technobabble etc. ad infinitum) the narrative truly shines in the BlazBlue's well developed characters. In the game's visual novel Story Mode, most of the fighters express striking personalities and quirks beyond their stereotyped exterior, and their relations to each other are reflected in almost every single aspect of the game.
Among the few peeves I've experienced is that some of the English voice actors are replaced in certain parts of the more recently recorded story/arcade dialogues. This, at least to me, breaks immersion quite a bit. A second issue is that the story can be unnecessarily convoluted and if you haven't played the first installment,
, the plot can prove extremely confusing even though it's not very deep at all.
Another double-edged sword is the "Stylish" input mode, which allows inexperienced players to execute combos without effort. Though this can be convenient in Story Mode where you just want to blaze through the action with a character you've never played, it backfires miserably in Matchmaking when
rookies mess your heck up even though they haven't earned that skill. Even I, a lowly noob who cannot even manage a single proper combo (...), valiantly avoids using the Stylish mode for this very reason. How else could I properly improve?

Pro's:
+Good netcode.
+Long and very good story mode. (all characters have a story mode, combining for 3 seperate endings per character and then a final "True" ending)

Trine is a charming puzzle platformer with some light action elements. The artwork is gorgeous, the  soundtrack is great and the gameplay is fun. The Enchanted Edition is a port of the original game to the Trine 2 engine and the improved graphics still hold up surprisingly well.
The game is rather reminiscent of Lost Vikings and puts you in control of three different characters with different abilities. Unlike in Lost Vikings, most of the puzzles in Trine are physics based. Unfortunately they all tend to be on the easy side. Especially late in the game you are given so many tools that pretty much any puzzle becomes trivial.
The combat is rather casual too, and overall I found the game quite easy even on hard difficulty. The last two levels are significantly more challenging, though. At least you can switch difficulty on the fly, so this shouldn't be a major issue.
Despite these minor faults Trine is a highly enjoyable game that's recommended to anyone who likes platformers.
The good:
- Beautiful art that still holds up quite well
- Fun Lost Vikings inspired gameplay
- Interesting fairytale story
- Great soundtrack
The bad:
- Big difficulty bump for the last two missions. The game is really easy even on hard before those two

A great idea albeit poorly executed
A quick copy-paste of the overall story so that you can follow on the review (Don’t worry there are no spoilers):
The game is set in the year 2084, in a futuristic version of Paris called Neo-Paris. The Memorize corporation has invented a new brain implant called the Sensation Engine (Sensen), which enables roughly 99% of the population to upload and share their memories on the net, as well as remove unhappy or unpleasant memories. This gives Memorize an immense degree of control over the population and enables them to establish a surveillance state. This, in turn, leads to a small group of rebels forming under the name "Errorists": their mission is to bring down Memorize. The invention of the Sensen has also resulted in the creation of Leapers; memory-addicted humans who have absorbed so many memories that their Sensen has degraded and they have mutated into a subhuman form, now living in the sewers of Neo-Paris.
The game's plot focuses on Nilin, a memory hunter working for the Errorists. When the game starts, she has been stripped of nearly all her memories by mega-corporation Memorize. With the help of a mysterious man named Edge, she goes on a quest to bring down Memorize and recover her lost memories.
On to the review
Pros:
-Interesting dystopian world you’re bound to enjoy especially if you’re a sucker for screwed up versions of our future.
-Builds an interesting climax and keeps you on the edge because the game is not afraid to yell at your face from the very beginning THERE’S A HUDGE TWIST SOMEWERE IN THIS GAME!!!
-A couple of interesting characters and collectables that give more information about Neo-Paris which help to essentially flesh out a very beautiful city full of contrasts.
-Nice, fluid combat with an interesting mechanic to create your own combos. It’s not ground-breaking but I had tons of fun punching people in this game.
-One or two nice puzzles in the game. They felt off and I really didn’t like that if you stood a while the game just gave you the answer but they were smart and short - just enough to break the tension I guess.
-This game does boss fights right! When you meet a boss it’s time to use whatever you’ve learnt so far against it and not mash the X button or play the game of “Find the exploit”.
-The very concept of the game, although not original (what is original anyways?) is hard to swallow and should make you question a few things.
Is it a good idea to let the general public get a hold of a technology that lets them digitize their memories?
Is it a good idea to let the public change their memories?
If we are what we remember, can we really change from one moment to the next providing that someone changed our memories?
Isn’t that a threat to free will? Imagine if a terrorist group could erase the memory of 9/11 from the minds of a population.
-The game also provides a few very difficult moments where you have to twist someone’s memories and eventually change their character. Even the fact that Nilin (the protagonist) is actually an (T)Errorist and goes about doing things what (T)Errorists do while balancing in that grey area of “The reason Justifies the Means” is a bit unsettling. It’s food for thought which is always very welcome in a game.
-I suppose the first twist is easy to read. The second one never crossed my mind. It didn’t blow it – but it was a cool twist non the less.
-Changing someone’s memories is by far the best mechanic of the game.
Cons:
-God awful story-telling. The worse thing is that you only become aware of how bad the story-telling is after you’ve spent a good three hours in the game.
-There are a few plot holes that really degrade the experience.
-Some minor camera glitches (didn’t really bother me. I’ve also heard that the game suffers from a few bugs but I didn’t encounter any).
-It’s quite short and somewhat easy. I would recommend upping your difficulty a bit to enjoy it.
-A very poor protagonist. I would call Nilin boring but that could be misinterpreted as if she had a boring character. Well Nilin has NO character. I get that she’s confused and that she can’t decide what to do and who to trust because of her memory wipe. But what we get in the game is a woman who has no sense of purpose other than follow the path laid for her from Edge. She does question his motives and his decisions a couple of times through the game but the answers she gets are poor and she doesn’t press harder. It’s as if she doesn’t care for whatever is happening around her – so long as she gets her memories back - and those moments of gallant clarity and distrust towards Edge are coming out more fake than they should.
Nilin doesn’t even question some of the most controversial things that she herself does in the game which is… bad… We spend a minute or two in the beginning of every level listening to her inner battles and those never include some of the dirtiest things a person has to do directly. Let alone the things that Edge did with her assistance.
-The very best mechanic of the game – the thing that it does best – the most innovative thing it had to show is changing someone’s memories. Well, you’ll only get to do it three times.
Conclusion
All in all I would recommend that you try out the game first and if you really dig in the dystopian Paris or if you get an itch to see what the hell is the game all about THEN buy it.
I personally (if anyone gives a flying tard about my opinion) enjoyed the game. But I fill the profile of a person who’s a sucker for dystopias and an intriguing story. Even if it’s presented in a lukewarm, sporadic rain of brilliance amongst ♥♥♥♥♥♥ plot holes and poorly written characters.

I have just finished the game and I can say, I am ashamed to have waited until the game was on sale to buy it. I feel as if I have stolen an impressive and visionary game. It's the Mirrors Edge of 2013 - heavily underrated and undeservedly ignored by the masses. The art design is gorgeous and really looks new - even if they only let us play through linear tube levels. The sound and music perfectly fits the mood and the story is interesting (especially the ending), let alone the memory fiddling and Nilin's special abilities which are really cool.
Most negative reviews focus on the "hand-holding" during the climbing sequences. Well, it should be an optional assistance feature. But it's not as bad as most reviews might want you to believe. After all, every Tomb Raider and even the Assassin's Creeds have obvious climbing path visualisations that are just as easily deciphered as street signs smeared in your face.
Another point in negative reviews is the supposedly bad fighting system. I don't understand this criticism. DONTNOD has simply stolen Batman's free-flow fighting system - which earned heavy praise when it first appeared in Arkham Asylum and is still pretty cool - and spiced it up with a flexible combo system that you can modify as you wish. Might not be a new manifestation of game design genius but its fun to play and no flaw at all.
I can only say that Remember Me is one of my favourite games of the last 10 years, right next to Batman (AA and AC), Assassin's Creed, Half-Life, Mirrors Edge, The Saboteur and Max Payne 3. On a more objective game score scale I would give it something in the low eighties.

I started Sine Mora as a casual game to play between “long games” since according to online sources you can get through it in about 2 hours. I don’t think so. I’ve played the game about 2 and a half hours and there is no way I’m ever going to finish it. Not because the game is bad, but because it’s too hard. The “easy” mode still fills the screen with enemy fire and I don’t see how a casual player can get through it without retrying a million times. I thought maybe I could get a few achievements out of the game at least, but I only got 2 out of the 12 possible and don’t think I’ll be able to advance further.
The first thing you’ll notice on starting the game is that it’s in a different language, with subtitles. I’m not sure what language it is but it sounds Eastern European. The story is difficult to understand since it deals with time travel, revenge, and some sort of interplanetary rebellion. The narration that starts each mission is mostly philosophical and adds very little to the story, just the speaker’s “motivation.” You also constantly switch characters as you play and they all have different backstories. Some of the people are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s too, so I wouldn’t call them the “good guys” either. From what I understood, you're playing the members of a rebel team trying to cause damage to the Empire in 2 different time lines (constantly switching between past and present).
Sine Mora is a side scrolling “bullet hell” game where you control a small aircraft usually traveling from left to right across the screen with lots of little ships flying past and shooting at you. There is a lot of variety in the game, planes, helicopters, boats, and even a lot of underwater combat. Every level seems to have multiple large boss enemies with various weak points that need to be blasted off. Similar to the old Raiden games (Super Nintendo) you collect weapon power-ups and screen clearing “bombs” (every character has a different secondary weapon, not always bombs). You do not have “lives” or a health bar, but instead you have a timer counting down to zero. When you kill an enemy you get a few seconds added to the clock, and if you take damage you lose some time. Of course when you reach zero you die. One annoying thing is that your weapon power-ups can be lost (they fly off when you take damage) and you have to chase after them before they leave the screen. You do have one big advantage though; all of your characters can slow down time (limited use) and use this to dodge the lasers and missiles flying at you.
Pros:
-Sine Mora is actually pretty fun in the beginning (before it gets insanely hard).
-Surprisingly good graphics for a game that’s only 300 megabytes. The visuals / bosses seriously look amazing.
-Many boss battles, which are great in shoot-em up games.
Cons:
-Totally unfairly unbeatably hard by the end. And I was playing “amateur” mode. I’m sure some people can do it, but they’re probably the guys doing 100 hit combos in Marvel vs Capcom. I lost a lot of weapon power-ups to enemy fire and then lost even more when I chased after them trying to collect what I lost. There are also a bunch of instant kill shots that you don’t get warned about.
-The steam achievements are “chained.” You can’t get the later ones without getting the early ones. For example, Airman, Sargent, Lieutenant, Major, etc. You can’t get Major without getting Lieutenant and I couldn’t even unlock Sargent! Each achievement has a SET of requirements to unlock. So it’s not like “Kill this boss.” To unlock 1 achievement might require: 1) Crash 15 times 2) Get 100% accuracy on any level 3) kill 100 ships, etc. I was stuck on a requirement to finish any level with A rank. Best I could get was a D rank…
-The story is practically incomprehensible at times. This might be because it’s in another language and is “narrated” to you with heavy character bias.
-Some of the later bosses will make you tear your hair out. They fill the screen with 100000000 fast moving bullets and half of them are homing. One of them knocked me out in about 20 seconds every time and it wasn’t until my 10th try that I realized he was actually reflecting my bullets back at me (so fast they’re almost invisible). The time slowing power might be enough to get through a boss fight, but each level seems to have at least 2 bosses.
Overall I do not recommend the game to casual players and only to people who have awesome hand eye coordination. It’s a shame too because I really liked the graphics and shoot-em up in the beginning of the game. The difficulty killed it for me though. I can’t say I enjoyed the experience overall.

Normally I don't write reviews.  I would rather have people play games for themselves and decide what score to give them or whether or not it is a "good" game.  I felt compelled to write a review for Ori and the Blind Forest because of the quality of the game.  Every piece of art, sound, and animation is done in a beautiful and profound way.  The platforming design is solid throughout the game with some truely devious segments at the end.  Each new environment felt fresh and unique with always the perfect selection of music to fit the atmosphere.   Perhaps the greatest aspect of the gameplay is the sheer mobility of the main character.  At the start of the game you are moving at a slower pace because you are a little bit limited in powers which gradually increase your mobility and the damage you do/receive.  Towards the end of the game, you are leaping, floating, richocheting and rocketing around the environment in some truly crazy and deadly areas.  I feel the difficulty is perfect for seasoned games.  You will die.....a lot, but with instant reload to your last conviently spammable save point after your die, death becomes simply a brief delay to victory.
There are 3 linear skill trees you can go into, but only 2 of them are really worth your hard earned experience points from killing enemies or hidden treasures.
I found myself becoming addicted to finding all the hidden rooms and health upgrades.  This is a sign of an effective platformer in all the important ways.  For what this game lacks in depth of story, it makes up for it with ample heart.  The animation and music work together to paint a heartfelt tale told in a excapist's dreamworld. Although it only took me around 8 hours to complete it, I plan on playing through it several more times; its just that good.
Not only is this one of my favorite platformers this decade, it may be one of my favorite games since they early 2000's.  Moon Studios has made a spectacular platformer in every way. 10/10.

Summary: Finished after 13.5 hours of play (in-game time). Was a fun game, but would have benefitted from a bit more vaiety towards the end.
Pros:
+ Engaging story. Outstanding cut-scenes.
+ Well fleshed-out NPC's that you spend time with between missions and start to really care for by the end of the game.
+ Fun gunplay. Enemy soliders seem to posess sqaud AI and will regularly flank you and try to flush you out. I played on "Do or Die" difficulty and this posed just the right level of challenge for me.
+ Some great locations.
+ One of the most well realized and perfectly chilling villains I've ever seen in a computer game.
+ Multiple ways of approaching battles, and weapon customizations add a tactical element to the gamplay.
Cons:
- Stealth AI can be .. questionable. Luckily the game doesn't focus too much on stealth, so this is not a big issue.
- Some long cut-scenes. We're talking 10 or 15 minutes. They're good, but after a few of them, occasionally feel like they get in the way of the shooting.
- No pause button in said cut-scenes.
- I felt it peaked at about 3/4 of the way through and then didn't offer much new material while getting to the end.
All in all, one of the best single-player linear FPS games I played in a long time. Would recommend.

A humble, but very solid indie metroidvania. Good platforming and combat, a great soundtrack, simple but well articulated graphics, bosses that can get pretty challenging, and lots to explore, discover and uncover (especially in regards to secrets!) combine to form a true gem for the genre. There's even some 'La-Mulana'-esque puzzles to solve (if you're into that kinda thing), but you'll have to do a fair bit of digging to even find them, let alone figure them out.
If you enjoy metroidvanias, or, if you're like me, and even just think you might enjoy games like that, then you should definitely pick this up. It's well worth the surprisingly low price.

Are you hungry for a new Metroid game but sick of Nintendo sitting on their asses doing nothing? I've got great news, everyone; this game is fantastic and exactly what you're looking for. Great graphics that never seem repetitive or dull, nice atmospheric music setting the tone for each level, plenty of power-ups that aren't boring or derivative, level-progression that requires you to explore and never feels guided or linear, a bunch of challenging and fun bosses, and more than 10 hours of content for a blind playthrough.
Not only is it good to see the platformer/action-adventure genre get some love, but it's great to see such a charming and genuine example such as this game. Whether it's on sale or not, you wouldn't regret supporting this game.

I really hope this is the beginning of the end of AAA gaming culture. Going the way of the music industry went, allowing indie artists to no longer have to be tied to a label to be successful since they can market, publish and control their own content these days for cheap, something labels used to have a monopoly over.
This game is truly amazing for an indie project, and for an indie title with no publisher that means no day one DLC, no microtransactions or tact on multiplayer nonsense or pre-order garbage. Just a great game and great story/mythology without all the strings attached to a AAA title.
The game has a great art style with an amazing attention to detail thanks to it's state of the art animation technology and it's amazing depiction of someone suffering from a mental illness, with voices floating around your head, filling you with doubt or giving you hints. This may turn off some people but it's the reality when dealing with a mental illness you can't just turn something like that off. It's worth something experiencing, but be warned that it can hit close to home if it's touchy subject you are keenly familiar with.
The combat is simplistic at best but is still fun, especially for the more casual gamer, but if you are a hardcore action fan the combat may be a bit boring for you as there are a lot better contenders that do that bit better.
There is no permadeath in the game, so if that was something you heard that turns you off, don't worry about it, it's part of the narrative. Although I went into it not reading the articles or anything about permadeath and then saw that message in the game. I thought it was real and subsequently fought every enemy like an angry bull backed into a corner and it fit into the narrative so well. But in the end it was just the game's misinformation trying to throw me off and it was genius.
If you like, action story based games. This should be right up your alley. If you like horror games, there is something here for you too (full disclosure, it's about the creep factor then it is 'jump-scare' scary so if you♥♥♥♥♥♥your pants easy don't sweat it too much)
Let's hope we see more games like this in the future!

First off, let me say Hellblade was a game that snuck up on me. I remembered watching a trailer on Youtube a while back, and during the timeframe between seeing said trailer, and the release day of the game, it kind of drifted off, became muddled in the vast sea of ever flowing video games that are offered to us.
When this game finally released, and I purchased, and downloaded it, I was eager to experience the story, and immerse myself. I can safely say I was blown away by this game.
Tackling a rather taboo topic, one oozing and writhing with a heavy stigma, Hellblade communicates to us the daily and eternal struggles of psychosis in fantasy-like setting. Fully adorned with chilling graphics, lush, rich sound design, and voice acting nothing short of exceptional, Hellblade puts you into the muddy, blood stricken boots of Senua; a young Celtic Woman suffering from deep and meaningful loss.
The gameplay involves puzzle solving elements, laced with combat stages and world building through dialogue provided by both internal, and external persons. This is a game where headphones will open your listening experience, and allow optimal fidelity, paving the way to immersion on an unprecedented scale. The puzzle elements are mostly a series of eye/I-spy scenarios, and aren't too hard to decipher. Combat is fluid and brutal, dynamic but grounded as Senua twists and turns in a series of graceful positions with an unseen strength as she courts with death. Her functionality is impressively easy to master, and so highly satisfactory and pleasing to the senses as she moves almost too realisticly.
The sound design is opulent, as you lavish on binaural audio; a soup of voices, nature, and steel cooked to perfection. You will not be disappointed here. The accompanying soundtrack further enforces this notion, with a mixture between chilling and ominous tunes, to pumping and pounding rhythms of heavy percussion, and the croaky chanting of druids. Some pieces even remind me of Enya, and in this I can assure you, you will enjoy it.
The visuals perfectly convey the intended message, and a genuine sense and grasp of the bleak and soggy landscape is painted before you. You will notice some 'shortcuts', namely objects and landmarks at long distances, but the real treat is what is within your line of sight for the entirety of the game; Senua herself. Unreal Engine 4 works wonders here, and the motion capture reproduces and replicates her emotions with frightening precision, as her eyes light up your screen. A doorway into the soul, should resound constantly during your playthrough. This is one of the few games where you truly get to see a character in their purest, and you can read them with no struggle.
Overall Verdict:
Gameplay: 9/10
Sound Design: 10/10
Graphics: 8-9/10
Performance: 8-9/10
Controls: 10/10
Story: 10/10
This may just be my game of the year, but even if it should not top my chart, it is a journey so engaging and riveting that I cannot fault it on anything outstanding. You will not be disappointed, this is one of the few games that cover such a controversial topic in a manner so lovingly crafted, and comes shining through the gates of Valhalla.
