I remember when I first played the Party Pack games at a late night event... I felt like I was struck with a bolt of amazement. I decided to buy all 3 during the holiday price drop, and I love them. Although... I should probably go through the games one at a time...
YOU DON'T KNOW JACK 2015: It's just classic You Don't Know Jack. Don't get me wrong, I absolutely LOVED YDKJ 2011, but if you played that, you kinda know what you're getting in 2015, except for E, P, AE, or U?! and Foggy Facts. The music, intros, questions, they're all great, though, so if you're new to the franchise, you NEED to play this. If you came straight from the 2011 release, there ARE new questions, but don't expect many new elements.
FIBBAGE XL: I once played Fibbage 2 in the 2nd pack with some friends, but it seemed like you couldn't be smart AND funny at the same time. But... I played it again, and... you CAN?! Yeah, it was actually really fun, coming up with lies to bizarre prompts. Not all of them were winners, but some of my prompts (and this game) definitely take home some Olympic medals... metaphorically speaking, obviously.
DRAWFUL: Clever game. Drawing pictures and making up titles just goes to show how awesome your friends are... or how sucky their art skills are. My only complaint is that the drawings can get a bit glitchy, since I'm on a tablet, not a phone, but it's only a minor annoyance. Definitely better than Pictionary.
WORD SPUD: This is the least favorite for many people, but I actually really like this game. It's like that game show Chain Reaction, but with other people to judge you on your word skills. I especially enjoy reading out the messed-up paragraphs at the end. It's not really a game for winning, just a game for laughing... at others.
LIE SWATTER: While the 100 player cap is fascinating, this is sadly the weakest in this pack. Yes, the facts and lies are weird, but you can easily do that for free. And besides, Fibbage XL is EXTREMELY similar and a better experience, anyway. I'd play this at least once or twice, but maybe not more than that.
This package, despite not having the Family Filter and Audience features, is still a great one. It's not the best of the Party Packs, but I still enjoy it nonetheless.
GAMES RANKED FROM WORST TO BEST:
Lie Swatter
You Don't Know Jack 2015
Word Spud
Fibbage XL
Drawful

Don't be fooled by its calming exterior; Depth Hunter 2: Deep Dive is THE world premier underwater terrorist fish murder simulator!
Loading the game up for the first time, you're shipped off to Thailand to take revenge on the local cell of Al Qaeda's Aquatic Jihad Division. 9/11 NEVER FORGET! As a righteous, God-fearing 'Murican, it is your duty to murder every single terrorist fish in sight. Not only does the game allow you to murder to your heart's content, but it encourages you by giving you two missions where you must murder the most amount of fish you can in five and ten minutes, respectively. The only fish you cant kill will be displayed with a red indicator on your HUD, because righteous 'Muricans only murder civilian fish with bombs. In between killing terrorists, you can also
liberate them of their terrorist treasure. There's also a camera, in case you are a damn dirty peace-loving HIPPY COMMUNIST who loves to shoot pictures instead of bullets.
Pros:
1. Lots of terrorist fish to murder.
2. 'MURICA!
3. Soothing music will help reduce 'Nam PTSD attacks.
4, Bullets are hitscan, so us 'Muricans don't have to worry about such things like aiming or simple math.
Cons:
1. The game uses the metric system. I suspect the developers are dirty commies.
2. You cant murder sting rays. Seriously, they killed Steve Irwin, you don't F' with Steve Irwin.
3. There's only one gun. Come on, you would think a standard shotgun or a rocket launcher would make it in. I guess you play an ultra black ops 'Murican who has to supply himself.
4. No exploding barrels.

I can't say enough of the BlazBlue series, the younger cousin to Guilty Gear.. Tight controls, intuitive mechanics, diverse selection of characters for many different playstyles. You've got your fast rushdowns, zoners, grapplers, puppets, and more. Every character is unique. Every character has a decent chance at winning against everyone else. The only one who seems to be at a disadvantage is Tager against good zoners and range. However, he is still deadly upclose and can quickly turn the tide. There are no clones here. The only exeption is Nu-13 and Lambda-11. However that doesn't really count as Nu-13 is only available as Lambdas unlimated form and isn't tourney legal. Moving on, the story in BB is surprisingly engaging for a fighter. Continuum Shift expands on the universe laid out by Calamity Trigger. Now, when I played CT, I was a little confused to what the actual ♥♥♥♥ is going on, but CS cleared all of those questions up while, naturally, leaving its own wtf is going on moments for the next game to answer. Also, to those who skipped on CT, CS includes an abbreviated version of CT. My favorite parts of the story are th gag reels. My personal favorite gag scenes being for: Relius, Arakune, Tager, Bang, Noel, Valkenhayn, Rachel, and Ragna. As for my favorites to play: Jin, Tager, Hakumen, Nu-13/Lambda, Makoto, Litchi, and Hazama.
Now hurry up and give me my Chronophantasma! I need my Terumi fix!!!!! And Kagura looks awesome as hell!
Would love to see BBCP on Steam, but this will do for now.

Definite buy if the game goes on sale, lowest price is $14.99
Overall 9/10- Great experience, great time waster, enjoyed it and was well worth my money.

Loyal readers and strangers of the internet, ‘tis I. It certainly has been a while, and I just know you’re all itching to read another page long review (This is the part you skip to the end, read the summary and leave.) Today you’re going to suffer through a review of a game that got huge amounts of hype, but was neglected when it game out. “Why?” you ask. Don’t interrupt me; I’m going to tell you why. What’s wrong with you? I go to all the trouble to write a review for the game, and you just come on in like you own the place. God, the nerve of you readers. Anyway, let us begin.
Remember Me is set almost 80 years in the future in “Neo-Paris.” (Which is future talk for “Paris.”) Society has been completely ruptured and as a result of new technology known as “Sensen” that allows real memories to be digitised, manufactured, sold, bought and traded. Because of this, people have chosen to remove or replace any bad memories. This has drastic effects on people’s personalities, which we see often in the game when a single altered memory can turn friend from foe. Throughout the game, we see too very distinct classes. The upper class, who live in a beautiful utopian society, without any cares. This contrasts with the majority of people, who live in decaying ruins, desperate for money, work, memories, Ect. As you can see, this game has an abstract, beautiful concept, above and beyond most games produced now (*Cough Cough FC3 Blood Dragon.*)
You take on the role of Nilin, an errorist agent who fights Memorise, the company who owns Sensen and have developed an immense power over 99% of the population, who are virtually addicted to Sensen. Nillin’s past shows her to be an elite errorist agent, capable of not only of stealing other’s memories, but altering and rewriting them. This power unlocks a unique mechanic that I’ll talk in a minute. You start the game in the clichéd manner of amnesia, having you memory recently been entirely wiped. The voice of the errorists, who goes by the name of “Edge” is the only thing that gets you out of the prison you and the other errorists are being kept in. As the game progresses, we see what the Sensen technology, despite having good intentions, has done to the world. In prisons, prisoners have their memories taken from them to prevent rebellions. People who have become so addicted to the technology, they’ve lost everything trying to afford it. However, as your actions, which are influenced by edge, have extremely negative consequences which impact on many innocent people, you start to doubt if you’re a vigilante, or a renegade.
Now, moving on to mechanics. Remember Me’s combat is primarily based on combos, comprised of left and right clicks and dodging. The basic idea was, you were given a combo. (E.G Punch, kick, kick, punch, kick, kick) and you can change the effects on these different attacks (E.g., one of the punches could do extra damage, another could heal you slightly, Ect) The dodging system was integrated quite well into the combat, with the exception that if you dodged, you would have to restart the combo. The system was very good, especially when integrated with different unlockable abilities which were all creative and innovative, and a single ranged weapons, although, neither of these things was crucial to combat. I liked the combat system all in all, what I didn’t like was how clunky it felt. Often, because there was no particular was to select your targets (which I honestly didn’t mind, don’t get me wrong) you would attack whichever enemy was closest, in range and looking at. This system reminded me of the Batman: Arkham series, although, unlike the Arkham games, there was no easy way to move from target to target. In fact, it was almost impossible. Another problem was that sometimes you would try and fight an enemy, and the game would outright choose a different target. I don’t blame the developers for this, but allowing freeflow would’ve reduced this problem. Finally, I found that combat was often too busy, especially with enemies such as Leapers, who could jump onto walls and stay there before producing an attack that can only be dodged. This meant that, if fighting a hoard of leapers, one would constantly have to be dodging, and that can be a bit trying, especially when you were unable to complete any combos.
The platforming aspect to the game had its problems as well. Every level design, regardless of how unique the art style, felt linear, like the world was closed, and didn’t exist short of this one path. The game even threw in little arrows on platforms you were meant to jump on, which was nice of them but really did take away the challenge of a platformer with such a strong puzzle aspect, although it was, undoubtedly, necessary, as the paths didn’t stick out like a sore thumb like they do in Assassin’s Creed (Seriously, God in that game must’ve been a parkourist.) All I’m saying is that this game would’ve sold much better with a slightly more open world.
I’m going to touch on the art style and soundtrack by saying that they’re both great. The art style really brought to life the contrasts of the classes of Neo-Paris and the soundtrack contributed heavily to the atmosphere
Finally, the mechanic that allows Nilin to enter somebodies memory and alter it was simply astounding. The way it was structured was a little bit of a trial at the time, having to re-watch the same cutscène over an over again to find memory glitches (Things in the memory you can change) and having you go back and select different glitches to change the outcome was tedious, especially because you had to deselect everything before re-watching the cutscène to find out what was wrong. Not even mentioning how memory glitches were only fractions of seconds long. I didn’t miss any memory glitches (Their animation was just the right amount of subtle to make it difficult, but entirely possible to find them if you were paying attention) but rewinding and replaying and pausing and fast forwarding and rewinding again trying to land on the exact place where the glitch was, was severely annoying, especially later on when they become even shorter.
SUMMARY:
Look, this game really tried to be a classic. Its storyline, art style, soundtrack and voice acting easily qualify. However, the clunky mechanics and linear environment didn’t work in the games favour. I enjoyed playing this game, but only for its storyline. It almost felt like it would’ve made a better movie than a game.
Storyline 10/10
Mechanics 4/10
Art style & Soundtrack 9/10
Overall: 7.5/10
Thanks for reading.
P.S, the game is pretty demanding of your computer, maybe free up some space or improve the RAM. You’ve been warned

I was really excited to play this game. It's a sidescroller (very similar to the arcade classics Raiden, Gradius, Life Force, etc) so I wanted to try it out. Sine Mora is essentially the same game so I don't want to go into too much detail about how to play it. Though this game has one of the best dynamic backgrounds/foregrounds I have ever seen a game, it is that very feature that also leads to its downfall. Things will frequently fly in and out of "the middle area" where you play in and it's very hard to tell whether or not you can actually shoot it, or go through them. It's not always a problem on its own but when combined with others, it's hard to deal with.
Another problem is just its difficulty. The game allows you to use a slo-mo effect to dodge many attacks but its very limited. Very limited being a couple of seconds during a long assault. It doesn't recharge until you reach certain powerups as far as I can tell so once you use it all, you're going to be dying a lot. That leads to points being lost and many penalties in your overall grade. Not to mention the enemies that come from behind you; these enemies cannot be hit since your ship doesn't have a backwards attack.
How did they not notice these problems in the final product? Sine Mora runs great and plays fine but the gameplay is a major set-back.

Ori and the Blind Forest was suggested to me because of my love of "Metroidvania" games. I put off buying it because, you know... poor. But when I finally got it, It was completely worth it.
The game is simple at its core: a forest spirit, Ori, is searching for a being that took care of it and was basically a parent to them - and that's pretty much all I can say about the plot. It throws you in immediately and sets the tone for the rest of the story.
The game is absolutely stunning, and at times I lost lives because I was distracted by the amazing backgrounds or boss designs.
As I said before, this is a metroidvania and I LOVE a good exploration, get xp, get powerups, MORE exploration type game. The powers, skills, and abilities you find throughout your journey through the forest are fun and useful. There are some times when I didn't know how to defeat a certain enemy, but for the most part the level design is well done. You get an ability and the game gives you a gradually increasing difficulty using them. I used a controller while playing, so I cannot speak to the keyboard setup.
It was wonderful to play this, and just writing about it makes me want to play it again. A note to anyone who is looking for a fun/silly exploration game... this story can get pretty real. I suggest HELL YEAH! for something like that, which hopefully will be my next review.
On a personal note, I sometimes suffer from bouts of depression. The weekend I bought this was one of those times - there were things going on in the midwest that really got to me, and I was thinking I would just get some game on my wishlist to distract me. Playing this, going through such an emotional story with moments of pure catharsis got me through that dark time.
That may not be the case for you, everyone is different. But I would tell anyone to try playing through this game when your soul just feels run down. I think it would help.

It is confusing to me how a supposed sequel can do worse in almost every regard to its predecessor. Whilst it is not a terrible or broken game (technical issues for many users aside), I cannot recommend it. I simply did not enjoy it a great deal, not compared to
(TNO) and
(TOB). For a full priced game, there is not enough good content here to justify the investment, and I confess myself extremely disappointed.
If you haven’t played Wolfenstein, try TNO, then maybe TOB. If you loved those games, then you can get this (on sale), which is more of the same, albeit in a way that feels weaker.
Fundamentally, the gameplay is moderately good. It follows much the same course as its predecessor, with tight, intense combat and plenty of stealth options. The loud gameplay is the meat of the game, and still delivers the usual gore/action/adrenaline. However, the set pieces don’t feel as strong. The combat AI is weak. The weapon selection is poor.
The stealth is wonky at best, with a lazy detection scheme. If one guard sees you, everyone instantly knows where you are. Leaning around cover to remain undetected feels much more awkward now too. TNO had fewer stealth sections, but those sections felt deliberately built for a choice of approach. In TNC, stealth in offered frequently, but the level design makes it feel like a continuous afterthought.
The level design also squanders potential. It has some lovely attention to detail in places, and there are some great areas; but too much of the rest is incredibly drab. Remember the trailers showing a vision of America under Nazi occupation? Well, you can have a few minutes of that and spend the rest in bunkers and brown, wrecked cities. There were so many imaginative environments in TOB and TNO, so it was so incredibly disappointing to see how little thought was put into these environments.
The campaign is a decent length if you play on the harder difficulties which prevent you from rushing everything. Along with some side missions and collectibles, there's probably 20-25 hours here for most people (not including any DLC that may be added further along the line).
At the same time, playing on the hardest difficulty (excluding the extra-hard difficulty where you can’t save and get no checkpoints) is painful. It is a significant challenge, but in a way that is ugly and brittle rather than intense and rewarding. Only the fact that you can quick save (which, incidentally, is never communicated to the player) makes it viable.
Don't worry though, there's no way to replay levels! There are post-game side missions where you can return to some areas which have been refilled with enemies and a mini-boss, but it's not the same. Perhaps there's no way to replay levels properly because the developers knew that no one would care!
All in all, the mechanical gameplay is fun, but everything else is more than a little underwhelming, Once you've shot your way through a section with the one or two guns that are actually useful and you get tired of frantic, chaotic gunfights, there's very little else in the gameplay department that is satisfying.
The story is occasionally interesting, but mostly ham-fisted. It sporadically preaches and incites, but never draws the player in. It's difficult to make out what is satire and what is genuine. That's not necessarily bad in a game that strives to be ridiculous, but the tone of the game changes too frequently.
At times, it went to great effort to build emotional resonance, tension or dread ... then changed to extreme levity, satire and gore. The result is that you either turn off your brain and focus on the shooting, or are left disappointed and annoyed when any narrative potential is squandered.
Moreover. plenty of the characters are flat out annoying or tedious. One, in particular, stands out as the most relentlessly crass, obnoxious and unpleasant character that I have ever encountered in a video game. Satire and charicatures are one thing, but her writing ruined every scene she was in. And with charicatures, your scope for any kind of character development vanishes.
TNO told a story of desperation, frenzy and resilience set in a tone of cynicism and dread. It wove its introspections about conflict through an increasingly careworn and jaded BJ. The action could then be construed as his own rage, desperation and hatred against a monolith of evil. All of it was modulated by levity, a focus on the good, to remind BJ what he was fighting for … as well as a healthy dose of satire. Successfully, TNO strode a line between the serious and the silly. But TNC lost its way completely.
There are some serious points buried in the game. In early sections, it dwells a great deal on death, heroism and self-sacrifice. It deals with ideas about courage, choices and ethics. There are moving elements, particularly from BJ’s internal monologue and Anya. But all of it is washed away, cut up and mismanaged.
In essence, I am not convinced that the game knew what story it was trying to tell. For a game with a deluge of cut-scenes, it falls far short of saying anything meaningful. Its predecessors cut a careful line between a serious narrative and a fun experience, but this game is just muddled and unconvincing.
It is not helped by the politically charged themes that are relevant to modern America. The game is careful to hold no serious ideological sympathies and mock everything … which inevitably leads to its own uncertainty about exactly what the point of the game is.
The narrative itself reaches an ending point somewhere in the middle, but then limps on for the second half of the game, before finishing abruptly. Except, nothing is really decided (so that you can fork out for DLC and a sequel).
Outside of a few teething problems, the game ran fine for me. It is quite pretty, but too many environments are dull. There's just no sense of ambition or spectacle. Dirt and concrete gets tiresome, no matter how pretty it is. The sound effects are very monotone and dull, though the musical score is a strong point.
There are lots of niggling frustrations with this game. I gained a very real sense, when playing, that it hadn’t been thoroughly play-tested. Whilst individual sections worked, it never quite came together. And that’s exempting the occasionally odd AI behaviour, the handful of glitches and the weak stealth. So much of the game feels like a step back from TNO.
The in-game map is annoying. The menus are awkward. The disparity in weapon quality is severe, particularly when you get the top upgrades. There’s no way to replay some levels. Many characters are annoying. The leaning system is clunky. The list goes on.
Among many minor frustrations, the weapon wheel deserves to be singled out. It is possibly the most unpleasant experience I have ever had in a video game. Not only is it awkward, but it breaks the flow of everything else, ruining the fun of combat, which is the best thing about this game.
The more I wrote this review, the more strongly I realised that I felt. I assumed that I felt quite balanced, even cautiously positive, about this game. In fact, having laid it out, I realise just how much of it annoyed me.
There is the kernel of a good game in here. There are good ideas. There are good elements. The shooting and combat remains fun long enough to get through the game. But too much is weak, lacking or poor. Without the energy and care of its predecessors, TNC feels like a rushed, cynical sequel that barely forms a coherent game.

I am not sure whether this game is underrated or misunderstood and misrepresented.  If you think of it as a game it is probably 7/10 due mainly to its great graphics.  If you think of it as a casual diving simulator it is, in my opinion at least a 9/10.  The gameplay sends you on quests that you must finish to unlock other diving areas.  The quests include spearfishing, photography, and treasure hunting in open ocean and caves.  You also gather coins from the ocean floor as well as from the quest rewards in order to upgrade your speargun, camera, fins etc.  In my opinion the neatest part of the game is the photography.  It is fun swimming around trying to get a great pic of a beautiful fish with a background of a wreck or coral reef.  Then later you can go through your album and make them your pc background.
One of the main cons I see to this game is working towards a perfect game.  Three of the achieves are going to be a grind now that I have run out of quests and new dive spots to unlock.  Though living as far from the ocean as I am I will probably never go scuba diving.  So for 15 bucks this was a very fun experience for me.
The graphics are lovely.  The music is a bit repetitive but peaceful and pleasant.  It is a great option for those who do not want their children playing shoot em ups and don't mind if they spear fish.  It is not gruesome.  The sharks don't bite.  So if you are looking for a fun dive experience I would give it a try.

Being a huge fan of water in video games, this game immediately appealed to me. Water can be quite impressive when rendered correctly and seeing how new games handle it always seems to interest me; something that began ever since I first laid eyes on the 'Nintendo 64' version of 'Wave Race'. Then I came to realize that the 'Depth Hunter' series were originally mobile games with micro-transactions up the wazoo and I was immediately turned off. Surprisingly enough however, this game is actually quite enjoyable if you're in the mood for a serene experience with a minimal challenge, and don't worry, none of those pesky micro-transactions made their way into the PC version, either.
The atmospheres in 'Depth Hunter 2' are gorgeous, the music is relaxing, the game  works with a gamepad, and the controls and character animations are quite realistic in feel. There are five areas to hunt within and challenges range from snapping photographs of creatures and shipwreck, to hunting fish and collecting treasure at the bottom of the ocean. An XP system is in place as well, although I'm not quite sure what it does, but it's always nice to see a character leveling up. Purchases can also be made to upgrade equipment, such as a larger USB stick to hold more pictures, a longer spear, bigger oxygen tank, etc. So there is some depth to the game, although minimal, no pun intended.
The two downsides to this game are the fact that the campaign is short and can be beaten in a few hours, and the lack of any story whatsoever. Personally, the lack of story didn't bother me at all though, as I don't really see how the game would benefit from one. In conclusion, I can definitely see why people don't like this game, but for me, sometimes it's fun to just turn on a game and admire the atmosphere. So if you're looking for something with some action or a challenge, look elsewhere. The price-tag is a bit high, so I would wait until this game goes on sale to pick it up, but other than that 'Depth Hunter 2' is quite enjoyable after a long day with a nice cold beer.
Maybe one day Capcom will get another license for Marvel games. It's ok, because in the meantime this game more than scratches that itch.

Fun for the whole family excluding; die-hard conservatives, young children, overly competitive try-hards, etc. In actuality, this game really is fun for a large portion of your family and friend group. The only one that is firmly questionable is "You don't know Jack", and the others only get as bad as the players let it, and you know that your friends will let it get pretty bad. Full of laughs and enjoyment, the party pack contains many of those games that are reminiscent of the classic party game such as "Drawful" being similar to pictionary, "Fibbage" being similar to two lies and a truth, and "Lie Swatter" being similar to a classic game of true and false trivia. It truly is fun, and will have all of your gatherings laughing at the answers that you come up with.

Ah, Party Pack 1. This is definitely the weakest out of the three packs, but You Don't Know Jack makes up for that, and I would honestly pay this price for the value that You Don't Know Jack brings alone. This pack's got a few gems, but definitely isn't as good as its predecessors. Let's talk about each individual game now, shall we?
You Don't Know Jack - 9.8/10 - This game takes the cake in this pack, and is definitely a favorite of mine throughout every Jackbox Game. This is the 2015 take of the popular YDKJ Series that has been going on since the 90's. 50 Episodes of Pure Comedy Gold and Genius Comedy Questions, this game is very witty, and constantly has me shivering with excitement for the next episode and redfaced from laughing too hard. The greatest part of this game isn't the questions though, it's Cookie Masterson and his puppet Billy O'Brien. The two best hosts you could ask for. I honestly could go on about this game for hours, it is super genius and VERY VERY well done. Think this is it? Well, you're wrong! When an episode ends, it takes you to the credits where you can sit and listen to over 50 advertisements that they added in for entertainment purposes. The sole reason that this game doesn't get a 10/10 from me is because it only has 50 Episodes which seems to go by fast when you love the game so much.
Fibbage XL - 8.0/10 - I'd like to thank Party Pack 1 for being the birthplace of the most successful Jackbox Game Series after You Don't Know Jack, the Fibbage series! The fans love Fibbage and so do the creators! The next pack brought Fibbage 2, and Fibbage 3 has been confirmed for The Jackbox Party Pack 4! Fibbage XL is a creative take on a trivia game. Not only are you trying to guess the truth, but you and your friends are making up lies to try and fool each other into picking! But wait, it gets better! Cookie Masterson hosts the Fibbage series as well! Let's get a big WOOT for that! This game is just as hilarious as You Don't Know Jack, and is definitely a work of art to check out!
Drawful - 6.0/10 - Seems like Party Pack 1 is the birthplace ot tons of Jackbox series. The Drawful Series started here as well. While Drawful isn't my favorite, nor even one of my favorite Jackbox series, it is still a fan favorite, and is still very fun to play! Don't know how to draw? GOOD FOR YOU! Drawful gives wacky prompts for you and your friends to draw, and then guess on! It's really fun to play at a party, while livestreaming, AND with friends and family! Drawful 2 is definitely an upgrade though, as Drawful brings a host with a muffled voice, repetitive prompts, and only one color. Drawful 2 allows you to create your own prompts, draw with TWO colors, AND listen to a host with a clear voice. But still no eraser. :(
Lie Swatter - 5.3/10 - Lie Swatter is fun for a few rounds, but gets boring AND very repetitive after a while. I've gotten the Shaquille O' Neal question like 10 times now, no joke, and I've only played about 14 Rounds! Anyway, Lie Swatter is a fast-paced trivia game for up to ONE HUNDRED PLAYERS. That is a key feature right there, as all other Jackbox Games are for 1-8 Players.
Word Spud - 3.0/10 - What'd you do Jackbox? Such geniuses made a big mistake! Yeah, in my opinion, Word Spud is a waste of a game slot. You know that game you play in the car when you're bored where one person says a word or a sentence, and you build on to it using the last letter/word used by the previous person? Well they made THAT into a video game. Pretty lame, but I will say it *does* have a tiny bit of a higher replay value than Lie Swatter and isn't as boring as it sounds. Still a lame choice of a game though! Come on Jackbox, you could've done better! And the worst part is, they often bring up Word Spud 2. Jackbox jokes so much, you don't know when they're joking, and when they're telling the truth, so I hope they're not trying to hint that Word Spud 2 is confirmed. Would be an even bigger waste of space than the first.
FINAL THOUGHTS:
Jackbox Games is a genius company, and never in a million years would I rate anything by them negatively. Keep going strong, Jackbox! Can't wait for the Party Pack 4!

This game is probably one of my favorites that is considered a lego game. Looking at this game back then, it was barebones in my opinion but now that's not the case here. The game has something different from other lego games, because this game is non-linear and open world. Licenses restricted those games, but this game takes advantage of the lego name because you are the builder. The games sandox mode is for the players who just want to build stuff feely. It's also for players who want to make sweet/cool builds and share with friends. This also makes lego building easy because now, you don't need to go to a retail store to purchase legos. The adventure mode takes inspiration from the Lego movie in which you explore different worlds, rank up, unlock new stuff, and become a master builder. I prefer this mode than sandbox because i'm not a fan of sanboxes. But still, two modes that i believe are really solid and fit the Lego name. However this game still is in early access and does have some problems that i have came across.

9/10

Enviroments can kill you

Combat is very basic but feels solid, similar to how you can "feel" the impact of the weapons hitting enemies in the Souls games.
The only major two gripes I have so far are sometimes wonky physics, which happens with engines like these, and truly horrid hitboxes on some traps, especially the spiked balls on chains. I've been hit by more than one from several character widths away.
Overall though if you enjoy platforming games, give this one a shot.

Some of it probably has to do with a fairly uninspired loot system lacking many interesting and meaningful modifiers, and having it reduced to simply red or green numbers to tell you straight up if it was more dps or not. I'm sure the writing did its share to help out, which seemed to think that if it was somewhat self-aware about being terrible it would be less terrible. The companion system was ok, but didn't feel like it really differentiated itself from, say, Torchlight 2. The tower-defense portion was pretty interesting, but felt kind of tacked-on, and like it took up a lot of space for being so ultimately meaningless. The infusion/enchanting system also seemed to have potential, but most of the ones I found didn't seem like they were that useful so I never really bothered with it.
Overall, it was a thoroughly mediocre hack-n-slass. I can't think of any good reason to play it over its competitors. It just kind of exists.

I have played Fallout 3 for years, first on PS3 and I am playing it again on PC heavily modded (Primarily through a mod called Tale of Two Wastelands)
You will see Negative Reviews of this game, you will see people complain that it doesn't work and to avoid it. But it does. And on the latest OS to boot.
It's a really, REALLY, simple fix. You download the game, and yes, it will not start just yet. First you need to go the Fallout 3 Community Hub then to Discussions, and you will find a Stickied Post directly explaining that you need to install GFWL. There will be a link there.
Once that's downloaded and installed, you will be able to play the game from then on.
It takes literally 10 seconds. But everyone who gives this a negative review whining "IT DOES NOT WORK BECAUSE I AM A SPANNER" apparently has the attention span of your common gold fish.
The game is ten years old, the OS that was around when it originally came out (Windows Vista) had GWFL by default, or shipped with the game on Disc). Sometimes things are a little more complex than download and run. And if people don't have the patience for that happening on occasion with older games, then they don't belong on PC, they should stick to consoles.

Fallout 3 has borne the brunt of some criticism for things like its gunplay and VATS system.  However, it all pales in comparison to the exploration, the stories, and the sheer amount of breathtaking detail you will find in the wasteland and beyond.
I don't want to give anything away so I'll keep this relatively short--just one example:  The final thing I did in this game was make a moral decision which went against what I believe in, but resulted in the greater good.  It actually took it out of me.  That was the point where, apart from a few side-quests, I'd done everything I could.  So I returned my character to the player home, sat him down on a chair and left the game for good.  He will spend the rest of his life there, safe but always wondering if he did the right thing--the hero they needed, but perhaps not the hero they wanted.
10/10 would get traumatised again.
Anyway, just one more thing: mod this game.  There's graphics mods and all kinds of mods available.  It's a little tricky but worth it.  The graphics are dated, but really stunning at the same time.  The developers pushed that game engine as far as it could go!
Note:  Steam says I only played 70 something minutes of this, but that's because I used the excellent Fallout Script Extender to load it, instead of Steam.  But yes, I've completed the main game and all the DLC.

I was eyeballing this game for a while, but was unsure, then my wonderful girlfriend gifted it to me.
Ok, let me start with the bad first so I can get it out of the way.  This game is linear.  If you are wanting open world gameplay, look elsewhere.   This game has a few bugs, but most of the bugs can be overcome with a re-load.  The major game-breakers were patched quickly from the get go.
The combat can sometimes be repetitive, and the enemies are pretty much the same across the board except for the boss monsters.
Now on to the good.
This game is outright a work of art.
The graphics are breathtaking, the soundtrack captivating, the voice acting superior.
The voices…oh my, the voices.  This game should only be played with headphones.
When I find myself fighting a monster and hearing in one ear “You got this” hearing in another ear “You’re going to die” and hearing behind me “You’re weak” I found myself realizing that this game is unique in it’s field.
The best comparison I can give to other games is a mix of Tomb Raider, Dark Souls, Heavenly Sword, and a pinch of Legacy of Kain thrown in for good measure.
Add on top of all of this, a clearly well researched subject of psychosis being brought into the limelight and exposed for the problem it is in our society and not being looked upon as a shameful thing, or something that is to be scorned, but instead offering some insight for the average person as to an illness that many people suffer with daily.
Finally, yes it's a short game in comparison.  Only about 6-8 hours worth of gameplay without much replay value.  But it's also $20 less than other games that are shorter, and not as wonderful on the market.
To all of this I say to the developers “Bravo!”

I have a disease. Somehow, I don't feel like I've "finished" a game unless I've gotten literally every achievement in the game. Ori and the Blind Forest took that dedication to its limit; getting 100% in it was an episode in torture. On the bright side, I feel now like I'm fairly qualified to leave a review for this lovely game. For a beautiful game it is, despite, or perhaps because of, its difficulty. Every time I replayed it for different achievements (I had separate playthroughs to obtain Immortal, Elite, and Supersonic, for no deaths, no skill points, and under three hours respectively), I saw something I hadn't seen before, discovered a better solution to a puzzle I didn't previously conceive. That power of Ori and the Blind Forest to continually delight speaks volumes to its power in both gameplay and storytelling. At times, the distinction between the two did not at all seem distinct; the gameplay itself feeds the story, in areas such as the Misty Woods, or the Forlorn Ruins, names that might sound alien to you now, but you will grow to both love and hate should you play. ;)
tl;dr if you replay to 100% this game, you might feel absolutely overwhelmed, but the thrill of the achievements and the power of its story to constantly amaze make it positively worthwhile.
I should also like to add that Ori and the Blind Forest was the first platformer video game I ever played. Accordingly, the learning curve was fairly steep. But if I could go from a 28 hour first playthrough down to a sub three hours fourth playthrough, so can you. ;)
Edit: I have since played the Definitive Edition (where One Life mode will probably be my life's work) and am absolutely impressed by how much work the devs have continued to put into this game. They fixed many of my notable issues with the game, such as lack of speed travel (more notably felt when going for the Supersonic achievement), added more abilities, added entirely new areas further fleshing out the backstory, and have made this game simply an endless source of both frustration and wonder. This is truly a labour of love on the part of the devs, and hope they receive the full recognition they deserve.

Honestly, this one was a borderline call from me to recommend.
On the plus side, it's pretty much Metroid.  "Spiritual successor" is an apt description.  Metroid 1 sensibilities, but with a lot of the abilities and puzzle cleverness of Super Metroid.  It's really good, and when it's fun it's fun.
But this game is HARD.  Maybe I'm a sissy, I never got into Dark Souls, but this thing is crazy hard.  Like "neighbors think I have Tourettes" hard, "Smash a controller like it's 1997" hard.  It's so hard I almost want to downvote it, because it's "almost feels like a personal insult" hard.
This is not the cushy Super Nintendo style Level->Save->Boss->Save progression.  There are multiple bosses in every level, and rarely is there a save point directly in front or directly after it.  Right now I'm at the 2nd boss of the Temple level, and I can't even reach the boss with 50% of my health.  I haven't seen a life tank or powerup for 3 or 4 bosses.  Not mini-bosses, legit bosses.
So there you have it.  Recommended if you like getting your face smashed in old-school.

The Jackbox Party pack really has something for everyone. After trying it out at a friends house, I had to get it for myself and show basically everyone I know this wonderful bundle. I play this frequently with my family and friends. It wonderful, since there really is something for everyone.
Drawful:
My favorite in the pack. The game takes wit and creativity to match a saying with a user generated drawing. Seems simple? Well the game will try and trip you up via mispelling words or adding in weird punctuation. It's wonderful and hilarious to see what some of your friends will come up with to get their promt across.
Fibbage:
The game that started this all for me. A game of lying and wit, Fibbage takes trivia guessing games to the next level by allowing players to put in what they think other will fall for. Then, everyone is on the hunt for the truth to get those juicy points. It's generated some amazing inside jokes among my friends and has me learning new (and useless!) facts every time I play.
Lie Swatter:
I love the fact that this game can take in so many players. Its fun to play with online friends or to stream on Twitch and have players from all over the world join in. Lie Swatter focuses on finding which fact is a lie, and swatting it, and which are in fact true! Some thing really do seem so farfetched at times, I'm always dumbfounded.
Word Spud:
This game takes a little more patience than the others, in my opinion. You need to build words off of one another and create a block of text from that. This game can be played with 3 people, but honestly, its not that fun unless you have 6+ people. The way you win points is based on people voting for yours, and sometimes people will vote just to be nice. The more people you have, the more outspoken others will be without seeming like their unfairly targeting any one person.
You Don't Know Jack:
Another amazing addition to the YDKJ series. It's great. Simple as that. I just wish you could play with more people, since it's the only game on the pack that can hold less than 8 people!
All in all, if you want a game pack you can play with everyone, look into the Jackbox Party Pack. I really love every game provided. They all have wonderful music, and spark amazing laughs. Just make sure you charge your phone before booting it up.
Wicked good fun for the holidays!  Had a great time playing Fibbage XL with/against my brother, sister-in-law, wife, mom and father over Thanksgiving.  Highly recommended!

A year later. I've been following the steady stream of updates to the game, wondering if the game would get to the point that it was playable/interesting, or began to resemble what we were promised at launch.
I decided to give the game another try, and selected the "survival" difficulty. I spawn on a planet nine minutes away from my ship and with radiation damage eating away at my shields. I begin the mad dash for resources to repair my various devices and my ship.
I quickly realize that the radiation is ticking away at about 1% per second--that's one and a half MINUTES of real time moving around on the surface before I have to either restore my radiation shield with (extra-rare) resources, or find cover in a structure, in my ship (9 minutes away), or underground.
This isn't my only problem though--my life support is also ticking down--at a slower rate, but if I run or use my jetpack (or both!) the tick down doubles, or increases three-fold. Life support *also* requires rare resources to restore.
Between these two clocks and the rarity of resources, I die a number of times before reaching my ship. When I do--it's floating 20 ft in the air (?!?), but I don't have the jetpack fuel to boost up to it, because I've used it all in the mad run TO the ship. So I die again--and this time I have to make the run without any of the resource caches I used the first time.
I FINALLY reach the ship. I FINALLY scrounge around on the planet, collecting the MEAGER resources to repair the ship. I enter the ship, but it won't move at all--even though every system is repaired and functioning "normally".
I exit the ship and get insta-killed. "Radiation damage" is the reason when I respawn. I enter/exit the ship again and again, get insta killed.
I'm sure this is some sort of rare glitch (couldn't find any record of it online), nonetheless, I'm *extremely* disappointed. It takes me right back to launch and the barrel-load of bugs and glitches at that time as well.
One year later and still an un-polished, glitchy, disappointing product. For. shame.

Every 50 experience points, each character is given one point towards the purchase of upgrades to their abilities.

I thought that Remember Me was a GOOD (not great) game. It did have linear gameplay and level design as well as limitations in the combat (combos). But the game's foundations were pretty great, the story was good (had much more potential— some cringe-worthy moments could've been taken out and some others exploited), the art design and environments were incredibly well crafted, and (SPOILER ALERT) your electronic teddy bear was the bad guy all along— 10/10 would play again.

This is a very stylistic experience and there is a good story buried somewhere in that experience.
Unfortunately, it is barely a game.  Remember Me can best be described as a series of large circular arenas to fight groups of enemies in connected by linear jump-to-the-next-ledge "hallways."  Every so often the game rewards you with a cutscene or zoom out to show all the beautiful scenery.
The combat is repetitive and clearly takes a back seat to the scenery.  This is best illustrated by the final boss fight which is made maddeningly frustrating by changing the camera angle for the fight, making it different from every other fight in the game, and thus making it near impossible to see what the hell you're doing.
The best part of the game is the "mixup" sequences.  These are best described as cutscenes you can fastforward or rewind through to find parts of it to manipulate.  These sequences end up being puzzles to find the right combination to achieve a desried result [generally to kill somebody].  If the game had focused far more on these, the game would have been much better.  These were the best part of the experience, but unfortunately there were only 4-6 of them in the entire game.
If you can pick this game up for 5 dollars, I'd say it is worth playing through just for the mixup sequences.  I played on hardest difficulty which was really, really easy for anyone who has played a Batman game.  There was a good story, which suffered from the haphazard pointless fights the game felt the need to force you through.  Had they abandoned combat entirely and made it a more Heavy Rain/Beyond Two Souls experience, this could have been something amazing.

I understand I may get some backlash for this, since I am a big fan of the series, but screw it.
I think Fallout 3 gets alot of undeserved flack, and while it certainly is one of the weaker entries in the series, it is certainly not the worst *COUGH*(((Fallout 4)))*COUGH*
So let's get riiiiiiiiiiiiggggggggggggggghhhhhhhhhhhhttttttttttt into the review:
PROS:
+The world is vast with a lot to explore.
+Quests offer verticality in how you complete them i.e. You Gotta Shoot 'Em In The Head, Oasis, Wasteland Survival Guide, Trouble on the Homefront.
+Transition from tabletop to a First/Third Person perspective was a good one.
+Your Karma actually has an impact in terms of how characters interact with you and which companions you could hire or  what quests become available to you. Mercenary groups will also start to pursue you based on your karma level.
+Too add on to that, Karma is very flexible, so even if you're the devil incarnete you could redeem yourself and become Mr. Roger's post nuclear descendant if you're willing.
+Dialogue checks aren't just limited to the speech skill, high skills or stats can open up more options in conversation during various points in the game.
+Inclusion of V.A.T.S. was a good one in terms of both adding a more strategic element to combat whilst also perserving the aimed shot mechanic from the previous games.
+Envoirmental Storytelling was a brilliant inclusion and makes use of gaming as a visual medium.
Now, enough sucking the game's wee wee, lets get into the bad:
CONS:
-The game can be almost childishly black and white with the morality. You thought A New Hope had basic and unnuanced morality? Ho! You haven't seen anything yet. Honestly it feels like I'm playing a Saturday morning cartoon sometimes
-While the flexibility of the Karma system is superb, its flexibilty also works against itself. One way of gaining karma is to give vagrants water, and you do this repeatedly until you get the "Very Good" ranking.  considering one of the potential outcomes for an early quest is to help (((Allistar Tenpenny))), an aristocrat, blow up a city with a nuke. An action the should result in the wasteland collectively shunning you, but since you gave that homeless guy a caravan's worth of clean water, you're pardoned, like wtf. Things like that makes the game come off as ridiculous.
-"Traits? the hell are those"? - Todd Howard, 2007
-Combat can be rather clunky, you'll find yourself relying on V.A.T.S. very frequently in firefights.
-Very few Unarmed related weapons and perks, making it an almost pointless skill to invest in.
-Many of the early perks (Level 2-6) are stat boosts, and many of the later perks(Level 24-30) are either too beneficial or utterly pointless.
-Speech as a skill is somewhat pointless as speech checks are based on precentages and probability, investing in speech doesn't always mean that you'll pass every check, just increases your odds.  all you really have to do is reload the save until you succeed.
-Bethesda thought mixing 1 & 2's plot was an adequate substitute for good writing.
-Some of the DLC, like Operation Anchorage, falls flat.
-Little Lamplight and Bigtown....why
-That's not how FEV works, Bethesda.
Overall:
While a weaker entry in terms of story, mechanics, and overall role playing, Fallout 3 is still an entertaining, if very flawed Fallout game. It's a great way to introduce newcomers into the franchise if nothing else.

Why Challenge mode was separated from the Tutorial section is anyone’s guess, you’ll only be learning character specific combos there.

Sine Mora is a SHUMP that is not only ball busting hard its at times rage inducing on some of the cheapness of the hits you'll receive. But as much as I would normally say that this is a bad thing Sine Mora uses this to its advantage, as previously said this game is absolutely ball busting hard even on the lowest difficulty and I don't even want to go in to how hard the highest is. The achievements you can get in this game as well reflective this difficulty making it all the more satisfying when you get those achievements and succeed in get the higher ranks in a stage. The gameplay is your basic SHUMP with your upgradable weaponry and visually stunning super moves to help clear the screen or do more damage. The thing that sets Sine Mora apart from the others is its ability to manipulate time allowing you to dodge barrage of bullets easier as well as think your next step or two ahead of time. The game also has not only spectacular visual that engross you as well as some amazing music to accompy you. The game also offers some amazing boss fights and some decent variety in patterns of its bullets requiring some fancy flying. The story however can be a bit confusing and distracting as the entire cast of what might as well be an adult version of the star fox team speak in a different language and requires the player to read the subtitles to understand the story (which is no problem personally for me). But for a SHUMP the story is very complex and does have some interesting characters to go with it.
Overall Sine Mora is a great example of a modern SHUMP that neither sacrifice story for graphics or graphics for story and is a good buy for both hardcore SHUMP fans and those interested in getting into the series as long as you’re ready to get your reproduction organs smash to bits.

I always have been a side-scrolling 2-D shooter fan from the days of Galaga, Gradius, and R-Type.  Sine Mora is in the same vein as those afforementioned games and I also consider it more difficult.  It's like Grasshopper/Digital Reality took elements from top-down bullet hell shooters such as Radiant Silvergun/Ikaruga/Do Don Pachi and implemented it into this game.  It is highly addictive nonetheless.  Dying then learning from your mistakes to master the levels is rewarding.  The graphics are nice and it does have a convoluted story like most games in this genre do.  The amount of play time directly depends on how much time the player is willing to spend to perfect the art.  There's different combinations of ships you can use so it adds an element of replayability.  There are a few different modes as well such as Boss Training and Score Attack.  Also, you can pit yourself against other players through the leaderboard to see how you stack up.  I can't recall if I paid the full 10 bucks for the game but it's on promotion quite a bit so anyone can pick it up for a decent price, however, Sine Mora isn't for all gamers unless you enjoy the difficulty of what the genre brings to the table.

Sine Mora and I have a pretty unique relationship. I first played it just before I really started to get into shmups, and a lot of the unique mechanics really hooked me, despite the incredibly high difficutly. However, after having broadened my horizons to a greater variety of traditional shoot 'em ups, a lot of the fondness I once had for it isn't there anymore. That isn't to say Sine Mora is a bad game--not at all, I still find it to be quite a unique, enjoyable game--but it doesn't convince me its time-manipulating mechanics are as refined as they could have been, or provide as much a benefit to the gameplay as they could be.
All that said, if you're a seasoned shmup fan, you'll find the change of pace with Sine Mora very refreshing, and defintely worth a look.
Varying sections of stages have a time limit which goes up for every enemy you destroy, and getting hit--instead of taking away a life and/or placing you back to the nearest checkpoint--takes time away from you. If time runs out? Boom! Back to the next checkpoint. This creates a very intresting risk/reward environment, one where the entire game feels like one giant game of tug-of-war. However, taking damage also send all of your collected weapon power-ups flying, making for some Gradius-level frustration when you repeatedly take hits trying to regain your lost power. That being said, your control is still very sharp, but performs much better with an analog stick, as the game was designed around it instead of the standard eight-way digital movement. It takes some getting used to, but is a much smoother experience that the genre should have adopted a long time ago.
Finally, your ship also has a limited capacity ability that allows time to be slowed down for better, more careful navigation of more intense fire patterns. Though, more likely than not, you'll save it for when you have to collect lost powerups, as the bullet patterns rarely acheive danmaku levels of insanity.
Overally, if you enjoy shmups, you will enjoy this game. The story is, hands down, one of my favorite stories told in video games, the gameplay and visuals provide a very fresh experience in what I would argue is a stagnating genre. If you're not into shmups, I'm sorry; this game is punishingly difficult, and you'll quickly get frustrated if your skills aren't up to par. Definitely watch a Let's Play for the story, however; it'll be worth it.

I really like Metroid and Castlevania games and I really looked forward to Environmental Station Alpha.
But sadly the game just continues to confuse and annoy me that I no longer want to complete it anymore. I quit at the part where some enemies were following you on the Y axis in the Volcano area, next to a room with fireball spitting Piranha plants.
=============
Its
aspects:
- It is aesthetically a nice game, very loyal to the 8-bit graphics I liked with NES games.
- It has a nice soundtrack and atmosphere, it really felt like a Metroid inspired game.
- The boss battles I did were fun, you may need to learn a pattern, but they were fun to play.
=============
But, its
aspects:
- It is a difficult game, you dont have a lot of health. The enemies and the environment tend to do a lot of damage later in the game. You can crank up your HP by editing the game's config, but I think the ingame upgrades should do this.
- It is a cryptic game, I often did not know what I had to do in order to progress. At first the game helps out with messages on ingame computers, but later on I often had the feeling I was missing certain items in order to progress like a vertical boost jump. I spent a lot of time looking for a fourth energy source in the Temple area, it turned out you had to move through a wall to get to it. I had to look on a YouTube video to figure this one out, that area just looks too much like a plain wall. In Metroid, a Zoomer (enemy) would have crawled along the wall and disappeared inside the hidden part to give a hint. If it were for a secret item like the disks, it would be fine. But not in order to progress in the storyline.
- It is a hard platformer, where you really need to master the hookshot jumps to get where you need to go. Too often I get knocked off by Rinka enemies, falling stalagtites or projectiles and drop into acid or lava. It just becomes annoying after too many times. However, some people may think this is where the challenge of the game is and consider it a good point.
- It is not very rewarding, I think it would have been better if boss battles rewarded you with upgrades rather than having to search for them. Also the heat suit kind of disappointed me, I need it just to get through a few areas. The Metroid Varia suit, deducts damage done from enemies and allows you to walk in lava. Also, killing enemies become a bit of a chore, they do not drop anything usefull like health.
=============
Because of these points I do not recommend this game to other players. Im just a casual gamer however and people with more skill and patience probably will find this game enjoyable.

As pretty much everyone has stated the first thing that comes to mind is Metroid. Very concise. You're in space. There are familiar figures, but with alien colors and features. Looks like Metroid. Feels like Metroid. Styling and rich art. I'm a big fan of the realistic figures they have designed with such a limited pixel pallette per figure. It looks and feels like a tight old school NES game, which as I'm sure you already realize is a phenomenal thing. I have to say, I was equally impressed to see the limited number of people accredited on the dev team. I believe it was four...my apologies if I am wrong. This game feels like a high quality 8-bit era game, so all praises due to the limited number of people who developed it. The controls are tight, like you would hope in this genre. But. just to specify there are a heavy amount of platforms elements, which for me is a good thing. It's something I personally find synonomous with Metroid or SOTN, but they also have a heavy combat element. And, Metroid in particular uses a blaster. Of course, there are combat elements in this game, and they are fun (see epic boss fights). But, they are closer to something like Alucard in SOTN, because of the limited range on your weapon. A meaningless distinction to some, sure, but I think it has weight to others. If only, stylistically. Ahh, yes. The boss fights. So far, I have participated in what I would deem a thorough amount. About one per hour. Granted, I have only played several hours. So, if this is isn't true in later stages, I apologize. But, I suspect it will be. Boss battles are HARD! Not impossible, but don't expect to get through it on your first time. Most of them have taken me about a half dozen times if not more. It's not just learning the NPCs patterns either. You have to be pretty dynamic with your strategy if you want to beat them. I have been playing on Normal mode for reference. All in all. This is one great Metroidvania style platformer, and highly suggest it at full price, if you're a fan of the genre. And, if you're not ABSOLUTELY try it out on sale. Great game. Excellent so far. And not to SPOIL anything. But, the story about a rogue AI has not been cliche yet, nor predictable. Which, in this day and age is an impressive thing.

I went into this game with mixed expectations. On the one hand I utterly adore underwater games and their setting, on the other I hate hunting in every way, shape or form.
What I figured would happen is that there would be the fun underwater exploration and swimming around competing with the actively hurting fish aspect and that depending on which part was more prominent I'd give it a positive or a negative review...
Turns out it went a different way.
There are three locales in the game, which you'll go through in order. Each has a variety of missions... which you'll go through in order. They range from catching specific fish, to catching as many fish as you can in a specific amount of time (no minimum amount for success) to finding treasures or taking pictures.
To summarize, these are... lacklustre. At no point did I feel challenged, engaged or even relaxed by these missions.
The hunting aspect of the game is present, but forgiveable as there is no blood, no real skill involved and as long as you're super close to the fish not even any animations... I'm not sure that's a good thing in general, but for me it was.
Progression through the missions as well as capturing / photographing fish and finding coins and treasures give you money and EXP. Money is used for upgrades which make you swim a bit faster, require you to go up for a air less and to make the fishing and photographing slightly easier.
I will
approve of an upgrade system, and I'm glad it's there... but I wish it would do a bit more. It's easy to get everything and the levels you gain do little more than unlock a few of the upgrades and then just give you bonus coins, and if I were to play a level on somebody else's profile and then be asked if he or she had all of the upgrades or none of them I wouldn't be able to tell.
Lacklustre is the name of the game here, and I can't say I recommend it.
It's better to just wait until
makes it out of early access.

This is the game that got me into fighting games. It has an amazing tutorial explaining the mechanics of the game and fighting games in general, there is a very well made Infinite prevention system combined with a system to prevent Touch of Death combos. The inputs are very forgiving, to the point where I can do the 360 motion on a keyboard. Plus, all the characters feel unique, including Fukua (A joke character made as a half April Fool's joke half shot at Capcom's Decapre reveal who the players liked so much she was made a permanent addition to the cast). Going beyond the mechanics, the game is amazing to look at, with every frame of animation in the game being hand-drawn, and there are a TON of frames in this game. The only downside is the online, but not because of the netcode (The netcode is pretty damn good, you only really have problems if your ping is 200+). I am going to be blunt, this is the kind of game you only play quick match on if you REALLY know what you are doing. Still, for $10(Originally $15) to start off and another $10 for all the DLC characters (Who were free for the first 3 months after their release, so Lab Zero was still taking a pretty big hit to their wallets after releasing them, all things considered), there are far worse titles on this platform you could buy and play with your friends.

Despite a lot of little problems and imperfections at the time of writing I am really enjoying Lego Worlds. I had a small play with it during early access but only really decided to sit down and give it more town since the full release. I did not pay full price because of aquiring during early access but I have paid much more for games that have held my attention for less time. We are still far from a "perfect" Lego game if there even is such a thing but this is an interesting take with a lot of fun elements among the more shallow gameplay decisions. I have written a long review below because I have a lot to say about the game but in short if you dont mind the kind of vapid gameplay in the usual Traveller's Tales Lego games and want to be able to build in a fully rendered Lego world then this game is for you.
1. As a Lego Game
I have played Lego games for a long time, way back into the old Lego Creator and Island days and I would just like to point out how insane I would've found this game back then. You can build your town out of Lego, populate it, walk around it and even interact with parts of it. That was basically everything I wanted but never really got from a Lego game as a child. I will admit that currently you cannot build vehicles which I think was a major part of every child's enjoyment of Lego but you can discover real sets that are identical to their real world counter parts. Even things like the modular sets! and you can walk around them in first person! As an adult who is still kind of a lego fan and has a few friends who make modular towns as a hobby this is a really cool thing to be able to do.
2. As a Survival, crafty, explorey... thingy
Trying to make Lego World's more than a creative tool has resulted in some interesting decisions when it comes to gameplay. Some I think work and some definately need fleshing out. There was some controversy about locking most of the games content behind a slightly odd unlock system rather than leaving the game as a sandbox creative tool like it was during early access but you can now choose to play a sandbox mode rather than the full game. I'm actually going to recomend giving the "adventure" mode a try as this is how I have mostly played the game and have gotten quite a bit of enjoyment out of its implimentation.
There is an inevitable comparison to be made to Minecraft and in my experiance, as with Minecraft, simply being able to build and create with no limits can be a very entertaining experience but there is definately some satisfaction to be had from putting in the work that the regular "survival" mode in minecraft makes you do to be able to create. Adventure mode in Worlds gives me a similar experience though rather than you having to "mine" every block you wish to place your self. (A mechanic I'm glad they avoided because I have done more than enough of that now in my gaming lifetime). Instead, in World's a lot of what you need to create can be discovered through exploration and questing in the game world... sort of.
I do get a sense of reward and achievement for finding new sets (which you can copy and paste anywhere into the world), new weapons (some are more fun than others) and new vehicles. Some of these discoveries open up fun little deviations in gameplay and not all of them are there to compliment the building and creative aspect of the game. There is an emphisis on exploration over surival which I do enjoy as the terrain and building generation has on numerous occasions, surprised me with how interesting or beautiful a location can look in Lego.
I would like more of a survival aspect in some ways as the game has potential to include that as a more major mechanic rather than an occasional digression into defending yourself from skeletons or a giant ape. The only real punishment for death is a loss in "studds" which is the currency to purchase things you have unlocked. I have never found myself short on studds...
The only issue with all of this is everything feels a little shallow for lack of a better term. Most of the mechanics seem to try and reward exploration which is a good thing. You find new sets and vehicles in the world to unlock them. Certain items and minifigures are only unlocked by having a different item already on you, which you would have had to have found elsewhere in the world. Different worlds have different quests to complete which forces you to keep moving to keep unlocking features through the gold brick suedo-levelling system. Those quests sometimes require you to use the creative tools to build or colour or destroy something to complete them. These things knit nicely together but all of them are quite basic in their execution.
Building quests for example, can be very easily completed without really much effort. Some require certain conditions which do force you to make an actual building for example, but I suspect the win conditions could be easily tricked. I like building in the game so I choose not to try and trick them and will often go above and beyond what the quest requires to make my creation look presentable but I would have liked to have been rewarded for doing a "proper job" in some way.
There are a couple of gameplay mechanics that just aren't complimented by the others. Most of the different lego building blocks you can use are locked from the start. Things like doors and windows and other fixtures and fittings can be unlocked through discovering generated buildings that already have them. I like this it again rewards exploration. Many of the regular building blocks however are only unlocked when a  little gremlin burrows out of the ground holding it over his head then forces you to run and catch him. At first I thought the occurence of these guys in game was tied to exploring and travelling but during a long (and fun I might add) building session many of the little fella's kept popping out of the ground right next to where I was working. This is an odd system, in a game about LEGO why is most of the LEGO only unlocked by a random number generator. Unlocking these different building blocks thus far have not been required for any of the quests through out the game so this whole aspect is completely seperated from the rest of the game. They tried to tie building and a questing/exploration game together with the quests mentioned before but just did not go any further with it.
I could go on with little complaints as many have in other reviews but there also a ton of little things I love. I love how the first time I found a raptor in a world I died almost instantly. I love the designs of the terrains and settlements you find. I love the variety in the different biomes, I could go on. My over all conclusion is that I do have fun in game. A game with a few let downs due to not reaching its potential is better than a game that never had any. Lego World's makes me feel like a kid with lego again which is surprisingly rare for a Lego Game and for all of it's lack of depth I am going to continue having a good time with it for quite some time I feel. I havent even tried playing with a friend yet which I can imagine will  add another host of little problems and little moments I will love.
The game (like most games these days) Seems like it may continue to be developed beyond release. I'd never suggest buying a game based on the fact it might be good some day. Lego World's is already good. But that fact might persuade you to ignore some of the problems some people have with the experience. Lego is a very subjective experience in general. No kid played with their Lego the same so what people want from a Lego Game will always be different but this is as close as we have got to having a creative Lego tool that is also an engaging experiance beyond the simple joys of creation.

After the first update, Foundation Update, the game started to feel more coherent in some parts, it was taking a direction in what it wanted to turn into.
After 1.2, the game got even more into the way I felt perfect for me personally: Exploration.
And after 1.3, Atlas Rises, we finally got the No Man's Sky that was promised to us. We still miss some small things, but nevertheless this game took up the shape of what it was originally supposed to be, and will probably follow through to in a few more updates, finally reach the No Man's Sky we dreamed with.
The major problem with people is: They think this was supposed to be like a CoD or Battlefield in space. This wasn't the original promise. People want to like a game that isn't for them. And then they get angry when they feel wronged... by themselves.
Today, after 1.3, No Man's Sky takes the #1 place in my personal list. 10/10 - Do recommend.

Before I bought it, I looked for some reviews of this game on inumerous sites and, even with an average score, I decided to give it a try.
All right, this is not an open world game, it won't take more than 5~6 hours to finish it and the story is linear.
But, what's the matter about playing a linear story? A book is linear, a movie is linear, can't a good game be it too?
Even that you can't move freely through it, the environment is rich in details, the story is well narrated and the protagonist is so captivating that you want to discover her past and help her cause. For so many times I just relaxed and started to take screenshots to remember the places and the action scenes.
The combat system is quite fun. While you advance in the game, you can mix buttons to create COMBOS and easily execute them. But, this is not the BATMAN ARKHAM SERIES combat system, so you CAN'T have a free flow between enemies and link the created combos. So don't expect huge combos like DEVIL MAY CRY for example.
The Memory Remix is quite a piece of art. You really feel like you are in command. You can and you will modify people's memories to change history. And it's so easy and fun, that it invites you to try different combinations just to see what happens.
If you're not a big fan of Achievements, just let the game take you through the story. I started to look for colectibles like an Achievement Hunter and soon the game became boring. So I just started to play the game despite of looking for trophies and it was a much better experience.
So, to summarize it:
Nice story, great soundtrack, captivating protagonist, amazing memory remix moments and everything placed on a beautifull, yet limited, fantasy world.
Play it, you sure will remember.

I understand I may get some backlash for this, since I am a big fan of the series, but screw it.
I think Fallout 3 gets alot of undeserved flack, and while it certainly is one of the weaker entries in the series, it is certainly not the worst *COUGH*(((Fallout 4)))*COUGH*
So let's get riiiiiiiiiiiiggggggggggggggghhhhhhhhhhhhttttttttttt into the review:
PROS:
+The world is vast with a lot to explore.
+Quests offer verticality in how you complete them i.e. You Gotta Shoot 'Em In The Head, Oasis, Wasteland Survival Guide, Trouble on the Homefront.
+Transition from tabletop to a First/Third Person perspective was a good one.
+Your Karma actually has an impact in terms of how characters interact with you and which companions you could hire or  what quests become available to you. Mercenary groups will also start to pursue you based on your karma level.
+Too add on to that, Karma is very flexible, so even if you're the devil incarnete you could redeem yourself and become Mr. Roger's post nuclear descendant if you're willing.
+Dialogue checks aren't just limited to the speech skill, high skills or stats can open up more options in conversation during various points in the game.
+Inclusion of V.A.T.S. was a good one in terms of both adding a more strategic element to combat whilst also perserving the aimed shot mechanic from the previous games.
+Envoirmental Storytelling was a brilliant inclusion and makes use of gaming as a visual medium.
Now, enough sucking the game's wee wee, lets get into the bad:
CONS:
-The game can be almost childishly black and white with the morality. You thought A New Hope had basic and unnuanced morality? Ho! You haven't seen anything yet. Honestly it feels like I'm playing a Saturday morning cartoon sometimes
-While the flexibility of the Karma system is superb, its flexibilty also works against itself. One way of gaining karma is to give vagrants water, and you do this repeatedly until you get the "Very Good" ranking.  considering one of the potential outcomes for an early quest is to help (((Allistar Tenpenny))), an aristocrat, blow up a city with a nuke. An action the should result in the wasteland collectively shunning you, but since you gave that homeless guy a caravan's worth of clean water, you're pardoned, like wtf. Things like that makes the game come off as ridiculous.
-"Traits? the hell are those"? - Todd Howard, 2007
-Combat can be rather clunky, you'll find yourself relying on V.A.T.S. very frequently in firefights.
-Very few Unarmed related weapons and perks, making it an almost pointless skill to invest in.
-Many of the early perks (Level 2-6) are stat boosts, and many of the later perks(Level 24-30) are either too beneficial or utterly pointless.
-Speech as a skill is somewhat pointless as speech checks are based on precentages and probability, investing in speech doesn't always mean that you'll pass every check, just increases your odds.  all you really have to do is reload the save until you succeed.
-Bethesda thought mixing 1 & 2's plot was an adequate substitute for good writing.
-Some of the DLC, like Operation Anchorage, falls flat.
-Little Lamplight and Bigtown....why
-That's not how FEV works, Bethesda.
Overall:
While a weaker entry in terms of story, mechanics, and overall role playing, Fallout 3 is still an entertaining, if very flawed Fallout game. It's a great way to introduce newcomers into the franchise if nothing else.
